column4: Question
column5: A
column6: B
column7: C
column8: D
column10: Explanation

column4: Bank A faxes Bank B an offer to sell currency, valid for 24 hours. Bank B faxes its acceptance after 10 hours. When is the exchange contract complete?
column5: At the moment Bank A transmits its offer
column6: When the 24-hour offer period expires
column7: As soon as Bank B's acceptance is transmitted to Bank A
column8: When both parties take possession of the countervalues
column10: Per 2/8/2, the contract is not completed until acceptance by the offeree and possession (actual or constructive) of the countervalues by both parties.

column4: Ahmad holds EUR in his account at Bank A and buys USD from the Bank in a spot contract; the USD is credited to his account. Has possession occurred?
column5: Yes, the credit entry is constructive possession
column6: No, possession requires physical handing over of the notes
column7: No, he must first withdraw the USD in cash from the Bank
column8: No, unless the Bank also issues him a cheque
column10: Per 2/6/5(a)(2), a spot purchase of currency against another currency already in the customer's account, credited to it, is constructive possession.

column4: In a Mudarabah dealing in currencies, the Mudarib offers to guarantee the Rabb al-Mal against currency risk. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, since the Mudarib bears no capital loss anyway
column6: No, one partner may not guarantee the other's currency risk
column7: Yes, if the guarantee is written into the Mudarabah contract
column8: Yes, if it covers only half of any currency loss
column10: Per 2/9/3, a partner in Musharakah or Mudarabah may not be a guarantor for the other partner against the risks of dealing in currencies.

column4: Ahmad and Bakr conclude a currency exchange and appoint agents only to take possession. Whose departure before possession invalidates the exchange?
column5: The departure of either agent from the place of the contract
column6: No departure matters once agents are appointed
column7: The departure of both principals from the contract place
column8: The departure of the buyer's agent alone
column10: Per the Basis, where agency is for possession only, the rule relates to both principals leaving before possession is taken, not to the agents doing so.

column4: A customer gives Bank A a cheque as the countervalue in a currency exchange. When does receiving the cheque count as constructive possession?
column5: When the balance is available in its currency and blocked
column6: Only when the cheque is endorsed to a third party
column7: When the cheque is post-dated by no more than a week
column8: Whenever the drawer is a known and trusted customer of the Bank
column10: Per 2/6/5(b), receipt of a cheque is constructive possession if the balance is available in the issuer's account in the cheque's currency and blocked for payment.

column4: Bank A offers credit facilities letting a customer trade currencies in amounts exceeding the funds he owns. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the Bank caps the leverage ratio
column6: Permitted if the customer pledges his balance
column7: Not permitted under the standard
column8: Permitted if every trade is settled spot
column10: Per 2/12/1, it is not permitted for a customer to trade currencies beyond what he owns using credit facilities from the Institution handling the trading.

column4: A merchant receives a voucher signed by a credit card holder for a purchase. When is this constructive possession of the voucher amount?
column5: When the merchant deposits it within the grace period
column6: When the voucher amount is within the card's limit
column7: When the cardholder settles with the issuer at month end
column8: When the card issuer pays the merchant without deferment
column10: Per 2/6/5(c), a signed voucher is constructive possession provided the card issuing Institution pays the amount to the merchant without deferment.

column4: A compliance officer at Bank A asks whether the standard on trading in currencies governs the discounting of bills of exchange. What is the position?
column5: It is covered as a deferred exchange of currencies
column6: It is expressly excluded from the standard's scope
column7: It is covered only when two currencies are involved
column8: It is covered as a form of al-Muqassah (set-off)
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard does not cover the discounting of bills of exchange, nor debt transfers without currency exchange or goldsmithery.

column4: Bank A buys USD from Bank B on condition that Bank B buys EUR from it in a second exchange, with no delivery of the currencies. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as a parallel purchase and sale
column6: Permissible, as the two exchanges offset each other
column7: Permissible if the net amount is settled at maturity
column8: Permissible if each exchange is in a separate document
column10: Per 2/9/2, parallel purchase and sale of currencies is not permissible: no delivery, one exchange conditional on another, or a binding bilateral promise.

column4: In the Hadith of Ibn Umar about selling camels for dinars and taking dirhams, which condition did the Prophet (pbuh) set?
column5: Delivery within one day of the camel's sale
column6: The rate fixed on the day the camel was sold
column7: Equal amounts, as dinars and dirhams are one kind
column8: Price of the day, leaving no debt owing between them
column10: Per the Basis, the Prophet allowed taking the other currency at the price of the day, provided they did not part with anything remaining owed as a debt.

column4: A customer owes Murabahah instalments in USD. When settling an instalment, he and the Institution agree he will pay in local currency. Which rate applies?
column5: A rate fixed in advance in the Murabahah contract
column6: The spot exchange rate on the day of payment
column7: The rate prevailing on the Murabahah contract date
column8: The average rate over the whole instalment period
column10: Per 2/5, at settlement of instalments the parties may agree on payment in another currency, applying the spot exchange rate on the day of payment.

column4: Bank A in Dubai and Bank B in London conclude a spot currency exchange by electronic messaging, each in its own office. How is the contract treated?
column5: As binding only after courier confirmation is received
column6: As void, since the parties are not in one session
column7: As if concluded in one place, with the same consequences
column8: As a forward contract owing to the distance involved
column10: Per 2/8/1, contracting between remote parties by modern means of communication has the same juristic consequences as a contract made in one place.

column4: In a sale of 10,000 currency units, the parties complete possession of the countervalue for only 6,000 units before dispersing. What is the result?
column5: Valid in full, since part was possessed at closing
column6: Valid for the 6,000 possessed; invalid for the rest
column7: Void in full, since possession was not complete
column8: Valid in full if the rest is delivered within two days
column10: Per 2/6/2, partial possession is valid only for the part fully possessed; the remaining part of the transaction remains invalid.

column4: Bank A argues that a binding bilateral promise to exchange currencies later is not itself a contract. Why do most jurists still prohibit it?
column5: It is equivalent to a contract without immediate possession
column6: It breaches the rule of equality between countervalues
column7: It involves an interest-bearing loan between the two parties
column8: It always leads to a monopoly in the currency market
column10: Per the Basis, binding bilateral promises equal a contract, and they are not immediately followed by possession of the countervalues.

column4: Bank A converts a customer's funds and transfers them to a payee abroad; per market practice the transfer takes two days. May the payee dispose of the funds meanwhile?
column5: No, and the exchange is void because of the delay
column6: Yes, constructive possession occurred at the order
column7: Yes, provided Bank A guarantees the transfer
column8: No, not until the transfer takes effect
column10: Per 2/6/5(a), a customary delay in transfer is allowed, but the payee may not dispose of the currency until the transfer takes effect.

column4: Ahmad gives Bank A local currency and asks it to remit the equivalent in USD abroad. Bank A converts the money and charges a fee. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as exchange and transfer are combined
column6: Permissible, but no fee may be charged for the transfer
column7: Permissible, and a fee may be charged for the transfer
column8: Permissible only if the remittance is in local currency
column10: Per 2/11, a money transfer in a currency different from that presented is permissible (exchange then transfer), and the Institution may charge a fee.

column4: Ahmad exchanges USD 100 spot for an unequal amount of Indian rupees. What is the Shari'ah basis for allowing the inequality?
column5: Only coins, not paper notes, must be exchanged equally
column6: Each country's currency is a separate kind, like gold and silver
column7: Paper money is outside the rules applied to gold and silver
column8: Inequality is allowed in any exchange the parties agree to
column10: Per the Basis, scholars likened paper money to gold and silver; each country's currency is a different kind, so amounts may differ if possession is mutual.

column4: A customer wants Bank A to finance his currency trading. Per the Shari'ah basis, which arrangement is the permissible alternative?
column5: A facility repaid with a fixed increase over the principal amount
column6: A facility letting him sell amounts he does not own
column7: A loan so he deals in amounts he owns, without conditions
column8: A loan on condition he trades only through Bank A
column10: Per the Basis, the Institution may lend so the customer deals in amounts he owns; requiring him to trade with the lender combines loan and exchange.

column4: Ahmad appoints an agent to carry out a currency exchange for him. On what basis does the standard permit agency in currency exchange?
column5: Agency is allowed in any act the principal may do himself
column6: Agency turns the exchange into a transfer of debt
column7: Agents are exempt from the possession requirement
column8: Agency is allowed only for possession, not contracting
column10: Per the Basis, agency is permissible for an activity the principal could undertake personally; possession must still occur by the parties or their agents.

column4: Bank A lends a customer money interest-free on condition that he conducts his currency trades only with Bank A. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since the loan itself is interest-free
column6: Not permitted, as any loan for currency trading is barred
column7: Permitted if the Bank's rates are competitive
column8: Not permitted, because of the trading condition
column10: Per 2/12/2, lending on condition that currency dealing be done with the lender is not permitted; without such a condition there is no prohibition.

column4: Bank A has an account payable exposure in Currency Y and wants a permissible way to hedge against devaluation. Which method does the standard allow?
column5: Giving a binding bilateral promise to buy Currency Y later
column6: Buying Currency Y in the forward market at a fixed rate
column7: Selling goods on credit or by Murabahah in Currency Y
column8: Having a Mudarabah partner guarantee Currency Y losses
column10: Per 2/4/2, where the exposure is an account payable, the Institution may hedge by selling goods on credit or by Murabahah in the currency of the exposure.

column4: A customer exchanges a one-pound note for coins of the same country worth 0.98 pound, both handed over on the spot. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, because both were delivered hand to hand
column6: Not permissible: equal amounts are required
column7: Permissible, as the difference is a minor handling cost
column8: Permissible, since a note and a coin are different kinds
column10: Per 2/1/2, countervalues of the same currency must be equal even if one is paper money and the other coin, e.g. a one-pound note for a one-pound coin.

column4: Company X, not a party to a Musharakah, volunteers to guarantee one partner against currency losses. When is this permissible?
column5: When the other partner requests it as a condition
column6: Never, as all guarantees of currency risk are void
column7: When the guarantee is stated in the Musharakah contract
column8: When the guarantee is not stated in the Musharakah contract
column10: Per 2/9/3, a third party may volunteer to guarantee against currency risks, provided the guarantee is not stated in the contract.

column4: Bank A e-mails a customer an offer to sell USD at a set rate, open for two days. After one day, before any reply, Bank A wants to withdraw it. Is this allowed?
column5: No, the offer binds the offeror for its stated period
column6: Yes, offers sent electronically are never binding
column7: Yes, if it compensates the customer for the change
column8: Yes, at any time before acceptance is received
column10: Per 2/8/2, an offer made for a stated period and sent by a prescribed means of communication remains binding on the offeror during that period.

column4: In a spot currency exchange, Company X asks to include a three-day conditional option allowing it to cancel the deal. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed if the option is granted to both parties
column6: Allowed if the countervalues are delivered at once
column7: Allowed if the option period is three days or less
column8: Not allowed: no conditional option may be included
column10: Per 2/1/3, a currency exchange contract shall not contain any conditional option or deferment clause regarding delivery of one or both countervalues.

column4: Bank A and Bank B agree today to exchange USD for EUR in three months at today's rate, settled through deferred transfers of debt. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, because the rate is fixed at contracting
column6: Prohibited, as a forward currency contract
column7: Permitted, if the two banks are Islamic Institutions
column8: Permitted, if settlement is netted on maturity
column10: Per 2/2, forward currency contracts are prohibited, whether effected by exchanging deferred transfers of debt or by a deferred contract without concurrent possession.

column4: A customer alone gives Bank A a binding promise to buy USD from it next month; the Bank makes no promise in return. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible: a one-party promise is allowed even if binding
column6: Permissible only if the Bank also promises to sell
column7: Permissible only if the promise is non-binding
column8: Forbidden, as any binding promise in currency trading is void
column10: Per 2/9/1, while a binding bilateral promise is forbidden, a promise from one party is permissible even if it is binding.

column4: Bank A credits purchased USD to a customer's account instead of handing over cash. Why does the Shari'ah basis treat this like actual possession?
column5: The Bank guarantees the customer against any loss
column6: The parties may waive the possession requirement by mutual agreement
column7: Shari'ah prescribed no particular method of taking possession
column8: Currencies are not subject to the rules of exchange
column10: Per the Basis, constructive possession equals actual possession because Shari'ah prescribed no method; custom giving power to dispose and risk transfer governs.

column4: Ahmad pays Bank A local currency for a USD remittance abroad. What is the Shari'ah basis for combining the exchange with the transfer?
column5: The exchange may be completed after the funds arrive
column6: Constructive possession via a bank draft, exchange first
column7: The transfer fee replaces the need for possession
column8: Remittances are exempt from currency exchange rules
column10: Per the Basis, the combination is allowed because a bank draft achieves constructive possession; the exchange takes place before the transfer.

column4: To hedge devaluation, Bank A lends Bank B USD interest-free, and Bank B lends Bank A the equivalent in EUR. When is this permissible?
column5: If the two loans are made conditional on each other
column6: If both loans are repaid at a pre-agreed forward exchange rate
column7: If no extra benefit is given and they are not linked
column8: If each loan carries the same modest rate of return
column10: Per 2/4/1, back to back interest-free loans in different currencies are allowed without extra benefit, provided the two loans are not contractually connected.

column4: Bank A expects a currency to decline and wants to protect its profit on a transaction by buying in the forward currency market. Is this allowed?
column5: No, forward dealing is prohibited even for hedging
column6: Yes, if the hedge does not exceed the exposure
column7: Yes, if the forward rate equals the spot rate
column8: Yes, because hedging is a legitimate purpose
column10: Per 2/3, dealing in the forward currency market is prohibited even if the purpose is hedging against a loss of profit due to an expected decline.

column4: Ahmad buys USD from a money changer against local currency. He pays now, and the changer will deliver the USD tomorrow. What is the status of the deal?
column5: Valid, if the exchange rate is fixed at the time of contracting
column6: Valid, since Ahmad's payment is actual possession
column7: Valid, because the two currencies differ in kind
column8: Invalid: both sides must be possessed before parting
column10: Per 2/1/1 and 2/6/2, both parties must take possession (actual or constructive) of both countervalues before dispersing; one-sided possession is not enough.

column4: A trader buys up a currency in a small market, aiming to dominate its supply and dictate its price. All deals are spot. How is this dealing treated?
column5: Not permissible: it aims at establishing a monopoly position
column6: Permissible, if the purpose is hedging devaluation
column7: Permissible, if the trader is a licensed Institution
column8: Permissible, since the countervalues are possessed spot
column10: Per 2/1/4, currency dealing shall not aim at a monopoly position nor entail evil consequences to the interests of individuals or societies.

column4: Company X owes Company Y 1,000 dinars and Company Y owes Company X 5,000 dirhams. They agree a rate to extinguish both debts. What is this?
column5: Permissible only if the debts share one currency
column6: Permissible only at the exchange rate when the debts arose
column7: A prohibited sale of a debt for a debt
column8: A permissible set-off (al-Muqassah) of the two debts
column10: Per 2/10/1, parties owing debts in dinar and dirham may agree a rate to extinguish the debts wholly or partially; this is al-Muqassah (set-off).

column4: Ahmad appoints Bakr as agent to sell currency on his behalf but does not authorise him to receive the price. What keeps the exchange valid?
column5: Possession may follow within the customary settlement cycle
column6: Ahmad or another agent takes possession before parting
column7: The buyer may defer payment since Bakr lacks authority
column8: Bakr must still take possession as contracting agent
column10: Per 2/7/2, an agent may sell currency without authority to receive, provided the principal or another agent takes possession before the principals disperse.

column4: To hedge devaluation risk, Bank A and a customer each give a binding promise to exchange USD for EUR in three months. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since a promise is not a contract
column6: Permitted, since hedging justifies the promises
column7: Forbidden, even though the purpose is hedging
column8: Permitted if the future rate is left open
column10: Per 2/9/1, a binding bilateral promise to buy and sell currencies is forbidden, even for hedging against currency devaluation risk.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A asks whether it may issue a credit card that is free from Riba and any other Shari'ah prohibition. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the answer?
column5: Yes, such a credit card is permissible
column6: No, only debit cards may be issued
column7: Yes, if interest applies to cash withdrawals only
column8: No, every credit card is prohibited
column10: Per the Basis (3), credit cards are prohibited where they rest on interest-bearing revolving credit; issuing credit cards free of Riba or other prohibition is permissible.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A charges its cardholders a membership fee, a renewal fee, and a fee for replacing a lost card. Is this allowed?
column5: Only if each fee varies with the amount spent
column6: No, card fees may be charged to merchants only
column7: Yes, the standard permits these fees
column8: Only the replacement fee is permissible
column10: Per 4/3, the issuing Institution may charge the cardholder membership fees, renewal fees and replacement fees.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, how is the percentage commission that Bank A charges merchants accepting its card justified?
column5: As compensation for the credit given to the merchant
column6: As brokerage, marketing and a debt collection fee
column7: As a share of the profit on the merchant's sale
column8: As a penalty for the merchant's late settlement
column10: Per the Basis (5), the commission is partly a brokerage and marketing fee and partly a service charge for collecting the debt.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A wants to charge cardholders for cash withdrawals made with its card. Which fee structure does the standard permit?
column5: A fee that rises with the time until repayment
column6: A fee set as a percentage of the amount withdrawn
column7: A percentage fee only on amounts above the balance
column8: A flat fee proportionate to the service offered
column10: Per 4/5/2, the issuer may charge a flat service fee for cash withdrawal, proportionate to the service, but not a fee that varies with the amount withdrawn.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Ahmad buys currency from a merchant with his debit card and signs the payment coupon. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the possession condition satisfied?
column5: Card purchases are exempt from possession rules
column6: Possession occurs when the statement is issued
column7: The accounting entry counts as constructive possession
column8: The signed coupon counts as actual delivery of the price
column10: Per the Basis (7), buying with a debit card is constructive possession, since an accounting entry is considered constructive possession (Fiqh Academy decision).

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: A charge cardholder disputes the quality of goods bought from a merchant. Does this affect the issuer's duty to pay the merchant within the card limit?
column5: Yes, the obligation lapses if the goods prove to be defective
column6: Yes, the issuer pays only if the holder approves
column7: Yes, payment is suspended until the dispute ends
column8: No, the issuer's obligation is direct and independent
column10: Per 2/2/6, the issuer's obligation to pay the merchant is direct and independent of the relationship between the merchant and the cardholder.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A's charge card terms impose a percentage interest charge if the holder pays after the free credit period. May the Bank issue this card?
column5: No, he must not be obliged to pay interest for delay
column6: Yes, since charge cards give no revolving credit
column7: Yes, if the rate is below that charged on conventional cards
column8: Yes, as interest applies only after the free period
column10: Per 3/2/1, charge cards are permissible only if the cardholder is not obliged to pay interest in case of delay in paying the amount due.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A issues a card only to customers with available funds; purchases and withdrawals are debited to the account at once. Which feature marks it as a debit card?
column5: It gives revolving credit within a set ceiling
column6: It gives no credit and is limited to the credit balance
column7: It must be settled in full at the end of a credit period
column8: It gives free credit until the monthly statement is issued
column10: Per 2/1/1-2/1/2, a debit card is issued against available funds, debits the account immediately up to the credit balance, and provides no credit.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A's card gives credit up to a ceiling; the holder must pay all purchases by the end of a set period after receiving a statement. How is it classified?
column5: A charge card, as it gives no revolving credit
column6: A credit card, as it carries a credit ceiling
column7: A debit card, as payment is made in full
column8: A credit card, as it is also a means of payment
column10: Per 2/2/1-2/2/3, a charge card gives credit up to a ceiling for a set period, without revolving credit: the holder pays by the end of the credit period.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A requires a charge card applicant to deposit 1,000 as a guarantee, which he cannot use while he holds the card. What must the Bank make clear?
column5: It pays a fixed annual return on the deposit
column6: It keeps all profit on the deposit as a card fee
column7: It holds the deposit idle as an interest-free loan to the Bank
column8: It invests the deposit by Mudarabah and shares the profit
column10: Per 3/2/2, an unusable guarantee deposit must be invested for the cardholder on a Mudarabah basis, with profit shared at a specified percentage.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A charges merchants that accept its card a commission of 2% of the purchase price of goods bought with the card. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it is interest on the credit
column6: Permissible as a percentage of the purchase price
column7: Permissible only if borne by the cardholder
column8: Permissible only as a flat fee per transaction
column10: Per 4/2, the issuer may charge the party accepting the card a commission at a percentage of the purchase price of items and services bought with it.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Ahmad holds a debit card issued by Bank A. In which case would he normally pay a charge for using the card?
column5: When his balance falls below a minimum amount
column6: When paying a merchant for goods out of his own credit balance
column7: When withdrawing cash through Bank B, a different Institution
column8: When withdrawing cash at Bank A's own machines
column10: Per 2/1/3, no charges normally apply, except when the card is used to withdraw cash or buy another currency through an Institution other than the issuer.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: A charge cardholder uses his card to pay for things prohibited by the Shari'ah. Which right must Bank A have stipulated when issuing the card?
column5: The right to charge interest on such purchases
column6: The right to cancel its payment to the merchant
column7: The right to double the annual membership fee
column8: The right to withdraw the card for this violation
column10: Per 3/2/3, the Institution must stipulate that the card may not be used for prohibited purposes and that it may withdraw the card if this is violated.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A plans a card letting holders pay off purchases in instalments, paying interest for the deferment on a revolving basis. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if issued only to its own depositors
column6: It is not permissible to issue such a card
column7: Permissible if the interest is disclosed upfront
column8: Permissible if a free credit period comes first
column10: Per 3/3, an Institution may not issue credit cards with an interest-bearing revolving credit facility where the holder pays interest to pay in instalments.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: An international card organization raises its service charge to Bank A to cater for credit granted. May Bank A pay the increased charge?
column5: Yes, as it is labelled a service charge
column6: Yes, since membership itself is permissible
column7: No, as it would be an indirect interest payment
column8: Yes, if paid in the organization's currency
column10: Per 4/1/2, fees to card organizations are allowed only if they include no interest, even indirectly, such as raising a service charge to cater for credit.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A requires a deposit before approving a card and forbids the cardholder from investing it. Why does the Shari'ah basis reject this?
column5: It amounts to a loan that draws extra benefit
column6: It makes the deposit a gift to the Bank
column7: It turns the card into a revolving credit card
column8: It breaches the card's approved credit limit
column10: Per the Basis (9), barring the holder from investing the deposit is like a loan drawing extra benefit; it should be invested for him on a profit and loss basis.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Ahmad's balance is 300. With Bank A's agreement, he uses his card to withdraw 500 in cash. When is this permissible?
column5: Never, withdrawals may not exceed his balance
column6: If the excess carries a modest fixed return
column7: Only if the card is a revolving credit card
column8: If no interest is charged on the excess
column10: Per 4/5/1, a holder may withdraw within his available funds, or more with the issuer's agreement, provided no interest is charged.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Ahmad buys gold from a jeweller using his charge card issued by Bank A. When is this purchase permissible?
column5: When the issuer can settle the jeweller without delay
column6: Only with a debit card, never a charge card
column7: Only if he repays the issuer within the free credit period
column8: Never, as gold must be bought only with cash in hand
column10: Per 4/4, gold, silver or currency may be bought with a debit or charge card where the issuer can settle the amount due to the merchant without delay.

column3: Debit Card, Charge Card and Credit Card
column4: Bank A offers cardholders free conventional life insurance and discounts on airline reservations. Which of these privileges is permitted?
column5: Only the conventional life insurance
column6: Neither, as all card privileges are barred
column7: Only the discounts on airline reservations
column8: Each of them, since they are free gifts
column10: Per 4/6, privileges prohibited by the Shari'ah, such as conventional life insurance, are barred; others, like airline or hotel discounts, are permitted.

column4: Bank A wants to put a defaulting debtor on a black list and warn other companies that enquire about him. Is this allowed?
column5: Only after a court declares him bankrupt
column6: Yes, as a non-material punishment for default
column7: Only with the debtor's prior written consent
column8: No, it is prohibited slander of the debtor
column10: Per 2/4, the Institution may list a defaulting debtor as undesirable and warn other companies on enquiry or when black lists are exchanged.

column4: Bank A wants to enforce an agreed acceleration clause against a procrastinating debtor who missed an instalment. What does the standard consider preferable?
column5: Adding a late charge on the debtor before accelerating it
column6: Applying it at once on the missed due date without any notice
column7: Notifying him and allowing a reasonable period first
column8: Obtaining a court order first before applying the clause
column10: Per 2/1/6, it is preferable to implement the acceleration clause only after notifying the debtor and after a reasonable period of time has lapsed.

column4: A contractor is late completing a building and owes an amount under the contract's penalty clause. Is his case within the procrastinating debtor standard?
column5: No, only debtors under Murabahah are covered
column6: Yes, he becomes a debtor by virtue of the penalty clause
column7: Only if the contractor has become insolvent
column8: No, penalty clauses on contractors fall outside the standard
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard covers a contractor or concessionaire who is late in completing work and becomes a debtor by virtue of a penalty clause.

column4: Late payers at Bank A customarily add 2% when finally settling, though no contract mentions it. May the Bank accept this extra under the standard?
column5: No, the custom on the extra makes it impermissible
column6: Yes, if the debtor hands it over willingly
column7: Yes, since nothing is written in any contract with the debtor
column8: Yes, as it counts as good settlement of debt
column10: Per 2/5/2, an excess may be accepted only where there is no condition, whether written or verbal, or custom or mutual agreement relating to it.

column4: Bakr guaranteed Ahmad's debt on condition that payment is first sought from Ahmad. An instalment is now overdue. How should Bank A proceed?
column5: Treat the guarantee as void for the condition
column6: Demand payment from whichever it chooses
column7: Demand payment from Bakr directly
column8: Demand payment from Ahmad before turning to Bakr
column10: Per 2/2(a), where the guarantor stipulated that settlement be first sought from the debtor, the creditor must start with the debtor.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a penalty clause apply to late construction work but not to a debtor's late payment?
column5: Debts are always secured by a mortgaged asset
column6: Penalty clauses suit only non-financial obligations
column7: Contractors are presumed solvent under the standard
column8: Construction contracts are not binding contracts
column10: Per the Basis, penalty clauses are valid in construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts, but are permissible only for non-financial obligations; a debt increase is Riba.

column4: Bank A wants to stipulate that a late payer compensates it for its loss of income, measured by its average profit rate during the delay. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, if a court determines the amount
column6: Yes, if it is based on the Bank's actual average profit rate
column7: Yes, if paid in kind rather than in cash
column8: No, opportunity loss compensation is not permitted
column10: Per 2/1/2, stipulating compensation for a debtor's delay is not permitted, including compensation for loss of income (opportunity loss).

column4: Bakr, a solvent guarantor, delays paying a guaranteed debt after Bank A's demand. Which rulings apply to him?
column5: None, since he is only a guarantor and not the original debtor
column6: Only the black list ruling, not the recovery of expenses
column7: The same rulings as apply to a defaulting debtor
column8: Only the rulings on penalty clauses agreed in the contract
column10: Per 2/2(b), all rulings applicable to debtors in default are equally applicable to guarantors in default.

column4: Bakr guaranteed Ahmad's debt to Bank A, with no condition on the order of claims. Ahmad defaults. From whom may the Bank demand payment?
column5: From either Ahmad or Bakr
column6: From Bakr only, once Ahmad defaults
column7: From Ahmad first, then Bakr if he refuses
column8: From Ahmad only, until he is insolvent
column10: Per 2/2(a), a creditor may demand settlement from the debtor or the guarantor, unless the guarantor stipulated that it be sought from the debtor first.

column4: Bank A still holds a Murabahah asset when the buyer becomes bankrupt. Per the Shari'ah basis, why may it take the asset ahead of other creditors?
column5: The Bank's claim ranks first as a loan
column6: The sale is void due to the buyer's non-payment of the price
column7: The asset is deemed mortgaged to the Bank
column8: A Hadith gives the seller priority over other creditors
column10: Per the Basis, Abu Hurayrah reported that a seller who retains the asset when the buyer becomes bankrupt is more qualified to take it than other creditors.

column4: Bank A suspects a defaulting debtor is hiding assets and wants to investigate his financial status and activities. What does the standard allow?
column5: Investigation only under a court order
column6: Investigation only of assets mortgaged to it
column7: Investigation by all permissible and legitimate means
column8: No investigation, as it intrudes on his private affairs
column10: Per 2/5/1, the Institution may monitor and investigate the financial status and activities of a defaulting debtor through all permissible and legitimate means.

column4: A defaulting debtor claims that Bank A's warning to other companies about him is slander. Per the Shari'ah basis, how is the warning viewed?
column5: As advice which it is a duty to give
column6: As slander, tolerated for large debts
column7: As a right arising only from the contract
column8: As slander, allowed only with his consent
column10: Per the Basis, a public complaint about a solvent debtor's default is not prohibited slander; warning others is advice that it is a duty to give.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, what makes a clause accelerating all instalments upon a missed instalment valid?
column5: The guarantor alone agrees to the clause
column6: The debtor consented to it when the contract was agreed
column7: A court orders it after the first missed instalment of the debt
column8: Prior notice is given, as a condition of validity
column10: Per the Basis, the Fiqh Academy allows acceleration if the debtor consented at contracting; prior notice is merely a reminder giving him reasonable time.

column4: A Murabahah contract makes all instalments due if one is missed. The customer missed an instalment due to force majeure. May Bank A accelerate the debt?
column5: Yes, but only for the next two instalments
column6: Yes, as the clause was agreed in the contract
column7: No, the clause cannot apply where force majeure caused it
column8: Yes, after giving him notice and allowing a reasonable period
column10: Per 2/1/6, unless the failure was caused by force majeure, all outstanding instalments may be stipulated to fall due when the debtor fails to pay one.

column4: Ahmad cannot pay a due debt to Bank A because he is genuinely insolvent. Per the Shari'ah basis, how should he be treated?
column5: All his instalments fall due immediately
column6: He should be granted a grace period
column7: He may be publicly dishonoured and punished
column8: He must compensate the Bank for the delay
column10: Per the Basis, punishment applies to a solvent defaulter, whereas an insolvent debtor should be granted a grace period.

column4: Bank A's contract lets it recoup late amounts from the customer's accounts. The debt is in USD; his investment account is in EUR. How may the Bank proceed?
column5: Recoup it at the then prevailing exchange rate
column6: It may not touch investment accounts
column7: Recoup it at the rate on the contract date
column8: Recoup it only with his fresh consent
column10: Per 2/5/3, a stipulated set-off from current or investment accounts needs no further consent; if currencies differ, the then prevailing rate is used.

column4: When settling, a defaulting debtor voluntarily pays Bank A more than the debt. There was no condition, custom or agreement on any extra. May the Bank accept it?
column5: No, any excess over the debt is Riba
column6: Only if the excess is given to charity
column7: Only if the extra was agreed verbally
column8: Yes, it may accept the extra amount
column10: Per 2/5/2, the Institution may accept an excess payment from a defaulting debtor if there is no written or verbal condition, custom or agreement on it.

column4: Which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite for prohibiting default in payment by a debtor able to pay?
column5: The best of you is the one who is best in the settlement of debt
column6: Muslims are bound by their contractual conditions
column7: Default in payment on the part of a solvent debtor is unjust
column8: Take what would suffice you and your child amicably
column10: Per the Basis, the Prophet (pbuh) said: Default in payment on the part of a solvent debtor is unjust; scholars agreed such a debtor may be punished.

column4: Bank A sets off a defaulter's overdue debt against his current account under a contract clause. Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports this right?
column5: The debtor's silence, deemed as his consent
column6: The rule that deposits belong to the Bank once they are placed
column7: A court order, which is always required
column8: The amicable right of recovery (Hadith to Abu Sufyan's wife)
column10: Per the Basis, set-off rests on the amicable right of recovery (Hadith to Abu Sufyan's wife); it needs no consent but is best documented in the contract.

column4: Bank A sold a machine by Murabahah. The buyer defaulted and later became bankrupt; the machine is still available in the same condition. What may Bank A do?
column5: Repossess the machine instead of seeking a bankruptcy order
column6: Sell the machine and keep any surplus above the price as profit
column7: Only claim as one of the creditors in bankruptcy
column8: Claim compensation for the delay in payment
column10: Per 2/1/7, if the sold asset is available in its sold condition and the buyer defaulted then became bankrupt, the Institution may repossess it.

column4: Ahmad's instalment was due on 1 May. Bank A made a normal demand; he has not proved insolvency and has not paid. Is default in payment established?
column5: No, unless a penalty clause was agreed
column6: Yes, default is established
column7: No, three instalments must be missed
column8: No, a court ruling is needed first
column10: Per 2/6, default is established when, after a normal demand, a debtor who has not proved insolvency fails to settle the debt on its due date.

column4: A customer of Bank A stops paying Murabahah instalments because he has become insolvent. Does the standard on the procrastinating debtor govern his case?
column5: No, insolvent or bankrupt debtors are outside its scope
column6: Yes, it governs every debtor who fails to pay
column7: Yes, once the delay exceeds a reasonable period
column8: No, it governs only guarantors who are in default, not debtors
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard covers solvent debtors and guarantors in default, not insolvent or bankrupt debtors or those delaying for a Shari'ah reason.

column4: Bank A argues that a late payment compensation clause is valid since the customer freely agreed to it. Why is it null and void per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Courts cannot reliably assess such losses
column6: It conflicts with the acceleration clause
column7: It is unfair to debtors who are insolvent
column8: Any increase in the amount of a debt is Riba
column10: Per the Basis, compensation for delay in a debt is Riba and void; conditions that make the impermissible permissible are not binding.

column4: Bank A incurs legal and other expenses to recover a debt from a procrastinating debtor. Who bears these expenses?
column5: Bank A, as the creditor
column6: The court, as a public cost
column7: The procrastinating debtor
column8: The two parties equally
column10: Per 2/1/4, the procrastinating debtor is liable for legal and other expenses incurred by the creditor to recover his debt.

column4: In an Istisna'a contract, the manufacturer agrees to pay a fixed amount for each day of late delivery. Is this penalty clause valid?
column5: No, it is Riba, just like a penalty imposed on a debt
column6: Yes, penalty clauses are allowed in Istisna'a
column7: Yes, but only in construction contracts, not manufacturing
column8: No, unless the buyer proves actual loss
column10: Per 2/3, penalty clauses may be included in construction, Istisna'a and supply contracts.

column4: Bank A stipulates that late payers must deliver goods worth 1% of the debt for each month of delay. Is this stipulation valid?
column5: Yes, since the amount is pre-determined
column6: Yes, as it is not cash compensation
column7: No, compensation in any form is not permitted
column8: Yes, if the debtor agreed at contracting
column10: Per 2/1/2, financial compensation for delay may not be stipulated, whether in cash or in other consideration, and whether pre-determined or not.

column4: A solvent customer deliberately delays paying a debt due to Bank A, though he is able to pay. How does the standard classify his conduct?
column5: Permissible within a 30-day grace period
column6: It is Haram (prohibited)
column7: Prohibited only if the contract says so
column8: Permissible if he later pays in full
column10: Per 2/1/1, default in payment by a debtor who is capable of paying the debt is Haram (prohibited).

column4: With no clause in the contract, Bank A sues a solvent defaulter, asking the court to award financial compensation for the delay. Is this permitted?
column5: No, a judicial demand for such compensation is barred
column6: Yes, if the award is in goods, not cash
column7: Yes, if the court sets a fair amount
column8: Yes, since nothing was stipulated in the contract beforehand
column10: Per 2/1/3, it is not permitted to make a judicial demand on a defaulting debtor for financial compensation, in cash or other consideration, for delay.

column4: A customer challenges Bank A's clause obliging him to donate to charity if he defaults. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is this clause based on?
column5: A right of set-off against his accounts
column6: Compensation for the creditor's actual loss
column7: A penalty clause, as accepted in the Hanbali school of law
column8: A commitment to donate, established in the Maliki school
column10: Per the Basis, this is a commitment to make a donation, well established in the Maliki school (Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar).

column4: A supply contractor owes Bank A 20,000 under a penalty clause but refuses to pay. The Bank still owes him 50,000 under the contract. What may the Bank do?
column5: Waive the penalty as unenforceable
column6: Cancel the contract and keep the 50,000 it still owes him
column7: Deduct the 20,000 from the amount it owes him
column8: Charge him an extra penalty on top for his refusal to pay
column10: Per 2/3, if the contractor refuses to pay a penalty, default rulings apply, and the amount may be deducted from amounts outstanding to the contractor.

column4: Bank A's Murabahah contract says a late payer must compensate the Bank for any fall in the value of the currency of the debt. Is this clause allowed?
column5: Yes, if the amount is not pre-determined
column6: Yes, if paid in goods rather than in cash
column7: Yes, as it covers actual loss, not opportunity loss
column8: No, such compensation may not be stipulated
column10: Per 2/1/2, no compensation (cash or other, pre-determined or not) may be stipulated for delay, including for loss due to a change in the currency's value.

column4: Bank A's financing is secured by a mortgaged asset. May the contract require the debtor to mandate the Bank to sell the asset without recourse to the courts?
column5: Yes, but only after the debtor's death
column6: Yes, such a mandate may be stipulated
column7: No, any sale must be ordered by a court
column8: No, the Bank may only retain the asset
column10: Per 2/1/5, the creditor may apply for sale of the mortgaged asset and may stipulate a mandate from the debtor to sell it without recourse to the courts.

column4: Bank A's Murabahah contract obliges the customer, if he procrastinates, to donate a percentage of the debt to charitable causes through the Bank. Ruling?
column5: Permissible, as an undertaking by the debtor to donate
column6: Permissible if the Bank keeps it as income
column7: Permissible only if a court orders each individual donation
column8: Not permissible, as it is a penalty on a debt
column10: Per 2/1/8, a debtor's undertaking to donate an amount or percentage of the debt to charity through the Institution if he procrastinates is permissible.

column4: Bank A accepts a cheque and set-off with the drawer then takes place through the clearing-house. How is this set-off classified?
column5: Always a contractual set-off, as the drawer agreed to it
column6: Not a set-off at all, but a transfer of debt (Hawalah)
column7: Either type, depending on which conditions are met
column8: Always a compulsory set-off, as the clearing-house imposes it
column10: Per 4/2, set-off between an Institution accepting a cheque and the drawer through the clearing-house may be compulsory or contractual, per the conditions met.

column4: X owes Y 5,000 due now; Y owes X 5,000 of the same currency due in six months. Neither has asked for set-off. Does a compulsory set-off occur?
column5: No, compulsory set-off requires equal maturity
column6: Yes, as each party is creditor and debtor
column7: Yes, as the amounts and currency are equal
column8: Yes, with a discount for the earlier maturity
column10: Per 2/1/2(b), compulsory set-off requires the debts to be equal in kind, type, description and maturity.

column4: In a contractual set-off, X owes Y 8,000 and Y owes X 5,000. What is the result?
column5: The 3,000 balance is waived by agreement
column6: 5,000 is set off and Y may claim the remaining 3,000
column7: The whole 8,000 is extinguished and X owes Y nothing more
column8: The set-off fails because the two amounts are not equal
column10: Per 2/2/3, if the debts are unequal, an equivalent amount is set off and the party owed the larger debt may request payment of the balance.

column4: Bank A's claim on Company X is secured by a mortgage; X's equal claim on Bank A is unsecured, same currency and maturity. When can set-off on demand occur?
column5: Never, since the debts differ in quality
column6: Only if the two parties sign a new agreement
column7: If Company X requests it, even without Bank A's consent
column8: If Bank A requests it and relinquishes the mortgage
column10: Per 2/1/4(b), a mortgage makes a debt superior in quality; set-off on demand needs its creditor to request it and relinquish that privilege.

column4: X owes Y 5,000 and Y owes X 5,000, same currency and maturity, but X's claim on Y is mortgaged to Bank B. Does compulsory set-off occur?
column5: No, the third party's right over the debt prevents it
column6: Yes, if X notifies Bank B in writing
column7: Yes, but Bank B then receives the set-off amount from Y
column8: Yes, as the debts are equal in every respect
column10: Per 2/1/2(c), neither debt may be encumbered by a third party's right, such as a mortgagee's, to protect rights belonging to third parties.

column4: Bank A and Bank B exchange promises that future debts between them, one in USD and one in EUR, will be settled by set-off. Which rate must the promise use?
column5: The rate prevailing on the date the promises are exchanged
column6: The current exchange rate at the time of actual set-off
column7: The average rate over the life of the debts
column8: A fixed rate agreed in the promise itself
column10: Per 3, for future debts in different currencies, the promise must be based on the current rate at the time of actual set-off, to prevent roundabout Riba.

column4: Company X owes Bank A USD; Bank A owes X EUR at a different maturity. They mutually agree to set off the debts. Is this allowed?
column5: No, debts must be of the same kind and type
column6: Yes, but only if the two amounts are exactly equal in value
column7: Yes, contractual set-off needs no similarity of debts
column8: No, maturities must coincide in any set-off
column10: Per 2/2/3, contractual set-off is permissible without the debts being similar in kind, type, description or maturity, as each party relinquishes privileges.

column4: Ahmad, owed a debt now due, forgoes that privilege and demands set-off against his deferred debt to Bank B. Why does Shari'ah not object, per the basis?
column5: A court approves every set-off on demand
column6: The creditor of the lesser debt always consents to the set-off
column7: Debts set off on demand are deemed equal
column8: The creditor of the superior debt has forgone his advantage
column10: Per the Basis, set-off on demand is permissible because the person entitled to the superior debt agreed to forgo its advantage; Shari'ah does not object.

column4: Bank A pre-stipulates set-off and consolidation of future debts in its deferred sale agreements with customers. What is the stated benefit?
column5: It allows late payment compensation by set-off
column6: It makes every future set-off compulsory regardless of its conditions
column7: No new agreement is needed if currencies differ or a debt is superior
column8: It transfers the Bank's receivables to other Institutions
column10: Per 4/1, pre-stipulating set-off means a fresh agreement may be avoided at the time of set-off when currencies differ or one debt is superior.

column4: Bank A is offered a currency swap in which interest-based securities are set off against interest-based securities. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the parties mutually consent
column6: Not permissible, as it is based on Riba
column7: Permissible as a contractual set-off
column8: Permissible because the currencies differ
column10: Per 5, currency swaps concluded on the basis of Riba are not permissible, since interest-based securities are set off against interest-based securities.

column4: Company X owes Company Y USD 10,000 and Y owes X USD 6,000, both due on 1 June and unencumbered. Neither party asks for anything. What happens?
column5: Full set-off, with the 4,000 excess waived by operation of law
column6: No set-off without both parties' consent
column7: Set-off only if Company Y requests it
column8: Compulsory set-off of 6,000; Y remains owed 4,000
column10: Per 2/1/1-2/1/2, compulsory set-off occurs without request or consent; with unequal amounts, an equivalent amount is set off and the balance remains owed.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is settling debts by set-off in line with the objectives of the Shari'ah?
column5: It discharges liability without futile recovery processes
column6: It removes the need for any consent of parties
column7: It lets creditors earn a return on their debts
column8: It is expressly ordered for all debts in the text of the Quran
column10: Per the Basis, set-off has been practised without disapproval and serves Shari'ah objectives by discharging debts without futile recovery processes.

column4: Company X and Bank A agree by contract to set off their mutual debts. On what Shari'ah basis does a contractual set-off rest?
column5: Necessity overrides the rules on debts between the parties
column6: The ruler may order mutual debts to be set off in all cases
column7: Custom alone determines how debts are settled between parties
column8: Muslims are bound by the conditions they have agreed
column10: Per the Basis, contractual set-off rests on the Hadith: Muslims are bound by their conditions, except one that makes the unlawful lawful or the lawful unlawful.

column4: Ahmad owes Bank A 1,000 due now; Bank A owes Ahmad 1,000 due in a year. Who may trigger a set-off on demand?
column5: Ahmad, by forgoing his deferred maturity
column6: Neither, because the maturities differ
column7: Bank A, by forgoing the privilege of its due debt
column8: Either party, but only with the other party's consent
column10: Per 2/1/3-2/1/4, the creditor of the superior debt (here the one now due) may demand set-off by forgoing his privilege, whether or not the other consents.

column4: Bank A discharges a customer's liability by waiving the obligation. Is this discharge governed by the standard on settlement of debt by set-off?
column5: No, waiving of obligation is covered by another standard
column6: Yes, as a form of compulsory set-off
column7: Yes, if the waived debt equals another debt between the parties
column8: Yes, as a form of contractual set-off
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard does not apply to discharge by transfer, waiving of obligation, composition or bilateral cancellation; other standards cover them.

column4: Bank A prices a letter of guarantee at 1% per quarter of the guaranteed amount, as consideration for the guarantee itself. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the letter of guarantee is fully covered in cash
column6: Not permissible, as it is a fee for the guarantee per se
column7: Permissible if the guarantee is uncovered
column8: Permissible as it reflects the risk taken
column10: Per 6/1/1, no remuneration may be taken for a letter of guarantee per se (covered or not), as it is usually computed on amount and duration guaranteed.

column4: A depositor demands that Bank A, holding his goods on trust, be liable for their loss in all cases. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the Bank not liable?
column5: Deposits are owned by the trustee once received
column6: Loss of trust assets is borne by the trustee as a matter of principle
column7: The depositor waived his rights by depositing
column8: A trustee is liable only for misconduct, negligence or breach
column10: Per the Basis, a trustee is not liable for loss except for misconduct, negligence or violation of conditions; otherwise liability conflicts with the nature of trusts.

column4: Bakr, guarantor of a debt to Bank A, incurs actual expenses during the period of his personal guarantee. May he claim them?
column5: Only if they are below 1% of the debt
column6: Yes, actual expenses incurred may be claimed
column7: No, a guarantee must be wholly cost-free
column8: Only if the debtor later defaults
column10: Per 3/1/5, no remuneration is allowed for the guarantee itself, but the guarantor may claim expenses actually incurred during the guarantee period.

column4: Two parties conclude a deferred sale. Under the standard, what is the status of documenting it in writing?
column5: Unnecessary, as attestation always suffices
column6: Obligatory, so that failing to write it down is a sin
column7: Recommended; custom governs form and evidential value
column8: Valid only in official, not private, documents
column10: Per 2/4/1, written documentation is recommended (private or official); customary practice governs drawing up documents and their evidential value.

column4: A customer pays a Hamish Jiddiyyah of 5,000 and breaks his binding promise. Bank A bought the asset for 100,000 and resells it for 97,000. What may it keep?
column5: 3,000 for actual damage, refunding 2,000
column6: Nothing, as no contract was concluded
column7: The full 5,000 as forfeited 'Arboun
column8: 5,000 plus a claim for lost profit
column10: Per 6/8/2, Hamish Jiddiyyah is held on trust; on breach the Institution may deduct only actual damage: cost minus the sale price to a third party.

column4: Bakr guaranteed a 10,000 cash debt and agreed with the creditor to settle it by delivering goods worth 9,000. How much may he recover from the debtor?
column5: Nothing, since he settled in kind
column6: 10,000, the full amount of the debt originally owed
column7: The goods' value plus a profit margin
column8: 9,000, the lesser of the goods' value and the debt
column10: Per 3/3/2, if the guarantor settles with a different commodity, he recovers the commodity's amount or the debt's amount, whichever is less.

column4: A successful bidder withdraws, causing actual financial damage of 3,000 in the tender. His final cash security is 10,000. What may be confiscated?
column5: 3,000, equal to the damage actually sustained
column6: Half the security (5,000) as an agreed penalty
column7: The full 10,000 security, as the bidder withdrew
column8: Nothing, as the security is held in trust for him
column10: Per 6/8/1, tender securities may not be confiscated except as compensation for an equivalent amount of financial damage actually sustained.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the authority for taking 'Arboun (earnest money) to secure performance of a contract?
column5: The Hadith that the guarantor is liable
column6: The Hadith on the seller who finds his goods with a bankrupt buyer
column7: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab, permitted by Imam Ahmad
column8: The consensus of all four schools of law
column10: Per the Basis, taking 'Arboun is based on the practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab before companions, permitted by Imam Ahmad, and a Fiqh Academy resolution.

column4: Without any stipulation in the agency contract, Bakr, an investment agent, voluntarily gives his clients an independent guarantee. He is later removed as agent. Status?
column5: The guarantee was void from the start
column6: He remains liable as guarantor
column7: He is liable only for his negligence
column8: His guarantee ends with the agency
column10: Per 2/2/2, a voluntary guarantee given independently of the agency contract makes the agent a guarantor in another capacity; he stays liable after discharge.

column4: Bank A wants to market its Musharakah investment product to customers as a guaranteed investment. Is this allowed?
column5: No, it may not be marketed or operated as guaranteed
column6: Yes, if the product is low risk
column7: Yes, if all the partners agree to it
column8: Yes, if only the profit, not the capital, is described as guaranteed
column10: Per 2/2/1, it is not permissible for Musharakah and Mudarabah contracts to be marketed or operated as a guaranteed investment.

column4: In a deferred sale, Bank A stipulates that if the buyer fails to pay within a set period, it may revoke the sale and repossess the asset without court. Ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as revocation needs a court
column6: Permissible, as the seller may stipulate this
column7: Not permissible, as a concluded sale is final
column8: Permissible only if the buyer is bankrupt
column10: Per 5/2, in a deferred sale the seller may stipulate a right to revoke and repossess the asset without recourse to the courts if the price is not paid in time.

column4: Bank A sells goods on deferred payment and stipulates a guarantee in the body of the same sale contract. Does this affect the permissibility of the sale?
column5: Yes, the condition renders the sale void
column6: No, but only if the guarantee is a mortgage
column7: Yes, a guarantee must always be made in a separate contract
column8: No, the guarantee does not affect the original contract
column10: Per 2/1/1, a guarantee is permissible in contracts of exchange and does not affect the permissibility of the original contract; it may be stipulated within it.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, how does the evidential value of attestation compare with written documentation?
column5: Equal to writing in every era and every legal system
column6: Rejected entirely as evidence by the traditional Fuqaha
column7: Traditionally stronger; modern laws favour writing
column8: Always weaker than writing, both traditionally and today
column10: Per the Basis, traditional Fuqaha held attestation stronger than writing, but in modern times laws rely on witnesses rarely and favour documentary evidence.

column4: A trainee says failing to put a deferred deal in writing is a sin. Per the Shari'ah basis, whose view is this?
column5: Ibn Hazm's; the majority regard writing as recommended
column6: The view of the Hanafis alone
column7: The majority's view; Ibn Hazm saw writing as merely recommended
column8: The consensus of all the Fuqaha
column10: Per the Basis, the majority hold written documentation is recommended; Ibn Hazm held it obligatory, relying on the literal meaning of the verse of debt.

column4: Bakr agrees to guarantee Ahmad's debt to Bank A, but asks Ahmad for a fee of 1% of the amount in return for the guarantee. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the fee is modest and fixed
column6: Permissible if based on the amount at risk
column7: Not permissible to take remuneration for a guarantee
column8: Permissible if Ahmad offered the fee himself without being asked
column10: Per 3/1/5, no remuneration whatsoever may be taken for a personal guarantee per se, nor commission paid for obtaining one.

column4: Bank A is asked for a letter of guarantee to back an interest-based loan. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is issuing it prohibited?
column5: Letters of guarantee are void in all cases under the Shari'ah
column6: It aids sin, as the guarantor helps establish the Riba debt
column7: The Bank would earn a fee on the guarantee
column8: Guarantees may only cover Murabahah debts
column10: Per the Basis, it is like assisting in sin; the Hadith cursing the writer and witnesses of Riba applies, as a guarantor has a stronger role than they do.

column4: The holder of an asset mortgaged to Bank A is using it in a way that may cause losses to be borne by the Bank. What may the Bank do?
column5: Charge the debtor a misuse penalty
column6: Nothing until the debt falls due
column7: Take the asset into full ownership
column8: Take legal action against the misuse
column10: Per 6/9/2, the Institution may protect the integrity of the subject of a guarantee, such as a mortgaged asset, and pursue legal action against its misuse.

column4: A third party promises to cover losses in a Mudarabah bond issue but fails to pay. May the Mudarib refuse its own obligations on that ground?
column5: Yes, as the promise was a contract condition
column6: No, the promise is independent of the Mudarabah
column7: Yes, if the bonds' prospectus mentioned it
column8: Yes, but only for the uncovered loss amount
column10: Per the Basis (Fiqh Academy), the third party's promise must be independent; the parties may not avoid their obligations because the volunteer failed to perform.

column4: Bank A's contract makes future instalments due on default. Ahmad misses an instalment, with no force majeure involved. When does the term take effect?
column5: After a reminder notice and a reasonable period
column6: At once, on the missed due date, without any notice
column7: Only after three or more consecutive instalments are missed
column8: Only after a court order is obtained
column10: Per 5/1, acceleration on default (not caused by force majeure) is permitted, but is not effective until a reminder notice is served and a reasonable time elapses.

column4: Bank A acts as investment agent for a client and, within the same agency contract, guarantees the client's capital. Why is this prohibited?
column5: Agents are never liable for anything, even for negligence
column6: Guarantees must always be paid for by the client as a fee
column7: Agency contracts may not contain conditions
column8: It turns the transaction into an interest-based loan
column10: Per 2/2/2, combining agency and guarantee conflicts with their nature; guaranteeing capital plus returns is like a loan repaid with an increase (Riba).

column4: Bank A undertakes to underwrite any shares left unsubscribed after an offer period. Which arrangement is permitted?
column5: Taking them at a discount to the offer value
column6: Taking them with a guaranteed resale price
column7: Taking them at offer value, with no fee for the underwriting
column8: Charging a commission for the underwriting undertaking itself
column10: Per 6/7/1, the Institution may underwrite remaining shares at the offer value, without any consideration for the underwriting per se.

column4: Bakr signed his guarantee for Ahmad's Murabahah debt one week after the Murabahah contract was concluded. Is the guarantee valid?
column5: Yes, it may come before, with or after the credit contract
column6: No, it must be signed together with the credit contract itself
column7: No, it must precede the credit contract
column8: Only if it is in the same document
column10: Per 3/3/3, a personal guarantee may be a separate contract, concluded together with, before, or after the credit transaction.

column4: Bank A is asked to guarantee a client's debt without any right of recourse to the client. When may it do so?
column5: Never, as non-recourse guarantees are void
column6: Only if it charges a fee for the guarantee
column7: Whenever its management finds the guarantee commercially useful
column8: Only if shareholders and investors authorised such donations
column10: Per 3/1/3, an Institution may not be a non-recourse guarantor unless its shareholders and investors have authorised it to make donations or acts of benevolence.

column4: In an Ijarah, Bank A as lessor requires the lessee to provide a guarantee covering damage to the leased asset from any cause. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, since the lessee holds and uses the asset throughout the lease
column6: No, unless restricted to misconduct, negligence or breach
column7: No, a lessor may never require any guarantee
column8: Yes, if the lessee is given a lower rental
column10: Per 2/3, the lessor bears the risk and the lessee holds the asset on trust; a guarantee may cover only misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the core justification for stipulating guarantees in contracts?
column5: They allow a return to be earned on debts
column6: They are needed only for non-Muslim parties
column7: They protect property, an objective of Shari'ah
column8: They replace the need for written contracts
column10: Per the Basis, stipulating guarantees is permissible because it protects property, which is one of the objectives of Shari'ah.

column4: Bank A manages a Mudarabah in foreign currency and offers to guarantee investors against exchange rate fluctuations. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as it amounts to guaranteeing the capital
column6: Permitted if limited to major currencies
column7: Permitted if disclosed in the prospectus
column8: Permitted, as it covers only currency risk and not the capital
column10: Per 3/3/4, a Mudarib, partner or investment agent may not guarantee currency fluctuations, as this amounts to guaranteeing others' capital.

column4: Bank A requires both a personal guarantee and a mortgage of security in one Murabahah contract. What is the ruling?
column5: Only one form of security may be taken per contract
column6: Permissible only if the guarantor owns the mortgaged asset
column7: Permissible only if each is in a separate document
column8: Permissible to include several guarantees in one contract
column10: Per 2/1/2, there is no Shari'ah objection to including a number of guarantees in one contract, such as a personal guarantee together with a mortgage.

column4: Bank A wants to secure its debt obligations against doubtful or bad debts through insurance. Which cover is permitted?
column5: Conventional credit insurance
column6: Islamic insurance coverage only
column7: Either Islamic or conventional insurance
column8: Conventional insurance, if Islamic is unavailable
column10: Per 6/4, subscribing to Islamic insurance as security for debt obligations is permissible; insuring debts on a conventional insurance basis is not.

column4: A Murabahah contract requires Ahmad to provide a guarantor, but he fails to do so. What may Bank A do?
column5: Charge him a monthly late penalty
column6: Raise the agreed Murabahah profit
column7: Sue to force him to provide one, or terminate the contract
column8: Nothing, as a condition to provide a guarantor is unenforceable
column10: Per 3/3/5, if a debtor fails to provide a stipulated guarantor, the Institution may initiate legal action to force him to provide one or terminate the contract.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a deferred-sale seller stipulate termination if the price is unpaid?
column5: He agreed to defer only if it causes him no loss
column6: A sale on deferment is a trust contract
column7: The Hanafis require termination of such sales in every case
column8: Courts may not hear claims on deferred sales
column10: Per the Basis, the seller consented to deferment only if it would not lose what is due to him (majority view); Hanafis confine him to litigation unless stipulated.

column4: As underwriter of a share issue, Bank A also conducts the feasibility study and markets the shares. May it charge for these?
column5: Only if no shares remain unsubscribed
column6: No, all underwriting must be free
column7: Yes, for services other than the guarantee
column8: Yes, as a percentage of shares underwritten
column10: Per 6/7/2, the underwriter may receive consideration for services other than the guarantee, such as a feasibility study or marketing the shares.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a creditor demand all instalments on default instead of waiting for each due date?
column5: The creditor is owed compensation for delay
column6: Deferred instalments are unlawful in principle under Shari'ah
column7: The guarantor's liability ends on default
column8: The debtor might hide his assets and claim insolvency
column10: Per the Basis, the creditor may accelerate because during the delay the debtor may conceal assets and claim insolvency; deferral is the debtor's right he may forgo.

column4: A leased machine needs major maintenance to keep providing the benefits agreed under the lease. Who bears the expense?
column5: The two parties equally
column6: The lessor
column7: The lessee, through the guarantee
column8: The lessee, as user of the asset
column10: Per 2/3, the lessor bears the expense of major maintenance needed to keep the leased property providing the contractual benefits, and related insurance.

column4: Investors ask Bank A, acting as Mudarib of their fund, to guarantee their capital in the Mudarabah contract. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted: the Mudarib may not guarantee the capital
column6: Permitted if the guarantee is written into the Mudarabah contract
column7: Permitted if the Mudarib takes a lower share
column8: Permitted for the capital but not for profit
column10: Per 2/2/1, a Mudarib, Musharakah manager, investment agent or partner may not be required to guarantee the capital or promise a guaranteed profit.

column4: Company Z guarantees to refund the price to a buyer if the sold commodity proves to belong to someone other than the seller. What is this guarantee called?
column5: A subscription guarantee
column6: Daman al-Dark
column7: 'Arboun
column8: Hamish Jiddiyyah
column10: Per 3/2, a guarantee to refund the price if the sold item belongs to another is Daman al-Dark, a market (business) guarantee of contractual obligation.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, which evidence supports guaranteeing a debt whose amount is not yet known?
column5: The rule that Gharar is always tolerated
column6: The Hadith on the bankrupt's sold goods
column7: The general Hadith that the guarantor is liable
column8: The consensus that debts must be fixed first
column10: Per the Basis, the Hadith 'The guarantor is liable' makes no distinction between known and unknown, and the uncertainty causes no dispute; also the Yusuf verse.

column4: Bank A takes cheques from Ahmad as security for his Murabahah instalments. Ahmad pays every instalment on time. What happens to the cheques?
column5: The Bank may present them for an added amount
column6: The Bank keeps them as its own property
column7: They are kept and a holding fee is charged
column8: They are returned to him
column10: Per 6/3, cheques or promissory notes may be taken to ensure timely payment; if the debtor pays on time they are returned, and on default they may be presented.

column4: In a Murabahah, Bank A stipulates a right to freeze Ahmad's current account until the price is paid. When is such a stipulation allowed?
column5: Always, as the Bank's security for the debt owed to it
column6: Only if he freely, willingly and absolutely agrees
column7: Never, under any circumstances, even with consent
column8: Only if the account balance at least equals the debt
column10: Per 6/5/2, the Institution may not stipulate freezing a current account in a credit transaction, unless the customer freely, willingly and absolutely agrees.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Islamic insurance an acceptable security for bad debts while conventional insurance is not?
column5: It is free of any element of guarantee
column6: It guarantees full recovery of every debt
column7: It is provided in return for a set consideration
column8: It rests on donation, where Gharar is tolerable
column10: Per the Basis, Islamic insurance is based on donation for mutual benefit, so Gharar is tolerable and the guarantee is not given for conditional consideration.

column4: A claimant asks whether the standard on guarantees governs securities for compensation arising from torts. What is the position?
column5: No, guarantees against torts are outside its scope
column6: No, it covers only mortgages, cheques and promissory notes
column7: Yes, if the tort arose within a contract
column8: Yes, it covers guarantees of every kind
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard covers securities protecting debts and obligations (documents, guarantees, mortgages, cheques) but not guarantees against torts.

column4: Bakr stipulated that Bank A must first claim from the solvent debtor. Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports such a stipulation?
column5: A Hadith requiring creditors to sue debtors first
column6: The consensus of the Fuqaha that guarantors are never claimed first
column7: Maliki and Hanafi views: claiming the guarantor is then pointless
column8: The rule that guarantees are trust contracts
column10: Per the Basis, the sequence condition rests on Maliki and Hanafi opinions: if the debtor is solvent, claiming the guarantor is pointless unless the debtor refuses.

column4: Company X deposits goods with Bank A for safekeeping and requires a mortgage from the Bank to cover any loss of the goods from any cause. Is this allowed?
column5: No, no security may ever be sought in deposits
column6: No, unless limited to misconduct, negligence or breach
column7: Yes, as a guarantee may be stipulated in any contract whatsoever
column8: Yes, if the Bank charges a safekeeping fee
column10: Per 2/2/1, stipulating a guarantee or mortgage in trust contracts (agency, deposits) is not allowed, except to cover misconduct, negligence or breach.

column4: To secure Ahmad's deferred debt, Bank A blocks an amount equal to the debt in his investment account. How is profit on the account treated?
column5: He earns no profit on the blocked amount
column6: The Bank keeps all the profit earned on the blocked amount as security
column7: He shares profit on the whole balance, after the Mudarib's share
column8: Profit accrues only on the unblocked portion
column10: Per 6/5/1, freezing or blocking is allowed (blocking an equal amount is preferred), but the customer shares profit on the whole balance after the Mudarib's share.

column4: Bank A charges an applicant administrative expenses for issuing a final letter of guarantee. What limit applies to these charges?
column5: They may not exceed 1% of the guaranteed amount
column6: They must reflect the amount and the duration of the guarantee
column7: No limit applies, as expenses are freely agreed
column8: They may not exceed what others charge for such services
column10: Per 6/1/2, administrative expenses may be charged for preliminary or final letters of guarantee, provided they do not exceed the commission others charge.

column4: Bank A sells by Murabahah on condition that it may freeze the buyer's current account. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this barred?
column5: It combines a deferred sale with a condition of a loan
column6: It deprives the buyer of the profit he would earn on the account
column7: Current accounts cannot be pledged at all
