column8: It makes the Murabahah price uncertain
column10: Per the Basis, freezing a current account is like a deferred sale conditioned on a loan, which Shari'ah prohibits; freezing investment accounts is a pledge of funds.

column4: A customer wants Bank A to issue a letter of guarantee that he will use to obtain an interest-based loan from another bank. May Bank A issue it?
column5: Yes, if the customer provides full cover
column6: Yes, if the Bank charges no fee for it
column7: No, it may not issue it for such a purpose
column8: Yes, as the guarantee itself bears no interest
column10: Per 6/1/3, the Institution may not issue a letter of guarantee for an applicant who will use it to acquire an interest-based loan or a prohibited deal.

column4: A notary is asked to witness and certify an interest-based loan between two companies. What is the ruling under the standard?
column5: Permitted if he receives no fee for his services
column6: Permitted, as a witness does not himself take interest
column7: Permitted if he discloses the interest rate in the certificate
column8: Not permitted, as it is an act prohibited by Shari'ah
column10: Per 2/4/3, it is not permitted to scribe or witness acts prohibited by Shari'ah, such as certifying or witnessing borrowing on the basis of interest.

column4: Bank A discharges Ahmad from a debt that Bakr had guaranteed. What happens to Bakr's liability?
column5: He remains liable for half the debt
column6: He is automatically discharged
column7: He remains liable for the full debt
column8: He becomes the principal debtor
column10: Per 3/3/2, if the creditor discharges the debtor, the guarantor is automatically discharged; discharging the guarantor does not discharge the debtor.

column4: Company X paid a primary cash security to join a tender that it lost. The tenderer had mixed the money with its own funds. What applies?
column5: It is held on trust and must be returned
column6: It is 'Arboun and may be kept
column7: It may be retained as a tender fee
column8: It is lost because it was intermingled
column10: Per 6/8/1, tender securities are held on trust, are not 'Arboun, and are recoverable even if intermingled with other money.

column4: Bakr guaranteed Ahmad's 10,000 debt at Ahmad's request. Bakr obtains a discount and pays the creditor 8,000. How much may he recover from Ahmad?
column5: 10,000, the full original debt
column6: Nothing, as he chose to settle early
column7: 8,000, the amount he actually paid
column8: 9,000, sharing the discount equally
column10: Per 3/3/2, a guarantor who secures a discount recovers only what he actually paid, not the full debt; this prevents a procedure potentially leading to Riba.

column4: Company Z, not a party to a Mudarabah, voluntarily undertakes to compensate the investors for any investment loss. When is this permissible?
column5: If it is not linked in any way to the Mudarabah contract
column6: If it is stated as one of the terms of the Mudarabah contract
column7: If the Mudarib co-signs the undertaking
column8: If Company Z receives a fee for it
column10: Per 6/6, a third party (not the Mudarib, agent or partner) may volunteer to compensate investment loss, if not linked in any way to the financing contract.

column4: A buyer pays 'Arboun when concluding a sale and does not terminate within the agreed option period. What becomes of the 'Arboun?
column5: It is kept by the seller as a fee
column6: It is refunded to the buyer
column7: It remains held on trust
column8: It becomes part of the price
column10: Per 6/8/3, if the contract is not terminated within the option period, the 'Arboun is considered part of the consideration for the contract.

column4: Bakr guarantees Ahmad's future debt, with liability starting on 1 July. On 1 June, before any debt arises, Bakr wants to withdraw. Can he?
column5: Only with the debtor's written consent
column6: Yes, by notifying the creditor before the debt arises
column7: No, a guarantee once given can never be withdrawn by the guarantor
column8: Yes, even without notifying the creditor
column10: Per 3/1/4 and 3/2, a guarantee contingent on a future date may be withdrawn by notifying the creditor before the guaranteed obligation arises.

column4: Bakr guaranteed Ahmad's debt with no condition on the order of claims. Ahmad is solvent and the debt is due. May Bank A claim directly from Bakr?
column5: Yes, it may claim from either of them
column6: No, it must claim from Ahmad first
column7: Only after a judgment against Ahmad
column8: No, unless Ahmad becomes insolvent
column10: Per 3/3/1, the creditor may claim from either debtor or guarantor, unless the guarantor stipulated at contracting that the debtor be claimed first.

column4: Company Y guarantees a customer's debt to Bank A at the customer's own request. Which type of personal guarantee is this?
column5: A voluntary guarantee without recourse
column6: A guarantee held on a trust basis
column7: A non-recourse guarantee, since the debtor himself asked for it
column8: A guarantee with a right of recourse to the debtor
column10: Per 3/1/2, a guarantee given at the debtor's request or with his consent carries recourse; a non-recourse guarantee is offered without his request or consent.

column4: Bakr guarantees whatever Ahmad will come to owe Bank A on future purchases, the amount being unknown today. Is the guarantee valid?
column5: No, the guaranteed amount must be known at the outset
column6: No, only existing debts may be guaranteed
column7: Yes, unknown and future debts may be guaranteed
column8: Only if Bank A first approves each purchase
column10: Per 3/2, a valid guarantee may be given for debts whose exact amount is unknown and for debts that will arise in the future.

column4: In a debtor's liquidation, whose claims for the cost of services provided in the liquidation process have priority over other creditors?
column5: The unsecured trade creditors of the debtor company
column6: The parties in charge of the liquidation
column7: The guarantors of the debtor, as they back its debts
column8: The shareholders of the debtor, as its owners
column10: Per 6/9/4, in bankruptcy or liquidation, those in charge of the liquidation have priority over other creditors for the cost of services they provide.

column4: Bakr asks why he cannot charge Ahmad a fee for guaranteeing his debt. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is it prohibited?
column5: A guarantee is charitable, so a fee for it is Riba
column6: Guarantors may not claim any expenses they incur at all
column7: Guarantees are invalid whenever any fee is paid for them
column8: Only Institutions may charge for guarantees, not individuals
column10: Per the Basis, guarantee is a charitable act implying readiness to lend; taking consideration for giving away a loan amount is Riba, as the Fuqaha agree.

column4: A lessee pays 'Arboun to Bank A and then fails to perform within the option period. The Bank may retain it. What does the standard consider preferable?
column5: Donating the whole amount to charity through the Board
column6: Refunding the balance above the actual damage
column7: Keeping the whole amount as profit, as the lessee defaulted
column8: Claiming further compensation on top
column10: Per 6/8/3, the seller or lessor may retain the 'Arboun, but it is preferable to refund any balance after deducting damage actually sustained.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why must a converting bank still repay the principal of its pre-conversion interest-based loans?
column5: Principal and interest form one indivisible debt in the contract
column6: Repaying principal avoids court penalties
column7: The lender may waive interest, not principal
column8: The loan is valid; only the interest condition is void
column10: Per the Basis, following the Hanafi view, the loan contract itself is valid and the interest condition void; acts of Muslims are deemed valid as far as possible.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may premises once used for impermissible services be converted for permissible use rather than sold or destroyed?
column5: Destroying property is never permitted under Shari'ah
column6: Real estate is exempt from all Shari'ah rules on use
column7: The prohibition concerns the use, not the location
column8: Premises are owned by the shareholders, not the bank
column10: Per the Basis, locations used for impermissible services may be transformed because the prohibition relates to the use of the location, not the location itself.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A needs funds to meet its liabilities. Which of these funding methods is listed as permissible in the standard?
column5: Issuing bonds with a fixed coupon
column6: Issuing preference shares carrying a fixed rate of return
column7: Taking interbank loans with interest
column8: Issuing Mudarabah, Musharakah or Ijarah certificates
column10: Per 6/2, permissible funding includes capital increases, Islamic certificates (Mudarabah, Musharakah, Ijarah), Salam, Istisna'a, sale-and-leaseback and Tawarruq.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: In an external conversion, the assets of the bank being acquired carry impermissible mortgages. What must the buyer stipulate?
column5: That depositors guarantee the mortgages
column6: That the seller replace them with permissible mortgages
column7: That the buyer will pay the interest secured by the mortgages
column8: That the mortgages stay until they lapse
column10: Per 9/3, shareholders must accelerate redemption of impermissible mortgages; in external conversion, the buyer must stipulate that the seller replaces them.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Investors acquire a conventional bank in order to convert it. The bank earned interest before the acquisition. Must the new owners dispose of it?
column5: Yes, if it remains in the bank's reserves
column6: Yes, all past interest must go to charity
column7: No, they are not obliged to dispose of it
column8: Yes, for the last five financial periods
column10: Per 8/1/1, new owners acquiring a conventional bank to convert it are not obliged to dispose of interest and impermissible earnings earned before acquisition.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A asks which Shari'ah governance bodies it must set up as part of the necessary measures for conversion. What does the standard require?
column5: A Shari'ah supervisory board and internal compliance department
column6: Only a Shari'ah adviser for new products
column7: Only an external Shari'ah auditor appointed on a yearly contract basis
column8: A Zakah committee in place of a Shari'ah board
column10: Per 3/4, the bank must form a Shari'ah supervisory board and an internal Shari'ah compliance department per AAOIFI Governance Standards.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, on what contracts does a converted bank's provision of banking services (not interest-based loans) rest?
column5: Salam and Istisna'a with advance payment
column6: Qard and Hawalah with a fee on each service
column7: Mudarabah and Musharakah with profit sharing
column8: Ijarah and agency with remuneration
column10: Per the Basis, providing banking services not related to interest-bearing loans is a practical application of Ijarah and agency with remuneration.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: After conversion, Bank B holds impermissible commodities, and some it sold earlier remain unpaid. What is required?
column5: Destroy those held; collect and donate the unpaid price
column6: Sell those held and keep all proceeds
column7: Destroy those held, and waive the unpaid price of those sold
column8: Hold them all until the Shari'ah board meets
column10: Per 8/1/5, the converted bank must destroy impermissible commodities it holds; the unpaid price of those already sold must be received and donated to charity.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Before deciding to convert, Bank A issued preference shares and interest-based certificates on which it pays interest. What must it do?
column5: Keep them outstanding but cap the interest rate paid on them
column6: Keep them until their maturity dates
column7: Liquidate them as traces of conventional transactions
column8: Keep them if held by central banks
column10: Per 6/1, all traces of conventional transactions on which the bank pays interest, including deposits, preference shares, bonds and certificates, must be liquidated.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A needs liquidity from the central bank. Which approach does the standard give as an example?
column5: Discounting commercial bills at the central bank for a fee
column6: Opening investment accounts for the central bank
column7: Repurchase agreements at a fixed rate of return
column8: Interest-bearing overnight borrowing from the central bank
column10: Per 4/1, the bank should adapt its dealings with the central bank for liquidity, for example by opening investment accounts for the central bank.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: A board member asks why training staff and redesigning contracts can become obligatory during conversion. Which principle does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: A means needed to fulfil an obligation is itself obligatory
column6: Necessity renders prohibited things permissible in such cases
column7: Custom is an arbiter in commercial dealings
column8: Harm is removed to the extent possible
column10: Per the Basis, conversion is obligatory; if it can be realised only by certain procedures and tools, using them also becomes an obligation.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may impermissible earnings be donated to charity, becoming lawful for the beneficiaries?
column5: Beneficiaries are not bound by Shari'ah
column6: The earnings were lawful from the outset
column7: Charity purifies the whole capital of the bank that gives it
column8: Transfer of ownership changes their prohibited character
column10: Per the Basis, transferring ownership changes the prohibited characterisation; what is prohibited for one may be permissible for another (the usurped goat Hadith).

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank B plans to use its interest earnings to fund training for its own staff. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, if the staff are newly recruited
column6: No, though training people other than its staff is allowed
column7: Yes, since training is one of the charitable channels listed
column8: Yes, if management approves the budget
column10: Per 10/2, the bank may not use such money directly or indirectly for its own benefit; listed channels include training people other than the bank's staff.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Investors buying a conventional bank to convert it can negotiate to exclude interest receivables and leave impermissible liabilities with the seller. Must they?
column5: Only for receivables, not liabilities
column6: No, they must take over all assets
column7: Yes, Shari'ah requires them to do so
column8: No, it is merely a recommendation
column10: Per 9/2, if the purchaser can exclude non-permissible receivables and leave the seller liable for non-permissible liabilities, Shari'ah requires it to do so.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A asks whether it may take a commission for providing a mere credit facility to a customer. What is the ruling?
column5: Yes, provided no interest is charged
column6: Yes, as a percentage of the facility
column7: No, and no charge may be made even for actual expenses
column8: No, but a charge may be linked to expenses incurred
column10: Per 5, no commission may be taken for providing a mere facility; however, the commission may be linked to expenses incurred in executing it.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Bank B cannot legally avoid paying interest on an old loan without facing penalties. Per the Shari'ah basis, why may it pay?
column5: Necessity, as acts done under compulsion are forgiven
column6: Paying interest is allowed if the amount is donated later
column7: Interest is a valid debt that must always be honoured
column8: The loan was taken before the conversion decision was made
column10: Per the Basis, interest is not a valid debt, but necessity allows payment where avoidance lacks legal protection; Allah forgave acts done under compulsion.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Paying all of Bank B's pre-conversion impermissible earnings to charity at once would lead to its collapse. What does the standard allow?
column5: Using them to fund bonuses for the bank's staff
column6: Disposal may reasonably take place gradually
column7: Keeping them permanently as part of its capital base
column8: Returning them to former depositors as extra profit
column10: Per 10/1, impermissible earnings go to charity without delay unless that would cause collapse or bankruptcy; then implementation may be reasonably gradual.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Bank A cannot terminate a long-term interest-based loan it granted before its decision to convert. What must it do with the interest?
column5: Keep it, as it was earned on a loan predating the conversion
column6: Add it to the bank's capital reserves
column7: Dispose of it to charity as the standard sets out
column8: Write off the principal amount instead
column10: Per 7/2, the bank must try to terminate pre-conversion interest loans; if unable, it must dispose of the interest earned as explained in 10/2.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: A converting bank offers a safe deposit box service that is naturally permissible. Does the conversion standard require it to change this activity or its profits?
column5: No, naturally permissible activities are outside its scope
column6: Yes, all pre-conversion activities must cease
column7: Yes, its past profits must be given to charity
column8: Yes, it must be suspended until the conversion process ends
column10: Per the Scope (1), naturally permissible activities and profits made by permissible means are not the subject of conversion; the bank may continue them.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Before converting, Bank B committed to provide a non-permissible service to a client. What must it do after converting?
column5: Assign the obligation to a conventional bank in return for a fee
column6: Perform it, as the contract is binding
column7: Terminate it, refunding the price even with compensation
column8: Perform it and donate the fee received
column10: Per 9/1/2, the bank must strive to terminate obligations to provide non-permissible services by refunding the consideration, even if it must pay compensation.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A's articles of association include objectives that contradict the nature of Islamic banking. What must be done?
column5: Disclose them in the annual report only
column6: Add a Shari'ah clause overriding them
column7: Keep them unchanged until the next renewal of its licence
column8: Amend the by-laws and cleanse them of anything contrary
column10: Per 3/2, by-laws must be amended through the required procedures to include objectives suited to Islamic banking and cleansed of anything contradicting it.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: A buyer converting Bank C offers creditors early repayment of Riba loans in return for a discount. Which principle supports this, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Ibra', if the discount is fixed in the loan
column6: Da' Wa Ta'jjal, if the discount was not agreed earlier
column7: Muqassah, if the two debts are of equal amount and maturity
column8: Hawalah, if the creditor consents in advance
column10: Per the Basis, early repayment for a discount rests on Da' Wa Ta'jjal, endorsed by the Fiqh Academy, provided the discount was not agreed upon earlier.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A's current account with the central bank, kept for set-off, earns interest it cannot avoid. What should the Bank do?
column5: Dispose of the interest earned
column6: Distribute it to its depositors
column7: Retain it in reserves for Zakah
column8: Keep it to cover clearing costs
column10: Per 4/1, for set-off the bank should keep current accounts accruing no interest or, if that is impossible, dispose of the interest earned.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a converting bank keep income it received under a qualified Ijtihad later seen as doubtful?
column5: The income was earned before the conversion decision was taken
column6: Shari'ah validates acts on a believed interpretation
column7: The Shari'ah board may waive disposal of any such income
column8: Doubtful income is always lawful to keep, whatever its source
column10: Per the Basis, Shari'ah validates actions based on an interpretation believed valid until proved wrong, by analogy with insurgents who act on Ijtihad.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Bank B's existing shareholders convert it into an Islamic bank. From when must the bank dispose of interest and impermissible earnings?
column5: From the bank's date of incorporation
column6: From the date of the new licence
column7: From the start of the financial period of conversion
column8: From the first financial period after the conversion is complete
column10: Per 8/1/2, for conversion by existing shareholders, disposal commences at the beginning of the financial period in which the conversion takes effect.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A used to charge interest on uncovered documentary credits. What alternative does the standard require?
column5: Charging a commission for the facility itself
column6: Charging interest on the credit and donating it all to charity
column7: Charging a percentage of the credit amount
column8: Treating them through Murabahah, Musharakah or Mudarabah
column10: Per 5, the bank may not receive interest for services; an Islamic alternative is needed, e.g. uncovered credits via Murabahah, Musharakah or Mudarabah.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: After internal conversion, Bank B still owes interest on old borrowings, in addition to the principal. What does the standard require?
column5: Refuse to repay the principal as well
column6: Pay interest and principal as contracted
column7: Avoid paying it by all lawful means, unless in dire need
column8: Pay the interest amount to charity instead of to the lender
column10: Per 9/1/1, the bank should use all lawful means to avoid paying interest (not principal) and pay interest only on the basis of dire need.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Before converting, Bank B distributed dividends derived from interest to its shareholders. Who should dispose of these earnings?
column5: No one, as the distributions were final and cannot be reversed
column6: The bank itself, out of its current profits after conversion
column7: The Shari'ah board, out of the bank's general reserves
column8: The shareholders personally, on ethical grounds
column10: Per 8/1/2, impermissible earnings distributed before conversion should be disposed of personally by the shareholders and depositors who received them; the bank is not bound.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Investors acquired Bank C to convert it. Zakah was not paid for past financial periods. Who bears Zakah for those periods?
column5: No one, as conversion cancels the past Zakah
column6: The previous owners; the new owners from the decision date
column7: The new owners, for all unpaid past periods
column8: The bank's depositors, in proportion to their account balances
column10: Per 11, outsiders acquiring a bank to convert it owe no past Zakah, which is the previous owners' liability; their liability starts from the decision to convert.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: A buyer converting Bank C must take over all assets, including interest-based liabilities. What must the buyer do with these liabilities?
column5: Dispose of them quickly, even via early repayment at a discount
column6: Transfer them to the bank's depositors in proportion to balances
column7: Keep paying them until their maturity
column8: Refinance them with new interest loans
column10: Per 9/2, if all assets must be acquired, the buyer must quickly dispose of non-permissible liabilities, even proposing early repayment for a discount.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Shareholders of Bank D decide to convert it. Zakah was unpaid in past periods, partly on impermissible earnings. Must they pay it?
column5: No, Zakah starts only from conversion
column6: No, since those earnings will be given to charity in any case
column7: Only on permissible earnings of past periods
column8: Yes, for past periods, even on impermissible earnings
column10: Per 11, converting shareholders must pay past Zakah even on impermissible revenues; Zakah is part of the obligation to dispose of such earnings.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank B is entitled to receive certain prohibited non-monetary assets from a counterparty. What may it do?
column5: Use them in its own operations
column6: Receive them with the intent to destroy them
column7: Sell them and keep the price
column8: Keep them in stock until a buyer appears
column10: Per 8/1/4, if the bank has rights to prohibited non-monetary assets, it may receive them with the intent to destroy them.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Bank A, a conventional bank, opens an Islamic window. Does the standard on conversion of a conventional bank govern the window's activities?
column5: No, Islamic windows are outside its scope
column6: Yes, once the window is licensed
column7: Only for the deposits of the window
column8: Yes, as a form of partial conversion
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard does not cover activities of Islamic windows, departments or units in conventional banks.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: A customer owes converting Bank B for a non-permissible service supplied before conversion and argues he need not pay. What applies?
column5: He is released, as the service was prohibited
column6: He pays only half, the rest being waived
column7: He must pay; the bank donates it to charity
column8: He pays and the bank keeps it as income
column10: Per 8/1/4, the bank receives such consideration to donate it; the customer may not avoid paying, or he would get both the service and its price.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A buys a commodity on deferred payment and sells it for cash to raise liquidity through Tawarruq. To whom may it sell?
column5: The original seller, at a lower price
column6: A third party other than the original seller
column7: Only the bank's own subsidiary
column8: Any party, including the original seller
column10: Per 6/2/5, Tawarruq means buying a commodity on deferred payment and selling it for immediate payment to a third party other than the previous seller.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A keeps accounts with conventional correspondent banks. What does the standard require regarding these relationships?
column5: Keep them unchanged until their maturity
column6: Convert them into interest-bearing deposits
column7: Revamp them and limit dealings to the extent of need
column8: Close all of them on the very day of the decision to convert
column10: Per 3/6, the bank opens accounts with Islamic banks and revamps conventional bank accounts; dealings with conventional banks are limited to the magnitude of need.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A must terminate all its previous interest-based transactions. Which verse does the Shari'ah basis cite for this?
column5: Render back your trusts to those to whom due
column6: No ground of complaint against those who do right
column7: And get two witnesses out of your own men
column8: Give up what remains of your demand for usury
column10: Per the Basis, terminating previous impermissible transactions rests on: Give up what remains of your demand for usury (Al-Baqarah 278).

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Bank B received revenues believed permissible under a position of an authoritative school, though now doubtful. Must it dispose of them on converting?
column5: No, they are not subject to compulsory disposal
column6: Yes, half of them must be donated
column7: Yes, all revenues of doubtful permissibility must be donated
column8: Yes, if received in the conversion period
column10: Per 8/1/3, received revenues of doubtful permissibility, believed permissible per a qualified Ijtihad, an authoritative school or eminent scholars, need not be disposed of.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank A sells some premises for liquidity and leases them back by Ijarah. Which requirement applies?
column5: The sale must be made conditional on the signing of the lease
column6: The sale contract must be independent of the lease
column7: The rental must equal the sale price
column8: The lease must be signed before the sale
column10: Per 6/2/4, sale-and-leaseback must follow the Ijarah standards; the contract of sale must be independent and separate from the contract of lease.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: The central bank requires a cash reserve from converting Bank A. Which alternative to freezing the cash account does the standard suggest?
column5: Borrowing the reserve from another bank
column6: Accepting interest on the frozen reserve and giving it to charity
column7: Depositing receivables represented by commercial paper
column8: Buying interest-bearing treasury bills
column10: Per 4/1, alternatives to the legal reserve include depositing receivables represented by commercial paper instead of freezing the cash account.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a converting bank clear non-permissible previous transactions gradually, for necessity or need?
column5: Shareholders may profit from them in the meantime
column6: Past contracts remain valid until each one matures
column7: Gradual conversion is the preferred model
column8: Clearing them all at once is not feasible
column10: Per the Basis, gradual clearance is allowed because immediate clearance of all non-permissible transactions is not feasible; the bank disposes of their effects.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: To raise funds, converting Bank A enters Istisna'a contracts as manufacturer. Which condition does the standard attach for this purpose?
column5: The Istisna'a price is paid to the bank in advance
column6: The price is paid by a third-party guarantor on delivery
column7: The price is paid on delivery of the asset
column8: The price is deferred over instalments
column10: Per 6/2/3, the bank may act as manufacturer in Istisna'a for funding, on condition the price is paid in advance, though deferment is generally allowed.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: After deciding to convert, Bank A wants to keep its non-permissible transactions running for two more years for convenience. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, if done within the announced period
column6: Yes, until the existing contracts mature
column7: No, delay is allowed only for necessity or pressing need
column8: Yes, if the resulting profits are given to charity meanwhile
column10: Per 2/1, pre-decision transactions must in principle cease or be disposed of immediately; delay is not permissible unless it is a necessity or pressing need.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Bank B decides on a gradual, partial conversion over ten years instead of an immediate comprehensive one. Can it be licensed as an Islamic bank meanwhile?
column5: No, not until the conversion process is completed
column6: Yes, once a Shari'ah board is appointed
column7: Yes, once half of its assets have been converted to Islamic ones
column8: Yes, once it announces its conversion plan
column10: Per 2/2, a bank adopting gradual or partial conversion is not regarded as converted and may not be licensed as Islamic until conversion is completed.

column3: Conversion of a Conventional Bank to an Islamic Bank
column4: Converting Bank B owns premises that were designated for non-permissible activities. What should it do with them?
column5: Sell them and donate the full sale price to charity at once
column6: Leave them unused permanently, to avoid any doubt
column7: Demolish them, as prohibited assets cannot be reused
column8: Change them to locations for permissible operations
column10: Per 8/1/6, property assets designated for non-permissible activities should be changed to locations designated for permissible operations and services.

column4: A trainee at Bank A describes Hawalah as a sale of one debt for another. Is this correct under the standard?
column5: No, it is a form of personal guarantee
column6: No, it is an independent courtesy contract, not a sale
column7: Yes, it is a sale of a debt at a discount to its face value
column8: Yes, it is a sale of a debt for a debt
column10: Per 3/1, Hawalah is a legitimate, independent contract made out of courtesy, not a contract of sale, permitted to facilitate payments and recovery.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports the majority view that a transferee who stipulated the payer's solvency has recourse if the payer is insolvent?
column5: The Hadith that Muslims are bound by their conditions
column6: The Hanafi rule on unrestricted Hawalah
column7: The analogy with a deferred guarantee
column8: The report of Uthman Ibn Affan on the payer's bankruptcy
column10: Per the Basis, the majority rely on the Hadith that Muslims are bound by their conditions; the solvency condition serves the contract's purpose.

column4: Ahmad, who owes Bakr nothing, directs Bakr to collect 1,000 from Zaid, who owes Ahmad that amount. How is this transaction characterised?
column5: An unrestricted Hawalah, since Bakr collects from Zaid
column6: An agency for collection, not a Hawalah
column7: A transfer of right by sale of the debt to Bakr
column8: A restricted Hawalah, since Zaid owes Ahmad that amount
column10: Per 6/2, Hawalah requires the transferor to be a debtor to the transferee; if a non-debtor transfers another, it is an agency contract for collection.

column4: Bakr finds that Zaid, the payer, has died bankrupt. Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports Bakr's recourse to the transferor?
column5: The Hadith that the guarantor is liable
column6: The rule that death annuls all contracts
column7: Uthman's report that a Muslim's right cannot go unfulfilled
column8: The consensus that Hawalah never discharges the transferor at all
column10: Per the Basis, the Hanafi view rests on Uthman Ibn Affan's answer that the transferee returns to the transferor, as the right of a Muslim cannot go unfulfilled.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a Hawalah not be concluded on a temporary basis or contingent on a future event?
column5: Contingent contracts are void in all cases
column6: The payer cannot know the debt in advance
column7: The transferee may refuse a transfer that is set for the future
column8: Its nature is the immediate transfer of the debt to the payer
column10: Per the Basis, Hawalah has the character of an immediate exchange creating a new relationship at once; a temporary or contingent transfer conflicts with its nature.

column4: Ahmad transfers his debt to Zaid on terms that the transfer takes effect only if Ahmad's shipment arrives next month. Is this Hawalah valid?
column5: Yes, a Hawalah may be made contingent on a future event
column6: No, a Hawalah must take effect immediately
column7: Yes, provided the arrival date is fixed in the contract
column8: Yes, once the shipment has arrived
column10: Per 4/3, a transfer of debt must take effect immediately; it may not be suspended, temporary or contingent on future events.

column4: Ahmad asks Bank A to transfer USD 1,000 from his USD current account to his creditor Bakr; the Bank charges a fee. How is the fee viewed?
column5: As a discount on the transferred debt
column6: As a guarantee fee for the transfer
column7: As Riba over the amount transferred
column8: As consideration for delivering the money
column10: Per 12/6, a same-currency remittance to the applicant's creditor is a transfer of debt; the fee is consideration for delivery, not an excess over the amount.

column4: Bank A's operations team asks whether the Hawalah standard governs all of the bank's banking remittances. What is the position?
column5: It excludes remittances in every case
column6: It covers every type of banking remittance
column7: It covers only remittances taking the form of Hawalah
column8: It covers only remittances made in a currency other than the original
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard covers Hawalah involving a change of debtor and excludes banking remittances except those taking the form of Hawalah.

column4: Ahmad, the transferor, dies after a Hawalah. His creditors ask that the debt Zaid owes under the Hawalah be shared among them pro rata. Is that right?
column5: No, the transferee is its sole owner
column6: Yes, but the transferee ranks first
column7: Yes, as the Hawalah is annulled by death
column8: Yes, it forms part of Ahmad's estate
column10: Per 10/1, Hawalah is not annulled by the transferor's death; the transferee solely owns the debt, which is not distributed among the transferor's creditors.

column4: Ahmad, Bakr and Zaid conclude a Hawalah through clear offer and acceptance showing intent to shift the debt, but never use the word transfer. Is it valid?
column5: No, it must be written and witnessed
column6: Yes, the word transfer need not be used
column7: Yes, but only between Institutions
column8: No, the word Hawalah must be stated
column10: Per 4/1, Hawalah is concluded by offer and acceptance clearly indicating the intention to transfer the debt; it is not necessary that the word transfer be used.

column4: Ahmad issues a cheque on his current account at Bank A to Bakr, to whom he owes that amount. How is this characterised?
column5: Agency: Bakr collects on behalf of Ahmad
column6: Sale: Bakr buys Ahmad's balance at Bank A
column7: Hawalah: Ahmad transferor, Bank A payer, Bakr transferee
column8: Hawalah: Bank A transferor, Ahmad payer, Bakr transferee
column10: Per 12/1, a cheque on a current account to the issuer's creditor is Hawalah, with issuer, bank and beneficiary as transferor, payer and transferee.

column4: Company X draws a bill of exchange on Bank A in favour of its creditor, but no debt exists between Company X and Bank A. How is this classified?
column5: An unrestricted Hawalah
column6: An invalid transaction
column7: A restricted Hawalah
column8: An agency for collection
column10: Per 12/4/1-12/4/2, a bill to the drawer's creditor is Hawalah; with no debt between the drawer and the paying bank, it is an unrestricted Hawalah.

column4: Zaid, the payer, dies solvent before paying the transferred debt. What is the effect on the Hawalah?
column5: It stands, but payment waits for the heirs' consent
column6: It is annulled; the debt is extinguished
column7: It is annulled; the transferee claims from Ahmad
column8: It stands; the transferee claims from Zaid's estate
column10: Per 10/2, the payer's death does not annul Hawalah; the transferee has recourse against his estate or guarantor, and to the transferor only if he died bankrupt.

column4: Ahmad owes Bakr 1,000. With everyone's consent, Bakr will now collect the 1,000 from Zaid instead of Ahmad. What has changed, per the standard's definition?
column5: The debt amount, so it is a set-off
column6: The debtor, so it is a transfer of debt
column7: The debt's currency, so it is an exchange
column8: The creditor, so it is a transfer of right
column10: Per 2, Hawalah of debt transfers the debt from the transferor (Muheel) to the payer (Muhal Alaihi): one debtor replaces another. A transfer of right changes the creditor.

column4: A client endorses a bill of exchange to Bank A, asking it to collect the amount and credit his account. How is this classified, and may the Bank charge?
column5: Hawalah, with a fee based on the amount
column6: Hawalah, with no fee permitted
column7: Agency, which must always be free of fee
column8: Agency, permissible with or without a fee
column10: Per 12/5/2, endorsing a bill so the Institution collects and credits the client is not Hawalah but agency, permissible with or without consideration.

column4: Zaid owes Ahmad nothing but, on Ahmad's order, agrees to pay Ahmad's creditor from his own funds and recover later from Ahmad. What is this?
column5: A permissible unrestricted Hawalah
column6: A transfer of right to Zaid
column7: A restricted Hawalah on Zaid's funds
column8: An invalid Hawalah, since Zaid owes nothing
column10: Per 5/1/2 and 6/3, where the payer is not the transferor's debtor and pays from his own funds with recourse, on the transferor's order, it is unrestricted Hawalah.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why must the transferee in a restricted Hawalah take no more than the amount of his own debt?
column5: To preserve the transferor's recourse
column6: To keep the two debts in one currency
column7: To avoid Riba
column8: To protect the payer's other creditors
column10: Per the Basis, the required similarity in amount means the transferee must not take more than his actual debt, the intention being to avoid Riba.

column4: Which of the following brings a Hawalah liability to an end under the standard?
column5: Unilateral notice by the transferor
column6: Death of the transferor
column7: Liquidation of the transferee Institution
column8: Write-off of the debt by the transferee
column10: Per 11, a Hawalah liability ends by settlement of the debt, mutual agreement to terminate it, or write-off of the debt by the transferee.

column4: Ahmad and Zaid agree to transfer Ahmad's debt to Zaid without asking Bakr, the creditor. Is the Hawalah valid?
column5: Yes, if Zaid is known to be solvent
column6: Yes, the creditor's consent is not needed
column7: No, the transferee's consent is required
column8: Yes, if Bakr is notified afterwards
column10: Per 6/1, the permissibility of Hawalah requires the consent of all parties: the transferor, the transferee and the payer.

column4: Zaid holds goods belonging to Ahmad. Ahmad's creditor Bakr is to be paid from the value of those goods held by Zaid. What type of Hawalah is this?
column5: A sale of the goods to Bakr
column6: A restricted Hawalah
column7: An agency for collection
column8: An unrestricted Hawalah
column10: Per 5/1/1, restricted Hawalah limits the payer to settling from a financial or tangible asset of the transferor in his possession.

column4: A Hawalah takes effect today, but the parties agree that Zaid, the payer, will pay the transferred debt on 31 December. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, payment of the transferred debt may be deferred
column6: Yes, if Zaid pays an added profit
column7: No, deferring payment makes the Hawalah itself contingent
column8: No, payment must be made on the spot
column10: Per 4/3, the transfer itself must be immediate, but it is permissible to defer payment of the transferred debt until a future specified date.

column4: In a restricted Hawalah, Zaid's debt to Ahmad was secured by a mortgage. After the Hawalah, who holds the rights and legal protections against Zaid?
column5: Ahmad keeps the mortgage rights
column6: The mortgage lapses on the Hawalah
column7: Ahmad and Bakr share them equally
column8: Bakr, the transferee, in Ahmad's place
column10: Per 9/2, in restricted Hawalah the transferee takes the place of the transferor in respect of all rights, legal protections and obligations against the payer.

column4: Bakr accepted a Hawalah on condition that Zaid, the payer, is solvent. Zaid proves to be insolvent. What is Bakr's position?
column5: He has recourse to the transferor
column6: He must wait until Zaid becomes solvent
column7: He loses his claim entirely
column8: He may claim only from Zaid's guarantor
column10: Per 7/1, if acceptance was conditional on the payer's solvency, the transferee has a right of recourse to the transferor if the payer is not solvent.

column4: Ahmad's creditor Bakr agreed to Zaid paying Ahmad's debt, but Ahmad himself was not asked. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Ahmad's consent required?
column5: He must confirm the amount Zaid owes him and its due date
column6: He might not want a third party to pay his debt
column7: He alone can fix the date of payment to Bakr
column8: He must approve the fee paid to Zaid for paying
column10: Per the Basis, the transferor's consent is required because he might not want a third party to pay the debt on his behalf.

column4: After a Hawalah is validly concluded, Ahmad, the transferor, wants to cancel it on his own. Can he?
column5: Yes, while the debt is not yet due
column6: Yes, by giving notice to the payer
column7: No, Hawalah is a binding contract
column8: Yes, until the payer makes payment
column10: Per 4/2, Hawalah is a binding contract and therefore is not subject to unilateral termination.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, which school alone permits unrestricted Hawalah, and on what ground?
column5: The Hanafis, as the order to accept did not require a debt
column6: The Malikis, as market custom has always favoured this practice
column7: The Hanbalis, as it is a kind of guarantee
column8: The Shafi'is, as it resembles a sale of debt
column10: Per the Basis, restricted Hawalah is agreed; unrestricted Hawalah is permitted by the Hanafis only, as the order to accept did not require the payer to be a debtor.

column4: The transferred debt is already due, but Zaid, the payer, requires that it be paid at an agreed future date. May Bakr, the transferee, demand earlier payment?
column5: Yes, since the debt was already due
column6: Yes, after giving reasonable notice
column7: Yes, if Ahmad guarantees payment
column8: No, not before the agreed date
column10: Per 5/1/4, in a deferred Hawalah where the payer required future payment at an agreed date, the payer cannot be asked to pay before that date.

column4: Ahmad issues a cheque to his creditor Bakr on an account with no balance, and Bank A accepts the overdraft. How is this classified?
column5: Not a transfer, as there is no balance
column6: An agency for collection
column7: An unrestricted transfer of debt
column8: A restricted transfer of debt
column10: Per 12/2, a cheque to a creditor without balance is an unrestricted transfer of debt if the bank accepts the overdraft; if rejected, there is no transfer.

column4: Bakr is transferred to a payer whose creditworthiness he does not know. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is accepting still permissible?
column5: The payer's solvency is always presumed by law
column6: The Hadith sets no condition of the payer's solvency
column7: The transferor guarantees the payer in all cases
column8: Gharar is always tolerated in Hawalah, as in all transfers
column10: Per the Basis, the Hadith's order does not make the payer's solvency a condition for Hawalah's permissibility, so acceptance remains Mubah.

column4: Ahmad owes Bakr 10 dinars and is owed 20 dinars by Zaid. He transfers Bakr to Zaid in a restricted Hawalah. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid, and Bakr may collect all 20
column6: Invalid, as the debts are unequal
column7: Valid, but Bakr may receive only 10 dinars
column8: Valid if Bakr pays Ahmad the difference
column10: Per 6/6, a lesser debt may be transferred against a larger one, on condition the transferee is entitled only to the equivalent of his own debt.

column4: One of the three parties to a proposed Hawalah lacks legal competence to act independently. What is the effect?
column5: It is valid if the other two consent
column6: It is valid if the debt is small
column7: It is valid as an unrestricted Hawalah
column8: The Hawalah is not valid
column10: Per 6/4, it is a condition that all parties to a Hawalah be legally competent to act independently.

column4: In an unrestricted Hawalah, Zaid objects that he never agreed to pay Ahmad's creditor. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Zaid's consent needed?
column5: There is no liability without first accepting it
column6: His consent replaces the consent of the transferee
column7: He must agree to the exchange rate used for the debt
column8: He must agree to waive any recourse against Ahmad
column10: Per the Basis, the payer must consent in unrestricted Hawalah because it makes him liable, and in principle there is no liability without prior acceptance of it.

column4: Bank C, the payer in a Hawalah, is declared bankrupt by a court order before paying the transferee. What may the transferee do?
column5: Claim from Bank C's depositors
column6: Have recourse against the transferor
column7: Only claim pro rata in Bank C's bankruptcy
column8: Nothing, as the transferor is discharged
column10: Per 7/2, the transferee has recourse to the transferor where the payer Institution is declared bankrupt by court order, or liquidated in bankruptcy before payment.

column4: A holder offers to transfer a bill of exchange to Bank A before its due date in return for immediate payment of a discounted amount. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it is a form of Riba
column6: Permissible as a successive Hawalah
column7: Permissible if Bank A is the drawee
column8: Permissible if the discount is small
column10: Per 12/5/4, discounting bills of exchange by transferring their value before maturity for a discounted immediate payment is not permissible: it is Riba.

column4: After a restricted Hawalah, Ahmad, the transferor, asks Zaid to pay him directly the amount Zaid owes him. Is Ahmad entitled to it?
column5: Yes, but only for half of the amount
column6: No, that right has passed to the transferee
column7: Yes, because Zaid's debt is still legally owed to Ahmad
column8: Yes, if Bakr has not yet claimed it
column10: Per 8, after a restricted Hawalah the transferor may not reclaim from the payer the amount transferred, as the right to receive it has passed to the transferee.

column4: After a valid Hawalah, Zaid delays paying Bakr. There was no solvency condition, and Zaid is neither dead nor bankrupt. Can Bakr go back to Ahmad?
column5: Yes, after a formal demand on Zaid
column6: Yes, for half of the transferred debt
column7: No, Ahmad has been discharged
column8: Yes, at any time Zaid delays
column10: Per 7/1, a valid Hawalah discharges the transferor from the debt and any claims; the transferee has no recourse against him except in stated cases.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, by analogy with which contract is a Hawalah with deferred payment permitted?
column5: A loan contract with a deferred maturity date
column6: A Salam contract with a deferred delivery of the goods
column7: A sale contract with a deferred price payable by instalments
column8: A guarantee contract concluded on a deferred basis
column10: Per the Basis, deferred Hawalah is analogous to a deferred guarantee: a right due by Hawalah is like one due by guarantee, which may be deferred.

column4: Ahmad paid Bank A for a travellers' cheque and later endorses it in favour of his creditor Bakr. How is this endorsement classified?
column5: A sale of the cheque to Bakr at a discount
column6: An unrestricted transfer of debt owed by Ahmad
column7: A restricted transfer of debt against Bank A
column8: An agency for collection by Bakr from Bank A
column10: Per 12/3, the holder is Bank A's creditor; endorsing the cheque to his creditor is a restricted transfer of debt for the value the Institution received.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, which Hadith shows that transfer of debt is legal?
column5: If one of you is transferred to a solvent person, he must accept
column6: Muslims are bound by the conditions they made
column7: Allah curses the one who gives Riba and the one who takes it
column8: The guarantor is liable for what he guarantees
column10: Per the Basis, the Prophet ordered that one transferred to a solvent person must accept the transfer, which shows Hawalah is legal; Ijma' also supports it.

column4: Bakr claims the transferred debt from Zaid, who refuses, saying he only ever owed money to Ahmad. What is Zaid's position?
column5: He may refuse and pay Ahmad instead
column6: He may refuse until the original due date
column7: He may pay only if Ahmad confirms
column8: He is obliged to pay Bakr
column10: Per 9/1, the transferee may claim the debt from the payer per the Hawalah terms; the payer is obliged to pay and has no right to refuse.

column4: Bakr, the transferee, dies before collecting the transferred debt from Zaid. What happens to the Hawalah?
column5: It is annulled, and Zaid is discharged
column6: It continues, and Bakr's heirs replace him
column7: It continues only if Ahmad consents
column8: It is annulled, and Ahmad becomes liable again
column10: Per 10/3, Hawalah is not annulled by the transferee's death; his heirs replace him (for an Institution, the liquidator takes its place).

column4: Bank A signs a Murabahah sale with a customer today and signs its own purchase contract with the supplier tomorrow. What is the status of the Murabahah?
column5: Valid, provided the mark-up is disclosed
column6: Valid, but binding only after the supplier delivers
column7: Not valid: the Bank must first buy and possess the item
column8: Valid, since the customer gave a binding promise
column10: Per 3/1/1, the Institution may not conclude a Murabahah before it concludes the purchase from the supplier and acquires actual or constructive possession.

column4: Ahmad tells Bank A informally that he would like to acquire a car through the Bank. Nothing is signed. What is the status of this expressed wish?
column5: It becomes a binding promise once the Bank buys the car
column6: It is a concluded Murabahah awaiting delivery
column7: It is a binding promise to purchase the car
column8: It is not a promise unless expressed in due form
column10: Per 2/1/3, the customer's wish to acquire the item does not constitute a promise or commitment except when it has been expressed in due form.

column4: Company X sells machinery to Bank A, and the Bank immediately sells the same machinery back to Company X by Murabahah on deferred payment. What is the status of the transaction?
column5: Void, as it is tantamount to 'Inah
column6: Valid but the Bank's profit must go to charity
column7: Valid if the Bank takes actual possession first
column8: Valid if the mark-up is disclosed to Company X
column10: Per 2/2/3, the seller must be a third party other than the customer; a customer selling to the Institution and buying back via Murabahah is void as 'Inah.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis disallow a promise that is binding on both the Institution and the customer?
column5: It turns the Murabahah into 'Inah between the parties
column6: It amounts to a contract before the item is acquired
column7: It leaves the mark-up unknown to both the Bank and customer
column8: It is a form of commitment fee charged by the Bank
column10: The basis: a bilateral binding promise amounts to a contract prior to acquisition of the item to be sold.

column4: Bank A approves a Murabahah credit facility limit for Company X and charges a fee for providing the facility. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible to charge a fee for the facility
column6: Permissible if added to the Murabahah cost
column7: Permissible if it is a fixed lump sum amount
column8: Permissible if Company X uses the facility
column10: Per 2/4/2, it is not permissible for the Institution to receive a fee for providing a credit facility.

column4: Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite for allowing a rebate when a Murabahah debtor pays early?
column5: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab on 'Arboun in sale contracts
column6: The Prophet asking Ubay Ibn Ka'b to write off part of a debt
column7: The Prophet's purchase of a she-camel from Abu Bakr
column8: The Hadith of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on options
column10: The basis: early payment discount is a settlement; in Ubay Ibn Ka'b's case the Prophet suggested: 'write off a portion of your debt.'

column4: Customer C fulfils his promise and the Murabahah contract is executed. What should Bank A do with the Hamish Jiddiyyah C paid?
column5: Hold it as security until the last instalment is paid
column6: Keep it as a fee for arranging the deal for the customer
column7: Keep it as earnest money for the Bank once the deal is done
column8: Refund it, or deduct it from the price if so agreed
column10: Per 2/5/5, once the promise is fulfilled the Institution must refund Hamish Jiddiyyah, or may agree with the customer to deduct it from the Murabahah price.

column4: In which situation may Bank A take Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit) from a customer?
column5: Only when the customer suggests the supplier
column6: Only when the price is payable on spot terms
column7: When the customer has given a binding promise
column8: Only after the Murabahah sale is concluded
column10: Per 2/5/3, the Institution may take Hamish Jiddiyyah in the case of a binding promise by the customer, to secure compensation for any breach.

column4: Customer C suggested Supplier S to Bank A, and the Bank asks C to guarantee S's good performance. In what capacity does C give this guarantee?
column5: In his personal capacity
column6: In his capacity as the Bank's agent
column7: In his capacity as co-buyer with the Bank
column8: In his capacity as purchase orderer
column10: Per 2/5/1, the customer guarantees the supplier's performance in his personal capacity, not as purchase orderer or as the Institution's agent.

column4: Bank A asks the purchase orderer to bear the transport risk of goods it is buying. Why is this disallowed, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: It would be a commitment fee in disguise
column6: Transport risk is always borne by the supplier alone
column7: The owner bears the risk, as profit goes with risk
column8: The customer is the agent of the supplier in all cases
column10: The basis: the goods' safety is the owner's responsibility; the customer is not the owner, and the right to profit is associated with bearing risk.

column4: A Murabahah contract says the car stays the Bank's property until full payment. Why is such a stipulation disallowed, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: It makes the price unknown, as it varies with the payment period
column6: It amounts to a sale of debt for debt between the parties
column7: It is a form of commitment fee charged by the Bank
column8: It contradicts the immediate transfer of ownership in a sale
column10: The basis: delaying transfer of ownership is against the effect of a sale, which is immediate transfer; delaying registration does not affect ownership.

column4: Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of taking 'Arboun (Earnest Money)?
column5: The Prophet's purchase from Abu Bakr
column6: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab
column7: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh
column8: The case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b
column10: The basis cites the practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab in the presence of Companions, permitted by Imam Ahmad, and a Fiqh Academy resolution.

column4: Bank A requires post-dated cheques from a customer before executing a Murabahah, in a country where cheques can be presented before their due date. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible in such a country
column6: Permissible if the cheques are post-dated
column7: Permissible with a written undertaking
column8: Permissible if the customer agrees
column10: Per 5/3, requiring cheques as security is not permissible in countries where they could be presented for payment before their due date.

column4: Customer C pays his Murabahah debt early, and Bank A wishes to give up part of the price. The contract was silent on this. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if stipulated in the contract
column6: Not permissible; the full price is owed
column7: Permissible, as it was not part of the contract
column8: Not permissible, as it resembles Riba
column10: Per 5/9, the Institution may give up part of the selling price on early payment provided this was not part of the contractual agreement.

column4: Customer C, acting as Bank A's agent, asks that the price be paid into his account. Why does the standard require the Bank to pay the supplier directly, per the basis?
column5: To pass the risk of the goods over to the supplier
column6: To avoid the deal becoming interest-based financing
column7: To let the Bank earn a fee for transferring the payment
column8: To make C liable for the risk of the goods
column10: The basis: requiring the Institution to pay the supplier directly avoids the risk of the contract degenerating into mere interest-based financing.

column4: Bank A cannot buy an item directly from the supplier and needs an agent. Whom should it preferably appoint?
column5: The purchase orderer, if he gave a binding promise
column6: Any party, as the standard sets no preference
column7: The purchase orderer, as he knows the item best
column8: A party other than the purchase orderer
column10: Per 3/1/3, the Institution may appoint an agent other than the purchase orderer; the customer should not be agent except in case of dire need.

column4: Bank A and a customer have not agreed who will bear the expenses of preparing their Murabahah contract documents. Who bears them?
column5: Each party in proportion to its benefit
column6: The Bank and the customer, evenly
column7: The Bank alone, as the seller
column8: The customer alone, as the purchase orderer
column10: Per 2/4/3, document preparation expenses are borne evenly by the two parties unless they agree that one party bears them wholly.

column4: Bank A wants to take 'Arboun from Customer C at the time C signs his promise to purchase. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as it shows how serious C is about his promise
column6: Permitted only for a binding promise
column7: Not permitted; 'Arboun is taken on concluding the sale
column8: Permitted if refunded in full when the sale is done
column10: Per 2/5/6, 'Arboun may be taken upon conclusion of the Murabahah sale, but not during the stage at which the customer has given his promise to purchase.

column4: Bank A buys goods directly from Supplier S without any agent. The supplier prepares the sale documents in the purchase orderer's name. Is this proper?
column5: No, the documents should be in the Bank's name
column6: Yes, as the customer will own the goods later
column7: Yes, if the customer signed a promise
column8: Yes, either name is equally acceptable
column10: Per 3/1/6, all documents for the sale must be in the Institution's name, not the customer's, unless the customer acts as the Institution's agent.

column4: Murabahah is held analogous to a sale at the purchase price without profit, based on the Prophet's purchase of a she-camel from Abu Bakr. What is that sale called?
column5: 'Inah
column6: Bay' al-Bara'ah
column7: 'Arboun
column8: Tawliyyah
column10: The basis states Murabahah is analogous to Tawliyyah (sale at purchasing price without profit), as the Prophet took Abu Bakr's she-camel at its acquisition price.

column4: After concluding an 'Arboun-based Murabahah, the customer revokes the contract. What is preferable for Bank A to do with the 'Arboun?
column5: Refund the remainder after deducting actual damage
column6: Refund the 'Arboun in full without deduction
column7: Keep the 'Arboun and also claim the lost mark-up
column8: Keep the full 'Arboun as its right
column10: Per 2/5/6, it is preferable that the Institution deducts actual damage (cost minus third-party price) and refunds the rest of the 'Arboun.

column4: A Murabahah customer asks Bank A for six more months to pay an instalment. The Bank agrees but requires an extra payment for the additional time. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the customer is solvent
column6: Permitted if agreed by mutual consent
column7: Not permitted to demand extra payment for time
column8: Permitted if the extension exceeds 3 months
column10: Per 4/8, once the price becomes a debt, no extra payment may be demanded for extra time or for delay in payment, with or without reason.

column4: Two partners in a Musharakah with Bank A want one to promise to buy the other's share. Which arrangement is permissible?
column5: A promise at the capital originally contributed by the partner
column6: A promise at cost plus a pre-agreed Murabahah mark-up
column7: A promise by Murabahah, payable only on deferred terms
column8: A promise at market price, with a new contract at the sale
column10: Per 2/2/5, a partner may promise to buy the other's share at market price or a price agreed at the time of sale, provided a new contract is drawn up.

column4: A Murabahah debtor is insolvent. Bank A agrees to reschedule the debt to a later date in return for an additional amount. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, since the debtor is insolvent and needs time
column6: Not permissible for a solvent or insolvent debtor
column7: Permissible if the extra amount is less than the mark-up
column8: Permissible if the extra goes to charity
column10: Per 5/7, it is not permissible to extend the payment date in exchange for an additional payment on rescheduling, whether the debtor is solvent or insolvent.

column4: Bank A's Murabahah contract mentions only the total selling price, without stating the cost or the profit. Is this sufficient?
column5: Yes, a known total price is enough
column6: No, the Bank's staff costs must also be shown
column7: Yes, if the customer accepts the total
column8: No, the profit mark-up must be known
column10: Per 4/7, the Institution's profit mark-up must be known; the mere mention of the total selling price is not sufficient.

column4: Bank A wants to refinance a Murabahah by renewing it on the same commodity with the same customer. Under which prohibited heading does this fall, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Sale before acquisition
column6: Sale of debt
column7: Bay' al-Bara'ah
column8: Gharar in the subject matter
column10: The basis: tradable Murabahah securities and refinancing a Murabahah fall under the sale of debt, which Shari'ah prohibits.

column4: Bank A stipulates in a Murabahah that it is free from responsibility for defects (Bay' al-Bara'ah). Which risk can it NOT exclude by this condition?
column5: All hidden defects of the asset unknown to the Bank
column6: Defects the supplier also knew about
column7: Destruction before the customer's possession
column8: Some specified defects of the asset named in the contract
column10: Per 4/9, the Institution may disclaim all or some defects, but not destruction before the customer's possession or diminution of the quantity sold.

column4: Bank A and a customer amend the mark-up and duration of a promise before the Murabahah is concluded. Why is this not prohibited debt rescheduling, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: A promise is not a contract, so no debt exists yet
column6: Because the customer had already paid Hamish Jiddiyyah
column7: Because the Bank already owned the item being sold
column8: Because the mark-up was only reduced and never raised
column10: The basis: amending the promise is allowed because a promise is not a contract, so changing profit or duration is not rescheduling of debt.

column4: After the Murabahah contract is drawn up, the supplier grants Bank A a discount on the same item. What happens to this discount?
column5: It is paid to charity under Bank supervision
column6: The Bank keeps it, as the contract is concluded
column7: The customer's price is reduced in proportion
column8: It is shared equally by Bank and customer
column10: Per 4/5, even after the contract, the customer should benefit from such a discount by a proportional reduction of the total Murabahah price.

column4: A customer breaches his binding promise. Bank A's cost was 100,000; it resells the item to a third party for 92,000. Its expected mark-up was 10,000. How much may it deduct from Hamish Jiddiyyah?
column6: The entire Hamish Jiddiyyah
column10: Per 2/5/4, the Institution may deduct only actual damage: cost minus the third-party price (100,000 - 92,000). Lost mark-up is not included.

column4: A jeweller asks Bank A to sell him 1 kg of gold by Murabahah with the price payable in 6 months. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the profit is a lump sum amount
column6: Permitted if the gold is in the Bank's possession
column7: Permitted for gold but not for currencies
column8: Not permitted for gold, silver or currencies
column10: Per 2/2/6, Murabahah on deferred payment terms is not permitted where the asset is gold, silver or currencies.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis forbid one Musharakah partner from promising to buy the other partner's share by Murabahah?
column5: Because Murabahah requires a third party as the seller
column6: It makes the buyer guarantee the other's share, which is Riba
column7: Because shares in a Musharakah can never be sold to a partner
column8: Because a partner may not buy anything from a partner
column10: The basis: such a promise leads to the buying partner guaranteeing the share of the other partner, which is Riba.

column4: Bank A and a customer want to exchange a bilateral promise before a Murabahah. When is such a bilateral promise permissible?
column5: Only if the customer pays Hamish Jiddiyyah with it
column6: Only if it is signed after the Bank buys the item
column7: Only if it is binding on both parties without option
column8: Only if one or both parties have an option to cancel it
column10: Per 2/3/3, a bilateral promise is permissible only if there is an option to cancel exercisable by both promisors or by either one of them.

column4: Out of dire need, Customer C is appointed as Bank A's agent to buy goods for a Murabahah. How should the price be paid to the supplier whenever possible?
column5: Into C's account, as the Bank's agent
column6: Bank A pays the supplier directly
column7: By C, who is later reimbursed by the Bank
column8: Half by Bank A and half by Customer C
column10: Per 3/1/4(a), the Institution itself must pay the supplier and not pay the price into the customer-agent's account, whenever possible.

column4: What evidence underlies the ban on deferred Murabahah in gold, silver and currencies?
column5: The Hadith requiring such exchange 'hand to hand'
column6: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab among the Companions
column7: The Hadith 'Do not sell what you own not' about absent goods
column8: The Hadith of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on the option of cancelling
column10: The basis cites the Prophet's saying that exchange of gold with silver be 'hand to hand', without delay; currencies take the ruling of gold and silver.

column4: Bank A's purchase contract with the supplier of an item later turns out to be void. What is the effect on its Murabahah with the customer?
column5: It is voidable only at the customer's option
column6: It remains valid, but the mark-up must be reduced
column7: It is also void, as the Bank lacked complete title
column8: It remains valid, as the customer acted in good faith
column10: Per 3/1/1, the Murabahah is void if the contract with the supplier is void, because the Institution would fail to acquire complete title to the item.

column4: Bank A paid insurance on goods during its ownership, before selling them by Murabahah. How may it treat this expense?
column5: Include it in the Murabahah cost price
column6: Charge it to the customer as a separate fee
column7: Bear it only, with no addition to cost
column8: Deduct it from the Hamish Jiddiyyah
column10: Per 3/2/6, the Institution may include insurance expenses in the Murabahah cost price; insurance must be on a Takaful basis whenever possible.

column4: Bank A plans to issue negotiable Sukuk whose underlying assets consist only of its Murabahah receivables. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the Murabahah sales were concluded validly
column6: Permissible if the Sukuk holders consent to the risk
column7: Permissible if the receivables are secured by mortgage
column8: Impermissible, as the assets are receivables only
column10: Per 2/2/7, it is impermissible to issue negotiable Sukuk where the underlying asset consists of Murabahah receivables or other receivables only.

column4: On which juristic ground does the Shari'ah basis allow a defaulting debtor's undertaking to donate a sum to charity?
column5: Compensation for the Bank's opportunity loss
column6: The commitment to donate in the Maliki school
column7: The Hanafi rule on penalty clauses
column8: A late payment fee due to the creditor
column10: The basis: it is an instance of the commitment to make a donation, well established in the Maliki school (Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar).

column4: After a customer's breach of promise, Bank A claims its lost mark-up. Why does the Shari'ah basis call this claim irrational?
column5: The mark-up belongs to the supplier
column6: Mark-up may only be taken as 'Arboun
column7: No mark-up exists without an actual Murabahah
column8: Mark-up is always refunded to the customer
column10: The basis: a claim for lost mark-up is irrational since there is no mark-up unless there is actually a Murabahah, and here there is none.

column4: Bank A wants to apply the Murabahah standard to a deferred payment sale that is concluded on a basis other than Murabahah. Does the standard govern that sale?
column5: No, such deferred payment sales are outside its scope
column6: Only if the Institution takes Hamish Jiddiyyah in the sale
column7: Yes, it covers every deferred payment sale of the Institution
column8: Yes, provided the sale is preceded by a promise to purchase
column10: Per clause 1, the standard does not cover deferred payment sales on a basis other than Murabahah, nor other trust and bargaining sales.

column4: Customer C asks Bank A to prepare a feasibility study for C's own benefit before a Murabahah and agrees to pay for it. What is the ruling?
column5: No fee; the study is part of the Murabahah cost
column6: The fee is allowed only if the Murabahah is executed
column7: The Bank may charge the fee, and C may get a copy
column8: The fee is allowed, but the study stays with the Bank
column10: Per 2/4/5, the Institution may receive a fee for a feasibility study requested by and for the benefit of the customer who agrees to pay; he may obtain a copy.

column4: A Murabahah customer undertakes to donate a percentage of the debt if he pays instalments late. How must Bank A handle these amounts?
column5: Return them to the customer later
column6: Spend them on charitable causes, not for itself
column7: Add them to its own income as fees for late payment
column8: Keep them to offset its funding costs for the period
column10: Per 5/6, the undertaking to donate is allowed, and the Shari'ah Supervisory Board must know the amounts go to charity, not to the Institution itself.

column4: Bank A sold an asset to a customer by Murabahah without stipulating any defect exclusion. A hidden defect that existed before the sale appears after the contract. Who is responsible?
column5: The supplier alone, not the Bank
column6: Nobody, since the contract is concluded
column7: The customer, who accepted the asset
column8: Bank A, as the seller
column10: Per 4/10, the Institution is responsible for pre-existing hidden defects that appear after the contract, unless it stipulated otherwise.

column4: Bank A buys goods on a 'sale or return' basis with a 10-day option. It presents them to the customer, who declines to buy. May the Bank still return them within the 10 days?
column5: No, presenting the goods to the customer ends the option
column6: Yes, but only with a new consent from the supplier
column7: Yes, mere presentation to the customer does not end the option
column8: No, the option ended when the customer signed his promise
column10: Per 2/3/5, the option between the Institution and the supplier does not expire by mere presentation of the item to the customer, but by the actual sale to him.

column4: Bank A's promise form, signed by the customer, makes the promise binding on both the Bank and the customer with no option to cancel. Is this acceptable?
column5: Yes, if Hamish Jiddiyyah is taken from the customer
column6: Yes, if the Shari'ah Supervisory Board approves the form
column7: Yes, as it protects both parties equally
column8: No, a promise binding on both parties is not permissible
column10: Per 2/3/1, the promise document may not include a bilateral promise binding on both the Institution and the customer.

column4: Bank A's Murabahah contract says ownership of the car stays with the Bank until the customer pays the price in full. Which alternative is permissible?
column5: Retaining title until the last instalment
column6: Postponing registration in the customer's name
column7: Keeping ownership but passing all risk
column8: Transferring ownership only on spot payment
column10: Per 5/4, delaying transfer of ownership until full payment may not be stipulated, but registration in the customer's name may be postponed as a guarantee.

column4: After a customer has given his promise, but before the Murabahah is executed, Bank A wants to increase the mark-up. Can it do so?
column5: Only with the customer's consent
column6: Yes, unilaterally, as only the customer is bound
column7: No, the terms of a promise can never be revised
column8: Yes, by giving the customer written notice
column10: Per 2/3/4, the terms of the promise (deferment, mark-up, etc.) may be revised before execution, but only by mutual consent of both parties.

column4: Customer C buys goods as Bank A's agent, and the Bank then sells them to C by Murabahah. How are the Bank's liability and C's liability as agent kept separate?
column5: By having the supplier insure the goods
column6: By placing the risk on C from his appointment
column7: By signing the agency and the sale in one document
column8: By a time interval between the agency and the Murabahah
column10: Per 3/1/5, the two risk liabilities are separated by an interval of time between performance of the agency and execution of the Murabahah.

column4: Bank A buys a building. The seller vacates it, but Bank A is not able to have disposal of it. Has Bank A taken possession?
