column5: Yes, vacating real property always conveys possession
column6: No, vacating without disposal is not possession
column7: Yes, once the sale contract is signed
column8: Yes, if the customer has already promised to buy
column10: Per 3/2/3, real property is possessed by vacating it and placing it at the acquirer's disposal; if he cannot dispose of it, vacating is not possession.

column4: A supplier gives Customer C a price list that is not addressed to any named customer. C plans to use it for a Murabahah with Bank A. How is this price list treated?
column5: As a sale already concluded with Customer C on those prices
column6: As an offer of sale made to Bank A as the buyer
column7: As an invitation to negotiate, not an offer of sale
column8: As a binding offer of sale made to Customer C by the supplier
column10: Per 2/1/4, a general offer with no named addressee is considered an invitation to negotiate and not an offer of sale.

column4: Bank A authorises Agent B to buy an item in B's own name without disclosing the agency to the supplier. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, though disclosure is preferable
column6: Permissible, and non-disclosure is preferable
column7: Not permissible; the agency must be disclosed
column8: Permissible only if B is the purchase orderer
column10: Per 3/1/7, the agent may act as principal without disclosing the agency, on behalf of the Institution; however, disclosure of the agent's role is preferable.

column4: Bank A asks the purchase orderer to guarantee the goods against damage and destruction while they are shipped and stored for the Bank. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if he suggested the supplier
column6: Permitted if it is offset by a lower mark-up
column7: Not permitted to impose this guarantee on him
column8: Permitted, since he will buy the goods anyway
column10: Per 2/5/2, it is not permitted to impose on the purchase orderer a guarantee for hazards such as damage and destruction during shipment or storage.

column4: Under the customer's authority, Bank A sells a Murabahah asset after the customer fails to pay on the due date. The sale yields more than the debt. What must the Bank do?
column5: Recover its due and return the balance
column6: Keep the surplus as a late payment fee
column7: Keep all proceeds as compensation
column8: Give the surplus to charitable causes
column10: Per 5/4, if the Institution sells the asset on default, it must confine itself to the amount due to it and return the balance to the customer.

column4: Bank A appoints the customer as its agent to arrange insurance cover for goods while the Bank is acquiring ownership. Who must bear the insurance cost?
column5: The customer, as agent
column6: Bank A and the customer equally
column7: The supplier of the goods
column8: Bank A
column10: Per 3/2/7, agency in obtaining insurance at the acquisition stage is permitted, but the Institution must bear the cost of insurance.

column4: The owner selling a house to Bank A for a Murabahah is the customer's brother. What must the Bank do before entering into the Murabahah?
column5: Nothing, since family ties have no effect on Murabahah
column6: Verify it is not a fictitious sale or stratagem for 'Inah
column7: Refuse the deal, since sales between close relatives are barred
column8: Require the brother to guarantee the customer's debt to the Bank
column10: Per 2/2/4, where the supplier has a blood or marital relationship with the customer, the Institution shall verify the sale is not fictitious or a stratagem for 'Inah.

column4: A Murabahah contract stipulates that all instalments fall due early if the customer delays payment without valid reason. How may Bank A apply this condition?
column5: Immediately on the first day of any delay in payment
column6: Only if a court approves the acceleration in advance
column7: After notice and lapse of the time specified in it
column8: It may not apply it at all, as the condition is invalid
column10: Per 5/1, acceleration may be stipulated for refusal or delay without valid reason, after lapse of the time in a notice sent within a reasonable period.

column4: Bank A already owns a stock of goods that it can readily sell to other buyers. Must it obtain a promise to purchase before selling them by Murabahah?
column5: No, but it must then take 'Arboun from the buyer
column6: No, the promise is not integral to Murabahah
column7: Yes, a Murabahah is invalid without a promise
column8: Yes, whenever the price is paid on deferred terms
column10: Per 2/3/2, the promise is not integral to Murabahah; it only assures completion, so if the Institution has other ways to sell, it may not need it.

column4: At the time of payment, a customer wants to pay his Murabahah instalment in a currency other than the Murabahah currency. Bank A agrees. What condition applies?
column5: Full payment of the agreed amount, leaving nothing due
column6: Part of the amount may remain due as a debt for later payment
column7: The exchange must be stipulated in the original contract
column8: The Bank may add a margin for the exchange
column10: Per 5/10, payment in another currency is allowed with the Institution's agreement at payment if paid in full with nothing remaining; it may not be stipulated.

column4: Bank A buys goods on the international market and its agent receives the bill of lading while the goods are at sea. What is the Bank's status?
column5: It has no possession until the goods arrive
column6: The customer has possession of the goods
column7: It has actual possession of the goods
column8: It has constructive possession of the goods
column10: Per 3/2/4, the receipt of a bill of lading by the Institution or its agent when buying on the international market is considered constructive possession.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis of the standard, what is a Murabahah concluded with a prior promise to buy from a person seeking goods through the Institution called?
column5: Banking Murabahah, or Murabahah to the purchase orderer
column6: Bay' al-Bara'ah, a sale free from liability for defects
column7: Ordinary Murabahah, a sale at cost plus a disclosed profit
column8: Tawliyyah, a sale at cost price without any profit
column10: The basis defines Murabahah without a prior promise as ordinary Murabahah, and with a prior promise as banking Murabahah (to the purchase orderer).

column4: Bank A concludes a Murabahah where the profit will be set by the LIBOR rate prevailing on each future instalment date. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the customer agrees to it in writing
column6: Not permitted, as profit is left to future variation
column7: Permitted, as LIBOR is a known and published public rate
column8: Permitted, if a ceiling rate is stated in the contract
column10: Per 4/6, price and profit must be fixed and known at signing; they may not depend on future variations such as a future LIBOR rate.

column4: At contracting, Bank A did not disclose transportation and storage expenses it incurred on the item. May it include them in the Murabahah cost?
column5: No, unless they are paid to the Bank's staff
column6: No, undisclosed expenses can never be included
column7: Yes, but only if the customer later agrees
column8: Yes, as they are customarily normal expenses
column10: Per 4/3, undisclosed expenses cannot be included unless customarily normal, such as transport, storage, letter of credit fees and insurance premiums.

column4: Customer C accepted a supplier's offer addressed to him personally but has not paid yet. He then asks Bank A to finance the same goods through Murabahah. What is the Bank's position?
column5: It may proceed because C has not yet paid the price
column6: It may proceed if C signs a binding promise to purchase
column7: It may not do Murabahah, as the sale is concluded with C
column8: It may proceed if the supplier assigns C's contract to it
column10: Per 2/2/1, once the customer accepts the supplier's offer, the sale is concluded with him and the Institution may not carry out Murabahah on the same item.

column4: The supplier's owner is the customer's wife. Why does the Shari'ah basis allow Murabahah in such a case, absent 'Inah?
column5: Both parties have independent legal liability
column6: Family sales are exempt from 'Inah rules
column7: The wife's consent cures any defect
column8: The Bank bears no risk in such deals
column10: The basis: a relative or spouse may be the supplier because both have independent legal liability, unless they are involved in an 'Inah transaction.

column4: Supplier S is 60% owned by Customer C. C asks Bank A to buy goods from S and sell them to him by Murabahah. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since S is a separate company
column6: Not permitted, since S is majority owned by C
column7: Permitted, as C's share in S is below 75%
column8: Permitted if the Bank takes Hamish Jiddiyyah
column10: Per 2/2/3, the supplying party may not be wholly or majority (more than 50%) owned by the customer; such a deal is tantamount to 'Inah.

column4: Customer C accepted a supplier's offer but argues no sale exists because he has not paid yet, so Bank A can still do Murabahah. Why is he wrong, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Payment is always made before acceptance can take place
column6: The supplier's offer had no addressee, so acceptance failed
column7: Payment results from the contract; it is not a condition
column8: Acceptance is binding only after delivery of the goods
column10: The basis: the sale is concluded once C accepts; payment of the price is a consequence of a contract, not a condition of its validity.

column4: Bank A takes a mortgage from a Murabahah customer. May it stipulate that it can sell the mortgaged asset to recover its debt without going to court?
column5: No, only a court may order the sale of a mortgaged asset
column6: No, unless the customer is declared insolvent by a court
column7: Yes, but it may keep the full proceeds of the sale
column8: Yes, via the customer's assignment to the Bank
column10: Per 5/5, the Institution may stipulate an assignment from the customer enabling it to sell the mortgaged asset without recourse to the judiciary.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis accept constructive possession as fulfilling the possession requirement?
column5: Shari'ah sets no form for possession; custom decides
column6: Because physical delivery is always impractical for a bank
column7: Because the customer bears the risk anyway
column8: Because possession is not needed in a Murabahah sale
column10: The basis: Shari'ah did not state a particular form of possession; it is left to custom, and any procedure giving control counts as possession.

column4: A customer asks Bank A to buy equipment from Supplier S. The Bank finds another supplier that is more suitable for it, but the customer refuses that offer. What may the Bank do?
column5: Buy from the other supplier and oblige the customer to purchase
column6: Proceed with Supplier S only after charging a commitment fee
column7: Nothing; it is bound to buy from the supplier the customer named
column8: Decline to carry out the transaction
column10: Per 2/1/2, the customer may name a source of supply, but the Institution may decline if the customer refuses more suitable offers from other suppliers.

column4: After a Murabahah is executed, the customer refuses to take delivery at the prescribed time. The contract has a condition for this case. What may Bank A do?
column5: Raise the price to cover storage costs
column6: Revoke, or sell to a third party for his account
column7: Charge him a daily fee for each day until delivery is taken
column8: Keep the asset and also the price already paid by him
column10: Per 4/11, the Institution may stipulate that on such refusal it may revoke the contract or sell the asset to a third party on the customer's behalf and account.

column4: Bank A arranges a syndicated financing for a large Murabahah and claims an arrangement fee. Who pays this fee?
column5: Nobody, as such a fee is not allowed
column6: The supplier of the financed goods
column7: The participants in the syndicate
column8: The customer, as a facility fee
column10: Per 2/4/4, in syndicated Murabahah the arranger Institution is entitled to an arrangement fee paid by the participants in the syndicate.

column4: Bank A takes possession of goods ordered by Customer C and treats the Murabahah as automatically concluded with C at that moment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since C had given a binding promise to buy
column6: Not permitted; mere possession does not conclude it
column7: Permitted, if C was informed of the possession in advance
column8: Permitted, if C paid Hamish Jiddiyyah
column10: Per 4/1, the Institution may not consider the Murabahah automatically concluded by its mere taking possession of the asset.

column4: Customer C is struggling to pay a Murabahah debt. Bank A proposes a new Murabahah with C on the same commodity to refinance the old one. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if C is proven to be insolvent
column6: Permitted after the Bank re-registers the commodity
column7: Permitted if the new mark-up is lower than the old one
column8: Not permitted, as it renews Murabahah on the same item
column10: Per 2/2/8, it is not permitted to renew a Murabahah on the same commodity with the same customer, i.e. to refinance the transaction.

column4: Bank A argues it may charge a commitment fee because it reserved funds for the customer. Why is such a fee impermissible, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: It is not proportional to the work and effort done by the Bank
column6: It is part of the cost of the item sold to the customer
column7: It is paid for a right to contract, which is not exchangeable
column8: It is paid to a third party rather than to the Bank itself
column10: The basis: a commitment fee is in exchange for the right to contract, a mere intention and wish that is not a subject of exchange.

column4: Bank A adds to the cost of a Murabahah item the salaries it paid its own staff for processing the deal. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted; only direct third-party costs count
column6: Permitted, as they are customary expenses of the business
column7: Permitted up to a reasonable amount
column8: Permitted if the salaries are disclosed to the customer
column10: Per 4/4, only direct expenses paid to a third party may be included in base cost; payments to the Institution's own staff may not be added.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis prefer that the Institution appoint an agent other than the purchase orderer to acquire the item?
column5: Because agency fees would be too high
column6: Because the supplier prefers other agents
column7: Because the customer cannot hold title
column8: To avoid a fictitious transaction on paper
column10: The basis: appointing someone other than the purchase orderer avoids a fictitious transaction, shows the Institution as real buyer and demarcates liabilities.

column4: Bank A bought an asset from the supplier on a deferred price and now intends to sell it to a customer by Murabahah. What must it do?
column5: Disclose that it bought the asset on deferred terms
column6: Pay the supplier in full before it sells the asset on
column7: Nothing, the payment terms are its own affair
column8: Sell it only on spot terms to the customer, not deferred
column10: Per 4/3, when the Institution purchased an asset for a deferred price for sale by Murabahah, it must disclose this to the customer.

column4: Bank A has paid a supplier but has not yet taken possession of the goods at the delivery location. Under the standard, when does the risk of the goods transfer to the Bank?
column5: Upon the signing of the Murabahah contract
column6: Upon the Bank's payment of the price
column7: Upon the Bank's taking possession of the goods
column8: Upon the customer's promise to purchase
column10: Per 3/2/5, responsibility for the risk attached to the item is transferred to the Institution upon its taking possession of the item.

column4: Goods insured by Bank A are destroyed before their sale to the customer. The insurance payout exceeds their purchase price. Who is entitled to the payout?
column5: The customer, as the intended buyer
column6: Bank A exclusively
column7: Bank A up to cost; the rest to the customer
column8: Bank A and the customer equally
column10: Per 3/2/6, insurance before sale lies with the Institution as owner; any recovery belongs to it exclusively, even if it exceeds the purchase price.

column4: Under the Murabahah standard, what is the specific purpose of requiring the Institution to take possession of the item before selling it to the customer?
column5: So that the Institution assumes the risk of the item
column6: So that the Institution may add storage costs
column7: So that the Institution can inspect it for the customer
column8: So that the item can be registered for the customer
column10: Per 3/2/2, possession ensures the Institution assumes the item's risk, moving it from the supplier's responsibility to the Institution's.

column4: During the promise stage Bank A refers to a known benchmark index, then fixes its profit at signing as 6% of cost. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted; the profit must be a lump sum
column6: Permitted; the index was only a comfort indicator
column7: Not permitted; benchmarks may never be mentioned
column8: Permitted only if profit floats with the index
column10: Per 4/6, a known indicator may be referred to in the promise stage as a comfort indicator, if profit at conclusion is a set percentage of cost.

column4: Bank A takes the Murabahah asset itself as a mortgage to secure the customer's debt, without taking possession of it. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, but only if a third party guarantees too
column6: No, a mortgage requires taking possession
column7: Yes, as a fiduciary mortgage or registered charge
column8: No, the sold asset cannot secure its own price
column10: Per 5/2, the Institution may take the Murabahah subject matter as fiduciary mortgage (registered charge), with or without possession.

column4: Bank A charges Customer C a fee in return for the Bank's commitment to execute a Murabahah with him later. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if it reflects the Bank's actual costs
column6: Permissible if disclosed in the promise document
column7: Permissible if deducted later from the price
column8: Not permissible; a commitment fee is prohibited
column10: Per 2/4/1, it is not permissible for the Institution to receive a commitment fee from the customer.

column4: Customer C signed a supply contract with Supplier S. C asks Bank A to take over that contract by assignment and then sell him the goods by Murabahah. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the Bank pays Supplier S directly
column6: Not permissible to assign C's contract to the Bank
column7: Permissible as long as C has not paid Supplier S
column8: Permissible if Supplier S consents to the assignment
column10: Per 2/2/2, any prior contractual relationship between customer and supplier must be genuinely excluded; assigning their contract to the Institution is not permissible.

column4: A customer defaults on Murabahah instalments that are due, and no donation undertaking exists in the contract. What may Bank A claim?
column5: Only the unpaid amount of the selling price
column6: The whole price including future instalments
column7: The unpaid price plus a delay charge
column8: The unpaid price plus its funding cost
column10: Per 5/8, on default the amount due is just the unpaid selling price; the Institution may not impose any additional payment for its own benefit.

column4: A lessor dies mid-lease and his heirs want to end the Ijarah. Why may they not, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: The lessee must consent to any change
column6: Only the lessor himself had that right, and it ended
column7: They suffer no damage, as they receive the rentals
column8: The lease converts into a gift to the heirs on death
column10: The basis: the lessor's heirs may not terminate because there is no potential damage to them, as they receive the rentals for the rest of the term.

column4: Bank A sells a leased building to Investor Z, who knows of the lease and accepts it. The lessee was not asked. What is the outcome?
column5: Valid, but the lease ends once the sale is concluded
column6: Void, as the sale needed the lessee's prior consent
column7: Valid, but the remaining rentals stay with the Bank
column8: Valid; Z replaces the Bank for the remaining rentals
column10: Per 7/1/2, the lessor may sell to a third party without the lessee's consent; a buyer who knows of and accepts the lease takes the place of the lessor.

column4: Bank A signs an Ijarah contract for a machine that a third-party supplier still owns, intending to buy it next week. What is the status of the lease?
column5: It may not be executed until the Bank owns the machine
column6: Valid, as the customer already knows the supplier well
column7: Valid, if the supplier guarantees delivery to the Bank
column8: Valid, if the rent starts only after the purchase date
column10: Per 3/1 and 3/1/2, a lease of a specified asset must be preceded by acquiring the asset or its usufruct; it is not executed until the Institution acquires it.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis require a lapse of time before selling a sale-and-leaseback asset back to the original seller-lessee?
column5: To allow the lessee time to save up the price
column6: It gains a different asset's traits, avoiding 'Inah
column7: To let the Bank earn enough rental income on the asset
column8: To allow registration of the asset in the Bank's name
column10: The basis: the time lapse prevents 'Inah, as physical changes or value changes during it give the asset the economic characteristics of a different asset.

column4: Company X wants to use a building owned by a third party. It asks Bank A to acquire the usufruct of that building and lease it to X. Is this possible?
column5: No, the Bank may lease only assets it owns outright
column6: No, a usufruct cannot be the subject of an Ijarah
column7: Yes, but only if X guarantees the owner's rentals
column8: Yes, the Bank may acquire the usufruct and lease it on
column10: Per 2/1, Ijarah is executed on an asset owned by the lessor or a usufruct owned by the sub-lessor; a customer may ask the Institution to acquire either.

column4: Bank A is asked to lease a vehicle to carry prohibited merchandise. Which principle does the Shari'ah basis apply in barring this?
column5: The rental would be uncertain until the goods arrive
column6: The vehicle would perish by its use in transport
column7: The lessor would be an accomplice in doing evil
column8: The lessee would not own the usufruct of the vehicle
column10: The basis: leasing for impermissible use makes the lessor an accomplice in evil, contrary to 'Help you one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa'.

column4: A farmer leases a tractor from a cooperative and agrees that the rental will be ploughing the cooperative's land for a season. Is this a valid rental?
column5: No, rental may be cash or goods only
column6: No, rental must be paid in cash
column7: Yes, but only if it is valued in cash
column8: Yes, rental may be a benefit (service)
column10: Per 5/2/1, the lease rental may be in cash, in kind (goods) or a benefit (service), and must be specified.

column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, the lessee paid rentals above market rate. The asset is destroyed with no fault of the lessee, so the lease cannot continue. What follows?
column5: The lessee must pay the Bank the full value of the asset
column6: Rental is adjusted and the excess over market refunded
column7: The lessee loses the excess he paid above the market rental
column8: The lessee receives back the full cost of the asset
column10: Per 8/8, the rental is adjusted to prevailing market value and the excess over the market rate is refunded to the lessee.

column4: A lessee who paid 'Arboun withdraws, so the Ijarah is not executed for a reason attributable to him. What is preferable for Bank A to do?
column5: Keep the full 'Arboun and claim lost rent
column6: Refund the full 'Arboun without deduction
column7: Forgo any amount above its actual damage
column8: Keep the 'Arboun and charge a penalty
column10: Per 4/1/4, the lessor may retain the 'Arboun, but it is preferable for the Institution to forgo any amount in excess of the actual damage it suffered.

column4: Part of a leased building collapses, impairing the expected benefit. The lessee is not at fault. What options does the lessee have?
column5: Terminate, or waive it and agree an amended rent
column6: Only claim the cost of repairs from the lessor
column7: Only continue the lease at the full agreed rent until term
column8: Only sub-lease the remaining part of the building
column10: Per 7/1/5, on partial destruction impairing benefit, the lessee may terminate; or he and the lessor may agree to amend the rent if he waives termination.

column4: Why may a lessor sell the leased asset to a third party without the lessee's consent, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Because the lease ends automatically upon any sale of it
column6: Because the buyer pays the lessee compensation for the loss
column7: He acts within his ownership and does not harm the usufruct
column8: Because the lessee has no rights at all in the asset
column10: The basis: the lessor owns the asset and acts within his ownership without affecting the lessee's right, which is the usufruct attached to the asset.

column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek with a gift contingent on paying the remaining instalments, the lessee pays all but one instalment. What happens to ownership?
column5: It passes pro rata to the paid instalments
column6: It does not pass, as the condition is not met
column7: It passes after a new contract is signed
column8: It passes, as the shortfall is minor
column10: Per 8/4, under a gift contingent on paying the rentals, title passes without further procedure on fulfilment; if even one instalment is short, it does not pass.

column4: Bank A's lease stipulates that the lessee shall carry out, at his own cost, the major maintenance needed to keep the asset able to provide the contractual benefits. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as the lessee is the one who uses the asset
column6: Permitted if the rent is lowered by a matching amount
column7: Permitted in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek contracts only
column8: Not permitted; it may be delegated at the Bank's cost
column10: Per 5/1/7, the lessor may not stipulate that the lessee undertake major maintenance; it may delegate the task at the lessor's cost. Ordinary maintenance is the lessee's.

column4: At the end of an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, the lessee is to acquire the asset by sale under Bank A's earlier promise. What must be done?
column5: A new contract of sale must be drawn up
column6: The lessee only needs to notify the Bank
column7: Nothing; title passes under the promise
column8: The original lease is simply re-signed
column10: Per 8/3, in transfer by gift or sale, a new contract must be drawn up on fulfilling the promise; ownership does not pass automatically under the promise document.

column4: A customer promises to lease an asset that Bank A will acquire. The Bank requires a sum of money to confirm his seriousness. What may the Bank deduct from it?
column5: The rentals it expected to earn over the whole lease term
column6: The whole sum, as the customer broke his promise
column7: A fixed penalty amount agreed in the promise document
column8: Only the actual damage it suffers from his breach
column10: Per 2/3, nothing may be deducted from the sum except in proportion to the actual damage suffered by the Institution if the customer does not fulfil his promise.

column4: Which Qur'anic command does the Shari'ah basis cite for the binding nature of an Ijarah contract?
column5: 'Fulfil (your) obligations'
column6: 'Allah has permitted trade'
column7: 'O my father engage him on wages'
column8: 'Help you one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa'
column10: The basis: Ijarah transfers ownership by exchange of counter-values, and such contracts are binding per the verse 'Fulfil (your) obligations'.

column4: Ahmad leases a shop from Bank A. The lease says nothing about subletting. Ahmad sublets the shop to Karim for a higher rent. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as Ahmad does not own the shop itself
column6: Permissible only with the Bank's approval
column7: Permissible, at the same, a lower or a higher rent
column8: Permissible only at the same or a lower rent than his own
column10: Per 3/3, a lessee may sublet to a party other than the owner for the same, lower or higher rent, unless the owner stipulated against it or required approval.

column4: During the lease, the lessee's misconduct makes a leased machine unusable for two months. Who restores it, and what of the rent for those months?
column5: The lessee repairs it, and the rent is waived
column6: The lessee repairs it, and the rent is not waived
column7: The lessor repairs it, and the rent is waived
column8: The lessor repairs it, and the rent stays due
column10: Per 5/1/6, if benefit is impaired by the lessee's misconduct, he must restore or repair the usufruct, and rent for the lost time is not waived.

column4: To secure rentals, Bank A takes an assignment of the lessee's rights to a permissible property insurance indemnity held by a third party. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as insurance is the lessor's
column6: Permissible only for misuse, not for rent
column7: Permissible only for life insurance
column8: Permissible as security for the rentals
column10: Per 6/1, permissible security of all kinds may be taken, including assignment of rights held by third parties, even a permissible insurance indemnity.

column4: A customer buys a building jointly with Bank A, owning 30% while the Bank owns 70%. He then leases the Bank's share. On what is the Bank's rental based?
column5: Any amount the two parties freely agree
column6: Only its 70% share of the building
column7: The whole building, as the customer uses it all
column8: The whole building less a 30% discount fee
column10: Per 3/6, the rental receivable by the Institution is only in proportion to its ownership share, since the lessee pays rent only on the share he does not own.

column4: Bank A wants the right to terminate an Ijarah if the lessee fails to pay rent on time. Can it include this?
column5: Yes, it may stipulate termination for non-payment
column6: No, termination always requires mutual consent of both
column7: Yes, but only after a court ruling
column8: No, only force majeure permits termination of a lease
column10: Per 7/2/2, the lessor may stipulate that the Ijarah be terminated if the lessee does not pay the rent or fails to pay it on time.

column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, which of these is a recognised method of transferring title to the lessee?
column5: A sale contract signed now, effective at lease end
column6: Transfer on registration under local law
column7: A promise to give it as a gift for no consideration
column8: A transfer clause inside the Ijarah contract itself
column10: Per 8/1, methods include a promise to sell (token, market value or accelerated rental), a promise of gift, or a gift contingent on paying remaining instalments.

column4: In an Ijarah Mawsufah fi al-Dhimmah, the vehicle delivered to the lessee is destroyed. Nothing else was agreed. What must the lessor do?
column5: Provide a substitute of similar specification
column6: Nothing, as the lease automatically ends
column7: Repair it at the lessee's cost
column8: Refund all rentals paid so far
column10: Per 7/1/6, in a lease of a described asset the owner must offer a substitute of similar specification and the Ijarah continues; if impossible, it terminates.

column4: A lessee stops using a leased office and returns the keys to Bank A without the Bank's consent, mid-term. What follows?
column5: The Bank must lease it to someone else
column6: The lease ends on return of the keys
column7: Rent remains due for the remaining period
column8: Rent stops, but a penalty is due
column10: Per 7/1/7, rent continues for the remaining period and the lessor keeps the asset at the lessee's disposal, unless the lessee relinquishes the remaining period.

column4: Ahmad, a lessee, invites two friends to share the usufruct he owns, and they then sub-lease the asset. When must the friends have joined?
column5: Only after the sub-lease, sharing the rental equally
column6: Before the sub-lease, then share rental pro rata
column7: Never; a lessee may not share his usufruct with others
column8: At any time, even after the sub-lease has been made
column10: Per 4/2/4, a lessee may make others co-owners of the usufruct only before a sub-lease; each then shares the sub-lease rental pro rata to his share.

column4: Bank A buys a building from Company X and leases it back to X on Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek. When may the Bank sell the building back to X?
column5: At any time, since the lease itself is a genuine contract
column6: Immediately after the lease is signed by both parties
column7: Only at the same price the Bank originally paid to X
column8: After a reasonable period in which value could change
column10: Per 8/5, a reasonable period must lapse between the lease and the sale to the lessee, long enough for the asset or its value to change, to avoid 'Inah.

column4: Bank A leases a delivery van to Ahmad, who overloads it far beyond common practice and damages it. Which duty did Ahmad breach?
column5: Paying all rentals in advance
column6: Carrying out major maintenance of the van
column7: Using the asset suitably and avoiding misuse
column8: Insuring the asset at his own expense
column10: Per 5/1/4, the lessee must use the asset in a suitable manner per common practice and avoid causing damage by misuse through misconduct or negligence.

column4: Under a lease of a described asset, Bank A delivers a vehicle that does not conform to the agreed specifications. What may the lessee do?
column5: Keep it, since the lease is already binding
column6: Only claim a reduction in the rental
column7: Terminate the lease and claim a penalty
column8: Reject it and demand one that conforms
column10: Per 3/5, if the lessee receives an asset that does not conform to the description, he is entitled to reject it and demand a conforming asset.

column4: Bank A wants to raise funds by signing new leases on an asset already leased to Company X for the same period. Why does the Shari'ah basis reject this?
column5: The usufruct is already sold; this sells rent receivable
column6: The asset would need fresh insurance for each new lessee
column7: The rentals would become a floating amount over the period
column8: The existing lessee did not approve the new lease
column10: The basis: after the first lease, the usufruct no longer belongs to the owner; re-leasing amounts to an impermissible sale of the rent receivable.

column4: How does the Shari'ah basis distinguish permissible Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek from conventional hire-purchase?
column5: Title passes at the start, as in a sale
column6: Ijarah rules apply until the end, then title passes
column7: Sale and lease rules apply together throughout the term
column8: The lessee bears ownership risk from the start
column10: The basis: in hire-purchase, sale and lease apply at the same time and title passes on the last payment; in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Ijarah rules apply until term end.

column4: In a floating-rental Ijarah, Bank A ties later rentals to a benchmark with a clear formula but sets no limits on its movement. What does the standard require?
column5: A ceiling on the maximum level only, not a minimum
column6: A floor on the minimum level only, not a maximum
column7: No limits, as a clear formula is enough
column8: A ceiling on both maximum and minimum levels
column10: Per 5/2/3, the benchmark must use a clear formula not subject to dispute and should be subject to a ceiling on both maximum and minimum levels.

column4: Along with an Ijarah, Bank A and the lessee sign a sale contract of the asset that will become effective at the end of the lease. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the price is only a token amount
column6: Permitted in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek contracts
column7: Not permitted as a means of transferring ownership
column8: Permitted, as the sale takes effect only at the end
column10: Per 8/7, transfer of ownership cannot be made by executing, along with the Ijarah, a sale contract that will become effective on a future date.

column4: Bank A is asked to lease office premises to be used as headquarters by an institution dealing in interest. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as the use is impermissible
column6: Permissible if the rent is given to charity
column7: Permissible, as the Bank only leases the premises
column8: Permissible if the lessee is not a Muslim
column10: Per 5/1/1, the benefit from Ijarah must be permissible; e.g., premises may not be leased as headquarters for an institution dealing in interest.

column4: Bank A leases one holiday flat to several lessees for the same usufruct and duration, without fixing a period for each; each uses it in the time assigned to him by set rules. What is this?
column5: Void, as each lessee's period is not fixed
column6: A permissible form of Muhaya'ah (time-sharing)
column7: Two contracts on the same asset and period
column8: A sale of the flat in undivided shares
column10: Per 4/2/3, a lease with several lessees entitled to the same usufruct without fixing a period per person is a form of Muhaya'ah (time-sharing).

column4: An Ijarah is signed on 1 May, but Bank A makes the asset available to the lessee only on 15 May. From when is the Bank entitled to rental?
column5: From the first payment date in the contract
column6: From 1 May, the date of signing
column7: From the end of the first month
column8: From 15 May, when the usufruct is made available
column10: Per 5/2/2, entitlement runs from when the lessee starts benefiting or the usufruct is made available, not necessarily from the signing date.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow an Ijarah to take effect from a future date, even though a sale cannot?
column5: Rentals are paid only at the end
column6: Ijarah is a contract that involves time
column7: Ijarah needs no specified duration
column8: Ijarah is not a binding contract
column10: The basis: unlike a sale, Ijarah is a contract that involves time, so it is relevant for it to be contingent on future events.

column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Bank A promises to transfer ownership, and the lessee also binds himself to acquire it. What is wrong with this?
column5: Only one party may be bound; the other has an option
column6: The Bank's promise may never be binding on the Bank
column7: A promise must be made by the lessee only, not the Bank
column8: Nothing, as both binding promises protect both parties
column10: Per 8/2, the lessor's promise is binding on one party only; the other must have the option not to proceed, to avoid an impermissible bilateral promise.

column4: Bank A leases out a machine it has not yet acquired, as a specified asset. On what ground does the Shari'ah basis reject this?
column5: The lessee must see and inspect the asset before contracting
column6: Leasing requires a master agreement to be signed first
column7: Ijarah sells usufruct; one may not sell what he does not own
column8: Ijarah is a loan of the asset, and loans need collateral
column10: The basis: the Hadith prohibits selling what one does not own, and Ijarah proper is a sale of usufruct.

column4: Bank A already owns a fleet of trucks. A customer agrees with the Bank on leasing two of them. When may the Ijarah contract be executed?
column5: Only after a master agreement is signed
column6: Only after the customer pays rent in advance
column7: Only after the trucks are insured by the customer
column8: As soon as the two parties reach agreement
column10: Per 3/1/1, if the asset or its usufruct is owned by the Institution, as it should in principle be, the Ijarah may be executed as soon as agreement is reached.

column4: Bank A has bought a building under a sale contract, but the title is not yet registered in its name. Can the Bank lease it?
column5: Yes, ownership exists under the sale contract
column6: No, title must be registered in its name first
column7: No, until the seller vacates and registers it
column8: Yes, but only as an agent of the seller
column10: Per 3/1/2, ownership is possible under a sale contract even if title is not registered in the purchaser's name; the purchaser may obtain a counter-deed.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis say that things that perish by use cannot be leased?
column5: Their rentals cannot be specified in advance
column6: The subject of a lease is usufruct, not the asset
column7: Such things cannot be insured by the lessor against loss
column8: They cannot be delivered on time
column10: The basis: the leased asset must be usable while preserved, because the subject of a lease is usufruct, not the asset; things that perish by use cannot be leased.

column4: Bank A links later rentals to a benchmark. To which principle does the Shari'ah basis liken this method?
column5: Hamish Jiddiyyah (security deposit taken from the customer)
column6: Bay' al-Bara'ah (sale on an 'as is' basis without liability)
column7: Ujrat al-Mithl (prevailing market rate of rental)
column8: Muhaya'ah (time-sharing of usufruct between co-owners)
column10: The basis: using a benchmark for later rentals makes them known, is similar to Ujrat al-Mithl and does not lead to dispute.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis say that ownership in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek cannot be passed by a sale effective on a future date?
column5: The price cannot be known so far in advance
column6: A sale's effect, transfer of ownership, is immediate
column7: The lessee may die before that future date arrives
column8: Future sales always involve Riba and Gharar together
column10: The basis: a sale contract cannot depend on a future date, since 'sale' means its effect, transfer of ownership, takes place immediately.

column4: Bank A drafts an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek with the clause on transferring title placed inside the lease contract itself. What does the standard require?
column5: It must be stated in the master agreement only
column6: It must be inside the lease contract itself, as a clause
column7: It may be oral if both parties agree to it beforehand
column8: The transfer method must be in a separate document
column10: Per 8/1, the method of transferring title must be evidenced in a document separate from, and independent of, the Ijarah contract.

column4: Bank A's lease states that the lessee may not sublet without the Bank's approval. The lessee sublets without asking. What is the position?
column5: Not permitted; he needed the Bank's approval
column6: Permitted, as the lessee owns the usufruct
column7: Permitted if the sub-lease rent is not higher
column8: Permitted if the sub-lessee is a Muslim
column10: Per 3/3, sub-leasing is allowed unless the owner stipulates that the lessee should not sublet, or not do so without his approval.

column4: Land leased for crop cultivation reaches the end of its term, but the harvest is late. What is the position of the lease?
column5: It continues at the original rental until the harvest
column6: It ends at once, and the crop must be removed
column7: It continues at the prevailing market rental
column8: It continues free of rent until the harvest
column10: Per 7/2/6, the lease may remain operative for a good cause such as a late harvest, continuing at a rental based on prevailing market value.

column4: In the first lease period, Ahmad pays rent of 100 on a spot basis and leases the same asset back to its owner for 120, also on a spot basis. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if the second rent is lower
column6: Not permissible, as the second rent is higher
column7: Not permissible, as lease-back to the owner is barred
column8: Permissible, as both rentals are paid on spot basis
column10: Per 3/4, the lessee may lease the asset back to its owner for a lower, same or higher rent if both rentals are paid on a spot basis.

column4: According to the Shari'ah basis, why is Ijarah also acceptable by reasoning?
column5: It replaces the need for Murabahah
column6: It lets people use assets that they do not own
column7: It is a way of lending money with a return
column8: It lets the lessor avoid risks of ownership
column10: The basis: Ijarah is acceptable by reasoning as a convenient means for people to acquire the right to use assets they do not own.

column4: Bank A and Company X sign a master agreement setting general terms for many future Ijarah transactions. How may each individual lease then be concluded?
column5: Only by signing a new master agreement for each asset
column6: Only by a separate signed lease document, never by offer and acceptance
column7: By a separate contract, or by offer and acceptance under it
column8: By the master agreement alone, with no further contract or step
column10: Per 2/2, under a master agreement each lease may be a separate signed contract, or the parties may exchange offer and acceptance referring to its terms.

column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, title cannot pass because the asset is destroyed without the lessee's fault, so rentals are adjusted to market rate. To what does the basis liken this?
column5: Reducing the price of a crop hit by natural calamities
column6: Rebating part of a debt paid before its due date
column7: Refunding 'Arboun after deducting the actual damage incurred
column8: Returning goods within a three-day option period
column10: The basis: retrospective adjustment to market rental protects the lessee and is analogous to discounting the price of a sold crop damaged by natural calamities.

column4: A rental has two parts: one paid to Bank A, and one held by the lessee for approved costs such as major maintenance. The held part exceeds the actual costs. How is the excess treated?
column5: As a penalty payable to charity
column6: As the lessee's own money to keep
column7: As a reduction of the asset's price
column8: As an advance to the lessor on account
column10: Per 5/2/4, the excess of the second part is treated as an advance to the lessor on account, while the lessor bears any shortage.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis reject making a purchase contract contingent on a lease contract?
column5: It falls under the Hadith barring two sales in one
column6: It makes the rental amount uncertain for the lessee
column7: It turns the lease into a loan with a benefit
column8: It delays the transfer of ownership of the asset
column10: The basis: making purchase contracts contingent upon leasing contracts is impermissible, prohibited by the well-known Hadith barring two sales in one sale.

column4: A lease runs from 1 March, but Bank A delivers the asset on 1 April. Nothing else was agreed. What happens to March's rental?
column5: March's rent is due once delivery takes place
column6: No rental is due for March; rent is reduced
column7: Full rent is due as the contract is signed
column8: Half the March rent is due as compensation
column10: Per 4/1/3, no rental is due between the agreed and actual delivery dates, unless it is agreed to extend the lease by an equivalent period after expiry.

column4: A customer breaks his promise to take an asset on operating Ijarah. Bank A bought it for 200,000 and sells it to a third party for 185,000. What may the customer be charged?
column5: Nothing, as a promise to lease is not binding
column6: The rentals for the whole intended lease term
column8: The whole security amount he deposited
column10: Per 2/3, in operating Ijarah the breaching promisor is charged the difference between the cost of acquisition and the selling price to a third party.

column4: Bank A leases a car described by accurate specifications that it does not yet own, undertaking to deliver it during the term. Must the rental be paid in advance?
column5: No, unless the lease is executed as a Salam
column6: Yes, as in every lease of a described asset
column7: Yes, the first year's rent must be paid upfront
column8: No, and the Bank need not deliver to the specs
column10: Per 3/5, advance rental is not a requirement in a lease of a described asset as long as the lease is not executed according to Salam (Salaf).

column4: Bank A is asked to lease a house to a non-Muslim for residential purposes. The Bank has no reason to presume any impermissible use. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only for commercial purposes, not residential
column6: Not permissible to lease a residence to a non-Muslim
column7: Permissible only with a guarantor
column8: Permissible, as the intended use is permissible
column10: Per 5/1/3, an Ijarah may be executed with a non-Muslim if the use is permissible, unless the lessor knows or has reason to presume an impermissible use.

column4: An Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek contains an undertaking by the lessee to donate a percentage of late rentals if he delays without good reason. How must the amounts be used?
column5: Used to reduce the Bank's maintenance and insurance costs
column6: Added to the Bank's rental income for that period
column7: Paid to charity under the Shari'ah Board's coordination
column8: Returned to the lessee at the end of the lease
column10: Per 6/4, such a donation should be paid to charitable causes under the co-ordination of the Institution's Shari'ah Supervisory Board.

column4: Bank A takes an office building on lease from a landlord, so the Bank is the lessee. Does the Ijarah standard apply to this lease?
column5: No, it applies only to Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek leases
column6: Yes, it applies to the Institution as lessor or lessee
column7: Yes, but only if the lease ends with transfer of ownership
column8: No, it applies only where the Institution is the lessor
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers operating leases and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek whether the Institution is the lessor or the lessee.

column4: Bank A plans to issue Sukuk al-Ijarah and asks whether the Ijarah and Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek standard governs this issuance. What is the answer?
column5: No, they fall under the standard on Investment Sukuk
column6: Only if the Sukuk end with transfer of ownership
column7: Yes, it covers every instrument based on Ijarah
column8: Yes, if the Sukuk are backed by leased property
column10: Per clause 1, the standard does not cover Sukuk al-Ijarah, which are covered by the Shari'ah Standard on Investment Sukuk, nor labour contracts.

column4: Bank A takes 'Arboun at the execution of a lease, and the lessee may terminate within a set period. If the lease proceeds, how is the 'Arboun treated?
column5: As a security held for misuse
column6: As an advance payment of the rental
column7: As a deposit refunded at lease end
column8: As a fee earned by the Bank
column10: Per 4/1/4, 'Arboun may be taken at execution of the lease with the lessee's right to terminate within a period, and it is treated as an advance payment of rental.

column4: Bank A has leased a building to Company X for two years. In the second year, it signs a lease of the same building with Company Y for the remaining period. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if X is informed of the new lease in writing
column6: Permitted as a successive lease for the rest of the period
column7: Permitted if Y agrees to pay a higher rent than X pays
column8: Not permitted during the existing Ijarah period
column10: Per 4/2/2, once the lessor leases an asset for a period, it cannot sign another Ijarah with another lessee for the existing period or any remaining part of it.

column4: Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite for the validity of a gift contingent on a condition, as used in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek?
column5: The Prophet's purchase of a she-camel from Abu Bakr
column6: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab on 'Arboun in sales
column7: The Prophet's gift to Negus, conditional on survival
column8: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on options in sales
column10: The basis: a conditional gift is valid; the Prophet sent a gift to Negus on condition that he was alive when the messenger arrived.

column4: A lessee of a large warehouse dies. His heirs prove the lease is now too onerous for their resources and exceeds their needs. What is the position?
column5: The heirs must continue to the end
column6: Only the lessor may terminate it
column7: The lease ends automatically on death
column8: The heirs may terminate the Ijarah
column10: Per 7/2/3, Ijarah does not end with death of a party, but the lessee's heirs may terminate if they prove it is too onerous and exceeds their needs.

column4: Six months into a lease, the lessee simply wishes to end it as he no longer needs the asset. There is no force majeure, defect or option. May he terminate alone?
column5: No, the lease is binding; he needs the lessor's consent
column6: Yes, by giving the lessor one month's notice in writing
column7: Yes, by paying the lessor a fixed termination fee
column8: Yes, as a lessee may always end a lease at his own will
column10: Per 4/1/1 and 7/2/1, Ijarah is binding; neither party may terminate or alter it without the other's consent, save force majeure, material defect or an option.

column4: Midway through a lease, Bank A sells the leased asset to the lessee himself. What happens to the Ijarah contract?
column5: It continues unchanged until the original term ends
column6: It terminates, as the lessee becomes the owner
column7: It becomes a sub-lease granted back to the Bank
column8: It continues at a reduced rental for the lessee
column10: Per 7/1/1, if the lessor sells the leased asset to the lessee, the Ijarah terminates due to transfer of ownership of the asset and usufruct to him.

column4: A lessee pays a rental of 100 dinars on a spot basis and then sublets the asset to the lessor for 110 dinars payable on a deferred basis. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the lessor consents to it
column6: Permissible, as rent may be higher on sublease
column7: Not permissible, as it leads to 'Inah
column8: Permissible if the deferral is under one year
column10: Per 3/4, leasing back to the owner is barred where varying rent or duration leads to 'Inah, e.g. 100 spot followed by 110 deferred.

column4: Bank A's lease contract states that the Bank bears no liability for any defect impairing the intended use of the leased equipment. Is this clause valid?
column5: No, the lessor may not exclude such liability
column6: Yes, if the rental is reduced in return
column7: Yes, for defects caused by events outside its control
column8: Yes, if the lessee accepts it in writing
column10: Per 5/1/5, the lessor must accept responsibility for defects impairing intended use and may not exclude liability, even for events outside its control.

column4: An identified leased vehicle is totally destroyed without the lessee's fault. The lease says the remaining instalments are still payable. What is the position?
column5: The lease ends, but the instalments stay due
column6: The lessee must pay half the remaining rent
column7: The lease ends; that stipulation is not allowed
column8: The lease continues with a substitute vehicle
column10: Per 7/1/3, Ijarah on an identified asset terminates on its total destruction, and it may not be stipulated that the remaining instalments be paid.

column4: A leased machine is destroyed due to the lessee's negligence. The machine is replaceable. What is the lessee's liability?
column5: He pays its value fixed by the lessor
column6: He must replace the machine
column7: He pays only the remaining rentals
column8: He has no liability, as he is a trustee
column10: Per 7/1/4, the lessee holds the asset in a fiduciary capacity and is liable only for misconduct or negligence; then he replaces it if replaceable, else pays valued damage.

column4: A customer paid Bank A a security deposit for his promise to lease. When the lease contract is executed, what may the parties agree about this deposit?
column5: That it is held until the end of the lease term
column6: That it becomes 'Arboun owned by the Bank on execution
column7: That the Bank keeps it as a fee for arranging the lease
column8: To treat it as an advance payment of rentals
column10: Per 2/4, it is permissible to agree, upon execution of the lease, that the deposit shall be treated as an advance payment of the lease rental instalments.

column4: A lessee owes two unpaid past rentals. Bank A and the lessee agree to restructure rentals. Which rentals may they increase?
column5: Only future rentals for unused periods
column6: The unpaid past rentals as well
column7: Past rentals, if the lessee consents
column8: All rentals, if the term is extended
column10: Per 5/2/5, future rentals may be amended by agreement; unpaid rentals of past periods become a debt owed by the lessee and cannot be increased.

column4: Bank A wants floating rentals for a 10-year Ijarah tied to a benchmark. What must it do for the first rental period?
column5: Set it as an average of past benchmarks
column6: Link it to the benchmark like later periods
column7: Specify its rental as a lump sum
column8: Leave it open until the period ends
column10: Per 5/2/3, with a floating rental, the first period's rental must be specified as a lump sum; later periods may follow a benchmark.

column4: Bank A leases a car by specification, not yet owned. Per the Shari'ah basis, which contract is this similar to, and what should the lessor avoid?
column5: It is similar to 'Inah; avoid the transaction
column6: It is similar to Istisna'a; avoid fixed rentals in advance
column7: It is similar to Murabahah; avoid any mark-up
column8: It is similar to Salam; avoid requesting advance rentals
column10: The basis: leasing on specifications does not lead to dispute and is similar to Salam, but the lessor should not request advance rentals per a Shafi'i and Hanbali view.

column4: A customer breaks his promise to take an asset on operating Ijarah. Bank A keeps the asset and does not sell it. What compensation may the Bank claim?
column5: A fixed amount stated in the promise
column6: None, since the asset was not sold
column7: The difference between cost and market value
column8: The first year's expected rentals
column10: Per 2/3, in operating Ijarah the charge is cost minus the third-party selling price; if the asset is not sold, the promisee is not entitled to any compensation.

column4: Bank A argues that, since local law treats its Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek as an instalment sale, the lessee should bear major maintenance. Is this acceptable?
column5: No, the rules of Ijarah still fully apply
column6: Yes, local law governs the parties' duties
column7: Yes, as the lessee will become the owner
column8: Yes, if the rentals resemble sale instalments
column10: Per 8/6, Ijarah rules apply to Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek and may not be breached because local laws or conventional practice treat it as an instalment sale.

column4: Bank A insures a leased asset. After the contract is signed, the insurance cost rises above what the Bank anticipated when fixing the rent. May it charge the excess to the lessee?
column5: Yes, as insurance costs always follow the leased asset
column6: No, it may not charge cost beyond that anticipated
column7: Yes, if the lessee is notified in advance in writing
column8: Yes, but only half of the increase in cost
column10: Per 5/1/8, the lessor bears insurance and may factor it into the rent, but after signing may not charge the lessee any cost exceeding that anticipated.

column4: After a lessee's default, Bank A forecloses on his security. What may the Bank deduct from the proceeds?
column5: Future rentals for the full remaining term
column6: Only past rentals, never compensation
column7: Past rentals due plus legitimate compensation
column8: All rentals, including those not yet due
column10: Per 6/5, the lessor may deduct only rentals due for past periods, not future ones, plus legitimate compensation for the lessee's breach of contract.

column4: A customer breaks his promise to take an asset on Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek. Bank A then leases it to a third party on the same basis. What may the customer be charged?
column5: The Bank's expected profit on the lease over its full term
column6: Cost of the asset minus its market value at the date of breach
column7: All rentals the customer would have paid over the lease
column8: Cost of the asset minus total rentals from the third party
column10: Per 2/3, for a promise of Ijarah with transfer of ownership, the breaching promisor is charged the difference between the asset's cost and total rentals from the third-party lease.

column4: Bank A buys a machine from Company X and will lease it back to X. The purchase contract says the sale is conditional on X taking the lease. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid, if the rent is fixed in the purchase
column6: The lease must not be a condition of the purchase
column7: Leasing back to the seller is never allowed
column8: Valid, as the lease is the purpose of the deal
column10: Per 3/2, an asset may be acquired from a party and leased to it, but the Ijarah should not be stipulated as a condition of the purchase contract.

column4: Bank A appoints a customer as its agent to buy equipment that the customer will later lease from the Bank. What does the standard say about this agency?
column5: Permissible, but another agent is preferred if possible
column6: Permissible, and the customer is the preferred agent for it
column7: Not permissible; the Bank must buy the equipment directly
column8: Permissible only if the customer pays the price
column10: Per 3/7, the Institution may appoint the customer as agent to acquire the asset, but it is always preferred that the agent be someone other than the customer.

column4: Bank A leases a hall to Company X for January to June, and the same hall to Company Y for July to December. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible; one asset, one lessee
column6: Permissible only if both pay the same rent
column7: Permissible as successive leases
column8: Permissible only with Company X's consent
column10: Per 4/2/1, one asset may be leased to several lessees for different periods, provided two contracts are not made for the same period (successive leases).

column4: An Ijarah allows Bank A to accelerate remaining instalments if the lessee delays without valid reason after due notice. What must the Bank still provide?
column5: Nothing, as the lease ends on acceleration
column6: A refund of all accelerated rentals at once
column7: A new lease at a reduced rental
column8: The asset for use for the remaining period
column10: Per 6/2, acceleration may be stipulated provided the asset is made available for the remaining period; accelerated rent is settled at the end or termination.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis bar a lessor from excluding liability for defects in the leased asset?
column5: Rent for impaired usufruct is unjust enrichment
column6: Defects are always caused by the lessee's own use
column7: The lessee bears all major maintenance of the asset
column8: Such clauses are allowed only in sales, not in leases
column10: The basis: such a condition defeats the purpose of exchanging usufruct for rentals; if usufruct is impaired, receiving rentals becomes unjust enrichment.

column4: Bank A and a lessee raise the rentals for future periods not yet due. Why is this not prohibited rescheduling, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Because the lessee freely agreed to the increase in rentals
column6: Because the rentals were floating anyway under the contract
column7: Because the asset's market value has risen since the lease
column8: It creates a new contract for rentals not yet a debt
column10: The basis: restructuring future rentals is a new contract for a term whose rentals are not yet due, so they are not a debt; raising due rentals for time is Riba.

column4: In January, Bank A signs an Ijarah contract under which the lease period starts in March. What is this arrangement?
column5: A promise to lease, not a contract
column6: A valid future Ijarah
column7: Valid only if rent is paid from January
column8: Void, as Ijarah must start on signing
column10: Per 4/1/2, the period starts on execution unless the parties agree on a future commencement date, resulting in a future Ijarah.

column4: A lessee pays a monthly rental late. Bank A's contract adds 2% to the rental due for each month of delay, for the Bank's own account. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if stated clearly in the written contract
column6: Permissible if the lessee is solvent and delays without excuse
column7: Not permissible; no increase for delay is allowed
column8: Permissible up to the Bank's actual cost of funds
column10: Per 6/3, no increase in the rental due may be stipulated by the lessor in case of delay in payment by the lessee.

column4: Bank A pays the full Salam capital at signing and agrees that the rice will be delivered in four instalments on four different dates. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only for goods sold by number
column6: Permissible, as the capital was paid at conclusion
column7: Permissible only if the capital is also split
column8: Not permissible; there must be one delivery date
column10: Per 3/2/9, there is no objection to setting various delivery dates in instalments, provided the capital was paid at the time the contract was concluded.

column4: Bank A and a seller disagree on how to describe the grade of cotton in a Salam. What is the reference for determining such descriptions?
column5: The buyer's own internal standards
column6: Whatever the Shari'ah Supervisory Board decides
column7: Customary practice and the experience of experts
column8: The seller's description alone
column10: Per 3/2/6, the reference for descriptions used to specify al-Muslam Fihi is customary practice and the experience of experts.

column4: A trading company asks whether Salam may finance its working capital, given Salam is mostly used by farmers. What does the Shari'ah basis say?
column5: Salam is limited to agricultural produce and farmers
column6: Salam is allowed only for small farmers
column7: Salam may be used only for exports
column8: Salam is not limited to farming; traders may use it
column10: The basis: though commonly used in agriculture, Salam's permissibility is not confined to it; it can be used in industry or trade.

column4: A Salam buyer accepts a substitute worth more than the original al-Muslam Fihi at delivery. Why does the Shari'ah basis forbid this?
column5: To stop the buyer making compound profit on one deal
column6: Because substitution is never allowed in a Salam deal
column7: Because the substitute must be the same genus
column8: Because the seller would lose his capital
column10: The basis: a substitute priced above al-Muslam Fihi's market value at delivery is barred to deter the buyer from making a compound profit on one deal.

column4: Bank A bought wheat by Salam from Farmer F and sold similar wheat by Parallel Salam to Mill M. F fails to deliver. May the Bank delay its delivery to M?
column5: Yes, if M was told of the first Salam
column6: No, the two contracts stand alone
column7: Yes, and it may also cancel M's contract
column8: Yes, as M's contract depends on F's
column10: Per 6/3, obligations of the two Salam contracts may not be linked; breach in one gives no right to terminate or delay performance of the other.

column4: Bank A has bought 500 tons of wheat by Salam for delivery in June. In March, it wants to sell the same wheat to a mill before receiving it. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as the Bank already paid
column6: Permitted if the mill pays in advance
column7: Not permitted before taking possession
column8: Permitted at a price not above cost
column10: Per 4/1, the buyer may not sell al-Muslam Fihi before taking possession of it.

column4: Bank A wants to issue tradable Sukuk representing its Salam receivables (the commodities owed to it by sellers before delivery). What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted to issue tradable Salam debt Sukuk
column6: Permitted if the sellers consent to the transfer
column7: Permitted if the commodities owed are fungible goods
column8: Permitted after half the term has passed
column10: Per clause 7, it is not permitted to issue tradable Sukuk based on the debt from a Salam contract (see 4/1 on selling before possession).

column4: After the delivery date, a Salam seller offers barley instead of the agreed wheat; no such swap was stipulated. On what condition may Bank A accept it?
column5: The swap must have been stipulated in the contract
column6: The barley must be of the same genus as the wheat
column7: The barley must be worth more than the wheat sold
column8: The barley must not be worth more than the wheat
column10: Per 4/2, after the due date the buyer may take other goods (not currency) if not stipulated, if suitable as al-Muslam Fihi and not worth more than it.

column4: Bank A signs a Salam for a fruit that is normally not available at the delivery place on the agreed delivery date. Which condition is missing?
column5: Immediate payment of the capital in the same session
column6: Common availability at the delivery place and date
column7: A known place of delivery stated in the contract
column8: A known quantity of the fruit, stated by weight or measure
column10: Per 3/2/8, al-Muslam Fihi must be commonly available under normal circumstances where it should be on the delivery date, so the seller can deliver.

column4: A Salam for delivery in four months stipulates that Bank A will pay the capital two days after the contract. What is the status of the Salam?
column5: Valid only if the delay had not been stipulated
column6: Valid only if the seller gives a guarantee to the Bank
column7: Void, as the capital must be paid on the spot, at the session
column8: Valid, as a delay of two or three days is tolerated
column10: Per 3/1/3, the capital must be paid immediately, but may be delayed two or three days at most, even if stipulated, if shorter than the delivery period.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis say Iqalah is easily applicable to Salam?
column5: Regret is more likely, as Salam is a low-cost sale
column6: Salam capital is never paid in advance of delivery
column7: Iqalah applies only to Salam contracts and no others
column8: Salam is not a binding contract until goods are delivered
column10: The basis: the Prophet encouraged Iqalah; in Salam, a low-cost sale, the parties are more likely to regret it, so Iqalah is easily applicable.

column4: A Salam seller offers to deliver conforming goods one month before the due date. The buyer has no valid reason for refusing. What is the position?
column5: Early delivery voids the Salam
column6: The buyer may accept only at a discount
column7: The buyer will be forced to accept them
column8: The buyer may refuse until the due date
column10: Per 5/5, early delivery of conforming goods is allowed; a buyer with a valid reason is not compelled, otherwise he is forced to accept.

column4: Bank A pays US dollars as Salam capital and wants al-Muslam Fihi to be a quantity of gold delivered in six months. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the delivery is under a year
column6: Permissible if the gold is weighed
column7: Permissible, as gold is a commodity
column8: Not permissible when the capital is currency
column10: Per 3/2/4, al-Muslam Fihi may not be currency, gold or silver if the Salam capital was paid in currency, gold or silver.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis treat granting the usufruct of an asset as immediate receipt of Salam capital?
column5: Usufruct is a form of cash under commercial custom
column6: Salam capital need not be received at all before delivery
column7: Possessing part of a thing is like possessing the whole
column8: Usufruct is received only when the term ends
column10: The basis follows the Maliki view and the maxim 'Taking possession of part of a thing is like taking possession of the whole thing'; so it is not a sale of debt.

column4: Bank A sold 1,000 tons of rice by Salam to Company X. To meet this, it buys similar rice by a separate Salam from a farmer. What is the Bank's role in the second contract?
column5: Seller, as in the first contract
column6: Buyer in an independent Parallel Salam
column7: Guarantor of the farmer's delivery
column8: Agent of Company X in a single deal
column10: Per 6/1, the seller may make a separate, independent Salam with a third party to acquire similar goods; the seller in the first becomes buyer in the second.

column4: Bank A signs a contract with a factory to manufacture machines to order. Does the Salam and Parallel Salam standard govern this contract?
column5: No, Istisna'a is covered by a separate standard
column6: Only if the machines are fungible goods
column7: Yes, if the Bank pays the price in advance
column8: Yes, as it is a sale for deferred delivery
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers Salam, Parallel Salam and Salam Sukuk, but not Istisna'a (manufacturing contract), which has a separate standard.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis reject a Salam for the produce of one specific farm?
column5: Salam is limited to manufactured goods
column6: Farm produce cannot be measured or weighed accurately
column7: The seller cannot own his farm's produce
column8: The farm may yield nothing by delivery (Gharar)
column10: The basis: per the Hadith ('but not for the products of the kin of so and so'), produce from a specific farm may not exist at delivery, leading to Gharar.

column4: When Salam delivery falls due, the seller offers Bank A cash equal to the wheat's market value instead of the wheat. May the Bank accept this as a replacement?
column5: No, replacement by currency is excluded
column6: Yes, if paid in the capital's currency
column7: Yes, as the market value is fair
column8: Yes, if the cash is less than the capital
column10: Per 4/2, the buyer may exchange al-Muslam Fihi for other goods after the due date, except currency.

column4: Bank A and a farmers' cooperative sign a memorandum of understanding setting quantity, specifications and pricing basis for successive Salam deals. When is each Salam concluded?
column5: Automatically, at the start of each harvest season
column6: All at once, upon signing the memorandum of understanding
column7: Separately, when each contract is executed
column8: Only when the goods are delivered
column10: Per 2/1/1, a memorandum may set the framework for successive Salam contracts; the execution of each Salam then takes place separately at the appropriate date.

column4: Bank A's Salam contract stipulates at signing that the seller may deliver olive oil instead of the agreed wheat. What is the problem?
column5: Oil cannot be sold by Salam as it is a processed good
column6: Replacement may not be stipulated in the contract
column7: Replacement is never permitted in Salam, even afterwards
column8: Oil and wheat are of the same genus under Riba rules
column10: Per 4/2, exchange for other goods is allowed after the due date only as long as such substitution was not stipulated in the contract.

column4: A farmer owes Bank A 50,000 from a previous transaction. They agree that this debt will be the capital of a new Salam for the farmer's wheat. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted to use a debt as Salam capital
column6: Permitted if the debt is already due
column7: Permitted, as the amount is known
column8: Permitted if the farmer agrees in writing
column10: Per 3/1/4, a debt may not be recognised as the capital of Salam, such as loans or debts owed by the seller to the Institution from previous transactions.

column4: Bank A wants its Salam contract to stipulate a penalty payable by the seller for each week of delay in delivering al-Muslam Fihi. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the seller is solvent
column6: Permitted if stated at contracting
column7: Permitted if the penalty goes to charity
column8: Not permitted in respect of delay in delivery
column10: Per 5/7, it is not permitted to stipulate a penalty clause in respect of delay in the delivery of al-Muslam Fihi.

column4: Bank A's Salam requires that the dates delivered must come from the seller's own farm in a named village. What is the ruling?
column5: Required, so that the source of the dates is known
column6: Not permitted to name a specific piece of land
column7: Permitted if the farm's yield is normally large
column8: Permitted, as it improves certainty about the dates
column10: Per 3/2/3, it is not permissible to stipulate that al-Muslam Fihi be from a specific piece of land; the seller may deliver conforming items from anywhere.

column4: On the due date, only part of the dates sold by Salam are available to the seller. What options does Bank A, the buyer, have?
column5: Take the dates' market value in cash
column6: Claim compensation from the seller for its lost profit
column7: Wait for availability, or cancel and recover capital
column8: Force the seller to buy dates at any price from others
column10: Per 5/8, the buyer may wait until al-Muslam Fihi is available or cancel and recover the capital; the parties may also agree to replacement under 4/2.

column4: Bank A wants a Salam for branded products made in approximate units with standardised specifications, regularly available at any time. May they be al-Muslam Fihi?
column5: Yes, they are goods without significant variation
column6: Yes, but only if one specific unit is named in the contract
column7: No, manufactured goods can be sold by Istisna'a only
column8: No, Salam is limited to agricultural crops and livestock
column10: Per 3/2/2, products identified by trademarks and standard specifications and commonly available are items where variations make no difference (read with 3/2/8).

column4: Bank A pays the capital of a Salam by granting the seller the use of a ship for one year, delivering the ship to him at once. What is the status of the capital?
column5: Invalid; usufruct is received only over time
column6: Valid only if the ship is later sold to him
column7: Invalid; Salam capital must always be paid in cash
column8: Valid; delivering the ship is immediate receipt
column10: Per 3/1/1, the capital may be the usufruct of an asset such as a ship; granting access through delivery of the asset is regarded as immediate receipt.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis prohibit penalty clauses for delay in delivering al-Muslam Fihi?
column5: The buyer bears the risk of delay
column6: Delay is always caused by force majeure, never by the seller
column7: It is a debt, so nothing above the principal is allowed
column8: Penalties go only to the Institution, never to charity
column10: The basis: al-Muslam Fihi is considered a debt, and it is not permitted to stipulate payment in excess of the principal amount of debts.

column4: A Salam seller delivers goods of lower quality than the contract specifications. What are the buyer's options?
column5: He must accept them and pay the full price agreed
column6: Reject them, or accept them, possibly at a discount
column7: He must wait for the seller to replace them
column8: He must accept them and also claim a penalty from the seller
