column10: Per 5/3, the buyer may reject or accept inferior goods; acceptance is ethical, and the parties may settle on acceptance even at a discounted price.

column4: Bank A wants to buy 'this car parked in the dealer's yard' by Salam, for delivery in three months. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as the car is clearly identified and seen
column6: Permitted if the price is paid on the spot
column7: Not permitted, as Salam is not for a specific item
column8: Permitted if the dealer gives a guarantee
column10: Per 3/2/3, Salam is not permitted for anything specific like 'this car'.

column4: On the due date, a Salam seller delivers goods meeting all contract specifications, but Bank A refuses them as prices have fallen. What is the position?
column5: The seller must offer a price discount
column6: The Bank shall be compelled to accept them
column7: The Bank may refuse and recover its capital
column8: The Bank may refuse but must pay a fee
column10: Per 5/1, the buyer must accept goods that meet the contract specifications; if he refuses, he shall be compelled to do so.

column4: A Salam seller cannot deliver on the due date because he has become insolvent. How should Bank A treat him?
column5: Demand delivery of currency instead
column6: Charge him a penalty for the delay in delivery
column7: Sell his debt to a third party
column8: Grant him an extension of time for delivery
column10: Per 5/6, if the seller fails to perform owing to insolvency, he should be granted an extension of time for delivery.

column4: Bank A and a Salam seller agree to cancel delivery of 40% of the cotton. What is the correct treatment?
column5: Return 40% of the capital to the Bank
column6: Return the cotton's current market value
column7: Partial cancellation is not allowed
column8: Return the capital plus a profit margin
column10: Per 4/3, Iqalah of the whole Salam for full return of capital, or partial cancellation for return of a corresponding part of the capital, is permissible.

column4: According to the Shari'ah basis, how does the buyer in a Salam contract usually benefit?
column5: By selling the commodity before delivery
column6: By receiving interest on the capital paid
column7: By charging the seller a fee for financing
column8: By acquiring the commodity below market price
column10: The basis: Salam finances those needing working capital, and the buyer benefits by acquiring the commodity at a price below the market price.

column4: A contract says Bank A 'buys' 100 tons of wheat of set specifications for delivery in six months, paying the full price now. The word Salam is not used. Is it a Salam?
column5: Yes, but only if a master agreement exists
column6: Yes, any term indicating such a sale suffices
column7: No, it is an ordinary sale of goods
column8: No, the word Salam or Salaf must be used
column10: Per 2/2, Salam may be concluded using Salam, Salaf, sale or any term indicating sale of a prescribed commodity for deferred delivery against immediate payment.

column4: A Salam contract does not state the place of delivery, and delivery at the place of contracting is possible. Where must delivery take place?
column5: At the place where the contract was concluded
column6: At a place chosen later by the seller alone
column7: At the seller's farm, factory or place of business
column8: At the buyer's main warehouse, whichever town it is in
column10: Per 3/2/10, if no place is set, the place of contracting is the place of delivery; if that is impossible, it is determined by customary practice.

column4: A Salam seller delivers wheat of better quality than specified, asking no higher price. The specified grade was not vital to the buyer. What must the buyer do?
column5: Cancel the Salam and recover capital
column6: Accept them and pay the extra value
column7: Accept the goods
column8: Reject them as non-conforming
column10: Per 5/2, the buyer must accept superior goods if the seller seeks no higher price, unless the inferior specified description is itself vital.

column4: Bank A's Parallel Salam has the same commodity description as its first Salam. Why is this not 'two sales in one', per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: They are two separable Salam deals
column6: Because the second is a promise only
column7: Because the parties are the same
column8: Because only one price is paid
column10: The basis: Parallel Salam is two Salam deals separable from each other despite similar descriptions, so it does not lead to two sales in one.

column4: Bank A and a seller part without the Salam capital being paid, leaving it for a month. Per the Shari'ah basis, what does this turn the transaction into?
column5: A Murabahah to the purchase orderer
column6: A permitted Parallel Salam
column7: A prohibited sale of debt for debt
column8: A valid deferred Salam
column10: The basis: delay in paying capital with dispersal of the parties renders the transaction a sale of debt for debt, prohibited by scholarly consensus.

column4: A Salam contract is concluded on the basis of an earlier memorandum of understanding, and the parties say nothing about it at signing. What is the status of the memorandum's terms?
column5: They are merely moral, not contractual
column6: They lapse once the contract is signed
column7: They bind only the seller, not the buyer
column8: They become part and parcel of the contract
column10: Per 2/1/2, the memorandum's contents become part of the contract, unless the parties agreed at conclusion to exempt themselves from some obligations.

column4: An Istisna'a makes the manufacturer the buyer's agent to sell the goods if the buyer delays taking delivery. The sale brings less than the contract price. What follows?
column5: The maker bears the shortfall itself as the buyer's agent
column6: The maker has recourse to the buyer for the balance
column7: The buyer may cancel the contract and take his money back
column8: The shortfall is written off
column10: Per 6/5, the manufacturer sells on the buyer's behalf, keeps the price and returns any surplus; if short, it has recourse to the buyer, who bears sale expenses.

column4: A manufacturer goes bankrupt while making goods under an Istisna'a, none yet delivered. Does the ultimate purchaser have a prior right over those goods against third parties?
column5: No, unless they were wholly or partly delivered
column6: Yes, if he paid part of the price
column7: Yes, over the goods and the materials
column8: Yes, as the goods are being made specially for him
column10: Per 3/1/3, unless the items are delivered, the ultimate purchaser has no prior right over a third party to items still being produced if the supplier is bankrupt.

column4: Bank A agrees to sell to a customer 'the factory located at Plot 12', which already exists, on an Istisna'a basis. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid, if the price is paid in stages
column6: Valid, if the Bank owns the factory
column7: Invalid, as it is an existing identified asset
column8: Valid, if the factory is described in detail
column10: Per 3/1/3, the subject of Istisna'a may not be an existing identified capital asset, e.g. a designated car or factory; Istisna'a is for items identified by specification.

column4: Bank A sells a building to a customer by Istisna'a on deferred payment, and buys it from a builder by Parallel Istisna'a on immediate payment. What is required?
column5: Both must be on the same payment terms
column6: The builder must sign the customer's contract
column7: The customer must approve the builder's price
column8: The two contracts must remain separate
column10: Per 7/2, the Institution may sell on deferred terms and buy on immediate payment through Parallel Istisna'a, provided the two contracts remain separate.

column4: Bank A ordered 10 buses by Istisna'a. Before taking any possession, it wants to sell those same buses to a transport firm. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the Bank has already paid the maker in full
column6: Not permissible before actual or constructive possession
column7: Permissible at a price not above cost
column8: Permissible if the firm pays in advance
column10: Per 6/7, the subject-matter may not be sold before possession; the Institution may instead sell similar items by description through Parallel Istisna'a.

column4: On what does the Shari'ah basis ground the legitimacy of Istisna'a from the Sunnah?
column5: The Prophet's request to make a pulpit and a finger ring
column6: The Prophet's purchase of a she-camel from Abu Bakr
column7: The Hadith on paying with specified scale and weight
column8: The practice of Umar Ibn Al-Khattab on 'Arboun
column10: The basis: Istisna'a's legitimacy rests on the Prophet's request that a pulpit and a finger ring be manufactured for him, plus Istihsan and Shari'ah objectives.

column4: An Istisna'a customer pays early and Bank A grants an unstipulated rebate. Which precedent does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: The Prophet's request that a carpenter make a pulpit for him
column6: The Prophet asking Ubay Ibn Ka'b to write off part of a debt
column7: The Prophet's gift to Negus, conditional on survival
column8: The case of Hibban Ibn Munqidh on the option in a sale
column10: The basis: discount for unconditional early payment rests on the Prophet's saying in the case of Ubay Ibn Ka'b and his debtor: 'Write off a portion of your debt'.

column4: Bank A acts as a mere financier of a deal already concluded between a supplier and a customer, calling it Istisna'a. Why does the Shari'ah basis reject this?
column5: The price is not known at signing
column6: The Bank cannot own manufactured goods in Istisna'a
column7: It is a Riba deal, with Istisna'a as a cover-up
column8: The supplier's role is not specified in the contract
column10: The basis: a mere financier role leads to a Riba transaction, making the Istisna'a a mere cover-up and not a real Istisna'a.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis say a defect exclusion clause, valid in some sales, is invalid in Istisna'a?
column5: Istisna'a goods are always defect-free
column6: Defects in Istisna'a are the buyer's risk
column7: Only the buyer may stipulate such a clause in a contract
column8: It is valid only for specific, identified goods
column10: The basis: Istisna'a sells specified goods for future delivery, and exclusion of defect liability is valid only in the sale of particular identified goods.

column4: Bank A concludes an Istisna'a with a customer for a ship before the Bank owns the ship or any of the materials to build it. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, but only after a binding bilateral promise
column6: No, the Bank must first own the finished ship itself
column7: Yes, Istisna'a may precede owning the materials
column8: No, the Bank must first own the materials
column10: Per 2/1/1, the Institution and customer may conclude Istisna'a before the Institution has title to the subject-matter or the materials it will be made from.

column4: Bank A completes a building under an Istisna'a. Must the Bank and the customer exchange a new offer and acceptance to sell the completed building?
column5: Yes, unless the price was paid in advance
column6: No, the binding Istisna'a already governs the sale
column7: Yes, a sale needs a separate final contract
column8: Yes, as in a Murabahah, after the Bank takes possession
column10: Per 2/2/2, Istisna'a is binding, so no new offer and acceptance is needed after completion, unlike the promise in Murabahah.

column4: After an Istisna'a is concluded, the customer and the contractor agree to add an extra floor to the building. On what condition is this permissible?
column5: Only if a new Istisna'a contract replaces the old one
column6: Adjust the deadline but not the price
column7: Keep the original price and deadline
column8: Adjust the price and allow a reasonable period
column10: Per 4/1/1, amending or adding specifications is permissible if the price is adjusted and a reasonable period is granted for the new requirements.

column4: Bank A agrees to complete a customer's project left unfinished by the previous contractor. Who bears the cost of assessing the project's existing status?
column5: The customer
column6: Bank A
column7: Bank A and the customer equally
column8: The previous contractor
column10: Per 4/2/2, the project is assessed on its existing status at the customer's cost; debts from the incomplete Istisna'a are the customer's personal responsibility.

column4: As manufacturer in an Istisna'a, Bank A has a Parallel Istisna'a with a builder. Before delivery to the customer, who bears ownership risk and insurance costs?
column5: The customer, as the ultimate purchaser
column6: Bank A, which cannot shift that risk to the builder
column7: The builder and the customer equally
column8: The builder, under the terms of the Parallel Istisna'a
column10: Per 7/3, the Institution as producer bears ownership risk, maintenance and insurance before delivery and may not transfer its risk towards the customer to the maker.

column4: A government grants a builder the right to operate a toll road for 25 years as the price for building it under Istisna'a (BOT). Is this a valid price?
column5: Yes, usufruct of the subject-matter may be the price
column6: No, the Istisna'a price must always be paid in cash
column7: Yes, but only if a cash amount is also added to it
column8: No, usufruct can be paid only from another unrelated asset
column10: Per 3/2/1, the price may be cash, goods or usufruct for a period, including usufruct of the subject-matter itself, as in Build Operate Transfer (BOT).

column4: A contractor stops building on the purchaser's land due to his own misconduct. What is the purchaser's position regarding the partly built structure?
column5: He pays the full contract price
column6: He takes it without paying anything for the work done
column7: He pays its value and claims his actual damage
column8: He pays its value with no damage claim
column10: Per 4/2/4, where failure is due to the contractor's misconduct, the purchaser is liable only for the structure's value and the builder compensates actual damage.

column4: A manufacturer delivers items of better quality than specified, for no extra charge. The buyer had not particularly pursued the specified quality. What must the buyer do?
column5: Accept and pay for the extra quality
column6: Reject them as non-conforming
column7: Accept only at a discounted price
column8: Accept the items
column10: Per 6/1/2, the purchaser shall accept better quality offered without extra charge, unless the contract quality was particularly pursued by him.

column4: According to the Shari'ah basis, whose view supports Istisna'a being a binding contract, and why?
column5: The Maliki view: a promise is always binding
column6: Abu Yusuf's: the maker spends money to produce to specs
column7: Imam Ahmad's: 'Arboun makes contracts binding
column8: Ibn Rushd's: all sales are binding by scholarly consensus
column10: The basis cites Abu Yusuf's view in the Mejelle: the manufacturer spends money to produce to specification and would suffer loss if the buyer could refuse.

column4: Bank A, as manufacturer, wants the ultimate purchaser to supervise the construction to ensure conformity. How may this be arranged?
column5: By a clause making him a co-manufacturer
column6: By transferring the work's risk to him
column7: It cannot be arranged, due to conflict
column8: By a separate, independent agency contract
column10: Per 5/2, the Institution as manufacturer may draw up an independent and separate agency contract appointing the ultimate purchaser to supervise production.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis bar selling Istisna'a items before taking actual or constructive possession of them?
column5: It is selling a non-existent item one does not own
column6: It doubles the profit made by the Institution on the deal
column7: It breaches the defect liability rule
column8: It makes the price unknown to the final buyer
column10: The basis: selling items before possession is selling a non-existent item and what one does not own, as it is not available to the seller at contracting.

column4: An Istisna'a stipulates that Bank A will produce the subject-matter using its own resources. The Bank later wants another company to build it. What is the position?
column5: It may assign it if the quality is the same as promised
column6: It may assign it via Parallel Istisna'a
column7: It must abide by the condition and may not assign it
column8: It may assign it with notice to the buyer
column10: Per 3/1/4, if the contract stipulates production by the Institution's own resources, it must abide by this and has no right to assign production to another entity.

column4: An Istisna'a includes a fair penalty clause for late delivery by the manufacturer. The delay is due to force majeure. Is the penalty due?
column5: Yes, a penalty clause applies regardless of the cause
column6: No, penalty clauses are never allowed
column7: Yes, but reduced by half for force majeure
column8: No, it applies only if delay is not force majeure
column10: Per 6/6, a fair penalty for late delivery may be stipulated, but compensation is permissible only if the delay is not due to force majeure.

column4: Company X has a construction contract with Builder B but cannot pay him. It asks Bank A to step in purely to pay B on X's behalf, calling it Istisna'a. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if B agrees to the arrangement
column6: Permissible, if X repays the Bank later in instalments
column7: Not permissible to be a mere financial intermediary
column8: Permissible, as long as work has not started
column10: Per 2/1/3, the Institution may not be a financial intermediary between a buyer and a third party, especially if the buyer cannot pay, before or after work starts.

column4: A customer orders ships from a shipyard by Istisna'a through Bank A. The customer owns 40% of the shipyard. The deal was won by competitive bidding. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as he owns a third or more
column6: Permissible, as bidding was competitive
column7: Permissible, as he owns less than half
column8: Permissible if the Bank pays the shipyard
column10: Per 2/2/4, Istisna'a is impermissible where one third or more of the producing facility belongs to the customer, even if won by competitive bidding.

column4: Bank A, as ultimate purchaser, pays 'Arboun to a manufacturer. The Bank then rescinds the Istisna'a. What is preferable regarding the 'Arboun?
column5: Forfeit it and add a penalty for the rescission
column6: Limit the forfeiture to the actual damage
column7: Refund the 'Arboun in full to the Bank, whatever the damage
column8: Treat it as part of the price of a new contract
column10: Per 3/3/1, 'Arboun becomes part of the price if fulfilled or is forfeited on rescission, but it is preferable to limit forfeiture to the actual damage.

column4: Bank A buys equipment from a contractor for cash and sells it back to the same contractor on deferred terms at a higher price, labelled Istisna'a. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it is an interest-based device
column6: Permissible if the equipment is new
column7: Permissible if the contractor won it by competitive bidding
column8: Permissible, as the price is agreed by both parties
column10: Per 2/2/4, buying from the contractor for cash and selling back to him deferred at a higher price is a device for interest-based financing ('Inah).

column4: An Istisna'a links payments to completion of each construction stage. On what condition is this permissible?
column5: The total price is left open until completion
column6: Stages are customarily specified, without dispute
column7: The buyer pays the full price in advance at signing
column8: The stages are fixed by the contractor alone
column10: Per 3/2/2, payment may be tied to stages of completion if, by custom, such stages are subject to specification and identifying them will not lead to dispute.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis forbid pricing an Istisna'a on a Murabahah cost-plus basis?
column5: Istisna'a prices must be paid in cash
column6: Murabahah is valid only for sales of gold and silver
column7: Murabahah needs an existing owned item of known cost
column8: Cost-plus profits are always excessive
column10: The basis: Murabahah requires an existing owned item of known cost, while Istisna'a precedes ownership, its actual cost is known only on completion, and its price must be known at signing.

column4: A manufacturer asks Bank A, as ultimate purchaser in an Istisna'a, for a guarantee. Which may the Bank give?
column5: None, since the Bank is the buyer
column6: An interest-bearing deposit placed with the maker
column7: An undertaking to pay an extra amount if it pays late
column8: Consent to blocking withdrawals from an account
column10: Per 3/3/2, as ultimate purchaser the Institution may give guarantees such as a mortgage, personal guarantee, assignment, accounts or consent to blocking withdrawals.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow a penalty for late delivery in Istisna'a, though not for late payment of debts?
column5: Penalties are paid to charity in Istisna'a
column6: It concerns items to be produced, not a monetary debt
column7: The manufacturer is always the wealthier of the parties
column8: Istisna'a is not a binding contract
column10: The basis: the penalty clause serves the contract and relates to an obligation to produce and deliver items in the future, not to a monetary debt.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why can animals, fruits and vegetables not be the subject of an Istisna'a?
column5: They are sold only by weight
column6: They perish before the delivery date
column7: They are not transformed by human manufacture
column8: They cannot be described by specification
column10: The basis: Istisna'a means a sale of materials to be transformed by manufacture or construction; natural things like animals, fruits and vegetables are not covered.

column4: A manufacturer fulfils an Istisna'a by delivering conforming items produced by another firm before the contract. The buyer set no own-resources condition. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible; he must make the items himself
column6: Not permissible; the items existed beforehand
column7: Permissible only if the buyer is told first
column8: Permissible, as no own-resources condition was set
column10: Per 3/1/5, the manufacturer may use items by others existing before the contract if the buyer did not stipulate own resources, but not as a device to defer both counter-values.

column4: Bank A is asked to conclude an Istisna'a for fresh fruit and livestock to be supplied in six months. Is Istisna'a the right contract?
column5: No, Istisna'a is for items made or constructed
column6: Yes, Istisna'a covers any goods delivered at a later date
column7: Yes, if the items are fully specified in the contract
column8: Yes, if the price is paid in instalments over six months
column10: Per 3/1/1, Istisna'a is permissible only for materials transformed by a manufacturing or construction process involving labour.

column4: Bank A proposes an Istisna'a price set as 'actual cost of construction plus 10%', to be computed on completion. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the costs are audited by an auditor
column6: Permitted, if a ceiling on the cost is added
column7: Permitted, as the 10% margin is known in advance
column8: Not permitted; Istisna'a cannot be cost-plus
column10: Per 3/2/5, an Istisna'a cannot be drawn up on the basis of Murabahah, e.g. by determining the price on a cost-plus basis.

column4: Bank A buys turbines by Istisna'a for June delivery, paying cash to give the maker liquidity. It then sells similar turbines by Parallel Istisna'a. Which delivery date is acceptable for that sale?
column5: July, after the original June delivery
column6: Exactly the signing date of the sale
column7: Any date the buyer prefers
column8: May, before the original delivery
column10: Per 7/1, in this Parallel Istisna'a the delivery date in the parallel sale must not precede that in the original purchase, and the contracts stay separate.

column4: A contractor building on the purchaser's land under Istisna'a halts work. The contract has a clause for this case. What may the purchaser do?
column5: Charge the contractor interest on the delay
column6: Take the structure without paying anything
column7: Complete the work at the contractor's expense
column8: Nothing until a court ends the contract
column10: Per 4/2/3, on the purchaser's land it may be stipulated that he may perform the contract at the manufacturer's expense from the date work halted.

column4: Costs rise in Bank A's Parallel Istisna'a with a manufacturer. The Bank wants to raise the price in its Istisna'a with the customer accordingly. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the customer is duly notified in writing
column6: Not permissible; the two contracts are not linked
column7: Permissible, if the rise exceeds 10%
column8: Permissible, in proportion to the rise
column10: Per 7/4, no link may be made between the two contracts; a party may not raise the price due to cost increases in the Parallel Istisna'a.

column4: Bank A contracts by Istisna'a to sell a specific, identified car it does not own. Which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite against this?
column5: 'Muslims are bound by their conditions'
column6: 'Give a worker his wages before his sweat dries'
column7: 'Do not sell what you own not'
column8: 'Write off a portion of your debt'
column10: The basis: Istisna'a is a sale by specification; selling a specific identified item not owned violates the Hadith 'Do not sell what you own not'.

column4: Under an Istisna'a with stage payments, a contractor completes stage two in line with the specifications. What may he do?
column5: Wait for final delivery to be paid
column6: Request payment for that completed stage
column7: Request a bonus for early completion
column8: Request the full remaining price
column10: Per 3/2/3, where work or payment is divided by stages, the manufacturer may request payment for each stage carried out according to specification.

column4: Bank A's actual cost of completing an Istisna'a proves much lower than estimated, thanks to a discount in its Parallel Istisna'a. Must it pass a discount to the customer?
column5: No, the customer has no claim to the saving
column6: Yes, if the saving exceeds 10%
column7: Yes, in proportion to the saving
column8: Yes, the full amount of the saving made by the Bank
column10: Per 3/2/6, the Institution need not give a discount when costs are substantially lower; likewise it cannot charge more if they are higher.

column4: A contractor cannot finish a building on the purchaser's land. Why may the land owner not take the structure without paying, per the Shari'ah basis?
column5: The owner must pay the full contract price for the structure
column6: The contractor has become the owner of the land under it
column7: The structure is a gift to the owner
column8: Built at his request, which is stronger than permission
column10: The basis: construction was started by the builder at the purchaser's request, which is stronger than a mere permission to build on his land.

column4: Bank A acts as the builder (contractor) for a customer's office tower under an Istisna'a. Does the Istisna'a standard cover the Bank in this role?
column5: No, it covers the Institution only as the ultimate purchaser
column6: No, construction contracts fall outside Istisna'a
column7: Yes, it covers the Institution as purchaser or maker
column8: Only if the Bank builds with its own staff
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a whether the Institution is the ultimate purchaser or the manufacturer or builder.

column4: A buyer refuses without good reason to take finished goods after being enabled to take possession. They stay with the manufacturer. Who bears safekeeping costs?
column5: The two parties equally
column6: Nobody, until a court rules
column7: The manufacturer
column8: The ultimate purchaser
column10: Per 6/4, the goods remain with the manufacturer on trust, who is liable only for negligence or misconduct; the purchaser bears safekeeping expenses.

column4: A manufacturer offers to deliver conforming items two months early. The buyer refuses but has no good reason. What is the position?
column5: The buyer is obliged to accept them
column6: The buyer may refuse until the due date
column7: The buyer may accept at a discount
column8: Early delivery cancels the contract
column10: Per 6/2, early delivery of conforming items is allowed; the buyer must accept unless he has a good reason for refusing.

column4: A customer gives Bank A price quotations he obtained from several builders before an Istisna'a. How may the Bank use them?
column5: Only to fix the Istisna'a price at cost plus
column6: To help assess costs and its prospective profit
column7: It may not use them; that would be Murabahah
column8: Only by assigning those builders' contracts to itself
column10: Per 2/1/2, the Institution may benefit from price offers obtained by the customer to evaluate expenses and compute prospective profit.

column4: After an Istisna'a is signed, the authorities impose new safety requirements that add costs not borne by the manufacturer under the contract or by law. The contract has a clause for this. Who pays?
column5: The ultimate purchaser
column6: The manufacturer
column7: The Institution's Shari'ah Board
column8: The two parties equally
column10: Per 4/2/5, a clause may provide that extra expenses from later directives of the authorities, not borne by the manufacturer, are borne by the ultimate purchaser.

column4: After production, the manufacturer enables the buyer to take control of the goods. Later the goods are damaged with no negligence by the manufacturer. Who bears the loss?
column5: The manufacturer, until the goods are physically delivered
column6: The ultimate purchaser
column7: Both parties equally, as neither was negligent
column8: The Institution that financed the Istisna'a
column10: Per 6/3, delivery may be constructive by enabling the buyer to take control; the manufacturer's liability then ends and the purchaser's liability begins.

column4: A manufacturer inserts a clause in an Istisna'a contract stating that it is not liable for any defects in the goods. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the price is reduced
column6: Permitted if the buyer signs it
column7: Not permitted in an Istisna'a contract
column8: Permitted for hidden defects only
column10: Per 2/2/3, the manufacturer may not stipulate in the Istisna'a contract that he is not liable for defects.

column4: During an Istisna'a, a force majeure event sharply raises the cost of materials. How may the contract price be amended?
column5: It may never be changed once it has been agreed
column6: Only upwards, by the manufacturer acting alone
column7: Only by adding a charge for the extra time needed
column8: By agreement, arbitration or court, up or down
column10: Per 4/2/1, the price may be amended upwards or downwards for force majeure by agreement, arbitration or judicial procedure, read with 4/1/3.

column4: Bank A offers a customer: 1,000,000 if the plant is delivered in 12 months, or 950,000 if delivered in 18 months; one offer is chosen at conclusion. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, price may vary with the delivery date
column6: No, it is a sale of debt for debt
column7: No, the price must be one single fixed amount
column8: Yes, but the choice may be left open
column10: Per 3/2/4, the Istisna'a price may vary with delivery date, and several offers may be negotiated provided only one is finally chosen to conclude the contract.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow the Istisna'a price to be deferred or paid in instalments without being a sale of debt for debt?
column5: Because Istisna'a is a form of Salam
column6: Because the price is not treated as a debt at all
column7: Labour makes it like leasing, with deferred rents
column8: Because the goods are delivered in full at signing
column10: The basis: labour (transformation and added value) is a key part of the item, making Istisna'a similar to leasing where rentals may be deferred.

column4: Midway through an Istisna'a, the ultimate purchaser demands design changes. The manufacturer refuses. Can the purchaser oblige him?
column5: Yes, if he pays for the changes
column6: No, not without the manufacturer's consent
column7: Yes, if the changes are minor
column8: Yes, as the buyer controls the design
column10: Per 4/1/2, the ultimate purchaser cannot oblige the manufacturer to introduce modifications without the manufacturer's consent.

column4: An Istisna'a customer pays early. Bank A wants to give him a rebate, which was not stipulated in the contract. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it resembles Riba
column6: Not permissible; the full price is due
column7: Permissible only if stipulated in the contract
column8: Permissible, as it was not stipulated at conclusion
column10: Per 4/1/3, a rebate for pre-payment is permissible provided it is not stipulated at the conclusion of the contract.

column4: After taking possession of Istisna'a goods, Bank A appoints the manufacturer as its agent to sell them to the maker's customers for a percentage fee. When is this permissible?
column5: Never, as the maker is the seller
column6: If agency and Istisna'a were not made in connection
column7: Only if the fee is a fixed amount
column8: Only if the agency is given free of any charge or fee
column10: Per 6/8, after possession the Institution may appoint the manufacturer as selling agent, free or for a fee, if the agency and Istisna'a were not connected.

column4: An Istisna'a customer asks Bank A for six more months to pay the price. The Bank agrees if the customer pays an extra amount for the extension. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the work is already complete
column6: Permissible as an agreed contract amendment
column7: Not permissible to charge for an extension
column8: Permissible if the price was left unpaid by him
column10: Per 4/1/3, amendments may not provide an additional sum for extending the payment period; a rebate for pre-payment is allowed if not stipulated at conclusion.

column4: A contractor cannot continue an Istisna'a because the ultimate purchaser obstructed the work through misconduct. What is the contractor entitled to?
column5: Nothing, as the work is incomplete
column6: The full contract price only, whatever work was done
column7: The value of the work done only, without compensation
column8: The value of the work done plus compensation
column10: Per 4/2/4, if failure is due to the purchaser's misconduct, the contractor is entitled to the value of the completed work and compensation for damage.

column4: Bank A offers two prices depending on whether a plant is delivered in 12 or 18 months. To which ruling does the Shari'ah basis liken this?
column5: Giving a labourer wages that differ by finishing time
column6: Setting the profit as a percentage of cost
column7: Charging more for extending a debt's due date for payment
column8: Taking 'Arboun to secure performance
column10: The basis: Istisna'a is analogous to Ijarah, where a labourer may be offered two dinars if he finishes in one day or one dinar if in two days.

column4: A machine delivered under an Istisna'a does not conform to the agreed specifications. What right does the customer have?
column5: Only to wait until it is rebuilt
column6: Only to accept it at the full price
column7: Only to demand a penalty payment
column8: To accept it or to refuse it
column10: Per 2/2/1, Istisna'a is binding when type, kind, quality, quantity and price are known; if the item does not conform, the customer may accept or refuse it.

column4: Bank A takes over a project abandoned by a customer's previous contractor. Must the Bank use that previous contractor to finish the work?
column5: Yes, the previous contractor must finish his own work
column6: No, it may finish the work by any means it sees fit
column7: Yes, unless the customer agrees to another contractor
column8: No, but the customer must choose the builder
column10: Per 4/2/2, the Institution is not bound to deal with the previous contractor and may stipulate that the work be completed by any means it deems fit.

column4: Bank A, as manufacturer in an Istisna'a, wants a penalty clause against the customer for late payment of the price. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if paid to the Bank's charity fund
column6: Permitted, in the same way as for late delivery penalties
column7: Not permitted against the purchaser for late payment
column8: Permitted if the penalty is fair
column10: Per 6/6, a penalty clause may be stipulated for late delivery by the manufacturer, but not against the ultimate purchaser for default on payment.

column4: A customer insists that Bank A itself manufacture his order. Why does the Shari'ah basis accept such a condition?
column5: He may want a maker known for competence and quality
column6: It removes the Bank's liability for defects in the goods
column7: It lets the Bank charge a higher profit
column8: It makes Parallel Istisna'a unnecessary
column10: The basis: the buyer may be interested in a particular supplier's distinguished competence and the quality of its manufacturing or construction.

column4: Why is Parallel Istisna'a not 'two sales in one', according to the Shari'ah basis?
column5: The second contract is merely a promise
column6: Only one single price is paid for the two deals together
column7: The same parties sign the two contracts together
column8: They are two separate deals with no link between them
column10: The basis: Parallel Istisna'a involves two separate Istisna'a deals with no link, so it is not two sales in one, and it is non-Riba-based financing.

column4: Company X contributes a business whose assets include a negligible amount of receivables. On which principle does the Shari'ah basis accept this?
column5: Necessity making the prohibited permissible
column6: Taba'iyyah: things that follow another thing
column7: Maslahah for the public good
column8: Custom as a source of rulings
column10: Per the basis, receivables combined with other assets at a negligible ratio may be contributed under the principle of Taba'iyyah (dependent things follow the principal).

column4: In a service partnership of two printers, one partner provides the printing machine required for the work. Which arrangement does the standard permit?
column5: He provides it for a fee charged against the Sharikah as an expense
column6: The machine automatically becomes common capital of the Sharikah once he brings it
column7: He receives a guaranteed fixed share of profit for it
column8: He must sell the machine to the partnership at its original purchase price
column10: Per 3/3/4, a party may provide the capital goods for fees charged against the Sharikah as expenses; each may also provide and own his own goods.

column4: Bank A asks whether the Sharikah standard governs its rules for a building that two heirs jointly own by inheritance, with no partnership contract. What is the position?
column5: Covered only if the heirs later convert it to diminishing Musharakah
column6: Covered, as a form of Sharikat al-'Inan between the two heirs, since both own shares
column7: Not covered: it excludes ownership partnership in jointly owned assets
column8: Covered, as a modern corporation of the allotment (Muhassah) type
column10: Per clause 1, the standard does not cover ownership partnership where the parties jointly own an asset; it covers Sharikat al-'Aqd (contractual partnership).

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah, Bank A's equity falls from 80% to 50%, but the parties keep the original profit ratio. Is that allowed?
column5: No, the profit ratio must fall with Bank A's share
column6: Yes, and losses may also stay at the original ratio if the parties so agree
column7: No, profit must always match the equity ratio as it changes after each unit sale
column8: Yes, if losses still follow the ratio of equity ownership
column10: Per 5/5, partners may keep the profit ratio despite changes in equity, or amend it, provided losses are allocated according to the equity share of ownership.

column4: Company G offers to guarantee the capital of Partner P in a Sharikah, free of charge. Company G owns 60% of Partner P's capital. Is this third-party guarantee acceptable?
column5: No, the guarantor must not own more than half of the guaranteed entity
column6: Yes, provided Company G is not itself a partner in the Sharikah
column7: Yes, since the guarantee is given without any consideration or fee
column8: No, unless Company G owns the whole of Partner P's capital
column10: Per 3/1/4/3(III), the third-party guarantor should not own more than half of the capital in the entity to be guaranteed.

column4: Three engineers form a service partnership to render consultancy. One of them performs far more of the services than the others. What is the Shari'ah implication?
column5: He is entitled to all of the profit of the partnership
column6: He must receive a fixed lump sum from the profit first
column7: None; unequal services rendered have no Shari'ah implication
column8: The partnership is void unless every partner renders an equal share of the services
column10: Per 3/3/2, there is no Shari'ah implication regarding any disproportion in the services that the partners or their representatives may have rendered.

column4: In a Sharikat al-'Inan with no restriction on management, partner Ahmad sells partnership goods on deferred payment and rents out a partnership asset without consulting others. Was he entitled?
column5: No, only the partner with the largest capital share may act for the partnership
column6: Yes, each partner may in principle do such acts in the partnership's interest
column7: Yes, but only for spot sales; renting out partnership assets needs consent
column8: No, deferred sales require the prior consent of all the other partners
column10: Per 3/1/3/1, each partner may in principle act for the partnership in spot or deferred sales, renting its assets and what is customary in trading.

column4: Bank A (an Institution) plans a partnership with a conventional bank for a Shari'ah-acceptable project. Which arrangement is among the guarantees the standard calls for?
column5: Profit is fixed in advance as a percentage of the capital invested
column6: The conventional bank first converts to Islamic banking before signing
column7: The conventional bank guarantees Bank A's capital against any loss
column8: Operations managed or supervised by an entity observing Shari'ah rules
column10: Per 3/1/1/2, assurances must be obtained that Shari'ah is observed, such as having the operations managed or supervised by an entity that observes Shari'ah rules.

column4: A Sharikah contract assigns Partner A a predetermined 50,000 of profit. The clause is never amended and a profit is realised. How is profit divided?
column5: 50,000 to Partner A and the remainder to the others
column6: Equally among all partners per head
column7: By each partner's respective share in capital
column8: By a ratio chosen by the managing partner
column10: Per 3/1/5/7, a predetermined amount is void; if not amended before profit comes forth, profit is divided based on each partner's share in capital.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis reject a partner contributing receivables alone as Sharikah capital?
column5: They are not assets in possession and may lead to Riba
column6: Debts can never be owned or transferred between persons under Shari'ah rules
column7: Receivables have no monetary value until they are collected in cash
column8: Only the Institution may contribute debts, and individuals may not
column10: Per the basis, debts cannot actually be used in operations as they are not assets in possession, and this may lead to Riba when the partner is the debtor.

column4: A Sharikah reaches its expiry date and all assets are sold at market value. What is paid first from the proceeds?
column5: The financial liabilities of the partnership
column6: Liquidation expenses
column7: The profit shares of the partners
column8: The partners' capital contributions
column10: Per 3/1/6/3, proceeds are used for (a) liquidation expenses, then (b) financial liabilities, then (c) distribution of the remainder to partners.

column4: On what principle does the Shari'ah basis rest the permissibility of modern corporations?
column5: Necessity makes the prohibited permissible, and corporations arise from necessity
column6: Custom overrides explicit texts in all commercial matters of the age
column7: Human transactions are in principle permissible (Mubah)
column8: Modern laws are binding on all parties dealing within a given State
column10: Per the basis, transactions are in principle permissible (Mubah) absent a clear injunction, and these corporations parallel 'Inan, Mudarabah and the like.

column4: On the date of distribution, a partner in a Sharikah decides to give part of the profit due to him to another party. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, since ratios are fixed at conclusion
column6: Permissible to relinquish part of his profit on that date
column7: Not permissible, as it changes the loss-sharing ratio
column8: Permissible only if agreed in the original contract
column10: Per 3/1/5/2, a partner may relinquish, on the date of distribution, a part of the profit due to him in favour of another party.

column4: A partner wants to lend a large sum of partnership funds to a friend for a year. The other partners have not been asked. What is the ruling?
column5: Not allowed unless all the partners consent
column6: Allowed if the friend gives a mortgage as security
column7: Allowed if the partner later repays any loss himself
column8: Allowed, as each partner may act for the partnership
column10: Per 3/1/3/1, a partner may not give out grants or loans that may damage the partnership unless all partners consent; only minor customary short-term loans are allowed.

column4: Before any valuation, partners pay themselves amounts 'on account' each quarter. What condition applies under the standard?
column5: The amounts become final profit once paid and are not reviewed
column6: The amounts must be fixed as a percentage of each partner's capital
column7: Such payments are prohibited before the partnership is liquidated
column8: They undertake to reimburse any excess over their final profit share
column10: Per 3/1/5/11, funds may be allocated on account before valuation, provided parties undertake to reimburse any excess over their share after valuation.

column4: Company X issues shares and adds a percentage to their actual value on the subscription date to recover issuing costs. Under what condition is this allowed?
column5: The percentage is paid as an extra dividend to the old shareholders of the company
column6: The percentage is approved by the licensed stockbroker
column7: The percentage reflects an appropriate estimate of actual expenses
column8: The percentage does not exceed 10% of nominal value, whatever the expenses are
column10: Per 4/1/2/2, the issuer may add a percentage to recover issuing expenses provided it is appropriately estimated to reflect the actual expenses incurred.

column4: Before signing, Bank A learns that the funds a conventional bank will contribute to a proposed Sharikah clearly come from non-permissible sources. May Bank A proceed?
column5: No, partnership is not permissible when this has become evident
column6: Yes, if Bank A takes a higher profit share as purification
column7: Yes, since the funds are mixed once contributed to capital
column8: Yes, provided the conventional bank manages the operations
column10: Per 3/1/1/2, partnership with non-Muslims or conventional banks is permissible unless it has become evident that their funds are from non-permissible sources.

column4: For final profit distribution, the partners use constructive valuation of Sharikah assets. How must outstanding receivables due in two years be valued?
column5: At face value plus a time-value increment
column6: At the amount a buyer would pay for early settlement of the debt
column7: At present value, discounted at a market interest rate
column8: At expected cash value after allowing for doubtful debts
column10: Per 3/1/5/9, receivables are valued at expected cash value after allowance for doubtful debts; time value of money or discount for early payment is not allowed.

column4: In a Sharikah, the customer gives a binding promise to buy all the partnership assets at liquidation. On what price basis is this promise permissible?
column5: The face value of the partners' contributions
column6: Market value or a price agreed at the date of buying
column7: The original cost of the assets plus a fixed margin
column8: The capital of the other partner, whatever the value
column10: Per 3/1/6/2, a partner may promise to buy the assets at market value or as agreed at the date of buying; a promise at face value is not permissible.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow current account balances to be used as Sharikah capital although they are loans?
column5: They become the bank's own capital once they are deposited
column6: Banks guarantee a fixed return on current account balances
column7: They are deposits held on trust by the bank, not loans
column8: They are presumed possessed as available to holders on demand
column10: Per the basis, current accounts are presumed possessed by the holders because the Institutions must pay on demand irrespective of their financial situation.

column4: A customer wishes to use the balance of his current account with Bank A as his capital contribution in a Sharikah with Bank A. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only after the funds are converted into commodities
column6: Permissible, though current accounts are juristically loans to the bank
column7: Permissible only in a Sharikah with a third party, not with Bank A
column8: Not permissible, since current accounts are loans to the bank
column10: Per 3/1/2/5, current account funds, though juristically loans, can be contributed to a Sharikah with the Institution itself or with a third party.

column4: A partnership in commendum fails with debts exceeding its assets. What is the liability of a sleeping partner?
column5: Limited to the lots he owns, not his personal assets
column6: Unlimited, but only after the managing partners pay
column7: Joint with the managing partners from personal wealth
column8: Nil, since sleeping partners bear no losses
column10: Per 4/3/1/2, managing partners are jointly liable from personal wealth, while each sleeping partner's liability is limited to the number of lots he owns.

column4: A company proposes Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares: they share in net profit without voting and are gradually redeemed through profit distributions before termination. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if holders agree in advance
column6: Permitted if they carry voting rights
column7: Not permitted to issue them
column8: Permitted for bearer shareholders only
column10: Per 4/1/2/15, it is not permitted to issue Tamattu' (enjoyment) shares, which share in net profit without voting and are gradually redeemed from profits.

column4: The Sharikah contract grants partner Ahmad, who keeps the partnership's accounts, a fixed monthly fee in addition to his profit share. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since accounting is a service and not capital
column6: Not permitted, but he may get a greater profit share instead
column7: Permitted, provided the fee is charged as an expense
column8: Not permitted, and he may not receive any extra profit either
column10: Per 3/1/3/4, a fixed remuneration for a partner who manages or provides services in the Sharikah contract is not permitted; a greater profit share is allowed.

column4: In a three-partner Sharikah with no agreed term, one partner gives due notice and withdraws. What is the effect?
column5: He forfeits his share as a penalty for leaving
column6: The whole partnership terminates automatically, as it lacks an agreed term
column7: He takes his share; the other partners' partnership continues
column8: He may not withdraw until the venture is complete
column10: Per 3/1/6/1, each partner may withdraw after due notice and take his share; this does not necessitate termination of the remaining partners' partnership.

column4: Under the standard, Sharikat al-'Aqd (contractual partnership) is defined as an agreement between two or more parties to combine what, for the purpose of making profits?
column5: Their assets, labour or liabilities
column6: Their labour only, under a fixed wage
column7: Their debts owed by third parties only
column8: Their assets only, in monetary form
column10: Per 2/1, Sharikat al-'Aqd is an agreement between two or more parties to combine their assets, labour or liabilities for the purpose of making profits.

column4: A partner asks why contributions in a different currency must be converted at the current exchange rate. Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: The hadith of the co-owner who frees a slave
column6: The partnership of Al-Sa'ib with the Prophet
column7: The saying of Ali Ibn Abu Talib on loss sharing
column8: Ibn Umar's camel sales at Al-Baqi' at the day's rate
column10: Per the basis, conversion is a currency exchange allowed at the current rate, as the Prophet endorsed Ibn Umar's sales at Al-Baqi' at the current rate.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is underwriting a share issue without consideration permissible?
column5: It is a gift from the company to the underwriter
column6: It is a form of interest-free loan to the company, repaid at its nominal value
column7: It involves no impermissible act like a fee for a guarantee
column8: The underwriter becomes a sleeping partner in the company for the unsubscribed shares
column10: Per the basis, underwriting without consideration is an undertaking not involving an impermissible act, such as taking a commission for a guarantee.

column4: Partners in a joint-liability company agreed on a ten-year duration. In year four, one partner notifies the others he is withdrawing. What is the ruling?
column5: He may withdraw without notice at any time
column6: He may not withdraw, as the agreed duration must be observed
column7: He may withdraw since the contract is not binding on any of the partners
column8: He may withdraw if he brings in a substitute partner approved by the court
column10: Per 4/2/2/2, withdrawal is allowed if no duration was set; if partners agreed on a duration it must be observed. Notice and no damage are also required.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow tangible assets, after valuation, as Sharikah capital?
column5: The aim of free use of funds and profit sharing is still realised
column6: Cash contributions would involve Riba between partners, so capital must be in kind
column7: The Hanafi school requires capital to be tangible goods
column8: Tangible assets carry no risk of loss for the partners, unlike cash contributions
column10: Per the basis, Sharikah aims to let partners use the money freely and share profit, which is realisable with tangible assets as with cash (Maliki and Hanbali view).

column4: In a Sharikah whose currency is the dinar, one partner pays his capital in US dollars and another in euros. How are their shares determined?
column5: By the nominal amounts in each currency, unconverted
column6: By the exchange rates prevailing at liquidation
column7: By an exchange rate fixed by the managing partner
column8: By translating both into dinars at current exchange rates
column10: Per 3/1/2/2, contributions in different currencies must be translated into the Sharikah's currency at current exchange rates to determine shares and liabilities.

column4: Sara did not stipulate that she would be a sleeping partner. In fact she did no work, but the agreement gives her profit above her capital share. Is she entitled?
column5: Yes, she may stipulate extra profit though she did not work
column6: Yes, but only if she also bears extra losses
column7: No, extra profit requires actual work by the partner herself
column8: No, profit must always match each partner's capital contribution
column10: Per 3/1/5/3, a partner who did not stipulate being a sleeping partner is entitled to stipulate an additional profit share even if he did not work.

column4: Partners hire an outside manager for a fixed salary and also set aside part of the investment profit for him as an incentive. Is this permissible?
column5: No, a manager may receive either a salary or a share of profit, not both
column6: No, an incentive from profit makes the salary void
column7: Yes, but only if the manager also contributes capital
column8: Yes, a fixed remuneration plus a portion of profit as incentive
column10: Per 3/1/3/3, it is permissible to set aside a portion of the investment profit plus a fixed remuneration as an incentive for the manager.

column4: A sleeping partner in a partnership in commendum wants to take part in managing the company. What does the standard say?
column5: He may manage if he holds the largest lots
column6: Sleeping partners are not entitled to manage or interfere
column7: He may manage jointly with a joint-liability partner
column8: He may manage if the other partners consent by majority
column10: Per 4/3/1/3-4, sleeping partners may not interfere in operations; management goes to a joint-liability partner or a third party.

column4: An investor undertakes to subscribe all unsubscribed shares of an issue at nominal value and asks a fee for this underwriting. What is the ruling on the fee?
column5: Permitted, as a commission for the guarantee he has given
column6: Permitted if the fee is a percentage of the total issue size, not a lump sum
column7: Not permitted for underwriting; fees for other services are allowed
column8: Not permitted, nor are fees for feasibility studies or marketing
column10: Per 4/1/2/4, underwriting must be without consideration; the shareholder may charge for services other than underwriting, such as feasibility studies or marketing.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis apply the general rules, especially of 'Inan, to diminishing Musharakah?
column5: To keep it from becoming mere interest-based financing
column6: Because it has no juristic personality separate from that of the partners
column7: Because the Institution manages it and bears the whole risk of loss
column8: Because it is a form of Mudarabah in which the customer is the Mudarib
column10: Per the basis, applying 'Inan rules safeguards diminishing Musharakah from becoming a mere interest-based financing with payment beyond a share of income.

column4: Which of the following is listed by the standard among the traditional Fiqh-nominate partnerships rather than the modern corporations?
column5: Partnership in commendum, with managing and sleeping partners
column6: Company limited by shares, with managing and sleeping partners
column7: Allotment (Muhassah) partnership, a private form of company
column8: Sharikat al-Wujuh (partnership of creditworthiness or reputation)
column10: Per 2/2/1, the traditional Fiqh-nominate partnerships are Sharikat al-'Inan, Sharikat al-Wujuh (or Al-Dhimam) and Sharikat al-A'mal; the others are modern corporations.

column4: Ali stipulated he would be a sleeping partner and provides 30% of the capital, yet asks for 50% of the profit. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, provided Ali also bears 50% of any loss of the Sharikah
column6: No, unless Ali brings additional capital to match his profit share
column7: No, extra profit above capital share may not go to a sleeping partner
column8: Yes, the profit ratio may always be agreed freely among the partners
column10: Per 3/1/5/3, profit may be disproportionate to capital provided the additional percentage over contribution is not in favour of a sleeping partner.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis prohibit a fixed remuneration in the Sharikah contract for a partner who helps manage?
column5: Management work cannot be valued in money, so no wage can be fixed for it
column6: It may guarantee his capital or shield him from loss
column7: It would make him a sleeping partner who bears no liability for losses
column8: Partners may not perform any management work in the company at all
column10: Per the basis, a fixed remuneration for a partner who assists in management may lead to guaranteeing his capital or to his not bearing loss in proportion to capital.

column4: A partner in a Muhassah partnership wants to terminate his participation unilaterally. What does the standard require?
column5: Notice to the partners and no damage to partners or clients
column6: Sale of his share to an outside buyer first
column7: Approval of the company's creditors and clients before he may leave
column8: Consent of the majority of the other partners given in a general meeting
column10: Per 4/5/2/4, he may terminate if he notifies other partners and the withdrawal does not cause damage to other partners or clients of the company.

column4: A company plans two share classes: Class P gets priority in profit distribution and at liquidation; Class V gets only extra voting rights. Which may it issue?
column5: Neither class
column6: Class V only
column7: Class P only
column8: Class P and Class V
column10: Per 4/1/2/14, preference shares with financial priority at liquidation or profit distribution are not permitted; procedural privileges such as voting are allowed.

column4: Bank A enters a Sharikah with a customer and asks that the contract stipulate that the customer guarantees Bank A's capital. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the customer receives a higher profit ratio in return
column6: Permitted if the guarantee is limited to half of the capital
column7: Permitted if the customer is the managing partner
column8: Not permitted: a partner may not guarantee another's capital
column10: Per 3/1/4/1, partners hold Sharikah assets on trust; it is not permitted to stipulate that a partner guarantees the capital of another partner.

column4: From the outset, partners engage Omar, a non-partner, to manage their Sharikah solely for 10% of the profit earned. How is Omar classified?
column5: As a partner bearing a share of losses from his own funds
column6: As an agent entitled to a fee even if there is no profit
column7: As a Mudarib, entitled only to a share in profit, if any
column8: As an employee entitled to a fixed wage plus 10% of profit
column10: Per 3/1/3/3, if management is from the outset for a percentage share in profit, the manager is a Mudarib entitled only to profit, if any, with no further remuneration.

column4: Ahmad contributes 60% and Bilal 40% of the capital of a Sharikat al-'Inan. They agreed to share profit 50:50. The venture loses 100,000. How is the loss borne?
column5: Each partner bears 50,000 as agreed for profit
column6: Ahmad bears 60,000 and Bilal bears 40,000
column7: Ahmad bears the whole loss as the larger partner
column8: Bilal bears 60,000 since he takes a larger profit ratio
column10: Per 3/1 and 3/1/5/4, profit follows the agreement but losses are borne according to each partner's contribution to the capital.

column4: Two traders form a partnership to buy goods on credit on their reputation; liability is 50:50 but profit is 70:30. Is it valid for these two ratios to differ?
column5: No, such a partnership is invalid without monetary capital
column6: No, the liability and profit ratios must always be equal, as profit follows liability
column7: Yes, the liability ratio may by agreement differ from the profit ratio
column8: Yes, but only if the difference between the ratios is small
column10: Per 3/2/1, in a partnership of creditworthiness the parties set each partner's profit and liability share; the liability share may differ from the profit share.

column4: A Sharikah contract gives Bank A a profit of 8% of its capital each year, with the rest of the profit to the customer. What is the status of this clause?
column5: Valid if the customer is the managing partner
column6: Valid if Bank A also bears losses by its capital share
column7: Valid, as the percentage is fixed at the outset
column8: Not valid: profit must be an undivided percentage of profit
column10: Per 3/1/5/1, each partner must get an undivided percentage of profit, not a sum of money or a percentage of the capital.

column4: Company G owns Partner P and offers to guarantee P's capital in a Sharikah. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is such ownership a problem?
column5: It is in substance a partner guaranteeing a partner's capital
column6: The guarantee would amount to contributing debts as capital of the Sharikah
column7: Company G would become a sleeping partner in the Sharikah with no right to manage
column8: The guarantee would then be given for consideration paid out of the profit
column10: Per the basis, the guarantor must not own the guaranteed or vice versa, since ownership makes it in substance a guarantee by a partner of another partner's capital.

column4: Company Z, independent of a Sharikah, offers to guarantee the capital of one partner against loss in return for an annual fee. Is this third-party guarantee acceptable?
column5: Yes, a third party may guarantee capital on any terms
column6: Yes, provided the fee is paid out of partnership expenses
column7: No, a third party may never guarantee a partner's capital
column8: No, a third-party guarantee must not be for consideration
column10: Per 3/1/4/3, a third party may guarantee capital loss, but the guarantee should neither be for consideration nor linked in any manner to the Sharikah contract.

column4: A manufacturing firm contributes its net assets, which include some receivables, as its share in a Sharikah. Is the inclusion of receivables acceptable?
column5: Yes, since the debts are inseparable from the other assets
column6: Yes, but only if the receivables exceed the tangible assets
column7: No, any debt in a contribution invalidates the capital
column8: No, the receivables must first be removed from the net assets
column10: Per 3/1/2/4, debts may form part of the capital contribution where inseparable from other assets, e.g. a manufacturing firm contributing its net assets.

column4: Subscribers to a new stock company pay the first instalment of their shares and the rest is deferred. Under what condition is this permissible?
column5: Only the paid instalment counts and the rest is waived
column6: The subscribers pledge their shares to an interest-based lender to fund the rest
column7: Instalments cover all shares; liability is confined to subscribed shares
column8: The deferred instalments carry a fixed markup to compensate the company for the delay
column10: Per 4/1/2/5, instalment subscription is allowed provided the instalments cover all the shares and the company's liability is confined to the value of subscribed shares.

column4: A Sharikah contract between Bank A (70% of capital) and a customer (30%) stipulates that the customer will bear all losses. What is the status of this term?
column5: Permitted since the customer consented to it
column6: Not permitted: losses follow each partner's capital share
column7: Permitted if the customer has a higher share of the profit
column8: Permitted if the customer manages the partnership
column10: Per 3/1/5/4, losses must be commensurate with capital contributions; it is not permitted to hold one partner liable for the entire loss.

column4: The rules of Sharikat al-'Inan apply to a stock company except in which respects?
column5: Agency of the managers and trust in holding assets
column6: Profit sharing and loss bearing in proportion to the capital shares held
column7: Use of capital in monetary form and the valuation of non-monetary contributions
column8: Shareholders' limited liability and no unilateral termination
column10: Per 4/1/1/1, the 'Inan rules apply except the limited liability of shareholders and that the company cannot be unilaterally terminated by one party or a minority.

column4: Bank A requires its partner to provide a mortgage over his house, to be used only if he commits misconduct, negligence or breach of contract. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as it secures misconduct, negligence or breach
column6: Not permissible, as partners act on a trust basis
column7: Permissible only if it also covers ordinary business losses
column8: Not permissible, as it amounts to guaranteeing capital
column10: Per 3/1/4/2, a partner may stipulate that another partner provides a personal guarantee or mortgage to cover misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah, the customer promises to buy Bank A's units at their original value whatever the market value. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the promise is non-binding on the customer and Bank A
column6: Not permitted: it guarantees Bank A's equity value
column7: Permitted as the price is known in advance and removes uncertainty for both
column8: Permitted if the units are bought gradually
column10: Per 5/7, acquisition must be at market value or a price agreed at the time; face or original value would mean the customer guarantees the Institution's equity.

column4: At expiry, after expenses and liabilities, the remaining assets do not cover the partners' full capital. How is the remainder distributed?
column5: Equally among the partners per head
column6: First to the managing partner, then the others
column7: Pro rata to each partner's share of capital
column8: According to the agreed profit-sharing ratio
column10: Per 3/1/6/3(c), if assets fall short of the contributed capital, distribution takes place on a pro rata basis to the shares of capital.

column4: A partner is appointed manager by a separate independent contract with a wage. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the wage allowed?
column5: The wage is a gift from the other partners and not a binding obligation
column6: He acts as an employee of the company, not as a partner
column7: Wages are part of his profit share, paid in advance of the final distribution
column8: He bears more risk than the other partners, so he is compensated with a wage
column10: Per the basis, under a separate independent contract the partner becomes an employee of the company and is not acting in the capacity of a partner.

column4: A shareholder in a stock company wants to dissolve the company with respect to his own shares and take back his capital. What is the ruling?
column5: He may not dissolve it for his shares but may sell them
column6: He may withdraw his capital at nominal value
column7: He may dissolve it for his shares if he holds more than 10% of the capital
column8: He may dissolve it for his own shares after giving due notice to the board
column10: Per 4/1/2/1, the stock company contract is binding; no one may dissolve the company in respect of his shares, but he may sell or relinquish them.

column4: Partners in a Sharikah agree to set aside 2% of the profit as a charitable donation to a hospital that is not a partner. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if the hospital becomes a partner
column6: Permissible only from the capital, not the profit
column7: Permissible
column8: Not permissible, as profit belongs only to partners
column10: Per 3/1/5/14, it is permissible to agree on setting aside a proportion of profit for non-partners as a charitable donation.

column4: Bank A and a customer are partners. The customer is appointed manager under a separate contract, independent of the Sharikah, and may be dismissed at any time. May he earn a specific remuneration?
column5: Yes, but only if the remuneration is a percentage of capital
column6: No, unless the Sharikah contract is amended to include the fee
column7: No, a partner may never receive remuneration for management work
column8: Yes, as the appointment is independent of the Sharikah contract
column10: Per 3/1/3/5, a partner may be appointed by an independent contract, dismissable without amending the Sharikah, and may then earn a specific remuneration.

column4: Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for the rule that losses must be borne in proportion to capital contributions?
column5: A resolution of Al Baraka Forum
column6: The saying of Ali Ibn Abu Talib
column7: The hadith of Ibn Umar at Al-Baqi'
column8: The hadith of Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi
column10: The basis cites Ali Ibn Abu Talib: 'Profit distribution is according to agreement of the partners and loss must be borne in proportion to the contribution in the capital.'

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah for a house, Bank A requires the customer to bear all insurance and maintenance costs since he will eventually own the house. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted as he will become the owner
column6: Permitted for insurance but not maintenance
column7: Not permitted to stipulate this
column8: Permitted if his profit share is raised
column10: Per 5/3, it is not permitted to stipulate that one partner bears all insurance or maintenance costs on the ground that he will eventually own the subject matter.

column4: Partners terminate a Sharikah on the basis of constructive liquidation; some assets are valued but not sold. How are these unsold assets treated?
column5: As a debt owed by the managing partner to the other partners after liquidation
column6: As property of the partner with the largest share
column7: As assets that must be sold within one year
column8: As the capital of a new partnership between the parties
column10: Per 3/1/6/3, in constructive liquidation the Sharikah is regarded as ended and a new partnership begun, with the valued unsold assets as its capital.

column4: Partners ask why they may not leave their profit ratios undetermined until profit is realised. What reason does the Shari'ah basis give?
column5: It involves uncertainty that may lead to dispute
column6: Ratios must always match capital shares
column7: It would make the capital a debt
column8: Profit belongs to the Institution until then
column10: Per the basis, deferring the profit ratio until profit is realised involves uncertainty which may potentially lead to dispute.

column4: Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for distributing profit on constructive valuation?
column5: The hadith of Al-Sa'ib, the Prophet's partner
column6: Ibn Umar's sale of camels at Al-Baqi' for dinars, taking dirhams
column7: The saying of Ali Ibn Abu Talib that loss is by the ratio of capital
column8: The hadith on valuing a slave partly freed by a co-owner
column10: The basis cites its use in Zakah and theft and the hadith: if a co-owner frees his part of a slave, the slave is valued by fair value and freed.

column4: Partner X wants to contribute a warehouse rather than cash to a Sharikah. What does the standard require?
column5: Only the rental income of the warehouse may be contributed
column6: It is rejected because Sharikah capital must be monetary only
column7: All partners must agree and value the warehouse in currency
column8: It is accepted at its historical cost without any valuation
column10: Per 3/1/2/1, tangible assets may be capital with all partners' agreement after their monetary value is determined in currency to know each partner's share.

column4: After a loss occurs, and without any prior condition in the contract, one partner volunteers to bear the entire loss. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid, as it was not a prior condition
column6: Valid only if he is the managing partner
column7: Void, since losses must follow capital shares
column8: Void unless approved by a court
column10: Per 3/1/5/4, it is valid that one partner takes, without any prior condition, the responsibility of bearing the loss at the time of the loss.

column4: Partnership goods held by the managing partner are destroyed by a fire with no misconduct, negligence or breach on his part. Is the managing partner liable?
column5: Yes, if he receives a larger profit share
column6: No, partners hold Sharikah assets on a trust basis
column7: Yes, for half the loss as a shared responsibility
column8: Yes, the managing partner always guarantees the assets
column10: Per 3/1/4/1, partners maintain the assets on a trust basis; no one is liable except for misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column4: In a partnership in commendum, the contract gives a sleeping partner a profit equal to 10% of his capital. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if profit exceeds 10% of capital
column6: Permissible if the managing partners agree
column7: Not permissible
column8: Permissible, as he cannot manage the company
column10: Per 4/3/2/2, it is not permissible to stipulate that a sleeping partner has a right to profit as a percentage of the capital or a lump sum.

column4: Two partners sign a Sharikah and agree to set their profit-sharing percentages later, once the profit is realised. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if losses are fixed by capital shares
column6: Not permitted: ratios must be set when the contract is concluded
column7: Permitted, as long as they agree on the ratios before distribution
column8: Permitted, since profit belongs to the partners
column10: Per 3/1/5/2, the profit percentage of each partner must be determined at conclusion of the contract and may not be deferred until profit is realised.

column4: A Sharikah owns assets acquired for leasing and distributes rental income to the partners every year. How are these annual distributions treated?
column5: As final profit that is not subject to any later settlement
column6: As a fixed remuneration of the partners for managing the leases
column7: As a return of capital to each partner in equal instalments
column8: On account, subject to settlement at the end of the Sharikah
column10: Per 3/1/5/12, where the subject matter is leased assets or services, the amount distributed annually is on account, subject to settlement and reimbursement at the end.

column4: A third party voluntarily promised to cover Partner A's capital loss in a Sharikah, then fails to do so. Partner A claims the Sharikah is void and stops meeting his obligations. Is he entitled?
column5: No, he cannot void the Sharikah or refuse his obligations
column6: Yes, but only for the portion of capital that was lost
column7: Yes, since he relied on the guarantee when contracting
column8: No, but the other partners must then cover his loss
column10: Per 3/1/4/3, the beneficiary may not claim the Sharikah is void or refuse his obligations if the guarantor fails to meet his voluntary promise.

column4: A stock company restricts its liability to its paid-up capital. What condition does the standard attach to this?
column5: Shareholders guarantee any shortfall from their personal assets on a pro rata basis
column6: The limitation is made public to inform the company's customers
column7: A court approves the limitation upon incorporation
column8: The company holds no debt above its paid-up capital at any time during its life
column10: Per 4/1/2/9, restricting the company's liability to paid-up capital is permissible if made public, so customers know its financial position without uncertainty.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may profit be disproportionate to capital contributions?
column5: Profit is deserved through funds, work or risk borne
column6: Losses are also disproportionate to the capital contributions
column7: Capital ratios are unknown until liquidation, so profit cannot follow them
