column8: Profit belongs only to the managing partner, who alone works for the Sharikah
column10: Per the basis (Hanafi and Hanbali view), one deserves profit by funds contributed, work done or risk borne, so the ratio may be agreed accordingly.

column4: Partners agree profit is shared 60:40 in year one and 50:50 in year two, depending on the profit level. Under what condition is this variable method allowed?
column5: It must be approved again by all partners at each period's end
column6: It is allowed only if the loss ratios vary in the same way
column7: It must match the partners' capital ratios in both periods
column8: It must not likely preclude any partner from sharing in profit
column10: Per 3/1/5/5, any permanent or variable profit allocation method is allowed if it does not lead to the likelihood of a partner being precluded from profit.

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah, the customer promises to set aside part of his profit share to buy Bank A's units at intervals. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it is a lump sum from profit
column6: Not permissible, as profit must be distributed
column7: Permissible as a way to acquire the Institution's equity
column8: Permissible only if the units are bought at face value
column10: Per 5/8, acquisition may include the client's promise to set aside a portion of his profit or return to acquire a percentage of the Institution's equity.

column4: Two years into a Sharikah with equal capital, the partners want to change the profit ratio from 50:50 to 60:40. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible at any time, while losses remain shared by capital shares
column6: Permissible only if the loss-sharing ratio is also changed to 60:40
column7: Not permitted once the contract has been concluded by offer and acceptance
column8: Permissible only at liquidation of the partnership, not during its term
column10: Per 3/1/1/4, partners may amend the terms and profit ratio at any time, taking into account that losses are shared according to each partner's share in capital.

column4: The partners of a Sharikah decide not to distribute this year's profit and to set aside a share of it as an investment risk reserve. Is this allowed?
column5: Only by a court order on the request of a partner
column6: Only a profit equalisation reserve is permitted
column7: Yes, both non-distribution and such reserves are permissible
column8: No, all realised profit must be distributed to partners at the end of each year
column10: Per 3/1/5/13, it is permissible not to distribute profits and to set aside a ratio of profit as a solvency, investment risk or profit equalisation reserve.

column4: A diminishing Musharakah contract gives Bank A the right to withdraw its share of capital at any time. What is the ruling on this clause?
column5: Permitted only after the first year
column6: Permitted if the customer has the same right to withdraw his share at any time
column7: Permitted, as Bank A is the financier and bears the main risk of the venture
column8: Not permitted under the rules of Sharikat al-'Inan
column10: Per 5/2, the general rules of partnership, especially 'Inan, apply; the contract may not give any party a right to withdraw his share in the capital.

column4: Mid-year, the partners want to allocate revenues as profit before deducting operating costs and taxes. What does the standard require before allocation of profit?
column5: Nothing; revenue may be allocated as received
column6: Costs, expenses and taxes deducted, capital kept intact
column7: Only taxes need be deducted before profit is allocated to partners
column8: Only the managing partner's fee must be deducted first
column10: Per 3/1/5/6, profit may not be allocated unless operating costs, expenses and taxes are deducted and the capital of the Sharikah is maintained intact.

column4: An investor buys shares with an interest-based loan from his broker, mortgaging the shares as security. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the broker is licensed
column6: Permitted if the shares are Shari'ah-compliant
column7: Permitted, as the shares secure the loan
column8: Not permitted
column10: Per 4/1/2/6, it is not permitted to purchase shares using interest-based loans from a broker or other person against mortgaging the shares.

column4: A student asks which Sunnah evidence the standard cites for the permissibility of partnership. Which is cited?
column5: Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi was the Prophet's business partner
column6: The Prophet's sale of camels at Al-Baqi' for dinars and dirhams
column7: The hadith of the co-owner of a slave who frees his part of him
column8: The hadith 'No harm and no reciprocal harm'
column10: The basis cites Al-Sa'ib Ibn Abu Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi, a partner of the Prophet in business, whom he welcomed as 'my brother and my partner'.

column4: An Institution arranges a Shari'ah-based syndicated financing and invites conventional banks to join as partners. Under what condition is this permissible?
column5: The conventional banks receive a fixed return on their portion of the funds
column6: The Institution secures the right to manage, under Shari'ah supervision
column7: The conventional banks take over management, with Shari'ah review afterwards
column8: The conventional banks contribute less than half of the funding
column10: Per 3/1/1/3, conventional banks may be included in a Shari'ah-based syndicated financing if the Institution manages it and operations are subject to Shari'ah supervision.

column4: A stock company issues new shares to increase its capital. Its old shares' fair value is above their nominal value. At what price may the new shares be issued?
column5: Only at a discount, to attract new subscribers
column6: Only at nominal value, to treat all subscribers equally and avoid disputes
column7: At the old shares' fair value, as assessed by experts
column8: At any price the board sets, regardless of the value of the old shares
column10: Per 4/1/2/3, new shares may be issued at the fair value of the old shares per expert valuation, i.e. at a premium, discount or market value.

column4: Which of the following arrangements falls within the scope of the Sharikah (Musharakah) and Modern Corporations standard?
column5: A diminishing Musharakah between an Institution and customer
column6: A Mudarabah between a Rabb al-Mal and a Mudarib
column7: An agricultural sharecropping or irrigation partnership (Muzara'ah)
column8: Regulatory market procedures and listing rules for modern companies
column10: Clause 1 applies the standard to modern partnerships including diminishing Musharakah, but excludes Mudarabah, sharecropping and market regulatory procedures.

column4: A creditor of a joint-liability company claims his whole debt directly from one partner, without first claiming from the company. Is he entitled?
column5: Yes, but only from the managing partner
column6: No, he may claim only each partner's pro rata part
column7: No, he must first claim from the company
column8: Yes, he may claim from any partner as he deems fit
column10: Per 4/2/2/1, a creditor may demand fulfilment of all or part of his rights from any partner; he is not obliged to claim from the company first.

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah, the customer leases Bank A's share of the jointly owned property. Who is responsible for periodical maintenance?
column5: The customer, as lessee of the whole property
column6: Each partner, for his own share
column7: Bank A, as the majority owner
column8: The customer, once he owns over half
column10: Per 5/9, either partner may lease the other's share for a specified amount and duration; each partner remains responsible for the periodical maintenance of his share.

column4: A partner in a joint-liability company wants to bring in his brother as a substitute partner in his place. The other partners object. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the brother is at least equally wealthy and creditworthy
column6: Permissible after giving due notice
column7: Not permissible without the other partners' agreement
column8: Permissible, as shares in such a company are freely transferable like stock
column10: Per 4/2/2/3, a partner in a joint-liability company may not bring in a substitute for himself without the agreement of the other partners.

column4: Company X offers, as its whole contribution to a new Sharikah, the receivables its customers owe it. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted: debts alone cannot be a capital contribution
column6: Permitted if valued at their face amount in currency
column7: Permitted if valued at a discount for early payment by debtors
column8: Permitted if the debtors are partners themselves
column10: Per 3/1/2/4, it is not permitted that debts (receivables) alone be used as a contribution to the Sharikah capital.

column4: At year end, partners propose a final allocation of profit based on the profit projected for the venture, without any valuation. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the projection is made by independent valuation experts
column6: Permitted if the partners later waive any difference that arises
column7: Not permitted: final allocation must rest on actual profit earned
column8: Permitted only where the Sharikah holds assets acquired for leasing
column10: Per 3/1/5/10, final allocation of profit may not be based on expected profit; it must be based on actual profit through actual or constructive valuation.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis permit a third party's promise to guarantee partners' capital?
column5: It is a guarantee given against a commission to the partners
column6: It is a charitable act independent of the partnership contract
column7: The third party shares in the profit of the partnership
column8: The third party acts as an agent of the partners in the venture
column10: Per the basis, a third party's promise to guarantee is a mere charitable act and an undertaking independent of the partnership contract.

column4: Bank A's Shari'ah board explains why partnership with conventional banks can be permitted despite a hadith restricting partnership with non-Muslims. What reason is given?
column5: Necessity always overrides the hadith, since banking cannot operate without them
column6: The hadith applies only to individuals, not to banks or other juristic persons
column7: The conventional bank's funds are purified once they are mixed with Islamic funds
column8: The feared Riba is absent where Shari'ah compliance is guaranteed
column10: Per the basis, the cause of the prohibition is fear of interest or impermissible contracts, which is absent when there are guarantees to apply Shari'ah rulings.

column4: A company limited by shares suffers a loss exceeding its capital. How are the excess losses treated under the standard?
column5: They are written off with no partner liable
column6: They are borne by the managing partners
column7: They are shared by all partners per head
column8: They are borne by the sleeping partners pro rata
column10: Per 4/4/2/4, losses are borne per capital shares and any excess losses are borne by the managing partners.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a joint-liability partner barred from bringing in a substitute without the other partners' consent?
column5: Shares in such companies cannot be sold at all, even with the other partners' consent
column6: The substitute would be a sleeping partner without any liability for the company's debts
column7: It would change the company's juristic personality and so dissolve it by law
column8: The partner's personality and personal assets matter to them
column10: Per the basis, the partner's personality is significant because the company's liability includes his personal assets, and a substitute may be in a weaker position.

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah, Bank A's contract states that the customer shall buy Bank A's units every quarter as part of the partnership contract itself. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as it is the essence of diminishing Musharakah
column6: Permitted if the customer signs each sale separately
column7: Not permitted; only an independent promise to buy is allowed
column8: Permitted if the price is the market value
column10: Per 5/1, the buying and selling must not be stipulated in the partnership contract; the buyer may give only a promise to buy, independent of that contract.

column4: Partners agree that any profit above 1 million belongs to the managing partner, and profit up to that ceiling is shared 50:50. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, profit above a ceiling may be given to a particular partner
column6: No, this is a lump sum that violates profit sharing
column7: Yes, but only if the managing partner is a sleeping partner
column8: No, profit must always follow capital shares
column10: Per 3/1/5/8 (subject to 3/1/5/3), it is permissible to agree that profit above a certain ceiling belongs to a particular partner.

column4: A service partnership contract states that one partner receives 20,000 from the profit as a lump sum before the rest is shared. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if he renders more services than the other partners do
column6: Not permitted: no lump sum may be specified from the profit
column7: Permitted, since there is no monetary capital in a service partnership
column8: Permitted if the partners agree unanimously
column10: Per 3/3/3, profit in a service partnership is shared by the agreed ratio, and the contract should not specify a lump sum from profit for a particular partner.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may a partner not promise to buy partnership assets at face value, while a promise at market value is allowed?
column5: Face value guarantees the capital; market value does not
column6: Market value is known at the contract date, so there is no Gharar in the promise
column7: Face value involves Riba, as it is in effect a currency exchange between partners
column8: Face value would make the partner a Mudarib rather than a partner in the Sharikah
column10: Per the basis, a promise to buy at face value constitutes a guarantee of capital, prohibited by Shari'ah; market value does not.

column4: An investor sells shares he does not own, relying on his broker's promise to lend him the shares by delivery date. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the investor pays no interest to the broker
column6: Permitted if delivery is made on the settlement date
column7: Permitted if the broker is licensed by the authorities
column8: Not permitted: the promise is not ownership or possession
column10: Per 4/1/2/7, one may not sell shares he does not own; a broker's promise to lend shares at delivery does not constitute ownership or possession.

column4: In a partnership in creditworthiness (Sharikat al-Wujuh), goods bought on credit are sold at a loss. How is the loss borne?
column5: By the partner who negotiated the purchases on credit
column6: Equally among the partners per head, whatever was agreed
column7: By the liability ratio each partner undertook for purchases on credit
column8: By the agreed profit-sharing ratio between the partners, whatever liability each undertook
column10: Per 3/2/3, profit follows the agreement, but loss is borne by each partner according to the ratio he undertook in the assets purchased on credit.

column4: Of the four categories of partnership classified by the Fuqaha, which does the Shari'ah basis describe as the most important?
column5: Sharikat al-Abdan
column6: Sharikat al-'Inan
column7: Sharikat al-Wujuh
column8: Sharikat al-Mufawadah
column10: The Shari'ah basis lists 'Inan, Abdan, Mufawadah and Wujuh, and states that Sharikat al-'Inan is the most important of all.

column4: A board member asks what the general basis of Sharikah is, since each partner acts for himself and for the others. What does the Shari'ah basis say?
column5: Charitable donation
column6: Guarantee (Kafalah)
column7: Agency (Wakalah)
column8: Mudarabah
column10: Per the basis, the general basis of Sharikah is agency (Wakalah): each partner acts as principal and as agent for the others; Mufawadah also adds guarantee.

column4: Partners agree that only partner Bilal will manage their Sharikah. Later partner Ahmad signs a sale on behalf of the partnership. What does the standard say?
column5: The other partners are bound by their consent not to act for the partnership
column6: Ahmad may act because he contributed part of the partnership capital
column7: Every partner keeps an unrestricted right to act on the partnership's behalf
column8: Restricting management to one partner is not permissible in Sharikah
column10: Per 3/1/3/2, partners may restrict management to one partner; the others are then bound to abide by their consent not to act on behalf of the partnership.

column4: Which Qur'anic verse does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of Mudarabah?
column5: 'And, verily, many partners oppress one another, except those who believe and do good'
column6: 'O you who believe! Fulfil your contracts and promises'
column7: 'Allah has permitted trading and forbidden Riba'
column8: 'Others travelling through the land, seeking of Allah's bounty'
column10: The basis cites the verse on those travelling through the land seeking Allah's bounty, interpreted as those who travel to trade and seek permissible income.

column4: A Mudarib has already bought goods with the Mudarabah capital. The capital provider now wants to terminate unilaterally. What is the ruling?
column5: The contract is binding until actual or constructive liquidation
column6: The contract becomes binding only from its maturity date
column7: He may terminate it if he pays the Mudarib a fair wage for the work already done
column8: He may terminate at once and reclaim the full cash value of the capital provided
column10: Per 4/3/1, once the Mudarib has commenced the business, the Mudarabah becomes binding up to the date of actual or constructive liquidation.

column4: In a three-year Mudarabah with a 50:50 ratio, year 1 loses 100,000 and year 2 earns 150,000. Nothing has been distributed. What profit is shareable at the end of year 2?
column5: Nothing at all until the Mudarib repays the loss
column6: 150,000, as each year's result stands on its own
column7: 50,000, after the loss is set off against later profits
column8: 150,000 less the Mudarib's share of the year 1 loss
column10: Per 8/7, no profit is recognised unless capital is intact; losses are compensated by profits of future operations and brought forward against them.

column4: A trainee asks how the Sunnah supports a capital provider restricting a Mudarib. Which report does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: Ali Ibn Abu Talib's saying on sharing profit and loss
column6: Ibn Umar's sale of camels at Al-Baqi' for dinars at the day's rate
column7: Umar Ibn Al-Khattab's restriction of an orphan's Mudarabah trade to Iraq
column8: Al-'Abbas's conditions to his Mudarib, approved by the Prophet
column10: Per the basis, Al-'Abbas stipulated that his Mudarib not travel by sea, pass valleys or trade in livestock, and the Prophet approved these conditions.

column4: Bank A manages its joint investment accounts on a Mudarabah basis and also issues Mudarabah Sukuk. Which of these does the Mudarabah standard cover?
column5: Neither, since the standard covers bilateral contracts only
column6: The joint investment accounts, but not the Mudarabah Sukuk
column7: Both, since each is based on the Mudarabah contract
column8: The Mudarabah Sukuk, but not the joint investment accounts
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers joint and special purpose investment accounts run on Mudarabah, but not Sukuk of Mudarabah, which have a separate standard.

column4: Company X owes Bank A 1 million. Bank A proposes to treat this debt as Mudarabah capital, with Company X as Mudarib. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the debt is already due and Company X is able to pay it
column6: Permissible if Company X has given adequate guarantees for the debt
column7: Not permissible to use a debt owed by the Mudarib as capital
column8: Permissible if the profit ratio is agreed in advance
column10: Per 7/3, it is not permissible to use a debt owed by the Mudarib or another party to the capital provider as capital in a Mudarabah contract.

column4: A Mudarabah contract is later concluded on the basis of a memorandum of understanding that is silent in the contract itself. What is the status of the memorandum's contents?
column5: They are part of the contract unless originally exempted from it
column6: They lapse once the actual Mudarabah contract has been signed
column7: They bind only the Mudarib and never bind the capital provider who signed the contract
column8: They apply only if repeated word for word in the new contract
column10: Per 3/3, the MoU contents become an integral part of any future contract unless the parties had originally agreed to exempt themselves from some obligations.

column4: Company X, acting as Mudarib for Bank A, is liquidated during the Mudarabah term. What is the effect on the Mudarabah?
column5: It continues with Company X's shareholders taking over as Mudarib
column6: It is liquidated, as the institution acting as Mudarib ended
column7: It continues until the agreed maturity date regardless
column8: It passes automatically to Company X's creditors to complete the term
column10: Per 10/1/5, a Mudarabah is liquidated on the death of the Mudarib or the liquidation of the institution that acts as Mudarib.

column4: Midway through a Mudarabah, the parties agree to change the profit ratio from 60:40 to 50:50 for the next year only. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if approved by an independent third party
column6: Permitted only at the final liquidation of the Mudarabah
column7: Not permitted once the contract has been concluded
column8: Permissible to change it at any time and set its duration
column10: Per 8/3, the parties may change the profit distribution ratio at any time and define the duration for which the agreement remains valid.

column4: Why, according to the Shari'ah basis, is Mudarabah needed instead of handing money to an investor for a periodic pre-agreed payment?
column5: Mudarabah avoids the need for any profit ratio
column6: A pre-agreed periodic payment would make it a debt with Riba
column7: Investors may not deal with capital belonging to others
column8: A pre-agreed payment would make the contract binding
column10: Per the basis, money cannot increase without work, and giving money for a periodic pre-agreed payment (rent) to an investor would be a debt with Riba.

column4: A Mudarabah contract omits the profit ratio and there is no customary practice on it. The Mudarib has worked for a year. What is the outcome?
column5: Void; the Mudarib gets a common market price for his work
column6: Void; and the Mudarib gets nothing for his year of work
column7: Valid; the profit is then shared equally by default between the two parties
column8: Valid; all of the profit goes to the capital provider, as the Mudarib took no share
column10: Per 8/4, absent a ratio and custom, the Mudarabah is void ab initio and the Mudarib receives a common market price for the services he provided.

column4: A Mudarib hires a worker to perform tasks that, by custom, any similar fund manager does himself. Who pays the worker's wages?
column5: The capital provider, from his profit share
column6: The Mudarabah funds, then deducted at liquidation
column7: The Mudarib, from his own personal funds
column8: The Mudarabah funds, as an operating expense
column10: Per 9/4, work customarily done by a fund manager is part of the Mudarib's duties; if he hires someone for it, wages come from his personal funds.

column4: Under a separate agreement independent of the Mudarabah, the Mudarib is hired for a fee to do work not customarily part of Mudarabah operations. If this agreement ends, what happens?
column5: The Mudarabah contract terminates as well
column6: The Mudarib loses his profit share
column7: The fee converts into a share of profit
column8: The Mudarabah contract is not affected
column10: Per 8/2, such a separate agreement is permissible; its independence means that terminating it will not affect the Mudarabah contract.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, besides the capital not being available, why is a debt owed by the Mudarib barred as Mudarabah capital?
column5: The Mudarib would become a sleeping partner with no right to manage
column6: The creditor may seek extra return for extending the debt
column7: Debts cannot be valued in any currency at all while they remain unpaid
column8: Debts carry no risk at all for the capital provider, who is the creditor
column10: Per the basis, it involves potential Riba: the creditor may be suspected of extending the debt tenure for extra consideration under the name of Mudarabah.

column4: A Mudarib wants to distribute profit while the Mudarabah capital is impaired. Which hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite against this?
column5: The co-owner who frees his part of a jointly owned slave and must value the rest
column6: Umar giving an orphan's funds for Mudarabah trade in Iraq, the profit being shared
column7: The Musali likened to a trader profiting only when capital is safe
column8: Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi, the business partner of the Prophet before his mission
column10: The basis cites the hadith likening a Musali to a businessperson who secures no profit unless the capital is secured; profit before capital recovery is invalid.

column4: A capital provider signs a Mudarabah but keeps the funds in his own locked account; the Mudarib has no access to them. What is the effect?
column5: Invalid: the capital must be available to the Mudarib
column6: Valid, since the contract was signed by both of the parties and its terms are clear
column7: Valid, but the Mudarib then becomes a guarantor of the funds
column8: Valid, as long as the capital is known in amount and currency
column10: Per 7/4, for validity the capital must be wholly or partly put at the Mudarib's disposal, or he must have free access to it.

column4: A Mudarib travels abroad for the Mudarabah. No amount for living expenses was agreed with the capital provider. What may he take from the Mudarabah funds?
column5: Nothing, unless an amount was agreed in advance
column6: Only travel costs, never living expenses
column7: A fixed daily amount set by the Mudarib himself
column8: Living and travel expenses as per custom and reason
column10: Per 9/7, absent agreement the Mudarib takes living expenses by custom and reason, and is also entitled to travelling expenses by custom and reason.

column4: A Mudarib wishes to accept funds from another investor on a Mudarabah basis while managing Bank A's Mudarabah. Under what conditions may he?
column5: With Bank A's permission, if his duties to Bank A are not affected
column6: Freely, since an unrestricted Mudarib may do so at will, without telling Bank A
column7: Only if he guarantees Bank A's capital in return for its consent to this
column8: Never, since a Mudarib may manage only one Mudarabah at a time
column10: Per 9/1/6(b), by permission of the capital provider, the Mudarib may accept funds from a third party if this does not affect his duties under the first Mudarabah.

column4: Ahmad gives Bilal funds under a contract titled 'Qirad', stating a profit ratio and Bilal's role as investor. Can this be a valid Mudarabah?
column5: No, Qirad refers to an interest-free loan only
column6: Yes, but only if a court registers the contract
column7: No, only the word Mudarabah concludes the contract
column8: Yes, Mudarabah may be concluded using the term Qirad
column10: Per 4/1, the Mudarabah contract may be concluded using terms such as Mudarabah, Qirad or Mu'amalah.

column4: A Mudarabah contract omits the profit ratio. Local custom is to share Mudarabah profit equally. How is profit distributed?
column5: Entirely to the capital provider
column6: By the ratio of capital to labour value
column7: Equally, following the customary practice
column8: The contract is void and the Mudarib gets a wage
column10: Per 8/4, if no ratio is stipulated, customary practice applies; if custom is equal distribution, profit is distributed equally.

column4: Bank A gives funds as a restricted Mudarabah. Which restriction is consistent with the definition of restricted Mudarabah?
column5: Requiring Bank A's staff to buy and sell jointly with the Mudarib in the market
column6: Limiting investment to a given location or type of investment
column7: Requiring the Mudarib to guarantee a minimum return on the capital provided
column8: Limiting the Mudarib to a commodity that is out of season
column10: Per 5/2, the capital provider may restrict the Mudarib to a location or type of investment, but not in a manner that unduly constrains his operations.

column4: Parties agree that profit up to 15% of capital is shared 70:30, and any profit above that ceiling goes to the Mudarib. What is the ruling?
column5: Void, as profit is linked to capital
column6: Permissible only if the excess goes to the capital provider
column7: Void, as it is a lump-sum stipulation
column8: Permissible; this ceiling arrangement is an exception
column10: Per 8/5, the lump-sum rule does not apply where parties agree profit over a ceiling goes to one party, and profit up to it is shared as agreed.

column4: Bank A gave funds to a Mudarib under a Mudarabah with no fixed term. Before the Mudarib has started any business, Bank A wants to terminate. May it?
column5: Yes, but Bank A must first pay the Mudarib a fixed fee
column6: Yes, the contract is not binding and may be ended unilaterally
column7: No, a Mudarabah becomes binding on both parties as soon as it is signed by them
column8: No, termination always requires the Mudarib's consent, even before any business starts
column10: Per 4/3, a Mudarabah is in principle not binding and either party may terminate it unilaterally, except after commencement or where a duration was agreed.

column4: Without the capital provider's consent, a Mudarib donates part of the Mudarabah funds to charity and waives a debt owed to the Mudarabah. What is the ruling?
column5: Each act is permitted in an unrestricted Mudarabah
column6: The debt waiver is allowed but not the donation
column7: Neither act is permitted for the Mudarib
column8: The donation is allowed but not the debt waiver
column10: Per 9/6, the Mudarib may not make a loan, gift or charitable donation from the funds, nor waive a Mudarabah right without the capital provider's consent.

column4: A capital provider gives a Mudarib two funds: profit on Fund 1 goes to the Mudarib and profit on Fund 2 to the capital provider. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible
column6: Permissible if the funds are invested separately
column7: Permissible if both funds are equal
column8: Permissible if losses are also split this way
column10: Per 8/6, it is not permissible to give two capitals on condition that profit of one goes to the Mudarib and profit of the other to the capital provider.

column4: A capital provider tells the Mudarib: 'Do business according to your expertise.' What limits still apply to the Mudarib's actions?
column5: None, he may act in any way he deems fit since the mandate is absolute
column6: He may only trade in the capital provider's own city
column7: He must obtain the capital provider's approval before each single transaction
column8: He must act in the parties' interest and per business custom
column10: Per 5/1, in an unrestricted Mudarabah the Mudarib's freedom must be exercised in the parties' interests and the profit objective, per business customs.

column4: At liquidation, a Mudarabah's total expenses exactly equal its total revenues. What do the parties receive?
column5: The Mudarib gets his profit ratio applied to the total revenues
column6: Capital back to the provider, nothing to the Mudarib
column7: The Mudarib gets a fair wage for his work, paid out of the capital
column8: The capital is reduced by the Mudarib's fee, which is due whether or not profit exists
column10: Per 8/7, if expenses equal revenues, the capital provider receives his capital back without profit or loss, and there is no profit for the Mudarib.

column4: Bank A is drafting a Mudarabah memorandum of understanding with a customer. Which item should the memorandum indicate?
column5: The type of guarantees from the Mudarib for negligence or misconduct
column6: A fixed annual amount of profit payable to Bank A on its capital
column7: A guarantee by the Mudarib of the capital against any market loss
column8: The Mudarib's fixed fee payable in addition to his profit share
column10: Per 3/2, the MoU should indicate restricted or unrestricted use, the profit ratio, and the guarantees from the Mudarib to cover negligence, misconduct or breach.

column4: In an unrestricted Mudarabah, the Mudarib appoints another person to buy a commodity and sells goods on deferred payment. Were these actions within his powers?
column5: No, he must personally do all the work himself
column6: No, deferred sales need the capital provider's consent
column7: Yes, each is within an unrestricted Mudarib's powers
column8: Only the appointment is allowed, not deferred sales
column10: Per 9/1/2 and 9/1/5, an unrestricted Mudarib may appoint another to carry out work, such as buying a commodity, and may buy and sell on deferred payment.

column4: For constructive valuation at the end of a Mudarabah, how must receivables due in a year be measured?
column5: At net realisable value, after a provision for doubtful debts
column6: At present value discounted at the market interest rate for the year of deferral
column7: At the price a third party would pay to buy the debt
column8: At face value plus a charge for the deferred period at the prevailing rate
column10: Per 8/8, receivables are measured at cash equivalent or net realisable value; neither time value nor discount for the payment period is considered.

column4: A Mudarib takes customary personal expenses from the funds though the contract is silent. Which principle in the Shari'ah basis supports him?
column5: Harm must be removed at any cost
column6: Certainty is not removed by doubt
column7: Necessity makes the prohibited permissible
column8: What is known by custom applies as a condition
column10: Per the basis, what is known by custom is deemed to apply as a condition even if not clearly stipulated, so custom permits common personal expenses.

column4: At liquidation, a Mudarabah shows a net loss and the Mudarib was neither negligent nor guilty of misconduct. How is the net loss treated?
column5: Recovered from the Mudarib's guarantee
column6: Deducted from the capital; the Mudarib is not liable
column7: Carried forward as a debt owed by the Mudarib
column8: Shared 50:50 between the Mudarib and the provider
column10: Per 8/7, if losses exceed profits at liquidation, the net loss is deducted from capital; the Mudarib, a trustee, is not liable absent negligence or misconduct.

column4: A Mudarib asks for a fixed monthly management fee in addition to his profit share for managing the Mudarabah. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if paid from the capital provider's share
column6: Permissible if agreed in the Mudarabah contract
column7: In principle not permissible to take both
column8: Permissible if the fee is below the profit share
column10: Per 8/2, in principle it is not permissible to earn a share of profit in addition to a fee in a Mudarabah contract.

column4: Bank A holds a guarantee from its Mudarib. The Mudarabah loses money due to a general recession, with no fault by the Mudarib. May Bank A enforce the guarantee?
column5: Yes, but only up to the amount of the profit expected from the Mudarabah
column6: Yes, guarantees in Mudarabah cover every capital loss, whatever its cause
column7: No, guarantees are never permitted in a Mudarabah
column8: No, only for misconduct, negligence or breach of terms
column10: Per clause 6, the capital provider may obtain adequate guarantees but may not enforce them except in cases of misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column4: A Mudarib sells Mudarabah goods below the market price to a friend, with no benefit to the Mudarabah. What does the standard say?
column5: He may sell at any price, being the manager of the funds
column6: He may do so as long as the price still covers the cost
column7: He is not entitled to sell below the common or market price
column8: He may do so freely in an unrestricted Mudarabah
column10: Per 9/5, the Mudarib may not sell below the common or market price unless it obviously serves an objective in the interest of the Mudarabah.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why does a Mudarabah end on the death of the Mudarib?
column5: The capital passes to the Mudarib's heirs, who must continue the Mudarabah
column6: It includes agency, which ends on the agent's death
column7: The profit ratio becomes unknown on his death, making the contract uncertain
column8: The Mudarib's guarantee lapses on his death, so the capital cannot be protected
column10: Per the basis, Mudarabah is similar to, or at least includes, agency, and an agency contract is terminable by the death of the agent.

column4: Parties agree a Mudarabah will run for three years. After one year, the Mudarib alone wishes to end it. What is the ruling?
column5: It cannot end before three years except by mutual agreement
column6: He may end it if he returns the capital without profit
column7: Only the capital provider may end it before maturity
column8: He may end it at any time as Mudarabah is non-binding
column10: Per 4/3/2, where the parties agree a duration, the contract cannot be terminated before the end of that duration except by mutual agreement.

column4: A Mudarabah contract gives the capital provider 6% of the capital each year as profit, and the rest to the Mudarib. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed if the 6% is paid only when profit exists
column6: Allowed, as the ratio is known at the outset and the Mudarib agreed to it
column7: Not allowed: profit must be an agreed percentage of profit
column8: Allowed if the Mudarib also gives a guarantee for the capital provider's share
column10: Per 8/1, profit must be distributed by an agreed percentage of profit, not a lump sum or a percentage of the capital.

column4: A Mudarib has begun trading when the capital provider seeks to cancel. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the contract now binding?
column5: Starting work turns the Mudarabah into a loan owed by the Mudarib
column6: Ending it may frustrate profit and leave the Mudarib unpaid
column7: The capital provider has become a guarantor of the Mudarib's work
column8: The Mudarib has become the owner of the capital once he began trading with it
column10: Per the basis, unilateral termination after work starts might frustrate the aim of profit and damage the Mudarib, who might get no compensation for his work.

column4: A capital provider hands over 'some funds' without stating amount or currency, and the parties agree to settle the figure later. What does the standard require?
column5: Capital must be clearly known in quality and quantity
column6: The Mudarib may determine the capital on his own
column7: The capital need only be stated in the accounts
column8: The capital may be fixed later at liquidation
column10: Per 7/2, Mudarabah capital must be clearly known and defined in quality and quantity so as to eliminate any uncertainty or ambiguity.

column4: Bank A restricts its Mudarabah to trading in a fruit that is out of season and very scarce, so the venture cannot make profit. What is the ruling on this restriction?
column5: Acceptable if the restriction is limited to a single year
column6: Acceptable if the Mudarib agreed to it in writing beforehand
column7: Acceptable, since the capital provider may restrict freely
column8: Not acceptable: restricted commodities must be commonly available
column10: Per 9/2, restriction to certain commodities requires them to be commonly available; they must not be scarce, seasonal or in very limited supply.

column4: A Mudarib hires a specialist for work that is not, by custom, the Mudarib's responsibility. May the specialist be paid from the Mudarabah funds?
column5: Yes, at any rate the Mudarib agrees
column6: Yes, at the prevailing rate
column7: No, such work may not be hired out
column8: No, only from the Mudarib's own funds
column10: Per 9/4, the Mudarib may hire, against the Mudarabah funds and at the prevailing rate, another party for work not customarily the Mudarib's responsibility.

column4: Contrary to the Mudarabah terms, the Mudarib invests the funds in a sector the capital provider excluded, and a loss results. What is the Mudarib's liability?
column5: He loses his profit share but owes no capital, as the provider bears the loss
column6: He is not liable at all, since he remains a trustee despite the violation
column7: He is liable only for half of the resulting loss, the rest falling on the provider
column8: He becomes liable for the amount of the Mudarabah capital
column10: Per 4/4, breach of the terms of the Mudarabah contract is a breach of trust making the Mudarib liable for the amount of the Mudarabah capital.

column4: A Mudarib with permission mixes 200,000 of his own funds with 800,000 of Mudarabah funds (ratio 50:50). Profit is 100,000. What does the Mudarib get?
column10: Per 8/9, profit is split by fund size: 20,000 to the Mudarib's own funds; the remaining 80,000 is shared 50:50, so he gets 20,000 + 40,000.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a Mudarabah initially a non-binding contract?
column5: The Mudarib is an agent, and agency is not binding
column6: The capital provider is a guarantor of the Mudarib
column7: The capital is a loan payable on demand
column8: The profit ratio is not yet known at signing
column10: Per the basis, the Mudarib uses the provider's funds with consent as an agent, and an agency contract is not binding.

column4: To what does the Shari'ah basis liken the Mudarib's preliminary entitlement to profit before final valuation?
column5: The contract of Qard, in which the borrower returns the like
column6: The contract of Ijarah, in which the usufruct is sold for rent
column7: The contract of Salam, in which the price is paid in advance
column8: The contract of sharecropping
column10: Per the basis, the Mudarib's preliminary entitlement to realised profit, known absolutely only after actual or constructive valuation, is analogous to sharecropping.

column4: A capital provider contributes trucks instead of cash as Mudarabah capital. How is the capital determined?
column5: By the trucks' value, per experts or as the parties agree
column6: By the trucks' original purchase price, with no new valuation needed at contract
column7: By the total rent the trucks will earn over the term
column8: It cannot be done, as capital must always be paid in cash at the contract date
column10: Per 7/1, capital may be tangible assets; their value is the contribution, determined by experts or as agreed by the parties.

column4: Bank A and Company X sign a memorandum of understanding for Mudarabah financing of up to 10 million over two years, to be implemented through successive transactions. Is this permissible?
column5: No, each Mudarabah must be negotiated without any framework
column6: Yes, if later implemented through specific or successive Mudarabahs
column7: Yes, and the memorandum itself transfers the 10 million at once
column8: No, a Mudarabah cannot be tied to a defined sum and duration
column10: Per 3/1, Mudarabah financing may be concluded under a general framework or MoU for a sum and duration, later implemented in specific or successive transactions.

column4: A Mudarabah contract stipulates that the Mudarib will receive 50,000 from the profit, the rest going to the capital provider. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid, but the 50,000 is treated as a fee
column6: Valid if profit exceeds 50,000
column7: The Mudarabah contract is void
column8: Valid, as the Mudarib's share is known
column10: Per 8/5, if one of the parties stipulates that he should receive a lump sum of money, the Mudarabah contract is void.

column4: Bank A, as capital provider, stipulates that its own staff will work alongside the Mudarib in buying and selling for the Mudarabah. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if Bank A's staff bear part of any loss that results
column6: Permitted if the Mudarib's profit share is raised to compensate for the interference
column7: Permitted in a restricted Mudarabah, where the provider may set such terms
column8: Not permitted for the capital provider to stipulate this
column10: Per 9/3, the capital provider may not stipulate a right to work with the Mudarib and be involved in selling and buying, or supplying and ordering.

column4: A Mudarib invested prudently within the contract terms, but a market fall caused a 20% loss of the capital. Who bears the loss?
column5: The Mudarib, who must restore the capital in full from his own assets
column6: The capital provider; the Mudarib is a trustee, not liable
column7: The Mudarib, up to the amount of his expected profit
column8: Both parties equally, as partners in the Mudarabah who share profit and loss
column10: Per 4/4, the Mudarib invests on a trust basis and is not liable for losses except in case of misconduct, negligence or breach of the contract terms.

column4: A Mudarib argues he may lend Mudarabah funds interest-free to a friend. Per the Shari'ah basis, why are loans, gifts and donations from the fund barred?
column5: They do not benefit the Mudarabah and risk loss to the provider
column6: They would turn the Mudarabah into a binding contract on the capital provider
column7: They would make the Mudarib a partner in the capital of the Mudarabah itself
column8: They would require a guarantee from the capital provider for the borrower
column10: Per the basis, loans, gifts and donations do not benefit the Mudarabah operation; rather, they involve potential loss to the capital provider.

column4: Midway through a Mudarabah, accounts show a profit. When does the Mudarib's entitlement to his share become absolute?
column5: Only when the capital provider pays him a separate fee
column6: As soon as any profit appears in the interim accounts
column7: Only after distribution on actual or constructive valuation
column8: On the date when the Mudarabah contract was concluded
column10: Per 8/8, the Mudarib is entitled once profit is realised, but this is subject to retention to protect capital and becomes absolute only after distribution.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, on which valid contracts does the permissibility of documentary credit rest?
column5: Mudarabah, Musharakah and Wakalah
column6: Murabahah, Ijarah and Salam
column7: Hawalah, Bay' al-Dayn and Qard
column8: Kafalah, Wakalah and Qard
column10: The basis states documentary credit relies upon contracts valid in the Shari'ah, such as Kafalah (personal guarantee), Wakalah (agency) and Qard (loan).

column4: Under a credit, the bank pays the exporter 20% before documents are presented, against his undertaking to repay if goods are not shipped. What is this credit called?
column5: A back-to-back credit guaranteed by another
column6: A revocable credit amendable at any time
column7: A red clause or advance payment credit
column8: A transferable credit for other beneficiaries
column10: Per 2/3/3, a red clause credit allows the bank to pay a percentage before submission of documents, against the beneficiary's undertaking to repay.

column4: A client asks why Bank A may charge him a percentage fee for credit services. What basis does the Shari'ah basis give?
column5: It is a wage for agency services, upheld by most Fuqaha
column6: It is a share of the profit on the imported goods sold to the client
column7: It is compensation for guaranteeing the payment, upheld by most Fuqaha
column8: It is a charge for the time until payment
column10: Per the basis, the fee is in lieu of services by the Institution as the client's agent; the majority of Fuqaha upheld charging wages for agency.

column4: In brief, how does the standard describe a documentary credit?
column5: A bank's undertaking to pay subject to inspecting the goods on arrival at port
column6: A bank's undertaking to pay against conforming documents
column7: A bank's purchase of the goods for resale to the buyer later
column8: A bank's loan to the buyer to settle the price of the goods
column10: Per 2/1, in brief, a documentary credit is an undertaking by a bank to pay subject to conformity of the documents to the contractual instructions.

column4: Bank A wishes to amend a documentary credit it issued without consulting the seller (beneficiary). For which type of credit is this possible?
column5: A standby credit
column6: An irrevocable credit
column7: A confirmed credit
column8: A revocable credit
column10: Per 2/3/1, a revocable credit can be amended or cancelled without consulting the beneficiary; an irrevocable credit needs the parties' consent.

column4: An exporter holds an accepted bill of exchange due in six months under a credit and offers to sell it to Bank A today at less than its nominal value. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible for Bank A to discount the bill
column6: Permissible if Bank A holds the bill to maturity
column7: Permissible if the discount equals actual expenses
column8: Permissible if the bill is accepted by a bank
column10: Per 3/7/2, the Institution may not discount accepted bills of exchange, i.e. purchase them before maturity at less than their nominal value.

column4: Bank B confirms Bank A's documentary credit. Per the Shari'ah basis, how is the confirming bank's undertaking characterised?
column5: As an agency for the beneficiary seller
column6: As a sale of the credit to Bank B
column7: As a back-up guarantee, which is permissible
column8: As a loan given to the issuing bank
column10: Per the basis, the undertaking of the confirming bank and similar participating banks is an act of back-up guarantee, which is permissible in the Shari'ah.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why can a revocable documentary credit not be classified as a guarantee contract?
column5: Guarantees must always be paid in cash at once
column6: An option is not permissible in guarantee contracts
column7: Guarantees cannot be given by a bank to a seller
column8: A guarantee cannot secure the price of a sale
column10: Per the basis, a revocable credit is a form of agency; it is not a guarantee because it conflicts with guarantee requirements and an option is not permitted in guarantee.

column4: A client wants to buy imported goods from Bank A through Murabahah financing of a documentary credit. Who should buy the goods from the supplier?
column5: The client, who then sells them to Bank A before it resells them to him
column6: The client, with Bank A paying the price to the supplier as a loan
column7: The supplier's bank, acting as agent of the client for the purchase
column8: Bank A, which then sells them to the client by Murabahah
column10: Per 3/5/2, the Institution should be the party that purchases from the supplier and then sells to the client through Murabahah.

column4: Bank A issues a credit under which payment to the project owner is due only if the contractor fails to perform. Which type of credit does this resemble?
column5: A standby credit, resembling a letter of guarantee
column6: A red clause credit paid in advance
column7: A transferable credit for other beneficiaries
column8: A revolving credit for repeat operations
column10: Per 2/3/3, a standby (guarantee) credit resembles letters of guarantee, with payment conditional upon the beneficiary's (contractor's) failure to perform.

column4: A seller requires the buyer to open a credit as a condition of the sale. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is this condition likened to?
column5: A stipulation to pay part of the price in advance, as in Salam
column6: A stipulation for a penalty on late payment of the price by the buyer
column7: A stipulation to provide a specific guarantor for payment
column8: A stipulation that the seller may revoke the sale if payment is late
column10: Per the basis, making a credit a condition in the sale is similar to a stipulation to provide a specific guarantor for payment, a valid condition in the contract's interest.

column4: Company X leases machinery from a foreign owner, who requires the rent to be paid through a documentary credit. Can a lease be the contract preceding the credit?
column5: No, rent can only be secured by letters of guarantee
column6: Yes; it may be a lease, agency or other contract
column7: Yes, but only if the lease is first converted into a sale
column8: No, the preceding contract must always be a sale contract
column10: Per 2/2/1, the preceding contract is usually a sale, but it may be a lease contract, agency with commission or any other contract.

column4: Bank A partners with a client in goods the client already bought, then plans to sell its share back to him on deferred payment. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this barred?
column5: It is a sale of a debt for a debt, as the price is deferred
column6: It is a sale before taking possession of the goods by the Bank
column7: It is a guarantee given for a fee, which is not permitted
column8: It amounts to a sale-buy back (Bay' al-'Inah)
column10: Per the basis, selling the Institution's share in goods purchased by the client back to him for deferred payment amounts to Bay' al-'Inah, prohibited by Shari'ah.

column4: In a Musharakah to import goods, Bank A wants to sell its share to its partner by deferred Murabahah after receipt of the goods. What condition applies?
column5: The sale must be made on a spot basis only, never deferred
column6: The sale must not rest on prior binding promises or the Musharakah
column7: The sale must be at the original face value of Bank A's share
column8: The partner must first buy the goods directly from the supplier
column10: Per 3/6/1, after receipt of goods the Institution may sell its share by spot or deferred Murabahah if not based on prior binding promises or stipulated in the Musharakah.

column4: A client has already bought goods and Bank A then joins him in a partnership over them. May Bank A sell its share to the client on deferred payment?
column5: No, it may not sell its share to the client on a deferred basis
column6: No, unless the client gave Bank A a binding promise beforehand
column7: Yes, by deferred Murabahah once the goods have been received
column8: Yes, provided the price is the market value of Bank A's share
column10: Per 3/6/2, the Institution may partner with the client in goods the client purchased, on condition that it does not sell its share to the client on a deferred basis.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may sight documents and bills of exchange not be negotiated for less than their nominal value?
column5: It breaches the rules of agency contracts
column6: It is a guarantee given in return for a fee
column7: It takes the form of a prohibited sale of debt
column8: It is a form of Bay' al-'Inah arrangement
column10: Per the basis, negotiating documents payable on sight, including bills of exchange, for less than nominal value adopts the form of the sale of debt, which is prohibited.

column4: Under a documentary credit, the beneficiary presents documents that do not conform to the credit instructions. What may the bank do?
column5: Accept, reject or seek amendment of the documents
column6: It must pay, since the documents were presented in time
column7: It must reject them and cancel the credit at once
column8: It must inspect the goods before deciding anything
column10: Per 2/2/4, if the documents do not conform to instructions, the bank reserves the right to accept, reject or seek amendment of the documents.

column4: Bank A opens a documentary credit not on a client's order but to import equipment for its own use. Does the Documentary Credit standard cover this?
column5: Yes, but only if the credit is also confirmed by another bank
column6: No, an Institution may never open credits for its own use under Shari'ah rules
column7: Yes, it covers both client-ordered credits and own-use credits
column8: No, it covers only credits opened on the order of a client of the Institution
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers documentary credit extended by an Institution on the basis of client orders or for the use of the Institution itself.

column4: A client asks Bank A to open a credit to import goods that are prohibited by the Shari'ah, for resale to non-Muslims. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, provided the client is not himself a Muslim
column6: Permissible, as the bank deals only in documents, not goods
column7: Permissible, if the bank only notifies and does not issue it
column8: Not permissible for the Institution to deal in such a credit
column10: Per 3/1/3, the Institution may not undertake documentary credit transactions, for itself or others, pertaining to goods prohibited by the Shari'ah.

column4: The seller presents conforming documents on time, but the buyer tells the bank he has heard the goods may be of poor quality. What must the bank do?
column5: Withhold payment until the goods are inspected on arrival
column6: Pay, as credit dealings are on documents alone, not the goods
column7: Cancel the credit at the buyer's request and notify the seller
column8: Pay half now and hold half pending the goods' arrival
column10: Per 2/4/1, documentary credit deals with documents alone without reference to the goods; the bank must execute when conforming documents are presented in time.

column4: A sale contract states its interpretation is subject to INCOTERMS. What condition does the standard attach to such a reference?
column5: The interpretation must not violate the rules of the Shari'ah
column6: The reference is void in any Islamic transaction, whatever its content
column7: INCOTERMS prevail over the Shari'ah in international trade matters
column8: It applies only if both parties are Institutions
column10: Per 3/2/3, a contract's reference to INCOTERMS or similar rules is circumscribed with a condition that it must not violate the rules of the Shari'ah.

column4: Bank A proposes to charge 0.5% of the credit amount for each month the credit remains open. What is the ruling on this commission?
column5: Permissible for import credits only, not for export credits
column6: Permissible, as a percentage of the amount is allowed and duration does not matter
column7: Not permissible: the duration must not affect the commission
column8: Permissible if the actual costs of the credit are also covered by it
column10: Per 3/3/1, a fee may be a lump sum or a percentage of the credit amount, provided the duration of the credit is not considered in determining it.

column4: A correspondent bank requires that a credit be subject to the uniform practices for documentary credit, which include interest clauses. What should Bank A do?
column5: Accept the practices in full as an accepted international industry standard
column6: Refuse any reference at all to the uniform credit practices
column7: Accept them in full and give any interest it receives to charity afterwards
column8: Qualify it as not violating Shari'ah, stating interest will not apply
column10: Per 3/7/1, such a reference must be qualified so it does not violate Shari'ah, and it must be explicitly stated that any interest provision will not be acted upon.

column4: Bank A and a client sign a Musharakah to buy imported goods before any credit is opened and before the client contracts with the supplier. In whose name may the credit be opened?
column5: Only in Bank A's name
column6: In the name of either partner
column7: Only in the supplier's bank's name
column8: Only in the client's name
column10: Per 3/6/1, where the partnership contract precedes the credit and the client's contract with the supplier, the credit may be opened in either partner's name.

column4: On what basis does the standard make documentary credit permissible?
column5: It is a loan from the seller to the buyer for the goods' price
column6: It is a sale of the goods by the bank to the importing buyer
column7: It includes agency for services and an institutional guarantee
column8: It is a Mudarabah between the bank and the importing client
column10: Per 3/1/1, documentary credit includes agency for procedural services (mainly document examination) and an institutional guarantee, both permissible.

column4: A client asks Bank A to amend a credit by extending its duration (rescheduling). What may Bank A charge for this amendment?
column5: Nothing at all, since amendments must always be free
column6: Only actual expenses, as a definite sum, not a percentage
column7: A lump-sum service fee plus a charge for the extra time
column8: A percentage of the credit amount for the extra period
column10: Per 3/3/1, where an amendment involves rescheduling the duration, the Institution may charge only actual expenses as a definite sum and not a percentage.

column4: Bank A pays the full value of a credit that was totally uncovered by its client. Per the Shari'ah basis, which element of the irrevocable credit comes into operation?
column5: The loan (Qard) element
column6: The mortgage (Rahn) element
column7: The partnership (Musharakah) element
column8: The agency (Wakalah) element only
column10: Per the basis, the loan element comes into operation when the Institution pays on behalf of the client in a credit that is totally or partially uncovered.

column4: Bank A structures a credit as a combination of contracts so it can take a higher fee that in effect prices its guarantee. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the client consents to it in writing and the fee is disclosed
column6: Permissible, since each contract in the combination is valid on its own
column7: Permissible as long as the fee is a lump sum, not a rate
column8: Not permissible: combined contracts cannot mask a guarantee fee
column10: Per 3/3/1(c), a combination of contracts may not be used as an excuse for prohibited transactions, such as a commission for a guarantee or a loan.

column4: After a credit is opened, a court declares the underlying sale contract null and void. How is the credit to be executed?
column5: Its execution becomes subject to a new agreement
column6: It lapses automatically and the buyer keeps the goods
column7: It is executed at half its amount, the other half being refunded
column8: It is executed as originally issued, because the credit is independent of the sale
column10: Per 3/1/4, if the contract concluded before the credit is nullified by a court decision, execution of the credit is subject to a new agreement.

column4: A credit secures a currency exchange contract. What must hold for the credit's subject to be permissible?
column5: Only the credit's own terms need be valid in Shari'ah
column6: Only the amount of the currencies must be fixed in advance
column7: The bank need not consider the underlying contract at all
column8: The exchange must be valid in its elements, conditions and type
column10: Per 3/1/3, the contract relied upon (currency exchange, ordinary sale or another) must be valid in Shari'ah in its elements, conditions and type of transaction.

column4: Company X has opened a valid credit in favour of its seller. Before the credit expires, the seller demands payment directly from Company X. Is he entitled?
column5: Yes, as opening the credit is not final payment
column6: Yes, at any time he chooses between the two
column7: No, not while the credit subsists and is valid
column8: No, the buyer is fully discharged by opening it
column10: Per 2/4/2, opening the credit is not final payment, but the seller has no right to request payment from the buyer as long as the credit subsists and is valid.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is it not permissible to take compensation for the guarantee aspect of a documentary credit?
column5: The agency services fee already covers the guarantee given by the bank
column6: A guarantee prepares for a loan, which is not compensated
column7: The guarantee is a sale of a debt for another debt owed by the bank
column8: Guarantees are void in international trade dealings under Shari'ah rules
column10: Per the basis, a guarantee is preparatory to extending a loan, which is not compensated; the four Fiqh schools are unanimous on not taking compensation for guarantee.

column4: A seller stipulates in the sale contract that the buyer must pay through a documentary credit. What is the status of this condition?
column5: Valid only if the buyer's bank is an Institution
column6: Valid, but only a recommendation to the buyer
column7: Void, as it adds a condition to the sale
column8: Valid, and its performance is binding on the buyer
column10: Per 3/2/1, the seller may stipulate payment through documentary credit; such a condition is valid and its performance is binding upon the buyer.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may the bank's guarantee in an irrevocable credit be conditioned on the documents conforming to the stipulations?
column5: The documents are themselves the subject of a loan to the buyer
column6: Kafalah accepts qualification through a stipulated condition
column7: Agency contracts may never be made conditional, so the guarantee cannot be either
column8: The credit is a sale subject to an option to cancel if documents are rejected
column10: Per the basis, the jurists ruled that Kafalah (guarantee) accepts qualification through a stipulated condition, so execution may depend on conforming documents.

column4: A client's credit is only partly covered. Bank A proposes to pay the uncovered part to the beneficiary as a loan to the client bearing interest. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the interest equals actual cost
column6: Permissible if the client agreed in advance
column7: Not permissible, as the credit would include interest
column8: Permissible, as the loan arises from a guarantee
column10: Per 3/1/3, the Institution may not deal in credit that includes interest, explicitly as in a loan on payment of amounts not covered, or impliedly.

column4: Bank A issues a shipping guarantee so the client can release goods before documents arrive. Which rule governs its commission for this letter of guarantee?
column5: The ruling on commission in the Shari'ah Standard on Guarantees
column6: A time-based fee for the period until the documents arrive from the seller
column7: The percentage-of-amount rule that applies to commission on credit services
column8: Free choice of the Institution and its client
column10: Per 3/3/3, commission for letters of guarantee accompanying credits, such as shipping guarantees, follows Shari'ah Standard No. (5) on Guarantees.

column4: Bank A is asked to confirm (endorse) a credit issued by Bank B, with no services required of Bank A. What may Bank A charge?
column5: Actual expenses plus a fee for the guarantee
column6: A percentage fee for the confirmation risk
column7: A lump-sum fee for guaranteeing payment
column8: Only the actual expenses it incurs
column10: Per 3/3/1(a), guarantee per se is not priced; confirming another bank's credit is an addition over guarantee, so only actual expenses may be charged.

column4: Bank A wants security for a credit it opens for a client. Which of the following may it accept as cover?
column5: Interest-based bonds held by the client
column6: Withholding the credit documents that stand for the goods
column7: Interest-based receivables owed to the client
column8: Shares in companies dealing in prohibited activities
column10: Per 3/4/1-2, cover may include cash, frozen permissible accounts and withholding the credit documents; interest-based bonds and receivables are not allowed.

column4: A supplier ships to Company X monthly and, within the credit's limit and validity, submits new documents for each new shipment under the same credit. What type of credit is this?
column5: A revolving or renewable credit
column6: A back-to-back credit backed by another
column7: A syndicated credit with several banks
column8: A standby credit conditional on failure
column10: Per 2/3/3, under a revolving or renewable credit the beneficiary can repeatedly submit new documents for new operations within the credit limits and validity.

column4: Before paying under a credit, Bank A obtains proof that the bill of lading presented by the beneficiary is forged. What is Bank A's position?
column5: It must pay and then claim from the beneficiary
column6: It must pay, as documents appear conforming
column7: It is under no obligation to execute the credit
column8: It must pay if the credit is irrevocable
column10: Per 2/4/3 and 3/1/4, the bank must pay against conforming documents except upon proof of fraud or forgery, in which case it is under no obligation to execute.

column4: A client deposits the cash cover for a credit with Bank A and asks that it earn a return until it is used. What does the standard permit?
column5: Investing the cash cover on a Mudarabah basis
column6: Paying a fixed interest on the cash cover
column7: Nothing; cash cover must remain idle
column8: Lending the cover to others at interest
column10: Per 3/4/3, the Institution and the applicant may agree on investing the cash cover of the credit in accordance with Mudarabah partnership.

column4: A credit expires before the seller presents the documents. The seller still delivered the goods under the sale contract. What can the seller do?
column5: Nothing, as the sale is revoked with the credit
column6: Claim the price plus compensation for delay
column7: Claim payment directly from the buyer
column8: Claim payment only from the issuing bank
column10: Per 2/4/2, if the credit expires before submission of documents, the seller may claim payment directly from the buyer, as expiry does not revoke the sale.

column4: A trader who is the beneficiary of a credit asks the executing bank to make part of the credit available to his own supplier. Which type of credit permits this?
column5: A standby credit
column6: A transferable documentary credit
column7: A revolving or renewable credit
column8: A red clause credit
column10: Per 2/3/3, a transferable credit entitles the beneficiary to request the executing bank to make it available, partially or totally, to other beneficiaries.

column4: Bank A is asked to act as intermediary, by payment or notification, so a beneficiary can sell deferred payment documents to the confirming bank below nominal value. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as Bank A itself is not the buyer of documents
column6: Permissible if Bank A charges only a fixed fee for its role
column7: Permissible for export credits but not for import credits
column8: Not permissible for Bank A to act as intermediary in this
column10: Per 3/7/3, the Institution may not trade in deferred payment documents below nominal value, nor act as intermediary between beneficiary and bank to facilitate it.

column4: Company X engages Ahmad under Ju'alah to obtain financing for it from banks. Which outcome may validly be the subject of this Ju'alah?
column5: Securing a loan with interest set by custom
column6: Securing a deferred-payment Murabahah facility
column7: Securing an interbank loan with interest
column8: Securing an interest-bearing loan from a bank
column10: Per 8/3/2, Ju'alah for facilities requires a valid subject, such as Murabahah on deferred payment, and not raising interest-bearing loans.

column4: An offeror promises a reward to a person for doing a task that this person is already obliged to do. Is this a valid Ju'alah?
column5: Yes, any task may be the subject of Ju'alah
column6: Yes, if the reward is known and deliverable
column7: No, the work must not be obligatory for the worker
column8: No, unless the worker accepts the offer first
column10: Per 5/3/1/5-6, it is a condition that the work involves some effort and that the work not be obligatory for the worker.

column4: A worker starts a Ju'alah task, then walks away from it on his own. The parties had made no special agreement. What can he claim?
column5: Nothing from the offeror
column6: Reasonable wages for work done
column7: The full reward if the offeror benefited
column8: A pro rata share of the reward
column10: Per 6/3-6/4, if the worker terminates after commencing work, he is not entitled to a reward and has no claim against the offeror unless otherwise agreed.

column4: A broker is engaged under Ju'alah to find a buyer for Company X's building. When is the broker's compensation earned?
column5: When he introduces any interested party to Company X, whether or not a deal follows
column6: When the buyer pays the last instalment of the price to Company X
column7: When he has spent a set number of days seeking a buyer for the building
column8: When the contract he intermediates is concluded
column10: Per 8/4, in brokerage under Ju'alah, entitlement to compensation is contingent upon the conclusion of the contract for which intermediation is undertaken.

column4: After a worker has started on a Ju'alah task, the offeror prevents him from continuing. What must the offeror pay?
column5: Only the worker's out-of-pocket costs
column6: Reasonable wages
column7: Nothing, since the result was not achieved
column8: The full agreed compensation
column10: Per 6/2, if the offeror prevents the worker from working after the work has commenced, the offeror is bound to pay reasonable wages.

column4: Bank A seeks guidance on a clause in an Istisna'a contract requiring the builder to maintain the building for two years. Does the Ju'alah standard cover this?
column5: Yes, all maintenance obligations in any contract are a form of Ju'alah
column6: Yes, since the extent of the maintenance work is unknown in advance
column7: No, maintenance stipulations in other contracts are excluded
column8: No, because Istisna'a is a form of Ijarah for service
column10: Per clause 1, the standard does not cover maintenance contracts or maintenance stipulations in other contracts, such as in a sale or Istisna'a contract.

column4: Bank A hires a collector under Ju'alah and offers him 10% of whatever debt he collects as his compensation. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, compensation may be a portion of the object of work
column6: No, compensation must always be a fixed, known sum
column7: Yes, but only if the whole debt is finally collected
column8: No, since the amount to be collected is unknown
column10: Per 5/3/2/2, compensation may be a portion of the object of work, e.g. a percentage of a debt agreed upon for collection.

column4: Ahmad offers a reward for finding his lost car. Bilal starts searching. Ahmad now wants to revoke the offer unilaterally. What is the ruling?
column5: It became binding on Ahmad as soon as he made the offer
column6: Ahmad may revoke freely as Ju'alah is never binding on the offeror
column7: Ahmad may revoke without any liability to Bilal for the search so far
column8: It became binding on Ahmad once the worker started work
column10: Per 4/1, Ju'alah is in principle not binding, but it becomes binding for the Ja'il (offeror) when the worker commences work.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Ju'alah not binding on the offeror before work starts?
column5: The worker is unknown to him, as in a gift made to the public
column6: Compensation is contingent on a condition, like a bequest
column7: The compensation is a debt on the offeror, as in a loan he has taken
column8: The work is fully certain, as in a sale where both counter-values are known
column10: Per the basis, accrual of the compensation is contingent upon a condition, so it resembles a bequest, which is not binding; for the worker, it resembles Mudarabah.

column4: Bank A pays half the Ju'l in advance for a study. The worker fails to achieve the required result. What is Bank A's right?
column5: It may reclaim the advance, which was subject to accounts
column6: It may reclaim only half of the advance it paid
column7: It must pay the remainder to him as reasonable wages
column8: It loses the advance, being a non-refundable fee
column10: Per 5/3/2/4, advance compensation is 'subject to accounts'; the worker is not entitled to it without the result, and the offeror may reclaim it.

column4: In a Ju'alah, the worker ('Amil) undertook not to revoke the contract during a six-month period. After two months he wants to withdraw. What is the ruling?
column5: He may withdraw if he returns any advance received
column6: He may withdraw if the offeror has not paid yet
column7: He may withdraw since Ju'alah is not binding
column8: He is bound to abide by his undertaking for that period
column10: Per 4/1, if the worker undertakes not to revoke the contract during a specified period, it is binding on him to abide by the undertaking.

column4: Which of the following distinguishes Ju'alah from Ijarah under the standard?
column5: Ju'alah is binding from conclusion, Ijarah is not
column6: Ju'alah requires the work to be clearly specified
column7: Ju'alah is valid even if the other party is not known
column8: Ju'alah requires acceptance by the worker
column10: Per clause 7, Ju'alah is valid despite uncertain work, needs no acceptance, pays on result, is valid with an unknown party, and as a rule is terminable.

column4: A client questions whether a bank, as a juristic person, can be the worker or offeror in a Ju'alah. What basis does the Shari'ah basis give for allowing it?
column5: Juristic persons act only through Mudarabah, not through Ju'alah or Ijarah
column6: Banks are agents of the state in all contracts they conclude with clients
column7: Ju'alah is a banking product by its nature, so only banks may use it
column8: Natural and juristic persons have equal capacity for Ju'alah
column10: Per the basis, an Institution may undertake Ju'alah as worker or offeror because natural persons and juristic persons have the same legal capacity for it.

column4: Bank A names Company Y as the worker in a Ju'alah to prepare a study. Company Y wants to hand the work to another firm. What does the standard require?
column5: Nothing; any worker may get help from anyone he likes
column6: It is never allowed; Company Y must do all the work itself
column7: Express consent of Bank A, with the firm under Y's supervision
column8: Only a notice to Bank A after the study has been completed
column10: Per 5/1, a specified worker must do the work himself or, with the offeror's express consent, through someone under his supervision and control.

column4: Company X announces publicly a reward to anyone who designs a new trade mark meeting its conditions. No specific person is named. Is the Ju'alah concluded?
column5: No, a worker must first formally accept the public offer
column6: Yes, Ju'alah may be concluded by an offer to the general public
column7: Yes, but only once Company X picks and names one worker
column8: No, the worker must be specified by name in the contract at the time of the offer
column10: Per 5/1 and 5/2, the worker need not be specified; Ju'alah is concluded by an offer to the public, and acceptance is not a condition.

column4: A student asks which Sunnah report supports Ju'alah. What does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri's Ju'l for curing a tribal chief
column6: Al-Sa'ib Al-Makhzumi's partnership with the Prophet
column7: Al-'Abbas's conditions to his Mudarib
column8: Umar's giving an orphan's funds for trade
