column10: The basis cites Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri's report of stipulating a Ju'l if the tribe's chief was cured through him, and the Prophet's tacit approval.

column4: Which Qur'anic evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of Ju'alah?
column5: The verse commanding the fulfilment of contracts
column6: The camel load promised for returning the King's beaker
column7: The verse on partners who oppress one another, except the righteous
column8: The verse on travellers seeking Allah's bounty while travelling through the land
column10: The basis cites the story of Yusuf: 'For him who brings it is the (reward of) a camel load; I will stand surety for it.'

column4: A Ju'alah offers 'a suitable reward' with no amount stated. The worker achieves the result. What is due?
column5: Whatever amount the worker demands
column6: Whatever amount the offeror chooses
column7: Reasonable compensation becomes binding
column8: Nothing, as the contract is void
column10: Per 5/3/2/1, compensation must be known, lawful and deliverable; if unknown, unlawful or not deliverable, payment of reasonable compensation becomes binding.

column4: Company X wants someone to find water on its land, but no one can say how much drilling will be needed. Why does Ju'alah suit this better than Ijarah?
column5: Ju'alah fixes the time the work will take in advance
column6: Ijarah cannot be used by companies for drilling or other exploration work
column7: Ju'alah requires the work to be precisely specified, which suits drilling better
column8: Ju'alah needs only a determined result, not specified work
column10: Per clause 3, Ju'alah is valid with uncertainty in the work if the end result is determined, so it suits activities for which Ijarah, needing specified work, does not.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is reasonable compensation due when the named Ju'l is vitiated (e.g. unlawful)?
column5: By analogy with Ijarah when the named wage is vitiated
column6: By analogy with a bequest when the bequeathed item is later revoked
column7: Because the offeror must pay a penalty for the unlawful stipulation
column8: By analogy with Mudarabah when the profit share is unknown or vitiated
column10: Per the basis, recourse to reasonable compensation is by analogy with Ijarah, where reasonable wages apply upon vitiation of the named wages.

column4: Under a Ju'alah, a collector is to recover a 100,000 debt for a 10,000 reward. He collects only 60,000. What is he entitled to?
column5: Nothing, as the whole debt was not collected
column6: Reasonable wages for his time and effort
column7: 6,000, in proportion to the amount collected
column8: The full 10,000, as he did the work
column10: Per 8/2, compensation may be contingent on collecting all the debt, or part of it so that compensation proportionate to the amount collected is due.

column4: A worker in a Ju'alah suffers an accident during the work causing loss, with no tort or negligence on his part. What is his entitlement?
column5: Half the agreed compensation
column6: Reasonable wages only
column7: No compensation at all
column8: Full compensation
column10: Per 5/3/2/3(b), where an accident during work causes loss not due to the worker's tort or negligence, the worker is entitled to full compensation.

column4: A worker not required to work personally hires helpers to finish a Ju'alah task. On what basis does the Shari'ah basis allow this?
column5: Ju'alah is a sale of the worker's own labour, so he may sub-contract it
column6: Ju'alah is similar to agency, where seeking help is valid
column7: Ju'alah creates a binding Ijarah on the helpers
column8: Ju'alah is a partnership in which all those present may work together
column10: Per the basis, the worker may seek others' help when personal service is not stipulated because Ju'alah is similar to agency, in which seeking help is valid.

column4: The period of a Ju'alah expires; the worker has done part of the work, which benefits the offeror, but the result is not near. What is the worker entitled to?
column5: Reasonable wages (Ujrat al-Mithl)
column6: A share of the offeror's profits
column7: The full agreed Ju'l
column8: Nothing, as the result was not achieved
column10: Per 5/3/1/3, when the period is over and the worker has done part of the work that will benefit the offeror, he is entitled to reasonable wages (Ujrat al-Mithl).

column4: A Ju'alah requires a mining result within one year. The year ends with the minerals almost reached. What happens to the worker's entitlement?
column5: He loses any right to compensation
column6: The period is automatically extended
column7: He receives half of the compensation
column8: The contract converts into an Ijarah
column10: Per 5/3/1/2, a period may be stipulated, after which there is no compensation, except when the period ends and the result is close: the period is then extended.

column4: Ahmad offers a Ju'alah reward and Bilal accepts but, before starting any work, Bilal revokes the contract. Is Bilal entitled to compensation?
column5: Yes, the full reward as agreed, since he had accepted the offer
column6: Yes, half of the agreed reward, as he accepted the offer
column7: Yes, reasonable wages for his readiness to work during the period
column8: No, revocation before work gives no compensation
column10: Per 6/1, if the offeror or the worker revokes the contract prior to commencement of work, the worker is not entitled to compensation.

column4: Bank A undertakes a Ju'alah as worker for a client, then contracts out the work to Company Y under a parallel Ju'alah. When is this permissible?
column5: If it was not stipulated that Bank A does the work itself
column6: Never, an Institution must always do the work itself under Ju'alah
column7: Only if both Ju'alahs are linked in one contract with the same terms
column8: Only if Company Y is paid the same Ju'l as Bank A receives from the client
column10: Per 9/1, an Institution may act as worker and contract out by parallel Ju'alah unless it is stipulated it will do the work itself; the two must not be linked.

column4: Under the standard, which description fits a bill of exchange?
column5: A certificate representing a common share in a stock company
column6: An order from a drawer to a drawee bank to pay a sum at sight
column7: A signed unconditional order to pay a sum to a third person or order
column8: A certificate whereby a debtor promises to pay a creditor a sum
column10: Per 2/1, a bill of exchange is a written, signed, unconditional order from one person to another to pay a sum at sight or a set date to a third person or order.

column4: A payee bank receives a crossed cheque bearing conditions set by the drawer. What is the bank's obligation?
column5: It is bound to fulfil the cheque's conditions
column6: It must cash it to any bearer who presents it at sight
column7: It may disregard the crossing at will, as it is only the drawer's wish
column8: It must refuse it as an invalid cheque, since it bears conditions
column10: Per 3/3(c), it is permitted to use a crossed cheque that binds the payee bank to fulfil its conditions.

column4: A holder sells a 100,000 promissory note not yet due to Company Y for 100,000 in cash today. How does the standard classify this sale?
column5: A permitted sale at par
column6: A valid Hawalah
column7: Riba al-Nasi'ah
column8: Riba al-Fadl only
column10: Per 6/2, selling commercial paper not yet due for an amount similar to its value is Riba al-Nasi'ah; for more than its value, it is Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl.

column4: Ahmad issues an account payee cheque to Bilal. Bilal asks the payee bank to cash it over the counter. What must the bank do?
column5: Return it to Ahmad for a new cheque
column6: Cash it if Bilal shows his identity card
column7: Cash it, since the cheque is payable at sight
column8: Credit the amount to the beneficiary's account
column10: Per 3/3(d), an account payee cheque binds the payee bank to fulfil its conditions by crediting the amount of the cheque to the beneficiary's account.

column4: In a currency exchange (Sarf), Company X offers to pay its side with a bill of exchange due in 30 days. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the bill's due date is within thirty days
column6: Not permissible, as Sarf requires possession of counter-values
column7: Permissible if the bill is first endorsed to the bank
column8: Permissible, as a bill is a valid form of commercial paper
column10: Per 3/2, bills of exchange and promissory notes may not be used in transactions requiring possession, such as counter-values in Sarf or Salam capital.

column4: Company X holds a 100,000 bill due in six months and offers to sell it to Bank A today for 95,000. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if Bank A charges no extra fee
column6: Permissible if the drawer has a good credit rating
column7: Permissible, as the discount reflects the time value
column8: Not permissible: it is discounting of commercial paper
column10: Per 6/1, it is not permissible to discount commercial papers.

column4: Ahmad buys gold from a dealer and pays with a certified cheque drawn on his bank. Is this a valid way to meet the possession requirement?
column5: Yes, a certified cheque counts as constructive possession
column6: Yes, but only if the cheque is cashed on the same day
column7: No, any cheque is merely a deferred promise to pay, even if certified
column8: No, gold may only be bought with physical cash in hand at the time of contract
column10: Per 7/1, receipt of a banker's or certified cheque is constructive possession of its amount, so it may be used where possession is required, e.g. buying gold.

column4: Company X issues a promissory note promising to pay Ahmad 50,000 in six months. How does the standard characterise this note in Shari'ah?
column5: As a contract of Sarf
column6: As a contract of agency
column7: As a certificate of debt
column8: As a restricted Hawalah
column10: Per 2/2, a promissory note is a certificate whereby the issuer (debtor) promises to pay a sum; in Shari'ah characterisation it is a certificate of debt.

column4: The drawer of a bill refuses to pay. The holder wants to claim from the endorser and the guarantor who signed the bill. What is his right?
column5: Recourse only to the guarantor
column6: Recourse to them severally or jointly
column7: Recourse only to the last endorser
column8: Recourse only to the drawer
column10: Per 8/2, all who signed (drawer, endorser, guarantor) are jointly responsible; the holder may have recourse to them severally or jointly after the drawer's refusal.

column4: A client with no balance draws a cheque on Bank A, which pays it (an overdraft). How is this treated and when is it permissible?
column5: As a guarantee, permissible for a fee
column6: As a Hawalah, permissible with interest
column7: As a loan (Qard), permissible if void of Riba
column8: As a sale of debt, permissible at a discount
column10: Per 3/3(b), a cheque drawn without a balance (overdraft) is from the Shari'ah perspective a loan (Qard), permissible if void of Riba.

column4: Ahmad, who neither owes Bank A nor has any balance or claim against it, draws a cheque on Bank A in favour of Bilal. How is the cheque characterised with respect to Ahmad?
column5: As an unrestricted Hawalah
column6: As a contract of Sarf
column7: As a restricted Hawalah
column8: As a certificate of debt
column10: Per 2/3, a cheque is a restricted Hawalah only where a debt exists between drawer and drawee; otherwise it is an unrestricted Hawalah with respect to the drawer.

column4: Ahmad wants to transfer dollars he holds to pay a supplier in euros through a bank transfer. What does the standard require?
column5: Transfer the dollars without any conversion
column6: Convert the currencies first, then make the transfer
column7: Transfer the dollars, then convert at maturity
column8: Convert at a rate fixed when the order is placed
column10: Per 7/3, where the currency differs, conversion must first be made (constructive possession sufficing), then the transfer: a combination of Sarf and Hawalah.

column4: Bank A, which holds a balance at one of its own branches, draws a cheque on that branch to pay a supplier. Is the use of this cheque permitted?
column5: Yes, but only if the supplier holds an account there
column6: No, only clients may draw cheques on banks where they hold balances
column7: No, a bank may not draw a cheque on itself, as it would be both drawer and drawee
column8: Yes, a bank may draw a cheque on its own branch
column10: Per 3/3(a), a cheque with a balance may be drawn by the client against the bank, or by the bank against another bank, itself or one of its branches.

column4: A trainee asks why a promissory note is permissible. Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: The hadith 'Muslims abide by their conditions'
column6: The command to fulfil obligations
column7: The command to write down debts for a fixed period
column8: The hadith on Banu Al-Nadir's debts
column10: Per the basis, a promissory note is a document acknowledging a debt, and Allah commanded securing debts: 'When you contract a debt for a fixed period, write it down.'

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is endorsement of commercial paper permissible?
column5: It is a sale of debt at a discount to the endorsee
column6: It is a gift from the endorser to the endorsee of the bill
column7: It is a form of Mudarabah between endorser and endorsee
column8: It does not go beyond Hawalah or Wakalah
column10: Per the basis, endorsement does not go beyond the meaning of either Hawalah (transfer) or Wakalah (agency), both of which are permissible.

column4: Bilal wants to use a note that is not yet due as the price of goods sold by description as a liability, to be delivered later. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible for goods sold by description as a liability
column6: Permissible if the note is first endorsed to the dealer
column7: Permissible if the goods are delivered on maturity
column8: Permissible, exactly as with ascertained goods
column10: Per 6/3, non-due paper may be the price of ascertained goods or usufruct, but not of goods sold by description as a liability.

column4: A banker argues that discounting a bill is merely a trade in paper. Per the Shari'ah basis, what does discounting amount to in reality?
column5: A fee for collecting the bill's value as agent
column6: A loan with interest, varying with value and maturity
column7: A permitted reduction of the debt for early payment
column8: A sale of goods for a deferred price to the bank
column10: Per the basis, discounting is in reality a loan with interest, as the charge varies with the paper's value and maturity date; loans with interest are prohibited.

column4: Under the law, a fixed amount is mandatorily held in a drawer's account for a cheque drawn between banks, so it is legally deemed certified. May it be used to buy silver?
column5: No, only physical cash is possession for silver
column6: No, only a banker's cheque is constructive possession
column7: Yes, but only once the cheque has been cleared
column8: Yes, its receipt is constructive possession of its amount
column10: Per 7/1, a banker's cheque, certified cheque or one legally deemed certified (an amount mandatorily maintained) is constructive possession, usable to buy gold or silver.

column4: A client gives Bank A a cheque to collect on his behalf, but no commission was agreed. What is the bank entitled to?
column5: Nothing, as collection is a free service that a bank owes its clients
column6: A share of the amount collected by the bank as its agent's profit
column7: Commission per prevalent practice among institutions
column8: Interest on the amount until it is credited to the client's account
column10: Per clause 5, collection is an agency; the institution gets the agreed commission or, absent agreement, the practice prevalent among institutions applies.

column4: Bank A pays a client's cheque without a balance but charges interest along with the cheque value. Per the Shari'ah basis, what is the ruling on writing and dealing in such a cheque?
column5: Permitted if the client consents to the charge
column6: Prohibited, since it includes Riba-bearing profits
column7: Permitted, as a form of absolute Hawalah
column8: Permitted, as an agency for borrowing
column10: Per the basis, a no-balance cheque is valid as absolute Hawalah or agency for borrowing, but if it includes Riba-bearing profits, writing and dealing in it is prohibited.

column4: Bank A asks whether the Commercial Papers standard governs a new instrument that has some attributes of commercial paper but is not a bill, note or cheque. What is the answer?
column5: No, the standard covers only bills, promissory notes and cheques
column6: No, the standard covers only cheques among bank instruments
column7: Yes, if the instrument is issued under the Geneva Convention
column8: Yes, it covers any instrument with commercial paper attributes
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers bills of exchange, promissory notes and cheques, and not anything else possessing the attributes of commercial paper.

column4: Bilal holds a note not yet due and wants to use it as the price to buy a specific, ascertained car from a dealer, who delivers the car at once. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as the note is not yet due
column6: Permissible, with actual or legal delivery of the car
column7: Permissible only if the car is delivered at maturity
column8: Not permissible, as it is a sale of debt for debt
column10: Per 6/3, a beneficiary may use commercial paper not yet due as price for ascertained goods or usufruct, with actual or legal delivery (commodity-based discounting of debts).

column4: A drawee bank accepts a bill and later seeks to avoid paying. Which hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite on the binding nature of such an undertaking?
column5: Ibn Abbas's taking silver at Mecca for notes payable at Kufa
column6: Al-Sa'ib's partnership with the Prophet in trade
column7: The Prophet's order to Banu Al-Nadir to reduce debts and hasten payment
column8: Abu Qatadah's taking on the two dinars of a deceased man
column10: The basis cites Jabir's hadith: Abu Qatadah undertook a deceased man's two dinars, the Prophet accepted it, and the deceased was absolved by that undertaking.

column4: Bank A issues travellers' cheques and wants to charge a commission on issue and on payment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only on issue, never at the time of payment
column6: Permissible only as a percentage for each day held
column7: Permissible for intermediation, provided it includes no Riba
column8: Not permissible, as travellers' cheques are loans
column10: Per 3/3(e), the institution issuing travellers' cheques may take commission for intermediation on issue or at payment, provided this does not include Riba.

column4: Which practice of the Companions does the Shari'ah basis cite to support dealing in bills of exchange?
column5: Ibn Abbas took silver at Mecca and wrote notes payable at Kufa
column6: Umar gave an orphan's funds to a trader for trade in Iraq
column7: Al-'Abbas set conditions on the travel of his Mudarib with his capital
column8: Abu Qatadah took on the two dinars of debt of a deceased man
column10: The basis cites Ibn Abbas taking silver from traders at Mecca and writing a demand note payable at Kufa, and Ibn Al-Zubayr's similar notes on his brother in Iraq.

column4: In a Salam contract, the buyer wants to pay the capital (Ras al-Mal) by handing over a promissory note. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the note is a certificate of debt
column6: Permissible if the note is payable at sight
column7: Permissible if the seller agrees to it
column8: Not permissible to use the note as Salam capital
column10: Per 3/2, a bill of exchange or promissory note may not be used as the counter-value for the capital (Ras al-Mal) in the contract of Salam.

column4: Ahmad owes Bilal 100,000 under a note due in six months. Ahmad, the debtor, offers Bilal, the first beneficiary, 95,000 now in full settlement. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted: it is Riba al-Nasi'ah since the debt is paid early for less
column6: Permitted to pay the first beneficiary less before maturity
column7: Not permitted: it is discounting of commercial paper at a lower amount
column8: Permitted only if a bank is the intermediary
column10: Per 6/1, discounting is not permitted, but it is permitted to pay an amount less than the value of the paper to the first beneficiary prior to maturity.

column4: The holder of a promissory note requires the issuer to provide a piece of land as tangible security for payment. How is this security treated?
column5: As a mortgage (Rahn), governed by the rules of Rahn
column6: As a Hawalah of the debt onto the land's value
column7: As a sale of the land to the holder of the note
column8: As a guarantee for which a fee may be charged
column10: Per 8/3, tangible security stipulated by the holder of commercial paper to secure his right is deemed a mortgage (Rahn) and governed by its rules.

column4: A holder of a note buys goods for delivery on the note's maturity date and, once the debt is established, transfers his creditor's claim to his debtor through the note. What is this transaction?
column5: A discounting of the note
column6: A Salam contract
column7: A Hawalah
column8: A sale of debt for a lesser sum
column10: Per 6/4, after the debt is established, the holder transfers his creditor's claim to his debtor through the paper; such a transaction amounts to Hawalah.

column4: In a Salam contract, the buyer pays the capital (Ras al-Mal) with a banker's cheque. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if it is cashed within one month
column6: Not permissible, as all cheques, even a banker's cheque, are deferred debts
column7: Not permissible, as Salam capital must be paid in physical cash at the session
column8: Permissible, as a banker's cheque is constructive possession
column10: Per 7/1, a banker's or certified cheque constitutes constructive possession and may be treated as the capital (Ras al-Mal) of Salam.

column4: Company X wants to exchange currencies with Bank A, paying with an ordinary (uncertified) cheque drawn on its account. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if Bank A collects the cheque some days later
column6: Permitted if Company X's account is usually well funded with sufficient balance
column7: Not permitted: it is not constructive possession of the amount
column8: Permitted, since all cheques are payable at sight, which equals possession
column10: Per 7/2, an ordinary cheque that is not banker's or certified is not constructive possession; it may not be used where possession is stipulated.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, on which hadith does the payee bank's duty to observe the conditions of crossed and account payee cheques rest?
column5: 'Muslims abide by the conditions they stipulate'
column6: 'Reduce the amount of the debts to hasten the payments'
column7: 'No harm and no reciprocal harm shall be inflicted in Islam'
column8: 'The delay of a rich man in paying his debt is oppression'
column10: The basis relies on the generality of the hadith 'Muslims abide by the conditions they stipulate', as such conditions promote the contract's interest.

column4: Bank A collects the value of a client's bills of exchange for him. How does the standard characterise this collection?
column5: As a loan by the bank to the client until the bills are collected
column6: As an agency, the client appointing the bank as agent
column7: As a purchase of the bills by the bank itself at a discount
column8: As a guarantee of the bills given by the bank to the client
column10: Per clause 5, collection of the amount of commercial papers is an agency, with the client appointing the institution as agent to collect on his behalf.

column4: Bank A, as drawee, accepts a bill of exchange due in three months. What is the effect of this acceptance?
column5: A guarantee for which the bank may take a fee
column6: A purchase of the bill by the bank at a discount
column7: A mere promise that has no binding effect
column8: An undertaking to pay the holder the debt at maturity
column10: Per 8/1, the drawee's acceptance is an undertaking and obligation to pay the debt in the paper to the holder at maturity, to be fulfilled per Shari'ah.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is an uncertified cheque not treated as possession of its amount?
column5: Receiving the cheque is a sale of a debt owed by the drawee's bank
column6: There may be no or insufficient balance to cover it
column7: Cheques can never represent money in Shari'ah, whether certified or not
column8: The drawer of the cheque may be a non-Muslim who deals in Riba
column10: Per the basis, an uncertified cheque is not possession due to the probability of no or insufficient balance; possession is based on customary practice.

column4: A bill of exchange is endorsed by its holder to a third party, meeting all legal conditions for endorsement. What is the effect of the endorsement?
column5: It is binding only if the drawer consents
column6: It is a mere promise with no legal effect
column7: It is binding in its legal effects
column8: It is void, as debts cannot be transferred
column10: Per clause 4, all forms of endorsement are binding with respect to their legal effects provided they fulfil the legal conditions and regulations set for them.

column4: Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for allowing a creditor to accept less for early payment (Da' Wa Ta'ajjal)?
column5: The Prophet's words to Banu Al-Nadir: 'Reduce and hasten'
column6: Ibn Abbas's taking silver at Mecca against notes payable at Kufa
column7: Abu Qatadah's taking on the debt of the dead man at the Prophet's request
column8: The verse commanding the writing of debts for a specified term
column10: The basis cites the hadith of Ibn Abbas: when Banu Al-Nadir had debts not yet due, the Prophet said 'Reduce the amounts to hasten payments'.

column4: A holder sells a 100,000 bill not yet due for 105,000 in cash today. How does the standard classify this sale?
column5: Riba al-Nasi'ah only
column6: Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl
column7: A permitted sale at a premium
column8: Riba al-Fadl only
column10: Per 6/2, selling commercial paper that has not become due for more than its value is Riba al-Nasi'ah plus Riba al-Fadl.

column4: Which of the following falls outside the scope of the standard on Investment Sukuk?
column5: Certificates of investment funds and portfolios
column6: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing or future assets
column7: Muzara'ah (sharecropping) certificates for agricultural land
column8: Investment agency (Wakalah) certificates issued for a specific project
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover shares of joint stock companies, certificates of funds and investment portfolios.

column4: Bank A undertakes to buy any unsubscribed portion of a Sukuk issue and asks the issuer for an underwriting commission. What is the ruling?
column5: The commission is allowed if it is a fixed lump sum
column6: Underwriting is not allowed as it is a mere promise to buy
column7: Allowed by binding promise, but no commission may be taken
column8: Both the underwriting and the commission are permissible
column10: Per 5/1/9, an institution may underwrite the unsubscribed issue on a binding promise, but should not receive any commission for the underwriting.

column4: The manufactured asset under Istisna'a Sukuk has been delivered to the ultimate purchaser on deferred payment. Why is trading in the certificates now subject to debt-trading rules?
column5: The Istisna'a contract is rescinded upon delivery
column6: The manufactured asset has been consumed and so no longer exists
column7: Ownership of the asset reverts to the manufacturer
column8: It represents the price owed by the purchaser, a monetary debt
column10: Per the Basis, after delivery to the ultimate purchaser the certificate represents the price in the purchaser's liability, a monetary debt, so debt-trading rules apply.

column4: An investor asks why Salam certificates may not be traded while certificates of leased assets may. What reason does the standard give?
column5: Salam goods are always perishable commodities that cannot be stored
column6: Salam certificates represent a share in the Salam debt
column7: Salam certificates have no fixed maturity date for delivery of goods
column8: Salam capital must remain held by the issuer until delivery
column10: Per 5/2/14 and its Basis, a Salam certificate represents a share in the Salam debt, so it is subject to the rules of debt trading.

column4: Which statement must a Sukuk prospectus explicitly include regarding Shari'ah compliance?
column5: That a Shari'ah Supervisory Board approved and monitors the issue
column6: That holders waive any claim if the project later breaches Shari'ah rules
column7: That the regulator certifies the profit rate as Shari'ah-compliant at issuance
column8: That Shari'ah review takes place only once, at the time of the issuance
column10: Per 5/1/8/4, the prospectus must mention the obligation to abide by Shari'ah and that a Shari'ah Supervisory Board approves the issue and monitors implementation.

column4: Investors trade certificates of ownership of leased assets on an exchange. Which reason justifies the permissibility of this trading?
column5: Market need permits trading in all kinds of certificates
column6: Sukuk are negotiable instruments of debt, just like conventional bonds
column7: The trading is in fact on the assets, which may themselves be traded
column8: The issuer guarantees the nominal value of the certificates
column10: Per the Basis, trading Sukuk representing tangible assets or usufruct is in fact trading the assets and usufructs; since these may be traded, so may the Sukuk.

column4: Ahmad leases a warehouse and issues equal-value certificates to sublease its usufruct, so that the holders own the usufruct and receive the rental. What type of Sukuk are these?
column5: Certificates of ownership in leased assets
column6: Certificates of ownership of services of a specified party
column7: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of described future assets
column8: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets
column10: Per 3/2/1/2, certificates issued by the lessee (owner of the usufruct) of an existing asset to sublease it are certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets.

column4: Ahmad holds 10% of the Sukuk of a project that suffers a loss. How is the loss allocated to him?
column5: The issuer bears it up to the nominal value of his Sukuk
column6: It is shared equally among all holders regardless of holding
column7: He bears 10% of the loss, in proportion to his holding
column8: He bears none, as Sukuk holders are creditors of the issuer
column10: Per 4/5, holders share the return as stated in the prospectus and bear losses in proportion to the certificates they hold.

column4: Thousands of investors accept a single prospectus that expressly states it is an offer. Someone objects that one offer cannot meet many acceptances. On what basis does the standard reject this?
column5: Contracts form by anything showing consent; one offer, many acceptances
column6: Necessity permits what would otherwise be an invalid contract
column7: Acceptance becomes valid only once the regulator approves the whole issue
column8: Each investor's acceptance creates a separate loan contract
column10: Per the Basis, valid contracts occur through anything indicating consent, so an offer from one person and acceptance from many is not objectionable.

column4: Sukuk holders ask the issuer to provide a mortgage and personal guarantees. For what may the issuer permissibly offer such guarantees?
column5: For a minimum fixed rate of profit to holders
column6: For the nominal value of the Sukuk in all cases
column7: For any fall in the market price of the Sukuk
column8: For its own wrongful acts or negligence
column10: Per 5/1/8/7, the issuer may offer some tangible or personal guarantees with respect to its wrongful acts or negligence.

column4: A Murabahah Sukuk commodity has been sold and delivered to the buyer on deferred payment. Why is trading in the certificates now restricted?
column5: The commodity can no longer be resold in the market
column6: They now represent a monetary debt against the buyer
column7: The buyer has not yet issued a promise to purchase
column8: The profit has already been distributed to holders
column10: Per the Basis, after the commodity is sold and delivered, Murabahah certificates represent a monetary debt against the buyer, so only debt-trading limits apply.

column4: Company X's draft Sukuk prospectus states that the issuer guarantees holders a fixed 6% annual profit. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the issuer charges no separate fee for giving the guarantee
column6: Permissible if the guarantee is disclosed in the prospectus
column7: Permissible if the Sukuk are of short-term maturity
column8: Not permissible: the issuer may not guarantee a fixed rate of profit
column10: Per 5/1/8/7, the prospectus must not state that the issuer guarantees a fixed percentage of profit.

column4: Sukuk proceeds are used, under a Mugharasah contract, to plant trees and cover the work and expenses of the plantation. What do the certificate holders become entitled to?
column5: Return of their capital plus an agreed fixed profit
column6: A share in both the land and the plantation
column7: A share in the crop only, without any share in land
column8: A fixed rental paid by the owner of the land
column10: Per 3/9, Mugharasah Sukuk holders become entitled to a share in the land and the plantation.

column4: Sukuk holders demand a say in managing the assets their certificates represent. On what basis does the standard recognise their right to management?
column5: They are creditors entitled to protect their loans to the issuer
column6: Management rights arise only where the Sukuk are based on investment agency
column7: They own the property represented, and management is part of ownership
column8: The prospectus grants it to them as a contractual favour only
column10: Per the Basis, holders have a right to management because they own the property their certificates represent, and management is part of ownership.

column4: Company X owns a building leased to tenants. It issues equal-value certificates to sell the building to subscribers so that they become its owners. Which type of Sukuk is this?
column5: Certificates of ownership in leased assets
column6: Investment agency (Wakalah) certificates
column7: Musharakah (participation) certificates
column8: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets
column10: Per 3/1, certificates issued by the owner of a leased asset to sell it, so that holders become owners of the asset, are certificates of ownership in leased assets.

column4: In the prospectus for negotiable Sukuk, the issuer undertakes to buy back any certificate offered to it after the issue. At what price may it make this undertaking?
column5: At the nominal value of the certificate
column6: At the market value of the certificate
column7: At nominal value plus any accrued profit
column8: At nominal value less a fixed discount
column10: Per 5/2/2, the issuer may undertake to purchase negotiable Sukuk at market value, but not at their nominal value.

column4: Investors have subscribed to a Murabahah Sukuk issue, but subscription has not closed and no allotment has been made. When does the issue contract take all the legal effects of its underlying contract?
column5: Only when the Murabahah commodity is delivered to the buyer
column6: As soon as each subscriber pays the subscription amount
column7: When the prospectus is approved by the regulator
column8: After subscription closes and the certificates are allotted
column10: Per 5/1/3, the issue contract has all the legal effects of its underlying contract after closing of subscription and allotment of the certificates.

column4: An independent third party, unrelated to the issuer, offers to guarantee the Sukuk holders against loss. Under what condition is this permitted?
column5: It must also guarantee a fixed rate of profit
column6: It must be a subsidiary of the Sukuk issuer
column7: It must provide the guarantee free of charge
column8: It must charge a fee equal to market rates
column10: Per 5/1/8/7, an independent third party is permitted to provide a guarantee free of charge.

column4: Istisna'a Sukuk funds have been converted, within the Istisna'a period, into assets owned by the holders. Why may these certificates be traded?
column5: The assets are properties that can be disposed of
column6: Istisna'a debts may be traded at any price
column7: The manufacturer guarantees the final sale price
column8: The ultimate purchaser has already paid in advance
column10: Per the Basis, trading Istisna'a certificates after funds are converted into assets is permissible because such assets are properties that can be disposed of.

column4: An investor argues that his Investment Sukuk are simply a debt claim on the issuer, like a bond. Per the standard, what do the Sukuk actually represent?
column5: A loan from the holder repayable with an agreed return
column6: A right to a fixed periodic coupon independent of the assets' performance
column7: A debt owed by the issuer for the nominal value of the Sukuk
column8: A common share in ownership of the assets made available for investment
column10: Per 4/2, Investment Sukuk represent a common share in ownership of the investment assets; they do not represent a debt.

column4: Bank A's Murabahah Sukuk commodity has been purchased and is held awaiting sale to a buyer. What reason does the standard give for allowing the certificates to be traded now?
column5: Debts may be traded freely before their maturity
column6: The buyer has issued a binding promise to purchase
column7: The certificates represent assets that can be traded
column8: The Murabahah profit has already been fixed and disclosed to holders
column10: Per the Basis, if the commodity has been purchased and is yet to be sold, trading is permissible because the certificates represent tradable assets.

column4: Certificates of ownership of an existing leased building have just been issued and ownership of the building has passed to the holders. When may they be traded?
column5: Immediately upon issue and up to the date of maturity
column6: Never, since they represent rental receivables
column7: Only after the first rental instalment is received
column8: Only on the maturity date of the Sukuk
column10: Per 5/2/4, Sukuk of ownership of existing leased assets may be traded immediately upon issue until maturity, after ownership passes to the holders.

column4: In Mugharasah Sukuk, the holders are workers rather than owners of the land. Subscription has closed, certificates are allotted and activity has commenced. May they trade?
column5: No, not before the maturity of the trees planted on the land
column6: Yes, whether holders own the land or are workers
column7: No, only land-owning holders may trade, not those who are workers
column8: Yes, but only under the rules for the trading of debts
column10: Per 5/2/18, Mugharasah certificates may be traded after closing, allotment and commencement of activity, whether holders are landowners or workers.

column4: Under Salam Sukuk, the issuer sells goods for future delivery and the subscribers pay the Salam capital. What are the certificate holders entitled to?
column5: Sale price of the certificates or of goods sold via Parallel Salam
column6: A fixed return on the Salam capital, paid periodically by the issuer
column7: The rental from leasing the Salam goods to the issuer
column8: A share of the issuer's overall profits for the period
column10: Per 5/1/5/3, holders own the Salam goods and are entitled to the sale price of the certificates or of the goods sold through a Parallel Salam.

column4: The owner of an orchard issues Musaqat Sukuk, and the subscribers assume the obligation of irrigation. What do the realised funds represent?
column5: The rental for the orchard land
column6: The maintaining cost of the trees
column7: The purchase price of the orchard
column8: The cultivation cost of new crops
column10: Per 5/1/5/10(a), where the landowner issues Musaqat Sukuk, subscribers undertake irrigation and the realised funds are the maintaining cost of the trees.

column4: Company X issued certificates of ownership of leased assets and wants to redeem some before maturity. At what price may it redeem them?
column5: At a price fixed in advance at the time of issue in the prospectus
column6: Only at the nominal value stated in the prospectus
column7: At nominal value less a fixed early-redemption fee
column8: At market price or a price agreed with the holder at redemption
column10: Per 5/2/5, the issuer may redeem certificates of leased assets before maturity at market price or at a rate agreed at the date of redemption.

column4: Bank A issues Wakalah Sukuk and invests the subscription funds as investment agent. What is the status of the subscribers?
column5: Creditors of Bank A entitled to a guaranteed return
column6: Owners of capital in a Mudarabah in which Bank A acts as the Mudarib
column7: Principals who own the assets with their benefits and risks
column8: Lenders whose funds Bank A must repay at nominal value
column10: Per 5/1/5/8, in Wakalah Sukuk the issuer is the investment agent and subscribers are principals who own the assets with their benefits and risks.

column4: Bank A plans to issue tradable Sukuk representing its portfolio of deferred Murabahah receivables owed by customers. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, if the Shari'ah Supervisory Board approves the prospectus beforehand
column6: No; debts owed as a liability may not be securitized for trading
column7: Yes, if the receivables are sold at their face value
column8: Yes, since any asset may be divided into equal shares
column10: Per 5/1/2, tangible assets, usufructs and services may be securitized, but debts owed as a liability may not be securitized for trading.

column4: A cultivator issues Muzara'ah Sukuk and uses the subscription amounts to buy farmland. What is the position of the subscribers?
column5: They are lenders to the cultivator, entitled to repayment in full
column6: They are lessees of the land, entitled to its usufruct
column7: They are owners of the land, entitled to a share of the produce
column8: They are the cultivators, entitled to a share of the produce
column10: Per 5/1/5/9(b), where the cultivator issues the Sukuk, subscribers are owners of the land and holders take a share of the produce as agreed.

column4: A Sukuk prospectus states that the issuer will compensate holders for loss of capital up to the nominal value. In which situations may such issuer liability be accepted?
column5: Only in cases of torts and negligence by the issuer
column6: In all cases, as long as it is stated in the prospectus
column7: Only during the first year after issuance of the Sukuk
column8: Only when the loss exceeds a set percentage of capital
column10: Per 5/1/8/7, the prospectus must not state that the issuer compensates holders up to nominal value in situations other than torts and negligence.

column4: Sukuk represent the usufruct of a described future building that has not yet been ascertained. An investor wants to buy them on the market. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the price does not exceed the nominal value
column6: Freely permissible, as the usufruct is already owned by the certificate holders
column7: Permissible only after the building has been fully leased out
column8: Not permissible except by observing the rules for disposal of receivables
column10: Per 5/2/8, usufruct Sukuk of a described asset may not be traded before the asset is ascertained, except by observing the rules for disposal of receivables.

column4: Company X has collected subscription money for its Sukuk, but subscription is still open and no funds have been employed yet. Per the definition, when do the Sukuk represent undivided shares in the project assets?
column5: Only on the maturity date when the assets are liquidated
column6: Once subscription closes and the funds are employed for the issue purpose
column7: From the date on which the prospectus is published
column8: From the moment each subscriber pays the full value of his Sukuk to the issuer
column10: Per 2, Sukuk represent shares in assets after receipt of their value, closing of subscription and employment of the funds for the purpose of issue.

column4: In a Murabahah Sukuk, subscription funds are used to buy a commodity which is then sold on Murabahah. What do the certificate holders own and receive?
column5: They own the commodity and are entitled to its sale price
column6: They own a debt on the issuer and receive fixed interest
column7: They own the usufruct of the commodity and receive rentals
column8: They own shares in the issuer and receive its dividends
column10: Per 5/1/5/5, Murabahah certificate holders own the Murabahah commodity and are entitled to its sale price.

column4: Certificates are issued to provide educational benefits from a university meeting stated specifications, without naming the university. How are these certificates classified?
column5: Certificates of ownership of usufructs of existing assets
column6: Investment agency certificates managed by the university
column7: Certificates of ownership of services of a specified party
column8: Certificates of ownership of described future services
column10: Per 3/2/4, services from a described provider (a university not named) are described future services; a nominated university falls under 3/2/3.

column4: Murabahah Sukuk funds have been used to purchase a commodity, which has not yet been sold to the buyer. May the holders trade their certificates?
column5: No, only after delivery to the buyer
column6: Yes, but only at their nominal value
column7: Yes, trading is permissible at this stage
column8: No, Murabahah certificates may never be traded
column10: Per 5/2/15, trading Murabahah certificates is permissible after purchasing the commodity and before selling it, but not after delivery to the buyer.

column4: In Muzara'ah Sukuk, the certificate holders act as workers who undertake the agricultural work. When may they trade their certificates?
column5: As soon as activity commences after allotment
column6: Not before the maturity of the fruits and plants
column7: Immediately after closing of subscription
column8: At any time, as with Mugharasah certificates
column10: Per 5/2/17, where Muzara'ah or Musaqat holders act as workers, trading is not permissible before the maturity of the fruits and plants.

column4: Istisna'a Sukuk proceeds were immediately paid as the price in a parallel Istisna'a contract. How is trading in these certificates treated?
column5: It is subject to the rules of disposal of debts
column6: It is freely permissible like trading in assets
column7: It is subject only to the rules of Salam
column8: It is permissible at market price without restriction
column10: Per 5/2/13, if funds are immediately paid as price in a parallel Istisna'a or the item is delivered to the ultimate purchaser, trading follows debt rules.

column4: Musharakah Sukuk have been subscribed and allotted, but the funds are still in cash and activity has not commenced. Ahmad wants to sell his Sukuk. Which rules must be observed?
column5: Only the rules on disposal of usufructs
column6: No special rules, as trading in Sukuk is freely permitted at any stage
column7: The rules of Sarf (currency exchange) and the rules for debts
column8: The rules of Salam applicable to deferred goods
column10: Per 5/2/1, trading or redemption before commencement of activity requires observing the rules of Sarf (currency exchange) and the rules for debts.

column4: Company X issues Mudarabah Sukuk to manage a trading activity with the subscription funds. What are the roles of Company X and the subscribers?
column5: Company X is an investment agent; subscribers are principals
column6: Company X is the owner of capital; subscribers are the Mudarib
column7: Company X is a borrower; subscribers are its creditors
column8: Company X is the Mudarib; subscribers are the owners of capital
column10: Per 5/1/5/7, in Mudarabah Sukuk the issuer is the Mudarib, the subscribers are the owners of capital and the funds are the Mudarabah capital.

column4: A Sukuk prospectus is silent on whether it is an offer. Ahmad submits a subscription and the issuer later approves it. How is the contract formed?
column5: The issuer's approval is the offer; Ahmad's payment is acceptance
column6: Ahmad's subscription is the offer; the issuer's approval is acceptance
column7: No contract arises until the Sukuk are listed and traded
column8: The prospectus itself is the offer; Ahmad's subscription is the acceptance
column10: Per 5/1/7, the prospectus is an invitation; subscription is the offer and the issuer's approval is acceptance, unless the prospectus expressly says it is an offer.

column4: Holders of Sukuk of ownership of usufructs of a tangible asset have subleased the asset to a second lessee. How is trading in these Sukuk now treated?
column5: As fully prohibited at all times, like Salam certificates
column6: As trading in tangible assets, freely permissible
column7: As currency exchange, under the rules of Sarf only
column8: As trading in debt, under the rules for disposal of debts
column10: Per 5/2/6, after sub-leasing the certificate represents rent receivables, i.e. a debt, so its trading is subject to the rules for disposal of debts.

column4: Company X, a manufacturer, issues Istisna'a Sukuk to produce equipment. In this structure, what do the funds realised from subscription represent?
column5: The cost of the product to be manufactured
column6: A deposit held in trust until the product is sold
column7: The rental for the use of the manufacturing plant
column8: A loan to the manufacturer repayable on delivery
column10: Per 5/1/5/4, the issuer is the manufacturer, the subscribers are buyers of the product and the subscription funds are the cost of the product.

column4: What is the Shari'ah basis for permitting the issue of investment Sukuk?
column5: Public need overrides the rules that would otherwise govern debt trading
column6: They are a permissible form of benevolent loan
column7: They are issued on the basis of Shari'ah-nominated contracts
column8: Market custom has accepted them like bonds
column10: Per the Basis, Sukuk are usually issued on Shari'ah-nominated contracts, so issuance on the basis of any of these contracts is acceptable.

column4: Bank A takes a mortgage over a customer's house, registered in the official register as valid under the law, while the customer continues to live there. What is the effect of the registration?
column5: It is a mere record without legal effects of possession
column6: It has no effect at all until Bank A takes physical possession of the house
column7: It transfers ownership of the house to Bank A
column8: It is constructive possession, standing in place of actual possession
column10: Per 3/4, registration of a mortgage of immovables valid under the law is constructive possession and stands in place of actual possession in its rules and effects.

column4: A lender asks why the borrower, not he, pays the delivery and recovery costs of a Qard. What reason does the Basis give?
column5: Custom in all markets places such costs on borrowers
column6: The lender does a good act, and costs are not imposed on one doing good
column7: The borrower owns the loan and so must bear all its risks
column8: The lender earns a return on the Qard that already covers all of these costs
column10: Per the Basis, the lender undertakes a good act, and 'no ground can there be against those who do good'; burdening him would deter lending.

column4: Bank A sells land to Company X. The parties made no stipulation on who pays the conveyancing and registration costs. How is this determined?
column5: By customary practice
column6: The seller always bears them
column7: The party who registers bears them
column8: They are split equally by law
column10: Per 4/1/2, expenses of conveyancing, witnessing, instruments and registration are borne as stipulated; if there is no stipulation, customary practice is relied upon.

column4: Bank A leases equipment to a customer under Ijarah. Absent contrary stipulation or custom, who bears the expenses of delivering possession of the leased equipment?
column5: Both parties equally
column6: The supplier of the equipment
column7: The lessor, Bank A
column8: The lessee, the customer
column10: Per 4/1/4, the expenses of possession of the leased property are borne by the lessor, while the lessee bears the expenses of delivering the rental.

column4: How does the standard define possession (Qabd)?
column5: The physical transfer of a thing from hand to hand in every case
column6: The registration of ownership of the thing in an official government register
column7: The payment of the full price of a thing to its seller
column8: The gathering of a thing or what takes its rule, per customary practice
column10: Per 2, possession is the gathering of a thing or what takes its rule, according to the requirements of customary practice.

column4: Two traders exchange gold for gold. Which evidence does the standard cite as the basis for actual physical possession in gold, silver and currencies?
column5: The hadith of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit: 'like for like... from hand to hand'
column6: The verse: 'No ground can there be against those who do good'
column7: The hadith: 'He who buys food is not to sell it until he has measured it'
column8: The maxim: 'Gains are based on the bearing of costs'
column10: Per the Basis, actual possession in gold, silver and currencies rests on the hadith of Ubadah Ibn Al-Samit: 'Gold for gold... like for like... from hand to hand.'

column4: Why does the standard refer to custom ('Urf) to determine how possession is realised?
column5: Custom always overrides texts specified by the Shari'ah
column6: Possession is defined precisely in the Arabic language
column7: The Lawgiver left 'possession' undefined; jurists agree on custom
column8: The Qur'an defines possession expressly as physical transfer by hand
column10: Per the Basis, there is consensus of the jurists on custom, as the Lawgiver used possession unqualified and it has no definition in language, so custom is referred to.

column4: A seller asks why he is discharged by relinquishing ascertained movables rather than placing them in the buyer's hands. What reason does the Basis give?
column5: The buyer always bears the delivery expenses, so the seller is discharged
column6: Physical taking is the taker's act, beyond the seller's ability
column7: Custom forbids sellers from touching sold goods once the price is agreed
column8: Movables have no value until they are physically moved by the buyer or seller
column10: Per the Basis, the obligor must be able to discharge himself; relinquishing is within his ability, while physical taking is a voluntary act of the taker.

column4: Ahmad lends 100 tons of wheat to Company X as Qard. Measuring is needed both on delivery and on recovery. Who bears these expenses?
column5: Ahmad on delivery; Company X on recovery
column6: Both parties equally
column7: The lender, Ahmad
column8: The borrower, Company X
column10: Per 4/2/1, the expenses of delivery and recovery in a loan, including ascertainment by customary units of measure, are borne by the borrower.

column4: Why does the depositor bear the costs of deposit and withdrawal in a Wadi'ah, per the Basis?
column5: The depositary is a trustee and therefore cannot bear any cost at all
column6: Gains are based on the bearing of costs, and the benefit is his alone
column7: The depositor is deemed the borrower of the depositary
column8: Custom always places costs on the weaker party
column10: Per the Basis, the burden of possession falls on the one who benefits from it ('Gains are based on the bearing of costs'); the benefit in deposit is the depositor's.

column4: Bank A buys an office building. The seller vacates it and leaves it to Bank A, enabling it to deal in the building freely. Has Bank A taken actual possession?
column5: No, not until Bank A physically occupies and uses the building
column6: No, until the full price is paid to the seller
column7: Yes, through relinquishment and enabling transactions in it
column8: No, until Bank A leases the building to a tenant
column10: Per 3/2, actual possession of immovable property is realised through relinquishment and enabling transactions in it.

column4: Why does the seller bear the costs of presenting and measuring the sold commodity, per the Basis?
column5: Delivery is his duty, and what an obligation requires is also obligatory
column6: The seller benefits more from the sale than the buyer
column7: The seller is a trustee who must bear all expenses relating to the goods
column8: The buyer has no duty to bear any cost of the sale
column10: Per the Basis, delivery is obligatory on the seller by the contract, and a thing without which an obligation cannot be fulfilled is also obligatory.

column4: A mortgaged, registered house still contains the tenant's household assets. Why does the registration still count as constructive possession?
column5: The tenant becomes the mortgagee's agent by law
column6: The household assets are part of the mortgage
column7: Registration transfers ownership of the house to the mortgagee by law
column8: Custom deems registration possession, even with such assets inside
column10: Per the Basis, custom in registration countries deems registration of a mortgage as constructive possession, even if the property holds the tenant's household assets.

column4: In a Sarf contract, Bank A exchanges US dollars for euros with Company X. What form of possession is stipulated?
column5: Constructive possession through a promise to deliver later
column6: Delivery of one currency now and the other within a week
column7: Reciprocal delivery within the contract session, on a spot basis
column8: Delivery of the two currencies at any time agreed by the parties
column10: Per 3/7, reciprocal possession in Sarf is delivery and acceptance of delivery within the session of the contract on a spot basis (Yadan bi Yadin).

column4: Bank A holds a customer's goods in trust (Amanah) as a depositary and then buys them, so its new possession entails liability for loss (Daman). How does its prior possession count?
column5: It counts only if the customer re-delivers the goods
column6: It stands in place of the new possession despite the difference
column7: It counts only if the goods are first insured
column8: It does not count, as possession in trust cannot become possession in liability
column10: Per 3/6, prior possession substitutes subsequent possession whether the prior was Daman or Amanah and whether the later entails liability or trust.

column4: Bank A's staff disagree on how possession of a newly traded type of commodity is achieved. Per the standard, what is the basis for determining the mode of possession in things?
column5: Custom ('Urf)
column6: The rules of the commodity exchange only
column7: Physical transfer by hand in all cases
column8: The terms set unilaterally by the seller
column10: Per 3/1, custom ('Urf) is the basis for determining the mode of possession; hence modes of possession differ with the nature of things and people's practices.

column4: Without the creditor's demand or consent, Ahmad deposits the amount he owes into an account maintained for Company X. What condition for constructive possession is missing?
column5: The deposit must be made in cash only, never by cheque or endorsement
column6: The deposit must be made at the creditor's branch
column7: The deposit must be witnessed by two persons
column8: The deposit must be upon the creditor's demand or with his consent
column10: Per 5/3, a deposit into a bank account maintained for a person is constructive possession when made upon his demand or with his consent.

column4: Company X receives a bank draft drawn on Bank B, though the actual cash is paid only some days later. How is Company X's receipt of the draft treated?
column5: As actual possession of the cash itself
column6: As no possession until the cash is received
column7: As constructive possession of the amount payable
column8: As a mere promise of payment by Bank B
column10: Per 5/1, possession of a bank draft or cheque is constructive possession of the amount payable by the drawee bank, even if actual payment is delayed.

column4: A heap of grain is sold by estimate without being weighed or measured. The seller relinquishes it to the buyer, enabling him to take it without obstacle. What is the status of possession?
column5: Constructive possession is realised by the relinquishment
column6: No possession, as grain must always be weighed first
column7: Possession occurs only if the sale is registered officially
column8: No possession until the grain is physically transported
column10: Per 3/3, relinquishment is constructive possession even where measures are applicable but not applied, as in sale by estimate.

column4: The buyer stipulates that goods located in Port A be delivered at his warehouse in City B at the seller's expense, and the seller agrees. Who bears the transport cost?
column5: The buyer, as the stipulation is invalid
column6: The seller, who must deliver at the specified place
column7: Both parties equally, as the place was changed
column8: The buyer, as transport is always his duty
column10: Per 4/1/3, where the buyer stipulates delivery at another place at the seller's expense, the seller must deliver there and bear the transport expenses.

column4: Ahmad deposits gold bars with Company X as Wadi'ah and later withdraws them; both steps involve handling costs. Who bears these costs?
column5: Company X on deposit; Ahmad on withdrawal
column6: Both parties equally
column7: The depositor, Ahmad
column8: The depositary, Company X
column10: Per 4/3, the expenses of deposit and withdrawal in a contract of deposit (Wadi'ah) are borne by the depositor (the owner of the deposit).

column4: In a Salam contract, Bank A is the buyer (Rab al-Salam). Absent contrary stipulation or custom, how are the delivery expenses allocated?
column5: Each party bears half of all delivery expenses of the contract
column6: Seller: delivery of goods; Bank A: delivery of the capital
column7: Bank A bears delivery of both the goods and the capital
column8: Seller bears delivery of both the goods and the capital
column10: Per 4/1/4, in Salam the seller bears the expenses of delivering the Salam commodity and the Rab al-Salam bears those of delivering the capital (Ras al-Mal).

column4: Company X sells 50 tons of rice to Bank A; weighing is needed to ascertain the rice. The contract and custom are silent. Who bears the wages of weighing?
column5: The seller, Company X
column6: Whoever requests the weighing
column7: The buyer, Bank A
column8: Both parties equally
column10: Per 4/1/1, expenses of delivering the sold commodity, including ascertaining it by weight or measure, are the seller's responsibility unless stipulation or custom differ.

column4: Bank A buys 100 tons of steel in the seller's warehouse. The seller weighs and sets them aside and releases them so Bank A can take them without obstacle; nothing is moved. Has Bank A taken possession?
column5: No, possession of steel requires physical delivery by hand
column6: Yes, but only once Bank A resells the steel to one of its customers
column7: No, possession requires transporting the steel to Bank A
column8: Yes, constructive possession after ascertainment and relinquishment
column10: Per 3/3, constructive possession of movables occurs, after ascertainment, by relinquishing them to the entitled person without obstacle, even with no transportation.

column4: Ahmad has been leasing a car from Company X and holds it. He then buys the same car from Company X. Is a fresh delivery needed for him to take possession under the sale?
column5: Yes; he must return the car and receive it again
column6: No; his prior possession stands in place of the possession due
column7: Yes, since his prior possession as lessee was not one of ownership
column8: No, but only if the sale contract is officially registered
column10: Per 3/6, prior possession of a tangible thing stands in place of subsequent lawful possession due to a cause acknowledged by the Shari'ah.

column4: Which of the following topics is excluded from the scope of the standard on Possession (Qabd)?
column5: Possession through bills of lading
column6: Constructive possession of ascertained movables
column7: Expenses of possession in a loan (Qard)
column8: Possession in set-offs
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover possession in set-offs or the nature of possession regarding liability for compensation; these have their own standards.

column4: Bank A orders a vessel from a shipyard under Istisna'a. Absent any stipulation or custom, who bears the expenses of delivering the vessel?
column5: The orderer (Bank A), who takes delivery of the vessel
column6: The ultimate purchaser, who buys the vessel from Bank A
column7: The manufacturer (the shipyard)
column8: Both parties equally, each bearing half of the expenses
column10: Per 4/1/4, in Istisna'a the manufacturer bears the expenses of delivering the subject matter, while the orderer bears those of delivering the price.

column4: Bank A receives a warehouse receipt issued in its name that identifies specific goods and allows it to deal in them. What does Bank A hold?
column5: Constructive possession of the goods the receipt represents
column6: A debt owed to it by the warehouse keeper
column7: Actual possession of the goods, through their physical delivery to it
column8: A mere promise from the warehouse to deliver later
column10: Per 3/5, holding documents like warehouse receipts in the possessor's name is constructive possession where the goods are ascertained and he can transact in them.

column4: A seller gives Bank A access to a warehouse holding 1,000 tons of wheat, of which Bank A bought 100 tons, but the 100 tons have not been measured or set aside. Has constructive possession occurred?
column5: Yes, provided the price has already been paid in full
column6: Yes, if Bank A insures the whole stock in the warehouse
column7: Yes; giving access to the whole warehouse is sufficient by itself
column8: No; the 100 tons must first be ascertained by a known method
column10: Per 3/3, constructive possession of movables takes place after their ascertainment by a known method, through relinquishment enabling delivery without obstacle.

column4: Ahmad sells a locked shop. Following the Hanafi view cited in the Basis, what suffices for delivery of possession?
column5: Handing over the key along with relinquishment
column6: Ahmad remaining present while the buyer enters
column7: Registering the sale before any handover
column8: Moving all goods out of the shop first
column10: Per the Basis, Hanafi jurists hold that for locked immovable property, delivering the key along with relinquishment suffices, enabling the possessor to open it easily.

column4: Suppose the custom of treating bills of lading as possession of goods changed in a market. Per the Basis, what follows?
column5: They remain possession only for perishable goods
column6: That mode would cease to be possession, as custom-based rules change
column7: They become possession only with a court order
column8: They remain possession forever, as the rule is fixed by an explicit text
column10: Per the Basis, where rules rest on custom they alter with a change in custom, except what the Shari'ah has specified; if custom changes, that mode ceases.

column4: Bank A buys a commodity, and paying the price to the seller involves a transfer charge. The contract and custom are silent. Who bears this charge?
column5: The seller of the commodity
column6: Both parties equally
column7: The buyer, Bank A
column8: The bank that executes the transfer
column10: Per 4/1/1, the expenses of delivering the price, if any, are the responsibility of the buyer unless there is a stipulation or custom to the contrary.

column4: A trainee asks whether the standard on Possession (Qabd) governs possession of a car taken by usurpation (Ghasb). What is the answer?
column5: No; it covers only possession of immovable property
column6: No; acts other than contracts, like Ghasb, fall outside its scope
column7: Yes, but only as regards the usurper's liability for compensation
column8: Yes; it covers every form of possession, whether by contract or not
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard covers possession in contracts and does not cover acts other than contracts, like possession in usurpation (Ghasb).

column4: An airline hypothecates an airplane to Bank A by valid registration under the law, and keeps operating the airplane. How is Bank A's position regarded?
column5: Bank A has constructive possession through the registration
column6: Bank A has actual possession by physical delivery
column7: Bank A has no possession, as airplanes cannot be held
column8: Bank A has possession only if the airplane is grounded
column10: Per 3/4, hypothecation of mobile movables like cars, trains, steamers and airplanes through valid registration is constructive possession.

column4: Bank A grants a Qard and requires promissory notes and documents to record the loan. Who bears the cost of preparing these documents?
column5: Both parties equally
column6: The lender, Bank A
column7: Whoever drafts the documents
column8: The borrower
column10: Per 4/2/2, the expenses of drawing up documents and promissory notes needed for a loan contract, its implementation or documentation, are borne by the borrower.

column4: A bailee holds a car, and the owner sells it to him. Why does the Basis treat his prior possession as sufficient for the sale?
column5: The owner's liability for the car ends at once
column6: His bailment is converted automatically into a loan, which counts as possession
column7: Possession aims at control and ability to transact, which he already has
column8: Possession is irrelevant to the validity of a sale
column10: Per the Basis, the purpose of possession is control over and ability to transact in the thing; if that state exists, possession exists too.

column4: Ahmad owes Company X 10,000. At Company X's request, he deposits that amount by cheque into Company X's bank account. What is the effect?
column5: Ahmad stays liable until Company X actually withdraws the cash amount
column6: It is constructive possession and Ahmad is absolved of the debt
column7: It is valid only if Company X signs a receipt
column8: It counts only if the deposit is made in cash
column10: Per 5/3, depositing an amount into a creditor's account at his demand or consent, by cash, endorsement or cheque, is constructive possession and absolves the debtor.

column4: Ahmad buys a laptop from a shop, and the shopkeeper physically hands it to him at the counter. What kind of possession has Ahmad taken?
column5: Prior possession standing in place of a later one
column6: Constructive possession, through registration
column7: Actual possession, through physical corporeal delivery
column8: Constructive possession, through relinquishment
column10: Per 3/3, actual possession of movables takes place through physical corporeal delivery.

column4: A merchant receives payment from a customer through a credit card. Per the standard, how is this payment regarded?
column5: As constructive possession of the payment
column6: As possession only when cash is withdrawn
column7: As a debt with no possession until settlement
column8: As actual possession of banknotes
column10: Per 5/2, payments made through a credit card are deemed constructive possession of such payments.

column4: Bank A holds a bill of lading in its name, but it does not identify any specific goods, and Bank A cannot transact in them. Is this constructive possession?
column5: Yes, as long as the bill is issued in Bank A's name
column6: No; documents can never amount to possession
column7: Yes; holding any bill of lading is always possession
column8: No; ascertainment and ability to transact are required
column10: Per 3/5, documents are constructive possession of what they represent only if goods are ascertained through them and the possessor is able to transact in them.

column4: In a sale of grain, the contract expressly stipulates that the buyer will pay the measuring costs. Who bears them?
column5: The seller, as measuring is always his duty
column6: Both parties equally, despite the stipulation
column7: The buyer, as the stipulation must be followed
column8: The seller, as the stipulation is void
column10: Per 4/1/1, measuring expenses fall on the seller unless there is a stipulation or customary practice to the contrary, which is then binding.

column4: Which text does the Basis cite for requiring ascertainment of movables by customary units of measure before possession is realised?
column5: 'He who buys food (wheat) is not to sell it until he has measured it'
column6: 'No ground can there be against those who do good; and Allah is Oft-Forgiving'
column7: 'Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat... like for like, hand to hand'
column8: 'A thing acted upon by the people must be accommodated'
column10: Per the Basis, the hadith 'He who buys food is not to sell it until he has measured it' shows possession in such cases is attained only through measure.

column4: To avoid interest, Bank A and a correspondent bank agree on a ceiling for overdrafts each may draw on the other, with no claim for profit. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as banks may not lend to each other
column6: Permissible; there is no restriction on this
column7: Prohibited as 'you lend me and I lend you'
column8: Permissible only if a profit rate is agreed
column10: Per 10/4, there is no restriction on agreeing with correspondents a ceiling on mutual overdrafts without any claim for profits (interest).

column4: Bank A wants its Qard service charge to include a share of staff salaries and office rent. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, if they are allocated on a reasonable basis
column6: Yes, as all costs of running loans may be recovered
column7: Yes, if the Shari'ah Supervisory Board is informed
column8: No; indirect expenses are not part of actual expenses
column10: Per 9/2, indirect expenses such as employee salaries, rentals of space, assets and transport, and general management expenses are not included in actual expenses.

column4: A borrower cannot repay a Qard on time. The lender agrees to extend the period if the borrower adds 2% to the amount due. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the 2% is given to charity
column6: Permitted, as it was not stipulated at the time of the original contract
column7: Prohibited: an excess stipulated during the delay is Riba
column8: Permitted, as compensation for the lender's delay
column10: Per 4/1, a stipulated excess is Riba whether stipulated at the contract, while setting the period of delay or during the period of delay.

column4: Ahmad borrowed 1,000 with no stipulation or custom of any excess. At repayment, out of goodwill, he voluntarily returns 1,050. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as any excess over a Qard is Riba
column6: Permissible, as an unstipulated excess at repayment
column7: Permissible only if the Qard was in kind, not cash
column8: Permissible only if the lender requests it
column10: Per 5/2, an excess in quantity or quality at repayment is permissible when not stipulated or customary, whether the Qard is cash or kind.

column4: Bank A sets up exclusive booths for depositing and withdrawing, available only to its premium current account holders. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as it relates to deposits and withdrawals
column6: Permissible only if the booths are offered for a fee
column7: Prohibited, as it is a benefit in lieu of the Qard
column8: Prohibited, as all lenders must be treated equally
column10: Per 10/1/3, there is no restriction if the institution distinguishes between current account owners in what relates to deposits and withdrawals, like exclusive booths.

column4: To attract current account balances, Bank A offers current account holders full exemption from credit card fees and transfer charges. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as they are only service exemptions
column6: Permitted, if the exemption is only partial and not a full exemption
column7: Permitted, as current accounts are deposits
column8: Not permitted: these benefits are given in lieu of the accounts
column10: Per 10/2, the institution may not give current account holders, in lieu of the accounts, benefits unrelated to deposits and withdrawals, including fee exemptions.

column4: Bank A's current account funds are lost through no negligence of the bank. Why must Bank A still repay the holders, per the Basis?
column5: The bank promised a return on current accounts and must honour its promise
column6: Current accounts are Wadi'ah, so the bank is a trustee liable only for negligence
column7: Current accounts are Qard, so the bank guarantees repayment
column8: Regulators require banks to insure all deposits against loss of any kind
column10: Per the Basis, the bank must return a similar amount even on loss without negligence; this is the purpose of Qard, unlike Wadi'ah, a trust not guaranteed absent negligence.

column4: Ahmad lent wheat to a farmer in City A, and the contract says nothing about the place of repayment. Where must the farmer return the similar wheat?
column5: At the farmer's place of residence
column6: At any place chosen by the farmer
column7: Wherever Ahmad happens to demand it
column8: In City A, where the loan was delivered
column10: Per 3/4/2, the applicable rule is the return of an amount similar to the loan amount at the place where it was delivered.

column4: Bank A lent Company X funds for a fixed period of one year. After four months, Bank A demands repayment. Must Company X repay now?
column5: No; the lender may not demand it before the period ends
column6: Yes; a Qard is always repayable on demand
column7: Yes, if Bank A gives Company X one month's notice before demanding it
column8: No, unless Company X's business is profitable
column10: Per 6, a period may be stipulated in Qard; the borrower need not repay before it ends, nor can the lender demand repayment before the end of the period.

column4: Bank A and Company X sign a Qard contract today, but the funds will be handed over next week. When does Company X come to own the loaned funds?
column5: Immediately on signing the contract
column6: When it takes possession of the funds
column7: When the first instalment is repaid
column8: On the maturity date of the loan
column10: Per 3/4/1, the borrower comes to own the subject-matter of Qard through possession, and becomes liable for repayment of a similar amount.

column4: Ahmad lends 100 kg of ordinary wheat on condition that the borrower returns 100 kg of premium-grade wheat. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since wheat is not a currency
column6: Permitted if the borrower agrees in writing
column7: Prohibited: a stipulated excess in quality is Riba
