column8: Permitted, as the quantity of wheat returned is exactly the same
column10: Per 4/1, stipulating an excess for the lender is Riba, whether the excess is in quality or quantity, tangible or a benefit.

column4: Bank A proposes to lend to a customer on condition that the customer buys goods from it. Which hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite against this?
column5: 'The best people are those who do better in repayment'
column6: 'He who buys food is not to sell it until he measures it'
column7: 'Gold for gold... like for like, from hand to hand'
column8: 'A Salaf and a sale (in one contract) are not permitted'
column10: Per the Basis, the hadith 'A Salaf (loan) and sale are not permitted' shows that combining a Qard and a sale in one contract is impermissible.

column4: Bank A charges current account holders a monthly fee for the services it renders to maintain their accounts. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only for accounts that are overdrawn
column6: Permissible to demand wages for services rendered
column7: Prohibited, as any charge on a Qard is Riba
column8: Prohibited, as the bank is the borrower
column10: Per 10/1/2, it is permissible for the institution to demand wages for services rendered to the holders of current accounts.

column4: Why does the borrower own the loaned wealth only upon possession, according to the Shari'ah basis?
column5: Qard is mainly donation, so like Hibah it is owned on possession
column6: Qard is purely commutative, so ownership passes like a sale on credit
column7: The lender keeps ownership until repayment
column8: Possession is needed to fix the price of the loan
column10: Per the Basis, Qard combines commutative and donation aspects with donation predominant, so its rule is like Hibah, in which ownership passes with possession.

column4: During the loan period, a borrower sends his lender an expensive gift because of the loan. They had never exchanged gifts before. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as it was not stipulated in the contract
column6: Permissible if its value is below 1% of the loan
column7: Permissible if the lender reports it to the borrower's bank
column8: Not permissible, as it is given for the sake of the Qard
column10: Per 5/1, the borrower may not give property or a benefit to the lender during the Qard for its sake, unless it was a practice between them before the Qard.

column4: Bank A charges credit card holders a fee of 3% of every cash amount withdrawn from an ATM. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible: the charge may not be linked to the amount
column6: Permissible, if it is capped at a maximum amount
column7: Permissible, if the percentage rate is disclosed to the cardholder in advance
column8: Permissible, as it is a charge for services
column10: Per 10/3/2, ATM cash withdrawal charges on credit cards must be a certain amount within reasonable limits; linking the charge to the amount withdrawn is not permissible.

column4: Ahmad lends money to a trader in City A and stipulates that it be repaid in City B, where Ahmad will be travelling. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if no benefit accrues to Ahmad
column6: Permissible to stipulate repayment at another place
column7: Prohibited, as Ahmad gains a benefit that is Riba
column8: Prohibited unless the trader also lives in City B
column10: Per 4/2, it is permissible to stipulate repayment of Qard at a place other than that where the loan was made.

column4: Nothing is written in a Qard contract, but local customary practice is that borrowers repay 5% more than they borrowed. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since nothing was stipulated in writing in the contract
column6: Permitted, as the excess is paid at repayment
column7: Prohibited, as a stipulation by custom is like a written one
column8: Permitted if the borrower is satisfied with it
column10: Per 4/1, the excess is Riba whether the stipulation is in writing or is part of customary practice.

column4: Ahmad keeps funds in a current account with Bank A, which uses them in its business. What is the legal nature of the current account?
column5: A loan: Bank A owns the funds and is liable to repay them
column6: A deposit (Wadi'ah) held in trust by Bank A
column7: A Mudarabah with Ahmad as owner of capital
column8: An investment account in which Ahmad shares in Bank A's profit
column10: Per 10/1/1, current accounts are loans and not deposits; the institution owns the amounts and a liability to repay them is established against it.

column4: Why does the Basis distinguish interest-free overdraft arrangements between correspondent banks from 'You give me a loan and I will give you a loan'?
column5: Overdrafts are always repaid on the same day
column6: The overdraft is a Mudarabah between the banks
column7: General need, and the benefit is mutual, not the lender's alone
column8: Banks are exempt from the rules of Qard when dealing with each other
column10: Per the Basis, such overdrafts rest on general need; the benefit is mutual, not specific to the lender, and it is a step for dealing with one's counterpart.

column4: Company X uses its credit standing to raise a loan for Ahmad from a lender and stipulates a reward for this service. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as any reward linked to a loan is Riba, even for a service
column6: Prohibited unless Company X guarantees the loan
column7: Permissible only if the reward is paid by the lender and not the borrower
column8: Permissible, as long as it is not a device (Hilah) for Riba
column10: Per 8, it is permissible to stipulate a reward for raising loans for another as long as it is not a fictional device (Hilah) for dealing in Riba.

column4: Besides the hadith, what reason does the Shari'ah basis give for prohibiting a sale stipulated within a Qard?
column5: Sales always require a separate session from loans
column6: It is a means to an excess in the Qard, so it is blocked
column7: A sale cannot be made between lenders and borrowers
column8: The sale price can never be agreed in a Qard
column10: Per the Basis, stipulating a sale in a Qard may oblige the borrower on the price for the sake of the Qard, creating a stipulated excess (Riba); such means are blocked.

column4: Ahmad lent money to his neighbour without stipulating any period. When must the neighbour return its substitute (Badal)?
column5: On demand by Ahmad
column6: After a customary period of one year
column7: Only when the neighbour can afford it
column8: Only after a court sets a date
column10: Per 6, if no period is stipulated in the Qard, it is binding on the borrower to return its substitute (Badal) on demand.

column4: During a loan, a borrower offers his lender a free ride on his animal. Per the hadith of Anas cited in the Basis, what should the lender do?
column5: Accept it, since only stipulated benefits are barred and this was not stipulated
column6: Accept it, then deduct its value from the debt when it is repaid
column7: Not accept it, unless such practice existed before the Qard
column8: Accept it, if he reciprocates within the same month
column10: Per the Basis, the hadith of Anas says the lender is not to accept a gift or free ride from the borrower unless such a practice was prevalent between them before the Qard.

column4: Bank A's actual direct cost of servicing a Qard is 50. It charges the borrower a service fee of 2% of the loan, which comes to 400. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as a percentage fee is common market practice for loans
column6: Permitted, if approved by the borrower
column7: Permitted, if disclosed before the loan is granted
column8: Prohibited: charges above actual direct costs are not allowed
column10: Per 9/1, a lending institution may charge only the actual amount directly spent on loan services; any charge in excess of that is prohibited.

column4: Two brothers have exchanged gifts every year for a long time. One borrows from the other and continues the usual gift during the loan period. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited unless the gift is deducted from the debt
column6: Permissible, as the practice existed before the Qard
column7: Permissible only after the loan has been repaid
column8: Prohibited, as any gift during the Qard is Riba
column10: Per 5/1, benefits during the Qard are not permissible when given for its sake, unless the practice continued between the parties from before the Qard.

column4: Ahmad offers to lend Company X a unique antique painting by way of Qard, to be returned later in kind. Is this a valid subject-matter of Qard?
column5: No; only cash may be the subject-matter of Qard
column6: Yes; any valuable property may be lent as Qard if returned in kind
column7: Yes, if its market value is agreed in advance
column8: No; the subject-matter must be known fungible (Mithli) wealth
column10: Per 3/4, the subject-matter of Qard must be known fungible (Mithli) marketable wealth.

column4: At repayment, a borrower voluntarily gives the lender a better camel than the one borrowed. Which evidence supports the permissibility of this?
column5: The hadith of Anas on refusing gifts and free rides from the borrower
column6: Abu Rafi': 'The best people are those who do better in repayment'
column7: The maxim: 'Gains are based on bearing of costs'
column8: The hadith: 'A Salaf and a sale are not permitted'
column10: Per the Basis, the hadith of Abu Rafi', where the Prophet repaid a young camel with a better one, supports an unstipulated excess at repayment.

column4: Bank A wants to apply the standard on Loan (Qard) to the deferred price owed by its Murabahah customers. Is that correct?
column5: No; the price in a credit sale is excluded from its scope
column6: Yes, but only once the customer delays payment
column7: No; the standard covers only loans made by individuals, not institutions
column8: Yes; every deferred amount owed to Bank A is a Qard
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover what is not a Qard, like the price in a credit sale and investment accounts, which have their own standards.

column4: Which reason does the Shari'ah basis give for permitting repayment of a Qard in a land other than where it was granted?
column5: The lender's benefit from travel is considered Zakat
column6: Any benefit to the lender in a Qard is permitted if both parties agree
column7: Basic rule in Mu'amalat is permissibility; no text prohibits it
column8: Necessity overrides the prohibition of Riba
column10: Per the Basis, the basic rule in transactions is permissibility; no text prohibits it, it benefits both parties without injury, and Companions' reports allow it.

column4: A loan agreement uses the word 'Salaf' rather than 'Qard', and the parties clearly intend a loan. Is the Qard concluded?
column5: No; the word 'Qard' must be expressly used
column6: Yes, but only if it is registered in writing
column7: No; a loan must be concluded by an act of delivery, not by words
column8: Yes; any word or act conveying the meaning of Qard suffices
column10: Per 3/1, Qard is concluded through offer and acceptance using the words Qard and Salaf or any other word or act that conveys the meaning of Qard.

column4: Bank A's system splits a single large ATM cash withdrawal by a credit card holder into several smaller ones, charging a fee on each. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible: slicing withdrawals to repeat charges is barred
column6: Permissible, if each fee is a fixed amount
column7: Permissible, if the card terms disclose the practice to cardholders
column8: Permissible, as each slice is a separate service
column10: Per 10/3/2, the institution may not slice withdrawals as a device for obtaining repeated charges, nor consider the repayment period in the charge.

column4: Bank A grants many small Qard loans in one group programme and cannot assign charges to each loan separately. How may it recover direct costs?
column5: Add a fixed percentage margin to every loan
column6: Charge direct collective costs, shared in proportion to each loan
column7: Charge each loan a flat fee set by Bank A's management
column8: Recover no costs at all, since each loan must bear its own charges only
column10: Per 9/1, where loan-by-loan charging is difficult, as in a group loan, direct collective charges may be borne on the entire sum, each loan bearing its share proportionately.

column4: Company X is about to lend money to Ahmad. Which legal capacities does the standard stipulate for the two parties?
column5: Lender: capacity to transact; borrower: capacity to donate
column6: Both: capacity to donate
column7: Lender: capacity to donate; borrower: capacity to transact
column8: Both: only the capacity to receive gifts
column10: Per 3/2 and 3/3, the legal capacity for donation is stipulated for the lender and the legal capacity to undertake transactions for the borrower.

column4: Bank A agrees to grant a Qard to a customer on condition that the customer leases equipment from Bank A under Ijarah. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible to stipulate an Ijarah within the Qard
column6: Permissible, if the Ijarah rental is at market rate
column7: Permissible, if the customer agrees in writing
column8: Permissible, as the two contracts are separate
column10: Per 7, it is not permissible to stipulate a contract of sale, Ijarah or other commutative contract within the contract of Qard.

column4: Company X lends Ahmad 5,000 on condition that Ahmad lets Company X use his delivery van free of charge during the loan period. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as no extra money is repaid
column6: Prohibited: a stipulated benefit for the lender is Riba
column7: Permitted, provided the loan has a fixed period
column8: Permitted, as the benefit is a use of property, not tangible property
column10: Per 4/1, a stipulated excess for the lender amounts to Riba whether it is a tangible thing or a benefit.

column4: Ahmad hands Company X 1,000 dinars, transferring ownership to it on condition that Company X returns 1,000 dinars similar to them. How is this contract classified?
column5: Mudarabah
column6: Wadi'ah (deposit)
column7: Qard
column8: Hibah (gift)
column10: Per 2, Qard is the transfer of ownership in fungible wealth to a person on whom it is binding to return wealth similar to it.

column4: A trainee asks why the subject-matter of Qard must be fungible. What reason does the Shari'ah basis give?
column5: Fungible items cannot be the subject of Riba, so they suit a loan
column6: Non-fungible items cannot be possessed by the borrower under a loan
column7: Only fungible items have a market price, which the borrower must repay
column8: Only a fungible item can be returned by a similar substitute
column10: Per the Basis, only a fungible item can be returned by the borrower; fungible items are also compensated by similar substitutes in usurpation and destruction.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: What is the Shari'ah basis for permitting international commodity sales that fulfil the elements and conditions of a valid sale?
column5: Custom of exchanges is sufficient by itself to validate any contract
column6: They fall under 'Allah has permitted trading'
column7: International conventions bind Muslim parties as a matter of Shari'ah
column8: Public need overrides the general rules of sale in international trade
column10: Per the Basis, such sales fall within the sale that Allah permitted ('Allah has permitted trading') and trade by mutual consent.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Company X, owner of assets, issues a binding promise to sell them to Bank A and asks Bank A for a fee in return for the promise. What is the ruling?
column5: The fee is allowed, as a promise is a service
column6: The fee is allowed if the promise is tradable
column7: The promise is void as all promises are non-binding
column8: The promise is allowed only without a counter-value
column10: Per 5/2/3/3, a binding promise to sell or buy is a substitute for options only without specifying a counter-value for the promise, and it is not tradable.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A's treasury proposes to buy futures contracts on crude oil and trade them before maturity. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, either in their formation or in trading them
column6: Permitted, if the contracts are ended by actual delivery of the oil
column7: Permitted, for hedging purposes only and not for speculation
column8: Permitted to trade them, but not to form them at the outset
column10: Per 3/3 and 5/1/2, futures transactions are not permitted according to the Shari'ah, either through their formation or through trading in them.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Why are options impermissible, according to the Shari'ah basis of the standard?
column5: They give rights to only one of the parties
column6: They always involve deferring the two counter-values of the contract
column7: Their subject-matter is not wealth that can be deemed compensation
column8: They are concluded outside organized markets
column10: Per the Basis, options are impermissible because the subject-matter of the contract is not wealth that can be deemed compensation under the Shari'ah.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A will pay a commodity's purchase price only if its agent guarantees that the end buyer will pay the deferred sale price. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the agent receives an extra fee
column6: Permitted, as it protects Bank A's funds
column7: Permitted, if the guarantee is given by a third person, not the agent
column8: Prohibited: payment may not be contingent on such a guarantee
column10: Per 4/2/11, the institution may not make payment of the purchase price contingent on the agent guaranteeing the sale price himself or through another person.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A pays a premium to acquire a right, but not an obligation, to buy shares at a set price within three months. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the premium is small relative to the share price
column6: Permitted, if Bank A genuinely intends to exercise it within the period
column7: Not permitted, either in its formation or in its trading
column8: Permitted, if traded only on a regulated exchange with a clearing house
column10: Per 5/2/1-5/2/2, options grant a right without obligation to buy or sell at a set price and period; they are not permitted in formation or trading.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A sells part of a stock of sugar it bought before the part sold is distinguished from the rest, so its sugar is mixed with the seller's. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the warehouse holds enough stock to cover both sales
column6: Prohibited, as the liabilities of buyer and seller overlap
column7: Permitted, if Bank A pays the full price to the seller on the spot
column8: Permitted, as long as the total quantity in the stock is known
column10: Per 4/2/2, selling the commodity before ascertaining it in a distinguishing manner is prohibited, as the liabilities of buyer and seller overlap.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: An agent buys a commodity and resells it before taking delivery, either actually or legally. What does legal delivery include?
column5: Transfer of liability by ascertaining the commodity sold
column6: Payment of the full purchase price to the seller of the commodity
column7: Signing a general memorandum of agency
column8: Receipt of the deferred price from the end buyer
column10: Per 4/2/4, selling before actual or legal delivery is prohibited; legal delivery includes transfer of liability by ascertaining the commodity from other things.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Company X enters an exchange contract for copper for a future date. Such contracts are usually closed by cash settlement or counter-contracts and rarely end in delivery. What type of contract is this?
column5: A Salam contract, with full advance payment of the price
column6: A futures commodity contract
column7: A spot contract, settled by immediate delivery and payment
column8: An Istisna'a contract, for the manufacture of goods
column10: Per 2/2/3, futures contracts take effect at a future date through liquidation, cash settlement or counter-contracts, and rarely end in actual delivery and possession.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A buys an existing, ascertained commodity in an organized market and takes delivery immediately, agreeing to pay the price in six months. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, as it is a forward contract
column6: Permitted only if the seller is an Islamic bank
column7: Permitted, as only one counter-value (the price) is deferred
column8: Not permitted, as the price must always be paid on a spot basis
column10: Per 3/2/4, there is no restriction in delaying one of the counter-values, such as the price, as in a deferred sale.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A orders machinery to be manufactured under Istisna'a, with delivery and price both deferred to a later date. What is the ruling?
column5: Invalid unless the machinery already exists
column6: Invalid, as the two counter-values are deferred
column7: Valid only if the full price is paid to the maker at signing
column8: Valid, as Istisna'a is valid even when the price is delayed
column10: Per 3/2/3, when the contract is Istisna'a, it is valid even when the price is delayed.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A appoints Company X to buy a commodity at a spot price and sell it on Bank A's behalf to a third party at a deferred price. How may Company X's compensation be set?
column5: As an amount or a percentage of the purchase price
column6: As a share of the deferred price owed by the buyer
column7: Only as an undivided share of the profit
column8: As interest on the deferred amount
column10: Per 4/1/1, in investment agency the agent's compensation may be set as an amount or a percentage of the commodity's purchase price.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Company X, as agent, reports to Bank A only an inclusive purchase price that silently includes its brokerage fee. What does the standard require instead?
column5: The fee must be an undivided share of the profit from the sale
column6: The fee may stay merged in the price if it is below the market rate
column7: The fee must be paid by the end buyer only and not by the principal
column8: The fee must be stated separately from the purchase price
column10: Per 4/2/9, merging the agency compensation into the price is prohibited; the fee must be mentioned and deducted from, or added to, the price.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A buys a specific, ascertained lot of cotton, stipulating that delivery will be in two months and that the price will also be paid in two months. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, as the two counter-values are delayed
column6: Permitted, if a portion of the price is deposited as security
column7: Permitted, if the delivery date is fixed
column8: Permitted, since the cotton is ascertained
column10: Per 3/2/2/2, where the commodity is ascertained but delay in its delivery is stipulated along with delay in the price, the contract is not permitted.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Why must Bank A state its commodity agent's wages separately rather than merge them into the price, per the Basis?
column5: 'O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations'
column6: 'He who hires a worker must make known to him his wages'
column7: 'Allah has permitted trading and forbidden Riba, so avoid it'
column8: 'Muslims shall abide by their conditions, except one that makes lawful the unlawful'
column10: Per the Basis, the hadith 'He who hires a hired worker must make known to him his wages' applies, as a rule of Ijarah, to agency for wages.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A buys a commodity on spot from Company X and sells it on deferred terms to Company Y, which owns 80% of Company X. How does the standard treat this?
column5: As a valid Murabahah, if the profit is disclosed
column6: As permitted, since Company Y is not the seller
column7: As a buy-back ('Inah) sale, which is prohibited
column8: As a valid sale, since the parties are separate entities
column10: Per 4/2/6, a spot purchase then deferred sale to the same seller or to its holding institution with majority ownership or effective control is 'Inah.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Company X agrees to sell described wheat for delivery in three months, with the price also payable in three months. The contract uses the word 'sale'. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted: it is a Salam whose capital is not paid promptly
column6: Permitted, if both parties are able to deliver
column7: Permitted, as a forward contract outside the exchange
column8: Permitted, as the word 'sale' rather than 'Salam' was used in it
column10: Per 3/2/2/1, a described commodity with deferred price is not permitted, whether called sale or Salam, as it is Salam without prompt payment of capital.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A stipulates that its commodity agent guarantee the sale price under all circumstances. On what basis does the standard reject this?
column5: Guarantees are never allowed in commodity sales, whether by agents or others
column6: The agent's wages would become unknown, which makes the contract invalid
column7: An agent is a trustee, liable only for transgression or negligence
column8: An agent is a debtor for all sums he handles on behalf of his principal
column10: Per the Basis, the agent is a trustee and gives no guarantee except for transgression, negligence or breach of the constraints of agency.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Company X, as agent, buys a commodity for Bank A and then wants to buy it from Bank A for itself. What is required?
column5: No step, as the agent already holds the commodity
column6: Only a single advice from Bank A confirming the sale
column7: Only the agent's notice to Bank A that it has bought the commodity
column8: Two independent offers and acceptances between the two parties
column10: Per 4/1/3, the agent may buy for himself only by distinguishing the two liabilities through two independent offers and acceptances, e.g. by exchanging two advices.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A buys copper on spot from Company X and sells it on deferred terms to a customer. The customer then sells it back to Company X at a lower spot price. What does the standard require?
column5: It is permitted if the customer holds it for a day
column6: Such buy-back must be avoided in this application
column7: It is permitted as the parties are different
column8: It is permitted if prices are at market rates
column10: Per 4/1/4, in spot purchase and deferred sale by the institution, avoidance of buy-back, like the buyer reselling to the original spot seller at a lower price, is stipulated.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: A commodity contract defers both the delivery and the price. Which reason does the Basis give for prohibiting it?
column5: It creates two liabilities, like delaying the capital of Salam
column6: It is not organized on an exchange under financial supervision
column7: The price cannot be known in advance
column8: The commodity may perish before delivery
column10: Per the Basis, delaying both counter-values creates two liabilities, and the jurists prohibit delaying the capital of Salam; it also opposes the contract's requirements.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: In a spot sale of an existing, ascertained commodity, delivery is delayed by a few days without any stipulation of delay. What is the effect on the contract?
column5: The contract becomes void for lack of spot delivery
column6: It does not affect the validity of the contract
column7: The contract turns into a forward contract
column8: The contract becomes a Salam contract
column10: Per 3/1/4, delay without stipulation in delivery of an existing and ascertained commodity, or in accepting the spot price, does not affect validity.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A buys aluminium on spot in an organized market. The seller provides documents proving the metal exists, is owned by him and is distinguished from other metal. Are the conditions met?
column5: No; Bank A must physically inspect the aluminium in the warehouse
column6: Yes, but only if the price is deferred
column7: Yes; such documents are sufficient proof of these conditions
column8: No; the aluminium must first be moved to Bank A
column10: Per 3/1/1-3/1/2, the commodity must exist, be owned and ascertained; documents establishing existence, ownership and distinction are sufficient proof.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A is offered a commodity swap as practised in exchanges. What reason does the Basis give for prohibiting such swaps?
column5: Commodity prices in swaps are unknown
column6: They are concluded for overly long periods with no fixed end date
column7: They are concluded only between banks
column8: No real exchange occurs; they usually involve interest, 'Inah
column10: Per the Basis, in swaps no actual exchange of counter-values takes place, and they usually constitute interest payment, 'Inah and deferment of one counter-value.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: A spot commodity contract contains a condition preventing the buyer from taking delivery and obliging him to accept a set-off for value. What is the ruling on such a condition?
column5: It is not permitted in a spot contract
column6: It is permitted if the price is paid on a spot basis
column7: It is permitted if the buyer is an institution
column8: It is permitted if the market rules require it
column10: Per 3/1/3, a spot contract must not include a condition that prevents the buyer from taking delivery and obliges him to accept a set-off for value.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: A general agency memorandum for commodity purchases denies the buyer (principal) any right to take delivery. Why is this prohibited, per the Basis?
column5: It creates two deferred liabilities
column6: It turns the commodity sale into a deferred currency exchange (Sarf)
column7: It makes the agent's wages unknown to him
column8: It negates transfer of ownership and the right to deal in the goods
column10: Per the Basis, stipulating no delivery negates the requirements of sale: transfer of ownership to the buyer and his right to transact in the sold commodity.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: A broker sells the same lot of metal to two institutions at once, using duplicated title documents. What does the standard require to prevent this?
column5: A guarantee from the broker for the sale price in all circumstances
column6: Precision on title document numbers and liability for the cause
column7: Registration of each sale with the regulator only
column8: Insurance of the metal by each buying institution
column10: Per 4/2/8, selling via fictitious documents or to several institutions is prohibited; title document numbers must be precise and liability fixed on the cause.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Which of the following is outside the scope of the standard on Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets?
column5: Commodity swaps and indexes
column6: Spot commodity contracts on an exchange
column7: Sales concluded outside the organized markets
column8: Commodity derivatives such as options and futures
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover financial and commercial paper or currencies, nor sales concluded outside the organized markets.

column3: Sale of Commodities in Organized Markets
column4: Bank A buys ascertained assets, paying part of the price as 'Arboun, with the right to revoke within 30 days and forfeit the 'Arboun. Can Bank A sell this right to another?
column5: No; the contract is valid but the right may not be traded
column6: No; the 'Arboun contract itself is invalid
column7: Yes, if the seller consents to the transfer
column8: Yes; it is a valid option that may be traded to another investor
column10: Per 5/2/3/1, a contract with 'Arboun and a right of revocation in a set period is permitted, but trading the right relating to the earnest money is not.

column4: Ahmad wants to sell shares he does not yet own. What reason does the Basis give for prohibiting this short sale?
column5: Shares cannot be sold before dividends are paid
column6: He sells what he neither owns nor is liable for
column7: Short sales always involve paying interest to the broker
column8: The price of shares is always unknown at sale
column10: Per the Basis, a short sale leads to the sale of something not within the liability of the seller nor in his ownership, which is prohibited.

column4: Why does the Basis prohibit the issuance of interest-bearing bonds?
column5: They give holders no voting rights
column6: They are sales of goods that are not yet owned by the issuer
column7: They are loans, and every loan yielding a benefit is Riba
column8: They are Salam contracts with deferred capital
column10: Per the Basis, bonds by nature are loans; as each loan yielding a benefit is Riba and bonds rest on interest-bearing loans, their issuance is prohibited.

column4: Ahmad buys shares of a permissible trading company only to benefit from short-term differences in prices, not for dividends. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if held for at least a year before being resold
column6: Not permissible, as it is speculation rather than genuine investment
column7: Permissible only if bought for dividends and not for price differences
column8: Permissible, whether for investment or for dealing
column10: Per 3/2, buying and selling shares of permissible corporations, spot or deferred, is permissible whether for investment or dealing to benefit from price differences.

column4: Why does the Basis reject the claim that holders of Tamattu' shares have been fully redeemed?
column5: Their new shares carry no voting rights of any kind
column6: They never paid in full for their original shares
column7: Redemption is only in form; they remain owners
column8: Their shares were originally issued at a discount
column10: Per the Basis, Tamattu' holders still claim profit rights and liquidation rights; their redemption is only in form, as they continue to be owners.

column4: A mixed company had prohibited income during the year but declared an overall loss and paid no dividends. Must its shareholders eliminate the prohibited income?
column5: No; nothing is due if no dividend is paid to the shareholders
column6: Yes, despite the loss and absence of distribution
column7: No; the loss offsets the prohibited income earned during the year
column8: Yes, but only half of the prohibited income, the rest being offset
column10: Per 3/4/6/2, the prohibited income specific to the share must be eliminated whether or not profits are distributed and whether a profit or a loss is declared.

column4: Bank A buys shares in a conventional bank in order to work to convert it. Which principle does the Basis cite for allowing this?
column5: Enjoining good and forbidding evil (al-Amr bil-Ma'ruf)
column6: What can be sold can be mortgaged
column7: The rule that the secondary is subservient to the primary
column8: Gains are based on the bearing of costs
column10: Per the Basis, participation by one able or striving to convert is a means to alter the rejected and falls under enjoining good and forbidding evil.

column4: Company X redeems Ahmad's shares during its life and gives him shares with lower profit rights and a claim at winding up only after capital shares are paid. What are these?
column5: Bearer shares, which are permissible
column6: Preference shares, which are permissible
column7: Ordinary shares, which are permissible
column8: Tamattu' shares, which are not permissible
column10: Per 2/7, Tamattu' shares, given in place of redeemed shares with lesser profit and deferred liquidation rights, may not be issued.

column4: Ahmad held shares of a mixed company for most of the year but sold them all before the end of the financial period. Must he eliminate the prohibited income?
column5: No; elimination is only due on distributed dividends
column6: No; elimination falls on the owner at the end of the period
column7: Yes, in proportion to the number of days during which he held them
column8: Yes, the full year's prohibited income per share
column10: Per 3/4/6/1, elimination is obligatory on the share owner at the end of the financial period; it is not obligatory for one who sells before then.

column4: Company X is being formed with the objective of manufacturing liquor and wants to issue shares to the public. What is the ruling on issuing these shares?
column5: Permissible, if the shares are sold only to non-Muslim investors
column6: Permissible, if half of its income is from lawful sales
column7: Permissible, as shares are mere evidence of ownership
column8: Not permissible, as the corporation's objective is prohibited
column10: Per 2/1, issuance of shares is permissible only if the corporation's objectives are permissible; they should not be prohibited, like manufacturing liquor.

column4: Ahmad lends his shares by way of I'arah to his brother so the brother can pledge them for a debt. May the brother sell the shares?
column5: Yes, at any time, as he holds them
column6: No, not even to execute the mortgage
column7: Only to execute the terms of the mortgage
column8: Yes, if he later returns similar shares
column10: Per 3/16, shares may be lent by I'arah for pledging; the borrower has no right to sell them except to execute the terms of the mortgage.

column4: Bank A accepts lawful shares as a mortgage for a customer's debt. Which principle does the Basis rely on to permit this?
column5: A thing can be mortgaged if its sale is permissible
column6: Gains are based on the bearing of costs, as in shared liability
column7: Necessity permits the prohibited, so any asset may be mortgaged
column8: The secondary is subservient to the primary, as in mortgages
column10: Per the Basis, a thing may be mortgaged if its sale is permissible; since shares may be sold, they may be mortgaged to secure and recover a debt.

column4: Company X's memorandum of association lists dealing in interest among its objectives, though actual interest income is small. May Bank A invest in its shares?
column5: Yes, as its interest income is below 5% of income
column6: No; such an objective in the memorandum bars investment
column7: Yes, if Bank A eliminates the interest income later
column8: Yes, if its interest-based debt is under the 30% limit of capitalization
column10: Per 3/4/1, the exemption requires that the corporation not state in its memorandum that one of its objectives is dealing in interest or prohibited goods.

column4: Bank A manages an equity fund that invests in shares of mixed companies. Who is responsible for eliminating the prohibited income?
column5: Each fund investor individually
column6: The custodian bank of the fund
column7: The companies whose shares are held
column8: Bank A, as it is managing the operations
column10: Per 3/4/6/6, the responsibility for elimination falls on the institution when it trades for itself or manages the operations.

column4: Why can shares of a named corporation not be the subject-matter of Salam, per the Basis?
column5: Salam's subject is a debt; such shares are ascertained
column6: Salam is valid only for food items and crops
column7: Shares cannot be described precisely enough to be the subject of Salam
column8: Shares have no reliable market price for Salam
column10: Per the Basis, the subject-matter of Salam is a debt, while shares of a named corporation are ascertained; Salam in them also sells what is not owned.

column4: Bank A invested in a compliant mixed company, but a year later its interest-based debt rose to 40% of market capitalization. What must Bank A do?
column5: Keep it and eliminate a larger share of the income
column6: Keep it, as it was compliant when it was bought
column7: Give up the investment, as the rules no longer apply
column8: Keep it until its market value recovers, then sell it at once
column10: Per 3/4/8, these rules must be observed throughout the period of participation; if they cannot be applied, it is obligatory to give up the investment.

column4: Ahmad wants to mortgage his shares of a lawful company whose assets are mostly debts and cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, whatever the mix of assets
column6: Permissible only if tangible assets predominate
column7: Not permissible, as shares cannot be mortgaged
column8: Not permissible, since debts predominate
column10: Per 3/10, lawful shares may be mortgaged whether the corporation's assets are cash, tangibles, debts or a mix, in line with the rules for selling at liquidation.

column4: Company X wants to issue its share certificates to bearer rather than in the shareholders' names. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as bearer documents involve Gharar
column6: Permissible: it may be in the name, to order or to bearer
column7: Permissible only for shares that are fully paid up by the subscribers
column8: Not permissible: it must be in the owner's name
column10: Per 2/8, the share certificate is evidence of the shareholder's undivided share in company assets and may be in the owner's name, to his order or for bearer.

column4: Why does the standard exempt trading in shares of permissible-activity companies that sometimes borrow or deposit on interest?
column5: Interest dealings by such companies are lawful
column6: Shareholders are not owners of the company's assets
column7: The prohibition of Riba does not apply to companies
column8: Removal of hardship, general need and predominance
column10: Per the Basis, the exemption rests on removal of hardship, general need, widespread practice, the principles of surplus, shortage and predominance.

column4: Ahmad resells shares before final registration formalities are completed. What justifies this, per the Basis?
column5: Registration of shares has no legal effect at all
column6: The broker guarantees delivery of the shares to him
column7: Daman has passed to him via constructive possession
column8: Shares are debts that may be traded without limits
column10: Per the Basis, transactions are allowed before final registration because liability for loss (Daman) passes to the buyer through constructive possession.

column4: A broker asks Bank A to lend it shares, to be repaid later with similar shares. Why does the Basis treat lending shares as impermissible?
column5: The broker would have to pay interest on the shares it borrows
column6: Lending of any kind of asset is prohibited
column7: Shares are not truly owned by their holders
column8: At repayment the share does not represent the same assets
column10: Per the Basis, lending shares is impermissible because, due to the constant change in the corporation's assets, the share at repayment does not represent the same thing.

column4: Company X holds interest-taking deposits equal to 25% of its market capitalization. Its other ratios are within limits. May Bank A invest in its shares?
column5: No; the limit for such deposits is 10% of the market capitalization
column6: Yes; interest-taking deposits are within the 30% limit
column7: Yes, as such deposits are not counted at all in the permitted ratios
column8: No; any interest-taking deposits bar investment in the company's shares
column10: Per 3/4/3, total interest-taking deposits must not exceed 30% of market capitalization; such deposits remain prohibited whatever their amount.

column4: Bank A proposes to swap the dividends of its share portfolio with a counterparty for an agreed return. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted: swaps on shares and their returns are barred
column6: Permitted, if no cash settlement occurs
column7: Permitted, if the underlying shares are all Shari'ah-compliant
column8: Permitted, if both parties use one currency
column10: Per 3/14, it is not permitted to conclude swap contracts with respect to shares and their returns.

column4: Bank A acts only as an intermediary executing share trades for clients in mixed companies. What is its duty regarding prohibited income?
column5: Eliminate the prohibited income itself from all client accounts
column6: Nothing, as the duty lies only with the company
column7: Inform clients of the elimination mechanism so they can do it
column8: Deduct the prohibited portion from its commission
column10: Per 3/4/6/6, in intermediation the institution must inform dealers of the elimination mechanism; it may also offer the service, with or without a charge.

column4: Shares of a goods-trading company may be traded even though more than half of its assets are cash and debts. Which principle supports this, per the Basis?
column5: Gains are based on the bearing of costs
column6: The secondary is subservient to the primary
column7: Necessity permits what is prohibited
column8: What can be sold can be mortgaged
column10: Per the Basis, cash and debts are secondary to the main activity; the secondary is subservient, as in the hadith on selling a slave who has wealth.

column4: Bank A buys a controlling stake in a conventional bank, able to pass a resolution at the first general meeting to convert it to Shari'ah compliance. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only after conversion is complete
column6: Not permissible, as the bank deals in Riba
column7: Permissible, as participation for purposes of conversion
column8: Permissible only if Bank A takes no dividends at all from the bank
column10: Per 3/3, participation or trading for conversion is permitted for one able to convert by a resolution at the first general meeting, or striving to do so.

column4: A trading company's tangible assets, benefits and rights are 40% of total assets; the rest is cash and debts. May its shares be traded without the rules of Sarf or debts?
column5: Yes, but only with spot payment and immediate delivery of the price
column6: No, as cash and debts exceed one-half of its assets
column7: No, its shares may be traded only at nominal value
column8: Yes; tangible assets are not below 30%, so the rest is secondary
column10: Per 3/19, where the activity is in tangible assets and benefits, shares may be traded freely if those assets are not less than 30% of total assets.

column4: An underwriter of a share issue also prepares the feasibility study and markets the shares, charging for this work. What is the ruling on this charge?
column5: Permissible, if it is not in lieu of the guarantee
column6: Not permissible, as the underwriter may take no fee
column7: Permissible only if equal to the underwriting risk
column8: Permissible only if done by a separate company
column10: Per 2/4, compensation for work like feasibility studies or marketing is permissible, by the underwriter or another, if it is not in lieu of a guarantee.

column4: Company X has 10,000,000 shares and prohibited income of 2,000,000 for the period. Ahmad owns 50,000 shares at period-end. How much must he eliminate?
column10: Per 3/4/6/4, total prohibited income / number of shares = 0.2 per share; multiplied by the 50,000 shares owned = 10,000.

column4: Shareholders object to a proposed class of shares with priority in profit. On what basis does the standard prohibit such preference shares?
column5: They prevent the shares from being traded on markets
column6: They make the market price of the shares unknown
column7: They turn the corporation into a Qard with its holders
column8: They sever participation in profit and wrong others
column10: Per the Basis, preference shares lead to severance of participation in profit and imposition of injustice on other shareholders.

column4: Which of the following is outside the scope of the standard on Financial Paper (Shares and Bonds)?
column5: Issuance of interest-bearing bonds
column6: Investment Sukuk
column7: Pledging and lending of shares
column8: Options and swaps based on shares
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard covers shares and interest-bearing bonds, but not investment Sukuk, which have a separate specific standard.

column4: A manufacturing company with permissible activity has interest-based loans equal to 35% of its market capitalization. May Bank A invest in its shares?
column5: No; interest-based borrowing exceeds the 30% limit
column6: Yes, if Bank A eliminates the interest portion
column7: Yes, as the limit for borrowing is 50%
column8: Yes, as its primary activity is permissible
column10: Per 3/4/2, the total amount of interest-based loans must not exceed 30% of the corporation's market capitalization.

column4: What is the Shari'ah basis for permitting the issuance of shares of a corporation with permissible objectives?
column5: The rule that a Qard may yield a benefit to the lender if agreed
column6: The custom of stock markets, without other evidence
column7: The rule that necessity permits what is prohibited
column8: Evidences on contracts, partnership, 'Inan and Mudarabah
column10: Per the Basis, it rests on the generality of evidences on abiding by contracts and conditions, partnership, 'Inan, Mudarabah, Musaqat and Muzara'ah.

column4: Company X's interest-based loans are 20% of its market capitalization, within the limit. Its CFO argues this makes the borrowing itself lawful. Is he right?
column5: No; only loans above 20% of capitalization are prohibited
column6: Yes; loans within the 30% limit are lawful for the company itself
column7: No; interest-based loans are prohibited whatever the amount
column8: Yes, as long as the loans are short-term facilities
column10: Per 3/4/2, the 30% limit only governs the exemption for investing; raising loans on interest is prohibited whatever the amount.

column4: Ahmad bought shares; the sale formalities are complete and liability has passed to him, but final settlement is pending. May he sell them now?
column5: Yes, even though final settlement is not yet made
column6: Yes, but only back to the original seller
column7: No, he must wait for registration in his name
column8: No, he must wait for final settlement first
column10: Per 3/7, the buyer may deal in the share after completion of the sale formalities and transfer of liability, even if final settlement has not been made.

column4: A retail company with permissible primary activity earns 7% of its total income from prohibited sources. May Bank A invest in its shares?
column5: Yes, if Bank A eliminates the 7% portion
column6: No; prohibited income exceeds 5% of total income
column7: Yes, as prohibited income is below 10%
column8: Yes, as its primary activity is permissible
column10: Per 3/4/4, income from a prohibited component must not exceed 5% of the corporation's total income, whatever its source.

column4: Bank A has calculated the prohibited income to be eliminated from its shareholdings and proposes to use it to pay its taxes. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible to use it in any way, even for taxes
column6: Permissible, if approved by the Shari'ah board of the Institution
column7: Permissible for half of the amount only, the rest going to charity
column8: Permissible, as taxes are a public obligation owed by the Bank
column10: Per 3/4/6/5, the prohibited component may not be utilised in any way, nor may a legal fiction be created to do so, even through payment of taxes.

column4: A company holding mostly receivables adds a small amount of tangible assets solely so that its shares can be traded freely. How does the standard view this?
column5: Acceptable, if a Shari'ah board approves it
column6: Acceptable, as any amount of tangible assets makes the shares tradable
column7: Acceptable, if the tangible assets are owned
column8: Not acceptable, as a legal device for trading in debts
column10: Per 3/20, the rule must not be used as a means for trading in debts by merging parts of tangible assets and benefits with debts as a legal device.

column4: A corporation's objective and usual activity is dealing in gold, silver and currencies (Sirafah). How must its shares be traded?
column5: Only under the rules of Salam
column6: In the light of the rules of Sarf
column7: Freely, like any trading company
column8: Only under the rules of Istisna'a
column10: Per 3/19, if the corporation's objective and usual activity is dealing in gold, silver or currencies (Sirafah), trading in its shares must follow the rules of Sarf.

column4: A corporation's entire assets consist of debts owed to it. Ahmad wants to trade its shares. What is required?
column5: No special rules, as shares are always tradable
column6: Observing the rules of Sarf only
column7: Observing the rules for dealing in debts
column8: Trading only at the nominal value of the shares
column10: Per 3/18, shares of a corporation whose entire assets are debts may not be traded unless the rules for dealing in debts are observed.

column4: A government issues zero-coupon bonds at a discount, repaying the full face value at maturity. What is the ruling on issuing them?
column5: Permitted, as no periodic interest is paid on them
column6: Prohibited, as the loan is repaid with an excess
column7: Permitted, as the issuer is a government, not a company
column8: Permitted, if the discount at issue is small
column10: Per 4, bonds stipulating return of the loan with any excess are prohibited, including zero-coupon bonds, whether private, public or governmental.

column4: Company X wants to issue a class of shares that receive profit and liquidation proceeds before ordinary shares. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the priority applies only at liquidation
column6: Permissible, if approved by the extraordinary general assembly
column7: Permissible, if the holders pay a higher price for them
column8: Not permissible: preference shares with financial priority
column10: Per 2/6, preference shares with financial features giving priority at liquidation or in profit distribution are not permissible.

column4: Bank A did not subscribe to a bond issue but wants to buy the bonds in the secondary market and pledge them. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as trading and pledging bonds are barred
column6: Only pledging is prohibited, not buying
column7: Permitted, if bought below face value
column8: Permitted, since Bank A was not the original lender to the issuer
column10: Per 5, trading in bonds, sale and purchase, is prohibited, and so is their pledging and endorsement.

column4: Company X lets subscribers pay 25% of the share value now and defer the rest in instalments. What conditions does the standard set?
column5: Instalments may apply to some shareholders only, at the company's choice
column6: Deferred instalments must carry a fixed profit for the company
column7: Instalments apply to all shares; liability limited to subscribed value
column8: Subscribers get full rights in all shares before full payment
column10: Per 2/5, share value may be paid in instalments provided they apply to all shares and the corporation's liability is restricted to the value of the shares subscribed.

column4: Company X issues new shares to increase its capital while the old shares' value is well above nominal value. At what price may the new shares be issued?
column5: Only at a premium fixed at 10% above the nominal value
column6: At the value of the old shares, by expert valuation or market value
column7: At any price chosen freely by the board of directors of the company
column8: Only at the original nominal value of the old shares
column10: Per 2/3, new shares may be issued at a price equivalent to the value of the old shares, by expert valuation of assets or market value, at a premium or discount.

column4: A broker earns commission on trades in shares of a mixed company. Must the broker eliminate part of its commission as prohibited income?
column5: Only if the broker also holds the shares
column6: Yes, the whole commission must be eliminated
column7: No; the commission is its right for the work done
column8: Yes, in proportion to the company's prohibited income
column10: Per 3/4/6/3, elimination is not obligatory for the intermediary, agent or manager out of their commission or wages, which are their right for their work.

column4: Ahmad sells shares he does not own, relying on his broker's promise to lend him the shares at the time of delivery. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the broker's promise secures delivery
column6: Permissible, if the shares are bought back on the same trading day
column7: Permissible, if the company's activity is lawful
column8: Not permissible; the broker's promise is of no consequence
column10: Per 3/6, selling shares the seller does not own (short sale) is not permissible, and the broker's promise to lend them at delivery is of no consequence.

column4: A broker offers Ahmad an interest-bearing loan to buy shares on margin, with the shares mortgaged for the loan. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, nor is mortgaging the shares for that loan
column6: Only the mortgage is prohibited, while the interest-bearing loan is permitted
column7: Permissible, if the interest rate is low and the shares are mortgaged
column8: Permissible, if the shares bought are themselves Shari'ah-compliant
column10: Per 3/5, buying shares with interest-bearing loans (margin sales) is not permissible, nor is mortgaging the shares for such a loan.

column4: Bank A pays Company X today for 10,000 shares of Corporation Y to be delivered in six months, on the basis of Salam. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if Corporation Y's activity is lawful
column6: Not permissible, as Salam in shares is not allowed
column7: Permissible, if the price is paid in full now
column8: Permissible, if the shares are described precisely
column10: Per 3/11, the contract of Salam is not permissible in shares.

column4: Company X rents shares from Ahmad for a fee, to show a stronger financial position at year-end, then returns them. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as renting shares is not allowed
column6: Permissible, if the rental is a fixed amount
column7: Permissible, if similar shares are returned
column8: Permissible, as it is an Ijarah of an asset
column10: Per 3/15, renting shares is not permissible, whether for pledging, selling and returning similar shares, acquiring profits or showing a stronger financial position.

column4: Company X wants to give founders' shares extra voting rights, with no priority in profits or liquidation. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it treats shareholders unjustly
column6: Not permissible, as all shares must be identical
column7: Permissible only if they also get priority in the distribution of profit
column8: Permissible, as the feature is procedural or administrative
column10: Per 2/6, certain shares may be granted procedural or administrative features, like voting rights, in addition to ordinary share rights.

column4: At subscription, Company X adds a fixed and reasonable percentage to the share value to cover the expenses of issuance. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it is an excess over the nominal value of the share
column6: Permissible at any rate the board decides
column7: Permissible, as long as the percentage is fixed and reasonable
column8: Permissible only if paid from the company's profits
column10: Per 2/2, a determined percentage may be added to the share value at subscription to cover issuance expenses if it is fixed and reasonable.

column4: During subscription, before business starts, a new corporation's assets are exclusively cash. Ahmad wants to sell his shares. On what terms is this permissible?
column5: At any market price agreed by the parties
column6: Only at nominal value, with delivery of possession
column7: At nominal value, with deferred payment allowed
column8: Only under the rules of dealing in debts
column10: Per 3/17, when the assets are exclusively cash, shares may be traded only at nominal value and with delivery of possession.

column4: Bank A is offered a call option on shares, traded on an exchange. Which reason does the Basis give for prohibiting options on shares?
column5: Options are concluded outside the exchange, so they lack transparency
column6: Options are only lawful for commodities, not for shares or currencies
column7: The option premium is always too high compared to the share price
column8: The right of option is not a right that can be sold
column10: Per the Basis, the right of option is not a saleable right: it is created by the contract and relates to an abstract thing; options also involve Gharar and gambling.

column4: Bank A agrees to subscribe at nominal value to any shares of a new corporation left unsubscribed, and asks a fee in return for this undertaking. What is the ruling?
column5: The fee is allowed if fixed as a lump sum and not as a percentage
column6: The fee is allowed as it is a market practice among underwriters
column7: Underwriting is allowed, but not compensation for it
column8: Underwriting itself is not permissible, whether or not a fee is taken
column10: Per 2/4, underwriting the issue is permissible when done without compensation in lieu of underwriting.

column4: Company X records shareholders' names in an electronic register only, not on certificates. Why is this valid, per the Basis?
column5: The Lawgiver set no particular form for recording rights
column6: Only bearer shares need to be recorded in a register
column7: Written records of rights are never required in Shari'ah
column8: Shares do not represent any ownership right at all
column10: Per the Basis, the Lawgiver wishes rights to be established through writing and other forms but has not determined a particular form.

column4: A government issues prize bonds: no interest is paid, but holders enter periodic draws for prizes. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as no interest is paid
column6: Permitted, as they are public bonds
column7: Prohibited, like other bonds
column8: Permitted, if prizes are small
column10: Per 4, prize bonds are also prohibited, irrespective of the bonds being private, public or governmental.

column4: What does the standard identify as the Shari'ah substitute for bonds?
column5: Preference shares
column6: Prize bonds
column7: Tamattu' shares
column8: Investment Sukuk
column10: Per 6, the Shari'ah substitute for bonds is investment Sukuk.

column4: Before production starts, the State sets how a licensee must dispose of its share of the extracted minerals and the value to be paid to it. Is this within the State's rights?
column5: No; only market forces may set the value
column6: Yes, taking into account public interest
column7: Yes, but only after production has begun
column8: No; the licensee freely owns its share
column10: Per 5/7/1, the State may determine in advance how the licensee disposes of its share of the products and the value paid, taking public interest into account.

column4: Why may the State regulate mineral exploration by granting exclusive utilization rights, according to the Shari'ah basis?
column5: It realizes public interest and prevents disputes
column6: Exploration is a form of Riba-free loan from the State to the licensee
column7: Private persons may not hold mineral rights of any kind whatsoever
column8: The State owns all land absolutely, including privately held land
column10: Per the Basis, State regulation realizes public interest and prevents disputes, as with fuqaha requiring State permission to develop wasteland.

column4: Company X leases land from the State and builds a hospital on it, which it must hand over to the State after 20 years. How is this contract adapted?
column5: As Salam, the hospital being the goods delivered after twenty years
column6: As Ju'alah, the Ju'l being the hospital to be handed over later
column7: As Istisna'a, the price being a money sum paid by the State in instalments
column8: As Ijarah, the rent being the project handed over
column10: Per 6/2/2, if the project is built on land leased from the State against handing the project over later, it is Ijarah and the rent is the project itself.

column4: Which of the following is outside the scope of the standard on Concession Contracts?
column5: Franchises
column6: Concessions for management of public utilities
column7: Concessions for the utilization of minerals
column8: Concessions for construction of projects
column10: Per Scope (1), the standard does not cover franchises, which should be dealt with by a separate standard, nor legal or consensual subsidiary concession rights.

column4: The State breaches a material condition of a utilization concession, causing Company X actual losses. What are Company X's rights?
column5: Only claim compensation for its losses; it may not revoke the contract
column6: Revoke the contract and claim compensation for actual damages
column7: Only revoke; no compensation is due
column8: Neither, as the State may amend at will
column10: Per 5/8, each party may revoke the contract when the other breaches a condition or commitment, and the breaching party compensates actual damages.

column4: The State grants a utilization concession directly to Company X without any prior survey or exploration licenses. Is this permissible?
column5: No; a survey license must always come first
column6: No; an exploration license must come first
column7: Yes; the State may offer concessions directly
column8: Yes, but only for water, not minerals
column10: Per 5/2/5, notwithstanding the procedural order, the State may offer exploration or utilization concessions directly without those procedures.

column4: The State provides land to Bank A to utilize on a set profit-sharing ratio, and Bank A engages an operator on a similar basis. Which form is this?
column5: Two-step Mudarabah
column6: Parallel Salam
column7: Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
column8: Parallel Istisna'a
column10: Per 7/3, Mudarabah may apply where the State provides land on a predetermined profit-sharing rate; Institutions may act directly or through two-step Mudarabah.

column4: A licensee is paid for building a project only by the right to use it for a period before handing it over. Why is this a valid price, per the Basis?
column5: Istisna'a needs no price at all when the orderer is the State itself
column6: The State owes the licensee nothing
column7: In Istisna'a, usufruct of the product may serve as its price
column8: Usufruct counts as a gift from the State
column10: Per the Basis, in Istisna'a temporary benefit from the product may be its price; the price may be money or usufruct, including of the product itself.

column4: Company X holds a concession license and wants to securitize it to raise funds. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only by selling the whole license outright to an investor
column6: Not permissible without the State as co-issuer
column7: Not permissible, as a license is not property
column8: Permissible per Shari'ah rulings and the licensor's conditions
column10: Per 9, a concession license is a financial right; its owner may sell, lease, mortgage, share or securitize it per Shari'ah rulings and the licensor's conditions.

column4: The State fixes the price at which a mining licensee sells its product. What justification does the Basis give?
column5: Avoiding competition among licensees in the mineral market
column6: Preventing social injury from unduly high prices
column7: Ensuring the licensee recovers its costs and earns a fixed profit
column8: Making a profit for the State treasury from the licensee's sales
column10: Per the Basis, the State's right to fix the product price rests on the need to prevent social injury that could result from licensees charging unduly high prices.

column4: Company X's exploration period ends without it discovering the minerals for which the license was obtained. Is it entitled to a utilization concession?
column5: Yes, if it pays an additional fee to the State for the concession
column6: Yes, for a reduced area of the license it originally held
column7: Yes, as it bore the costs and risks of exploration during the period
column8: No, it is not entitled at the end of that period
column10: Per 5/2/4, if the licensee does not discover the minerals or water by the end of the exploration period, it is not entitled to a utilization concession.

column4: Bank A obtains a mining concession for a share of the output and engages an operator to extract, paying it a share of output. Which form applies?
column5: Parallel Salam
column6: Parallel Ju'alah
column7: Parallel Istisna'a
column8: Diminishing Musharakah
column10: Per 7/1, Ju'alah or Parallel Ju'alah may be applied in utilization concessions where the licensee receives a specific share of the output.

column4: Company X, an exploration licensee, discovers water in its licensed area. The license is silent on later rights. What is Company X's position?
column5: It has no further rights once exploration ends
column6: It must compete with all other bidders for the concession on equal terms
column7: It is eligible for the exclusive right to the utilization concession
column8: It becomes owner of the water and the land
column10: Per 5/2/3, after discovery the exploration licensee becomes eligible for the exclusive right of obtaining the utilization concession, unless the license stipulates otherwise.

column4: Bank A funds part of the capital for a concession project and undertakes to sell its share gradually to the State over the term. Which form is this?
column5: Diminishing Musharakah
column6: Two-step Mudarabah
column7: Fixed Musharakah
column8: Parallel Ju'alah
column10: Per 7/4/2 and 8/3/2, in diminishing Musharakah the Institution contributes a share of capital and undertakes to sell its share gradually to the State.

column4: A licensee holds a concession area for years without working it. Which precedent underlies requiring continuity of utilization?
column5: The hadith 'Muslims shall honor their obligations'
column6: The hadith on not selling food that was bought before measuring it
column7: The rule that the secondary is subservient
column8: Umar's ruling on wasteland left undeveloped for three years
column10: Per the Basis, continuity derives from the ruling on retained, undeveloped wasteland: Umar said land left undeveloped three years becomes the developer's.

column4: A mining licensee stops extraction without a reasonable excuse, in breach of its duty to continue utilization. What may the State do?
column5: Give a reasonable grace period, then cancel if not resumed
column6: Cancel the license at once, without any notice or grace period
column7: Confiscate the licensee's equipment as a penalty
column8: Nothing, as the licensee owns the concession
column10: Per 5/6, a licensee who ceases without reasonable excuse may be given a reasonable grace period to restart; otherwise the State may cancel the license.

column4: A ministry plans to award a mining concession to a favoured company without giving other qualified bidders any chance. What does the standard require when offering concessions?
column5: Awarding it to whoever first applies for it
column6: Awarding it only to companies owned by the State
column7: Justice, equality of chances and realization of public interest
column8: Awarding the concession to the highest financial bidder in all cases
column10: Per 4, when offering concession rights, due consideration should be given to justice, equality of chances and realization of public interest.

column4: Company X builds a toll road on State land; the road and its usufruct belong to Company X for 25 years, then go to the State. What is this?
column5: A management concession contract under which Company X runs the road
column6: A form of construction concession contract
column7: A utilization concession contract for extracting natural resources
column8: A survey license, granting the right of preliminary study
column10: Per 6/1/2/2, a licensee building a project on State land, with the project and usufruct owned by it for a period then passing to the State, is a construction concession form.

column4: The State grants Company X the right to manage a port for an annual fee of 5% of the port's total income. How is the contract adapted?
column5: As Istisna'a
column6: As Ju'alah
column7: As Ijarah
column8: As Mudarabah
column10: Per 10/2/1, where the management concession price is a lump sum or percentage of total income, the contract between the State and licensee is Ijarah.

column4: The State hires a specialized body to conduct mineral exploration on the State's behalf. Which rulings govern this relationship?
column5: The rulings of Musharakah, as the State shares in the minerals
column6: The rulings of Ijarah and Ju'alah
column7: The rulings of Salam, as the exploration result is delivered later
column8: The rulings of Mudarabah, as the State provides the capital
column10: Per 5/2/6, when the State requests a specialized body to survey or explore on its behalf, the relationship is subject to the rulings of Ijarah and Ju'alah.

column4: In a construction concession structured as Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a, the State is al-Mustasni' and Bank A is al-Sani'. What is the price of the product?
column5: Income from fees or rent collected from the public
column6: A lump sum paid by the State to Bank A at completion of the project
column7: A share of the State's general tax revenue over the concession term
column8: Bank A's construction cost plus a fixed profit margin agreed upfront
column10: Per 8/2, in Istisna'a the State is al-Mustasni', the Institution al-Sani', and the price is income from fees or rent collected from the public for services.

column4: A licensee hires land from the State to build a power plant and hands it back to the State at the end on the basis of Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek. May it sublease the land to a builder?
column5: No, the licensee must build the power plant itself without sub-contracting
column6: No, as the land is owned by the State
column7: Yes, but only through a Salam contract
column8: Yes, through an operating or diminishing Ijarah sub-contract
column10: Per 8/1, the licensee may hire the land and present the project back under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, using an operating or diminishing Ijarah sub-contract.

column4: A licensee managing a public water utility wishes to rescind its fixed-term management concession. Under what condition may it do so?
column5: The State has breached a condition first
column6: It pays the State a set penalty for early exit from the contract
column7: It takes measures ensuring services to the public continue
column8: It may never rescind a fixed-term contract
column10: Per 10/3, the licensee may rescind on condition that it takes measures that ascertain the provision of services to the public.

column4: Company X pays the State a fee for an exploration license over an area for three years. What rights may this license give it?
column5: Ownership of the land in the licensed area
column6: The right to be sole explorer and to conduct exploration works
column7: The right to sell minerals without a concession
column8: Only a non-exclusive right to survey the area for a limited period
column10: Per 5/2/2, an exploration license may entitle its holder to become the sole explorer in the area and to conduct the works required for exploration.

column4: Besides its own share of output, the State wants to buy additional quantities from a licensee's oil output. On what terms may it do so?
column5: By preemptive right at prevailing prices and contract terms
column6: At a price that the State fixes unilaterally below market rates
column7: Only if the licensee chooses to offer them
column8: Free of charge, as a further share of output
column10: Per 5/7/2, the State has a preemptory right to buy the quantities it needs from the output at prevailing prices and contractual terms.

column4: Which hadith does the Basis cite to support giving the explorer an exclusive right?
column5: 'Muslims honor all their obligations except those which permit prohibited deeds'
column6: 'He who hires a worker must make known his wages'
column7: 'A Salaf and a sale are not permitted'
column8: 'Whom who develops a piece of wasteland shall become its owner'
column10: Per the Basis, offering the exclusive right to the explorer can be based on the hadith: 'Whom who develops a piece of wasteland shall become its owner.'

column4: The State leases land to Bank A for a rent equal to a set share of the mine's output, and Bank A leases it to a third party to build the project. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as Bank A may not sublease
column6: Permissible as Ijarah with sub-contracting
column7: Not permissible, as rent must be money
column8: Permissible only as a Ju'alah contract
column10: Per 7/2, Ijarah may be applied where the State leases land for a rent as a set share of output; the licensee may lease to a third party (sub-contracting).

column4: Why is a mining licensee entitled to build refineries and acquire transport facilities, per the Basis?
column5: They are part of the Ju'l paid by the State for the exploration
column6: The licensee owns the land of the concession and everything on it
column7: The State must provide them free of charge to every licensee
column8: They are complementary requirements of utilization
column10: Per the Basis, rights to production and transport devices are complementary requirements of utilization; the same applies to related easement rights.

column4: Minerals are found under Ahmad's private land. One view puts them at the State's (Bayt al-Mal's) disposal. What reason does the Basis give for this view?
column5: No one, the landlord included, brought the minerals into being
column6: Ahmad did not pay the Kharaj on his land
column7: Private land ownership never extends to resources under the ground
column8: The State always owns private land
column10: Per the Basis, this view holds that no one, including the landlord, can claim to have brought the minerals into being, which removes disputes with the discoverer.

column4: A State follows the Fiqh view that the landowner has the right to utilize minerals against a fee to the State. Can it grant a mining concession over privately-owned land?
column5: Yes; concessions may cover all types of land
column6: Yes, if the landowner is paid a fair fee for the use of the land
column7: No; privately-owned lands are not subject to concession
column8: Yes, but only if the land is vacant
column10: Per 5/4/2, under the view giving utilization of minerals to the landowner, privately-owned lands, vacant or built on, are not subject to concession contracts.

column4: A State agency charges Company X a fixed fee for the procedures of offering it a concession right, with no element of Riba or Gharar. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as the State may not take fees
column6: Permissible, as a fee stipulated in the contract
column7: Not permissible, as concessions must be granted free
column8: Permissible only if the fee is a share of output
