column10: Per 3/2, there is no Shari'ah objection to fees or compensation for procedures of offering concession rights, unless the deal involves Riba, Gharar or other banned practices.

column4: In a construction concession, the licensee does the construction works and also provides the materials, and is paid by the right to use the project for a period. How is it adapted?
column5: As Istisna'a, its value being the right to utilize the project
column6: As Ju'alah, its Ju'l being a share of output
column7: As Mudarabah, with the project as capital
column8: As Ijarah, its rent being the project itself handed to the State
column10: Per 6/2/1, if the licensee undertakes construction and materials (the predominant case), the contract is Istisna'a, its value being the right to utilize the project.

column4: Company X gets a utilization concession whose exploration effort is unknown, for a set percentage of the output. How does the Shari'ah classify it?
column5: Mudarabah: the State is owner of capital
column6: Ijarah: the State is lessor, Company X is lessee
column7: Salam: the State is buyer of the output
column8: Ju'alah: the State is Ja'il, Company X is 'Amil
column10: Per 5/3, a utilization concession is a form of Ju'alah: the State is the Ja'il, the licensee the 'Amil and its amount the Ju'l.

column4: A management concession is treated as Mudarabah though its capital is a facility, not cash. What view does the Basis rely on?
column5: Mudarabah capital may be any debt owed by the State to the licensee
column6: Facilities count as cash by custom
column7: The Hanbalis permit Mudarabah on income-generating assets
column8: The State is exempt from Mudarabah rules
column10: Per the Basis, the Hanbalis permit Mudarabah on income-generating assets like animals; net profit is shared after allocations to preserve the project's capital.

column4: Company X holds a survey license for an area and later finds signs of minerals. Does the survey license give it exclusive rights or the right to mine?
column5: Yes; it entitles Company X to start mining at once
column6: Yes; it makes Company X the sole surveyor in the whole licensed area
column7: It gives extraction rights but not exclusivity
column8: No; it gives neither exclusive survey nor extraction rights
column10: Per 5/2/1, a survey license does not grant the right of sole surveyor in the area nor the right to conduct extraction works or build facilities.

column4: The State inspects a licensee's management of an airport and finds a breach of contract conditions. What may it do under the standard?
column5: Impose any penalty it deems fit
column6: Impose the penalties stipulated in the contract
column7: Take the airport's revenue as compensation
column8: Only warn the licensee, without penalties
column10: Per 10/5, the licensor may monitor and inspect the contract's conditions and impose the penalties stipulated in the contract for breach.

column4: A management concession price is set as a percentage of the project's net profit after expenses and allocations. How is it adapted?
column5: As Mudarabah, with the facility itself as capital
column6: As Musharakah, with cash contributed by the State as capital
column7: As Ju'alah, with the profit share as Ju'l for managing the facility
column8: As Ijarah, with the profit share as rent for the facility
column10: Per 10/2/1, if the price is a percentage of net profit, the contract is Mudarabah, in which the capital is the original facility or the project itself.

column4: A licensee's pay for building a bridge is set as a sum of money, recovered through bridge tolls. The period ends before the full sum is received. What is its position?
column5: It must hand over the bridge at the end and lose the unpaid balance
column6: It may sell the bridge to a third party
column7: It keeps utilizing the project until the full sum is received
column8: It may raise tolls without the licensor's consent
column10: Per 6/3/2, where pay is a sum of money, the licensee keeps the project and utilizes it until receipt of the full amount, unless a clearance deal is made.

column4: Why does exploration, unlike survey, give the licensee exclusive status, per the Basis?
column5: Exploration is like Tahjir; survey is mere expectation
column6: Surveys are done only by the State itself, never by private persons
column7: Exploration licenses cost more than surveys and so confer more rights
column8: Survey is a Ju'alah and exploration a sale of the minerals in advance
column10: Per the Basis, survey rests on mere expectation, while exploration is like Tahjir (retention) in wasteland development, which precedes utilization.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a Fodooli's act suspended pending the owner's approval rather than treated as void?
column5: Gharar is always tolerated in sale contracts, so no sale is ever void
column6: The buyer's rights override those of the owner of the goods sold
column7: A Muslim's act should be preserved from cancellation if possible
column8: The Fodooli is considered a guarantor of the owner for the value of the goods
column10: The basis: a Muslim's act should be preserved from cancellation where possible; Ibn Al-Humam reconciled Gharar and benefit by permissibility with suspension.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Broker B is appointed as agent of a seller and, in the same deal, as agent of the buyer, to conclude the sale between them. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the price agreed between them is the market price
column6: Not permitted: an agent may not act for both parties
column7: Permitted, as long as he discloses both roles to the two principals
column8: Permitted, if both principals agree to pay his fee in equal parts
column10: Per 6/1/3, the agent should not act for both parties to the contract.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Which narration does the Shari'ah basis cite from the Sunnah as evidence that agency is permissible?
column5: The Prophet appointed a collector of Zakah to take it from a tribe
column6: The Prophet permitted Salam in fruits for a known term
column7: The Prophet bought food on deferred payment from a Jew, pledging his armour
column8: The Prophet gave Urwah Al-Bariqi a dinar to buy a sheep
column10: The basis cites the Hadith of Urwah Al-Bariqi, given one dinar by the Prophet to buy a sacrificial sheep, an incidence involving agency.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Goods held by Bank A as agent for a customer are destroyed in a fire. The Bank was not negligent and did not breach the contract. Who bears the loss?
column5: The Bank and the customer share the loss equally, as both gained from the agency
column6: The customer, as the Bank holds the goods as a trustee
column7: The Bank, as the goods were in its possession when they were destroyed
column8: The Bank, if it received a fee for the agency, as a paid agent guarantees
column10: Per 5/2, the agent is a trustee and is liable only for damage from his misconduct, negligence or breach of the contract terms.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An investment agency contract sets the agent's fee by reference to a published indicator quoted at the beginning of each quarter. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as fees must be a lump sum
column6: Not permissible, as the fee is unknown at signing
column7: Permissible only if the indicator is fixed for the term
column8: Permissible, as the fee will become known in the future
column10: Per 4/2/3, the fee may be an amount to be known in the future, as when linked to an indicator quoted at the beginnings of different intervals of time.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A discriminating minor appoints an agent to sell his bicycle. The agent sells it at a fair price. What is the status of the sale?
column5: It remains pending the approval of the minor's guardian
column6: It is valid because the price equals the market price
column7: It is void from the outset and cannot be approved
column8: It is valid and binding on the minor immediately
column10: Per 3/1/2, in acts that may be harmful or useful like buying and selling, a partially capable person's agent's acts remain pending the guardian's approval.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad appoints two agents in the same contract to sell his land. One of them sells it alone without the other. Ahmad never authorized sole action. What is the ruling?
column5: Each agent may act independently of the other, since both are appointed
column6: Sole action is allowed if the price obtained is fair and the principal benefits
column7: Neither may act as sole decision-maker without authority
column8: The first agent to act binds the principal and the second agent
column10: Per 6/5, where several agents are appointed in the same contract, none should become the sole decision-maker unless authorized by the principal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A non-paid agent has started a construction task that cannot be halted without harming the principal. The agent now wants to withdraw. What is the ruling?
column5: The agency is binding until the whole project is completed
column6: He may withdraw only if he pays the principal compensation
column7: He may withdraw at once, as non-paid agency is not binding on the agent
column8: The agency is binding until work can be suspended without injury
column10: Per 4/3/3, agency remains binding when the agent commences tasks that cannot be discontinued without injury, until they can be suspended without injury.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A paid agent completes useful partial work, then stops without any reasonable excuse, causing the principal an actual loss. What is the agent's position?
column5: Paid for the part done; liable for the principal's actual loss
column6: Entitled to nothing, and liable for the principal's loss and the lost profit
column7: Entitled to the full fee, with no liability for loss since he did useful work
column8: Paid for the part done, with no liability for the loss as he acted in good faith
column10: Per 4/2/7, the agent gets remuneration for beneficial work done within the contract value, and must indemnify the principal for actual loss from his refusal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad appointed Bank A as agent to sell his car, then sold the car himself before the Bank found a buyer. What is the status of the agency?
column5: It continues until the Bank is formally notified
column6: It becomes binding on Ahmad for the agreed term
column7: It expires, as the principal no longer owns the asset
column8: It continues for any similar car Ahmad buys later
column10: Per 7/1/3-7/1/4, agency expires when the principal performs the task himself or no longer owns the asset in question.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: In a paid procurement agency, Bank A's contract with its agent states that the agent shall bear transport, storage and insurance costs of the goods. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the costs are deducted from the fee he is paid for the agency
column6: Not permitted: these expenses are for the principal to bear
column7: Permitted, as the agent is paid a fee that is meant to cover such costs
column8: Permitted only for costs arising after delivery of the goods to the Bank
column10: Per 5/1/1, in procurement agency the principal bears the price and expenses; in paid agency these may not be stated as payable by the agent.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Under a general agency over Ahmad's assets, the agent donates part of the assets to a charity without Ahmad's authorization. What is the ruling?
column5: Not allowed: general agency excludes donations unless authorized
column6: Allowed, if customary practice accepts such gifts from an agent
column7: Allowed, since general agency covers all disposals, including donations
column8: Allowed, if the donation serves Ahmad's reputation and is reasonable
column10: Per 4/1/1, general agency covers all methods of disposing of assets but does not include making donations unless the principal authorizes it.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A broker known to provide agency services only against payment acts for Ahmad. Their contract is silent on any fee. Is the broker entitled to remuneration?
column5: No, unless Ahmad later agrees to pay him voluntarily after the work
column6: Yes, but only half of the usual market rate for such services
column7: Yes, remuneration ascertained by customary practice is valid
column8: No, since no fee was stipulated, the agency is unpaid despite the custom
column10: Per 4/2/1, paid agency is permissible whether the fee is stipulated or ascertained by custom, as when the agent provides such service only for a fee.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A Fodooli sells Ahmad's car. Before Ahmad approves, the buyer revokes the contract. Ahmad then approves. What is the effect of the approval?
column5: The sale becomes effective from the approval date
column6: None; a new contract has to be initiated
column7: The buyer's revocation is void and the sale stands
column8: The sale becomes effective from the date of the act
column10: Per 8/2, the owner's approval should precede revocation of the contract by either party; otherwise, a new contract has to be initiated.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Bank A's agent, without asking the Bank, appoints another firm as sub-agent to complete the task. What is the ruling?
column5: He may, as long as the task is completed on time
column6: He may, if the sub-agent is paid from his own fee
column7: He may, since he remains liable for the sub-agent
column8: He has no right to do so without the Bank's permission
column10: Per 6/4, the agent has no right to appoint a sub-agent except with the permission of the principal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Under an absolute agency to sell goods, the agent sells them on deferred payment without asking the principal. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, since the agency was absolute
column6: Not permissible without the principal's prior consent
column7: Permissible, if the deferred price is above market price
column8: Permissible, as long as the buyer provides a guarantee
column10: Per 4/1/2, in absolute agency barter and deferred payment sales are not permissible except with the prior consent of the principal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad instructs his agent to sell a car for 10,000. The agent sells it for 11,000. Has the agent breached the agency contract?
column5: Yes, any departure from the set price is a breach of the agency contract
column6: No, but Ahmad may declare the sale invalid and recover the car
column7: Yes, and the extra 1,000 belongs to the agent as his reward for the sale
column8: No, acts that serve the principal's interest are not a breach
column10: Per 5/2, breach does not include acts that serve the principal's interest, such as selling at a higher or buying at a lower price.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An agent told to buy for cash instead buys on deferred payment, which does not serve the principal's interest. What may the principal do?
column5: Either maintain the contract or declare it invalid
column6: He must accept it, but the agent pays any excess
column7: He can only claim compensation, not reject it
column8: He must accept it, as the agent acted in good faith
column10: Per 6/3/1, when the agent breaches in a way not serving the principal's interest (e.g. spot vs deferred), the principal may maintain the contract or declare it invalid.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad asks his friend Karim to collect a debt for him without any fee. Karim hears the request, says nothing and does not object. What is the status of the agency?
column5: The agency is void as no standard wording was used
column6: No agency arises until Karim accepts it expressly, in writing or orally
column7: Karim's silence counts as acceptance of the non-paid agency
column8: Silence counts as acceptance only in paid agency, not in non-paid agency
column10: Per 2/2/2, in accepting non-paid agency silence is sufficient acceptance, while a negative response indicates rejection.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A debtor agrees that, if he defaults, his own assets will be placed under the management of his creditor. What form of agency is this?
column5: Immediate agency
column6: Conditional agency
column7: Act of an uncommissioned agent
column8: Future agency
column10: Per 2/2/3/2, conditional agency makes validity subject to a condition, e.g. a debtor placing his assets under his creditor's management on default.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An agent wishes to sell the principal's property to his own wife. What is required under the standard?
column5: The agent should obtain the principal's consent
column6: Nothing, as long as the price is the market price
column7: Nothing, unless the deal involves favoritism
column8: The deal is prohibited even with consent
column10: Per 6/1/1, in deals that involve the agent's spouse or relatives under his guardianship, the agent should obtain the consent of the principal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A discriminating minor appoints an agent to receive, on his behalf, a gift that his uncle wants to donate to him. What is the ruling?
column5: Invalid, since a minor can never appoint an agent in any matter at all
column6: Invalid, since gifts cannot be received through agency
column7: Valid only after approval of the minor's guardian or the competent court
column8: Valid, since the act results in absolute benefit to the minor
column10: Per 3/1/2, a partially capable person such as a discriminating minor may appoint an agent in matters of absolute benefit, such as accepting donations.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An investor gives Bank A funds under absolute agency, authorizing it to use any form of investment without naming one. Does this Jahalah affect the agency?
column5: No, and the Bank is free of any customary restriction or duty to the investor
column6: Yes, the agency is void for unknown subject matter and cannot be corrected later
column7: No, it is overlooked, but the Bank must serve the investor's interest
column8: Yes, unless the investor names a specific asset later
column10: Per 3/3/1, Jahalah is overlooked when in absolute agency the principal allows any form of investment; the agent must observe his interest and customs.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Bank A appoints a broker as agent to sell its shares, effective today, but requires him to refer back to the Bank before each sale. What is the ruling?
column5: The agency becomes effective only after the first referral
column6: Valid: agency is effective now; disposal awaits the condition
column7: The condition is void and the broker may sell freely without referral
column8: Invalid: a condition may attach to the contract itself, not to the disposal
column10: Per 2/2/4, conditions may be confined to disposal: the agency is immediately effective but disposal awaits a condition like referring back to the principal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad tells his agent to buy a car for up to 100. Its market price is 110. The agent pays 120. How much must the agent compensate Ahmad?
column5: 20, the difference between 120 and Ahmad's limit
column6: Nothing, as the agent is a trustee
column7: 10, the difference between 120 and the market price
column8: 10, the difference between 110 and Ahmad's limit
column10: Per 6/3/2, if the agent buys above both market and set price, he compensates the difference between the purchase price and the market price.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An agent gets a fixed fee plus a pledged share of profit. Per the Shari'ah basis, how may that extra share be characterized?
column5: As a deferred part of the price
column6: As a Mudarabah profit share
column7: As a guarantee of minimum return
column8: As a conditional gift or as Ju'alah
column10: The basis: the pledge to give the agent a share of profit is a pledge to donate, so it can be a conditional gift or Ju'alah (or a subsidiary addition).

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Company X asks Bank A to act as its agent in extending interest-bearing loans to third parties for a fee. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible: the subject matter is a Shari'ah-banned practice
column6: Permissible, since the Company could lend such funds personally with interest
column7: Permissible, if the Bank's fee is fixed in advance and not a share of interest
column8: Permissible, as agency covers all financial contracts that clients request
column10: Per 3/3/3, the subject matter of agency should not involve a Shari'ah-banned practice, like trading in impermissible commodities or usurious lending.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An agent to sell a mortgaged asset dies before the sale. Per the Shari'ah basis, what happens to this agency?
column5: It passes to the mortgagee to sell for himself at the market price
column6: It expires, like any agency, on the agent's death, and cannot be inherited
column7: It does not expire and is pursued by the agent's inheritors
column8: It is suspended until the debtor appoints a new agent in place of him
column10: The basis treats agency to sell a mortgaged asset as an exception: it does not expire on the agent's death and is pursued by inheritors, to protect the mortgagee.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis allow agency to be tied to a condition or a future date?
column5: Agency is delegation of power, not a transfer of ownership
column6: Agency is a binding contract like Ijarah, so conditions may be attached
column7: Gharar is always tolerated in non-paid contracts such as agency
column8: Customary practice overrides Shari'ah rulings on conditions in contracts
column10: The basis: agency can be linked to a condition or future date because it is delegation of power rather than an act of ownership transfer required immediately.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the agent treated as a trustee rather than a guarantor of the asset he holds?
column5: He has no right to dispose of the asset except by the owner's order
column6: He works in the principal's interest and was trusted by him
column7: He receives no fee in most agency contracts, so he bears no liability
column8: The principal can revoke the agency at any time before the sale
column10: The basis: the agent works for the principal's interest, trusteeship is normal in such engagements, and choosing him shows the principal's good faith.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad appoints a discriminating minor as his agent to buy goods from the market. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, with commitments shared by Ahmad and the minor in equal parts
column6: Permitted only if the minor's guardian bears the commitments
column7: Not permitted, as an agent must be an adult of full legal capacity
column8: Permitted; all contractual commitments rest solely on Ahmad
column10: Per 3/2/1, a discriminating minor may become an agent provided that all the contractual commitments are the sole responsibility of the principal.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Karim, with no authority, sells Ahmad's goods without declaring that he lacks authority. Ahmad refuses to approve the sale. What is the result?
column5: The sale binds Ahmad despite his refusal
column6: The sale remains suspended indefinitely
column7: The act becomes binding on Karim himself
column8: The sale is binding on the buyer and Ahmad equally
column10: Per 8/2, if the owner does not approve, the Fodooli's act binds the Fodooli himself, if he did not declare at signing that he had no authority.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A debtor appoints his mortgagee as agent to sell the mortgaged asset on maturity. Later, the debtor tries to revoke this agency. What is the ruling?
column5: He cannot: the agency is binding as it involves others' rights
column6: He can, since agency is basically a non-binding contract for the principal
column7: He can, provided he notifies the mortgagee in writing and pays him damages
column8: He cannot, but only if the agency is a paid one
column10: Per 4/3/1, agency becomes binding when it involves rights of others, as when the mortgagor appoints the mortgagee as agent to sell on maturity.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: The principal under an ordinary agency to buy goods dies before the agent completes the purchase. What is the status of the agency?
column5: It continues until the purchase is completed
column6: It passes automatically to the principal's heirs
column7: It continues if the agency was a paid one
column8: It expires with the death of the principal
column10: Per 7/1/1, the agency contract expires when the principal or the agent dies or loses legal capacity, or the Institution is bankrupt or liquidated.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Karim sold Ahmad's car on Ahmad's behalf. Only afterwards did Karim learn that Ahmad had appointed him as agent before the sale. How is the sale treated?
column5: It falls under agency from the moment Karim learns of it
column6: The prior sale does not fall under the agency contract
column7: It binds Ahmad because an agent is a trustee
column8: It falls under agency, as the appointment came first
column10: Per 3/2/2, the agent must be aware of his status; an act done before he knows he is an agent does not fall under the agency (it may fall under Fodooli rules).

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Which Qur'anic passage does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of agency?
column5: The sending of one with a silver coin to buy food in Al-Kahf
column6: The verse on fulfilling contracts and obligations in all transactions
column7: The verse permitting trade and prohibiting Riba in all dealings
column8: The verse on recording debts in writing when dealing for a specified term
column10: The basis cites Al-Kahf: 19, where one was sent to town with a silver coin to buy food, as the agent of the others.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An investment agency contract stipulates that the agent guarantees the investors' capital. What is the ruling on this stipulation?
column5: Permissible, if the agent is paid a separate fee for giving the guarantee
column6: Not permissible: it turns the deal into an interest-based loan
column7: Permissible, if the guarantee is limited to a part of the capital
column8: Permissible, as it protects the investors' capital against any loss
column10: Per 5/2 (citing SS 5, 2/2/2), combining agency and guarantee in one contract is not permissible; an agent's capital guarantee makes it an interest-based loan.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Without any reasonable excuse, the principal forces a paid agent to stop work halfway through the agency period. What fee is the agent entitled to?
column5: Remuneration for the half already performed
column6: No fee, since the agency was revoked
column7: The full remuneration agreed upon
column8: The market rate for the work already performed
column10: Per 4/2/7, when the principal forces the agent to discontinue before the end of the period without reasonable excuse, the agent gets the full agreed fee.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis limit a breaching agent's compensation to the gap from the market price, not a pre-set profit?
column5: Because the agent is never liable for any loss
column6: Because the market price is always the fairest price
column7: Because the principal may otherwise revoke the deal
column8: To compensate loss without a pre-fixed return on capital
column10: The basis: compensating the market-price gap establishes justice without accepting capital on pre-fixed return, which entails a suspicion of Riba.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A one-year agency is silent on new operations. In month 11, the agent enters an Ijarah whose effects run beyond the year. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only with the principal's fresh consent
column6: Permitted, as it was commenced within the agency period
column7: Not permitted in the last quarter of the term
column8: Not permitted, as its effects exceed the agency term
column10: Per 4/4/3, unless the contract states otherwise, the agent may commence new operations during the period even if their effects succeed the period.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A paid agent has done part of the work when the subject matter is destroyed by a flood, with no fault of the agent. Must the principal pay?
column5: Yes, the full fee for the whole agency term
column6: No, damage of the subject matter cancels the fee
column7: Yes, for the part of the work already performed
column8: No, and the agent must indemnify the principal
column10: Per 4/2/8, damage of the subject matter does not relieve the principal from paying for work performed; the agent indemnifies only for misconduct or negligence.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Ahmad, who has no right over a property, tries to authorize an agent to sell it. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this agency invalid?
column5: The agent derives his right from a principal who has none
column6: Only paid agency can cover the sale of property owned by others
column7: Agency is not allowed in the sale of real estate or other fixed property
column8: The agent has not yet taken possession of it from the principal
column10: The basis: the principal must have the right to dispose because the agent derives that right from him; he cannot delegate a right he does not own.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Without any need or urgency and with no authority, Karim sells Ahmad's goods to a buyer. Ahmad later approves the sale. From when is the sale effective?
column5: From the date of Ahmad's approval only, as approval is not retroactive
column6: It is not effective; a new contract is needed between Ahmad and the buyer
column7: From the date the buyer takes delivery of the goods from Karim
column8: From the date of Karim's act, as approval is retroactive
column10: Per 8/4, when the owner approves the act of the uncommissioned agent, the contract becomes effective under agency rules, retroactively from the date of the act.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Bank A is reviewing four agency mandates. Which one falls within the scope of the standard on Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent?
column5: A mandate to handle documentary credits for importers
column6: A mandate to manage an investment fund for investors
column7: A mandate to pay the Bank's Zakah on its behalf to the Zakah collectors
column8: A mandate to act as advocate for a client in a court prosecution
column10: Per clause 1, the standard covers fund management, real estate and investment agency, but excludes worship (Zakah), legal advocacy and documentary credits.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Bank A's Shari'ah board rejects a broker acting for both buyer and seller in one deal. Per the basis, what is the main reason?
column5: To avoid giving both offer and acceptance to one party
column6: Because agency cannot cover sale contracts
column7: Because the broker would have to guarantee the price
column8: Because the broker would earn two separate fees
column10: The basis, following the Hanafi and predominant Shafi'i view, bars it to avoid assigning offer and acceptance to one party and prevent self bias.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: A collection agency contract lets the agent keep "whatever share it deems fit" from the amounts it collects for the principal. What is the ruling on this fee?
column5: Permissible, if customary practice supports it
column6: Permissible, as the agent's share is linked to output
column7: Permissible, if the principal may revoke at any time
column8: Not permissible, as the remuneration is left undetermined
column10: Per 4/2/3, it is not permissible to leave the agent's fee undetermined and allow him to take an unspecified share from the principal's entitlements.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Company X, as Bank A's agent, buys goods for the Bank. Company X then wants to buy the same goods from the Bank. What is the ruling?
column5: Not allowed, as an agent can never buy from his principal, even by offer and acceptance
column6: Allowed, with the goods staying at the Bank's risk after sale
column7: Allowed by new offer and acceptance, guarantees kept separate
column8: Allowed automatically, with no new offer and acceptance and no change of risk
column10: Per 6/1/4, an agent may buy what he bought for the principal by offer and acceptance; guarantees stay separate and after the sale goods are at the agent's risk.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: Bank A's Shari'ah board accepts an agency formed by any wording indicating delegation. On which fiqh principle does the standard base this?
column5: Harm should be removed, and rigid wording causes harm to the parties
column6: Necessity makes the prohibited permissible, so delegation is allowed by any wording
column7: Gain accompanies liability for loss, so the agent's wording binds him
column8: In contracts, intentions and meanings count, not wording
column10: The basis grounds forming agency in any wording on the principle that what matters in contracts are intentions and meanings rather than wording and constructions.

column3: Agency and the Act of an Uncommissioned Agent (Fodooli)
column4: An agent sells the principal's goods to his adult son, who is not under his guardianship, at a fair price. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible unless it involves injustice or favoritism
column6: Not permissible in any case, as the son is a relative
column7: Not permissible without the principal's consent
column8: Permissible only if the price exceeds market price
column10: Per 6/1/1, deals with ascendants or descendants not under the agent's guardianship (and not his spouse) are permissible unless they involve injustice or favoritism.

column4: Bank A wants to sell its share in a syndicate whose physical assets and usufructs exceed its cash and debts. On what terms may it sell?
column5: Only at face value plus a fixed profit agreed by the participants
column6: At the value agreed with the buyer, per the contract conditions
column7: Only at the nominal value of its contribution, whatever the assets are worth
column8: Only after the syndicate is fully liquidated and its assets are sold
column10: Per 10/2, an Institution may dispose of its share at the agreed value if physical assets and usufructs exceed cash, debts and financial rights.

column4: A board member objects that Bank A cannot be a partner with a non-Muslim conventional bank. Per the Shari'ah basis, what really matters?
column5: That the non-Muslim partner holds only a minority share in the syndicate
column6: That the non-Muslim partner pays a higher fee than Muslim partners
column7: The deal's conformity to Shari'ah, not the faith of the dealer
column8: That the deal is only with banks of the same country
column10: The basis: partnership with a non-Muslim is not prohibited except for banned dealings; what matters is the deal's conformity to Shari'ah, not who made it.

column4: From which contract does the Shari'ah basis derive the permissibility of syndicated financing?
column5: Musharakah
column6: Hawalah
column7: Qard
column8: Kafalah
column10: The basis states that the permissibility of syndicated financing is derived from Musharakah, which encounters no Shari'ah restriction.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is receiving a commitment commission prohibited?
column5: It is paid before any work has been done by the lead bank on the deal
column6: It always exceeds the actual cost incurred in arranging the financing
column7: It is paid for the right of contracting, a matter of will
column8: It is paid by the customer, not by the partners in the syndicate
column10: The basis: commitment commission is paid for exercising the right of contracting, a matter of will and desire, not a subject matter of compensatory deals.

column4: Bank A manages a syndicate as a paid agent for an agreed fee. The operation ends without any profit. Is Bank A entitled to its fee?
column5: No, the fee is converted into a share of loss borne by Bank A
column6: Yes, the fee is due whether profit materializes or not
column7: No, the fee is due only if profit is realized by the syndicate
column8: Only half of the fee, as no profit was made on the operation
column10: Per 6/3, in paid agency the agent becomes entitled to remuneration whether profit is actually materialized or not.

column4: Bank A, Bank B and Bank C join in a syndicated financing through Ijarah. How should the accounts of the syndicated operation be kept?
column5: Recorded only in the largest contributor's accounts, as it bears most risk
column6: Merged into the accounts of the lead manager for the whole operation
column7: Split pro rata into each participant's own accounts according to its share
column8: Independent of the participating Institutions' accounts
column10: Per clause 2, the accounts of the syndicated financing operation are kept independent from the accounts of the participating Institutions.

column4: The participants ask Bank A, the lead manager acting as Mudarib, to guarantee the syndication funds against any loss. What is the ruling?
column5: Not allowed: a trustee is liable only for misconduct or negligence
column6: Allowed, if it is paid an extra fee for giving the guarantee to participants
column7: Allowed, but only for half of the funds contributed by the participants
column8: Allowed, since it controls the funds as manager and can protect them better
column10: Per 8/1, the lead manager (Mudarib, partner or agent) is a trustee and should not guarantee funds except for misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.

column4: Which of the following is listed by the standard as a mode through which syndicated financing may be provided to customers?
column5: Term loans at a fixed rate of interest
column6: Discounting of commercial bills
column7: Muzara'ah, Musaqat and Mugharasah
column8: Overdraft facilities with a fixed fee
column10: Per 4/6, Muzara'ah, Musaqat and Mugharasah are among the Shari'ah-compliant modes listed, with Murabahah, Ijarah, Salam, Istisna'a, Mudarabah and Sukuk.

column4: Bank A prepared the feasibility study and contracts for a syndication. It asks for a commission higher than its actual cost. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if Bank A is also the lead manager of the syndication
column6: Permissible; it may equal, exceed or be below the cost
column7: Not permissible; preparatory tasks must be free of any charge
column8: Not permissible; it must equal the actual cost incurred, no more and no less
column10: Per 7/1, the leading Institution may receive commission for preparatory tasks, equal to, less or more than actual cost, whether or not it is lead manager.

column4: Bank A, an Islamic Institution, is invited to join a syndicated financing with two conventional banks. All funds are subscribed and used through Murabahah. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if the conventional banks convert to Islamic banks
column6: Not permissible, as syndication is only among Islamic Institutions
column7: Not permissible unless the conventional banks contribute less
column8: Permissible, since subscription and use of funds are Shari'ah-compliant
column10: Per 5/2, conventional banks may join Islamic Institutions in syndicated financing as long as subscription and utilization of funds follow Shari'ah-compliant forms.

column4: Four Institutions arrange a syndicated financing. Who should supervise its arrangement, implementation and follow-up?
column5: The Shari'ah supervisory board of the borrower only, as the beneficiary
column6: The participating Institutions' Shari'ah supervisory boards
column7: The central bank of the lead manager's country only, as the regulator
column8: The lead manager's internal audit department only, with no board role
column10: Per 5/4, it takes place under the participants' Shari'ah supervisory boards; preferably a joint committee of them makes decisions binding on all parties.

column4: Which narration does the Shari'ah basis cite for paying syndication contributions in another currency at the day's exchange rate?
column5: Ibn Umar selling camels at Al-Baqi' in dinars for dirhams
column6: The Hadith forbidding two sales in one
column7: Urwah buying two sheep with one dinar and selling one of them
column8: Hakim Ibn Hizam buying sacrificial animals with the Prophet's money for a dinar
column10: The basis cites Ibn Umar's Hadith on selling camels at Al-Baqi' in dinars and taking dirhams at the same day's rate before parting.

column4: Participants agree at the outset that the syndicated financing is closed, so no Institution may exit before its end. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only for paid agency arrangements, not for Musharakah
column6: Not permissible, as it contradicts the nature of Musharakah contracts
column7: Not permissible, as partners may always exit whenever they wish to
column8: Permissible; a closed syndication may bar premature exit
column10: Per 10/1, it is permissible to agree on a closed syndicated financing operation that does not allow premature exit.

column4: A syndicate is asked to finance a hotel project where one floor will house a nightclub serving alcoholic drinks. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the nightclub is a minor part of the whole project
column6: Permissible, if its income is given to charity by the syndicate
column7: Not permissible, even if only part of the funds go to it
column8: Permissible, as the hotel itself is lawful and the nightclub is incidental
column10: Per clause 3, syndicated financing must go to permissible activities and should not be totally or partially directed to projects with a Shari'ah restriction.

column4: A conventional bank is proposed as lead manager of a syndication in which Bank A participates. When is this acceptable?
column5: Only if the conventional bank holds the largest share of the financing
column6: Only if the contracts, projects and modes are Shari'ah-compliant
column7: Only if Bank A guarantees the conventional bank's acts to the participants
column8: Never, as the lead manager must always be an Islamic Institution itself
column10: Per 5/3, the lead is originally an Islamic Institution, but a conventional bank may lead if the contracts, projects and modes of financing are all Shari'ah-compliant.

column4: Bank A agrees to manage a syndicate for no reward, and the financing Institutions share the profit. What arrangement is this?
column5: Mudarabah
column6: Paid agency
column7: Musharakah with a management fee
column8: Non-paid agency
column10: Per 6/4, in non-paid agency the lead manager undertakes to manage the operations for no reward, and the financing Institutions share the profit.

column4: The participants in a syndicate arrange their relationship on a Mudarabah basis. What is the role of the syndication manager?
column5: He acts as Mudarib and is the exclusive operation manager
column6: He acts as a non-paid agent who receives a fixed bonus at the end
column7: He acts as a guarantor of the participants' capital against all loss
column8: He shares management equally with all participants in the syndicate
column10: Per 6/1, under Mudarabah the syndication manager acts as a Mudarib and becomes the exclusive operation manager according to the Mudarabah contract.

column4: In a syndicated Mudarabah, the investment agent undertakes to protect the participants against exchange rate fluctuations. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if all participants agree to it
column6: Permissible, if limited to the profit amount
column7: Impermissible for the agent or any other party
column8: Permissible, if the agent receives a fee for it
column10: Per 9/3, the investment agent or any party of the Musharakah or Mudarabah may not commit to safeguard another party against exchange rate fluctuations.

column4: A syndication is in US dollars. Bank B pays its contribution in euros. How is Bank B's contribution measured?
column5: Revalued in dollars at the exchange rate on the day of payment
column6: Revalued at a fixed rate agreed at the outset between the participants
column7: Revalued in dollars at the rate on the day of signing the contract
column8: Kept in euros, with profits paid in euros at maturity of the syndication
column10: Per 9/1, contributions in other currencies are revalued in the syndication currency at the prevailing exchange rate on the day of payment.

column4: Bank A's syndicate finances the power plant of a project via Istisna'a, while other banks finance the rest with interest-based loans. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if Bank A also leads the conventional loans for the project
column6: Permitted if Bank A shares the conventional lenders' risk
column7: Permitted if accounts and lead manager arrangements are separate
column8: Not permitted, as the whole project is tainted by Riba, even with separation
column10: Per 5/5, Institutions may finance parts of a project financed conventionally elsewhere, if accounts and lead manager arrangements of both are separate.

column4: The lead bank of a syndicated Musharakah asks participants to pay it a commitment commission. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if it does not exceed the actual cost of the commitment
column6: Permissible if disclosed to all participants before they subscribe
column7: Permissible if paid only by the customer and not by the partners
column8: It is not permissible to receive commitment commission
column10: Per 7/2, it is not permissible to receive commitment commission.

column4: Bank A manages a syndicate as a partner. Participants ask it to guarantee them against default by the syndicate's debtors. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if limited to the profit portion
column6: Not permissible for the managing Institution
column7: Permissible, if the debtors are its own customers
column8: Permissible, as it selected the debtors
column10: Per 8/2, the Institution managing the syndication as Mudarib, partner or agent may not guarantee the debtors of its partners or FX fluctuations of contributions.

column4: In a Musharakah syndicate, the partners delegate Bank A to manage the operation. How may Bank A be rewarded for managing it?
column5: By a fixed percentage of the total capital stated in the Musharakah contract
column6: By a guaranteed return on its contribution, whatever the syndicate earns
column7: By a higher profit share or a lump sum under a separate contract
column8: By a share of profits stated within the Musharakah contract only
column10: Per 6/2, partners may delegate one of them to manage against an increase in its profit share or a lump sum, with a separate management contract signed.

column4: A Mudarib in a syndicate offers to safeguard the capital providers against exchange rate fluctuations. Per the basis, why is this prohibited?
column5: It turns the Mudarabah into an agency with an unspecified fee
column6: It amounts to the Mudarib guaranteeing the capital
column7: It is a form of commitment commission
column8: Exchange rates cannot be known on the contract date
column10: The basis: such a commitment leads to the impermissible case of a partner or Mudarib guaranteeing the other party against loss of capital.

column4: In a Musharakah syndicate, Bank A contributes 40% and Bank B 60%; profit is agreed 30:70. The operation makes a loss. How is the loss borne?
column5: 40% by Bank A and 60% by Bank B
column6: 30% by Bank A and 70% by Bank B
column7: 50% by each bank equally
column8: Entirely by the bank that manages the operation
column10: Per 6/2, in Musharakah the Institutions provide funds and bear losses proportionately to their contributions, whereas profits are shared as agreed.

column4: A syndication contract states that any exiting participant will be bought out at the nominal value of its contribution. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if all participants accept it at the time of the contract
column6: Permissible, as it protects the exiting party from any loss in value
column7: Permissible, if the syndicate is profitable at the time of exit
column8: Not permissible to agree beforehand on exit at nominal value
column10: Per 10/2, it is not permissible to agree beforehand on transfer of shares at nominal value or on a guarantee of a certain limit of profits.

column4: In a combined set, a subsidiary contract is executed without separate offer and acceptance, to serve a lawful need of the parties. What is the ruling?
column5: Void, as offer and acceptance are always required for any contract
column6: Acceptable, given the lawful need in a subsidiary contract
column7: Valid only if confirmed later by a written offer
column8: Void unless both parties later sign a new contract
column10: Per 5/2/5, subsidiary and implicit contracts may be relieved of some validity prerequisites (such as offer and acceptance) when dictated by need or lawful interest.

column4: A trainee asks why two lawful acts can become prohibited when combined. Which example does the basis, citing Al-Shatibi, give?
column5: Combining Murabahah with a promise
column6: Combining sale with a gift of a pen
column7: Combining Ijarah with Wakalah
column8: Combining sale and lending
column10: The basis cites Al-Shatibi: combining may create restrictions absent individually, e.g. combining sale and lending, marrying two sisters, or a woman and her aunt.

column4: Ahmad lends Karim 10,000, stipulating in the loan contract that Karim must let him stay free of charge in Karim's house. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible: it uses the loan as an excuse for Riba
column6: Permissible, if it is written in a separate contract
column7: Permissible, if the stay is for a short period
column8: Permissible, as no extra money is repaid
column10: Per 4/3, combination must not be an excuse for Riba, e.g. a loan stipulating that the borrower offers accommodation in his house to the lender or a present.

column4: A combined set contains a subsidiary contract with an element of Gharar that would invalidate it if concluded alone. What is the ruling?
column5: The Gharar is overlooked only if minor in amount
column6: The subsidiary contract must be removed
column7: The Gharar may be overlooked in the subsidiary contract
column8: The whole set is void due to the Gharar in one of its contracts
column10: Per 5/2/1, Gharar, which affects financial contracts, may be overlooked in implicit and subsidiary contracts.

column4: Bank A offers a money transfer service combined with currency exchange, where spot delivery of the exchanged currency is not observed. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as it combines two contracts in one
column6: Prohibited, as spot delivery is always required in currency exchange
column7: Permissible only for amounts below a set limit
column8: Forgivable, as the exchange is subsidiary to the transfer
column10: Per 5/2/3, sale-based Riba and violation of exchange rules (e.g. ignoring spot delivery when exchange is combined with money transfer) are forgivable in subsidiary contracts.

column4: An investor provides Mudarabah capital to a Mudarib and, in the same set, lends him that same capital. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the loan protects the investor's capital from loss
column6: Not permissible, as Mudarabah and lending contradict
column7: Permissible, if profit is shared as agreed
column8: Permissible, if the loan is interest-free
column10: Per 4/4, combining Mudarabah with lending the Mudarabah capital to the Mudarib is an example of contradictory contracts that may not be combined.

column4: Bank A designs a new set of combined contracts. Besides the rules on combination, what else must it observe?
column5: Only the parties' agreed commercial terms and the Bank's internal policies
column6: Only the rules of the main contract in the set
column7: The general Shari'ah rules on structure, rulings and conditions
column8: Only the rulings on Muwata`ah
column10: Per 7/4 and 7/5, new combined sets must observe the general rules of Shari'ah on structure, rulings, requirements and conditions, and the rulings on combination.

column4: Bank A wants to apply a concession to an implicit contract in a combined set. How should the concession be judged?
column5: By tradition and practice, with Shari'ah Board clearance
column6: By the customer's consent alone, with no further review
column7: By the applicable conventional banking regulations only
column8: By the Bank's management, based on its expected profitability and risk
column10: Per 5/1, concessions are judged in the light of traditions, practice and professional experience, and subject to clearance by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.

column4: Which Hadith does the basis cite to show that Gharar may be forgiven in implicit aspects of a contract?
column5: Ibn Umar's sale of camels at Al-Baqi' for dinars against dirhams
column6: The prohibition of two sales in one deal
column7: The sale of a slave together with his money
column8: The buyer of an unpollinated palm may stipulate its fruits
column10: The basis cites the Hadith on buying an unpollinated palm: the buyer may stipulate its fruits; the Gharar is forgiven as it is an implicit aspect.

column4: Bank A and a customer stipulate their Muwata`ah as part of the contract. What is its effect?
column5: It becomes a condition precedent subject to Shari'ah rulings
column6: It has no effect on the contract, being only a moral promise between the parties
column7: It replaces the contract and needs no further rulings
column8: It becomes binding on Bank A only, not the customer
column10: Per 6/2/2, Muwata`ah stipulated in the contract becomes a condition precedent, and the contract becomes subject to rulings on permissibility, enforceability and validity.

column4: According to the majority of the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali Fuqaha cited in the basis, how is a set of combined contracts judged?
column5: Only as a single indivisible contract
column6: In the light of its individual components
column7: By the intention of the stronger party
column8: By the largest contract in the set
column10: The basis: per the majority of Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali Fuqaha, a combined set is judged by its components; if each is permissible, the set is too.

column4: Ahmad sells his land to Karim and rents him his car for one month, both for a total of one thousand dinars. What form of combined contracts is this?
column5: Combined contracts with one stipulated in the other
column6: Combined contracts concluded for separate values
column7: Combined contracts with a single lump sum counter value
column8: An exhaustive statement of successive stages
column10: Per 2/2/1, combined contracts may have a single lump sum counter value, e.g. selling land and renting a car for one month, both against 1,000 dinars.

column4: A party grants an asset to Ahmad as a gift and, at the same time, sells the same asset to him. What is the ruling on this combination?
column5: Permissible, if the price is only nominal
column6: Not permissible: the two contracts contradict each other
column7: Permissible, as both gift and sale are lawful when concluded separately
column8: Permissible, if the gift precedes the sale
column10: Per 4/4, combined contracts must not contradict each other, e.g. granting an asset as a gift while selling or leasing it simultaneously.

column4: Bank A and Company X agree to finance a machine, leaving it to be decided later whether the deal will take the form of Murabahah or Ijarah. How does the standard treat this?
column5: As a Muwata`ah to form up a Riba trick
column6: As an act of an uncommissioned agent
column7: As a single sale with a deferred price payable in instalments
column8: As one of the forms of combination of contracts
column10: Per 2/1/4, agreement to conclude the deal through any of different contractual forms to be finally decided in the future is a form of combination of contracts.

column4: In a combined set, the object of a subsidiary contract is not precisely known. Does this Jahalah invalidate it?
column5: No, it may be ignored in a subsidiary contract
column6: No, but only if the Jahalah is very minor
column7: Yes, unless the main contract is a sale
column8: Yes, Jahalah always invalidates a contract
column10: Per 5/2/2, Jahalah, which affects financial contracts, may be ignored with regard to the object of a subsidiary contract.

column4: An Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek set provides for Muwata`ah in the contract. The customer later wants to ignore it. What is the ruling?
column5: It is not binding, as it preceded the contract and was never written into it
column6: It is binding only after the last rental
column7: It stays binding, subject to permissible banking practice
column8: It binds only Bank A, not the customer
column10: Per 7/2, Muwata`ah provided for in the contract and used to combine contracts should be observed and remains binding, subject to permissible conventions.

column4: Ahmad tells Karim: "I sell you my house for 10,000 dinars on condition that you rent it back to me for two years at 1,000 a year." What form of combination is this?
column5: Two contracts for separate values with no link
column6: A prior agreement with no condition at all
column7: Two contracts for a single lump sum value
column8: One contract stipulated as a condition in the other
column10: Per 2/2/3, some combined contracts may be stipulated as conditions in the others, e.g. selling a house on condition the buyer leases it back to the seller.

column4: Two parties agree beforehand to a Bay' al-Wafa` structure to obtain a return on money. What is the ruling on this Muwata`ah and the contract?
column5: The contract and Muwata`ah are valid if the Shari'ah board approves them
column6: The Muwata`ah is valid if the price is fair and the buyer takes possession
column7: The Muwata`ah is prohibited and the contract is invalid
column8: The contract is valid but the Muwata`ah is void
column10: Per 6/3/1, Muwata`ah to form up Riba tricks, such as Bay' al-'Inah, Bay' al-Wafa` or Riba al-Fadl, is prohibited and the contract so designed is invalid.

column4: Citing Al-Qarafi, why does the basis bar combining contracts that contradict each other?
column5: Such contracts always involve excessive Gharar
column6: Contracts are means to objectives and cannot serve opposite ones
column7: Contradictory contracts always involve Riba, whatever their objectives
column8: They cannot be concluded by offer and acceptance
column10: The basis cites Al-Qarafi: contracts are devices to achieve specific objectives; one requirement cannot fit two contradicting positions at once.

column4: Per the basis, why is a Muwata`ah preceding a contemporary set like Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek treated as binding?
column5: It is part of a whole system that collapses if one part fails
column6: Because it is always written into each contract by the Bank's practice
column7: Because a court must enforce every promise made before a contract
column8: Because it turns the set into a single sale
column10: The basis: current banking tradition treats such Muwata`ah as binding; it is part of a system that collapses when any component loses balance.

column4: Per the Maliki Fuqaha cited in the basis, which requirement applies before using Sadd al-Zara`i' to bar a Muwata`ah?
column5: The deal involves more than two contracting parties
column6: The deal is concluded for a single lump sum price
column7: The deal is concluded through a paid agent of either party
column8: Resort to the excuse is very frequent and excessive
column10: The basis: per the Maliki Fuqaha, Sadd al-Zara`i' needs very frequent, excessive resort to the excuse and a strong accusation ruling out good intention.

column4: In a combined set, Bank A buys, on deferred payment, the shares of an indebted company. Does the rule against selling a debt for a debt bar this?
column5: Yes, unless the price is paid immediately in cash
column6: No, debt for debt may be ignored as a subsidiary contract
column7: Yes, debt may never be sold for another debt, even in a combined set
column8: Yes, unless the company's debts are settled first
column10: Per 5/2/4, selling a debt for another debt may be ignored in a subsidiary contract, e.g. purchasing (on debt) the shares of an indebted company.

column4: In a combined Murabahah set, the customer fails to honor its commitment, causing Bank A an actual loss. What may Bank A claim?
column5: Its full expected profit on the deal
column6: A pre-agreed penalty linked to the price
column7: Indemnity for the actual injury it encountered
column8: Nothing, as the commitments are not binding
column10: Per 7/6, failure of a party to combined contracts to honor its commitments gives the other party the right to claim indemnity for the actual injury.

column4: A trader wants high-quality dates for his low-quality dates. Per the Hadith in the basis, what should he do?
column5: Sell the low-quality dates, then buy the high-quality ones
column6: Exchange more low-quality dates for less of the high-quality dates
column7: Sell and buy back the dates in one pre-agreed contract
column8: Exchange equal amounts with a cash top-up
column10: The basis cites the Prophet's direction to sell low-quality dates first and then buy the high-quality ones, as two separate unrelated contracts.

column4: A trainee asks for the textual basis for ignoring currency exchange rules in subsidiary contracts. What does the basis cite?
column5: The Hadith on low and high quality dates
column6: The Hadith forbidding sale and lending
column7: The Hadith on buying a slave who has money
column8: The Hadith on the unpollinated palm tree
column10: The basis cites the Hadith on buying a slave with money: it may be bought with his money without the exchange rules, whether the money is known or not.

column4: A finance house offers hire-purchase in its traditional form, where one contract is at once a lease and a sale of the asset. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as leasing and selling contradict here
column6: Permissible, as it is like Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek
column7: Permissible, if the rentals equal the asset price
column8: Permissible, if ownership passes at the end
column10: Per 4/4, leasing with selling (hire-purchase in its traditional form) is listed among contradictory contracts that may not be combined.

column4: Per the basis, what is the status of a loan stipulating that the borrower must give the lender a present?
column5: Valid, if the present is of small value
column6: Valid, but the present is not enforceable
column7: Disliked but valid, by agreement of the Fuqaha
column8: Null and void, as the stipulated benefit is Riba
column10: The basis: Fuqaha unanimously agree such a loan becomes null and void; any loan with a prior condition of benefit to the lender is Riba.

column4: On what does the basis rely for allowing the sale of a debt for a debt within a subsidiary contract?
column5: Ibn Al-Qayyim's view on two separate sales combined in one contract
column6: Imam Malik's view in Al-Muwatta` on a slave owed a debt
column7: Al-Sayuti's view on implicit sales and the forgiveness of Gharar in them
column8: Al-Qarafi's view on contradictory contracts
column10: The basis relies on the slave Hadith and Imam Malik's view in Al-Muwatta` allowing sale of a slave whose money is a debt, even if sold on deferred payment.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is combining several permissible contracts in one transaction permissible?
column5: Customary practice overrides the rules of contracts
column6: Necessity makes all combined contracts permissible
column7: Combined contracts are never subject to Riba
column8: Freedom of contracting is acknowledged in principle
column10: The basis: freedom of contracting and honoring commitments is acknowledged in principle unless it leads to violation; Ibn Al-Qayyim affirmed this.

column4: In a Diminishing Musharakah set, the customer pledged to buy Bank A's units in stages. Is this pledge binding?
column5: Only if the pledge is repeated at each stage
column6: Only for Bank A, not for the customer
column7: Yes, pledges in such combined sets bind their parties
column8: No, pledges in combined sets are morally binding only, not legally
column10: Per 7/3, the pledges contained in such combined contract sets are binding to their respective parties.

column4: Bank A sells a commodity to a customer for 110 on deferred payment and, by agreement in the same set, buys it back at once for 100 cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited: it is Bay' al-'Inah used as a trick for Riba
column6: Permissible, if the two sales are on separate dates
column7: Permissible, if the commodity is actually delivered
column8: Permissible, since both sales are valid alone
column10: Per 4/2, combination of contracts should not be used as a trick for committing Riba, such as agreeing to practice Bay' al-'Inah or Riba al-Fadl.

column4: Bank A relies on a concession that applies to a subsidiary contract within a set. It then wants to apply it to the same contract concluded independently. What is the ruling?
column5: It applies if the contract value is small
column6: It cannot be granted to the independent contract
column7: It applies if both parties consent to it
column8: It applies equally to independent contracts
column10: Per 5/1, concessions granted to implicit and subsidiary contracts when combined cannot be granted to the same contracts concluded independently.

column4: Bank A offers a customer a sale of goods and, in the same contract, a loan to the same customer. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the sale is at market price
column6: Permissible, if the loan carries no interest
column7: Permissible, since each contract is lawful alone
column8: Not permissible: sale and lending is an explicit ban
column10: Per 4/1, combining contracts must not include cases explicitly banned by Shari'ah, like combining sale and lending in one contract.

column4: Company X proposes a set combining a permissible Ijarah with a contract that is impermissible on its own. Can the combination make the set permissible?
column5: Yes, since the set is judged only as a whole, not by its parts
column6: No, each combined contract must be permissible on its own
column7: Yes, if both share a single lump sum value
column8: Yes, if the impermissible part is subsidiary
column10: Per clause 3, combining contracts is permissible provided that each contract is permissible on its own.

column4: Bank A combines an Ijarah and a Wakalah in one set. Each is permissible on its own and neither is a condition of the other. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, barring an exceptional Shari'ah restriction
column6: Permissible only if both are concluded for a single lump sum value
column7: Prohibited unless one is made a condition of the other
column8: Prohibited, as two contracts may never be combined in one set
column10: Per clause 3, combining contracts each permissible on its own, without one as a condition in the other, is permissible unless an exceptional restriction applies.

column4: Before signing, Bank A and a customer agreed a condition that was not repeated in the signed contract. How binding is it?
column5: Not binding, as it is not in the contract text
column6: Binding only if a court later confirms it
column7: As binding as the normal conditions of the contract
column8: Binding only on the party who proposed it
column10: Per 6/2/3, a condition preceding the signing has the same validity and binding nature as normal contract conditions, being the agreed bases of the contract.

column4: Ahmad sells his house to Karim for 1,000 dinars and rents him his car for 100 dinars per month. Neither is a condition of the other. What form is this?
column5: Combined contracts with one stipulated in the other
column6: Combined contracts concluded for separate values
column7: Combined contracts with a single lump sum value
column8: A single contract with two instalments
column10: Per 2/2/2, combined contracts may be concluded for separate values, e.g. selling a house for 1,000 dinars and renting a car for 100 dinars per month.

column4: Bank A structures a Diminishing Musharakah as one agreement with successive parts and stages leading to the parties' goal. How does the standard describe such combined contracts?
column5: A prohibited combination of sale and lending
column6: A single lump sum combination of two separate contracts of sale
column7: An exhaustive statement of successive parts and stages
column8: Combined contracts for separate values only
column10: Per 2/2/4, combined contracts may be an exhaustive statement of successive parts and stages, e.g. Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Murabahah and Diminishing Musharakah.

column4: Two parties agree beforehand to combine Salam with Ju'alah for the same contract value. What is the ruling on this Muwata`ah?
column5: Permissible, if the Ju'alah is subsidiary
column6: Prohibited only if the Salam price is deferred
column7: Permissible, as each contract is lawful when concluded alone
column8: Prohibited, as the contracts contradict each other
column10: Per 6/3/4 and 4/4, Muwata`ah to combine contradictory contracts, such as Salam with Ju'alah for the same value, is prohibited.

column4: During preparatory negotiations, the intentions of Bank A and a customer coincide on a Murabahah to be signed later. What meaning of Muwata`ah does this reflect?
column5: Coincidence of intentions at the negotiation stage
column6: Agreement to contract with a third party
column7: A condition added after the contract is signed
column8: Intention to use a trick for practicing Riba
column10: Per 6/1/3, one meaning of Muwata`ah is the coincidence of the intentions of the parties at the stage of preparatory negotiations before signing.

column4: On the same day, Ahmad buys a car from Bank A and rents a warehouse from it. Neither contract is a condition of the other, and there was no prior agreement. How is this classified?
column5: Combining contracts by Muwata`ah without any condition
column6: Combining contracts without condition and without Muwata`ah
column7: Combining contracts with one as a condition in the other
column8: Agreeing to choose the contractual form in the future
column10: Per 2/1/1, one form is combining more than one contract without imposing any as a condition in the other and without prior agreement (Muwata`ah).

column4: Which of the following does the standard give as an example of contemporary contract sets agreed beforehand to be executed in successive stages?
column5: Traditional hire-purchase
column6: Sale combined with lending
column7: Murabahah on Order of Purchase
column8: Bay' al-'Inah
column10: Per 7/1, examples include Murabahah on Order of Purchase, Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek and Diminishing Musharakah.

column4: A Shari'ah board examines a Muwata`ah that might be an excuse for Riba. The intention is doubtful and there is a clear lawful need. Should it be prohibited?
column5: No; prohibition needs obvious intent and no lawful need
column6: Yes; a lawful need does not affect the ruling
column7: No; only Bay' al-'Inah can ever be prohibited
column8: Yes; any possible excuse for Riba is prohibited, even where intent is doubtful
column10: Per 6/3/2/1, prohibition requires that the intent to reach a banned deal be obvious beyond doubt and that no obvious need or lawful interest justify it.

column4: Bank A and a customer agree beforehand on a structure that violates no Shari'ah rule or objective and harms no one, as a Shari'ah exit. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as every prior agreement is a trick
column6: Prohibited, unless stated in the contract text
column7: Permissible only if never disclosed to others
column8: Permissible, as Muwata`ah for Shari'ah exits
column10: Per 6/3/3, Muwata`ah for Shari'ah exits that do not violate Shari'ah rules or objectives or harm others is permissible.

column4: Which of the following is one of the meanings of Muwata`ah stated in the standard?
column5: A written guarantee given by the agent to the principal against loss of the goods
column6: A unilateral promise made after signing the contract
column7: Unrevealed prior agreement on a permissible deal as a Shari'ah exit
column8: A sale whose price is later fixed by a third party chosen by both sides
column10: Per 6/1/2, one meaning of Muwata`ah is an unrevealed prior agreement between the parties to perform a permissible act or deal to find a Shari'ah-accepted exit.

column4: Per the basis, how does the company's role differ between Islamic and commercial insurance?
column5: Agent of the account vs original party in its own name
column6: Original party in its own name vs agent of the account
column7: Guarantor of all claims vs agent of the policyholders' account
column8: Mudarib in underwriting vs partner in the fund
column10: The basis: in Islamic insurance the company is the agent of the insurance account; in commercial insurance it is an original party contracting in its own name.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company T can settle with a party who caused damage to an insured car, for less than the full claim, in the participants' interest. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only with each participant's written consent
column6: Permissible if in participants' interest and compliant
column7: Not permissible, as the company is only an agent
column8: Not permissible; the full claim must be pursued
column10: Per 10/10, there is no restriction on reconciling with the injuring party if it serves the participants' interest and conforms to Shari'ah rulings.

column4: A participant claims indemnity but disputes who must prove the loss. Per the basis, on whom does the burden of evidence lie?
column5: On the Shari'ah Supervisory Board
column6: On the company, as the agent
column7: On the reinsurer of the fund
column8: On the participant, as the claimant
column10: The basis: responsibility of providing evidence lies with the participant, per the general rule that evidence should be established by the claimant.

column4: A company seeks Islamic cover against liability claims and breach of trust by staff. Which type of Islamic Insurance is this?
column5: Person Insurance (Takaful)
column6: Property Insurance, indemnifying actual injury
column7: Life insurance with an investment element
column8: Social insurance arranged by the state
column10: Per 6/1, Property Insurance indemnifies actual injury and covers fire, car and airplane accidents, liability, breach of trust, etc.

column4: An Islamic insurance company drafts its documents. What must be stipulated about each participant's contribution?
column5: He donates it and its returns to the insurance account
column6: He lends it to the company until the policy ends and then recovers it
column7: He sells it to the company against the cover
column8: He keeps ownership of it until a claim arises
column10: Per 5/1, it should be stipulated that the participant donates his contribution and its returns to the insurance account for paying indemnity.

column4: A brewery asks Islamic Insurance Company T to insure its stock of alcoholic drinks against fire. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the cover is against fire only and not against theft
column6: Permissible, if the claim is paid to charity
column7: It must refrain from covering Shari'ah-banned items
column8: Permissible, if the contribution is higher
column10: Per 5/8, the company must adhere to Shari'ah, especially refraining from providing coverage for Shari'ah-banned items, activities or purposes.

column4: Ahmad's car is covered by Islamic insurance for an insurance amount of 20,000. An accident causes an actual loss of 15,000. How much indemnity does he receive?
column5: 17,500, the average of the two figures
column6: 15,000 plus his share of the surplus as of right
column7: 20,000, the full insurance amount
column8: 15,000, the lesser of the loss and the insured amount
column10: Per 11/1, the participant receives either the loss he incurred or the insurance amount, whichever is less, as per regulations.

column4: Participants ask why Islamic Insurance Company T will not guarantee the insurance assets. Per the basis, what is the reason?
column5: It is a donor who may withdraw at will
column6: It is a partner bearing loss pro rata to its share in the fund
column7: It is an agent, who does not guarantee save for fault
column8: It is a Mudarib bearing all investment loss
column10: The basis: the company is an agent, and Fuqaha unanimously agree an agent does not guarantee property except for misconduct, negligence or breach.

column4: An Islamic insurance company records its own capital and the policyholders' contributions in a single account. What does the standard require?
column5: Two separate accounts: company and policyholders
column6: Separate accounts only when there is a deficit
column7: Separate accounts only for the investment returns
column8: One account is acceptable if it is audited annually by an external auditor
column10: Per 5/2, the company should maintain two separate accounts: one for its own rights and liabilities and one for those of the policyholders.

column4: Which principle does the basis cite as the ground for indemnity in Islamic insurance?
column5: What matters is intentions and meanings, not words and forms
column6: One should neither tolerate harm nor cause it
column7: Necessity makes the prohibited permissible
column8: Gain accompanies liability for loss, so the insurer takes the profit
column10: The basis grounds indemnity on the principle that one should neither tolerate harm nor cause it to others, with fair, non-obsessive indemnification.
