column5: The gift is void because it relates to the primary subject matter
column6: None; Gharar does not affect donation contracts such as gift
column7: The gift is valid only if the catch is estimated in advance
column8: The gift is void because the Gharar is excessive
column10: Per 4/1, Gharar violates only exchange-based contracts (sale, lease, partnership); it does not affect donation contracts such as gift and will.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A enters into a fixed-term Mudarabah with an investor. The outcome of the investment is uncertain. How does the standard treat the Gharar here?
column5: It is minor Gharar arising from the profit ratio
column6: It is permitted only because of a recognized need
column7: It is medium Gharar and does not affect the contract
column8: It is excessive Gharar and nullifies the Mudarabah
column10: Per 4/2/3, medium Gharar may exist in contracts like Ju'alah, guardianship, companies and fixed-term Mudarabah, and it does not affect the contract.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Company X agrees to buy fuel from a supplier at the market price on the day of purchase, without stating a figure. What is the ruling on this price term?
column5: Permitted only if a cap on the price is agreed
column6: Permitted; the Gharar in such a price is forgiven
column7: Void, as the price is left to an outside party
column8: Void, because no amount is stated in the contract
column10: Per 5/2/2, Gharar in the price is permitted when the sale is concluded at the market price on the day of purchase or the price people usually sell at.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: A farmer sells unripe fruits on his trees to Company X, apart from the trees and without any stipulation to await harvesting. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid: the Gharar is in a corollary of the trees
column6: Valid if the buyer pays the full price in advance
column7: Valid: unripe fruits involve only medium Gharar
column8: Void: the Gharar relates to the primary subject matter
column10: Per 4/3, Gharar in the primary subject matter, as when unripe fruits are sold apart from the trees without stipulating awaiting harvest, nullifies the contract.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis consider Gharar from failure in delivery as nullifying a sale?
column5: The seller gets the price while the buyer may not get the item
column6: The seller loses the option of viewing the item
column7: The price in such sales is always unknown to one of the parties
column8: Such sales are donation contracts by nature
column10: Per the basis, a sale safeguards both parties' rights; if the seller gets the price while the buyer cannot get the sold object, the contract's objective is violated.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: A sale contract gives the buyer an option to rescind with no time limit. What is the effect on the contract?
column5: The contract is valid but the price becomes deferred
column6: The option is void but the sale remains valid
column7: The contract is void, due to Gharar in its form
column8: The contract is valid; the option lasts three days
column10: Per item 7, a contract becomes null and void if it contains a condition causing Gharar in its form, such as an option without time limit.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: A seller releases a commodity to Bank A and facilitates its taking, but the Bank has not physically taken it. What kind of holding has occurred?
column5: Actual holding
column6: Holding only for goods sold by Juzaf
column7: No holding until the goods are moved
column8: Constructive holding
column10: Per 5/6, constructive holding indicates the act of releasing the commodity and facilitating the process of its holding.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, when does a suretyship (Kafalah) become affected by Gharar?
column5: When it is paid for, as it becomes exchange-based
column6: When it is made for an unknown period or an unknown amount
column7: When it is made subject to a condition
column8: When it covers a future obligation not yet due at the time
column10: Per the basis, suretyship tolerates Gharar as a corollary contract; if paid for, it becomes an exchange-based contract and thus affected by Gharar.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A leases a warehouse to Company X at a fixed monthly rent, but the lease contract specifies no period at all. What is the status of the lease?
column5: Valid, as the Gharar is only medium
column6: Void, as this is excessive Gharar
column7: Valid, but either party may end it on notice
column8: Valid, as the monthly rent is known
column10: Per 4/2/1, signing a lease contract for an unspecified period is an example of excessive Gharar, which sets the contract null and void.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Ahmad appoints an agent for a fee under a Wakalah whose subject matter is vague. How does the standard treat the Gharar in this paid agency?
column5: Agency is never affected by Gharar
column6: It is treated as a donation, so Gharar is ignored
column7: It is treated like Ijarah and is affected by Gharar
column8: It is valid as a general agency in all cases
column10: Per 6/3, agency may involve Gharar when free of charge; if paid, it is treated like Ijarah (hiring) and is affected by Gharar.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: A trader sells Ahmad a commodity he does not have and will have to purchase from the market later. Which contracts are exceptions to the nullity of such a sale?
column5: Salam and Istisna'a, subject to their conditions
column6: Murabahah and Musawamah, subject to disclosure
column7: Ijarah and Ju'alah, subject to known rent
column8: Any sale if the price is deferred
column10: Per 5/5, Gharar from sale of a non-owned commodity nullifies the sale; Salam and Istisna'a are exceptional cases subject to their conditions.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: A car showroom sells Ahmad "one of the cars in the showroom" without specifying which, and with no option to specify. What is the effect?
column5: The contract is valid with medium, forgivable Gharar
column6: The contract is valid; the seller picks any car
column7: The contract is valid if all cars have the same price
column8: The contract is void due to non-specification of the car
column10: Per 5/2/1/3, sale of a non-specified car from a number of cars in a showroom involves Gharar that nullifies the contract.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: For excessive Gharar to be justified by need under the standard, which description of the need is correct?
column5: It must amount to a threat to life or to the survival of the business
column6: It causes severe hardship and has no permissible alternative
column7: It must be approved by a regulator as a necessity
column8: It must be a public need, not a private one
column10: Per 4/4, need (public or private) means refraining leads to severe hardship, though not amounting to mortality, and it must be inevitable with no permissible way.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank B leases a car to a customer at a set rent per mile; the total rent will be known only after the trip ends. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid only if a maximum mileage is fixed
column6: Void, as the rent is left to one party's choice
column7: Void, since the total rent is unknown at contracting
column8: Valid; the unit price is known though the total is not
column10: Per 5/2/2, renting a car at a rent per mile, with the amount determined after reaching the destination, does not make the contract void.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank B buys in Salam a commodity that is not usually available in the market on the agreed delivery date. What is the ruling on this contract?
column5: Valid if the seller provides a guarantor
column6: Valid, since the Gharar is only minor
column7: Void, due to excessive Gharar
column8: Valid, as Salam is an exception for non-owned goods
column10: Per 4/2/1, sale of a Salam commodity that is not usually available on the date of delivery is an example of excessive Gharar that nullifies the contract.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A sells a house to a customer who has inspected the house but has not seen its foundation. What is the effect of this Gharar?
column5: The sale is void as the Gharar is excessive
column6: No effect; it is minor Gharar that a contract can hardly avoid
column7: The sale is valid only if the foundation is described in writing
column8: The sale is voidable at the buyer's option at any time
column10: Per 4/2/2, selling a house to a buyer who has not seen its foundation is minor Gharar, which does not affect the contract.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Why, according to the Shari'ah basis, does Gharar not affect donation contracts as it does exchange-based contracts?
column5: The donee incurs no loss, so no dispute arises
column6: Donations are always made under a recognized need
column7: Donation contracts are corollaries of exchange contracts
column8: Donation contracts never involve uncertainty
column10: Per the basis, Gharar in exchange contracts leads to unlawful acquisition of wealth; in donations no dispute arises since the recipient incurs no loss.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Which reported prohibition does the Shari'ah basis cite to support nullity of a contract whose duration is unknown?
column5: Bay' al-Munabadhah, throwing the sold goods
column6: Bay' al-Hasah, sale concluded by the throw of a stone
column7: Habal al-Habalah, price deferred to an unborn camel's birth
column8: Bay' al-Thunya, sale with an exception that is not specified
column10: The basis cites the prohibition of Bay' Habal al-Habalah, where the price is postponed until a camel's fetus is born and gives birth, and the verse on fixed-term debts.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: A trader sells a quantity of buried root crops (underground commodities) still in the ground to Company Y. How does the standard classify and treat this Gharar?
column5: Medium Gharar, which does not affect the contract
column6: Medium Gharar, which makes the contract voidable
column7: Minor Gharar, which nullifies only the price clause
column8: Excessive Gharar, which nullifies the contract
column10: Per 4/2/3, sale of underground commodities is an example of medium Gharar, which does not affect the contract.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Why is a contract involving Gharar in its form (offer and acceptance) null and void, according to the Shari'ah basis?
column5: It turns the contract into a donation
column6: Its subject matter cannot be delivered
column7: Its price becomes unknown to the parties until delivery
column8: It stays unconcluded, as finalization is only probable
column10: Per the basis, a contract with Gharar in its form remains unconcluded; such Gharar makes finalization of the contract probable rather than definite.

column3: Controls on Gharar in Financial Transactions
column4: Company Y sells a pregnant sheep to Ahmad. The condition of the fetus is unknown. What is the effect of this Gharar on the sale?
column5: The sale is void as the condition of the fetus is unknown to the buyer
column6: No effect, since the fetus is a corollary (Tabi') of the sheep
column7: The sale is valid only if the fetus is excluded
column8: The sale is valid only if the fetus is priced separately
column10: Per 4/3, Gharar in a corollary (Tabi') of the primary subject matter, such as a fetus sold with the pregnant sheep, has no effect on the contract.

column4: After an arbitration decision is issued, Company X says it does not consent to it. Is the decision binding on Company X?
column5: Yes, unless revoked as contrary to Shari'ah or public order
column6: Yes, but only once Company X signs it
column7: No, until it is registered with a court
column8: No; the decision needs the consent of both parties after it is issued
column10: Per 11/12, the decision need not meet the parties' consent; it is binding on them unless revoked for being counter to Shari'ah or public order.

column4: The parties require the arbitrator to consult two named experts before ruling. The experts' views differ from the arbitrator's own assessment. What applies?
column5: He must adopt the experts' views in his verdict, whatever his view
column6: He must refer the dispute back to the parties
column7: He must consult them but is not bound to accept their views
column8: He may ignore the requirement to consult them
column10: Per 9/5, the parties may require consultation with named experts, but the arbitrator is not bound to accept the experts' viewpoints.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, what conditions should, in principle, govern the selection of arbitrators?
column5: Only the conditions agreed by the parties
column6: Shari'ah conditions for selecting judges, incl. non-partiality
column7: Only the licensing rules of the host country
column8: Only the experience requirements of the Institution and the parties
column10: The basis states that selection of arbitrators should in principle follow the same Shari'ah conditions for selection of judges, including non-partiality.

column4: How does the Shari'ah basis of the standard characterize the nature of arbitration?
column5: A sale of the arbitrator's services to the parties, and nothing more
column6: A judicial function of the State
column7: A donation by the arbitrator to the parties
column8: Like agency for the parties, and like private custodianship
column10: The Shari'ah basis states that arbitration seems like agency on behalf of the two parties, while also seeming to involve private custodianship.

column4: An arbitrator has no proof either way and decides a disputed claim based on his own personal opinion. Is this an accepted method of judgment?
column5: No; he should not judge on the basis of his own opinion
column6: Yes, since he need not follow judicial procedure
column7: Yes, if the parties do not object later
column8: Yes, if he is a recognized expert in the subject of the dispute
column10: Per 10/1, the arbitrator may use legally accepted methods such as confession, attestation, oath or Nukul, but should not judge on the basis of his own opinion.

column4: Bank A and Company X had no arbitration clause. A dispute arises and the law of their country imposes arbitration on them. Is this a recognized form of resorting to arbitration?
column5: No; arbitration must be agreed at the time of dispute
column6: No; arbitration is valid only if agreed in the original contract
column7: Yes, but only if both parties later sign a new contract
column8: Yes; arbitration can also be legally imposed on the parties
column10: Per 3/1, arbitration can be sought by agreement at the time of dispute, by a previous agreement, or it can be legally imposed on the two parties.

column4: While deciding a dispute over delayed delivery, an arbitrator also rules on a separate lease issue that the parties never referred to him. What is the position?
column5: It is valid, since the parties are the same as in the referred dispute
column6: It is valid if it serves justice between them
column7: It is outside his mandate unless the parties agree
column8: It is binding if issued in the same decision
column10: Per 11/3, arbitration should not go beyond the subject matter of dispute, as further issues fall outside the arbitrator's mandate unless the parties agree.

column4: Company X refuses to implement an arbitration verdict, and the only available courts do not observe the rules of Shari'ah. What may Bank A do?
column5: Seize Company X's assets on its own
column6: Approach those courts to execute the verdict
column7: Restart the arbitration with a new arbitrator
column8: Nothing; it may only use Shari'ah courts
column10: Per 13/1 and 13/2, if a party refuses, the other may present the verdict to judiciary; it is permissible to approach courts not observing Shari'ah for execution.

column4: An arbitration decision does not state its Shari'ah basis or reasoning, and no law requires reasoning. What is the effect on its validity?
column5: It must be reissued with reasoning
column6: It is valid only if the parties consent
column7: It remains valid; reasoning is preferable, not a condition
column8: It is void for lack of reasoning, whatever the applicable law says
column10: Per 11/6, mentioning the basis of the decision (reasoning) is preferable but not a condition for valid arbitration, unless the law so requires.

column4: An Ijarah contract between Bank A and a customer contains an arbitration clause. When a dispute arises, the customer refuses arbitration. What is the position?
column5: The customer may choose the courts instead at any time
column6: Arbitration is binding as it was stipulated in the contract
column7: Arbitration is optional until both sign a new agreement
column8: Arbitration is binding only on the Bank, not the customer
column10: Per 5/1 and 9/3, arbitration is binding when stipulated as a condition in the contract; no further agreement is needed at the time of dispute.

column4: Two months after issuing his verdict, an arbitrator wishes to change it simply because he has reconsidered. When may he retreat from his verdict?
column5: At any time before the verdict is executed
column6: Whenever he changes his opinion
column7: Whenever either party asks him to, before the decision is executed
column8: Only when he declares he committed a mistake in it
column10: Per 13/3, the arbitrator has no right to retreat from his verdict unless he declares a mistake; then he can cancel or amend it per Shari'ah.

column4: An Institution concluded an arbitration verbally. According to the Shari'ah basis, what is needed for the arbitration to be legally accepted?
column5: It must be written and signed by arbitrators and parties
column6: Nothing; verbal arbitration alone is enough to be legally accepted
column7: It must be attested by two witnesses only
column8: It must be approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board
column10: Per the basis, arbitration may be verbal in Shari'ah, but to be legally accepted it needs to be written and signed by the arbitrators and the parties.

column4: Ahmad, appointed in person as arbitrator by Bank A, falls ill and appoints his colleague to replace him without asking the Bank. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed, as the arbitrator may delegate his task freely
column6: Allowed, if the colleague has the same qualifications
column7: Allowed, if the other party does not object
column8: Not allowed without the appointing party's permission
column10: Per 8/6, the arbitrator cannot appoint an alternate without permission of the party that appointed him, as he was accepted in person.

column4: An arbitrator's final decision settles only three of five disputed points between Bank A and a customer. What may the parties do?
column5: Demand a further decision on the remaining points
column6: Nothing, as the decision is final
column7: Treat the whole decision as void and restart the arbitration
column8: Only take the remaining points to court
column10: Per 11/2, partial resolution makes arbitration incomplete; the parties have the right to demand a further decision to resolve the remaining points.

column4: Bank A must comply with a certain national law in an arbitration it conducts as arbitrator. How should it handle a provision of that law contrary to Shari'ah?
column5: It may apply the law if both parties agree
column6: It should still not violate the rulings of Shari'ah
column7: It must apply the law, since the parties chose it
column8: It must stop the arbitration altogether
column10: Per 9/4, the arbitrator should apply the rulings of Shari'ah; if obliged to apply a certain law, he should still not violate the rulings of Shari'ah.

column4: Bank A signs a financing agreement governed by a law that contradicts Shari'ah. What does the standard recommend to avoid being forced to apply that law in disputes?
column5: Requiring the counterparty to waive all claims
column6: Leaving disputes to the courts of the host country
column7: Stipulating Islamic arbitration in the agreement
column8: Agreeing on arbitration only after a dispute arises
column10: Per 3/2, seeking Islamic arbitration should be stipulated in agreements so the parties cannot be forced to resort to laws that contradict Shari'ah.

column4: A Mudarib managing investment accounts is asked to accept arbitration over a dispute on the Mudarabah funds. When may he accept it?
column5: Only with approval of a court
column6: With the capital owners' consent or a Mudarabah clause
column7: At any time, since he manages the Mudarabah funds
column8: Only if the arbitrator is chosen by the other party to the dispute
column10: Per 8/7, a Mudarib may not accept arbitration except with the capital owners' consent or on the basis of a clause in the Mudarabah conditions.

column4: A government employee officially designated to perform arbitration asks the parties to pay him a fee for an arbitration. May he receive fees?
column5: Yes, if the fee is a percentage of the claim
column6: Yes, as any arbitrator may receive fees
column7: No; the fee entitlement excludes such a designated employee
column8: Yes, if the fee is fixed in the arbitration document by the parties
column10: Per 14/1, the arbitrator may receive fees if he is not a volunteer or a government employee designated for arbitration.

column4: The arbitration document set a 60-day period. The period ends without a verdict, and the parties have not agreed to extend it. What is the arbitrator's status?
column5: He may continue until he issues the verdict
column6: He must issue whatever verdict he has reached
column7: He may extend the period on his own
column8: He becomes terminated
column10: Per 9/6, when the period specified for arbitration expires without a verdict, the arbitrator becomes terminated unless the parties agree to extend it.

column4: Bank A operates in a country where an acute need arises to appoint a non-Muslim arbitrator for a dispute. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, provided the verdict conforms to Shari'ah
column6: Never permitted; the arbitrator must always be a Muslim
column7: Permitted, and he may apply any law he chooses
column8: Permitted only if the other party is also non-Muslim
column10: Per 8/2 and 11/1, an arbitrator is in principle a Muslim, but a non-Muslim may be appointed when acute need requires, to reach a Shari'ah-accepted verdict.

column4: Ahmad, a paid arbitrator, accepts a case and then withdraws mid-way, causing the parties actual harm. What is the ruling?
column5: He loses his fee but bears no other liability
column6: He may be liable for the actual harm caused
column7: He may not withdraw, and his withdrawal is ignored
column8: He has no liability, as arbitration is never binding on him
column10: Per 5/2, arbitration is binding on a paid arbitrator; if he terminates himself after accepting, he bears any actual harm resulting from his act.

column4: In an arbitration with no prior agreement on expenses, Bank A applied for an expert report for its own claim. Who bears the cost of that report?
column5: The arbitrator, out of his fees
column6: The party that loses the arbitration
column7: Bank A alone, as it relates to its own application
column8: Both parties equally, as a common expense of the arbitration
column10: Per 14/2, absent prior agreement, expenses relating to one party's application are borne by that party alone; common expenses are shared.

column4: Bank A and Company X ask an arbitrator to decide a matter that would establish a ruling against Company Y, which is not party to the arbitration. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible, as it proves a verdict against a third party
column6: Permissible, since the parties consented to the arbitration itself
column7: Permissible if the arbitrator is paid by both parties
column8: Permissible, if Company Y is notified of the verdict
column10: Per 7/2/2, arbitration is impermissible in cases that entail proving or disproving a verdict that concerns a third party.

column4: Bank A and Company X appoint two arbitrators. What does the standard provide for the case where the two arbitrators' votes are equal?
column5: The Bank's arbitrator has the deciding vote
column6: The arbitration becomes void as the panel is even
column7: The dispute must then be referred to the competent courts for ruling
column8: The parties may appoint a chairman with the casting vote
column10: Per 8/3, the number of arbitrators is preferably odd; otherwise the parties may appoint a chairman whose vote is the casting vote when votes are equal.

column4: Two traders ask an arbitrator to rule on whether one of them should receive a Hudud penalty for an offence. May this be arbitrated?
column5: No; Hudud are a right of Allah and not subject to arbitration
column6: Yes, if the arbitrator is a qualified Muslim scholar
column7: Yes, if both parties consent to the arbitrator's verdict
column8: Yes, provided the verdict is later registered in court
column10: Per 7/2/1, arbitration is impermissible in what constitutes a right of Allah, such as Hudud.

column4: An arbitrator issues a verdict on an issue that, under the standard, may not be resolved through arbitration. What is the status of that verdict?
column5: It is binding until revoked by a court
column6: It is valid but not enforceable in court
column7: It is null and void
column8: It is valid if both parties accept it
column10: Per 7/3, when the arbitrator issues a verdict on an issue that should not be resolved through arbitration, his verdict is null and void.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, which of the conditions applied to judges may be dropped for an arbitrator in case of necessity?
column5: That the verdict conform to Shari'ah
column6: That the arbitrator be non-partial
column7: That the arbitrator have full eligibility
column8: That the arbitrator be a Muslim
column10: The basis states that in necessity some judge conditions may be dropped, such as being a Muslim, but a non-Muslim arbitrator must not issue a verdict contradicting Shari'ah.

column4: A contract requires each party to appoint an arbitrator. Company X refuses to appoint its own, and the contract sets no other method. What may Bank A do?
column5: Appoint Company X's arbitrator itself, as the contract is silent
column6: Resort to the judiciary to appoint Company X's arbitrator
column7: Proceed with its own arbitrator as sole arbitrator
column8: Treat the arbitration clause as void
column10: Per 8/5, if a party refrains from appointing its arbitrator, the other may resort to the judiciary for that appointment, unless the contract specifies another way.

column4: Fatimah donates a farm as Waqf; half the income goes to her relatives and half to an orphanage. Which type of Waqf is this?
column5: Family Waqf (al-Waqf al-Ahli)
column6: Self-dedicated Waqf (al-Waqf 'Ala al-Nafs)
column7: Charitable Waqf (al-Waqf al-Khayri)
column8: Joint Waqf (al-Waqf al-Mushtarak)
column10: Per 2/3/3, a joint Waqf is where the property is donated to family as well as charitable purposes, with the income shared accordingly.

column4: A scholar asks why family Waqf is permissible though it benefits relatives. What reasons does the Shari'ah basis give?
column5: Relatives are always poor by presumption, so it is charity
column6: Umar's Waqf Hadith, and it finally becomes charitable
column7: The Waqif retains ownership of the asset through his family
column8: It is a form of inheritance before death
column10: The basis: family Waqf is permissible on the basis of the Hadith about Umar's Waqf, and because it is in fact charitable since it will finally become so.

column4: Ahmad, suffering a fatal illness, declares his land a Waqf. According to the Shari'ah basis, which rulings govern this Waqf?
column5: The rulings applicable to the will of such a person
column6: The rules of gifts with immediate possession
column7: The ordinary rules of Waqf by a healthy person
column8: The rules for Waqf of an irrational person
column10: The basis states that Waqf by a person suffering a fatal illness should be subject to the rulings applicable to the will of such person.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a Waqf superintendent barred from leasing the Waqf to himself or his son without the legal authorities?
column5: Because relatives cannot be tenants of any Waqf property
column6: Because such a lease is a form of Riba
column7: To guard against favoritism and neglect of the Waqf
column8: Because he is not allowed to collect rent
column10: The basis: the prohibition stems from fear of favoritism, part of human nature, and minimizes the chance of neglecting the interest of the Waqf.

column4: Ahmad makes a Waqf for his adult cousin Ali, who is legally competent. Ali rejects it. What happens?
column5: The Waqf is suspended until Ali changes his mind and accepts
column6: The Waqf stays valid and Ali's share goes to charitable purposes
column7: The property returns to Ahmad's ownership as a failed Waqf
column8: The Waqf becomes void, as the beneficiary did not accept it
column10: Per 3/1/1, Waqf needs only offer; if a competent beneficiary rejects it, the Waqf remains valid and his share goes to charitable purposes.

column4: A Waqf shop is leased below the normal rent. A new tenant offers the normal rent of similar property. What may the superintendent do?
column5: Nothing at all until the old lease term expires
column6: Raise the rent without needing the old tenant's acceptance
column7: End the old lease unless the old tenant accepts the increase
column8: Lease to both tenants and split the shop between them
column10: Per 6/2, if a new tenant can pay the normal rent, the superintendent may terminate the previous contract unless the old tenant accepts the rent increment.

column4: A Waqf has no income this year, and the superintendent wants to borrow so as to pay the beneficiaries their usual shares. What is the ruling?
column5: Not allowed; borrowing may not be to spend on beneficiaries
column6: Allowed if repayable from next year's expected income
column7: Allowed, as beneficiaries' rights come before all else
column8: Allowed with the judiciary's permission in such a case
column10: Per 5/3/6/3, borrowing for the Waqf should not be for the sake of spending on the beneficiaries of the Waqf.

column4: Ahmad declares a Waqf effective from next year. By analogy to which contract does the Shari'ah basis justify such a future-dated Waqf?
column5: 'Ariyah (lending)
column6: Ijarah (lease)
column7: Hibah (gift) with possession
column8: Wasiyyah (will)
column10: The basis states that permissibility of declaring Waqf effective from a future date is viewed by analogy between Waqf and Wasiyyah (will).

column4: Ahmad declares a shop as Waqf, keeping its rental income for himself while alive and naming a hospital to receive it after his death. Which type of Waqf is this?
column5: Family Waqf (al-Waqf al-Ahli) for his relatives
column6: Self-dedicated Waqf (al-Waqf 'Ala al-Nafs)
column7: Joint Waqf (al-Waqf al-Mushtarak) for charity and kin
column8: Temporary Waqf for the period of his own lifetime
column10: Per 2/3/4, in a self-dedicated Waqf the donor retains the income for himself while alive and indicates the charitable purpose entitled after his death.

column4: Company X's owner declares today that his warehouse will become a Waqf starting from next year. What is the status of this declaration?
column5: Valid only if made in a will
column6: Void; a Waqf must take effect immediately upon declaration
column7: Valid; a Waqf may be effective from a future date
column8: Valid only for family Waqf
column10: Per 3/1/3, Waqf can be declared effective from a future date, as when the donor declares his property to become Waqf starting next year.

column4: A Waqf building in a deserted area yields no income and no funds exist to develop it. The superintendent agrees a sale at fair value. What else is required?
column5: Permission of the judiciary
column6: Consent of the Waqif's heirs
column7: A vote of the beneficiaries
column8: Approval of the tenant in occupation
column10: Per 9/3, Istibdal conditions include no income and no development funds, no excessive injustice in price, Waqf interest, and permission of the judiciary.

column4: A Waqf tenant fails to pay the rent. The superintendent wants to waive the debt as a favour. Per the Shari'ah basis, may he?
column5: Yes, if the amount is small
column6: Yes, with the tenant's written request
column7: Yes, as manager he owns the Waqf's claims
column8: No; the debt is owed to the Waqf, not to him
column10: The basis: the Waqf has a legal personality separate from its superintendent; a party failing an obligation is indebted to the Waqf, so he cannot relieve the debtor.

column4: A Waqf superintendent leases a Waqf apartment to his wife at a rent slightly below the market rent of similar property. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed if the shortfall is under one third of the rent
column6: Allowed, as minor Ghabn is always forgiven in leasing
column7: Not allowed; even minor Ghabn is not forgiven for relatives
column8: Allowed if the wife pays the whole rent in advance
column10: Per 5/3/2, he may not lease to direct relatives or his spouse for less than the normal rent; minor Ghabn is not forgivable here, though forgivable for nonrelatives.

column4: A Waqif requires that Waqf income always be distributed to beneficiaries first, even when the Waqf building needs urgent renovation. What is the status of this condition?
column5: Invalid, as it hinders the interests of the Waqf
column6: Valid, but only for family Waqf
column7: Valid, as the Waqif's conditions are like Shari'ah texts
column8: Valid unless the beneficiaries waive it
column10: Per 4/1/3 and 8/1/1, a condition requiring income distribution first even when maintenance is needed is invalid as it hinders the interests of the Waqf.

column4: A Waqf has income held during the waiting period before its beneficiaries are identified. May the superintendent invest it, and how?
column5: Only with the Waqif's written condition
column6: Yes, in permissible low-risk modes such as Mudarabah
column7: No; Waqf income may never be invested in any mode
column8: Yes, in any investment offering the highest return
column10: Per 7/1, Waqf income may be invested per the Waqif's condition, during the waiting period, or from excess income, through permissible low-risk methods.

column4: Ahmad makes a Waqf for his future grandchildren, none of whom has been born yet. What is the status of the Waqf?
column5: Suspended until the first grandchild is born
column6: Valid only if a current beneficiary is added
column7: Void, as the beneficiary does not exist when the Waqf is declared
column8: Valid; the beneficiary need not be present at declaration
column10: Per 3/3/3, the Waqf beneficiary need not be present at the time of declaring the Waqf.

column4: The board of directors of Company X resolves to declare one of the company's buildings a Waqf. Who should make the Waqf decision for a legal person?
column5: The general assembly, not the board of directors
column6: The chief executive officer alone
column7: The board of directors, as it manages assets
column8: Any two directors acting jointly
column10: Per 3/2/1, if the Waqif is a legal person, the Waqf decision should be made by the general assembly and not the board of directors.

column4: A Waqif stipulated that his Waqf house be benefited from by residence for poor students. The superintendent finds leasing it would serve better. What applies?
column5: Leasing makes the Waqf void
column6: It may be used by residence or by leasing
column7: It may only be used by residence
column8: It may be leased only with court permission
column10: Per 4/1/4, when the Waqif stipulates benefit through residence, the Waqf can be benefited from in that manner or through leasing, and vice versa.

column4: A tenant of Waqf land built a new building on it at his own cost, raising the land's normal rent. The superintendent demands a rent increase. What applies?
column5: The tenant must accept the increase, as the land's rent has risen
column6: The building passes to the Waqf free of charge
column7: The tenant is not bound to accept the rent increment
column8: The lease is terminated automatically
column10: Per 6/2, if development and construction are done at the tenant's cost, he is not bound to accept the rent increment; if at the Waqf's cost, he is.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is Waqf regarded as the ongoing charity (Sadaqah Jariyah) mentioned in the Hadith?
column5: The income is paid only after the death of the Waqif himself
column6: The Waqif keeps ownership of the asset for all time
column7: The asset must be a mosque, a well or a school
column8: The beneficiary neither owns the asset nor disposes of it
column10: The basis states Waqf is the ongoing charity in the Hadith because the beneficiary does not own the Waqf asset and accordingly cannot dispose of it.

column4: A Waqf builds a maintenance reserve from its annual income. The beneficiaries demand a share of that reserve. What is their right?
column5: Right to half of the reserve each year as part of their income
column6: Full right, as all income of the Waqf belongs to the beneficiaries
column7: None, unless part of the reserve exceeds actual needs
column8: Right to the whole reserve once the Waqf asset has been repaired
column10: Per 8/1/2, the beneficiaries have no right in the maintenance reserve unless part of it turns out to be in excess of actual needs; its returns join the principal.

column4: A Waqif forbade any exchange of his Waqf. The Waqf property has since become ruined. May Istibdal take place?
column5: No; the Waqif's prohibition is binding
column6: Only if the beneficiaries unanimously agree
column7: Only if the Waqif's heirs consent
column8: Yes; Istibdal is allowed when the Waqf is ruined
column10: Per 9/2, Istibdal can take place per the Waqif's condition, or when the Waqf becomes ruined, even if prevented by the Waqif.

column4: A person whose legal competence is restricted for irrationality declares his land a Waqf for a school. What is the ruling?
column5: Invalid, unless he makes the Waqf for himself while alive
column6: Valid, as Waqf is a good deed open to everyone, even the incompetent
column7: Valid if his guardian later approves the Waqf
column8: Valid if it is made as a temporary Waqf only
column10: Per 3/2/3, the Waqf of a person restricted for irrationality is invalid, except when he declares his property as Waqf for himself as long as he is alive.

column4: A Waqf owns vacant land but has no funds. Bank A leases the land, builds on it, and leases the building to the Waqf, which owns it at the end. Which mode is this?
column5: Hikr, with the tenant paying a changing normal rent
column6: Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek of a property to be built
column7: Istibdal of the Waqf land in exchange for a building
column8: Diminishing Musharakah in which the land is shared too
column10: Per 7/2/3, under IMB the Waqf land is leased to the financier who builds and delivers the building to the Waqf; at term end the Waqf owns the building.

column4: A tenant pays a lump sum (Kardar) at signing for developing the Waqf, plus a rent below that of similar property, gaining Haqq al-Qarar. When is this permissible?
column5: Whenever the Waqif did not expressly prohibit it
column6: Whenever the lump sum exceeds one year's normal rent
column7: In necessity, if no tenant pays normal rent plus a lump sum
column8: Only if the Waqf already has sufficient income of its own
column10: Per 6/3/2, Haqq al-Qarar (al-Khulu) is permissible when dictated by necessity and no tenant will pay the normal rent along with a lump sum for development.

column4: Ahmad rents a building for five years and declares its usufruct a Waqf, subleasing it for beneficiaries. The owner permits subleasing. How long is this Waqf?
column5: Temporary, for the period of the original rent
column6: For Ahmad's lifetime
column7: Until the owner decides to sell the building
column8: Permanent, as Waqf is in principle eternal
column10: Per 3/4/6, Waqf of a usufruct acquired by rent is temporary according to the original rent period, and needs the owner not to bar subleasing.

column4: A Waqf superintendent wants to lease Waqf land for 50 years at a fixed rent. Under the standard, when may such a long lease be used?
column5: Whenever the Waqif did not forbid long leases
column6: Only for obvious interest, with a variable index-linked rent
column7: Only if the tenant is a Muslim institution
column8: Whenever the tenant pays the whole rent in advance for all 50 years
column10: Per 6/1, long leases should not be the normal practice for Waqf assets except for obvious interest, with a variable rent linked to an accurate, well-known index.

column4: A donor dedicates USD 1 million in cash as Waqf for students. How should this cash Waqf be used?
column5: Only interest earned on deposits may be spent
column6: The full amount is distributed to students at once
column7: It must be converted into real estate first
column8: Its income is spent while the principal is retained
column10: Per 3/4/3/2, Waqf in money is permissible; income from utilizing it (e.g., Shari'ah-based lending or Mudarabah) is spent while retaining the principal.

column4: Ahmad declares his apartment building a Waqf. A year later he wants to sell it to settle a personal expense. What is the ruling?
column5: He can, since a Waqf is a revocable gift to the beneficiaries
column6: He can, if he donates the sale price to charity
column7: He cannot; the Waqf is binding and ended his ownership
column8: He can, with the beneficiaries' consent
column10: Per 2/2, Waqf is a binding commitment; declaring a property as Waqf spontaneously deprives its donating owner of the right of ownership.

column4: A Waqf residential building earns little. The superintendent wants to convert it into a commercial building. Which of the following is a condition for this?
column5: That the Waqif stipulated conversion
column6: Unanimous consent of all beneficiaries
column7: Approval of the Waqif's heirs
column8: Permission of the concerned authorities
column10: Per 5/2/5, changing the operational form is allowed if it meets demand, generates more income and is done with the permission of the concerned authorities.

column4: Why, per the Shari'ah basis, must the Waqif have full legal competence?
column5: Because Waqf is an exchange contract
column6: Because Waqf in its essence is a donation (Tabarru')
column7: Because the Waqf needs judicial registration
column8: Because the beneficiary must accept the Waqf when it is declared
column10: The basis states the Waqif must have full legal competence because Waqf in its very essence is a donation (Tabarru').

column4: A Waqif stipulates that his Waqf may never be exchanged (Istibdal) under any circumstances. What is the effect of this condition?
column5: The condition is rejected; the Waqf remains valid
column6: The whole Waqf becomes void
column7: The condition binds only during his lifetime
column8: The condition is binding as a Waqif condition
column10: Per 4/1/3, absolute forbiddance of Istibdal is an invalid condition; such a condition is rejected while the Waqf remains valid.

column4: On what analogy does the Shari'ah basis base the view that a Waqf donation should not exceed one third of the donor's wealth?
column5: The analogy with Zakah on wealth, a fixed share of the wealth
column6: The analogy with Hibah (gift) in illness
column7: The analogy with Wasiyyah (will), leaving a share for heirs
column8: The analogy with 'Ariyah (lent thing)
column10: The basis grounds the one-third limit on the analogy between Waqf and Wasiyyah, where part of the wealth should be left to the heirs.

column4: A Waqf superintendent uses the Waqf's income to buy an extra building for the Waqf instead of paying beneficiaries. The Waqif set no such condition. Is this allowed?
column5: No; it requires a condition stipulated by the Waqif
column6: Yes, as it increases the Waqf's assets and its future income
column7: Yes, if the building yields higher income
column8: Yes, with judicial approval after the fact
column10: Per 5/3/3, the superintendent shall not use Waqf income to increase Waqf properties, except in fulfillment of a condition stipulated by the Waqif.

column4: A Waqf superintendent wants to lease the Waqf shop to his dependant son at a rent above the market rent. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed with the beneficiaries' approval
column6: Not allowed except through the judiciary
column7: Allowed, since the rent is above market
column8: Allowed if the lease is for one year only
column10: Per 5/3/2, the superintendent shall not lease the Waqf to himself or his dependant son, even at more than the normal rent, except through the judiciary.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may the superintendent borrow to protect the Waqf but not to pay beneficiaries when there is no income?
column5: Any debt taken for the beneficiaries' shares necessarily involves Riba
column6: The Waqif's heirs must pay the beneficiaries instead
column7: Beneficiaries are never entitled to any income at all
column8: Borrowing prevents the Waqf's ruin; unpaid shares do not
column10: The basis: borrowing safeguards the Waqf against being useless, whereas refraining from paying beneficiaries when there is no income involves no such harm.

column4: Ahmad makes a Waqf whose income goes to his children and grandchildren. Eventually none of them remains in existence. Where does the income go?
column5: Back to Ahmad's estate for his heirs
column6: To the State treasury as ownerless property
column7: To a charitable purpose
column8: To the Waqf superintendent
column10: Per 2/3/2 and 3/3/4, in a family Waqf the income goes to a charitable purpose when none of the specified persons is existent.

column4: A Waqf owns an indivisible share in a building jointly with Company X. The Waqf superintendent asks for division; Company X refuses. What applies?
column5: The superintendent's request is rejected
column6: The Waqf share is gifted to Company X
column7: Company X is forced to divide the building physically between them
column8: Company X must accept a sale; proceeds buy like property
column10: Per 3/4/4/2, for an indivisible Waqf, the refraining party is forced to accept selling, and the Waqf's proceeds buy a Waqf property of the same kind.

column4: Bank A offers a Waqf superintendent financing secured by a mortgage over the Waqf building. May the superintendent mortgage the Waqf asset?
column5: Yes, for a short-term debt only
column6: No; mortgaging Waqf assets is not allowed
column7: Yes, if the debt is for the Waqf's benefit
column8: Yes, if the beneficiaries agree
column10: Per 5/3/4, the superintendent shall not mortgage the Waqf assets for a debt to be obtained for the Waqf or the beneficiaries.

column4: Ahmad, whose legal competence is restricted because of indebtedness, declares his shop a Waqf. His creditors refuse to confirm it. What is the status?
column5: The Waqf becomes invalid
column6: The Waqf is valid for half the shop
column7: The Waqf is valid but suspended until he pays
column8: The Waqf stays valid; debts are paid from its income
column10: Per 3/2/3, the Waqf of a person restricted for indebtedness depends on his creditors' confirmation; if they refuse, the Waqf becomes invalid.

column4: A Waqf's building badly needs maintenance and the Waqf income is insufficient. The Waqif set no condition on borrowing. May the superintendent borrow?
column5: No; borrowing needs the Waqif's condition in the Waqf deed
column6: Yes, with the authorities' permission, if the Waqf can repay
column7: No; only beneficiaries may borrow for it
column8: Yes, freely, as maintenance precedes any distribution to beneficiaries
column10: Per 5/3/6, borrowing is allowed on permission of legal authorities in necessity, e.g. maintenance without sufficient income, considering the Waqf's ability to repay.

column4: Ahmad wants to make a Waqf whose income goes to a specific group of wealthy relatives, not to any charity. The purpose involves no sin. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible; a Waqf need not be charitable at inception
column6: Impermissible; every Waqf must be charitable from the start
column7: Impermissible; Waqf for the rich is barred
column8: Permissible only if the relatives are poor
column10: Per 3/3/1 and 3/3/2, Waqf must not be for an impermissible purpose but need not be charitable from inception; Waqf for the rich is permissible.

column4: Ahmad wants to dedicate his house as Waqf for students for ten years, then take it back. Is this temporary Waqf permissible?
column5: No; this is an 'Ariyah (lending), not a Waqf at all
column6: No; every Waqf must be eternal, so a time limit voids the whole Waqf
column7: Yes; temporary Waqf is permissible though eternity is the principle
column8: Yes, but only when the Waqf is made for a mosque or a school
column10: Per 3/1/4, Waqf in principle should be eternal, but temporary Waqf is also permissible when the donor wishes to get back his property after a specific period.

column4: An upper floor is declared Waqf, but the owner of the lower floor cannot construct his floor. Under the right of Ta'alli, what may be done?
column5: The Waqf lapses until the lower floor is built
column6: The Waqf may build only if the owner pays in advance
column7: The lower-floor owner must sell his land to the Waqf
column8: Build the lower floor at Waqf cost, repaid from its rent
column10: Per 3/4/5, the lower floor can be built at the Waqf's cost (with authorities' permission) and the cost reimbursed to the Waqf from its leasing income.

column4: A Muslim donor wishes to make a Waqf for a hospital that serves a non-Muslim community, for a purpose involving no sin. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if Muslims share the income
column6: Permissible, since the cause involves no sin
column7: Impermissible; beneficiaries must be Muslims
column8: Permissible only as a temporary Waqf
column10: Per 3/3/2, it is permissible to make Waqf for the benefit of non-Muslims, provided the cause to be served does not involve a sin.

column4: Why, per the Shari'ah basis, does a beneficiary's rejection of a Waqf not nullify it?
column5: He may drop his own rights but cannot nullify the Waqf
column6: Acceptance is needed only from the Waqif
column7: A Waqf can only be nullified by a court
column8: Rejection is valid only after the Waqif's death and not before it
column10: Per the basis (Hanafi view), the beneficiary can drop his own rights in the Waqf, but he cannot nullify the Waqf itself.

column4: A Waqf's annual income is ready for distribution, but its building needs scheduled maintenance. The Waqif set no condition on maintenance. What should the superintendent do?
column5: Distribute first, then maintain from next year's income
column6: Seek the beneficiaries' consent before maintaining
column7: Maintain only if the Waqif had stipulated it
column8: Spend on maintenance before distributing to beneficiaries
column10: Per 8/1/1, spending on maintenance and renovation precedes distribution of income, and does not require a prior condition stipulated by the Waqif.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, on which schools' views does the permissibility of temporary Waqf rest?
column5: The Shafi'i and Hanbali Schools, against the Maliki
column6: The Hanafi and Shafi'i Schools, by consensus
column7: The Maliki and Imami Schools, and a view of Abu Yusuf
column8: The Hanbali School alone, as an exception
column10: The basis states permissibility of temporary Waqf rests on the Maliki and Imami Schools, and what is reported of Abu Yusuf of the Hanafi School.

column4: On which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis rest the rule that the Waqif's permissible conditions must be observed?
column5: "Do not sell food until you hold it"
column6: "Muslims are bound to the conditions they make"
column7: "There is no misdemeanor on the one in charge of it"
column8: "When a person dies his deeds stop except in three"
column10: The basis cites the Hadith "Muslims are bound to the conditions they make", except a condition permitting the prohibited or prohibiting the permitted.

column4: A Waqf holds Sukuk whose issuer is liquidated, and the Waqf receives the liquidation proceeds. Which rulings should then apply?
column5: The Shari'ah rulings on Istibdal (exchange of Waqf property)
column6: The proceeds are distributed to beneficiaries as income
column7: The rules on dissolving a family Waqf
column8: The proceeds return to the Waqif
column10: Per 3/4/3/4, Waqf in Shari'ah-accepted shares and Sukuk is permissible; in case of liquidation, the rulings on Istibdal should be applied.

column4: A superintendent considers a Hikr lease that keeps Waqf land with a tenant as long as he pays the changing normal rent. Which is a condition for Hikr?
column5: The Waqf has surplus income
column6: The tenant pays the whole rent in advance
column7: Istibdal of the Waqf is not possible
column8: The Waqif expressly stipulated Hikr
column10: Per 6/3/1, Hikr requires that the Waqf has no income for development, no one will pay fixed-term rent in advance for it, and Istibdal is not possible.

column4: Ahmad bought land with an option for himself to cancel the purchase. During the option period he declares the land a Waqf. What is the effect?
column5: The Waqf is valid only after the option lapses
column6: The Waqf is valid and the option continues
column7: The Waqf is void while the option exists
column8: The Waqf is valid and his option is cancelled
column10: Per 3/4/1(c), if the Waqif himself has the option of disposing of the property, the Waqf becomes valid and the option is spontaneously cancelled.

column4: A real estate Waqf is to be exchanged, and there is no risk of misuse. How may the exchange be done?
column5: Sell for cash held by the judiciary until real estate is bought
column6: Exchange it for listed shares of equal market value
column7: Sell it and distribute the cash among the beneficiaries
column8: Sell and invest the cash in Mudarabah on a permanent basis, not in real estate
column10: Per 9/3/5, real estate Waqf is exchanged for real estate; where no risk of misuse, it can be sold for cash kept with the judiciary until a new real estate is bought.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, which school's view is followed in allowing a Waqf for a non-charitable but permissible purpose?
column5: The Hanafi School; the Maliki School requires charity
column6: The Maliki School; the Hanafi School requires charity
column7: The Hanbali School; all others require charity
column8: The Shafi'i School; the Hanbali School requires charity
column10: The basis: since Waqf is a donation, the only condition is a permissible purpose (Maliki view), whereas the Hanafi School holds the purpose should be charitable.

column4: A leased Waqf asset needs renovation, and the Waqf lacks funds. The tenant offers to carry out the renovation. What may the superintendent grant?
column5: A rent-free lease for as long as he lives
column6: Ownership of a share of the Waqf asset in return for the cost
column7: Nothing; tenants may never renovate Waqf assets
column8: Priority to remain tenant until his cost is fully repaid
column10: Per 8/1/3, the superintendent may allow the tenant to renovate, against priority to continue as tenant until he gets full repayment of his debt.

column4: The Waqf of Mosque A has unspent excess income, while nearby Mosque B lacks funds for its maintenance. What may be done with the excess?
column5: It must return to the Waqif's heirs
column6: It must stay with Mosque A
column7: It may be transferred to Mosque B
column8: It must go to the poor generally
column10: Per 5/4, excess unspent income of a specific mosque's Waqf may be transferred to another mosque lacking enough income for its expenses or maintenance.

column4: Bank A hired a well-defined service for future delivery. The service delivered turns out useless. What is the status of the contract?
column5: It remains valid; the employee must deliver a similar service
column6: The employer may only terminate it, with no other remedy
column7: It becomes null and void at once for lack of benefit
column8: The employer must accept it as delivered and pay in full
column10: Per 8/2/1, where the useless service pertains to future delivery of a well-defined service, the contract remains valid and the employee must deliver a similar service.

column4: A hiring contract's pay instalments are payable monthly. The parties now consent to raise the pay for months not yet served. Is this permitted?
column5: No; changes need a new framework agreement
column6: Yes, but only for past unpaid months
column7: Yes; pay for future periods can be amended by consent
column8: No; the agreed pay can never be changed once the contract is signed
column10: Per 5/2/5, it is permissible, with both parties' consent, to amend the pay of future periods in which the service has not yet been benefited from.

column4: Bank A, as employee, wants a clause protecting it if the employer defaults in paying. Which clause is permissible?
column5: A clause adding a late fee kept by the Bank as income
column6: A clause converting the debt into a higher deferred amount
column7: A clause increasing the pay by 2% per month of delay
column8: A pledge by the employer to donate a percentage to charity
column10: Per 5/2/8, no condition may increase the agreed pay on default; the contract may include a pledge to donate a percentage of the pay to charity under the Shari'ah Board.

column4: Ahmad is a private employee working full-time under the supervision of Company X. He wants to take a second job with Company Y during the same hours. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed, since he may serve several employers
column6: Not allowed without Company X's permission
column7: Allowed, as long as his work quality is unaffected
column8: Allowed, if Company Y pays him more
column10: Per 4/3, a private employee working for a single employer may not work for anyone else at the same time, except with his employer's permission.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why can the pay for future periods be adjusted by consent while past unpaid pay cannot be increased?
column5: Only increases in pay, not decreases, amount to Riba
column6: Past pay remains owned by the employer until it is paid to the employee
column7: Adjusting future pay renews it; increasing past pay is Riba
column8: Future pay is already a debt, while past pay is not
column10: The basis: adjusting future pay is a renewal for a coming period; increasing unsettled past pay against more time is Riba.

column4: Company X pledged to hire Bank A's services and paid a seriousness guarantee of 50,000. It then withdraws, causing the Bank actual harm of 20,000. How much may the Bank deduct?
column5: Nothing, since a pledge is not binding
column6: Only 20,000, the actual harm caused
column7: 20,000 plus the Bank's expected lost profit
column8: The full 50,000 as a penalty for withdrawal
column10: Per 3/2, upon the client's withdrawal, the deduction from the guarantee amount should not exceed the actual harm caused to the Institution.

column4: Company X proposes a hiring contract with no specified period. Per the Shari'ah basis, why must the hiring period be specified?
column5: The pay cannot be fixed without a period
column6: An unspecified period makes the employee a partner in the employer's business
column7: Hiring is a donation contract needing a term
column8: An unspecified period causes Gharar and leads to dispute
column10: The basis: non-specification causes prohibited Gharar and Jahalah leading to dispute; hiring is in essence a sale of service, so must be free of Gharar.

column4: Bank A has hired Company Y, an employee-institution, to provide IT staff support for two years. Company Y is then liquidated. What happens to the contract?
column5: It is terminated
column6: It is suspended until Company Y is revived
column7: It passes automatically to Company Y's shareholders
column8: It continues with Company Y's liquidator
column10: Per 8/1/1, a hiring contract relating to the employee in person is terminated when the employee-institution encounters liquidation, bankruptcy or freezing of activities.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, to which contract is hiring for a service delivered in the future compared?
column5: Mudarabah
column6: Wakalah
column7: Salam
column8: Murabahah
column10: The basis states a hiring contract for a future service is judged by analogy to Salam, as it does not lead to dispute; Shafi'is and Hanbalis do not require advance pay.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why does a private employee not guarantee what he works on, absent transgression or negligence?
column5: This is the general principle in trust-based contracts
column6: He is not paid anything for his work until the contract is complete
column7: He works for many employers at the same time
column8: The employer is presumed to be negligent instead
column10: The basis: a private employee not guaranteeing absent transgression, negligence or breach is the general principle in trust-based contracts.

column4: A private employee hired from 1 May reports to work only on 15 May without excuse. What applies?
column5: Full pay for the whole month, as the contract had already started
column6: No pay for the gap; termination allowed unless a make-up is agreed
column7: Pay for the gap is due, with a penalty deducted from his total pay
column8: No pay for the gap, but the employer may not terminate the contract
column10: Per 4/9, the employee gets no pay for the gap; the employer may terminate unless they agree on a compensatory period at the end of the contract.

column4: Bank A receives a seriousness guarantee from a client who pledged to hire its services. Which of the following is a permitted way to hold this amount?
column5: Treat it as the Bank's income on receipt
column6: Lend it to other clients at a fixed return
column7: Use it freely as the Bank's own funds without any return to the client
column8: Invest it for the client by Mudarabah or investment agency
column10: Per 3/2, the guarantee amount may be kept as a deposit not disposed of, invested for the client via Mudarabah or investment agency, or frozen in his current account.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may pay take the form of a common share of the output?
column5: It is in reality a form of Ju'alah, not hiring
column6: It can be known and does not lead to dispute or Gharar
column7: It turns the hiring into a partnership contract between the two
column8: The employer bears no risk in this form of pay
column10: The basis states the pay can be a common share because in this form it can be known and will not lead to dispute or Gharar.

column4: Which Qur'anic verse does the Shari'ah basis cite as evidence for the permissibility of hiring of persons?
column5: "Then if they give suck to the children for you, give them their payment"
column6: "O you who believe! Fulfill (your) obligations. Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle"
column7: "Help you one another in Al-Birr and Al-Taqwa"
column8: "When you contract a debt for a fixed period, write it down"
column10: The basis cites the verse: "Then if they give suck to the children for you, give them their due payment" (Al-Talaq: 6) for permissibility of hiring.

column4: A contractor and Company X agree: if the work is done in 30 days the pay is 10,000; if done in 20 days it is 12,000. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if the lower rate is paid first
column6: Impermissible, as the pay is uncertain
column7: Impermissible, as two sales in one sale
column8: Permissible; more than one rate of pay may be agreed
column10: Per 5/2/9, the parties may agree upon more than one rate of pay, e.g. one rate if done within a certain period and a higher rate for a shorter period.

column4: Ali is a private employee of Bank A. He leaves work for a day without permission, for no recognizable duty. What does the standard say?
column5: He may be absent if a colleague covers his work that day
column6: He may be absent if he makes up the lost time later
column7: He may not be absent without permission or a recognized duty
column8: He may be absent for up to three days in each month without pay
column10: Per 7/1/1, the private employee must render his service and observe the hiring period, not being absent except with the employer's permission or for a recognizable duty.

column4: A hiring contract gives Company X a conditional option (Khiyar al-Shart) to cancel within 15 days. On day 10, X cancels. What is the ruling?
column5: Invalid; hiring cannot be terminated unilaterally
column6: Valid only if X proves a defect
column7: Valid only if the employee also agrees
column8: Valid termination, as it is within the option period
column10: Per 8/2/2, the contract can be terminated on the basis of Khiyar al-Shart by the party that stipulated it, within its specified period.

column4: Six months into a two-year hiring contract, Company X wants to end it simply because it found a cheaper provider. The employee objects. What is the ruling?
column5: It may terminate if it pays a penalty
column6: It may not terminate without the other party's consent
column7: It may terminate since hiring is non-binding
column8: It may terminate with one month's notice to the employee
column10: Per 4/7, hiring of persons is binding; neither party can terminate or amend it without the other's consent, except for breach, emergent excuse or inevitable circumstances.

column4: Company X hires a contractor to translate a book within one month. He translates half; the half is useful, and Company X refuses to extend the period. What is he owed?
column5: The pay normally paid for similar work (Ajr al-Mithl)
column6: Half the agreed pay automatically by default
column7: The whole agreed pay for the translation, as half was useful
column8: Nothing, since the agreed work is incomplete
column10: Per 5/1/2, if the partial work is useful and the employer will not extend the period, the employee is entitled to Ajr al-Mithl; if useless, to no pay.

column4: Company X owes its contractor three months of unpaid past wages. They agree to defer payment by six months in return for a 5% increase. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible as an ordinary amendment of the future pay
column6: Permissible, since both parties freely consented to it
column7: Impermissible; unpaid past pay is a debt and cannot grow
column8: Permissible if the increase goes to the employee directly
column10: Per 5/2/5, unpaid pay for past periods is a debt owed by the employer; stipulating an increase (rescheduling) is impermissible. Future pay may be amended by consent.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, on what ground may the Institution take a seriousness margin from a party pledging to hire its services?
column5: Need and interest
column6: The rules of Rahn on existing debts
column7: The general rule of Kafalah
column8: The analogy with 'Arboun in sale
column10: The basis states that permissibility of receiving a seriousness margin from the party pledging to hire is based on need and interest.

column4: Bank A hires a well-defined consultancy service to be delivered in the future. Bank A then hires out an identical service to a client. What is this and is it allowed?
column5: Sub-hiring, allowed only with the provider's consent
column6: Sale of a debt, which is not allowed
column7: Parallel hiring, and it is allowed
column8: Two sales in one, which is not allowed
column10: Per 5/1/3, if the hired service is specifically defined and to be delivered in the future, the employer may hire out an identical service to another (parallel hiring).

column4: An employee hired to deliver a well-defined future service dies before delivery. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the contract not become void?
column5: The employee's heirs become the new employer
column6: The service, as a debt, is considered existent
column7: The pay has already been earned in full
column8: The employer has waived the service
column10: The basis: a contract for a future service does not become void on the employee's death because the service, as a debt, is considered existent.

column4: A hiring contract is executed as planned after the employee received 'Arboun at signing. How is the 'Arboun treated?
column5: As a deposit returned to the employer
column6: As a gift on top of the full pay
column7: As a seriousness margin held until expiry
column8: As a prepaid part of the employee's pay
column10: Per 4/11, if the hiring contract is implemented, the earnest money ('Arboun) becomes a prepaid part of the employee's pay.

column4: Which practice does the Shari'ah basis cite to support hiring a person for a deferred service?
column5: The Prophet and Abu Bakr hiring a guide to serve after three days
column6: Umar's taking of 'Arboun in the presence of the Sahabah
column7: The Prophet's hiring of a scribe to record the Qur'an
column8: Umar's donation of his land in Khaybar as a Waqf for the poor and kin
column10: The basis cites the Prophet and Abu Bakr hiring a man from Bani Al-Dail as a guide after three days; and hiring is a time-based contract.

column4: A fishing company hires a crew and agrees to pay them 10% of the catch as their pay. What is the ruling on this form of pay?
column5: Impermissible, as it turns hiring into Mudarabah
column6: Permissible only with a minimum fixed wage
column7: Impermissible, since the pay is unknown at signing
column8: Permissible; pay can be a percentage of the output
column10: Per 5/2/6, the pay can be determined as a percentage of the output (e.g., 10%) or as a part of the thing to be made.

column4: Company X hires Ahmad to do a specific job himself. Ahmad passes the job to an assistant without any contract clause permitting this. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed if the assistant is equally qualified for the job
column6: Not allowed; he must do it himself unless the contract allows
column7: Allowed, as only the end result matters to the employer
column8: Allowed if Ahmad pays the assistant out of his own pay
column10: Per 7/1/2, the employee is in principle to do the work himself unless the contract stipulates otherwise; for future defined services only the specifications matter.

column4: Ali, a private employee of Bank A, accidentally damages office equipment without any transgression, negligence or breach of a condition. Is he liable?
column5: Yes, for half of the cost of the damage
column6: Yes; employees are always liable for damage to the employer's property
column7: No; a private employee is liable only for such faults
column8: Yes, unless he was working overtime
column10: Per 4/5, a private employee is not responsible for damage unless it is due to his own transgression, negligence, or breach of a stipulated condition.

column4: A three-year hiring contract links pay after year one to a published wage index. What does the standard require for such variable pay?
column5: Known first-period pay and an agreed index with limits
column6: An index chosen by the employer alone at each new period
column7: A fixed amount for all three years with no indexation
column8: Approval of the regulator for the pay of each new period
column10: Per 5/2/4, pay can be variable if the first period's pay is known and an accurate, agreed indicator with an upper and a lower limit sets later periods.

column4: A tailor serving many customers (a shared employee) accepts an order from Bank A's staff club while serving others. Is he restricted from working for others at the same time?
column5: Yes; he must serve only one client at a time, in order of orders
column6: Yes, unless the first client permits it
column7: No; a shared employee is not subject to that restriction
column8: No, but only if he charges all clients equally
column10: Per 4/3, unlike a private employee, a shared employee working for more than one person is not restricted from working for others.

column4: On what does the Shari'ah basis rely for the permissibility of taking 'Arboun in hiring of persons?
column5: The analogy with Salam payment in advance, as a pledge of performance
column6: The Hadith "Don't sell what you do not have"
column7: The consensus of the four schools
column8: What Umar did before the Sahabah, adopted by Ahmad
column10: The basis derives 'Arboun permissibility from what Umar did in the presence of the Sahabah, adopted by Ahmad, and a Fiqh Academy of Makkah resolution.

column4: A contractor refuses to deliver the agreed service and fails to provide the suitable alternative agreed in the contract. What may the employer do?
column5: Claim the full contract value as a penalty
column6: Terminate and claim indemnity for the actual harm
column7: Only terminate, with no indemnity for any harm he has suffered
column8: Only wait until the contractor performs
column10: Per 8/1/2, if the employee refrains from delivering the service and fails to present the agreed alternative, the employer may terminate and claim indemnity for actual harm.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why may an Institution not hire out a specific service before owning and possessing it?
column5: By analogy to selling what one does not own
column6: Because services cannot be delivered constructively
column7: Because pay must always be in advance
column8: By analogy to the prohibition of 'Inah
column10: The basis: it is by analogy to the prohibition of selling things one does not own, and Hakim Ibn Hizam's Hadith "Don't sell what you do not have".

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why must a shared employee guarantee what he works on?
column5: He is a trustee in the same way as a private employee
column6: He works in the owner's absence and for many employers
column7: His pay is deemed to include an insurance premium
column8: He always owns the item that he is working on
column10: The basis cites Sahabah reports: the shared employee does his paid work in the owner's absence and works for many employers, not one.

column4: Bank A agrees to provide a client with a fully specified training programme to be delivered next year. The Bank does not yet own it. Must the client pay in advance?
column5: Yes, as future services require advance pay under every contract
column6: No, and the Bank must own the service first
column7: Yes, at least half must be paid at signing
column8: No, unless the contract is a Salam or Salaf contract
column10: Per 5/1/6, future well-described services need not be owned at signing, and the pay need not be in advance unless the contract is Salam or Salaf.

column4: An investment agent permitted to utilize a client's money incurs a loss without transgression or negligence. Unlike a shared employee, is he liable?
column5: Yes, if the client did not approve the investment in advance
column6: Yes, for any loss above 10% of capital
column7: No; he guarantees only for transgression or negligence
column8: Yes; like a shared employee he is fully liable
column10: Per 4/6, unlike the shared employee, the investment agent does not guarantee except in case of transgression or negligence.

column4: Bank A hired a specific, identified service. The service then becomes completely useless. What is the status of the contract?
column5: The contract becomes null and void
column6: The employee must deliver a similar service
column7: The contract continues and pay remains due
column8: The employer may only claim a discount
column10: Per 8/2/1, in specific hiring, when the service becomes completely useless the contract becomes null and void; if partially useless, the employer may terminate.

column4: A hiring contract says that if Company X defaults on an instalment without excuse after notice, all remaining instalments fall due. If X pays early, when does the employee finally own them?
column5: Immediately upon receiving the accelerated instalments
column6: At the end of the first year of the hiring contract
column7: Only once he completes the work of the whole hiring period
column8: Only after a court confirms the employer's default
column10: Per 5/2/7, an acceleration clause is allowed, but the employee does not own the prepaid instalments finally until he completes the work of the whole hiring period.

column4: Bank A signs a hiring contract on 1 March with an IT expert, agreeing that his work will start on 1 June. What is this arrangement called and is it valid?
column5: Forward hiring, and it is void
column6: Deferred hiring, valid only if paid in advance
column7: Conditional hiring, valid only with a guarantor
column8: Deferred hiring, and it is valid
column10: Per 4/8, the hiring period starts at signing unless the parties agree on a specific start date; this is known as deferred hiring (to be executed in the future).

column4: Bank A rents a consultant's service and then sub-hires it to a client with the contract's permission. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is sub-hiring permissible?
column5: Sub-hiring is a form of agency without pay
column6: Owning the service enables the employer to transfer it
column7: Services are not owned by the hirer, so no transfer of them occurs
column8: The client becomes a partner of the Bank
column10: The basis states sub-hiring is permissible because when the employer owns the service/work he becomes able to transfer it to someone else.

column4: A hiring contract for a private employee is silent on when pay is made. When is the pay due, and what may the employee do if it is delayed despite notice?
column5: Monthly by default; he must keep working
column6: At signing; he may then demand a late fee
column7: At expiry of the hiring period; he may then stop work
column8: At signing; he may then sue for damages only, but not stop work
column10: Per 7/2/1(a), absent agreement, pay is due after complete service or at expiry of the period for private employment; if delayed despite notice he may stop work.

column4: A provider delivers a future, well-described IT service that does not conform to the agreed specifications. What right does the employer have?
column5: Only terminate the contract with no other remedy
column6: Accept it, since delivery has occurred
column7: Only accept it with a reduced pay
column8: Reject it and insist on a conforming service
column10: Per 5/1/6, if the delivered service does not conform to what was agreed, the employer may reject it and insist on a service conforming to specifications.

column4: Bank A wants to sign a contract providing a specific, identified hospital service to a client, but it has not yet acquired that service. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if the Bank pays the hospital in advance for the service
column6: Impermissible until the Bank owns and can deliver the service
column7: Permissible since the client has promised to hire
column8: Permissible if the price is fixed in the contract
column10: Per 5/1/5, for a specific service the Institution must own it and be able to deliver it; it may not sign with the client before possessing it.
