column4: Company X hires a shared employee to print brochures, giving the work's type and specifications but no deadline. When must the work be done?
column5: Within the period set by normal practice
column6: The contract is void for lack of a period
column7: Within one month by default
column8: Whenever the employee chooses, without limit
column10: Per 4/4, the shared employee is informed of the work, its type and specifications; when no period is stated, resort is to normal practice.

column4: Bank A hires a contractor for a project and wants a clause making the contractor pay a set amount for delay in finishing the work. Is such a clause permissible?
column5: Yes, but only if the amount is paid to charity
column6: No; only the employer can be penalized for delay
column7: Yes, if set with regard to normal practice and justice
column8: No; penalties of this kind are Riba in all contracts
column10: Per 7/1/3, in hiring of persons a penalty code may require the employee to pay a specific amount for delay, determined by normal practice and justice.

column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is pay due even if the employer did not benefit from an employee who placed himself at his disposal?
column5: Pay in hiring is always due in full at signing
column6: The employee bears no duties at all under hiring
column7: The pay is in reality a donation from the employer, not a price
column8: The employee met the condition; the employer has no excuse
column10: The basis: the employee is entitled since he fulfilled the condition of being at the employer's disposal, while the employer has no excuse for not benefiting.

column4: Company X hires Ahmad personally to do a specific task. Without any clause or agreement allowing it, Company X hires out Ahmad's service to Company Y. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed, since Company X owns the hired service
column6: Not allowed unless the contract or the parties permit it
column7: Allowed, if Company Y pays a higher rate for it
column8: Allowed, as parallel hiring is always permitted in such cases
column10: Per 5/1/3, the employer may not hire out a specific person's service to a sub-employer unless the contract permits sub-hiring or the parties agree.

column4: A ship's crew hiring contract expires mid-voyage. Ending it now would cause harm. What does the standard provide?
column5: Hiring continues, at agreed pay or else normal pay
column6: The contract continues with no pay due
column7: The contract continues at the old pay only
column8: The contract ends and the crew is unpaid onward
column10: Per 8/2/3, hiring ends at expiry but remains when needed for a reasonable excuse or to avoid harm, for pay agreed or else the normal pay for similar services.

column4: Bank A signs a framework agreement with Company X setting general conditions for hiring its consultancy services over three years. How are individual hiring operations concluded?
column5: Only one hiring contract is allowed under a framework agreement
column6: Each operation is binding automatically once requested by Company X
column7: The framework agreement itself is the hiring contract for all operations
column8: By a separate contract, or offer and acceptance, for each operation
column10: Per 3/1, a framework agreement may set general conditions, but each operation needs a separate hiring contract or offer and acceptance referring to those conditions.

column4: A shared employee hired to design a website within 60 days fails to finish it in that period. What options does the employer have?
column5: Terminate the contract or agree on a new period
column6: Only claim a fixed penalty from the employee
column7: Keep the work and pay nothing
column8: Only extend the period without the employee's consent
column10: Per 4/10, when a shared employee fails to do the work in the specified period, the employer may terminate the contract or a new period can be agreed.

column4: An employee receives 'Arboun when signing a hiring contract. The employer later fails to execute the contract. What is the preferred treatment of the 'Arboun?
column5: The employee keeps all of it as profit
column6: The employee must return all of it to the employer, with no deduction
column7: The employee keeps only the part covering his actual harm
column8: It is split equally between the two parties
column10: Per 4/11, if the contract is not executed the 'Arboun goes to the employee, but he is preferably to take only the portion compensating his actual harm.

column4: Ahmad is hired and puts himself at Bank A's disposal from day one, but the Bank has not yet assigned him any task. Is his pay payable?
column5: No, until the Bank actually assigns him some task to perform
column6: Yes; making himself available makes the pay payable
column7: No, until the first task is completed
column8: Only half until a task is assigned
column10: Per 5/2/3, pay is payable on delivery of the work or making it available, i.e. when the employee is at the employer's disposal even if no task is assigned.

column4: An employee's pay was due in advance, but he agreed to wait two months. Later the employer claims a right to always pay two months late. What is the position?
column5: The delay was a respite he granted, not a right of the employer
column6: The pay is converted into deferred pay for the rest of the term
column7: The contract becomes void because its terms were changed
column8: The employer has now acquired a right to pay two months late
column10: Per 6/2, when the employee accepts a delay of pay due in advance, this is a respite he willingly granted and can by no means be considered a right of the employer.

column4: An employee wants the right to end the contract if the employer fails to pay one or more instalments of pay. May he stipulate this?
column5: Yes, but only after a court ruling
column6: Yes; this is Khiyar al-Naqd
column7: No; nonpayment only gives a right to sue
column8: No; only the employer may stipulate termination
column10: Per 8/2/3, the employee may stipulate termination when the employer fails or delays payment, or does not pay one or more instalments (Khiyar al-Naqd).

column4: Bank A wants its annual hiring contract with a consultant to renew automatically each year. What does the standard require for such spontaneous renewal?
column5: Nothing; all hiring contracts renew automatically each year
column6: A fresh signature at the start of each year
column7: A renewal clause, unless a party notifies its disinterest
column8: Approval of the Shari'ah Board each year
column10: Per 8/2/6, for spontaneous renewal a condition must state that the contract renews at a new period if neither party notifies the other of disinterest.

column4: Ahmad and Ali each own 25 goats that share the same facilities. How does the standard treat them for Zakah?
column5: As one herd only if in the same place
column6: As two herds, each paying half a goat
column7: As two herds, each below Nisab
column8: As one herd of 50 owned by one person
column10: Per 5/6/1, mixed ownership is recognized: animals owned by several persons are treated as owned by one when they share the same facilities.

column4: Company X owns goats that are mostly fed with purchased fodder for most of the year, kept for milk, not trade. Does the livestock Zakah rate apply?
column5: No; only animals for trade are Zakatable
column6: Yes, as goats are a Zakatable kind of livestock, whatever the way they are fed
column7: No; livestock rates apply only to free-grazing animals
column8: Yes, because they reach the Nisab
column10: Per 5/6, livestock are subject to the Zakah rate on livestock only if fed through free grazing most of the year.

column4: Company X's share capital and share issuance premium are shown under liabilities. Can they be deducted from Zakatable assets?
column5: Yes, as they are sources of funding that the company owes to its shareholders
column6: No; they are not debt obligations of the company
column7: Yes, only the issuance premium
column8: Yes, only the share capital
column10: Per 8/2/2, the capital account and issuance premium fund the company but are not its debt obligations, so they are not deductible from Zakatable assets.

column4: Company X has an interest-bearing loan with unpaid principal and unpaid interest outstanding. Can the unpaid interest be deducted from Zakatable assets?
column5: No; impermissible commitments are not recognized debts
column6: Yes, if it is actually paid within the year
column7: Yes, but only half of the unpaid interest
column8: Yes, as part of the company's current liabilities
column10: Per 6/2/4, unpaid interest is not deducted from Zakatable assets, because impermissible commitments cannot lead to a Shari'ah-recognizable debt.

column4: Bank A gives Zakah to a poor debtor, who then voluntarily uses it to repay his debt to the Bank, with no prior condition or collusion. Is this acceptable?
column5: No, unless a court approves it
column6: No, a debtor who receives Zakah may never use it to repay the payer
column7: Yes, even if it was a stated condition
column8: Yes, absent collusion or a pre-stated condition
column10: Per 10/1, Zakah recipients may repay their debts out of the Zakah they receive from their creditors, provided there is no collusion or pre-stated condition.

column4: Bank A's Zakah is due, but it wants to distribute it over a set schedule. For how long may it delay payment?
column5: Indefinitely, at its discretion
column6: For not more than one year
column7: Not at all; it must pay at once
column8: For up to three years
column10: Per 10/2, Zakah is to be paid when due but may be delayed for not more than one year for shortage of funds, a distribution schedule, or obvious interest.

column4: Company X harvests wheat twice a year and extracts minerals from a mine. Does the Hawl (Zakah year) apply to these?
column5: Yes for the wheat, no for minerals
column6: Yes for minerals, no for the wheat
column7: Yes; a full lunar year must pass for both
column8: No; harvesting and extraction are what matter
column10: Per 3/2/4, no consideration is given to the Hawl for agricultural products, since harvesting matters; for minerals and Rikaz, extraction is what matters.

column4: A customer paid Hamish Jiddiyyah to Bank A to confirm his binding promise to purchase in Murabahah. Who pays Zakah on this amount?
column5: Neither party, as it is a security
column6: The two parties equally
column7: The customer
column8: Bank A, as holder of the amount
column10: Per 5/1/5/1, Hamish Jiddiyyah is the advance paid by the client to confirm his binding pledge; Zakah on such amount shall be paid by the client.

column4: Company X grows two varieties of the same kind of dates on farms in different regions. Neither variety alone reaches 653 kg, but together they do. What applies?
column5: They are added together, so Zakah is due
column6: No Zakah, since varieties are never added
column7: No Zakah, since each farm is separate
column8: Zakah only on the larger variety
column10: Per 5/4/2, different types of the same kind are added together for Nisab; it makes no difference if the produce is in different geographical locations.

column4: Company X holds promissory notes from a buyer for goods sold on credit at a price including a mark-up. On what amount is Zakah paid?
column5: The cost of the goods only
column6: The mark-up only
column7: The face amount, including the mark-up
column8: The amount once the notes fall due
column10: Per 5/3/4/3, Zakah is paid on the principal of the debt (amount of the paper), including the increment added to the price, whether due or not.

column4: Company X bought goods for trade; the goods were earmarked for it after the contract, but it has not yet possessed them by the Zakah date. Who pays Zakah on them?
column5: Company X, the buyer, even before possession
column6: The seller, who remains the owner of the goods until delivery takes place
column7: The seller and the buyer equally
column8: Neither, until possession takes place
column10: Per 5/2/5, Zakah has to be paid on goods earmarked for the buyer after concluding the contract, even if he has not yet possessed them.

column4: Company X's goods in process have no known market value on the Zakah accrual date. How may they be valued?
column5: At the raw materials' purchase price only
column6: At cost
column7: At zero, as they are unfinished
column8: At the value of the finished goods
column10: Per 5/2/6/2, goods in process are valued at current market price on the day of Zakah accrual; if their market value cannot be known, they may be valued at cost.

column4: Company X paid 'Arboun to a seller. How is the 'Arboun treated in the Zakah of each party?
column5: Zakatable for the buyer; deducted by the seller
column6: Zakatable for both parties
column7: Not Zakatable for either party
column8: Deducted by the buyer; Zakatable for the seller
column10: Per 5/1/5/4, 'Arboun is deducted from the buyer's Zakatable assets, while the seller pays Zakah on it, since he gets it whether or not the contract is concluded.

column4: Company X has slow-moving trade goods and has made a provision for them. How are they treated for Zakah?
column5: Valued at market price as they are; the provision is not deducted
column6: Valued at cost, since they are slow-moving; the provision is deducted from their value
column7: Valued at market price; the provision is also deducted
column8: Excluded entirely from Zakatable assets
column10: Per 5/2/6/1 and 7/3/3, slow-moving goods may be valued at market price in their current form; an allocation for them is not deducted from Zakatable assets.

column4: Bank A sold a car in Murabahah for 120 (cost 100) on deferred payment; the full 120 is outstanding. On what amount does the Bank pay Zakah?
column5: 100, the cost of the car, with profit added on collection
column6: 20, the profit only, as the cost is not Zakatable until paid
column7: Nothing until collection
column8: 120, the total price including profit
column10: Per 5/3/4/9, Zakah on Murabahah debtors is payable on the total price including profits, as with cash debts under 5/3/1.

column4: Company X has set aside 10 million in cash, fully owned and controlled by it, to fund a future investment project. Is this cash Zakatable?
column5: No, not until the investment project starts
column6: Yes; allocation to a project does not affect full ownership
column7: Yes, but at half of the normal Zakah rate
column8: No; funds earmarked for a specific purpose are no longer fully owned by the company
column10: Per 3/2/1, full ownership exists even if the asset is allocated for a purpose other than settling debts, such as implementing investment projects.

column4: Company X trades in cattle, buying and selling them for profit. Which Zakah treatment applies to these cattle?
column5: Zakah on livestock only
column6: No Zakah, as they are not grazing
column7: Zakah on articles of trade only
column8: Both livestock and trade Zakah
column10: Per 5/2/3 and 5/6/2, when articles of trade are livestock or produce, they are subject to Zakah on articles of trade only, valued at selling market price.

column4: A Zakah fund wants to invest Zakah money in a project. Which condition applies under the standard?
column5: The project must remain owned by the Institution
column6: Only if the return is guaranteed by the Bank
column7: Only in projects run by the payer itself
column8: Only after the urgent needs of recipients are met
column10: Per 10/4, Zakah may be invested if need arises, after meeting recipients' urgent needs, with safeguards, and owned by recipients or supervised by the Shari'ah body.

column4: Ahmad receives a monthly salary. At what point is Zakah due on his salary income?
column5: Never, as salaries are exempt from Zakah
column6: On the portion that remains unexpended for a whole year
column7: On his annual gross salary at year end
column8: On each salary payment at the time of its receipt by Ahmad
column10: Per 3/1/3, Zakah is not due on wages and salaries upon receipt, but on that portion which remains unexpended for a whole year.

column4: Company X keeps laying hens to sell their eggs. How are the hens treated for Zakah?
column5: Like Mustaghallat: no Zakah on them, only on unexpended income
column6: As livestock, at the rates applicable to goats, since hens are kept for their produce
column7: Fully exempt, together with all of their income, as they are a means of production
column8: As articles of trade, valued at market price at the end of the Zakah year
column10: Per 5/6/7, Zakah is not due on chickens acquired for production; they are treated like Mustaghallat (productive assets) under item 4/2.

column4: Company X made an advance payment to a contractor on signing a construction contract. Is this advance part of Company X's Zakatable assets?
column5: Yes, at half its value
column6: Yes, until the work is delivered
column7: No, since it is no longer owned by Company X
column8: Yes, as a receivable from the contractor, repayable if the contract is not performed
column10: Per 5/3/4/5, no Zakah is paid on advance payments on signing contracts, since they are no longer owned by the Institution.

column4: Ahmad's only Zakatable wealth is trade goods. Which Nisab is widely recognized as applicable to articles of trade?
column5: The Nisab of gold: 85 grams of pure gold
column6: The Nisab of silver: 595 grams of pure silver
column7: 40 units, as for goats
column8: 653 kilograms, as for produce
column10: Per 3/2/2, the gold Nisab is 85 grams of pure gold; the Nisab widely recognized as applicable to articles of trade is that of gold.

column4: Company X holds cash in US dollars while its financial statements are in a local currency. How is Zakah on this cash determined?
column5: At the historical rate when the dollars were bought
column6: At the average rate of the year
column7: In local currency at the exchange rate on the due date
column8: Only in US dollars, without conversion
column10: Per 5/1/1, Zakah on foreign currency cash is paid from its local currency equivalent at the prevailing exchange rate on the date Zakah is due.

column4: Bank A covers a documentary credit for importing trade goods: it paid opening expenses and amounts retained by intermediary banks. What is Zakatable before the goods are owned?
column5: Neither, until the goods arrive
column6: The amounts retained for the credit, not the expenses
column7: Only the expenses of opening the credit
column8: The expenses and the retained amounts, as both are paid by the Bank for the goods
column10: Per 5/2/6/7, Zakah is paid on the amounts retained for the credit, not the expenses; once the goods are owned, Zakah is on their market value.

column4: Ahmad rents farmland from Company Y and grows wheat on it. Who pays the Zakah on the wheat?
column5: Neither, as the land is rented
column6: Company Y, the landowner
column7: Both equally
column8: Ahmad, the tenant
column10: Per 5/4/9, Zakah on produce of rented land is paid by the tenant; in Muzara'ah or Musaqat it is paid by the two parties proportionately.

column4: Company X, legally bound to pay Zakah, made a net loss this year, but its assets still exceed its liabilities. Is Zakah due?
column5: Yes, but only on the reserves and retained profits
column6: Yes; losses do not prevent Zakah unless liabilities absorb assets
column7: No; Zakah is due only in a year in which a profit is made on capital
column8: No; Zakah is levied on the income statement, not assets
column10: Per 2/3/2, the Institution need not make profits to pay Zakah; losses do not prevent it, except when liabilities absorb all its assets.

column4: Bank A sold goods in Salam and received the Salam capital, but has not yet delivered the goods. How is this treated in Bank A's Zakah?
column5: No effect until the goods are delivered
column6: Only the profit portion is deducted
column7: The Salam capital is fully Zakatable as cash held by the Bank, whatever its obligation
column8: The Salam capital is deducted from Zakatable assets
column10: Per 6/3/3, goods sold through Salam and not yet delivered are a debt, so the amount of Salam capital is deducted from the Zakatable assets.

column4: A non-profit educational institution with no specific owner, funded by allocated public property (Irsad), makes a surplus this year. Is Zakah due?
column5: Yes, on its annual surplus at the rate of 2.5%, like a trading company
column6: Yes, on the market value of the allocated property
column7: No; it is exempt like charitable Waqf, even with profits
column8: Yes, because it made a profit this year, as profit makes any institution Zakatable
column10: Per 3/1/7, the exemption of charitable Waqf also applies to trust funds and Irsad for non-profit institutions with no specific owner, even if they make profits.

column4: Ahmad has a long-term investment account at Bank A from which withdrawals are restricted. Must he pay Zakah on it?
column5: Yes, on its balance and profits despite the restriction
column6: No, since he cannot withdraw from the account until the term of the investment ends
column7: Yes, but only on the profits earned in the year
column8: No, not until the deposit term comes to an end
column10: Per 5/1/3/2(a), account owners pay Zakah on investment balances and profits, short or long term, even if drawing from the account is restricted.

column4: Company X, a textile trader, faces a severe trade recession and has little cash. May it pay its Zakah on trade goods in kind?
column5: Yes, at any time and with no condition
column6: No; Zakah on trade goods may be paid only in cash, as it is assessed at market value
column7: Yes, if the interest of Zakah recipients is achieved
column8: Only with the regulator's approval
column10: Per 5/2/4, Zakah on articles of trade is in principle paid in cash, but in a trade recession it can be paid in kind if recipients' interest is achieved.

column4: Bank A's board of directors decides the Bank should pay Zakah, but there is no Zakah law, no clause in the articles, and no general assembly resolution. Is the Bank committed to pay Zakah directly?
column5: No; the duty then lies with shareholders and account holders
column6: Yes, if the Shari'ah Board approves it
column7: Yes; every Islamic bank must pay Zakah directly
column8: Yes; a board decision is sufficient to commit the Bank directly
column10: Per 2/2/1 and 2/2/5, the Institution pays Zakah directly only under an enforceable law, its articles, or a general assembly resolution; otherwise the shareholders pay.

column4: A herder owns 45 free-grazing cows for a full year. What Zakah is due?
column5: One Tabee'a (in its second year)
column6: Two Tabee'a
column7: Nothing, below the Nisab
column8: One Musinnah (in its third year)
column10: Per the cow table in 11/2, 40 to 59 cows require one Musinnah (at the 3rd year of age); 30 to 39 require one Tabee'a.

column4: Company X keeps a current account with Bank B and (against Shari'ah) receives interest on it. How should it treat this for Zakah?
column5: Pay Zakah on the principal plus all the interest
column6: Pay Zakah on the principal and donate all the interest
column7: Pay Zakah on the interest only and keep the principal
column8: Pay no Zakah at all on a current account balance
column10: Per 5/1/3/1, Zakah is paid from current accounts with other Institutions; any interest (prohibited) is donated entirely to charitable purposes.

column4: Bank A holds a bad debt for four years and finally collects it. How much Zakah is due on it?
column5: Zakah for one year after collection
column6: Zakah for all four years, paid at once after collection of the debt
column7: No Zakah, as it was doubtful
column8: Zakah for two years
column10: Per 5/3/1, for bad and doubtful debts the Institution does not have to pay Zakah except for one year after their collection.

column4: Bank A owns its head office, computer software, and spare parts kept in its warehouse for operations. Which of these are Zakatable?
column5: Only the spare parts kept in the warehouse
column6: None of these operational assets is Zakatable
column7: Only the software, as an intangible asset
column8: All three, at their market value
column10: Per 4/1, Zakah is not due on operational fixed assets, intangible assets like software, or operational movable assets such as spare parts, even if warehoused.

column4: Company X inherited land, did not buy it, and now offers it for sale. Is the land an article of trade for Zakah?
column5: No; land is always a fixed asset
column6: No; trade goods must be acquired by purchase
column7: Yes, but only after a sale contract is signed
column8: Yes; the intention to offer it for sale suffices
column10: Per 5/2/1, articles of trade include anything offered for sale, whether acquired by buying or otherwise; the mere intention to offer it for sale is sufficient.

column4: Company X cannot tell which of its debts financed Zakatable assets. Zakatable assets are 40% of total assets and total debts are 10 million. What is deducted?
column5: 6 million
column6: Nothing
column7: 4 million
column8: 10 million
column10: Per 6/2/3, when it is difficult to know the debt from Zakatable assets, use their ratio to total assets; at 40%, 40% of total debts is deducted.

column4: Company X holds conventional bonds bought at 1 million that pay interest. How is Zakah applied?
column5: No Zakah, as bonds are prohibited
column6: Zakah on the 1 million cost; all interest donated to charity
column7: Zakah on the bonds' cost plus the interest, which the company may keep as income
column8: Zakah on the interest only
column10: Per 5/1/4/1, Zakah is paid on the principal of the bond (its cost), while the entire interest is donated for charitable purposes.

column4: A herder owns 150 free-grazing goats for a full year. What Zakah is due?
column5: One goat for every 40
column6: Three goats
column7: Two goats
column8: One goat
column10: Per the goat table in 11/3, 40 to 120 goats require 1 goat and 121 to 200 goats require 2 goats.

column4: A farm owns 50 camels used only for ploughing and irrigation. Are they part of its Zakatable assets?
column5: No; working animals are not Zakatable
column6: Yes, at the camel livestock rates
column7: Yes, if they reach the Nisab
column8: Yes, as articles of trade
column10: Per 5/6/3, working animals, such as those used in land plowing, irrigation and carrying, are not part of Zakatable assets.

column4: Bank A owns 70% of Subsidiary S, which does not pay its own Zakah. How is Zakah on Subsidiary S handled?
column5: Bank A pays all of S's Zakah, since it controls the subsidiary
column6: Bank A pays nothing; S's managers pay it
column7: Bank A pays Zakah on 70% of S's share price
column8: S's Zakah is computed alone; Bank A pays 70% of it
column10: Per 4/2/5, the subsidiary's Zakah is calculated independently; the mother pays its proportion and the rest falls on the other parties (minority rights).

column4: Company X failed to pay Zakah for several past years. Does that past Zakah lapse due to the passage of time?
column5: No; Zakah does not cease by prescription
column6: Yes, after one year, as the Zakah year has passed
column7: Yes, if the company was unaware
column8: Yes, after three years, as the right of the recipients lapses by prescription
column10: Per 10/5, Zakah does not cease to be valid by prescription.

column4: Bank A is not legally committed to pay Zakah, so Zakah is the responsibility of its shareholders and investment account holders. What must the Bank do?
column5: Deduct the Zakah from dividends without any disclosure to holders
column6: Nothing, as Zakah is a private matter
column7: Indicate the Zakah payable per share or per account balance
column8: Pay the Zakah anyway from retained profits
column10: Per 2/2/5, when Zakah is the shareholders' and account holders' responsibility, the Institution has to indicate the amount payable per share or per investment account balance.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company T asks whether Zakah is payable by its policyholders' insurance portfolio, which has an independent financial liability. What is the answer?
column5: Yes, at 2.5% of its surplus, as the portfolio is treated as a separate company
column6: Yes, on contributions received
column7: Yes, but only on investment income
column8: No Zakah is payable by the insurance portfolio
column10: Per 5/3/5, the contributions form a fund with independent liability given as donation, not returnable; so no Zakah is payable by the insurance portfolio.

column4: Company X wants to discharge its Zakah by writing off debts owed by its poor debtors. What is the ruling?
column5: Allowed, with the Shari'ah Board's approval
column6: Not allowed; relieving debtors does not discharge Zakah
column7: Allowed, if the debtors are eligible recipients of Zakah and cannot pay
column8: Allowed, up to the amount of Zakah due
column10: Per 10/1, the Zakah payer cannot discharge his Zakah by relieving his debtors, though recipients may repay debts from Zakah absent collusion or precondition.

column4: According to the Shari'ah basis of the standard, why is it impossible to imagine a debt arising from commodities purchased through Salam?
column5: The capital (price) has to be paid in advance
column6: The seller bears all the risk until delivery
column7: Salam goods are always exempt from Zakah
column8: The goods are delivered at the time of contract
column10: The Shari'ah basis states it is impossible to imagine a debt from commodities bought through Salam, because the capital (price) has to be paid in advance.

column4: Company X spends heavily on irrigation channels and on delivering the Zakah produce to recipients. Which cost may be deducted from Zakatable assets?
column5: The irrigation channel expenses
column6: Each of the two costs equally
column7: Neither cost
column8: The cost of delivery to recipients
column10: Per 5/4/7 and 5/4/8, irrigation and land development expenses are not deducted, while the cost of delivery to recipients is deducted.

column4: Ahmad holds Ijarah Sukuk. On what basis does he pay Zakah?
column5: Always on the Sukuk's face value
column6: Only on the periodic distributions received
column7: On the basis of the Sukuk's underlying assets
column8: On the market value regardless of assets
column10: Per 5/1/4/2, owners of investment Sukuk pay Zakah on the basis of the underlying assets of these Sukuk, as indicated in the standard.

column4: Bank A sets up a Zakah fund and disburses Zakah directly. Whose clearance is required for this, and what reporting is needed?
column5: The central bank's, with a monthly report
column6: The Shari'ah Board's, with an annual report on disbursements
column7: The external auditor's, with a quarterly report on the disbursements
column8: The board of directors', with no further report
column10: Per 2/2/4, establishing a Zakah fund and disbursing Zakah require Shari'ah Board clearance, with a comprehensive annual report on Zakah disbursements.

column4: Company X chose to postpone Zakah on a sound outstanding debt until it is collected. When it collects the debt after three years, what must it pay?
column5: Zakah only on the profit component
column6: Zakah for one year only
column7: No Zakah, as it chose to postpone
column8: Zakah for the whole past period
column10: Per 5/3/2, the Institution can postpone Zakah on outstanding debts until collection, but on collection it has to pay Zakah for the whole past period.

column4: Company X owes 3 million for trade goods bought on credit and 5 million for a factory machine bought on credit. Which debt is deducted from the Zakah base?
column5: The 5 million for the machine
column6: The 3 million for trade goods
column7: The two debts in full
column8: Neither debt
column10: Per 6/2/1 and 6/2/2, debts for Zakatable trade assets are deducted from the Zakah base, while debts for non-Zakatable fixed assets are not.

column4: Bank A holds shares in Company Z for retention (Nama'), not trading. Company Z reports its Zakatable assets per share. How does Bank A pay Zakah?
column5: On the market value of the shares at the end of the Zakah year
column6: On the cost of the shares
column7: On Company Z's Zakatable assets per share
column8: On dividends received only
column10: Per 4/2/4, for shares held for retention, Zakah is levied on the Zakatable assets per share if known; otherwise estimated; if none, on remaining net income.

column4: A first-instance court orders Company X to pay indemnity, and Company X appeals. It books a provision. When can it be deducted from Zakatable assets?
column5: Once a final verdict makes it due for payment
column6: Never, as it is a provision
column7: Immediately upon the initial verdict, since the court has already ordered payment
column8: When the appeal is filed
column10: Per 7/3/7, the indemnity provision is not deducted from Zakatable assets until it becomes due for payment by virtue of a final verdict.

column4: Ahmad paid a cash security for an electricity connection. He could not invest it, and it is refunded years later. When and how is Zakah paid?
column5: Every year while it is held
column6: Never, as it is a security
column7: On refund, for all past years
column8: On refund, for one year
column10: Per 5/1/5/3, Zakah on cash security for services such as electricity is paid by its owner on refund for one year, unless he was enabled to invest it.

column4: Bank A calculates its Zakah base by the net assets method. Which of the following is deducted from its Zakatable assets?
column5: Rights of holders of non-restricted investment accounts
column6: The paid-up capital and share premium of the Bank
column7: The statutory and voluntary reserves of the Bank
column8: The provision for slow-moving and perishable goods
column10: Per 2/1/1, the Zakah base equals Zakatable assets minus current liabilities, rights of non-restricted investment account holders, minority, Waqf and charitable rights, etc.

column4: Company X harvests 500 kg of dates and 400 kg of wheat from its farms. What is the Zakah position, given the 653 kg Nisab?
column5: Zakah on 900 kg, since crops of different kinds are added together to reach the Nisab
column6: Zakah on both, as the total exceeds Nisab
column7: No Zakah; different kinds cannot be added together
column8: Zakah on the dates only
column10: Per 5/4/1 and 5/4/2, the Nisab is 653 kg; types of the same kind may be added, but different kinds of produce cannot; each kind has its own Nisab.

column4: A bakery making bread for sale holds year-end stocks of flour and of cleaning materials and fuel. Which are Zakatable?
column5: Both, at their cost
column6: The flour, at market value before manufacturing
column7: Neither, as they are not finished goods
column8: The fuel and cleaning materials only, as consumables used up in the business
column10: Per 5/2/8, raw materials that remain components of goods made for trade are valued at market value; supporting materials such as fuel and cleaning materials are not.

column4: Company X bought fertilizers on deferred payment for its farm. How are they treated in calculating Zakah on the produce?
column5: Not Zakatable, and deductible since obtained through debt
column6: Zakatable as part of the farm's current assets, whether bought on credit or in cash
column7: Deductible from the Zakah base even if paid in cash
column8: Not Zakatable, and never deductible in any case
column10: Per 5/4/5, fertilizers and insecticides are not Zakatable assets and are not deducted from the Zakah base unless they were obtained through debt.

column4: Bank A calculates Zakah on its cash and trade assets using the solar year instead of the lunar year. Which rate applies in a normal (non-leap) year?
column10: Per 3/2/4, the Zakah year for cash and commercial assets is lunar (354 days); if the solar year is adopted, the rate becomes 2.577%.

column4: An expert estimates (Khars) Company X's ripe grapes. What may be deducted and left to the owner before Zakah is assessed?
column5: Nothing at all
column6: One fourth or one third
column7: One half of the estimated produce, left to the owner
column8: One tenth, which is the Zakah rate for rain-fed crops
column10: Per 5/4/3, Khars can be used when produce is ripe; one fourth or one third can be left to the owner, the rest being Zakatable after drying.

column4: A government ministry holds large public funds and runs an insurance fund for public institutions. Is Zakah due on them?
column5: Yes, if the funds are invested for profit
column6: Yes, but only on the insurance fund
column7: No; Zakah is not obligatory on public wealth
column8: Yes, at 2.5% of their year-end balance
column10: Per 3/1/5, Zakah is not obligatory on public wealth (public sector) or the insurance funds of public institutions.

column4: Bank A's Shari'ah Board decides to give all of this year's Zakah to the poor and debtors only. Must Zakah cover all eight heads?
column5: No, but it must cover at least four
column6: Yes, in equal shares to all eight heads, as stated in the Qur'anic verse
column7: Yes, at least one share to each head
column8: No; it may be confined to some of the heads
column10: Per 10/8, Zakah should not necessarily cover all eight heads of disbursement; it can permissibly be confined to some of them.

column4: Company X holds statutory and voluntary reserves that appear under liabilities. How are they treated under the net assets method?
column5: Only voluntary reserves are deducted
column6: Not deducted; they are Zakatable as owned by the company
column7: Deducted only if required by law
column8: Deducted, as they appear under liabilities in the balance sheet of the company
column10: Per 8/2/1, both statutory and voluntary reserves are not debts in Shari'ah and are not deducted; being owned, they are Zakatable under the net assets method.

column4: Bank A wants to send its Zakah from its home country to famine victims abroad. Who judges whether this transfer serves an obvious interest?
column5: The external auditor
column6: The central bank, as the supervisor of the Institution
column7: The Shari'ah board of the Institution
column8: The board of directors of the Institution, as the governing body
column10: Per 10/9, Zakah funds can be transferred from the place of payment to another place due to an obvious interest judged by the Shari'ah boards of the institutions.

column4: Bank A manages investment accounts as Mudarib. On what does the Bank itself pay Zakah regarding these accounts?
column5: Only its share of profit or commissions, as cash assets
column6: The balances plus profits of all accounts
column7: The full balances of all accounts, as they are liabilities of the Bank towards the holders
column8: Nothing at all
column10: Per 5/1/3/2(a), investment accounts are a trust (Amanah) for the managing Institution, which pays Zakah only on its share of profits or commissions.

column4: Company X holds real estate prepared for trade, bought at 5 million and now expected to sell for 7 million when Zakah is due. At what value is it assessed?
column5: 6 million, the average of cost and market
column6: The lower of cost or market value
column7: 5 million, its historical cost, as the gain is not yet realized
column8: 7 million, its expected cash (selling market) value
column10: Per 2/1/2 and 5/2/2, assets prepared for trade are assessed at their expected cash value (selling market value) when Zakah is due, not at cost.

column4: Company X prepares goods for export under a documentary credit in its favour. How are the amounts retained for the credit treated?
column5: Zakatable at half their value until shipment
column6: Zakatable in full as receivables of the company, since they are due from the issuing bank
column7: Neither Zakatable nor deductible, as not yet possessed
column8: Deductible from Zakatable assets as a liability
column10: Per 5/2/6/8, amounts retained for an export credit are neither Zakatable nor deductible since not yet possessed; goods still held remain Zakatable.

column4: Company X paid a bid security to a ministry and could not invest it. It was refunded after three years. How much Zakah does Company X owe on it?
column5: Zakah for two years
column6: Zakah for one year
column7: Zakah for all three years
column8: No Zakah at all
column10: Per 5/1/5/2, the owner pays Zakah annually unless he was not enabled to invest it before refund; when several years elapse before refund, Zakah for one year is paid.

column4: Company X has trade goods in its Zakah base at market value and has booked a provision for decline in their value. Is the provision deducted?
column5: No, since the goods are already at market value
column6: Yes, but only up to 50% of the provision
column7: Yes, if the provision is approved by auditors
column8: Yes, in full as a liability of the company
column10: Per 7/2/2, as Zakah uses market value, provisions on current assets are not deducted, unless assets are valued at book value above exchange value.

column4: A family Waqf (al-Waqf al-Ahli) pays income to Ahmad's children; part of the income remains unspent at year end. Who pays Zakah on it?
column5: The Waqf itself, on the whole property and all of its income at year end
column6: The beneficiaries, on the unexpended income at year end
column7: The Waqf superintendent, on the gross income
column8: Nobody, as all Waqf is exempt from Zakah
column10: Per 3/1/6, charitable Waqf is exempt; for family Waqf, the beneficiaries pay Zakah at year end on the portion of Waqf income that remains unexpended.

column4: Company X, a private firm, extracts oil it owns under a concession. Mining stops for an abnormally long period and then resumes. What applies?
column5: No Zakah, as minerals belong to the state
column6: Rate 20% as Rikaz, with no Nisab
column7: Nisab combines output before and after; rate 10%
column8: Nisab is assessed afresh from resumption; rate 2.5%
column10: Per 5/5/2, minerals' Zakah rate is 2.5%; if extraction is suspended for an abnormal period, Nisab assessment starts when extraction resumes.

column4: Bank A holds non-trading shares and makes an allocation for decline in their value. Can this allocation be deducted from Zakatable assets?
column5: No allocation for such deterioration may be deducted
column6: Yes, if the decline in value is judged permanent
column7: Yes, but only up to half of the decline in value
column8: Yes, in full, as it is treated as a liability
column10: Per 4/2/4 and 7/3/2, for shares owned for non-trading purposes, no allocation for deterioration in value should be made from Zakatable assets.

column4: A perfume trader's bottles and boxes are not sold separately, but they add to the value of the perfume sold. Are they included in valuing the goods?
column5: No, packing materials are never part of the goods being valued, whatever their effect on value
column6: No, because they are not sold separately
column7: Yes, because they increase the value of the goods
column8: Yes, but at cost rather than market value
column10: Per 5/2/10, packing materials not prepared for trade separately are excluded from valuation, but if such materials increase the value of the goods they should be included.

column4: A farm owned by Company Y is fully irrigated by pumps at the company's cost. What Zakah rate applies to its produce?
column5: 7.5% (three quarters of the tenth)
column6: 5% (half of the tenth)
column7: 2.5% as for trade goods
column8: 10% (one tenth)
column10: Per 3/3 and 5/4/1, the rate is 10% for non-irrigated lands, 5% for irrigated lands and 7.5% for partially irrigated lands.

column4: Bank A has a cash debt owed by a solvent client, payable in two years. Is Zakah due on it this year?
column5: Yes, but only on the profit portion of the debt
column6: No, not until the debt is actually collected, since Zakah is due only on cash in hand
column7: Yes, annually, whether due or not, as it will surely be paid
column8: No, not until the debt actually falls due, since the client has no obligation to pay before then
column10: Per 5/3/1, Zakah is due annually on cash debts owed to the Institution, whether due or not, since it will certainly receive them.

column4: The regulator requires Bank A to keep a legal deposit for its licence; the Bank can neither withdraw nor invest it. It is refunded after five years. What Zakah is due?
column5: Zakah for one year, at the time of refund
column6: Zakah every year as it is owned
column7: Zakah for all five years, due at the time of refund of the deposit
column8: No Zakah, as it was restricted
column10: Per 5/3/4/8, if the Institution was not enabled to invest the legal deposit, it pays Zakah on it for only one year at the time of refund.

column4: A client withholds 5% of contract payments as retention from Bank A until the project is complete; the Bank cannot invest it. How is Zakah treated?
column5: No Zakah at any time
column6: Zakah for all years on receipt
column7: Zakah every year while it is held, as it remains owned by the Bank
column8: No Zakah while held; one year's Zakah on receipt
column10: Per 5/3/4/4, if the Institution cannot invest retention amounts it pays no Zakah on them; on receipt it pays Zakah for only one year.

column4: A herder owns 30 free-grazing camels for a full year. What Zakah is due?
column5: Four goats
column6: One Bint Makhad camel (in its second year)
column7: Six goats
column8: One Bint Labun camel (in its third year)
column10: Per the camel table in 11/1, 25 to 35 camels require one Bint Makhad camel (at the second year of age).

column4: Company X has an end-of-service benefits provision; part is due for payment this year but unpaid. What may be deducted from Zakatable assets?
column5: Half of the provision
column6: The entire provision balance, as it is a liability of the company towards its employees
column7: Nothing in any case
column8: Only the part that is paid or due this year
column10: Per 7/3/6, end-of-service provisions are not deducted as merely allocated; they are deducted only when actually paid or when due in the current year.

column4: Bank A paid Salam capital to a farmer for wheat it bought for trading, not yet received. What Zakah treatment applies?
column5: Zakah on the wheat's expected market value
column6: No Zakah until the wheat is received
column7: Bank A pays Zakah on the Salam capital
column8: The farmer alone pays and the Bank pays nothing
column10: Per 5/3/4/10, the Institution pays Zakah on Salam capital if the goods were purchased for trading; the seller's received capital is Zakatable as his cash.

column4: Bank A agrees to act as agent for paying Zakah on behalf of some of its investment account holders. What is required?
column5: Funds must be available or submitted by the principals
column6: The Bank must pay from its own funds first
column7: The Bank may deduct Zakah from any client's account on its own
column8: The Bank must get a court order for each payment
column10: Per 2/2/2, when the Institution accepts agency for payment of Zakah for equity or account holders, funds should be available or submitted by the principals.

column4: Bank A included a full 100 receivable in Zakatable assets; 30 of it is doubtful and covered by an allocation. What may be deducted?
column5: Half the doubtful part
column6: The doubtful part of 30
column7: The full 100 debt
column8: Nothing, allocations are never deducted
column10: Per 5/3/2, when a debt is partially doubtful and an allocation is made, the doubtful part may be deducted if the total debt was initially included in Zakatable assets.

column4: Company X's trade goods were worth 10 million on the Zakah due date, and 9 million on the later date it actually paid Zakah. Which value applies?
column5: 9 million, the price on the date on which the Zakah was actually paid
column6: 9.5 million, the average of the two
column7: 10 million, the price at the date of Zakah accrual
column8: The lower of cost or market value
column10: Per 5/2/2, if prices change between the dates of accrual and payment of Zakah, the price at the date of Zakah accrual is adopted.

column4: Company X is building a hotel to operate (not to sell). During construction, part of it generates rental income. How is Zakah treated?
column5: Zakah on the unexpended income, added to Zakatable assets
column6: Zakah on the market value of the whole project
column7: No Zakah of any kind until construction ends
column8: Zakah on the full construction cost to date, as the hotel is still an asset under development
column10: Per 4/2/3, for capital projects not for trading, Zakah is due on the unexpended part of income they generate, added to Zakatable assets at year end.

column4: Company X received rent in advance for services not yet provided, and separately received earnest money on a sale whose goods are undelivered. Which is deducted?
column5: Neither of the two amounts
column6: Each of the two amounts in full
column7: The earnest money received on the sale
column8: The prepaid income for undelivered services
column10: Per 6/3/9, prepaid income for undelivered services is deducted since not finally owned; earnest money on exchange contracts is owned and not deducted.

column4: Company X receives a government cash subsidy for farming and free use of land and equipment. What is included in its Zakah base?
column5: The land and equipment only
column6: Both the cash and the land and equipment
column7: The cash subsidy only
column8: Neither of them
column10: Per 5/4/10, cash subsidies are included in the Zakah base as liquid assets, whereas free-of-charge land and equipment should not be included.

column4: Company X owns a building leased to tenants (Mustaghallat), not held for trade. How is Zakah applied?
column5: No Zakah at all, either on the building or on its rent
column6: Zakah on the full gross rent at the time it is received
column7: Zakah on the building's market value at each year end, as it is an asset of the company
column8: No Zakah on the building; Zakah on unexpended rent at year end
column10: Per 3/1/4 and 4/2/1, leased assets not for trade are not Zakatable; the unexpended rental is added to other Zakatable assets at year end.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: Bank A and a client mutually agree to end a Murabahah facility early. A trainee calls this a contingent incident. Is he right?
column5: No; it is a contingent incident only if a court approves the ending
column6: No; termination by mutual consent is not a contingent incident
column7: Yes; any early ending of a commitment, however it arises, is a contingent incident
column8: Yes, provided the termination causes harm to one of the parties
column10: Per 1 and 2, contingent incidents are sudden events with significant influence on commitments; termination on mutual consent or by a party's contractual right is distinct.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: After signing an Ijarah contract, the lessee claims his consent was defective from the very time of signing, though its effect appeared later. How does the standard on contingent incidents treat this?
column5: A defect of will, outside the standard, not a contingent incident
column6: It is a contingent incident that necessitates amending the rent
column7: It is an external reason that terminates the contract automatically
column8: It is a contingent incident because its impact appeared after signing
column10: Per 1 and 2, defects of will exist from the time of signing even if their impact occurs later; they differ from contingent incidents and are excluded from the standard.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: What is the Shari'ah basis for amending a commitment to absorb the impact of contingent incidents rather than ending it?
column5: Contracts are binding only until conditions change after signing
column6: A commitment may always be ended once either party suffers any harm at all
column7: Termination is the only way to remove harm under all Fiqh schools
column8: Muslims should seek appropriate disposition, not rush to termination
column10: Per the Shari'ah basis, amendment rests on striving for appropriate disposition without rushing to termination, a rule adopted by the various schools of Fiqh.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: A buyer finds that the sold asset was seized unlawfully and belongs to another person, so the commitment is ineffective. What is the Shari'ah basis for this?
column5: Possession for a long period always confers ownership
column6: The seller's good faith validates the sale of the asset
column7: Unlawful seizure is not recognised as a basis of ownership
column8: The buyer's Qabd cures any defect in the seller's title
column10: Per the basis, unlawful seizure is unrecognizable as a basis of ownership: 'An extorter is indebted with what he takes until he returns it back'.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: On which evidence are the rulings on Jawa'ih (calamities) based?
column5: The Hadith forbidding Bay' al-Sinin and permitting discounts on calamities
column6: The view of Al-Shatibi that Shari'ah has no room for futility
column7: The Hadith that an extorter is indebted with what he takes until he returns it
column8: The consensus that a lessor may cancel a lease for any excuse
column10: Per the basis, Jawa'ih rulings rest on the Hadith in which the Prophet forbade Bay' al-Sinin and permitted value discounts on calamities.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: A commitment becomes null and void when its fulfillment has become useless. On what principle is this ruling based?
column5: The prohibition of Bay' al-Sinin for agricultural produce
column6: Fulfilling a useless commitment is futility, alien to Shari'ah
column7: A commitment lapses whenever its performance becomes costly
column8: Every contract is voidable whenever one party loses interest in it
column10: Per the Shari'ah basis, implementing a useless commitment is an act of futility, and there is no room for futility in Shari'ah legislation, as Al-Shatibi indicated.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: Bank A buys a fleet of vehicles, then discovers that part of the fleet is owned by a third party, not the seller. What is the effect?
column5: That part is void; the Bank may accept the rest or terminate
column6: The whole contract is void and the Bank cannot keep any vehicle
column7: The contract stands in full and the Bank must claim from the third party
column8: The Bank must accept the rest at the full price without any option
column10: Per 5/3, if the object is partly owned by someone else, the commitment in that part is void; the committing party may accept the rest or terminate due to fragmentation.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: A sudden frost, not caused by any human act and unavoidable even if foreseen, destroys part of fruits sold to Bank A. What is the effect under the rules on Jawa'ih?
column5: The Bank pays the full price because the fruits were already sold to it
column6: The seller must replace the fruits with produce from another farm
column7: The price is discounted in proportion to the damage in the produce
column8: The whole sale is cancelled and the full price is refunded
column10: Per 5/5, Jawa'ih are non-human incidents that cannot be avoided even if known; in sale of fruits they lead to discounting the price in proportion to the damage.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, ownership cannot be transferred for a reason the lessee cannot stop. The rent was set above the normal rent of similar property. What applies?
column5: The lessor must transfer ownership despite the obstacle
column6: The rent above the normal rent of similar property is dropped
column7: All rent paid is refunded and the lessee pays nothing for use
column8: The lessee loses all rent paid, as he had full use of the property during the lease
column10: Per 5/5, in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek the rent exceeding normal rent of similar property is dropped when ownership cannot be transferred for a reason the lessee cannot stop.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: In an Ijarah, an incidental excuse arises causing the lessee abnormal harm, but the acceptability of his excuse is doubtful. How is the issue resolved?
column5: By continuing the lease with no possibility of termination
column6: By the lessor's sole decision, as owner of the leased asset
column7: By automatic termination of the Ijarah at the lessee's request
column8: By mutual agreement or by resort to law
column10: Per 5/4, the harmed party may terminate for abnormal harm, and an obvious excuse permits termination; a doubtful excuse is resolved by mutual agreement or by law.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: Company X is committed to deliver goods to Bank A. The goods are totally destroyed in Company X's warehouse before delivery to the Bank, with no act of the Bank. Who bears the loss?
column5: Both parties equally, since the loss was not caused by either of them
column6: Bank A, because ownership passed to it upon signing the contract
column7: Company X, the committed party, as delivery had not yet taken place
column8: An insurer only; neither party bears any loss in such a case
column10: Per 5/2, if the object of commitment is damaged before delivery to the committing party, the loss is borne by the committed party.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: Bank A agreed to lease imported equipment to a client in an Ijarah, but the State then bans import of such equipment. How does the standard classify this incident?
column5: A Jawa'ih incident requiring a discount of the full rent amount
column6: A defect of will existing at signing, which renders the whole lease void
column7: A matter outside the standard because it was caused by the State
column8: A contingency requiring amendment, not termination, of the contract
column10: Per 4/3, prevention of importation of goods for a Murabahah or Ijarah is an amendment-type contingency; actual harm is removed by reconciliation, arbitration or law.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: After Bank A signs a Murabahah contract, the government imposes a new customs duty on the imported goods. Who bears this new obligation?
column5: The party who must bear it by law or as stipulated in the contract
column6: The customer in all cases, as he is the final buyer
column7: Both parties equally, since neither caused the new duty
column8: The Bank in all cases, since as seller it imported and priced the goods
column10: Per 4/1, a new duty or tax affects the commitment of the party who has to bear the new obligation by virtue of law or the stipulations of the contract.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: A supplier fails to deliver on time and the delivery becomes useless. Which condition must exist for the commitment to become null and void?
column5: The failure originates from the supplier's own personal choice
column6: The failure originates from objective rather than personal reasons
column7: The failure is caused by an act of the supplier's own staff
column8: The failure could have been avoided with reasonable effort
column10: Per 5/1/1-5/1/3, failure must be absolutely inevitable, arise from objective rather than personal reasons, and be caused by an external party.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: Before actual or legal delivery to Bank A, part of the goods owed to it is damaged by a heavenly factor (Sabab Samawi) the supplier could not avoid. What right does Bank A have?
column5: No right; it must accept the remaining goods as they are
column6: Only a claim for the full price of the damaged part
column7: A right to demand a penalty for late delivery of the goods
column8: The right of option regarding the commitment
column10: Per 5/2, in partial damage before actual or legal delivery caused by an unavoidable heavenly factor (Sabab Samawi), the committing party has the right of option.

column3: Impact of Contingent Incidents on Commitments
column4: Supplier X undertook to supply a conference's requirements, but for objective external reasons it could not deliver before the conference was held. What happens to the commitment?
column5: It is suspended until the next conference of the same organizer
column6: It is converted into a debt owed by the supplier equal to the value of supplies
column7: It becomes null and void because fulfillment has become of no use
column8: It remains binding and must be delivered after the conference
column10: Per 5/1, when delivery becomes impossible or useless, e.g. supplies for a conference not delivered before it is held, the commitment becomes null and void under set conditions.

column4: In a sale, the buyer paid 'Arboun to Bank A, then used his right to terminate the contract. What happens to the 'Arboun?
column5: It is held in trust until a new buyer is found
column6: It is owned by the Bank as seller
column7: It is returned in full to the buyer
column8: It is returned after deducting actual harm
column10: Per 5/3/2/2, 'Arboun is part of the price paid in advance; it is owned by the seller or landlord when the buyer or tenant uses his right of terminating the contract.

column4: Bank A offers a client a choice between Murabahah and Musawamah to finance a machine. What distinguishes Murabahah from Musawamah?
column5: In Murabahah the Bank's cost of obtaining the good must be indicated
column6: Musawamah is a lease while Murabahah is a sale
column7: In Musawamah the Bank's cost of obtaining the good must be indicated
column8: Murabahah covers only movable assets, unlike Musawamah
column10: Per 3/2/1, both are sale-based financing methods; contrary to Musawamah, in Murabahah the cost incurred by the Institution for obtaining the good must be indicated.

column4: Bank A wants to charge a client a fee for allocating and specifying a facility limit for him, payable whether or not any deal is concluded. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, but only if the client actually uses the facility
column6: Yes, if the fee is disclosed in the facility letter in advance
column7: No; mere willingness to deal does not justify remuneration
column8: Yes, if it equals the actual cost of allocating the limit
column10: Per 5/3/1/2, commission for offering credit facilities is impermissible, as mere willingness to enter a lending and borrowing transaction does not justify remuneration.

column4: Bank A is Rab al-Mal in a Mudarabah; the Mudarib managed the project properly but it made a loss. Who bears the loss?
column5: Both parties, in proportion to time and capital
column6: The Mudarib, as he managed the project
column7: Both parties, in their profit-sharing ratio
column8: The Bank as Rab al-Mal bears the entire loss
column10: Per 3/2/2, in Mudarabah the entire loss is borne by Rab al-Mal unless it is due to transgression or negligence of the Mudarib.

column4: Within the period of an approved facility, Bank A rejects a client's application to use it for a Murabahah. The client claims compensation. What is the ruling?
column5: The Bank is not committed to pay any compensation
column6: The Bank must compensate the client for his actual harm
column7: The Bank must pay a penalty agreed in the facility letter
column8: The Bank must refund any commitment fee the client paid
column10: Per 5/2, the Institution is not committed to pay compensation on rejecting a request to utilize approved facilities, and the client is free to use them or not.

column4: A client asks Bank A to prepare a feasibility study of his project for his own interest. When may the Bank charge the cost of the study?
column5: Only if the Bank then finances the project
column6: When the cost of the study is agreed upon beforehand
column7: Only if the study proves the project feasible and financeable
column8: Never, as it is part of the financing service
column10: Per 5/3/1/5, the Institution may charge the cost of a feasibility study requested by the client for his own interest, when the cost is agreed upon beforehand.

column4: Bank A charges a client a commission for a credit study of his creditworthiness, and then rejects his request. What is the ruling?
column5: The commission is permitted, and the study belongs to the client
column6: The commission is permitted only if the facility is granted
column7: The commission must be refunded because the request was rejected
column8: The commission is permitted, but the study remains the Bank's
column10: Per 5/3/1/1, the commission is due as the client benefited regardless of acceptance or rejection; the study becomes the client's property.

column4: Bank A sends a client a letter approving a facility with a limit, validity period and conditions on guarantees. No transaction has started yet. What is the letter's effect?
column5: It binds the client to use the full limit within the period
column6: It creates a debt owed by the client equal to the whole approved limit
column7: It is no commitment by the Bank unless transactions actually commence
column8: It binds the Bank to finance up to the limit during the period
column10: Per 2/4, the decision letter indicates it does not constitute any commitment from the Institution unless transactions are actually commenced.

column4: Bank A requires that a client's credit study be prepared by a third party firm. Per the Shari'ah basis, may it do so?
column5: No; the study must be prepared internally by the Institution
column6: Yes; the Institution may stipulate preparation by a third party
column7: Yes, but then no fee may be charged to the client at all
column8: No; a third party may prepare it only if the client chooses
column10: Per the basis, the Institution can even stipulate a condition that the study be prepared by a third party.

column4: Under the Fatwa cited in the basis, how must the contract for preparing a client's credit study relate to the financing contracts?
column5: It must be a clause inside the Murabahah contract
column6: It must be part of the facility letter for the limit
column7: It must be merged into the Mudarabah or Musharakah deal
column8: It must be a special contract fully separate from them
column10: The cited Fatwa (Aayan: 189) requires special contracts for the study, completely separate from the financing and legal contracts of the deals.

column4: Bank A issues a letter of guarantee for a client; the client will owe the Bank only if the Bank later has to pay the beneficiary. How is this credit classified?
column5: Financing, since one of the two transacted objects is deferred
column6: Incidental credit, since indebtedness is only probable at the end
column7: Not credit at all, since no funds are presented to the client
column8: Direct cash credit, since the client's indebtedness arises at the beginning
column10: Per 2/1, indebtedness probable only at the end is incidental credit, e.g. bank suretyship, letters of guarantee, bills of acceptance and documentary credits.

column4: A client buys a commodity from Bank A in a transaction where both the price and the commodity are delivered instantly. Is this a credit facility?
column5: Yes, as an incidental facility owed by the Institution
column6: Yes, as a cash facility in the form of an asset
column7: No; transactions with instant delivery of both objects are excluded
column8: Yes; every sale by an Institution to a client is a credit facility
column10: Per 2/3, transactions that entail instant delivery of the transacted objects are not considered part of credit facilities.

column4: A client's credit facility with Bank A is about to expire and both want to continue dealing. How should the renewal be done?
column5: By extending the duration of the current contracts
column6: By adding a renewal commission to the existing debt
column7: By automatic rollover clauses in the original contracts
column8: By entering into new contracts
column10: Per 5/3/2/4/2, renewal and extension of facilities should be done by entering into new contracts rather than extending the duration of ongoing ones.

column4: Bank A wants to charge a fee on the unused part of a client's approved facility, as traditional banks do for loans and overdrafts. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted; it is the fee of interest-bearing facilities
column6: Permitted if called a financing fee and not a loan fee
column7: Permitted if the client uses less than half of the limit
column8: Permitted, as the Bank reserved and kept funds available for the client
column10: Per 5/3/2/1, the Institution should not charge the commitment fee (loan fee, overdraft facility fee, financing fee) of traditional interest-bearing facilities.

column4: Bank A charges a client a credit study fee higher than the study's actual cost of preparation. Per the Shari'ah basis, is this acceptable?
column5: No; only actual expenses may ever be charged to clients
column6: No; the fee must equal the actual cost of preparation
column7: Yes, but only if the facility is then granted
column8: Yes; the fee need not equal the actual cost of preparation
column10: Per the basis, the study fee need not equal the actual cost, since it is a service that can be performed independently within the contract.

column4: What is the Shari'ah status of a credit facility agreement signed between Bank A and a client before any utilization?
column5: It is a bilateral binding promise enforceable by the courts
column6: It is a binding loan contract for the full approved limit
column7: Mutual understanding and exchange of non-binding promises
column8: It is a binding sale contract from the date of signing
column10: Per 4, the decision and the facility agreement are means of mutual understanding and exchange of non-binding promises; utilization depends on the contract used.

column4: Bank A issues a letter of guarantee and also acts as agent in a documentary credit for a client. What may it charge?
column5: Actual expenses for the guarantee, and a return for the agency
column6: A percentage of the guaranteed amount for each service
column7: A return on both the guarantee and the agency
column8: A return on the guarantee, and only actual expenses for the agency
column10: Per 5/3/2/3, no returns on guarantee in DCs, letters of guarantee and suretyship except actual expenses, but returns may be obtained for agency in DCs.

column4: A client paid Hamish Jiddiyyah with his binding promise in a Murabahah, then retreated. Bank A suffered actual harm of 2,000 while the deposit is 5,000. What may the Bank do?
column5: Keep the whole deposit as part of the price
column6: Deduct 2,000 of actual harm and return the rest
column7: Return the whole 5,000 and claim nothing
column8: Keep the whole 5,000 as compensation
column10: Per 5/3/1/6, if the client retreats from concluding the contract, the amount of actual harm caused to the Institution is deducted from the seriousness margin.

column4: On what basis may an Institution charge a fee for preparing a credit study for a client?
column5: The fee is a guarantee return for assessing the client's risk
column6: The study is part of the financing and its cost is priced in the profit margin
column7: The study is a remunerable service apart from the financing contract
column8: The fee compensates the Institution for reserving the facility
column10: Per the Shari'ah basis, the credit study as such can constitute a remunerable service apart from the financing contract.

column4: A client asks Bank A to extend the repayment date of his Murabahah debt by six months. What may the Bank charge for the rescheduling?
column5: A fixed fee proportional to the extension period
column6: An additional return for the period of extension
column7: A share of the client's profits during the extension
column8: Only the actual expenses of the rescheduling transaction
column10: Per 5/3/2/4/1, the Institution should not obtain returns for extending the repayment date of debts; it charges only actual expenses of the rescheduling.

column4: Bank A prepares the Murabahah contracts to be signed with a client; the contract is silent on who bears the cost of preparing them. Who bears it?
column5: The cost is shared between the Bank and the client
column6: The Bank alone, as it drafts the contracts
column7: Neither party; the cost cannot be charged at all
column8: The client alone, as the beneficiary of the financing
column10: Per 5/3/1/4/1, the contract preparation cost is shared unless the contract says otherwise, and must be fair so it is not an implicit commitment fee.

column4: A client asks Bank A for a facility to buy and sell foreign currency on a deferred basis, as offered by traditional banks. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible as an incidental facility within the approved limit
column6: Impermissible, as it defers one of the two transacted objects
column7: Permissible if the exchange rate is fixed on signing the contract
column8: Permissible if no interest is charged on the deferred amount
column10: Per 5/1, traditional facilities are impermissible if they involve interest or lead to deferment of one of the two transacted objects, as in currency exchange contracts.

column4: Bank A provides capital to Company X under a Mudarabah within a credit facility. When would Company X owe the capital as a debt to the Bank?
column5: Only in case of transgression or negligence by Company X
column6: Always, since every cash facility creates a debt on the client
column7: Once the facility period expires, whatever the outcome
column8: Whenever the Mudarabah operation ends with any loss
column10: Per 2/2/1, Musharakah and Mudarabah are cash facilities but do not result in a debt owed by the client except in case of transgression or negligence.

column4: Why is charging the client for a credit study also justified, per the Shari'ah basis, even though the financier uses it to assess risk?
column5: The study fee is deducted later from the profit of the deal
column6: The study benefits both the financier and the financed party
column7: The client is a borrower and must pay all of the lender's own costs
column8: The benefit of the study is confined to the financier only
column10: Per the basis, the benefit from the study is shared between the financier and the financed party rather than confined to the former only.

column4: A client paid Company X for a credit study, then wants to use it with another financier. Per the Fatwa cited in the basis, may Company X refuse to hand it over?
column5: No, but it may hand over only a summary of the study
column6: Yes, unless the client also signs a financing deal with Company X itself
column7: Yes; the study remains Company X's confidential property
column8: No; the study is the client's once he pays, and must be handed over
column10: Per the cited Fatwa, the study becomes the client's property once he pays its cost; it must be handed over so he can use it with Company X or any other party.

column4: Bank A arranges a syndicated Murabahah financing with several banks and charges an arrangement fee. Who should bear it?
column5: The arranging bank itself, from its own profit
column6: No one; arrangement fees are impermissible
column7: The participants of the syndication
column8: The client being financed, in all cases
column10: Per 5/3/1/4/2, in syndicated financing the arranging Institution may charge arrangement fees to be borne by the participants of the syndication.

column4: A client finds that an online adhesion contract he joined carries an excessively unfair price. What remedy does the standard give him?
column5: No remedy, since he accepted the terms by adhering
column6: Resort to law to nullify the contract or amend its conditions
column7: Only a claim against the State for weak supervision
column8: Unilateral withholding of payment until the price is reduced
column10: Per 8/3/4, for an unfair price or an unjust condition, the adhering party may resort to law for nullification of the contract or amendment of its conditions.

column4: Bank A provides internet access service to subscribers against a specific fee. How is this contract characterised?
column5: A Ju'alah contract payable only when the service succeeds
column6: A Wakalah contract with the subscriber against a fee
column7: A shared-hiring contract (Ijarah Mushtarakah) with the beneficiary
column8: A sale of the network's usufruct outright to each individual subscriber
column10: Per 3/2, the online access contract is a shared-hiring contract (Ijarah Mushtarakah), subject to the rulings on hiring of persons and hiring a shared employee.

column4: Per the Al Baraka Seminar resolution cited in the basis, when is an online contract between parties in different places one between absent parties?
column5: When neither party can hear the voice of the other
column6: When the contract is concluded outside working hours
column7: When the parties are in different countries
column8: When either party uses a third-party website
column10: The cited Al Baraka resolution treats an online contract as between absent parties if neither can hear the other's voice, so message contracting rules apply.

column4: Bank A's website is trespassed, causing it direct financial loss and actual loss of earnings. What does the compensation comprise?
column5: Only the direct financial loss, excluding loss of earnings
column6: Only a fixed penalty set in advance by the Bank
column7: Only the expected profit the Bank had planned to earn
column8: Both the direct financial loss and the actual loss of earnings
column10: Per 8/1/5, compensation for trespassing comprises direct financial loss as well as actual loss of earnings; expert advice may be sought.

column4: Company X's website shows a product and states it may withdraw even after a customer accepts. A customer clicks to accept. What is the status?
column5: It was only an invitation; offer and acceptance must still take place
column6: The contract is concluded once the customer clicks to accept
column7: The contract is concluded, but Company X keeps an option to cancel it later
column8: The contract is void, since withdrawal conditions are prohibited
column10: Per 5/3, retaining the right of withdrawal even if accepted makes the message an announcement or invitation for contracting, not an offer.

column4: A client was deceived online by a forged identity of the seller. Per the basis, why may he terminate the contract?
column5: The forgery is a contingent incident after signing
column6: The forgery makes the price unknown to the buyer
column7: The forgery turns the contract into an adhesion contract subject to the State
column8: It affects his consent, a fundamental prerequisite of contracting
column10: Per the basis, forgery or error about a party can influence the consent of the deceived party, and consent is the fundamental prerequisite of contracting.

column4: Bank A wants to use electronic signatures to verify the identities of dealers on its website. When is this acceptable?
column5: Only when the dealer also signs a paper copy later
column6: When it is adoptable under the prevailing rules and regulations
column7: Only for contracts below a certain monetary limit
column8: Never; identity may be proved only by the dealer's personal presence
column10: Per 8/2/2, the electronic signature is acceptable for verifying dealers' identities if it is adoptable by virtue of the prevailing rules and regulations.

column4: Ahmad buys computer software from Company X's website. When does possession in the strict Shari'ah sense take place?
column5: When he clicks to accept the offer shown on the seller's website
