column6: When Company X sends him an invoice by e-mail
column7: When he downloads it to his computer after signing
column8: When he pays the price by bank card online
column10: Per 7/2, for software and the like, possession occurs when the purchaser, after signing, downloads it from the website to his personal computer.

column4: Two years after learning that its website was trespassed, Bank A claims compensation. Under the standard, is the claim barred by time?
column5: No; compensation is due even without any claim being made
column6: No; there is no specific time limit, subject to compatible rules
column7: Yes; compensation is due automatically and lapses if it is not paid on time
column8: Yes; it must be claimed within one year of the incident
column10: Per 8/1/6, compensation is due only when claimed, and claiming has no specific time limit after the trespass is known, observing compatible rules.

column4: Bank A and a client conclude a Murabahah over an online video call, each in a different city. Which rulings apply to the contract signing session?
column5: The rulings on contracts signed in the presence of the two parties
column6: No session rulings, as the parties are in different places
column7: The rulings on message contracting through a messenger
column8: The rulings on contracts signed in the absence of the two parties
column10: Per 4/1, audio or audiovisual contracting is subject to the rulings for contracts in the presence of both parties, e.g. Itihad al-Majlis and succession of offer and acceptance.

column4: Which aim of Shari'ah does the basis cite to support accepting electronic signatures to verify dealers' identities?
column5: Facilitation of trade through speed of contracting
column6: Preservation of lineage, one of the five main Maqasid
column7: Preservation of wealth, one of the five main Maqasid
column8: Removal of Gharar in the subject matter of sale
column10: Per the basis, Shari'ah encourages technological means to preserve people's wealth, as preservation of wealth is one of the main five aims (Maqasid).

column4: Bank A posts an e-mail message stating all rights and commitments of a sale without retaining any right of withdrawal if accepted. How is this message treated?
column5: As an invitation for contracting
column6: As a mere announcement to the public
column7: As a concluded contract in itself
column8: As an offer
column10: Per 5/2, a message containing all the rights and commitments, without retaining the right of withdrawal if accepted, is considered an offer.

column4: During a phone conversation about a sale, Bank A's offer is made, then the parties move on to discuss a different subject before any acceptance. What is the status of the session?
column5: The session continues for the whole working day
column6: The session continues until the call is finally ended by either party
column7: The contract signing session is considered to have stopped
column8: The offer remains open until expressly withdrawn
column10: Per 4/1/1, the session is the time of communication on the contract; if the conversation ends, is disconnected, or shifts to another subject, the session stops.

column4: Bank A concludes an online contract with someone who forged the identity of a well-known company. What right does Bank A have?
column5: Only a right to claim a reduction in price
column6: Only a right to require a new electronic signature
column7: No right, as the contract was validly accepted
column8: The right to terminate the contract
column10: Per 8/2/3, when forgery or error occurs regarding the personality or characteristics of a party, the other party has the right to terminate the contract.

column4: A monopoly supplier of an indispensable service offers uniform online terms the public cannot change; price and terms are fair. What is the status?
column5: It is permissible and binding on its two parties
column6: It is binding only on the supplier, not on the adhering party
column7: It is void because the adhering party cannot negotiate
column8: It is voidable at the option of the adhering party
column10: Per 8/3/3, if the price in an online adhesion contract is fair and the terms entail no injustice to the adhering party, it is permissible and binding.

column4: Why does the basis classify online contracts by audio or audiovisual communication as contracts between present parties?
column5: The communication is recorded and can later be used as evidence in court
column6: The parties are present at the same time, though not in one place
column7: Both parties are deemed to be present in the same place
column8: The contract is written down on screen during the call
column10: Per the basis, both parties are present at the same time though not in one place, so simultaneous presence in time is fulfilled when offer and acceptance are exchanged.

column4: After an online auction ends, the highest bidder wants to retreat. When is he barred from doing so?
column5: If the seller made the offer binding for a period or practice requires it
column6: Only if he had paid a deposit when placing his bid
column7: Never; once the auction is over he is free to retreat from his highest bid
column8: Only if the auction was run by an Institution
column10: Per 4/3, after bidding ends he may not retreat if the seller conditioned the offer to remain binding for a period, or if normal practice necessitates it.

column4: In an online auction run by Bank A, Ahmad is currently the highest bidder and wants to withdraw his bid before the auction ends. What is the ruling?
column5: He may retreat at any time before the auction closes
column6: He may retreat if he pays a cancellation fee to the Bank
column7: He may not retreat from his bid until the bidding is over
column8: He may retreat if another bidder matches his bid
column10: Per 4/3, in online bidding the highest bidder should not retreat from his bid until the bidding process is over.

column4: Bank A sends a sale offer to a client by e-mail. Which category of contract rulings applies to this deal?
column5: Rulings on adhesion contracts subject to state control
column6: Rulings on contracts signed in the absence of the two parties
column7: Rulings on online bidding and auction contracts
column8: Rulings on contracts signed in the presence of the two parties
column10: Per 4/2, written communication, e-mail or site access is subject to the rulings on contracts in the absence of the two parties, as it resembles message contracting.

column4: Bank A launches a commercial website to market its permissible Murabahah products, using impermissible advertising means to attract clients. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the products themselves are fully Shari'ah-compliant
column6: Impermissible only if the website charges users a fee
column7: Permissible, provided the contracts are concluded offline
column8: Impermissible, due to the impermissible means of promotion
column10: Per 2/1, launching commercial websites is permissible unless they involve impermissible acts, such as using impermissible means to promote permissible goods and services.

column4: A hacker trespasses Bank A's commercial website, causing it losses. How does the standard view the website?
column5: As property of the hosting provider, which alone can claim any compensation
column6: As public space, so no compensation is due for access
column7: As its owner's private property, so trespass may need compensation
column8: As a mere service, so only criminal penalties may apply
column10: Per 8/1/1, commercial websites are private properties of their owners, so trespassing them could necessitate compensation.

column4: On which view is the ruling based that an offeror may not retract an offer within its stated validity period?
column5: The general rule that every promise is binding in law
column6: The Hanafi view that an offer can be revoked before acceptance
column7: The view that silence of the offeree counts as acceptance
column8: The view of some Maliki scholars that a timed offer stays valid
column10: Per the basis, it rests on the view of some Maliki scholars (Al-Hattab quoting Abu Bakar Al-Arabi), supported by an International Islamic Fiqh Academy resolution.

column4: Why is an online contract valid once acceptance is given, even before the offeror learns of it, per the basis?
column5: Contracts are valid only after they are registered online
column6: A contract is the concordance of two wills, achieved on acceptance
column7: The offeror is deemed to know everything that is sent to his website
column8: Possession takes place at the moment of acceptance
column10: Per the basis, scholars define a contract as 'the concordance of two wills'; once the acceptor declares consent, concordance occurs and the contract is valid.

column4: A client buys gold from Bank A through the Bank's website. What is required regarding the two objects of the contract?
column5: Instant exchange (Taqabud) must be ascertained during the session
column6: Payment may be deferred if the gold is delivered at once
column7: Exchange may occur within any period agreed by the parties
column8: Delivery of gold may be deferred if the price is paid at once
column10: Per 7/3, for currency, gold, silver or any commodity requiring Taqabud, instant exchange of both objects must be ascertained during the contract session.

column4: Why is an e-mail that does not state all the rights and commitments of a contract not treated as an offer, per the basis?
column5: An offer is valid only if made in the presence of both parties
column6: An offer must be categorically obvious and bear no other meaning
column7: An offer must always include a period for its validity
column8: E-mail cannot carry an offer under the rules of message contracting
column10: Per the basis, such a message is not an offer because, from a Shari'ah point of view, an offer should be categorically obvious and cannot bear any other meaning.

column4: A client accepts Bank A's online offer on Monday, but the Bank learns of the acceptance only on Wednesday. When did the contract become valid?
column5: On Monday, when the client accepted the offer
column6: When the Bank sends confirmation of receipt
column7: On delivery of the subject matter to the client
column8: On Wednesday, when the Bank learned of the acceptance
column10: Per 6, an online contract is valid from the time the other party accepts the offer, whether or not the offering party has come to know of it.

column4: Bank A's website requires a client to confirm acceptance after clicking the acceptance icon. The client clicks the icon but never confirms. Is there acceptance?
column5: Yes, but the client has an option to rescind within three days
column6: Yes; clicking the acceptance icon is acceptance in all cases
column7: No, unless the Bank has already delivered the item
column8: No; acceptance needs the required confirmation
column10: Per 5/4, clicking the icon is acceptance if no confirmation is required; if the system requires confirmation, acceptance occurs only on confirmation.

column4: Money is stolen from Bank A's site, which had taken all possible protective measures and gave no pledge of liability. The thief cannot be charged. Who is responsible?
column5: The client whose money was stolen
column6: Bank A and the client, equally
column7: The one who facilitated the act of theft
column8: Bank A, as owner of the website through which the theft took place
column10: Per 8/1/7, liability rests on the direct thief, otherwise on the facilitator; the site owner is not chargeable if it took all measures and gave no pledge.

column4: Ahmad buys a car online based on a description and a model shown on the website. On delivery the car differs from the description. What may he do?
column5: He may only terminate and cannot keep the car
column6: He has no option, as he did not see the car itself
column7: He must accept it and claim only the price difference
column8: Choose to conclude, terminate, or negotiate a settlement
column10: Per 8/4, if the delivered object differs from the description, prior sight or model, the buyer may conclude, terminate or negotiate appropriate settlement.

column4: A call between Bank A and a client negotiating an Ijarah is cut off for a reasonably short while and then resumes. What is the effect on the contract session?
column5: The short disconnection does not stop the session
column6: The contract is deemed concluded at the time of disconnection
column7: The session stops, but the offer stays binding for a day
column8: The session stops and the offer must be issued anew
column10: Per 4/1/1, disconnection stops the session unless the disconnection of the conversation is for a reasonably short while.

column4: Company X wants to sell its online customers' data to a marketing firm without their permission. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the data are sold at a fair market price
column6: Strictly prohibited without the permission of the data owners
column7: Permitted if the marketing firm is a Shari'ah-compliant entity
column8: Permitted, since the data were collected by Company X
column10: Per 8/1/3, trespassing dealers' online data is impermissible; it is strictly prohibited to sell or transmit it to others without the owners' permission.

column4: Bank A e-mails an offer to sell a property and states that it remains valid for 10 days. On day 4, before the client replies, the Bank wants to withdraw. Can it?
column5: Yes, if it notifies the client by e-mail
column6: Yes, any time before the client's acceptance
column7: No; it may not withdraw during the specified period
column8: No, unless the client has not opened the e-mail
column10: Per 4/2/2, where the offering party specifies a validity period, acceptance time covers the whole period and the offeror has no right to withdraw during it.

column4: Per the basis, why does downloading purchased software after signing count as possession?
column5: The object is released and disposition is facilitated for the buyer
column6: Ownership of software passes only on full payment of the price, whatever the delivery
column7: The seller loses all copies of the software on download
column8: Downloading is a form of registration of the sale
column10: Per the basis, possession takes place when the sold object is released and disposition is facilitated; its form differs with the object and how it is perceived.

column4: Bank A, as mortgagee, decides to revoke a mortgage it holds before the debt is repaid. What is the ruling?
column5: It may not, as the mortgage binds both parties
column6: It may do so only with the mortgagor's consent
column7: It may do so only by a court order
column8: Yes; the mortgagee has the right to revoke it
column10: Per 3/1/1, the mortgage contract binds the mortgagor, who cannot revoke it, whereas the mortgagee has the right to revoke it.

column4: Bank A's mortgage contract states that on default the Bank automatically becomes owner of the mortgaged land. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the default lasts over 90 days
column6: This condition is not permitted
column7: Permitted, as both parties agreed to it
column8: Permitted, if the land's value equals the debt
column10: Per 3/4/2, the mortgagee may not stipulate that he owns the asset on default, but he may purchase it from the mortgagor at market value.

column4: A building mortgaged to Bank A increases in value and earns rental income. The contract is silent. What is the status of the increase and income?
column5: They belong to the mortgagor free of the mortgage
column6: Only the increase in value is mortgaged, not the income
column7: They are mortgaged along with the principal
column8: They belong to Bank A as compensation for waiting
column10: Per 3/2/8, appreciation in value and income of the mortgaged asset are mortgaged along with the principal, unless the parties agree otherwise.

column4: Bank A holds a mortgaged asset as a notary for the benefit of two other parties. Does the standard on mortgage cover this case?
column5: Yes; it also covers mortgages it keeps as notary or agent
column6: No; it covers only mortgages the Institution presents to others
column7: No; notary arrangements are governed only by agency rules
column8: No; it covers only mortgages requested by the Institution
column10: Per 1, the standard covers mortgages requested by the Institution, those it presents to others, and those it keeps as notary or agent for others.

column4: Bank A incurs costs for safekeeping and documentation of a mortgaged asset. The contract is silent on these costs. Who bears them?
column5: Both parties equally
column6: The notary, if one is appointed
column7: Bank A, the mortgagee
column8: The mortgagor, as owner of the asset
column10: Per 3/2/10, the mortgagee bears expenses of safekeeping, documentation and selling of the mortgaged asset, unless the parties agree the mortgagor bears them.

column4: In a spot sale, the commodity is still in the seller's hands, and the buyer wants a mortgage from the seller to secure its delivery. Is this valid?
column5: No, unless the price has been deferred
column6: Yes, if the commodity is a fungible asset
column7: Yes; any obligation of the seller, including delivery of the sold commodity, may be secured
column8: No; a spot sale commodity in the seller's hands is not a debt
column10: Per 3/3/1, a mortgage may not be for a non-debt deal, such as a specific price, usufruct of a specific asset, or a spot sale commodity still with the seller.

column4: Bank A, as Rab al-Mal in a Mudarabah, requires a mortgage from the Mudarib. In which case is this permissible?
column5: If the Mudarabah term exceeds one year
column6: If confined to indemnity for transgression, negligence or breach
column7: If it secures return of the capital to the Bank in all cases and events
column8: If it secures a minimum profit for the Bank
column10: Per 3/3/2, mortgage may not be stipulated in trust-based contracts (e.g. Mudarabah), unless confined to indemnity for transgression, negligence or breach.

column4: The mortgagor permits Bank A to use a mortgaged apartment free of charge during the mortgage. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the use is for a short period
column6: Permissible, since the mortgagor gave permission
column7: Impermissible, as the mortgagee may not use it at all, even for a fee
column8: Impermissible; the Bank may use it only against normal pay
column10: Per 3/2/9, the mortgagee may not enjoy free benefit of the asset with or without permission, but may use it with permission against the normal pay for similar assets.

column4: A mortgaged current account is converted by agreement into an investment account at Bank A. What are the parties' roles?
column5: The Bank is Rab al-Mal and the holder is Mudarib
column6: The holder is lender and the Bank is borrower
column7: The holder is Rab al-Mal and the Bank is Mudarib
column8: The holder and the Bank are Musharakah partners
column10: Per 5, on transfer to an investment account the holder gets his profit share as owner of capital (Rab al-Mal) and the Institution as worker (Mudarib).

column4: Bank A wants a client to sign a mortgage contract a week before signing the Murabahah that will create his debt. Is this valid under the standard?
column5: Yes; the mortgage may be signed before or with the debt contract
column6: Yes, but only if the debt is a Qard Hasan
column7: No; the debt must first be established before any mortgage is signed
column8: No; mortgage may be signed only after the debt is due
column10: Per 3/3/1, a valid mortgage need not be preceded by establishing the debt; it can be signed before or at the same time as the debt contract.

column4: One building is mortgaged to Bank A and Bank B with the same rank. A third mortgagee wants the same rank. How is the right shared and whose consent is needed?
column5: Consent of the first mortgagee only; the right is shared equally
column6: Consent of all; right shared in proportion to their debts
column7: Consent of the mortgagor only; shared equally
column8: No consent needed; first come, first served
column10: Per 3/2/3, where mortgages are of the same rank, all parties must consent and the mortgage right is shared in proportion to their respective debts.

column4: A mortgaged asset is insured by Islamic insurance and is damaged; cash compensation is received. What happens to the cash?
column5: It is paid to the mortgagor free of the mortgage
column6: It is kept by the insurer until the debt matures
column7: It is mortgaged, with its returns, in a frozen investment account
column8: It is paid to the mortgagee, who becomes owner of the asset's value
column10: Per 8, cash compensation replaces the asset and is mortgaged with its returns by depositing it in a frozen investment account owned by the mortgagor.

column4: A creditor argues that the Qur'anic verse makes taking a mortgage obligatory in every debt. What does the basis say?
column5: Mortgage is obligatory when there is no scribe
column6: Mortgage is obligatory whenever the creditor asks for it in the contract
column7: Mortgage is obligatory only on deferred sales
column8: Mortgage is not obligatory; the verse indicates guidance
column10: Per the basis, mortgage is not obligatory, without known dispute; the emphasis in the verse indicates guidance rather than obligation.

column4: With the owner's permission, Ahmad mortgages a borrowed house to Bank A; the house is sold to repay Ahmad's defaulted debt. What right does the owner have?
column5: No right, since he permitted the mortgage
column6: Recourse on Ahmad for its value, as a house is not fungible
column7: Recourse on Ahmad for a similar house in kind
column8: Recourse on Bank A for the full sale price of the house
column10: Per 3/2/6, if a borrowed mortgage repays the debt, the owner has recourse on the mortgagor: in kind for a fungible asset, or in value otherwise.

column4: A client who mortgaged his truck to Bank A wants to keep using it for his business. When may he do so?
column5: On the permission of the mortgagee
column6: Without any permission, since he is the owner
column7: Only after repaying half of the debt
column8: Never, as long as the truck is mortgaged
column10: Per 3/2/9, the mortgagor can benefit from the mortgaged asset on permission of the mortgagee.

column4: A client fully repays his debt, but Bank A wants to keep the mortgaged land as collateral for a new, separate debt. There is no prior agreement. May it?
column5: Yes, as the land is already in its possession
column6: No; it was not mortgaged for the new debt
column7: Yes, if the new debt is smaller than the old one
column8: Yes, if the new debt arises within one year
column10: Per 3/1/7, after repayment the mortgagee may not keep the asset for a new debt, unless both agreed it secures any debt between them within a specific period.

column4: A client offers Bank A shares of a company whose original activities are permissible and whose dealings are not predominantly Riba-based. May they be mortgaged?
column5: Yes; such shares can be mortgaged
column6: No; only Islamic Sukuk can be mortgaged
column7: No; shares represent common property
column8: Yes, but only shares of Islamic banks
column10: Per 4/1, Islamic Sukuk, shares of Islamic financial Institutions and shares of companies with permissible original activities may be mortgaged.

column4: A mortgaged car held by Bank A is destroyed in a flood with no transgression or negligence by the Bank. What is the effect?
column5: The Bank bears the loss and the debt is cancelled
column6: The Bank must replace the car with a similar one
column7: The debt is reduced by the car's value
column8: The Bank bears no liability and the debt remains valid
column10: Per 3/2/4, the mortgaged asset is a trust owned by the mortgagor; if it perishes without transgression or negligence, no liability arises and the debt remains.

column4: A mortgaged asset is sold on default for 70 against a debt of 100 owed to Bank A. What is the status of the shortfall of 30?
column5: It becomes a debt only if the mortgagor agrees
column6: It is borne by the notary who held the asset
column7: It remains a normal debt with recourse on the mortgagor
column8: It is extinguished, as the mortgage has been executed
column10: Per 3/4/1, if the sale value is less than the due debt, the difference is subject to the rulings on normal debt, with recourse on the mortgagor.

column4: A client repaid 80% of a debt secured by a mortgaged building and asks Bank A to release 80% of the building. The Bank refuses. Is it entitled to refuse?
column5: No; it must release the whole asset once most is repaid
column6: No; it must release the asset in proportion to repayment
column7: Yes, but only if the debt is now overdue
column8: Yes; it may keep the whole asset for any part of the debt
column10: Per 3/1/7, the mortgagee may keep the whole mortgaged asset for any part of the debt, unless he accepts partial release.

column4: Bank A, as mortgagee, pays for urgent repairs to a mortgaged building to prevent its decay. What right does it have?
column5: Only a right to add a profit margin to the debt
column6: Ownership of the building in proportion to the repair cost
column7: Recourse on the mortgagor, or an equivalent period of use
column8: No right, as it paid voluntarily without permission
column10: Per 3/2/10, reparation and preservation costs fall on the mortgagor; if the mortgagee pays, with or without permission, he has recourse or an equivalent period of benefit.

column4: Bank A's mortgage over a client's land is possessed legally through registration in the land registry, not by physically holding the land. How is it treated?
column5: As a mere promise to mortgage until physical delivery
column6: As a formal mortgage, with the same rulings as seizure mortgage
column7: As valid, but with weaker rulings than a seizure mortgage held by hand
column8: As invalid, since actual possession by hand is required
column10: Per 3/1/2, possession may be actual (seizure mortgage) or legal via registration (security or formal mortgage); both types are subject to the same rulings.

column4: A client mortgages his investment account managed by Bank A on an investment agency basis. The account earns profit. What is the status of the profit?
column5: It is mortgaged along with the principal unless agreed otherwise
column6: It is mortgaged only if the relationship with the Bank is Mudarabah
column7: It is free of the mortgage because of the agency basis
column8: It belongs to the Bank as compensation for the debt
column10: Per 6/2, income and growth of the units or account are mortgaged with the principal whether the relationship is Mudarabah or investment agency, unless agreed otherwise.

column4: Under the standard, what does it mean to mortgage an asset?
column5: To lease it to the creditor in exchange for deferring the debt
column6: To transfer its ownership to the creditor until the debt is paid
column7: To tie it to a debt so it or its value repays it on default
column8: To sell it to the creditor with an option to buy it back later
column10: Per 2, to mortgage means to make a financial asset tied to a debt so that the asset or its value is used for repayment of the debt in case of default.

column4: After concluding a mortgage contract with Bank A, the client wants to revoke it unilaterally before repaying the debt. May he?
column5: Yes, at any time before the asset is delivered
column6: Yes, if he provides a guarantor instead
column7: No, unless the Bank has not yet registered it
column8: No; it is binding on the mortgagor once concluded
column10: Per 3/1/1, the mortgage is binding on the mortgagor once concluded and he cannot revoke it from his side, whereas the mortgagee has the right to do so.

column4: A rented asset, mortgaged with the owner's permission, perishes in the mortgagor's hands without his transgression or negligence. Must he compensate the owner?
column5: Yes, as with a borrowed asset in all cases
column6: No; for a rented asset, only transgression or negligence
column7: Yes, at half its value on the date of perish
column8: No, but the mortgagee must compensate the owner for its full value
column10: Per 3/2/6, a borrowed mortgage perishing requires compensation to the owner, but for a rented asset only if due to transgression or negligence of the mortgagor.

column4: Per the basis, why is freezing a current account balance as mortgage at the same Institution permissible?
column5: It is like mortgaging an asset already under the mortgagee's guarantee
column6: It is a form of Mudarabah from the outset
column7: Current accounts are trust deposits with no guarantee by the Institution
column8: The balance becomes the Institution's own property
column10: Per the basis, it is similar to mortgaging assets previously held under the guarantee of the mortgagee (in the mortgagee's hands), which is permissible.

column4: A mortgaged warehouse burns down and the mortgagor receives compensation from a solidarity insurance scheme. What is the status of the mortgage?
column5: It ends, since the mortgaged asset has perished
column6: It continues over the land only, but not over the insurance compensation
column7: It ends, and the debt becomes due immediately
column8: It continues, with the compensation replacing the warehouse
column10: Per 3/1/6 and 8, a mortgage ceases when the asset perishes unless compensation is obtained (e.g. solidarity insurance), which then replaces it.

column4: In a deferred-price Murabahah, Bank A stipulates that the customer, after possessing the car, mortgage it to the Bank against the deferred price. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible, as the Bank cannot take the sold good as mortgage
column6: Permissible only before the customer possesses the car
column7: Permissible for the seller to stipulate
column8: Impermissible unless a third-party guarantor is added
column10: Per 3/2/7, the seller may stipulate that the buyer, after actual or constructive possession, mortgage the good to him against the deferred price.

column4: Investment accounts used as mortgage contain changing assets, involving some Gharar. Per the Maliki argument in the basis, why is this acceptable?
column5: The account is converted into cash on mortgaging
column6: Who may lend undocumented may accept documentation with some Gharar
column7: The Institution guarantees the account value
column8: Gharar is never relevant to mortgage contracts, whatever the asset type
column10: Per the basis, the Malikis argue that since the mortgagee may lend without documentation, he can accept documentation with some Gharar: something is better than nothing.

column4: Why is a mortgagee barred from benefiting free of charge from the mortgaged asset, per the basis?
column5: Otherwise he would be committing Riba
column6: Otherwise he would owe Zakah on the asset
column7: Otherwise he would breach the notary's rights
column8: Otherwise the mortgage would become a sale
column10: Per the basis, the mortgagee does not have the right to make free of charge benefit from the mortgaged asset because otherwise he would be committing Riba.

column4: On a client's default, Bank A wants to buy the mortgaged land from him and take from the price what it is owed. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, at the value fixed in the mortgage contract
column6: No; the mortgagee may never acquire the asset
column7: Yes, at a discount reflecting the client's default
column8: Yes, if it purchases at market value
column10: Per 3/4/2, though ownership on default may not be stipulated, the mortgagee may purchase the asset from the mortgagor at market value and take its due portion.

column4: A client wants to mortgage to Bank A the future rental income of a specified building he owns, without mortgaging the building itself. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if the building is mortgaged too
column6: Impermissible, as the income is not yet owned and may never come into existence
column7: Permissible, as the income-earning principal is specified
column8: Impermissible, as it involves excessive Gharar
column10: Per 7, mortgaging an income still to be owned is permissible if the principal is specified, whether with the principal or independently.

column4: Bank A appoints its subsidiary as agent to possess a mortgaged asset on its behalf. What rights of disposition does the agent have?
column5: The same rights of disposition as the Bank as principal
column6: Only the right to hold the asset, without disposition
column7: Wider rights than the Bank, as the actual possessor
column8: Only the rights the mortgagor separately grants it
column10: Per 3/1/3, the mortgagee may appoint an agent to possess the mortgage; the agent has the same rights of disposition as the principal.

column4: The verse on mortgage mentions travel. According to Ibn Al-Mundhir as quoted in the basis, why is travel mentioned?
column5: It limits mortgage to debts in foreign lands
column6: It is the predominant case of need, not a condition
column7: It is a condition for the validity of mortgage
column8: It shows mortgage is obligatory for travellers
column10: Per the basis, travel is mentioned as the predominant case where mortgage is needed (lack of a scribe); it is not stipulated as a condition.

column4: A mortgagor goes bankrupt. Bank A, his mortgagee, is owed 100, while the mortgaged asset sells for 60. How is Bank A treated?
column5: Priority over the whole 100, recoverable from all of his remaining assets
column6: Equal standing with other creditors for all 100
column7: Priority over the 60; the remaining 40 is waived
column8: Priority over the 60; equal standing with others for the 40
column10: Per 3/5/3, on bankruptcy the mortgagee has priority from the sale value; for any excess debt he stands equal with other creditors.

column4: On default, a mortgaged asset is sold for 120 against a debt of 100 owed to Bank A. What happens to the remaining 20?
column5: It is held as security for future debts
column6: It is given to the mortgagor
column7: Bank A keeps it as compensation for delay
column8: It is donated to charity on the mortgagor's behalf
column10: Per 3/4/1, after repaying the mortgagee's debt, the remaining value of the sold mortgaged asset is given to the mortgagor.

column4: Per the Shafi'i view cited in the basis, why may a mortgaged asset be kept with a notary?
column5: The mortgagor retains ownership of the asset
column6: A notary is required for every valid mortgage
column7: The right belongs to both parties, so they can agree on it
column8: The mortgagee is not trusted to keep the asset, so a neutral third party must hold it
column10: Per the basis, the Shafi'is permit keeping the mortgage with a notary 'because the right belongs to the two parties, so they can agree on that'.

column4: Bank A and a client agree to place a mortgaged machine with a notary. Later the Bank wants to move it to its own warehouse. May it?
column5: No; neither party may transfer it to another location
column6: Yes, since the Bank is the mortgagee
column7: Yes, after notifying the notary and the client in writing in advance
column8: No, unless the client is in default
column10: Per 3/1/3, the mortgage can be kept by a notary agreed by both parties; when kept by a notary, neither party has the right to transfer it elsewhere.

column4: A client mortgages his current account balance with Bank A to the same Bank. How does the Bank's status over the balance change?
column5: It does not change; the Bank still guarantees it as a loan
column6: It becomes the Bank's own property until repayment
column7: It changes from holding it on trust basis to holding it on guarantee basis
column8: It changes from holding it on guarantee basis to holding it on trust
column10: Per 3/2/5, when an asset held by the mortgagee as a guaranteed asset (e.g. a current account) is mortgaged, its status changes from guarantee to trust.

column4: A conventional lender asks Bank A to hold a mortgage as security for an interest-bearing loan it granted. Can a valid mortgage secure this debt?
column5: No; the debt secured must be a permissible debt
column6: Yes, if the interest is waived on default
column7: Yes, if Bank A acts only as notary
column8: Yes, since the mortgage is separate from the loan
column10: Per 3/3/1, the secured debt must be permissible (e.g. sale price, Salam or Istisna'a commodity); it should not be an impermissible debt such as a usurious loan.

column4: Which evidence does the basis cite for the mortgagor bearing the expenses of the mortgaged asset?
column5: The report that the Prophet mortgaged his armor to a Jew for barley
column6: The verse: if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, take a pledge
column7: The Hadith: one who mortgages gets its benefits and bears its expenses
column8: The verse: if one of you deposits a thing on trust with another
column10: Per the basis, the Prophet said: 'The one who mortgages the asset should get its benefits and bear its expenses', since the asset belongs to the mortgagor.

column4: A client offers Bank A preference shares and interest-based bonds as mortgage for a Murabahah debt. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the Bank donates the interest earned
column6: Impermissible, as Shari'ah bars their issue and trading
column7: Permissible, as the Bank only holds them as security
column8: Permissible if the bonds are government-issued
column10: Per 4/3, papers that may not be issued or transacted under Shari'ah, e.g. interest-based bonds, preference shares and enjoyment shares, cannot be mortgaged.

column4: A client offers Bank A a stock of wine as mortgage for a Murabahah debt. What is the ruling?
column5: Not acceptable; it must be Shari'ah-permissible property
column6: Acceptable, if its value exceeds the debt amount
column7: Acceptable, if the Bank never takes physical possession
column8: Acceptable, if the client is not a Muslim
column10: Per 3/2/1, the mortgaged asset must be Shari'ah-permissible property, well specified, and deliverable.

column4: With Bank A's permission, a mortgagor sells the mortgaged car to Ahmad, who does not agree to keep the mortgage. What happens to the mortgage?
column5: It continues and binds Ahmad as new owner
column6: It ceases, due to the permitted transfer of ownership
column7: It transfers automatically to another asset of the seller
column8: It continues, and the sale itself is void
column10: Per 3/1/6, the mortgage expires on transfer of ownership (sale, gift or will) with the mortgagee's permission, unless the new owner accepts to keep it.

column4: Bank A holds a client's documents of title to goods as mortgage. Per the basis, why is this permissible?
column5: Documents are cash and thus valid as mortgage, like any other monetary instrument
column6: Documents give the Bank ownership of the goods
column7: Possession of the documents counts as possession of the goods
column8: Documents are a debt owed by the shipper to the Bank, which the Bank may collect on demand
column10: Per the basis, holding documents representing ownership of goods as mortgage is permissible because their possession is considered possession of the goods.

column4: How do the Hanafi scholars justify stipulating a mortgage as a condition in a sale, per the basis?
column5: It transfers risk of the goods to the seller
column6: It is a condition that serves only the seller's profit, not documentation
column7: It is required to make any sale valid
column8: It suits the contract because it entails contract documentation
column10: Per the basis, the Hanafis see it as a condition that suits and conforms to the contract since it entails documentation, like stipulating the quality of the price.

column4: A seller in a deferred sale stipulates that he retains ownership of the sold item until the price is paid. Per the basis, why is this not allowed?
column5: Retention of ownership is a form of Riba
column6: Ownership can pass only after full payment anyway in all deferred sales
column7: He willingly gave up his right to spot payment of the price
column8: It makes the sale an adhesion contract
column10: Per the basis (Hanbali view), the seller cannot retain ownership until a deferred price is paid, since he willingly relinquished his right to spot payment.

column4: Those who validate a mortgage signed before the debt contract compare it, per the basis, to which arrangement?
column5: A Wadi'ah deposit kept on trust basis
column6: A Hamish Jiddiyyah paid with a promise to purchase, which the buyer forfeits if he withdraws
column7: An 'Arboun paid in advance in a sale
column8: A darak guarantee against a third party claim on the asset
column10: Per the basis, a mortgage before the debt documents a valid right and is for something in the future, similar to a guarantee and a darak guarantee.

column4: A buyer on deferred terms promised to give a mortgage as a condition of the sale but refuses to provide it. Per the Hanafi view in the basis, what does the seller have?
column5: The right of option
column6: The right to keep the price and the goods
column7: The right to charge a late payment fee
column8: No right, as the condition is void
column10: Per the basis, refraining from honoring a valid condition like the mortgage condition gives the concerned party the right of option (Hanafi view).

column4: Why must a mortgaged asset be Shari'ah-permissible property, per the basis?
column5: Only permissible assets may be held in trust by banks
column6: It must be sold to settle the debt, and banned objects cannot be
column7: Impermissible assets cannot be insured by the mortgagor under Islamic insurance
column8: Impermissible assets have no market value at all
column10: Per the basis, the objective is to sell the asset to settle the debt; a Muslim cannot repay debts with Shari'ah-banned objects such as alcohol and swine.

column4: A client who mortgaged his house to Bank A dies before repaying the debt. What happens to the mortgage contract?
column5: It remains valid only if the heirs renew it
column6: It terminates and the debt becomes unsecured
column7: It remains valid and his inheritors substitute him
column8: It terminates and the Bank becomes owner of the house
column10: Per 3/1/5, the death of the mortgagor or mortgagee has no effect on the validity of the mortgage; the respective inheritors substitute the dead party.

column4: A farmer offers Bank A a stock of fresh vegetables as mortgage for a debt. May perishable objects be mortgaged?
column5: No; perishable objects cannot be possessed
column6: Yes, as they can be sold and replaced by their value
column7: No; only tangible durable assets may be mortgaged
column8: Yes, but only if the debt matures within a week
column10: Per 3/2/2, perishable objects can be mortgaged as they can be sold and replaced by their value.

column4: Ahmad owns a 30% share in a jointly owned building and offers it to Bank A as mortgage. When is this permissible?
column5: Never; common property cannot be mortgaged
column6: Only when the Bank takes physical possession of the whole
column7: Only when the co-owners mortgage the whole building
column8: When the share can be identified and sold separately
column10: Per 3/2/2, a mortgaged object can be a share of common property which can be identified and sold separately.

column4: On what evidence does the basis rely to show that mortgage is permissible even when the parties are not travelling?
column5: The Prophet mortgaged his armor to a Jew in Al-Madinah for barley
column6: The verse on depositing a thing on trust with another
column7: The consensus that travel is a condition of mortgage
column8: The verse requiring a scribe to record every deferred debt in writing
column10: Per the basis, Anas reported that the Prophet mortgaged his armor plate to a Jew in Al-Madinah and took barley for his family.

column4: A client mortgages his current account to Bank A, where it is held. The Bank wants to use the balance in its operations. What is required?
column5: Payment of a fixed return to the client for the use
column6: Nothing; a current account is a loan that the Bank may freely use anyway
column7: The client's verbal consent only, with no change
column8: Agreement to convert it into a Mudarabah investment account
column10: Per 5, the Institution should not use the mortgaged current account unless both agree to transfer it to an investment account under Mudarabah, avoiding free benefit.

column4: Ahmad's zakatable assets are mortgaged to Bank A and he cannot dispose of them. Who must pay the Zakah on them?
column5: No one, since disposal is restricted
column6: Ahmad, as the owner of the mortgaged asset
column7: Bank A, as the possessor of the asset
column8: Ahmad and Bank A in proportion to the debt
column10: Per 9/1, the owner of the mortgaged asset pays Zakah if due; his inability to dispose of the mortgaged asset does not relieve him from Zakah.

column4: A client offers Bank A, as mortgage, usufruct-based Sukuk representing common shares in the usufructs of specific assets. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible, as usufructs cannot be sold
column6: Permissible only if converted into tangible assets
column7: Permissible to mortgage them
column8: Impermissible unless the lessee agrees
column10: Per 4/2, it is permissible to mortgage usufruct-based Sukuk representing common shares in the usufructs of specific assets.

column4: A client mortgages to Bank A a debt owed to him by Company X; other creditors of the client also claim that debt. Who has the stronger claim?
column5: Bank A, as mortgagee, is more entitled to it
column6: All creditors share it in proportion to their claims
column7: The earliest creditor of the client, whoever it is
column8: Company X decides whom to pay first
column10: Per 3/2/12, when a debt is mortgaged, the mortgagee becomes more entitled to it than anyone else.

column4: Bank A stipulated that the mortgagor appoint it as agent to sell the mortgaged asset on default without resort to judiciary. The mortgagor later wants to revoke this agency. Can he?
column5: Yes, but only before any default occurs
column6: Yes, since agency is a non-binding contract
column7: No, unless he deposits cash equal to the debt
column8: No; he cannot retreat from such agency once agreed
column10: Per 3/1/4, the mortgagee may stipulate this agency to sell without judiciary, and the mortgagor has no right to retreat from it once agreed upon.

column4: Through Bank A's negligence, a mortgaged machine is destroyed. What is the treatment?
column5: The Bank pays its value on the date of perish; the debt remains
column6: The Bank owes nothing, as the asset was a trust
column7: The debt is cancelled entirely, whatever the value of the destroyed machine
column8: The Bank compensates the value at the contract date
column10: Per 3/2/4, on perish due to negligence the mortgagee compensates the value on the date of perish; the debt remains and the parties may set one off against the other.

column4: A client mortgages to Bank A a debt owed to him by Company X. How does possession of this mortgaged debt take place?
column5: Only by Company X signing a new debt contract directly with the Bank
column6: By possessing the debt's document or attesting the debt
column7: Only by collecting the debt from Company X in cash
column8: It cannot take place, as debts cannot be mortgaged
column10: Per 3/2/11-3/2/12, debt may be mortgaged; possession is by possession of the debt's document or attestation of the debt when mortgaged.

column4: A client offers shares of a company with permissible original activities, but where Riba-based dealings form a predominant part of its activities. May Bank A accept them as mortgage?
column5: Yes, if the Bank purifies the dividends
column6: Yes, since its original activities are permissible, whatever the share of Riba dealings
column7: No; such shares are among papers that cannot be mortgaged
column8: Yes, if the company is listed on an exchange
column10: Per 4/3, impermissible mortgages include shares of companies with permissible original activities but where Riba-based dealings are a predominant part.

column4: Bank A issues a back-to-back documentary credit for a client against another credit. Per the basis, why is this permissible?
column5: A credit creates a bank debt to the client, which may be mortgaged
column6: Documentary credits are Mudarabah investments that may be pledged freely
column7: Documentary credits involve no debt at all
column8: The second credit is a gift from the bank
column10: Per the basis, a documentary credit results in a debt owed by the bank to the client, and such debt can be mortgaged to obtain a new debt.

column4: A client mortgages his units in an Islamic investment fund to Bank A. What may the Bank do with respect to his redemption rights?
column5: Take ownership of the units until repayment
column6: Suspend them absolutely or in proportion to the debt
column7: Sell the units immediately on signing
column8: Nothing; redemption rights cannot be restricted
column10: Per 6/1, the Institution as mortgagee can suspend the client's right to get back or draw, absolutely or in proportion to the debt, whichever is more suitable.

column4: A client defaults and fails to redeem his mortgaged asset. Per the Hadith on foreclosure cited in the basis, what follows?
column5: The mortgagee becomes owner after one full year of continued default
column6: The mortgagee becomes owner, as was the practice
column7: The asset passes to the State Treasury
column8: Failure to redeem does not make the mortgagee owner of the asset
column10: Per the basis, the Hadith 'Mortgage should not be foreclosed from its owner' means failure to redeem does not entitle the mortgagee to the asset, unlike Jahiliyyah practice.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A wants to charge a fee for opening investment accounts. How should this fee be set?
column5: As a monthly charge based on the account balance
column6: As a percentage of the deposit amount, charged annually for the account
column7: As a lump sum, charged once, preferably not above average actual cost
column8: As a share of the profit earned by the account
column10: Per 2/2/4, the opening fee should be a lump sum, preferably not exceeding average actual cost, and charged once at the time of opening the account.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A announced an expected rate of return of 7% based on a feasibility study, but actual realized profit is 5%. What is distributed?
column5: 6%, the average of expected and actual
column6: The actual realized profit after liquidation
column7: 7%, as the announced rate is binding
column8: 7%, with the Bank covering the shortfall
column10: Per 5/2, an expected rate of return is not binding if not achieved; final distribution is based on profit realized after actual or constructive liquidation.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A client transfers funds from his USD account to his EUR account at Bank A. What form of possession suffices for this exchange?
column5: Actual possession of cash in each currency
column6: Possession after two working days
column7: Constructive possession is sufficient
column8: Physical delivery of the euro banknotes
column10: Per 2/2/6, in transfers between accounts, constructive possession is sufficient, for the same or different currencies, as the process involves exchange and transference.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Why is a lump sum or percentage of capital as a party's return prohibited in Mudarabah, per the basis?
column5: It eliminates profit sharing, the essence of the partnership
column6: It makes the expenses too high for the Mudarib, who must pay them from his own pocket
column7: It conflicts with the scoring method of distribution
column8: It requires constructive liquidation every month
column10: Per the basis, it eliminates profit sharing, a fundamental aspect of Mudarabah; e.g. if profit only equals the lump sum, the partnership's essence is lost.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A paid monthly amounts to holders before liquidation. After constructive liquidation, a holder's actual share is lower. What must the Bank do?
column5: Nothing; advance payments are final
column6: Carry the difference into the next period's profit of the investment pool
column7: Cover the difference from its own Mudarib share
column8: Deduct the difference so each receives his exact profit share
column10: Per 5/3, advance payments are permitted; after liquidation the Institution makes necessary additions or deductions so each holder receives his exact share.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: After liquidation, Bank A's shareholders, as Mudarib, decide to give up part of their profit share to the account holders. What must the Bank do?
column5: Disclose that relinquishment
column6: Nothing, as it is a purely internal matter
column7: Obtain approval of each account holder
column8: Treat it as a binding term for future periods
column10: Per 5/6, when the shareholders as Mudarib relinquish part of their profit share to accountholders after liquidation, the Institution should disclose that.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A client deposits a large quantity of banknotes over the counter, while another transfers the same amount electronically to the Bank's account. For which deposit may a handling fee be charged?
column5: Neither deposit, as all deposit fees are prohibited
column6: Each of the two deposits, at the same rate
column7: Only the electronic transfer, for the processing and communication costs it involves
column8: Only the banknotes deposit, for transport, storage and counting
column10: Per 2/2/5, the Institution may charge a fee for transportation, storage and counting of cash handed to the cashier; this does not include amounts transferred to it.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A agrees with holders that profit is shared 30:70, but any profit above a 6% index goes to the Bank. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible, as profit must always be shared in ratios
column6: Impermissible, as it is a lump sum for the Bank
column7: Permissible; profit at or below the index is shared as agreed
column8: Permissible only if the excess goes to the holders
column10: Per 4/4, a lump sum for one party voids Mudarabah, but agreeing that profit above a limit or index goes to one party is allowed; up to it, profit is shared as agreed.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: To attract customers, Bank A offers to pay a small variable increment on current account balances in addition to full repayment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if it is called a gift in the account terms
column6: Impermissible, as such increment constitutes usurious interest
column7: Permissible, if it is paid from shareholders' profit
column8: Permissible, as it is variable and not fixed in advance, so it is not usurious interest
column10: Per 2/2/2, the Institution must guarantee current accounts but must not commit to any fixed or variable increment on them, as that constitutes usurious interest.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A cannot transfer funds to an account holder because he changed his address. After the specified period the funds go to charity, and later he reappears. What happens?
column5: The Bank keeps them as income for the period
column6: He loses them, as they were already given to charity
column7: He receives them only if he proves need
column8: The funds are paid to him from the charity account
column10: Per 2/2/7, such funds are kept in a suspended account then added to the charity account; if the owners' addresses become known, they are paid from the charity account.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A holder exits Bank A's investment pool. Per the Mubara'ah stipulation, what happens to his rights in the remaining reserves for investment risks?
column5: He receives his share of them in cash on exit
column6: He relieves the remaining holders of them
column7: They are transferred to the Bank as Mudarib
column8: They are held for him until the pool is liquidated
column10: Per 5/4, the exiting party relieves the holders of his rights in undistributed profit and the remaining reserves and allocations; holders relieve him of unapparent losses.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A's unrestricted investment accounts incur a loss with no transgression, negligence or breach by the Bank. Who bears the loss?
column5: The Bank as Mudarib, from its own funds
column6: The Bank and the holders in the profit-sharing ratio
column7: The account holders, in proportion to their shares in the capital
column8: The shareholders, as the Bank guarantees the investment accounts' capital
column10: Per 2/1/1, holders of unrestricted accounts bear all losses in proportion to their capital shares, except losses from transgression, negligence or breach, borne by the Institution.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A proposes that holders take all profit from Q1 operations while the Bank takes all profit from Q2 operations. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible to allocate a period's profit to one party
column6: Permissible, if agreed in the account opening form
column7: Permissible, as each party still shares overall
column8: Permissible, if the two periods are of equal length and the holders agree to it in advance
column10: Per 4/5, allocating the profit of a certain period or transaction to one party and of another period or transaction to the other is impermissible.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A plans to give its shareholders' funds better investment opportunities than the funds of its participatory Mudarabah account holders. What must it do?
column5: Nothing; shareholders always have priority in investments
column6: Obtain each holder's written consent after the investment
column7: Disclose that policy before disposition
column8: Compensate holders with a fixed return on their capital
column10: Per 2/1/3, equality in investment opportunities should in principle be ensured; a different policy must be disclosed before disposition.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A's investment accounts lost money in 2025. Bank A wants to cover the loss from 2026 profits directly. What is the ruling?
column5: Not allowed, except by covering the loss from reserves
column6: Allowed, but only from the Mudarib's share
column7: Allowed, as all periods form one continuing Mudarabah contract between the parties
column8: Allowed, if holders do not object
column10: Per 3/2/1, the loss of one financial period should not be covered from the profits of another period, except in the case of covering losses from reserves.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Per the IIFA resolution cited in the basis, how are current accounts in Islamic banks characterised?
column5: As loans only if the bank is insolvent
column6: As trusts that the bank must not use
column7: As Mudarabah funds sharing in the profit and loss of the bank
column8: As loans held under guarantee and repayable on demand
column10: Per the basis (IIFA 86 (9/3)), current accounts are loans; the bank holds them under guarantee and repays on demand; its solvency does not affect the ruling.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: In computing distributable profit, at what stage is the reserve for investment risks deducted?
column5: Only from shareholders' funds
column6: After deducting the Mudarib's share
column7: From gross profit, before the Mudarib's share
column8: From the capital of the investment accounts
column10: Per 3/1/2/3, allocations for bad debts and the reserve for rate of return are deducted from gross profit, while the reserve for investment risks is deducted after the Mudarib's share.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: An investment account holder demands that Bank A guarantee repayment of his deposit after an investment loss with no fault of the Bank. What is the ruling?
column5: The Bank must guarantee it, as all deposits are guaranteed
column6: The Bank guarantees half of it as Mudarib
column7: The Bank guarantees it if it was held for over a year
column8: No; investment accounts are held on trust
column10: Per 2/2/1-2/2/2, investment accounts are held on trust and not guaranteed except for transgression, negligence or breach; profit or loss is distributed as agreed.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A holder exits the Mudarabah with part of his funds before the period ends. Bank A sets the exit amount so that it earns less profit. How is this characterised?
column5: Impermissible penalty imposed on the holder for withdrawing before the period ends
column6: Permissible exit on the basis of supply and demand
column7: Impermissible deprivation of the holder from the profit he is entitled to receive
column8: Permissible only if the holder pays a fee
column10: Per 4/9, the holder may exit, and the Institution may set the exit amount to earn no or less profit; this is exit on supply and demand, not deprivation from profit.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Per the basis, which principle supports the approximation inherent in the scoring method of profit distribution?
column5: More exemptions are allowed in partnerships than in exchange dealings
column6: Each depositor's exact profit must be traced
column7: Exchange dealings tolerate more Gharar and approximation than partnerships
column8: Profit is deserved only for contribution of work
column10: Per the basis, much more exemptions are allowed in Musharakat than in Mu'awadah, and division (Qismah) by approximation of shares rests on mutual consent.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Holders deposit and withdraw at different times during the period in Bank A's general investment pool. Which method can be used to distribute profit among them?
column5: Equal shares for every account regardless of the amount deposited
column6: Shares based only on the opening balance
column7: The scoring method: amount multiplied by period of stay
column8: Shares based only on the year-end balance
column10: Per 5/1, the scoring method (currency unit x time unit) can be used; holders implicitly exchange Mubara'ah for aspects that cannot practically be catered for.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A uses current account balances to fund its own Murabahah deals. What is the status of these balances and the Bank's use of them?
column5: Loans it guarantees, which it may invest at its own risk and benefit
column6: They are Mudarabah funds; holders share the profit
column7: They are loans, but any profit earned on them must be shared with the holders
column8: They are trusts; it may not use them at all
column10: Per 2/2/1, current accounts are loans the Institution guarantees on demand; it may dispose of and invest them for its own benefit and under its own responsibility.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A Mudarabah investment account contract sets no profit ratios at signing, and there is no normal practice to refer to. What is the result?
column5: Ratios are set later by the Bank at distribution
column6: Void; the Mudarib gets a normal wage and Rab al-Mal all profit
column7: Profit is shared equally between the two parties
column8: The Mudarib takes the whole profit as reward for the work he performed
column10: Per 4/2, if ratios are unspecified and no normal practice exists, the Mudarabah is void; the Mudarib gets the wage for similar work and all profit goes to Rab al-Mal.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Two parties to a Mudarabah defer setting profit ratios until profit is earned. Per the basis, why is this impermissible?
column5: It makes the Mudarib a guarantor of capital
column6: It prevents covering expenses from the profit
column7: It turns the Mudarabah into a loan with interest
column8: It leads to Jahalah, which could lead to dispute
column10: Per the basis, postponing profit ratios leads to Jahalah (ignorance) which could lead to dispute; but agreeing at distribution to change ratios or donate is allowed.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A invests the liquidity portion of unrestricted investment accounts in short-term instruments without holders' consent; a loss arises without negligence. Who bears it?
column5: The Bank and holders equally
column6: The central bank holding the reserve
column7: The account holders as Arbab al-Mal
column8: The Bank, as it invested without consent
column10: Per 4/10/2, the Bank may invest liquidity funds without consent in unrestricted Mudarabah; returns join the investment base and losses without fault are borne by the holders.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A wants to charge investment accounts with the expenses of its investment department and its follow-up and accounting departments. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if disclosed in the account terms
column6: Permitted, as they relate to the accounts' investments
column7: Permitted, up to half of the gross profit
column8: Not permitted; these are tasks the Mudarib must perform
column10: Per 3/1/2/2, investment accounts are not charged with expenses of tasks the Mudarib must perform, e.g. investment departments, follow-up and accounting departments.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A wants to distribute profit without converting all Mudarabah assets into cash. Which method of liquidation may it use?
column5: Constructive liquidation, with expert valuation of assets and debts
column6: Estimation based on the expected rate of return
column7: Valuation of all assets by the Bank's own board at their book value
column8: None; actual liquidation into cash is always required
column10: Per 3/1/2/1, liquidation may be constructive: noncash assets are valued by experts, debts valued for collectability, with allocations for bad debts.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: An operation of Bank A's unrestricted investment pool spans two financial periods. How is its profit allocated?
column5: Entirely to the period in which it is completed
column6: Equally between the two periods, regardless of the time in each one
column7: Over the whole period of the operation, by each period's duration
column8: Entirely to the period in which it started
column10: Per 3/2/2, profit from operations extending to succeeding periods is distributed over the whole period of such operations in proportion to the duration of each operation.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A and its investment account holders agree to give a part of the profit to a charitable third party. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible, as profit belongs only to the parties
column6: Permissible by agreement of the two parties
column7: Permissible only from the Bank's share
column8: Permissible only if the third party contributed work
column10: Per 4/8, in principle profit belongs to the Institution and the holder, but they can agree to allocate a certain part of it to a third party.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: In one financial period, one Mudarabah operation of Bank A lost 50 while others earned 200. How is the loss treated?
column5: It is borne by the Bank as Mudarib, since it managed the operation that lost money
column6: It is carried forward to next period's profits
column7: It is charged to the capital before the profits
column8: It is covered from the profits of the other operations
column10: Per 3/2/1, a loss in one operation may be covered from the profits of other operations; if it exceeds them, from capital. The final liquidation result matters.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A restricted investment account suffers a loss because Bank A invested in a project outside the one specified by the account holder. Who bears the loss?
column5: The holder and the Bank equally
column6: The Bank, as it arises from breach of the contract
column7: The holder, as restricted accounts bear all losses
column8: The account holder, in proportion to his capital
column10: Per 2/1/2, the holder bears losses in proportion to his capital share, except losses from transgression, negligence or breach of contract, borne by the Institution.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A, as Mudarib, mixes its own funds with the investment account funds. How is the profit divided?
column5: The Bank earns only as Mudarib, not on its funds
column6: The Bank takes all profit attributable to the pool
column7: Between the two capitals; the Bank earns as partner and Mudarib
column8: The Bank earns only as partner on its funds, losing its Mudarib share
column10: Per 4/7, mixing makes the Mudarib a partner by its funds and Mudarib for the other funds; profit is divided between the two capitals.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Which Hadith does the basis cite for the rule that no profit is sought before preservation of capital?
column5: A prayer performer is like a merchant: profit only after capital
column6: Profit is distributed as agreed, while loss follows capital contribution
column7: The one who mortgages should get benefits and bear expenses
column8: When someone liberates a co-owned slave he should pay partners
column10: Per the basis, the Hadith likens a prayer performer to a merchant who obtains profit only after preserving his capital; profit is an increment on the principal.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A's account terms promise holders 5% of their capital annually as their share of profit. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the Bank has enough reserves
column6: Permissible, as the percentage is fixed and known
column7: Permissible, if it is called an expected return
column8: Impermissible; profit must be shared in ratios
column10: Per 4/1, profit must be distributed in ratios, never as a lump sum, a percentage of capital, or any method that could avoid sharing of profit.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Per the basis, on what ground is distributing profit on constructive liquidation permissible?
column5: Shari'ah accepts valuation in several applications, such as Zakah
column6: Expected returns are binding on the Institution
column7: Mudarabah profit is a lump sum fixed in advance
column8: Valuation is accepted in Shari'ah only where the assets are all in cash
column10: Per the basis, it rests on acceptance of valuation in Shari'ah in applications such as Zakah and theft, with the Hadith on valuing a co-owned liberated slave.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Ahmad opens a savings account at Bank A that carries no authorization to invest the funds for his benefit. Which rulings apply to it?
column5: The rulings on unrestricted investment accounts
column6: The rulings on current accounts
column7: The rulings on restricted investment accounts
column8: The rulings on investment agency accounts
column10: Per 2/2/3, savings accounts without authorization to invest for the holder are subject to the rulings on current accounts; with such authorization, investment account rulings.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Account terms state that Bank A's financial statements are authoritative. An account holder disputes a figure in them. What is the position?
column5: The Bank must prove each figure if challenged
column6: They are void, as clauses making the Bank's own statements authoritative are impermissible
column7: They are authoritative unless the holder proves them wrong
column8: They are authoritative and cannot be challenged
column10: Per 2/2/9-2/2/10, authoritative status of the Institution's statements may be stipulated unless proved wrong; the claimant holder bears the cost of proving the accusation.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A distributed profit to investment account holders mid-year, but at year-end the capital was not fully protected. How is the earlier distribution treated?
column5: As an advance payment, not realized profit
column6: As a loan from the holders to the Bank
column7: As a gift from the Bank to the holders
column8: As realized profit that cannot be adjusted
column10: Per 3/1/1, profit is not realized before protecting the capital; any amount distributed before that is an advance payment rather than realized profit.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Partners agree profit ratios that differ from their capital ratios. Per the Hanbali view in the basis, why is this allowed?
column5: Loss may also be shared by agreed ratios
column6: Profit ratios must follow the scoring method
column7: Profit is deserved for funds, work or guarantee
column8: Profit is deserved only for contribution of funds
column10: Per the basis, profit is deserved for contribution of funds, work or guarantee, so partners may set ratios not commensurate with their shares (Hanbali view).

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Why does ignorance about the profit share nullify a Mudarabah contract, per the basis?
column5: Profit must equal the expected rate of return
column6: Profit is the object of contracting and must be known
column7: Profit belongs only to the Mudarib, so the capital provider need not know its share
column8: Ignorance makes the capital guaranteed
column10: Per the basis, profit has to be known because it constitutes the object of contracting, so ignorance about it nullifies the contract.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Why is earmarking the profit of a specific portion of capital for one party prohibited, per the basis?
column5: It makes the capital unknown at the outset
column6: It requires the Mudarib to guarantee capital
column7: It breaches the rule on equality of investment opportunities for funds
column8: It could jeopardize profit sharing and lead to oppression
column10: Per the basis, earmarking the profit of a specific portion of capital for one party could jeopardize the process of profit sharing and lead to oppression.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: On final liquidation of Bank A's investment base, some reserves for investment risk and rate of return remain. Per the Mubara'ah stipulation, where do they go?
column5: They go to the Bank's shareholders
column6: They are devoted to charitable purposes
column7: They are added to the Bank's general reserves
column8: They are returned to the last holders only
column10: Per 5/4, the stipulation should indicate that on liquidation of the investment base the remaining reserves and allocations are devoted to charitable purposes.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: A Mudarabah term makes the Mudarib bear all losses. Which statement does the basis cite against such a term?
column5: The Hadith of the merchant who profits only after preserving his capital
column6: The IIFA resolution that deposits are loans
column7: Ali's saying: profit as agreed, loss per capital contribution
column8: The Hadith on discounts for calamities
column10: Per the basis, Ali Ibn Abu Talib said profit is distributed as agreed, while loss is borne per capital ratios; charging one party with the other's loss is oppressive.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A wants to change the profit sharing ratios of its investment accounts but finds individual correspondence too costly. What may it do?
column5: Change them without any notice, as Mudarib
column6: It may never change ratios once the account is opened, even with consent
column7: Apply the new ratios immediately to the current period
column8: Notify or advertise it; if no protest, it applies from next period
column10: Per 2/2/8, the Institution may notify or advertise on its website; implicit acceptance arises if no protest within a period, effective from the beginning of the next period.

column3: Distribution of Profit in Mudarabah-Based Investment Accounts
column4: Bank A manages some investment accounts on the basis of investment agency rather than Mudarabah. Does the standard on profit distribution in investment accounts cover them?
column5: No; agency-based accounts need a separate standard
column6: Yes; it covers all investment accounts of the Institution
column7: No; such accounts are treated as current accounts
column8: Yes, but only restricted accounts under agency
column10: Per 1, the standard covers Mudarabah-based investment accounts and does not cover accounts managed on the basis of investment agency, which require a separate standard.

column4: Allocations deducted from a solidarity reinsurance fund remain unpaid on liquidation. Per the basis, how are they treated?
column5: Returned to participants in proportion to contributions
column6: Paid to the company as Mudarib
column7: Spent on charitable purposes, not given to participants
column8: Transferred to the shareholders' equity
column10: Per the basis (j), such unpaid allocations at liquidation are spent on charitable purposes and not given to participants, unlike in commercial reinsurance.

column4: A traditional reinsurer pays Islamic Insurance Company X the amount of insurance coverage for a large claim. May X receive it?
column5: No; all amounts from traditional reinsurers are prohibited
column6: Yes; receiving the coverage amounts is permissible
column7: Yes, but it must be given to charity
column8: Only after deducting the interest component
column10: Per 7/1, it is permissible for Islamic insurance companies to receive the amounts of the insurance coverage from traditional reinsurance companies.

column4: In Islamic reinsurance, who owns the contributions paid in, per the basis?
column5: The reinsurance company
column6: The participants individually
column7: The company's shareholders
column8: The reinsurance account
column10: Per the basis (c), in commercial reinsurance the company owns premiums, while in Islamic reinsurance the company does not own the contributions; the reinsurance account does.

column4: On what ground does the basis hold commercial reinsurance impermissible?
column5: It rests on commercial insurance and involves prohibited Gharar
