column6: It is a donation contract lacking possession
column7: It involves deferment of both of the objects of exchange in the contract
column8: It gives the reinsurer no right of option
column10: Per the basis, commercial reinsurance depends on commercial insurance and involves prohibited Gharar; the Prophet prohibited Bay' al-Gharar.

column4: A reinsurance company acting as agent claims it must guarantee the reinsurance account's losses. Per the basis, what is the rule?
column5: An agent guarantees half of any loss
column6: An agent guarantees only for transgression, negligence or breach
column7: An agent guarantees if it charges a fee
column8: An agent always guarantees the principal's funds whether at fault or not
column10: Per the basis, by unanimous agreement of Fiqh scholars an agent should not guarantee except in case of transgression, negligence or breach of the contract.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X keeps all policies whose risks it can easily tolerate and reinsures only those whose risks it cannot tolerate. Which form is this?
column5: Excess risk reinsurance
column6: Comprehensive reinsurance
column7: Risk sharing reinsurance
column8: Loss reinsurance
column10: Per 5/2, in excess risk reinsurance the insurer keeps policies it can tolerate and seeks reinsurance for those involving risks it cannot tolerate.

column4: After expenses and compensations, part of the contributions and their returns remain in an Islamic reinsurance account. Per the basis, where does it go?
column5: To the traditional reinsurers as a rebate
column6: To the company as revenue and profit, as compensation for managing the reinsurance account
column7: To the company's shareholders as dividend
column8: To the policyholders' account as surplus for participants
column10: Per the basis (d), the remaining contributions and returns go to the policyholders' account as distributable surplus, unlike commercial reinsurance where they are revenue.

column4: A traditional insurer asks Islamic Reinsurer R, using an Islamic reinsurance contract, to reinsure the risks of a liquor factory. May R accept?
column5: Yes, since the client is a traditional insurer
column6: Yes, since the Islamic reinsurance contract is used
column7: No; the reinsurance must not involve a prohibited object
column8: Yes, if the premiums are given to charity
column10: Per 8/3, reinsurance for traditional insurers is permitted only if it does not involve a Shari'ah-prohibited object, among other conditions.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X can obtain full cover from Islamic reinsurers but prefers a traditional reinsurer for lower cost. May it reinsure with the traditional reinsurer?
column5: No; only a transitional need amounting to necessity permits it
column6: Yes, if the cost saving is passed to participants
column7: Yes, if the traditional reinsurer is highly rated
column8: Yes, if the Shari'ah Board approves the arrangement after signing it
column10: Per 3/1/1 and 3/2, reinsuring with Islamic reinsurers is permissible; with traditional ones it is impermissible except as a transitional arrangement from public need amounting to necessity.

column4: What distinguishes traditional reinsurance from Islamic reinsurance, according to the definition in the standard?
column5: It is formed by agreement among insurance companies
column6: It covers only part of the risks that the insurance funds may encounter
column7: It is based on exchange of premiums and compensation, not donation
column8: It has a fund with a distinct legal personality
column10: Per 2/2, Islamic reinsurance is the alternative to traditional reinsurance, which is based on exchange of reinsurance premiums and compensation rather than donation commitments.

column4: Per the basis, what supports Islamic insurers reinsuring with traditional reinsurers in some cases?
column5: The lower cost of traditional reinsurance cover
column6: Practical necessity and dire public need ranking as necessity
column7: The agency nature of traditional reinsurers
column8: The view that Gharar does not affect exchange-based reinsurance contracts
column10: Per the basis, permissibility rests on practical necessity from lack of Islamic cover and dire public need ranking as necessity, recognised by Qur'an and Sunnah.

column4: An Islamic insurance company asks whether the standard on Islamic reinsurance governs the Islamic insurance policies it issues directly to individuals. What is the answer?
column5: Yes, but only policies issued to companies
column6: Yes; it covers all Islamic insurance and reinsurance
column7: No; direct policies are governed by conventional law
column8: No; Islamic insurance is covered by a separate standard
column10: Per 1, the standard covers Islamic reinsurance and participation with traditional insurers or reinsurers; it does not cover Islamic insurance, covered separately.

column4: A traditional reinsurer asks Islamic Insurance Company X to keep cash reserves for ongoing risks that belong to the reinsurer, on which X pays interest. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the interest is paid only from the shareholders' own funds
column6: Not permitted; X should not keep such interest-bearing reserves
column7: Permitted, as the reserves belong to the reinsurer
column8: Permitted, if the reserves are held for under a year
column10: Per 6/2, Islamic insurers should not keep cash reserves for ongoing risks belonging to traditional reinsurers on which interest has to be paid.

column4: Islamic Reinsurer R is asked to provide reinsurance to a traditional insurance company. Which condition applies?
column5: R must first convert the traditional insurer into an Islamic insurance company
column6: It is never allowed for an Islamic reinsurer
column7: The traditional insurer's contract may be used if fair
column8: The Islamic reinsurance contract must be used, with no linkage
column10: Per 8/3, it is permissible subject to: use of the Islamic reinsurance contract, no linkage, and no Shari'ah-prohibited object.

column4: A participant company claims more compensation than the actual harm it suffered. Which principle in the basis limits reinsurance coverage?
column5: Coverage is set by the reinsurer at its discretion
column6: Coverage equals the contribution paid in
column7: Coverage is for actual harm only, not for making wealth
column8: Coverage includes expected profits of the insured
column10: Per the basis, coverage rests on 'No harm and no reciprocal harm' and the rule that coverage is for actual harms and not for making wealth out of it.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X earns a Mudarib share from investing premiums retained for a traditional reinsurer. Where is this share credited?
column5: To the account of the participants
column6: To the account of the traditional reinsurer
column7: To a charity account, as it arises from dealing
column8: To X's shareholders as a fee income
column10: Per 6/2, the reinsurer's profit share goes to its account with the Islamic insurer, while the Islamic insurer's share as an independent personality goes to the participants' account.

column4: On what basis are contributions made to an Islamic reinsurance fund out of the insurance funds?
column5: On the basis of a sale of risk to the reinsurer
column6: On the basis of Qard Hasan to the reinsurer
column7: On the basis of exchange of premium and compensation
column8: On the basis of donation
column10: Per 2/1-2/2, contributions are made out of insurance funds on the basis of donation, unlike traditional reinsurance based on exchange of premiums and compensation.

column4: For a large claim, Islamic Insurance Company X bears the first USD 20,000 and the reinsurer bears the rest of the compensation. Which form is this?
column5: Excess risk reinsurance
column6: Risk sharing reinsurance
column7: Loss reinsurance
column8: Selective reinsurance
column10: Per 5/3, in loss reinsurance the reinsurer bears losses beyond an agreed limit, e.g. the insurer bears the first 20 thousand dollars and the reinsurer the rest.

column4: Per the basis, the Islamic reinsurance contract is a binding donation by analogy to which practice?
column5: Hamish Jiddiyyah paid with a promise
column6: Munahadah: travelers' contribution to a pool of food
column7: Mudarabah between the reinsurance company and the reinsurance fund
column8: Bay' al-Gharar, the aleatory sale
column10: Per the basis, the contract is a binding donation, analogous to Munahadah (travelers' contribution to a pool of food victuals) or to a pledge of donation.

column4: A traditional reinsurer announces a redistribution of its insurance surplus to its clients, including Islamic Insurance Company X. What should X do?
column5: Not accept it, though it may request premium discounts
column6: Accept it and give it all to charity
column7: Accept it and credit it to participants' account, as it belongs to the insurance fund
column8: Accept it only if it is below a set limit
column10: Per 7/3, Islamic insurers should not accept redistributions of insurance surplus from traditional reinsurers, but may request premium discounts.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X needs traditional reinsurance for one year only, but the reinsurer proposes a five-year agreement. What does the standard require?
column5: The period is set by the reinsurer alone
column6: The period should be commensurate with the actual need
column7: Any period may be agreed once necessity to use traditional reinsurance exists
column8: The period must be at least five years
column10: Per 6/3, the periods of reinsurance agreements with traditional reinsurers should be commensurate to the actual need.

column4: Islamic Reinsurer R applies the Shari'ah controls set for Islamic insurance companies. Who are treated as the participants in R's scheme?
column5: The insurance companies
column6: The shareholders of the reinsurer
column7: The traditional reinsurers it deals with
column8: The individual policyholders of each insurer
column10: Per 8/1, Islamic reinsurers observe the controls of the Islamic insurance standard, considering that the participants in this case are the insurance companies.

column4: A new Islamic reinsurance company is being established. Which body should supervise its establishment and verify its contracts and documents?
column5: Its external auditor only
column6: The board of directors acting alone
column7: A Shari'ah Supervisory Board formed for it
column8: The Shari'ah board of the largest participant
column10: Per 8/2, a Shari'ah Supervisory Board is formed to supervise establishment, verify contracts and documents, review applications and report on activities.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X intends to sign a reinsurance agreement with a traditional reinsurer due to necessity. What must it do before signing?
column5: Seek approval of the traditional reinsurer's board
column6: Notify its Shari'ah Supervisory Board after signing
column7: Obtain consent of each individual participant
column8: Seek the approval of its Shari'ah Supervisory Board
column10: Per 6/4, before signing agreements with traditional reinsurers, Islamic insurance companies should seek the approval of their Shari'ah Supervisory Boards.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X needs reinsurance cover and may use a traditional reinsurer under necessity. Where must it first seek cover?
column5: With Islamic reinsurers, to the largest possible extent
column6: With its own shareholders' funds only
column7: With traditional reinsurers first, then with Islamic ones for the rest
column8: With the cheapest reinsurer, whatever its type
column10: Per 6/1, Islamic insurance companies should reinsure first with Islamic reinsurance companies to the largest possible extent.

column4: Islamic insurance companies form a reinsurance fund. On whose behalf do the companies agree to form it?
column5: On behalf of the traditional reinsurers
column6: On behalf of the insurance funds under their management
column7: On behalf of their own shareholders, who contribute the capital of the fund
column8: On behalf of the regulator of the market
column10: Per 2/1, Islamic reinsurance is an agreement among insurance companies, on behalf of the insurance funds under their management, to avoid part of the risks.

column4: Several Islamic insurance companies form a reinsurance fund from contributions out of their insurance funds. What is the nature of this fund?
column5: It is a traditional reinsurer owned by the funds
column6: It is a branch of the largest participating company
column7: It has a distinct legal personality and independent liability
column8: It is owned by the participating companies' shareholders in equal shares
column10: Per 2/1, a reinsurance fund with a distinct legal personality and independent financial liability is formed from contributions made out of insurance funds on donation basis.

column4: Per the basis, what is the capacity of the company in an Islamic reinsurance contract, compared to commercial reinsurance?
column5: It is a principal party that contracts in its own name for its own account
column6: It is the owner of the contributions received
column7: It is a guarantor of the reinsurance account
column8: It is an agent of the reinsurance account, not a principal
column10: Per the basis (b), the Islamic reinsurance company is an agent of the reinsurance account, whereas in commercial reinsurance the company is a principal in its own name.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X retains a portion of the premiums due to a traditional reinsurer and invests it by Mudarabah. What are the roles?
column5: The traditional reinsurer is Mudarib and X is Rab al-Mal
column6: X and the reinsurer are equal Musharakah partners
column7: X is Mudarib and the traditional reinsurer is Rab al-Mal
column8: X is borrower paying a fixed return to the reinsurer
column10: Per 6/2, retained funds may be invested through Mudarabah or investment agency, with the Islamic insurer as Mudarib and the traditional reinsurer as Rab al-Mal.

column4: Under a reinsurance agreement, Reinsurer R must accept all risks within the scope agreed with Islamic Insurance Company X. A new risk in scope arises. May R refuse it?
column5: No, unless the risk is above a loss limit
column6: Yes, if the risk exceeds Company X's capacity
column7: Yes; it may study each risk individually and decline any it does not want
column8: No; it is bound to accept all risks within the agreement's scope
column10: Per 4/2, in comprehensive reinsurance (reinsurance agreement) the reinsurer is committed to accept all the risks falling within the scope of the agreement.

column4: Per the basis, why may the reinsurance company manage the reinsurance account either for a fee or free of charge?
column5: Wakalah is permissible with or without remuneration
column6: Donation contracts permit any fee arrangement
column7: The company owns the account and sets its own fee
column8: Mudarabah allows the Mudarib to waive his share
column10: Per the basis, management rests on the agency (Wakalah) contract, which Fiqh scholars unanimously declare permissible with or without remuneration.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X reinsures 25% of every policy it issues, whether within or beyond its own capacity. Which form of reinsurance request is this?
column5: Loss reinsurance
column6: Risk sharing reinsurance
column7: Excess risk reinsurance
column8: Selective reinsurance
column10: Per 5/1, in risk sharing reinsurance the insurer seeks reinsurance for a percentage (e.g. 50% or 25%) of its policies, within or in excess of its own capacity.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X uses a traditional reinsurer under necessity. What limit applies to the size of such reinsurance?
column5: It is limited only by the reinsurer's capacity
column6: It may cover all risks once necessity exists
column7: Kept to the minimum, with Shari'ah Board follow-up
column8: It may cover up to half of all risks
column10: Per 6/5, Islamic insurers should stick to the minimum size of reinsurance with traditional reinsurers, and Shari'ah Boards should follow up.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X wants to hold back part of the premiums due to a traditional reinsurer to keep liquidity, without paying interest. What arrangement is allowed?
column5: Agree to retain a portion of the premiums due to the reinsurer
column6: Hold reserves for the reinsurer and pay it interest
column7: Lend the premiums to the reinsurer as Qard Hasan until claims are settled
column8: Withhold all premiums until claims are settled
column10: Per 6/2, the Islamic insurer and the traditional reinsurer may agree that a portion of premiums payable to the reinsurer be retained by the Islamic insurer.

column4: Per the basis, why does Gharar not invalidate cooperative (solidarity) reinsurance?
column5: Gharar is permitted in all insurance contracts
column6: The reinsurer guarantees all claims in advance
column7: Cooperative reinsurance involves no uncertainty at all
column8: Gharar does not affect donation-based contracts
column10: Per the basis, cooperative insurance rests on cooperation and donation, and it is a well-known Fiqh axiom that Gharar does not affect donation-based contracts.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X presents an individual risk, with a summary of its information, to a reinsurer, which studies it and decides whether to accept. What method is this?
column5: Excess risk reinsurance
column6: Selective reinsurance
column7: Comprehensive reinsurance (reinsurance agreement)
column8: Loss reinsurance
column10: Per 4/1, in selective reinsurance the insurer presents the individual risk with its information; the reinsurer decides whether to accept and is committed to what it accepts.

column4: Islamic Insurance Company X receives a surplus distribution from an Islamic reinsurance company. How is it treated?
column5: Lawful gain, credited to policyholders' account as revenue
column6: As income of X's shareholders
column7: As a reserve to be returned to the reinsurer at the end of the year
column8: As an unlawful gain to be given to charity
column10: Per 9, all financial gains from Islamic reinsurers are lawful and credited to the account of policyholders (participant companies) as part of revenues.

column4: A traditional reinsurer offers Islamic Insurance Company X a reinsurance commission. What is the correct position?
column5: X may take it if the Shari'ah Board approves
column6: No commission, but it may seek premium discounts
column7: X may take it, as it reduces the participants' cost
column8: X may take it and credit it to its shareholders
column10: Per 7/2, an Islamic insurer may not receive reinsurance commission from a traditional reinsurer, but it has the right to seek premium discounts.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: The lease of a shop ends, and the incumbent tenant agrees to hand over occupancy to a new tenant for a payment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the owner receives a share of it
column6: Permitted, as goodwill belongs to the tenant who built up the customer base
column7: Not permitted, as his right in the usufruct has expired
column8: Permitted, if it does not exceed one month's rent
column10: Per 8/3, after the end of the lease the incumbent tenant may not take any payment to hand over occupancy, because his right in the usufruct has expired.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A shareholder with a pre-emptive subscription right wants to assign it to a third party. Under the standard, how may it be assigned?
column5: Only for consideration at market value, as for any financial right
column6: It may not be assigned at all
column7: Only to another existing shareholder
column8: Without consideration, subject to law and supervisory rules
column10: Per 13/2, it is permissible to assign the right of priority to a third party without consideration, subject to law and the rules of company supervisory bodies.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Company X holds a license to use a software product and wants to transfer this licence to Company Y. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as it is a usufruct owned by Company X, which may transfer it for a price
column6: Permitted, if Company X stops using the software
column7: Not permitted; a license to use gives personal use only
column8: Permitted, if Company Y pays a fair price
column10: Per 4/3, ownership of a license to use gives the licensee the right to personal use only, which cannot be transferred to a third party.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Bank A sells a car on instalments and stipulates that it retains ownership until the last instalment. Per the basis, what is the correct position?
column5: Invalid; it may instead retain possession as security
column6: Invalid, and no security of any kind may be taken
column7: Valid, as the seller may protect its deferred price
column8: Valid only if the buyer agrees in writing
column10: Per the basis and IIFA 51 (6/2), transfer of ownership is a legal effect of sale; the seller may not retain ownership but may retain possession as security.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Company X holds a call option on shares and wants to sell the option to Bank A for a price. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the price is fair
column6: Permissible, if the option is not yet due
column7: Permissible, as it is a financial right
column8: Not permissible to take consideration for it
column10: Per 10/1, it is not permissible to take consideration for transfer of put or call option rights, whether by sale or otherwise.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Ahmad's house neighbours a house that is sold, but the two share no common easement rights. Does Ahmad have Shuf'ah as a neighbour?
column5: Yes; every adjacent neighbour has Shuf'ah, whether or not they share common easements
column6: No; a neighbour's Shuf'ah applies only with common easements
column7: Yes, if he offers a higher price than the buyer
column8: Yes, if his house is larger than the sold one
column10: Per 7/1/2, the right of Shuf'ah enjoyed by a neighbour is applicable only when the two properties share common easement rights.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Ahmad holds a commercial license from the authorities and wants to transfer it to Company X for a price. The law does not prohibit this. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as a license is personal to its holder
column6: Permissible only without consideration
column7: Permissible, for or without consideration
column8: Permissible only with the consent of a court
column10: Per 3/3/3/3, a license holder may dispose of a commercial license for or without consideration unless specifically prohibited by law.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Ahmad learned of the sale of his co-owner's share but delayed claiming Shuf'ah for months, beyond what custom allows. What is the effect?
column5: His right remains valid for one year
column6: His right remains, but he pays a higher price
column7: His right passes to his heirs
column8: His right of Shuf'ah lapses
column10: Per 7/2/4, Shuf'ah must be claimed immediately on becoming aware of the sale in accordance with custom or law, failing which it lapses.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A creditor did not claim a debt for many years, and the law sets a limitation period for court claims that has passed. What is the status of the right itself?
column5: It is not extinguished, though a court claim may be barred
column6: The right is transferred to the state treasury
column7: The right is reduced in proportion to the delay
column8: The right is extinguished by the mere passage of a long period of time
column10: Per 12/2 (a), rights are not extinguished by the passage of time, but there can be a limitation period after which a claim cannot be made in court.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Bank A holds a mortgage over a client's land as security for his Murabahah debt. How is the Bank's right in the land classified?
column5: A primary proprietary right of full ownership
column6: A secondary proprietary right protecting a personal right
column7: A personal right against the client, with no link to specific property
column8: A right to an intangible asset
column10: Per 3/2/2, secondary proprietary rights only protect fulfilment of personal rights, e.g. the creditor's rights in security provided by an obligor.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A workshop repaired a client's machine, and the client has not paid. May the workshop retain the machine?
column5: Yes, and it may sell it immediately to recover its fee, without notice to the client
column6: No, unless the client signed a mortgage
column7: Yes, it may retain the machine until it is paid
column8: No, it must return it and sue for payment
column10: Per 12/2 (b), a creditor has a right of lien; e.g. a manufacturer or worker may retain the product of their work until they receive the payment due.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Which Hadith does the basis cite for the recognition of rights to tangible or intangible assets?
column5: The neighbour of the house has a greater right to it
column6: No harm and no reciprocal harm
column7: The heirs of a deceased person inherit his estate
column8: People share in three things: water, pasturage and fire
column10: Per the basis, the recognition of rights, whether to tangible or intangible assets, rests on the Prophet's saying: 'No harm and no reciprocal harm'.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Per the basis, which Hadith grounds the right of Tahjir and rights established by first use?
column5: Anyone who first uses what no Muslim used is more entitled to it
column6: No harm and no reciprocal harm
column7: The best amongst you is the one who is best in settlement of his obligations
column8: People share in three things: water, pasturage and fire
column10: Per the basis, Ibn Qudamah cites: 'Anyone who first uses what no other Muslim has previously used is more entitled to it'.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Bank A is an unsecured creditor of Company X, while Bank B holds a proprietary right over Company X's building. What can Bank A do that differs from Bank B?
column5: It can seize Company X's building directly using permissible means
column6: It can enforce its right against any asset it chooses
column7: It has priority over Bank B on the building
column8: It cannot enforce its right by claiming any specific property
column10: Per 3/2/3, the owner of a proprietary right can directly enforce it over specific property; the owner of a personal right cannot claim any specific property.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A building's ground floor collapses due to its owner's fault, harming the upper-floor owners. What is the ruling?
column5: The court must sell the land and split the price
column6: The ground floor owner is liable to reconstruct it
column7: Each owner bears his own loss
column8: The upper owners must reconstruct and claim later
column10: Per 6/2/1, if a lower storey collapses due to its owner's fault, he is liable to reconstruct it so the upper-storey owners are not harmed.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Company X copies the registered trademark of Company Y for its own products, claiming trademarks have no value in Shari'ah. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, unless Company Y sells the trademark
column6: Permissible, if Company X's products are better
column7: Not permissible; trademarks are protected rights
column8: Permissible, as trademarks are not tangible property
column10: Per 3/3/3/1, rights to trade names, trademarks, copyrights and patents have recognised monetary value and are protected by Shari'ah; violating them is not permissible.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Co-owners divide their land and demarcate boundaries and paths; then one sells his part. Per the Hadith in the basis, is there a right of Shuf'ah?
column5: Yes, if the sale is to an outsider
column6: Yes; co-owners always keep Shuf'ah, even after boundaries and paths are set
column7: Yes, if claimed within one year
column8: No; once boundaries and paths are set there is no Shuf'ah
column10: Per the basis, Abu Salamah narrated the Prophet ruled for Shuf'ah in undivided property; if boundaries are assigned and paths demarcated, there is no Shuf'ah.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A co-owner with a right of Shuf'ah agrees to waive it in return for a payment from the buyer. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as Shuf'ah is granted only to prevent harm
column6: Permissible, if the payment is below the property price
column7: Permissible, as any financial right can be waived for a fee
column8: Permissible, if the waiver is documented in court
column10: Per 10/2, it is not permissible to take consideration for transfer or waiver of rights granted only to prevent harm, such as the right of Shuf'ah.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Midway through a lease, the owner offers the tenant a payment to vacate and waive his right to the remaining period. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, as it is payment for vacating
column6: Permitted only if the tenant pays a matching fee
column7: Permitted only after the lease has expired
column8: Permitted, as compensation for the waived usufruct
column10: Per 8/2, the owner may pay the tenant during the lease for waiving his right to the usufruct for the remaining period; after expiry without renewal, no payment is allowed.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A buyer becomes insolvent before paying for a machine, and the seller finds that same machine among the insolvency assets. What right does the seller have?
column5: A priority proprietary right to it, if local regulations allow
column6: Only an equal claim with all other creditors
column7: Ownership of it in all cases, regardless of the law of the jurisdiction
column8: No right, as ownership passed to the buyer
column10: Per 12/2 (c), the seller has a priority proprietary right to the specific item found in the insolvent buyer's assets if the applicable regulations allow it.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: With government permission, Ahmad marked a plot of unappropriated land (Tahjir) but has not developed it. He wants to sell the land to Omar. What is the ruling?
column5: He may sell the land, as Tahjir confers ownership
column6: Waive his entitlement for consideration, but not sell the land
column7: He may sell the land after one year of possession
column8: He may neither sell the land nor waive his entitlement in any manner
column10: Per 9/2-9/3, Tahjir gives exclusivity and priority but not ownership; the holder may waive his entitlement for consideration but may not sell the land.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Ahmad carried out Tahjir on a plot but left it unutilised for three years, with no different regulatory period. What is the status of his right?
column5: It passes automatically to the state treasury as ownership
column6: It becomes full ownership
column7: It expires
column8: It remains valid indefinitely
column10: Per 9/4, the right of Tahjir expires if the land is not utilised for three years, or as provided by applicable regulations.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Company X bought a co-owned plot on deferred payment over two years. The co-owner Ahmad exercises Shuf'ah. On what terms does he acquire it?
column5: On the buyer's terms, including deferral, with the usual costs
column6: At the market value on the date of exercise
column7: On deferred terms, but the conveyancing costs fall on Company X as buyer
column8: Only for immediate cash payment of the price
column10: Per 7/2/1, the preemptor takes the buyer's place and buys on the same terms (e.g. deferred payment), also assuming the buyer's liabilities such as usual conveyancing costs.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A tenant agrees to pay the owner a lump sum on top of periodic rent for a five-year lease, and the lease ends after two years. How is the lump sum treated?
column5: As an impermissible payment that must be refunded to the tenant in full
column6: As a non-refundable key money gift to the owner
column7: As a security deposit returned in full
column8: As part of the agreed rent, governed by rental payment rules
column10: Per 8/1, the lump sum is permitted if treated as part of the agreed rent for the entire lease; on early termination, the rules on rental payments apply to it.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Per the basis, from which Qur'anic indication is the right of retention (lien) derived?
column5: The command to record debts in writing
column6: The prohibition of consuming wealth unjustly
column7: The permissibility of reciprocal treatment
column8: The command to fulfil all contracts
column10: Per the basis, the verse 'And if you punish, then punish them with the like...' indicates reciprocal treatment, so one may retain property until receiving his rights.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A landowner holds a right of passage over his neighbour's land and agrees to waive it in return for a payment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only if the waiver is without consideration
column6: Permissible for an easement, unlike Shuf'ah
column7: Not permissible, as easements prevent harm like Shuf'ah
column8: Not permissible, as easements have no monetary value
column10: Per 10/3, it is permissible to take consideration for transfer or waiver of easement rights, by sale or otherwise.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A client asks whether the standard on financial rights governs his Khiyar al-Shart (option to revoke within a set period) in a sale with Bank A. What is the answer?
column5: No; Khiyarat are excluded, being covered elsewhere
column6: Yes, as Khiyar al-Shart is a proprietary right
column7: No; options are not recognised by the Shari'ah
column8: Yes; it covers all rights that arise in sale contracts with Institutions
column10: Per 1, the standard does not cover non-financial rights, Khiyarat (e.g. Khiyar al-Shart, Khiyar al-Naqd) or Waqf rights, as these are covered in separate standards.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Ahmad and Omar co-own a fleet of trucks not attached to any real estate. Omar sells his share. Does Ahmad have a right of Shuf'ah?
column5: No, unless the trucks are all used together in a single joint business
column6: Yes, if he claims it immediately
column7: Yes; Shuf'ah applies to any co-owned property
column8: No; Shuf'ah covers only immovables and movables attached to them
column10: Per 7/1/1, the right of Shuf'ah exists only in relation to immovable property or movable property attached to it.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Omar gives his share in a co-owned house as a gift to his nephew, without consideration. The other co-owner claims Shuf'ah. What is the ruling?
column5: Shuf'ah applies at the market value of the share
column6: Shuf'ah applies at a price set by the court
column7: No Shuf'ah, as the transfer was not a sale
column8: Shuf'ah applies, since ownership was transferred
column10: Per 7/2/6, there is no Shuf'ah where ownership is transferred without a sale or similar transaction, e.g. inheritance, bequest or gift without consideration.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: A plot is co-owned by A (50%), B (30%) and C (20%). C sells his share to an outsider, and A and B both claim Shuf'ah. How is the right shared?
column5: To whichever of them claims first
column6: In proportion to their shares in the property
column7: Entirely to A, as the largest co-owner, who holds the greatest share
column8: In equal shares to the two claimants
column10: Per 7/2/2, where a jointly owned property has more than one preemptor, each has the right of Shuf'ah proportionate to his share in the property.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: In the basis, the right of Shirb is distinguished from the right of Shafah. What is the right of Shirb specifically?
column5: The right of passage to a water source
column6: The right of humans and animals to drink
column7: The right to use water for ablution
column8: The right to water crops and trees
column10: Per the basis, Shirb is specifically for watering crops and trees, while Shafah is the right of humans and animals to drink and use water for ablution, bathing, etc.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Company X wants to sell its patent to Company Y for a price. When is this transaction permissible?
column5: Only if the patent is attached to a tangible asset
column6: When it is free of Gharar, deception and fraud
column7: Only if the patent is transferred without consideration
column8: Never, as patents are not financial rights
column10: Per 3/3/3/2, rights to intangible assets are financial rights and may be disposed of or transferred for consideration if free of Gharar, deception and fraud.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: In a long-term lease, local law allows the tenant to sub-lease for payment without the owner's consent. Per the Shari'ah, may he do so?
column5: No, except with the agreement of the owner
column6: Yes, since local law permits it
column7: Yes, if the new tenant uses it for the same purpose
column8: Yes, if the payment does not exceed the rent
column10: Per 8/3, in long-term leases, contrary to laws in some jurisdictions, Shari'ah does not permit sub-leasing or assigning for payment except with the owner's agreement.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Per the basis, why is selling abstract rights such as Shuf'ah or options impermissible?
column5: They are protected as intangible assets
column6: They are rights in rem attached to property and so are inseparable from the owner
column7: No Shari'ah monetary value, plus Gharar and Jahalah
column8: They can be inherited by the heirs
column10: Per the basis, the impermissibility of selling the abstract rights in item 10 rests on their lack of monetary value in Shari'ah and the presence of Gharar and Jahalah.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: How does the basis reconcile the Hadith 'The neighbour of the house has a greater right to the house' with the Hadiths limiting Shuf'ah?
column5: By applying it to all adjacent neighbours
column6: By treating the neighbour Hadith as abrogated by the later Hadiths
column7: By limiting it to movable property only
column8: By applying it to a neighbour who is co-owner or shares easements
column10: Per the basis, the Hadiths are reconciled by ascribing the neighbour Hadith to a neighbour who is also a co-owner or shares easement rights.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Company X's bylaws give existing shareholders priority to subscribe in a capital increase. How is each shareholder's priority right determined?
column5: Only for shareholders with a majority stake
column6: In proportion to his respective share before the issuance
column7: Equally among all shareholders, whatever their holdings before the issuance
column8: According to the order of applications
column10: Per 13/1, bylaws may give existing shareholders priority to subscribe; each may subscribe in proportion to his respective share prior to the issuance.

column3: Financial Rights and How They Are Exercised and Transferred
column4: Ahmad co-owns a plot with Omar. Omar sells his share to Company X without Ahmad's consent. What right does Ahmad have?
column5: To take the share from Company X at its sale price
column6: To cancel the sale and have the share returned to Omar
column7: Only to claim compensation from Omar
column8: To acquire the share at its current market value
column10: Per 7/1, Shuf'ah is the right of a neighbour or co-owner of real estate to acquire the sold property from the buyer, with or without consent, for the sale price.

column4: Ahmad, facing an insolvency claim, plans a long trip abroad that would harm his creditors. What may the creditors seek?
column5: An order that he pay all debts in full before departing
column6: An absolute travel ban for the whole period of the claim, even if guarantors are provided
column7: Prevention of the travel unless he appoints a surety for his attendance
column8: Nothing, as travel can be restricted only after a declaration
column10: Per 4/2/7, creditors may seek to prevent travel that harms them where the debtor does not appoint a surety to ensure his attendance, providing guarantors.

column4: After his declaration of insolvency, Ahmad exercises an option to terminate a purchase contract he concluded before the declaration. What is the effect?
column5: It is effective only with the creditors' unanimous approval
column6: It is effective, since it relates to a previous transaction
column7: It is effective only if the court later ratifies it
column8: It has no legal effect, like all his post-declaration acts
column10: Per 5/3, post-declaration sales, gifts and endowments have no legal effect, except acts relating to previous transactions such as exercising an option to terminate.

column4: An insolvent debtor's admission that his property belongs to a friend is not enforced without the creditors' approval. What is the Shari'ah basis for this?
column5: The principle that the deferred period has a share in the price
column6: The rule that a debtor's admissions are never valid evidence
column7: The Maliki view that admissions require a judge's approval
column8: Preventing harm to creditors: "No harm and no reciprocal harm"
column10: Per the basis, non-enforcement of the insolvent's admissions and ownership-transferring dispositions prevents harm to creditors, per the Hadith "No harm and no reciprocal harm".

column4: Company X suffers a temporary liquidity shortfall and delays some payments, but no declaration of insolvency follows. Is this situation governed by the Insolvency standard?
column5: No; delays not leading to a declaration of insolvency are outside its scope
column6: Yes; any delay in payment of a due debt is treated as insolvency (Iflas) by the court
column7: Yes, once the delay exceeds the agreed grace period
column8: No, because the standard covers individuals only, not companies
column10: Per 1, the standard does not cover financial difficulties, liquidity shortfalls or delays in payment that do not lead to a declaration of insolvency.

column4: After his declaration of insolvency, Ahmad buys a car on credit from Dealer Z. Can Dealer Z share in the sequestered assets with the existing creditors?
column5: Yes, pro-rata with the existing creditors
column6: Yes, with priority as the most recent creditor
column7: No; Z's claim attaches to Ahmad's future liability
column8: No, unless Z files his claim before distribution
column10: Per 5/4, post-declaration purchases attach to the debtor's future liability, not to the sequestered assets; such parties do not share those assets.

column4: After his assets are sequestered, Ahmad receives a plot of land as a gift from his uncle. How is this land treated?
column5: It remains the uncle's property until the declaration is revoked
column6: It is excluded, having been acquired after sequestration, so it is his own free property
column7: It attaches only to his future liability, not to the creditors
column8: Creditors' debts attach to it, as it accrued to him without his dealing
column10: Per 5/2, debts attach to the debtor's existing property at sequestration and to property accruing to him without his dealing, such as gifts.

column4: A lessee becomes insolvent in the middle of an Ijarah term. Regarding rent for the period in which the usufruct was already enjoyed, what is the lessor entitled to?
column5: That rent only if he terminates the whole Ijarah
column6: Nothing, since the lessee is now insolvent
column7: That rent, on a pro-rata basis along with other creditors
column8: Full priority for the rent of the entire Ijarah term
column10: Per 5/5/2, the lessor is entitled, pro-rata with other creditors, to the rent for the period during which the usufruct was enjoyed.

column4: Company X asks the court to declare its own insolvency. On what basis does the standard permit this?
column5: The Hanafi opinion that only the debtor may apply
column6: The Shafi'i opinion, and his interest in stabilizing his finances
column7: The Maliki opinion that creditors must consent first
column8: The rule that a court may act only on the debtor's own request, never on creditors' claims
column10: Per the basis, the debtor's right to request his own insolvency rests on the Shafi'i opinion and his interest in stabilizing his financial situation, excluding fraud.

column4: Proceeds from selling an insolvent debtor's assets are available. Which claim should be paid first?
column5: Fees of the administrators who manage the sale and distribution
column6: Claims of the creditor holding the largest debt
column7: Claims of unsecured creditors on a pro-rata basis
column8: Claims of secured creditors, as they hold a security over specific assets of the debtor
column10: Per 8/3/1, priority goes to the fees of the administrators and their assistants who manage the sale and distribution, then secured creditors (8/3/2).

column4: Bank A, owed a deferred price not yet due, joins a demand for Ahmad's insolvency. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a demand on undue debt not warranted?
column5: Bank A must first prove that it is the sole creditor
column6: Debts arising from Murabahah are never subject to insolvency
column7: Deferred debts are extinguished upon any insolvency, so Bank A would lose its claim
column8: No demand lies for undue debt, as the deferred period has a share in the price
column10: The basis states insolvency must be demanded by owners of due debts: there is no demand for undue debt, as the deferred period has a share in the price.

column4: After Ahmad's assets have been distributed, creditor E proves a debt that existed before the insolvency. How does E obtain his share?
column5: From each existing creditor, by mutual consent or litigation
column6: From the fees paid to the administrators
column7: He cannot, since the distribution is final
column8: From Ahmad's tools of trade and his home, which were left to him after sequestration
column10: Per 8/3/6, if a debt is discovered after distribution, the new creditor obtains his share from each existing creditor by mutual consent or through litigation.

column4: Upon Ahmad's insolvency, his undue debt of 100,000 is accelerated. Creditors approve reducing it to 80,000. A guarantor had guaranteed the original debt. What is the guarantor liable for?
column5: Only the 20,000 difference waived by creditors
column6: 80,000, the reduced amount
column7: Nothing, as the reduction discharges the guarantee
column8: 100,000, the amount originally guaranteed
column10: Per 5/6, with creditors' approval the accelerated undue debt may be reduced, and guarantors are liable for the reduced amount, not the amount originally guaranteed.

column4: After revocation of his first insolvency, Ahmad buys on credit, acquires property through new transactions and is declared insolvent again. What are the first-insolvency creditors entitled to?
column5: Priority over the creditors of the second insolvency
column6: A pro-rata share alongside the new creditors
column7: No share in the assets of the second insolvency
column8: A share only if the second insolvency is within a year
column10: Per 10/3, creditors of the first insolvency are not entitled to share assets of the second insolvency acquired through new transactions (unlike gifts).

column4: All creditors of Company X sign an agreement declaring X insolvent and sequestering its assets without going to court. Is this a valid declaration of insolvency?
column5: Yes, if Company X itself countersigns the declaration
column6: Yes, provided every creditor has signed the agreement
column7: Yes, if the central bank is notified of the agreement
column8: No; the court has the sole authority to declare insolvency
column10: Per 4/5, the court has the sole authority to declare a person insolvent.

column4: Supplier S sold machinery to Company X on credit and received 20% of the price. X is declared insolvent and the machinery is among the sequestered assets. Does S have the right of claw-back?
column5: Yes, because the machinery is still identifiable
column6: Yes, if X's other creditors give their consent
column7: No; the right is for a seller who has received no part of the price
column8: Yes, upon returning the 20% he has received, since the rest of the price remains unpaid
column10: Per 6, the right of claw-back is established for the seller who has not received any part of the selling price.

column4: Company X is declared insolvent. Customer Y owes X a deferred amount due in one year. How is this receivable treated?
column5: It is written off to protect Customer Y
column6: It stays deferred, joins the insolvency assets and is paid out when collected
column7: It becomes due immediately upon X's insolvency, so Customer Y must pay it at once to the creditors
column8: It is excluded from the insolvency assets
column10: Per 5/7, undue debts owed to the insolvent do not become due; they are included in the insolvency assets and distributed to creditors as and when paid.

column4: Creditors of Ahmad ask why they cannot simply declare him insolvent themselves by agreement. What is the Shari'ah basis for requiring a judicial ruling?
column5: The case of Mu'adh, and because insolvency needs consideration and Ijtihad
column6: Because the debtor's consent is needed for any sequestration of his property by the creditors
column7: Because creditors of undue debts must be represented
column8: Because a declaration transfers ownership to the creditors
column10: Per the basis, a judicial ruling is required following the Prophet's act in Mu'adh's case, and because insolvency needs consideration and Ijtihad.

column4: Bank A's Murabahah receivable from Ahmad falls due in two years, while his other creditors' debts are already due. Can Bank A, on its own, demand a declaration of insolvency now?
column5: Yes; any creditor may demand it regardless of maturity, since the debtor is already in default
column6: No, unless Ahmad has first refused a request to travel
column7: No; creditors of undue debts have no present right to demand it
column8: Yes, provided Bank A's receivable is the largest debt
column10: Per 4/3/1 and 5/5/1, the application is by creditors of due debts; creditors of undue debts have no present right to demand a declaration of insolvency.

column4: Supplier S, unpaid, finds goods he sold to Company X among X's assets after its insolvency, but X had pledged them to Bank B as security. Can S reclaim them?
column5: Yes, provided a judge approves the reclamation
column6: No, unless Bank B renounces its right to the mortgage
column7: Yes; the seller's right overrides any pledge
column8: Yes, but only for the part exceeding Bank B's debt
column10: Per the basis, reclamation requires that no right of another person relates to the asset, e.g. a pledge, except when the mortgagee renounces his right.

column4: After Ahmad's insolvency is revoked, it emerges that before the declaration he had received a gift that was not sequestered. What happens to it?
column5: It is sequestered for creditors whose debts predated the declaration
column6: Ahmad keeps it, since the insolvency has been revoked and his property is free again
column7: It goes to the creditors whose debts arose after revocation
column8: It is shared among all present and future creditors
column10: Per 10/2, such an asset acquired before the declaration without reciprocal consideration is sequestered and distributed among the creditors whose debts predated it.

column4: Shortly before his declaration of insolvency, during a period the competent authority assesses as a period of uncertainty, Ahmad endowed a building as Waqf. What is the effect?
column5: It is valid, but the building's rent goes to the creditors
column6: It is valid, since it preceded the declaration
column7: It is valid, since endowment is an act of charity
column8: It has no legal effect, as the rule extends to that period
column10: Per 5/3, the lack of legal effect of sale, gift or endowment also applies during the period of uncertainty preceding the declaration, as assessed by the authority.

column4: After being declared insolvent, Ahmad admits that he owes 50,000 to Mr. B in relation to his sequestered assets. What is the effect of this admission?
column5: It is binding provided Mr. B is not one of his relatives
column6: It is binding whenever the debt was in fact incurred earlier
column7: No effect, unless creditors accept the debt predates the declaration
column8: It is binding on all creditors, as an admission is the strongest evidence against oneself
column10: Per 5/1, such an admission has no legal effect, whether the debt arose before or after the declaration, unless the creditors accept it was incurred before.

column4: Bank A, which manages, as a paid agent, an investment fund it does not own, is declared insolvent. How is the fund treated?
column5: It is shared equally between fund investors and creditors
column6: It is part of the insolvency assets up to the agency fee
column7: It is part of the insolvency assets as Bank A manages it
column8: It is not part of Bank A's insolvency assets
column10: Per 9/2, investment vehicles independent of the institution, not owned by it and managed on a paid agency or Mudarabah basis, are not part of the insolvency assets.

column4: What is the Shari'ah basis for the obligatory ruling of declaring insolvency and interdiction against a debtor whose debts exceed what he can pay?
column5: The Prophet's interdiction of Mu'adh Ibn Jabal and sale of his property
column6: The principle that the deferred period has a share in the price
column7: The Hadith that a sold item found with the buyer reverts to the seller
column8: The Maliki opinion on the three stages of insolvency
column10: Per the Shari'ah basis, the Prophet (peace be upon him) interdicted Mu'adh Ibn Jabal, sold his property and distributed it among his creditors; this is the majority view.

column4: In the second stage of insolvency, creditors fear that Ahmad will admit a debt owed to his first cousin to divert assets. What may they ask the competent authorities to do?
column5: Nothing, since only admissions to his own children can be restricted, not those to other relatives
column6: Prevent admissions of liability to relatives up to four vertical steps
column7: Have the cousin declared insolvent jointly with Ahmad
column8: Annul all contracts he has ever concluded with his relatives, whenever they were made
column10: Per 4/2/4, creditors may seek to prevent the debtor admitting liability to those who may be preferred, e.g. blood relatives up to four vertical steps such as a first cousin.

column4: Seller S reclaims livestock he sold to an insolvent buyer. While with the buyer, the animals gained considerable weight. Who gets the weight increase?
column5: The other creditors, through the value of the increase
column6: The insolvent buyer, whom S must compensate for the fodder and care that produced it
column7: S and the insolvent buyer, shared equally between them
column8: S, since an inseparable increase goes with the reclaimed asset
column10: Per the basis, if an inseparable increase occurs, like livestock weight, and the seller chooses reclamation, he takes only the asset as is; a separate increase belongs to the insolvent.

column4: After distribution of Ahmad's assets, his creditors have recovered only 60% of their debts. What is the position on the remaining 40%?
column5: Creditors may legally demand it immediately
column6: No legal right to demand it, but Ahmad is morally bound to pay it
column7: Ahmad has no obligation of any kind to pay it
column8: Creditors may have him declared insolvent again to recover it
column10: Per 5/8, after distribution creditors have no legal right to demand unpaid debt, but the debtor has a moral obligation in Shari'ah to pay all debts in full.

column4: Creditors of Company X, whose debts exceed its assets, want to act before going to court. What does the first stage of insolvency involve?
column5: Demanding pro-rata payment and no donations, loans or preferences
column6: Filing a petition for an immediate declaration of insolvency
column7: Selling the debtor's tools of trade by public auction
column8: Seizing the debtor's assets directly without any authority
column10: Per 4/1, in the first stage creditors demand pro-rata payment and that the debtor refrain from donations, loans and preferential dealings.

column4: Bank A's deferred Murabahah receivable from Ahmad is not yet due when he is declared insolvent. What happens to this receivable?
column5: It becomes due but ranks after all originally due debts
column6: It is extinguished by the declaration of insolvency
column7: It becomes due and Bank A shares the assets with due creditors
column8: It stays deferred and Bank A must wait until maturity, being paid after all due creditors
column10: Per 5/5/1, all the debtor's undue debts become due, and their creditors share the sequestered assets with the creditors of due debts.

column4: Creditors Ali and Omar obtained a declaration of Ahmad's insolvency. Before the distribution, creditor Karim appears with a proven claim. What is Karim entitled to?
column5: Nothing, since he did not join the application
column6: A pro-rata share of the distribution
column7: Only what remains after Ali and Omar are paid in full
column8: Payment only after the declaration is revoked
column10: Per 4/4, creditors need not prove they are the sole creditors; another creditor appearing before distribution is entitled to a pro-rata share.

column4: Ahmad, a carpenter, is declared insolvent. He owns his carpentry tools and a large villa far exceeding his needs. How are these assets treated?
column5: The tools are sold; the villa is kept as his residence
column6: Both the tools and the villa are sold for the creditors
column7: Tools are kept; the villa is sold and replaced by a suitable home
column8: The villa is kept and the tools are leased out for creditors
column10: Per 7/2, tools of trade and a suitable home are excluded from the sale; a home exceeding his requirements is sold and replaced by a suitable one.

column4: Ahmad's debts exceed his assets, but no court has declared him insolvent yet. He plans to give a valuable property to his brother. What is his position in Shari'ah?
column5: He is morally bound to refrain from acts that may harm his creditors
column6: He may make the gift if at least one creditor approves it
column7: He must first pre-pay his deferred debts, then he may make the gift
column8: He is free to dispose of his property until a declaration is made
column10: Per 3/1, a person whose debts exceed his assets has a moral obligation in Shari'ah to refrain from any action that may harm the creditors, even before a declaration.

column4: The sale proceeds of Ahmad's sequestered assets do not cover his debts. Creditors ask the court to oblige him to work or borrow to pay the shortfall. What is the ruling?
column5: He must do so if a majority of creditors demand it
column6: He must work until the debts are fully paid
column7: He must take a loan to settle the remaining debts
column8: He is not required to earn or take out a loan
column10: Per 7/3, the debtor is not required to earn or take out a loan if the proceeds of sale are insufficient to pay off his debts.

column4: Company X, whose due debts exceed its assets, applies to the court to have itself declared insolvent. How does the standard treat this application?
column5: It is allowed only for individuals, not for companies
column6: It is not allowed; only creditors may make the application
column7: It is a valid basis unless the court considers it fraudulent
column8: It is allowed only if all creditors give written consent
column10: Per 4/3/2, a declaration may be based on an application by the debtor himself, except where the competent judicial authority considers it fraudulent.

column4: Seller S meets all conditions for reclaiming goods from an insolvent buyer and verbally cancels the sale. Is a court decision needed for the reclamation?
column5: Only once the goods can be delivered to him
column6: No; it takes place immediately without a judge's decision
column7: Yes; reclamation requires a judicial order, as it affects the rights of other creditors
column8: Only once the competent authority is informed
column10: Per the basis, reclamation is cancellation of the sale, verbal or otherwise, taking place immediately without a judge's decision, the authority's knowledge or ability to deliver.

column4: Islamic Bank A faces a one-week cash gap and considers an interest-bearing overdraft from a conventional bank. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted if the facility is arranged through a subsidiary
column6: Permitted for one week as a matter of necessity, since the gap is short and temporary
column7: Permitted if the interest paid is small and fixed in advance
column8: Prohibited, whether direct, by overdraft or by a commission-based facility
column10: Per 4/1, obtaining liquidity through interest-bearing loans is prohibited, whether directly or through overdrafts or interest-bearing or commission-based facilities.

column4: Bank A securitises some of its assets by selling them to Sukuk subscribers and remains manager of those assets. At what price may it promise to repurchase them?
column5: At the market price or at a price to be agreed
column6: At face value, since it manages the assets
column7: At original cost plus a fixed periodic return
column8: At book value as on the date of issuance
column10: Per 4/2/5, an institution managing securitised assets may promise to purchase them at the market price or at a price to be agreed.

column4: To raise liquidity, Bank A concludes an Istisna'a sale stipulating advance payment and a parallel Istisna'a purchase on instalments. Is advance payment obligatory in the Istisna'a sale?
column5: Yes, but only in the parallel Istisna'a purchase
column6: No; it may be stipulated, although it is not obligatory
column7: No; advance payment is prohibited in Istisna'a
column8: Yes; the Istisna'a price must always be paid in advance
column10: Per 4/2/2, the institution may conclude an Istisna'a sale stipulating advance payment, although advance payment is not obligatory, with a parallel Istisna'a on deferred terms.

column4: The central bank wishes to provide liquidity support to Islamic Bank A during a market squeeze. How must this support be provided?
column5: Through an interest-bearing facility, as central banks are exempt from the Riba prohibition
column6: Through a commission-based overdraft facility
column7: Through any mode, since the support is only temporary
column8: Only through Shari'ah-compliant modes, e.g. Mudarabah or investment agency
column10: Per 4/1, liquidity support from supervisory or regulatory bodies such as central banks must be provided only through Shari'ah-compliant modes, e.g. Mudarabah and investment agency.

column4: In a Sukuk issuance, Bank A is only the lessee of the Sukuk assets and is not their manager. What purchase undertaking may it give?
column5: No promise to purchase of any kind
column6: A promise to purchase only at the market price
column7: A promise to purchase the assets at face value
column8: A promise at a price fixed by the subscribers later
column10: Per 4/2/5, if the institution is only the lessee and not the manager of the Sukuk assets, it may promise to purchase them at face value.

column4: Bank A may need to liquidate assets before distributing profits to investors. What is the Shari'ah basis for linking profit distribution to liquidity?
column5: No profit exists until capital is protected, which liquidation achieves
column6: Profits may only be paid from central bank support funds, never from the investors' assets
column7: Distribution before liquidation would amount to Riba
column8: Investors are entitled only to cash, never to assets
column10: Per the basis, profit distribution depends on liquidity because there is no profit except after protection of capital, realised by liquidating the assets.

column4: Bank A invites investors into a Musharakah to finance its working capital. The venture will use Bank A's office building. How is the building treated?
column5: It is valued and added to the investors' share of the capital
column6: It is contributed as part of Bank A's share of the capital
column7: It is used by the venture free of charge, outside the accounts
column8: It is lent or leased to the venture, rent being a venture expense
column10: Per 4/2/4, the institution contributes its current assets after valuation; fixed assets are not part of the Musharakah but are lent or leased, with rent as an expense.

column4: Under the standard on obtaining and deploying liquidity, what does the term "liquidity" refer to?
column5: Any asset recorded on the institution's balance sheet
column6: Cash balances held in current accounts only
column7: Cash or that which can be easily converted to cash
column8: Funds obtained through central bank support facilities
column10: Per 2/1, liquidity refers to cash or that which can be easily converted to cash.

column4: Bank A's treasury committee is drafting its liquidity management objective. Which formulation matches the standard's definition of liquidity management?
column5: Drawing on central bank facilities whenever cash is short
column6: Balancing swift, cheap obtaining of liquidity with its effective deployment
column7: Investing all available cash in long-term assets for return
column8: Holding maximum cash in reserve to cover any withdrawal at all times, whatever the cost to returns
column10: Per 2/2, liquidity management means achieving a balance between obtaining liquidity as swiftly and cheaply as possible and investing and deploying it effectively.

column4: Bank A needs cash. It sells its office building for immediate cash and then leases it back on rent payable in arrears. How does the standard treat this?
column5: As a permissible mode of obtaining liquidity
column6: As permissible only if the rent is paid in advance
column7: As permissible only for assets the bank does not use
column8: As prohibited, being a disguised interest-bearing loan
column10: Per 4/2/3, the institution may sell some of its assets for immediate cash and then, if required, lease them back on rent payable in arrears.

column4: Bank A sells commodities on a Salam basis, receives the price up-front, and obtains a promise to sell from a third-party commodity broker to hedge price fluctuation. Is this permitted?
column5: No; any promise connected to a Salam sale is prohibited
column6: Yes; securing a third-party broker's promise to sell is permitted
column7: Yes, but only if the broker is also the Salam buyer
column8: No; Salam may not be used to obtain liquidity, since the price is received before delivery
column10: Per 4/2/1, selling on Salam and buying for delivery at maturity is permitted; securing a promise to sell from a third-party broker to mitigate price risk is permitted.

column4: Bank A does not sell its commodities but evaluates them to arrive at the expected monetary value they could realise. In the traditional terminology cited by the standard, this is:
column5: Tandid by estimation
column6: Actual Tandid
column7: Securitisation of assets
column8: Liquidity management
column10: Per the basis, liquidity is traditionally Tandid: actual Tandid is selling commodities for cash; Tandid by estimation is evaluating them to arrive at expected monetary value.

column4: Bank A deploys surplus cash by buying wheat on Salam and, in a separate contract, appoints the Salam seller to sell the wheat to his customers. When may the wheat be sold?
column5: Never; the Salam seller cannot sell on the bank's behalf
column6: At any time, even before the delivery date
column7: After Bank A takes physical or constructive delivery
column8: Only after the seller returns the Salam price
column10: Per 5/3, commodities bought on Salam may be sold after taking physical or constructive delivery, personally or by appointing the seller, in a separate contract, as agent.

column4: Why are supervisory bodies, such as central banks, the entities most responsible for ensuring institutions' liquidity is Shari'ah-compliant?
column5: They are the institutions' main providers of liquidity and can set the terms of such support
column6: They appoint the institutions' Shari'ah boards
column7: They hold the institutions' reserves as custodians
column8: They licensed the institutions to operate by Shari'ah-compliant procedures
column10: Per the basis, supervisory bodies are most responsible because they licensed the institutions to operate by Shari'ah-compliant procedures and prohibited what violates Shari'ah.

column4: Bank A commissions a project on Istisna'a with immediate payment, then sells the same project to Company X through a second Istisna'a for deferred price and delivery. What condition applies?
column5: The two Istisna'a contracts must not be linked
column6: The second contract must be concluded first
column7: The two contracts must carry exactly the same price
column8: The manufacturer must guarantee Company X's payment
column10: Per 5/4, Istisna'a and parallel Istisna'a are used to deploy liquidity without linking the two contracts.

column4: In a capital protection structure, Partner A contributes 60% of a Musharakah's capital but stipulates that he will bear only 30% of any loss. Is this acceptable?
column5: Yes, if both partners agree to it in writing, since Musharakah terms are set by agreement
column6: Yes, since it serves the aim of protecting capital
column7: No; partners must bear losses per their shares in the capital
column8: Yes, if Partner A accepts a lower profit share
column10: Per 4/1/1, a condition of capital protection instruments is that investment partners bear risks and losses according to their respective shares in the capital.

column4: A Mudarabah agreement drafted by Bank A states that the Mudarib is liable for any loss of capital, whatever its cause. Is this stipulation permissible?
column5: Yes, if the Mudarib freely agrees to it when signing the contract
column6: No; liability is limited to misconduct, negligence or breach
column7: Yes, but only in a restricted Mudarabah with a specified activity
column8: Yes, if the Mudarib's profit share is raised in return for it
column10: Per 3/6 and 5/1, it is not permissible to stipulate that the manager is unconditionally liable for loss of capital beyond wilful misconduct, negligence and breach.

column4: To protect a fund's capital against currency moves, a manager proposes conventional currency swaps and options. What does the standard say?
column5: Permissible if the counterparty is an Islamic bank
column6: Permissible if investors consent in advance
column7: Permissible, since currency risk may be protected by any available hedging contract
column8: Not permissible; conventional hedging contracts are excluded
column10: Per 5/5, protecting capital by conventional hedging contracts such as futures, options and swaps is not permissible.

column4: Investors question why Takaful cover may protect capital while conventional insurance may not. What is the basis given by the standard?
column5: Takaful is an undertaking to donate, not an exchange of counter-values
column6: Takaful cover is issued only by government-owned institutions
column7: Takaful covers only those losses caused by the manager's negligence
column8: Takaful contributions are lower than conventional insurance premiums
column10: Per the basis, Takaful is an undertaking to make donations among participants, not Mu'awadah, aiming at cooperation; prohibitions on commercial insurance do not apply.

column4: A critic says splitting a fund's capital between Murabahah and Musharakah is a prohibited combination of contracts. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is it not?
column5: Musharakah and Murabahah are one type of contract
column6: The Shari'ah board has waived the prohibition
column7: Combining contracts is always permitted in funds, whatever the link between them
column8: Each part is invested independently in a separate contract
column10: Per the basis, diversification is not combining contracts in one, as each contract is conducted independently, each part of capital invested in a different contract.

column4: A fund places part of its capital in Murabahah with strongly rated parties so that principal plus profit protects the initial capital, and invests the rest in Musharakah. Ruling?
column5: It is prohibited as it amounts to guaranteeing the capital
column6: It is permissible only if the Murabahah buyer guarantees the rest
column7: It is a permissible diversification method to protect capital
column8: It is a prohibited combination of two contracts in one
column10: Per 4/2/7(b), dividing capital between Murabahah with strong-rated parties and Musharakah is a permissible diversification method to protect capital.

column4: Under the standard, what is the Shari'ah ruling on protecting capital by permissible means?
column5: It is obligatory on every capital provider in every investment
column6: It is desirable, as it serves the objectives of Shari'ah regarding wealth
column7: It is disliked, as it conflicts with the sharing of risk and reward
column8: It is merely permissible, with no preference either way in Shari'ah and no link to wealth
column10: Per 3/1, protecting capital by permissible means is desirable in Shari'ah as it serves the objectives of Shari'ah with regard to wealth.

column4: A Musharakah contract stipulates that the managing partner guarantees the capital absolutely. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this condition void?
column5: It gives the managing partner an excessive share of the profit
column6: It is valid in Shari'ah but cannot be enforced before a court
column7: It strips the contract of its essence, turning it into a guaranteed loan
column8: It is void only if it was not disclosed to the other partners before the contract was signed
column10: Per the basis, such a condition strips partnership and agency contracts of their essential content, turning them into a guaranteed loan, and violates their trust-based nature.

column4: Bank A, as Mudarib, asks why no reserve deduction is taken from its own profit share. Per the Shari'ah basis, why?
column5: Liability for loss is borne by the capital providers, not the manager
column6: Any deduction from the Mudarib's share would amount to Riba
column7: The Mudarib's profit share is fixed by contract and cannot change
column8: Reserves are effectively a fee paid for the Mudarib's own work
column10: Per the basis, reserves come from investors' profits with consent and in their interest; none is taken from the manager's share as loss is borne by capital providers.

column4: A fund manager wants to protect a fund against exchange-rate fluctuation and inflation using Shari'ah-compliant instruments. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible only through conventional swaps and options
column6: Permissible only if the manager guarantees the outcome
column7: Not permissible; only loss of the capital itself may be protected, not currency or inflation
column8: Permissible; such risks may be covered by compliant instruments
column10: Per 3/3, Shari'ah-compliant instruments and processes may protect investment from risks such as loss of capital, depreciation, inflation or exchange-rate fluctuation.

column4: A Rabb al-Mal claims compensation for opportunity cost after the Mudarib's negligence. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is unrealised profit not compensated?
column5: Profit belongs entirely to the Mudarib until distribution
column6: It is non-existent wealth that has not yet been realised
column7: Compensation of any kind is Riba in Mudarabah
column8: The Rabb al-Mal waived profit by entering the contract
column10: Per the basis, opportunity cost is not compensated because it is non-existent wealth not yet realised; realised profit after liquidation is treated like capital.

column4: A fund protects capital with Murabahah and uses the rest to buy assets under 'Arboun contracts. The assets' value then falls sharply. What happens?
column5: The Murabahah buyers must bear the decline in value
column6: The sellers must refund the 'Arboun to the fund
column7: The fund must complete the purchases and sell at a loss, as the 'Arboun binds it
column8: The purchases are not completed; loss is limited to the 'Arboun
column10: Per 4/2/7(d), if asset values decline, the purchase contracts are not completed and the loss is limited to the 'Arboun amount, with capital protected by Murabahah.

column4: Bank B, unrelated to the fund manager, undertakes free of charge to indemnify investors for losses caused by the manager's negligence, with recourse to the manager. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, but only if Bank B charges a fee for providing the guarantee
column6: Yes, but only if Bank B waives every right of recourse to him
column7: Yes; recourse is allowed for losses from misconduct or negligence
column8: No; any recourse by a guarantor to the manager is prohibited
column10: Per 4/2/5, a third party may, without consideration, indemnify against loss from the manager's misconduct or negligence and has a right of recourse to the manager.

column4: A Mudarib stores Mudarabah goods in an unlocked, unguarded warehouse, contrary to the usual means of protection, and they are stolen. Who bears the loss?
column5: The Mudarib, for failing to use usual means of protection
column6: The Rabb al-Mal, since the Mudarib is a fiduciary and does not guarantee the capital
column7: The two parties equally, as partners in the venture
column8: The Mudarib only if the contract expressly says so
column10: Per 3/2, the investment manager must exercise due diligence to protect the funds; if he fails to do so using usual means of protection, he is liable.

column4: An investor required the manager to obtain Takaful cover for the investment. The manager did not, and an uninsured loss of capital occurred. Who bears the loss?
column5: The manager, but only for the lost profit
column6: The manager is liable for the resulting loss of capital
