column7: The investor and manager, in equal shares
column8: The investor, since protection is merely desirable
column10: Per 4/2/11, if the investor required the manager to adopt certain Shari'ah-compliant protection and he did not, he is liable for any resulting loss of capital.

column4: Under the Murabahah and 'Arboun protection method, the fund manager wishes to sell some of the fund's 'Arboun contracts to other investors before settlement. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, once half of the 'Arboun period has passed
column6: Yes, at their market value on the date of sale
column7: No; trading in 'Arboun contracts is impermissible
column8: Yes, provided the original sellers consent
column10: Per 4/2/7(d), the rules of 'Arboun must be observed, including reserving the assets until settlement and the impermissibility of trading in 'Arboun contracts.

column4: Due to the Mudarib's negligence, a deal that would have produced profit was missed; the capital itself is intact. Can the Rabb al-Mal claim the expected profit?
column5: No; the Mudarib is liable for loss of capital, not of profit
column6: Yes, the full amount of the profit that was expected from the deal
column7: Yes, but only half of the expected profit, as a compromise
column8: Yes, at the prevailing market rate of return for the period
column10: Per 3/7, in case of the Mudarib's misconduct, negligence or breach, the capital provider may hold him liable for loss of capital but not loss of profit.

column4: An investor asks Bank A whether its commitment to "protect" his capital means the Bank guarantees it. How does the standard distinguish protection from guarantee?
column5: They are synonyms; both mean that the manager undertakes to bear any loss of the capital
column6: A guarantee is wider, covering inflation and exchange rates
column7: Protection is narrower, covering only destruction of capital
column8: Protection is safeguarding; a guarantee is an undertaking to bear any loss
column10: Per 2, protection is wider than a guarantee: a guarantee is a party's undertaking to bear any loss, while protection refers to safeguarding capital.

column4: Which of the following is listed by the standard as a permissible method of protecting capital?
column5: The manager's commitment to buy assets at nominal price
column6: A sale with an option to terminate for non-payment (Khiyar al-Naqd)
column7: Conventional futures, options and swaps
column8: A third-party guarantee of the capital against loss, given in return for a fee
column10: Per 4/2/9, a sale with Khiyar al-Naqd is a permissible method; fee-based guarantees, conventional hedging and nominal-price commitments are prohibited under 5.

column4: Company Y owns 60% of an investment manager and voluntarily undertakes to indemnify the fund's investors against any capital loss, without recourse to the manager. Is this undertaking valid?
column5: No; the ownership relationship exceeds one half
column6: Yes, if Company Y acts in the public interest
column7: Yes, since it has no right of recourse to the manager
column8: Yes, provided Company Y charges no fee for it
column10: Per 4/2/4, a valid third-party undertaking requires administrative independence and no direct or indirect ownership relationship of more than a half with the manager.

column4: Constructive liquidation of a Mudarabah shows profit of 100,000 added to the capital. Later the Mudarib's negligence wipes out that 100,000. Is he liable for it?
column5: No, he is liable only for the original capital
column6: Yes, since the profit had become part of the capital
column7: Yes, but only for half, as the Mudarib's share
column8: No, since he is never liable for loss of profit
column10: Per 3/7, if liquidation shows profit added to capital and it is lost through the Mudarib's misconduct, negligence or breach, he must indemnify it as part of the capital.

column4: An investment agent invests strictly within his mandate. A market downturn reduces the capital by 20%, with no misconduct, negligence or breach on his part. Who bears the loss?
column5: The agent, as he holds the funds in trust
column6: The agent, for any loss above 10%
column7: The investor; the agent is not liable
column8: The agent and investor, equally
column10: Per 3/4, the investment manager acts in a fiduciary capacity and is not liable for loss of capital except for wilful misconduct, negligence or breach of contract.

column4: An investor argues a Mudarib should bear a market loss because he held the money. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is the manager not liable absent misconduct or negligence?
column5: The Mudarib's possible loss is offset by his expected profit share in other operations
column6: Losses in Mudarabah are always borne by the state as guarantor
column7: A manager's liability exists only where the investor is a bank
column8: He holds it with the owner's permission, as if it were with the owner
column10: Per the basis, by consensus the manager takes capital with the owner's permission as his representative; loss in his hands is like loss in the owner's possession.

column4: Company Z offers to guarantee a fund's capital for a fee. Besides being akin to conventional insurance, what Shari'ah basis does the standard give for prohibiting it?
column5: The fee would be too small to cover the potential loss, so the guarantor would be harmed
column6: The extent of loss is unknown at inception, causing excessive ambiguity
column7: Guarantees may be given only by the investment manager
column8: A guarantee is valid only for debts, never for any capital
column10: Per the basis, a fee-based guarantee entails excessive ambiguity since the extent of loss is unknown at inception, and giving a guarantee for a fee is prohibited.

column4: Bank A, as Mudarib, proposes a capital protection reserve funded by deductions from both the investors' profit share and its own Mudarib share. What does the standard allow?
column5: Deductions from both shares in proportion
column6: Deductions only from the Mudarib's share
column7: Deductions from the capital before profit is computed
column8: Deductions only from the investors' share of profits
column10: Per 4/2/6, reserves to protect capital are created through deductions from the investors' share of profits but not from the manager's share as Mudarib.

column4: Company Z offers to guarantee a fund's capital against any loss in exchange for an annual fee. How does the standard classify this?
column5: Impermissible; it is a form of conventional insurance
column6: Permissible, as it is a form of Takaful
column7: Permissible if Company Z is independent of the manager
column8: Permissible if the fee is reasonable and disclosed
column10: Per 5/4, a third party's undertaking to guarantee the capital for a fee is not permissible; it is a form of conventional insurance.

column4: A fund manager obtains Takaful cover, on behalf of the investors, against the risks of the manager's own negligence, death or bankruptcy. Is this permissible?
column5: No, since it covers the manager's own negligence, which no cover may insure against
column6: Yes, but only against the risk of the manager's death
column7: Yes; the manager may obtain Takaful cover on the investors' behalf
column8: No; only the investors themselves may obtain such cover
column10: Per 4/2/1, Takaful may cover misconduct, negligence, breach, procrastination, death or bankruptcy, obtained by investors or by the manager on their behalf.

column4: In a Mudarabah fund, the Mudarib undertakes to buy the fund's assets at maturity at their nominal price, to reassure investors. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, as it makes the manager bear the loss
column6: Permissible if the price is agreed at the outset
column7: Permissible, as it is only a unilateral promise
column8: Permissible if investors pay a fee for the promise
column10: Per 5/3, a commitment by or obligating the manager to purchase the investment assets at nominal price or at an initially agreed price is not permissible.

column4: Bank A, as agent, receives all profit above the expected profit in addition to its fee. How does the Shari'ah basis characterise this excess?
column5: Compensation for the agent's cost of funds
column6: A form of agency fee fixed in advance
column7: A share of profit as in Mudarabah
column8: A type of conditional gift and an incentive
column10: Per the basis, allocating to the agent any profit in excess of the expected profit is a type of conditional gift and an incentive.

column4: As investment agent, Bank A sold the principal's goods on credit to Company X, which now delays payment. Who pursues Company X for payment, including litigation?
column5: The principal, as the owner
column6: Bank A, the agent
column7: Bank A and the principal jointly
column8: A court-appointed administrator
column10: Per 8, the results of the contract belong to the principal, but rights and obligations such as pursuing payment or delivery, including litigation, belong to the agent.

column4: Ahmad appoints Bank A to invest and grow his savings, and the Bank agrees to act without charging any fee. Is this an investment agency?
column5: No; it is a general agency to perform specific tasks
column6: No; without a fee it automatically becomes a Mudarabah
column7: Yes; investment agency may be with or without a fee
column8: No; investment agency must always be remunerated
column10: Per 2/1, investment agency means appointing another person to invest and grow one's wealth, with or without a fee.

column4: With the principal's permission, Bank A buys goods for him with its own money before receiving his funds, then asks for an extra 2% for the advance. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, as fair compensation for Bank A's own cost of funds
column6: Yes, if the principal agreed to the extra charge in advance
column7: No, since an agent may never start investing before funding
column8: No; the advance is an interest-free loan bringing it no benefit
column10: Per 6/3 and 6/4, the agent may start with permission by advancing a loan, but it is an interest-free loan that may bring no benefit to the agent.

column4: Company X signs an investment agency contract with Bank A in March, stating that the appointment takes effect from 1 July. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, but only for an unrestricted investment agency
column6: No; an agency must take effect upon signing
column7: Yes; it may take effect on a specified future date
column8: Yes, but only if the whole fee is paid in advance
column10: Per 3/2, the appointment of an agent may be contingent on conditions or made to take effect on a specified future date.

column4: Company X used investment agency financing from Bank A for working capital and no longer needs it. How may the relationship be ended?
column5: By Takharuj: pro-rata division or a buy-out at a price then agreed
column6: By a buy-out of Bank A's share at face value fixed at the outset
column7: By Bank A keeping its share until the original term ends
column8: By Company X repaying the amount plus a fixed return
column10: Per 12/2, the relationship may be terminated by Takharuj: the joint account is distributed pro-rata or one party buys the other's share at a price agreed at that time.

column4: An investment agency contract requires Bank A, as agent, to pay storage and insurance of the goods, reimbursed only if the investment yields a profit. Is this valid?
column5: Yes, if the expected yield is high enough to cover them
column6: No; such expenses are the principal's responsibility
column7: Yes, as long as the agent accepts it in the contract
column8: Yes, since the agent receives a fee for its work
column10: Per 6/2, investment expenses are the principal's; the agent may not be required to pay them, nor may reimbursement be deferred or tied to the investment's yield.

column4: A fixed-term investment agency gives the principal a right to terminate unilaterally if the agent's Shari'ah supervision licence is withdrawn. Is this clause permissible?
column5: Yes, but only in an unremunerated investment agency
column6: No; a binding contract of fixed term can contain no right of unilateral termination
column7: Yes; a unilateral right may be stipulated for specific circumstances
column8: Yes, but such a right may be given only to the agent
column10: Per 4/2, where the parties agreed not to terminate for a specified period, the contract may stipulate one party's right to terminate unilaterally in specific circumstances.

column4: A principal argues that agency is by nature non-binding, so he can exit a fixed-term investment agency at will. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is it binding?
column5: It is for a specific period that neither party may dissolve unilaterally
column6: The agent has invested some of its own funds alongside the principal
column7: Any contract signed by a licensed institution is binding
column8: The agent's fee for the whole term has already been paid in advance
column10: Per the basis, investment agency is binding because it is entered into for a specific period, the parties agreeing neither can unilaterally dissolve it except as specified.

column4: The principal told Bank A to sell an asset at 100. Bank A, in breach of this instruction, sold it at 120. What is the position?
column5: Bank A keeps the extra 20 as its own profit
column6: Bank A loses its right to any performance incentive
column7: Bank A is liable for breach and must undo the sale
column8: Bank A is not liable; the gain belongs to the principal
column10: Per 7/1 and 7/2, a breach advantageous to the principal does not make the agent liable; the gain belongs to the principal without affecting the agent's incentive.

column4: Bank A's agency contract gives it a fixed fee plus all profit above an expected 8%. The investment earns 10%. Is Bank A's claim to the extra 2% valid?
column5: Yes, but only for half of the excess profit
column6: Yes; the excess may be given as a performance incentive
column7: No; an agent is entitled to its fixed fee only, and any excess profit belongs to the principal
column8: Yes, but only if the fixed fee is waived
column10: Per 5/4 and 6/5, the agent may be entitled, in addition to its fee, to all or part of any amount above the expected profit as a performance incentive.

column4: An investment agency expires with receivables still uncollected and no renewal. The principal demands that Bank A pay them from its own funds or via Tawarruq. Must it?
column5: No; it must collect them but need not pay from its own funds
column6: No, and it has no duty to collect them either
column7: Yes; it must raise the amount through Tawarruq
column8: Yes; it must pay them from its own funds and then recover the amounts from the debtors
column10: Per 12/4, the agent must collect the receivables, but is not required to pay them from its own funds or to seek financing like Tawarruq.

column4: Bank A, as investment agent, negligently left the principal's funds uninvested for six months. The capital is intact. What is Bank A liable for?
column5: The expected profit stated in the contract
column6: Nothing for expected profit; only for capital
column7: Half of the expected profit for the period
column8: Market-rate profit for the six months
column10: Per 7/1, where the agent is liable, liability is limited to the capital; it is not liable for expected profit whether capital was invested late or not at all.

column4: With the principal's consent, Bank A appointed Company Y as sub-agent. Bank A now wishes to dismiss Company Y. Can it?
column5: No; nobody may dismiss it before term ends
column6: Yes, with notice to the principal
column7: Yes, as the agent who appointed it
column8: No; only the principal can dismiss Company Y
column10: Per 9/2, a sub-agent appointed with the principal's consent can be dismissed only by the principal, unless the agent was authorised to appoint any sub-agent at will.

column4: With the principal's consent, Bank A set aside part of the profit as a profit equalisation reserve. At liquidation, a balance remains. What happens to it?
column5: It is shared equally by Bank A and the principal
column6: It reduces Bank A's incentive for those periods
column7: It is returned to the principal, with Bank A's fee unaffected
column8: It goes to Bank A as an additional incentive for its management of the investment
column10: Per 6/7, upon liquidation the reserve balance is returned to the principal without affecting the agent's fixed fee or incentive for the periods concerned.

column4: An investment agency contract with Bank A is silent on any fee. Bank A customarily charges fees for such services, as is normal practice. What is Bank A entitled to?
column5: Whatever fee Bank A unilaterally sets
column6: Nothing, since no fee was stipulated
column7: A share of the profit as if a Mudarib
column8: The fee prevalent in the relevant markets
column10: Per 5/2, if the fee was not specified and the agent customarily charges a fee, it is entitled to the fee prevalent in the relevant markets.

column4: An agent breached a 12% minimum-yield restriction while the market average was only 7%. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is he not liable up to the stipulated 12%?
column5: That would be acquiring another's wealth by illegitimate means
column6: The stipulated rate is void in every agency contract, so no restriction can be enforced
column7: The principal should have consulted the market first
column8: The agent's breach was advantageous to the principal
column10: Per the basis, the agent compensates up to the market average for breach, but not a stipulated rate above it, as that would be acquiring another's wealth illegitimately.

column4: Which evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for the permissibility of investment agency?
column5: "No harm and no reciprocal harm" in all financial dealings
column6: The Prophet's interdiction of Mu'adh and sale of his assets
column7: "Engage in trade with the wealth of orphans" lest Zakah consume it
column8: "Muslims are bound by their conditions" stipulated in their contracts and agreements
column10: Per the basis, permissibility rests on the Hadith "Engage in trade with the wealth of orphans so that it will not be consumed by Zakah" and Verses on seeking sustenance.

column4: Bank A, an investment agent experienced in equity investing, wants to appoint a sub-agent to manage the principal's equity portfolio, without the principal's permission. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, at the agent's full discretion, since an agent may always delegate to a sub-agent
column6: No; the activity is within its expertise and capacity
column7: Yes, if the sub-agent is its own subsidiary
column8: Yes, if Bank A pays the sub-agent's fee
column10: Per 9/1, the agent may not appoint a sub-agent except for activities outside its expertise or capacity, or where the principal permits it.

column4: The agency requires investments yielding at least 10%. Bank A, without consulting the principal, invests at 5%, while the market average is 8%. What must Bank A compensate?
column5: Nothing, as profit is never guaranteed and the agent only owes his best effort
column6: 2%, the gap between market and stipulated profit
column7: 5%, the gap between the profit earned and the stipulated 10%
column8: 3%, the gap between the earned and average market profit
column10: Per 10/2, the agent compensates the difference between profit earned and the average market profit (if below the stipulated rate), not the stipulated minimum.

column4: Midway through an investment agency, the principal unilaterally notifies Bank A that it may now invest only in real estate. What is the status of this new restriction?
column5: Valid provided the agent's agreed fee remains unchanged
column6: Invalid; neither party may unilaterally amend the restrictions
column7: Valid, since the principal is the owner of the invested funds
column8: Valid if notice is given to the agent thirty days in advance
column10: Per 3/4, it is not permissible for any one of the parties to unilaterally amend the restrictions in the agency contract.

column4: A client asks how an investment agency differs from Mudarabah, given both aim to grow wealth. What distinction does the Shari'ah basis draw?
column5: Investment agency is a loan; Mudarabah is a sale
column6: Investment agency is a gift; Mudarabah is a guarantee
column7: Investment agency is a form of Ijarah; Mudarabah is a partnership
column8: Investment agency is a partnership in profit; Mudarabah is a contract of Ijarah for work
column10: Per the basis, investment agency, like Mudarabah and Musharakah, aims to increase wealth, but it is a form of Ijarah (hiring) while they are forms of partnership.

column4: Bank A's investment agency fee is linked to a benchmark known to both parties, referred to before each period after the first period's fee is fixed. No limits are set. What is missing?
column5: A cap and a floor setting maximum and minimum limits
column6: The principal's right to cancel before each period
column7: Conversion of the fee into a share of the profit
column8: Nothing; a known benchmark is sufficient by itself
column10: Per 5/1, a fee linked to a known benchmark referred to before each period is permissible but should be capped and floored with maximum and minimum limits.

column4: Bank A, as unrestricted investment agent, invests the agency funds in its Mudarabah portfolio. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is it entitled to the agency fee and not Mudarabah profit?
column5: The principal acts as Mudarib in the portfolio
column6: Mudarabah profit is always given to charity when the funds come from an agency
column7: Its contract with the principal is agency, not Mudarabah
column8: Agency funds cannot generate any profit
column10: Per the basis, the agent's contract is agency, not Mudarabah; even if funds go into a Mudarabah portfolio, it earns the agency commission, not Mudarabah profit.

column4: An investor appoints Bank A as unremunerated investment agent for a fixed three-year term. After six months, the investor wishes to terminate unilaterally. What is the position?
column5: It is binding only if Bank A receives a fee
column6: He may terminate at will, as unremunerated agency is a non-binding contract in all cases
column7: He may terminate if he pays the fee for the full term
column8: The contract is binding; he cannot terminate it unilaterally
column10: Per 4/1, investment agency contracts, remunerated or not, are binding on institutions as fixed-term contracts in which both parties agree not to terminate.

column4: Under an unrestricted investment agency, Bank A puts the principal's funds into a type of venture that customary practice would never accept for such funds. Was Bank A free to do so?
column5: No; it remains bound by custom and the principal's best interests
column6: No; an unrestricted agent may invest only in Murabahah deals
column7: Yes; an unrestricted agent may invest in anything at all
column8: Yes, as long as the agreed agency fee was not exceeded
column10: Per 3/3, an unrestricted agency is still restricted by customary practice and requires the agent to act in the principal's best interests.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A's regulator requires a customary accounting method for spreading profit on deferred sales over several periods. May Bank A adopt it?
column5: No; only methods invented by the Bank itself may be used
column6: Yes, if Shari'ah-compliant; AAOIFI standards preferred where possible
column7: No; all profit on a deferred sale must be booked in full at the date of the sale
column8: Yes, whether or not the method conforms to Shari'ah rules
column10: Per 8/1, customary accounting practices required by regulators may be adopted if Shari'ah-compliant; AAOIFI's Accounting Standards should be adopted whenever possible.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A sells a commodity in Murabahah at a 40% mark-up over cost, and the customer freely consents. Is there a maximum profit limit that makes this impermissible?
column5: No upper limit, given mutual consent and the values of kindness
column6: Yes; profit may not exceed the market interest rate
column7: Yes; profit may never exceed one third of the cost price, whatever the customer's consent
column8: Yes; profit is limited to the regulator's standard rate
column10: Per 4/1, there is no upper limit for profits, provided the transaction is based on mutual consent, with due consideration for kindness, contentment and clemency.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Company X earns a return under a sale contract that turns out to be invalid in Shari'ah. How is the return classified under the standard?
column5: Permissible profit if it was disclosed in advance
column6: Impermissible profit, as it results from an invalid contract
column7: Permissible profit if the buyer consented to it
column8: Permissible profit, since it arose from a sale contract concluded with mutual consent
column10: Per 3/2, impermissible profit is that which results from a prohibited transaction such as interest-based contracts, forbidden commodities or invalid contracts.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: A Mudarabah contract changes the profit ratio once a hurdle rate is reached. Per the Shari'ah basis, why are different rates permissible?
column5: Profit above a hurdle is not true profit
column6: The capital is guaranteed below the hurdle
column7: They do not disrupt the sharing of profit by all parties
column8: The Mudarib's work increases above the hurdle, so he deserves a larger share
column10: Per the basis, using different rates in Mudarabah is permissible because such a provision does not disrupt the sharing of profits by all parties.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: In a competitive market with no monopoly or extraordinary circumstances, a regulator proposes capping profit rates on all Murabahah sales. What is the ruling?
column5: Obligatory, in order to protect customers from excessive prices
column6: Permissible at all times, as part of the regulator's normal powers to protect customers
column7: Permissible only if all the licensed banks agree to it beforehand
column8: Impermissible in principle, save monopoly, extraordinary circumstances or public interest
column10: Per 4/2, a regulator may not in principle cap profits; fixing the rate is allowed in monopoly, extraordinary circumstances or clear public interest, if not prejudicial.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: A Murabahah customer cannot pay on time and asks for a longer term. Bank A proposes to extend the term and add further profit to the total amount. What is the ruling?
column5: Impermissible: rescheduling by raising profit for extension
column6: Permissible, since the customer himself requested the extension and agreed to the profit
column7: Permissible if the extension is shorter than one year
column8: Permissible if the Shari'ah board approves the amount
column10: Per 9, where the profit rate is time-bound, re-scheduling debt by increasing the profit or total amount through extending the duration is impermissible.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A uses an agreed benchmark to set Murabahah profit at the promise stage, and the contract makes later instalments vary with the benchmark's movement. Is this valid?
column5: Yes, provided that the benchmark used is a well-established one
column6: Yes, since the benchmark was mutually agreed by both parties
column7: No; benchmarks may never be referred to at all in Murabahah
column8: No; the total price and instalments must not vary with the benchmark
column10: Per 6/2, a benchmark may be used at the Wa'd or contracting stage, but the total price and instalments must be stipulated and must not vary with the benchmark.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: A Murabahah contract contains a clause obliging Bank A to grant a rebate if the customer pays early. Is this clause acceptable?
column5: Yes; early-payment rebates must always be stipulated in the contract to be valid
column6: Yes, provided the rebate equals the unearned profit
column7: No; a rebate may be granted but not stipulated in the contract
column8: No; rebates for early payment are prohibited outright
column10: Per 11, the institution may grant a rebate for early payment provided it was not stipulated in the contract, taking regulatory directives into account.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: A capital provider stipulates that the Mudarib must not invest in activities whose expected profit rate is below 6%. Is this stipulation permissible?
column5: Yes, and the Mudarib must make up any shortfall
column6: Yes, provided neither capital nor profit is guaranteed
column7: No; the Mudarib must be left fully unrestricted
column8: No; it amounts to guaranteeing the capital provider a 6% profit on his funds
column10: Per 7/2, the capital provider may stipulate the Mudarib avoid activities below a specific expected profit rate, but capital and profit may not be guaranteed.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A sells a car for 100,000 cash or 120,000 payable over two years. Is the higher credit price permissible?
column5: Yes, but only if the increase equals the prevailing interest rate
column6: Yes, and more may be added to the debt if payment is late
column7: Yes, if built into the price and the debt never rises for late payment
column8: No; any extra price charged for deferment of payment is Riba
column10: Per 5, profit in credit sales may exceed cash sales if incorporated into the price and the debt is not increased due to late payment.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: What evidence does the Shari'ah basis cite for not stipulating a maximum profit limit?
column5: "Allah has permitted sale and prohibited Riba" alone
column6: "...except it be a trade amongst you, by mutual consent"
column7: "No harm and no reciprocal harm"
column8: "Muslims are bound by their conditions"
column10: Per the basis, the absence of a profit cap rests on the Verse "...except it be a trade amongst you, by mutual consent", confirmed by an Islamic Fiqh Academy resolution.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: A Mudarabah contract sets a 60:40 profit split for a one-year tenor and 70:30 for a three-year tenor. Is setting different ratios by tenor permissible?
column5: No; ratios may change only on a hurdle rate
column6: Yes, but only if the capital is guaranteed
column7: No; one ratio must apply throughout the Mudarabah
column8: Yes; different ratios may be set for different tenors
column10: Per 7/1, in Mudarabah different profit ratios or rates may be set as per different tenors or triggered by a hurdle rate, without totally depriving any party.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: A customer argues that a higher deferred price is just like interest. Per the Shari'ah basis, on what ground is the increase in a credit sale permitted?
column5: "Allah has permitted sale", read as covering deferred sale
column6: Custom, since all markets charge more for credit
column7: The customer's consent, which validates any increase
column8: Necessity, as Islamic banks cannot otherwise operate in a market based on credit
column10: Per the basis, the increase is permitted by the Verse "Allah has permitted sale", referring to deferred sale, so the comparison between it and interest is addressed.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A wants to state the profit in its Murabahah contracts as 5% of the cost price rather than as a lump sum. Is this permissible?
column5: No; profit must always be a fixed lump sum, since a percentage makes the price unknown
column6: No; profit must be a percentage of the sale price
column7: Yes; profit may be a fixed amount or a percentage of cost
column8: Yes, but only if linked to an index benchmark
column10: Per 6/1, Murabahah profit may be stipulated as a fixed amount added to the cost price or as a percentage of the cost price.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A bought goods for 1,000 and sold them in Murabahah for 1,150. In the context of the standard on calculating profit, how is the 150 described?
column5: Interest: a charge for the time value of money
column6: Profit: the amount generated in excess of the cost
column7: Fee: consideration for the Bank's services
column8: Rebate: an amount owed back to the customer
column10: Per 2, profit means the amount generated in excess of the original capital or of the cost in financing and investment operations.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A calculates profit as an annualised percentage of the outstanding financing under an amortised payment schedule. When is this method permissible?
column5: When transparent, fully disclosed and the total price is fixed
column6: Never; only flat-rate profit methods are permissible, as reducing balances are Riba-based
column7: Always, even if the total sale price is left floating
column8: Only if the customer repays in equal monthly instalments
column10: Per 10, annualised methods on total or outstanding amounts are permissible if transparent, fully disclosed and the total sale price is stated as a fixed amount.

column3: Rules for Calculating Profit in Financial Transactions
column4: Bank A advertises "Home finance at only 4% profit!" without explaining how the profit is calculated. What does the standard require?
column5: Disclosure only if a customer complains
column6: Disclosure only once a contract is signed
column7: Nothing, as advertising is outside the contract and creates no obligation on the Bank
column8: Disclosure of the calculation method in its advertising
column10: Per 9, the institution must disclose its method of profit calculation, including when mentioning profit in advertising and marketing, to prevent deception.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite for revoking a contract due to price gouging of a trusting buyer?
column5: "No harm and no reciprocal harm"
column6: "Overcharging a trusting buyer (Mustarsil) is forbidden"
column7: "Allah has permitted sale and prohibited Riba"
column8: "Muslims are bound by their conditions", cited for binding contractual stipulations
column10: Per the basis, the Hadith states "Overcharging a trusting buyer (Mustarsil) is forbidden"; a variant narration says it is Riba.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: An elderly customer trusts a shopkeeper not to overcharge him, so he does not negotiate, and is charged far above the fair price. How does the standard classify him?
column5: A party who consented, with no option
column6: A party to Najsh, entitled to Khiyar al-Taghrir for the inflated price he was charged
column7: A victim of Tadlis, with Khiyar al-Tadlis
column8: A Mustarsil, a victim of price gouging with Khiyar al-Ghabn
column10: Per 4/3/1, sale to a Mustarsil, a purchaser who does not negotiate because he trusts the seller, is an example of price gouging.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Ahmad discovers the seller added substances to make a product look better. After discovering this, he uses up the product entirely. What happens to his Khiyar al-Tadlis?
column5: It transfers to a right of exchange for a new item
column6: It survives, since the deception was proven, and he may still revoke the sale after use
column7: It lapses, as he consumed it after discovering the deception
column8: It converts into a right to compensation
column10: Per 3/5, the option to revoke on grounds of deceptive conduct lapses if the item is consumed by the buyer after the deception is discovered.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: A dealer paints an old car to hide its age and make it appear new, and Ahmad buys it. On discovering this, what are Ahmad's options?
column5: Return the car, or keep it without compensation
column6: Return the car only within three days of purchase
column7: Nothing, since the dealer made no false statement
column8: Keep the car and claim compensation for the difference
column10: Per 3/3/2 and 3/4, painting an old car is deceptive conduct (Tadlis); the buyer may return or retain it, and gets no compensation if he retains it.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: In a Murabahah sale, the seller deliberately tells the buyer that his cost price was 100,000 when it was actually 90,000. What right does the buyer have?
column5: No option, since the buyer agreed to the price
column6: Only a claim for compensation, not revocation
column7: Khiyar al-Taghrir: an option to revoke for verbal deception
column8: Khiyar al-Tadlis: an option to revoke for deceptive conduct
column10: Per 2/1-2/2(a), deliberate misinformation on cost in Murabahah is verbal deception (Taghrir), giving the buyer the option to revoke.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: A seller argues that verbal deception should not allow revocation once the buyer has agreed to the price. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is revocation allowed?
column5: Deception defeats mutual consent, a pillar of valid contracts
column6: Any sale may be revoked within a customary period, without need for a ground
column7: The seller must always guarantee the market price
column8: Revocation punishes the seller for his deception
column10: Per the basis, verbal deception contradicts mutual consent, a basic pillar of valid contracts, since without it the buyer would not have purchased; the same applies to Tadlis.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Ahmad discovers he was overcharged excessively. Instead of revoking, he and the seller agree that the seller will pay him an indemnification amount. Is this permissible?
column5: No; his only remedy is revocation of the contract
column6: Yes; they may mutually agree on indemnification instead
column7: No; indemnification is permitted only by court order
column8: Yes, but only if it equals the full excess price
column10: Per 4/4/2, a buyer who accepts the contract has no right to compensation, but the parties may mutually agree upon an indemnification amount instead of revocation.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: At an auction, the seller's associate keeps raising the bid with no intention to buy, and Ahmad wins at an inflated price. How does the standard treat this?
column5: It is normal auction practice, so the sale is final and Ahmad has no option to revoke
column6: It gives no option, as no statement was made to Ahmad
column7: It entitles Ahmad only to a reduction of the price
column8: It is Najsh, giving Ahmad an option to revoke for verbal deception
column10: Per 2/2(b) and 2/3/1, raising bids by phantom bidding (Munajashah or Najsh) is verbal deception giving the buyer the option to revoke.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: A fruit shipment looks fresher than it really is because of unusually cool weather during transport, beyond the seller's control. Does the buyer have Khiyar al-Tadlis?
column5: No; the deception did not result from the seller's conduct
column6: Yes, but only if he returns the fruit the same day
column7: No, because fruit is excluded from this option
column8: Yes, since the buyer was misled about the condition, whatever the cause of the appearance
column10: Per 3/2/1, the deception must result from the seller's conduct or instructions; if caused by circumstances beyond his control, the option is invalid.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Ahmad knew, when buying, that the price was far above the market level, but bought anyway. He later seeks Khiyar al-Ghabn. Is he entitled to it?
column5: Yes; an excessive price alone gives the option, whether or not the buyer knew of it
column6: Yes, if he returns the item within a week
column7: Yes, but limited to partial compensation
column8: No; he must have been unaware of the gouging at inception
column10: Per 4/2, a prerequisite of Khiyar al-Ghabn is that the buyer was unaware of the price gouging at the inception of the contract.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Ahmad validly exercises Khiyar al-Taghrir and must transport the item back to the place of sale. Who bears the expenses of the return?
column5: Both parties, equally
column6: Whoever is nearer to the place of sale
column7: The seller
column8: Ahmad, as the party revoking
column10: Per 2/4/3, the seller is liable for expenses relating to the return of the item to the place of sale.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: After buying a property, Ahmad pledged it to Bank B as security. He then discovered he had been grossly overcharged. What is the status of his Khiyar al-Ghabn?
column5: It converts into a right to a price reduction
column6: It lapses, as a third-party right attached to the item
column7: It remains, as the pledge was made before he discovered the gouging
column8: It remains, subject to Bank B's consent
column10: Per 4/5(a), Khiyar al-Ghabn lapses on consumption of the item, and the attachment of a third-party right over it has the same legal effect.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: A seller hid a machine's defect by adding a substance. Before the buyer revokes, the machine's condition improves to no less than its original specification. Can he still revoke?
column5: No, unless the seller admits the deception
column6: Yes, but only with compensation to the seller
column7: No; the deception must be continuing at revocation
column8: Yes; the seller's deceptive conduct suffices
column10: Per 3/2/3, the deception must be continuing; if the item's condition improves to not less than the original specification before revocation, no right to revoke remains.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Ahmad paid 150,000 for equipment. Certified valuators' highest estimate is 110,000, which commercial custom deems excessive. Ahmad was unaware. What is his right?
column5: Khiyar al-Ghabn: to revoke the contract or accept it
column6: To revoke only if the seller made a false statement
column7: None, since the price was agreed by mutual consent
column8: To keep the item and claim back the 40,000 excess
column10: Per 4/1 and 4/4/1, if the price exceeds the experts' highest estimate and is excessive by custom, the buyer may revoke or accept without refund.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: Misled by the seller's false statements, Ahmad buys food and consumes it before discovering the deception. What is the position?
column5: Ahmad is entitled to a partial refund of the price
column6: The option lapses; the seller is entitled to the full price
column7: Ahmad may still revoke and recover the full price
column8: The seller must refund the excess over the market price
column10: Per 2/4/1-2/4/2, Khiyar al-Taghrir lapses if the item is consumed before the deception is discovered; the seller gets the full price and the buyer no refund.

column3: Options to Terminate Due to Breach of Trust (Trust-Based Options)
column4: After discovering verbal deception, Ahmad sells the item to a third party. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does his option to revoke lapse?
column5: The third party acquires the option instead of him, as it passes with the item
column6: Options lapse whenever the item changes hands
column7: The seller can no longer refund the price
column8: His disposal equals explicit consent to waive the option
column10: Per the basis, the option lapses on disposal of the item after discovering the deception, because disposal is equivalent to explicit consent to waive the option.

column4: Bank A and Company X sign a binding bilateral promise to sell and buy a commodity, solely to provide financing; no law or custom requires it. Is it legally binding?
column5: Yes, because both parties signed the document
column6: No, and fulfilling it is not even a religious duty
column7: No; it is only a religious obligation in this case
column8: Yes; all bilateral promises are legally binding
column10: Per 4/2, a bilateral promise is legally binding only where a commercial transaction is impossible without it due to law or custom, and the aim is not merely financing.

column4: Ahmad lends 100,000 to Company X. In a separate letter, X promises to let Ahmad use its warehouse free of charge during the loan. What is the ruling on this promise?
column5: Permissible, as it is outside the loan contract
column6: Permissible, as a promise is not legally binding
column7: Permissible if the warehouse use is of small value
column8: Prohibited, even though it is in a separate document
column10: Per 3/2, any promise in a loan that procures benefit for the lender beyond repayment is prohibited even if given in a document separate from the loan contract.

column4: Ahmad tells a shop he will buy a phone from it next month. The shop does nothing in reliance on this. Ahmad then changes his mind without excuse. What is the position?
column5: He breached a religious obligation, but is not legally bound
column6: He committed no wrong at all, legal or religious
column7: He is legally bound to buy the phone, since a promise to buy always binds the promisor
column8: He must pay the shop its expected profit
column10: Per 3/4, fulfilling a promise is a religious obligation and breaking it without excuse is a sin, but it is legally binding only when it causes the promisee to incur a liability.

column4: Relying solely on Ahmad's resolute promise to buy, Bank A buys a car for 50,000. Ahmad refuses to buy, and Bank A sells it to another buyer for 46,000. What must Ahmad pay?
column5: 4,000 plus the profit Bank A expected to earn
column6: 4,000, the actual loss suffered by Bank A
column7: Nothing, since a promise is only a moral duty
column8: 50,000, the full cost, in exchange for the car
column10: Per 3/4, a promisor who caused the promisee to incur liability must indemnify actual loss: the difference between cost and price obtained; actual loss excludes opportunity cost.

column4: A shop tells Ahmad: "If you buy this sofa from me, I will give you a lamp as a gift." Ahmad buys the sofa, but the shop refuses to give the lamp. Is the promise legally binding?
column5: Yes, but only if the promise was made in writing
column6: No; benevolent promises are only religiously binding
column7: No, unless the lamp's value is stated in the sale price
column8: Yes; it is conditional on Ahmad incurring a liability
column10: Per 3/6, a benevolent promise is not legally binding unless conditional on the promisee performing an act causing him to incur a liability, e.g. buying an item.

column4: Per the IIFA resolution cited in the Shari'ah basis, when can a bilateral promise be made binding on both parties?
column5: Whenever the subject is a financing transaction
column6: When a sale cannot yet be concluded and public interest requires it
column7: Whenever both parties sign a written undertaking in the presence of two witnesses
column8: Whenever the seller already owns the commodity
column10: The basis cites an IIFA resolution: a bilateral promise may bind both where a sale cannot be concluded (seller not owning the commodity) and public interest obliges it.

column4: Under a legally binding promise, the agreed date arrives. Bank A, the promisee, offers to sell the asset to the customer, the promisor. What is the status?
column5: The customer is bound religiously and legally to accept
column6: The sale was already concluded on the date automatically
column7: The customer may freely accept or reject the offer
column8: The sale needs no acceptance once the offer is made
column10: Per 3/8, the promised contract is not automatic; offer and acceptance must be exchanged; if the promisee makes the offer under a binding promise, the promisor must accept.

column4: In an Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, Bank A promises to gift the asset to the lessee if he pays all lease instalments. He pays them all, but Bank A hesitates. Is the promise binding?
column5: No; promises of gifts are never legally binding, even when conditional on full payment
column6: No; only the lessee's promises are legally binding
column7: Yes; it is legally binding as a conditional gift promise
column8: Yes, but only if the gift was priced in the rent
column10: Per 5/2 with 3/6, the institution's promise in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek to gift the asset conditional on payment of all instalments is legally binding.

column4: Bank A tells Company X of its resolute intention to lease it a building next year, leaving X free to take up the offer or not. What is this arrangement and X's role?
column5: A bilateral promise binding both parties
column6: A concluded Ijarah contract effective next year
column7: A unilateral promise; Company X is the promisor
column8: A unilateral promise; Company X is the promisee
column10: Per 2/1, a unilateral promise is informing another of a resolute intention to act in the future in its interest; the receiving party, the promisee, has the option to avail itself.

column4: Ahmad buys a car from Bank A on credit for 120,000 and, after the sale, promises to sell it back to Bank A on spot for 100,000. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, since the promise followed the sale and was not part of the contract
column6: Permissible, since a promise is not a contract
column7: Prohibited as 'Inah, though the promise came after the sale
column8: Permissible if a third party acts as intermediary
column10: Per 3/3, a promise resulting in a repurchase ('Inah) is prohibited whether part of the sale or given before or after it; using a colluding intermediary is also prohibited.

column4: Relying on a customer's binding promise to buy, Bank A acquires an asset, but then prefers to sell it to someone else. The customer insists on buying. Who is bound?
column5: Only Bank A, as the party that bought the asset
column6: Only the customer; Bank A may demand performance or waive it
column7: Both parties, equally, once the asset is bought on the strength of the customer's promise
column8: Neither party, as the promise was unilateral
column10: Per 3/5, a legally binding promise is enforceable only against the promisor; the promisee has the option either to demand performance or to waive it.

column4: Under a binding bilateral promise in a supply agreement, Company X refuses to conclude the purchase. Bank A sells the goods to a third party at a lower price. What may Bank A recover?
column5: Its actual loss from the lower price, excluding opportunity cost
column6: The full price promised, while keeping the third-party price
column7: Its actual loss plus the profit it expected to make
column8: Only an injunction; it may not claim any indemnity
column10: Per 4/3, the non-defaulting party may seek an injunction; if it mitigates by contracting with a third party at a lower price, the defaulter indemnifies actual loss, not opportunity cost.

column4: Bank A and a client sign a master agreement setting the process and terms for future Murabahah deals. Is the client obliged to enter into a Murabahah upon signing?
column5: Yes; the master agreement is a concluded sale
column6: No; each party keeps the option to enter each deal
column7: No, and its terms cannot apply to later deals
column8: Yes, for at least one Murabahah transaction
column10: Per 4/4, a master agreement is a non-binding bilateral promise; each party has an option, and once a Murabahah is concluded its terms apply as reconfirmed in each contract.

column4: Two institutions exchange back-to-back bilateral promises designed to replicate a derivative that Shari'ah prohibits. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if each promise is non-binding
column6: Permissible, since promises are not contracts and create no binding obligation
column7: Permissible if the subject matters differ
column8: Impermissible, as a circumvention of a Shari'ah prohibition
column10: Per 6, back-to-back bilateral promises entered to circumvent Shari'ah prohibitions, such as back-to-back derivatives, are impermissible.

column4: In a diminishing Musharakah, the client promised to buy units of Bank A's share at stipulated intervals. The client now wants to stop buying. Is his promise binding?
column5: Yes, but only for the first purchase of units
column6: No; it is only a religious obligation
column7: Yes; the client's promise is legally binding
column8: No; only Bank A's promises are binding
column10: Per 5/2 with 3/5, the client's promise in diminishing Musharakah to buy units of the institution's share at stipulated intervals is legally binding.

column4: An importer and Bank A use a binding bilateral promise when opening a letter of credit, as the seller does not yet own the goods. What does the Shari'ah basis rely on?
column5: An IIFA resolution permitting it where law, public interest or custom requires
column6: The rule that all bilateral promises bind both parties, as they are equal to contracts
column7: The Hadith "Muslims are bound by their conditions"
column8: The consensus that a promise always creates a contract
column10: The basis cites an IIFA resolution: where a sale cannot be concluded as the seller does not own the goods, and public interest, law or custom requires (e.g. LCs), it may bind.

column4: Bank A promises to sell a specific commodity to Company X in three months, and Company X promises to buy that same commodity from Bank A. What does the standard call this?
column5: Two unrelated unilateral promises
column6: A master agreement for future transactions
column7: A bilateral promise
column8: A concluded sale with a deferred delivery
column10: Per 2/2, a bilateral promise is the exchange of two back-to-back promises between two parties, each promising a future act relating to the same subject matter.

column4: The orchard needs a major new well drilled, work customarily beyond an irrigator's duties. How may the Musaqat worker arrange it?
column5: He may not arrange it; only the owner can
column6: He may hire others on the account of the partnership
column7: He must drill it himself at no extra cost, as it forms part of his husbandry duties
column8: He must hire others at his own sole expense
column10: Per 8/3, the worker may hire others, on the account of the Irrigation Partnership, to perform work customarily beyond the scope of his duties.

column4: A Musaqat worker falls seriously ill and cannot work, and the owner revokes the contract. What is the worker entitled to?
column5: A market wage for the period he worked
column6: His full stipulated share of the crop
column7: A wage, less the owner's actual loss
column8: Nothing, since he did not complete the work
column10: Per 13/2/1/1, if the worker cannot work for a reason outside his control, such as illness, he gets a market wage for the period worked.

column4: An owner sets a Musaqat term ending before the produce normally materializes. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is this impermissible?
column5: Harvest time must be fixed by a judge
column6: Short terms are prohibited in all contracts, as the parties cannot foresee the outcome
column7: The worker must always receive a market wage
column8: Justice: the owner must not get the produce while the worker gets nothing
column10: Per the basis, the term runs until produce materializes per the rules of justice, so the owner does not exclusively benefit and the worker is not deprived.

column4: A Musaqat worker demands a larger share of the crop for harvesting the fruit, as harvesting is hard work. Is he entitled to an increase?
column5: No; customary work is already his contractual duty
column6: Yes, if the harvest is larger than expected
column7: Yes, a reasonable increase for the harvesting
column8: No, but the owner must pay him a separate wage
column10: Per 8/3, customary work does not entitle the worker to any increase in his share, as he is already contractually obligated to do it.

column4: The crop did not materialize within the Musaqat term. In all, the worker worked 6 months, then stopped with a valid excuse; the crop took 12 months to materialize. What does he get?
column5: His full share, as he stopped with a valid excuse before the contract ended
column6: Nothing, since he stopped before the crop
column7: A market wage for the six months worked
column8: Half of his share, in proportion to time worked
column10: Per 10/2, a worker who stops with a valid excuse gets the portion of his share corresponding to time worked relative to the total time the crop took to materialize.

column4: A Musaqat worker dies mid-season. The contract does not stipulate that the work is non-assignable. What option do his heirs have?
column5: To claim his full share without further work
column6: To complete the work on the same terms, personally or by hiring
column7: None; the contract terminates on his death, as it rests on his personal work
column8: To renegotiate a higher share with the owner
column10: Per 12/3, absent a non-assignability stipulation, the successor may complete the work on the same terms, himself or by hiring workers, for the deceased's share.

column4: A Musaqat worker hires helpers at his own expense. Per the Shari'ah basis, what supports this, and what remains?
column5: Analogy with Ijarah; liability is shared equally
column6: Necessity; liability passes to the owner
column7: The Khaybar condition; his own liability does not cease
column8: Custom alone; liability passes to the helpers, who are paid from the partnership
column10: Per the basis, the Prophet allowed the people of Khaybar to use hired hands at their own expense; the worker's responsibility does not cease.

column4: Without the owner's permission, a Musaqat worker subcontracts his whole work to another irrigator. What option does the owner have?
column5: To ratify or reject the third-party contract
column6: Only to claim compensation from the subcontractor
column7: None; the worker may assign the work freely
column8: To void the Musaqat and keep the whole crop
column10: Per 6/1/2, the worker may not subcontract without the owner's permission; if he does, the owner may ratify or reject the third-party contract.

column4: A flood destroys 40% of a Musaqat crop; 60% survives. The worker's stipulated share is one half. How is the surviving crop divided?
column5: The worker bears the whole loss from his share
column6: Half each of what remains, per the stipulated shares
column7: The owner bears the whole loss from his share
column8: The owner first recovers the 40% that was lost, and the rest is shared
column10: Per 10/1, if a natural disaster destroys only part of the crop, the parties divide what remains according to their stipulated shares.

column4: After work began, an orchard owner claims Musaqat is non-binding and that he may cancel at will. Which Shari'ah basis supports its binding nature?
column5: "No harm and no reciprocal harm" in partnerships
column6: "Overcharging a trusting buyer is forbidden"
column7: "O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations"
column8: "Ill-gotten sapling shall have no right therein"
column10: Per the basis, Musaqat becomes binding once entered into or undertaken under the overarching Verse "O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations".

column4: A Musaqat contract gives the worker the first 1,000 kg of dates harvested and the owner the rest. Is this share arrangement valid?
column5: Yes, if the owner guarantees the 1,000 kg
column6: Yes, provided the harvest exceeds 1,000 kg
column7: Yes, since the worker's quantity is fixed and known, which removes any Gharar
column8: No; each party needs a defined, indivisible share of produce
column10: Per 5/1, the contract should stipulate for each party a predetermined, defined, indivisible share of the produce.

column4: During a Musaqat, the trees under contract die from disease and can no longer bear fruit. What happens to the contract?
column5: It terminates
column6: It converts into an Ijarah of the land
column7: It continues until the term expires
column8: The worker must replant the trees
column10: Per 12/4, the Musaqat contract terminates upon the death of the trees or their inability to bear fruit.

column4: Before the crop materializes, an orchard owner bars the worker from the trees and, when asked, still refuses to let him complete the work. What is the worker entitled to?
column5: Double his share, as a penalty on the owner
column6: His stipulated share of the expected crop
column7: Nothing, as no crop has materialized yet
column8: A wage at the market rate for similar work
column10: Per 8/5, if the owner does not enable the worker before the crop materializes and refuses when asked, the worker is entitled to the market wage for similar work.

column4: A Musaqat on mango trees sets a two-month term, although the crop normally needs six months to be ready. What is the problem?
column5: Musaqat must always be for a full calendar year
column6: The term must run to harvest or a period normally enough for it
column7: The term must be at least three years for trees
column8: None; the parties may set any term they wish, however short for the crop to mature
column10: Per 5/3, the contract is valid until harvest or for a defined period in which the crop is normally enough for harvest.

column4: An owner offers his Musaqat worker a lump sum of 5,000 instead of a share of the crop. Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a share required?
column5: A lump sum is always Riba in any contract, because it fixes the return in advance
column6: The worker must bear the risk of the land
column7: A lump sum diverts the contract from Musaqat's features
column8: Cash payments are not allowed in farming
column10: Per the basis, specifying lump-sum compensation diverts the contract from the features of Musaqat, based on the Khaybar Hadith; a known share averts Jahalah.

column4: An orchard owner refuses to allow the Musaqat worker to do his work. What right does the worker have regarding the contract?
column5: He is entitled to revoke the contract
column6: He must apply to the owner's heirs
column7: He has no right of revocation
column8: He must wait until the term expires
column10: Per 13/3, the worker is entitled to revoke the contract if the owner refuses to allow him to work (see 8/5).

column4: Two months into a binding Musaqat, before any crop materializes, the worker abandons the work and cannot be made to continue. What is he entitled to?
column5: A market wage for the two months worked
column6: Nothing; he gets no share of the crop
column7: A share proportionate to the time worked
column8: His full share once the crop materializes
column10: Per 8/4, if the worker stops working before the crop materializes, he is not entitled to any share.

column4: A Musaqat contract covers a grove of old trees that are no longer productive and cannot bear fruit. What is the status of the contract?
column5: Valid, but the worker gets a wage instead
column6: Valid, if the worker's share is increased
column7: Invalid; the trees must be arable and need husbandry
column8: Valid, since the trees are clearly identified and owned by the contracting party
column10: Per 4/3, the trees must be identified, arable (productive), and in need of irrigation and plant husbandry.

column4: An orchard owner stipulates in the Musaqat that the worker must also repaint the owner's house during the season. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, if the worker's share is raised to compensate him for the extra work
column6: Yes, as the owner may set any terms he wishes
column7: Yes, if the extra work is done after the harvest
column8: No; the work is restricted to husbandry of the crop and trees
column10: Per 5/2, the work should be restricted to the husbandry of the crop and trees; the owner may not demand additional work from the worker in this contract.

column4: An owner argues his Musaqat worker should guarantee the crop. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the worker act in a fiduciary capacity?
column5: He is the owner's agent in preserving the trees and fruits
column6: He has no share in the crop until division, so he cannot be a partner
column7: He is a lessee of the land under the contract
column8: He is a guarantor appointed by the owner
column10: Per the basis, the worker acts in a fiduciary capacity rather than a position of liability because he is an agent on behalf of the owner in caring for trees and fruits.

column4: Midway through a Musaqat, it transpires the trees actually belong to a third party, not the contracting owner. Who gets the crop, and what does the worker get?
column5: The worker and contracting party share it as agreed, since the worker acted in good faith
column6: The contracting party; the worker gets his share
column7: The third party; the worker gets nothing
column8: The third party; the worker gets a market wage up to his share
column10: Per 11/1, the crop belongs to the third party; the worker gets a market wage from the other party, not exceeding what his share would have been.

column4: A hailstorm completely destroys an orchard's crop under a Musaqat. The worker had worked diligently all season. What is he entitled to?
column5: Half of his expected share
column6: Nothing
column7: Compensation from the owner
column8: A market wage for his work
column10: Per 10/1, if the crop is completely destroyed by a natural disaster, the worker is not entitled to anything.

column4: Which of the following does the Shari'ah basis cite as Sunnah evidence for the permissibility of Musaqat?
column5: The Hadith on overcharging a trusting buyer
column6: The Hadith on the wealth of orphans and Zakah
column7: The Prophet gave Khaybar to its people for half of its yield
column8: The Prophet's interdiction of Mu'adh's property and sale of it to pay his creditors
column10: Per the basis, the Prophet gave the land of Khaybar to its inhabitants to work and cultivate for half its yield; Ijma', common sense and analogy with Mudarabah also apply.

column4: Under a Musaqat, at what point does the worker become entitled to his share of the crop?
column5: Only after the crop is harvested and sold, when the profit can be known
column6: Upon signing, as an advance on the crop
column7: Only at the end of the agreed contract term
column8: As soon as the crop materializes, on an indivisible basis
column10: Per 9/2, the worker is entitled to his share of the crop on an indivisible basis as soon as it materializes.

column4: Bank A does not own any orchards but wants to use Musaqat. Which structure does the standard recognise?
column5: Guarantee a fixed crop yield to tree owners
column6: Contract Musaqat with tree owners, then hire workers
column7: Lend money to tree owners in return for a share of their crop
column8: Buy the future crop at a discount via Musaqat
column10: Per 15/1, an institution may enter into Musaqat contracts with owners of trees and then hire workers (irrigators) to carry out the work.

column4: An orchard owner and a worker sign a Musaqat. Before any work starts, and with no agreement not to terminate, the owner wishes to withdraw. Can he?
column5: Only with the approval of a court
column6: Only if he pays the worker the market wage
column7: Yes; it binds only on commencing work or by agreement
column8: No; Musaqat is binding on both parties as soon as it is signed, before work starts
column10: Per 3, Musaqat is permissible and becomes binding on commencement of the work or if the parties mutually agreed not to terminate before expiry.

column4: A date-palm Musaqat is silent on by-products. Besides the dates, the palms yield palm leaves each season. How are the leaves treated?
column5: Shared as part of the crop per the agreed ratios
column6: They belong to the worker as a reward for work
column7: They are sold and given to charity
column8: They belong to the owner of the trees alone
column10: Per 9/1, all recurring produce such as fruits and palm leaves is shared as part of the crop, unless the parties agreed to restrict sharing to the fruits.

column4: Ahmad holds a long lease on an orchard (owning its usufruct, not the land). He contracts Karim to irrigate and tend it for one third of the produce. How is this contract classified?
column5: A Mudarabah, since Karim contributes only work
column6: An Ijarah of Karim's services, not a Musaqat
column7: Invalid, as only the orchard's owner may contract
column8: A valid Musaqat, as the owner of usufruct may contract
column10: Per 2, Musaqat is a contract between the owner of an orchard or its usufruct and a worker (irrigator), sharing the produce in ratios stipulated at contracting.

column4: The trees under a Musaqat become unable to bear fruit. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the contract terminate?
column5: "Neither harm nor malice": he would otherwise work gratis
column6: The owner may then take the land back for free, as the worker's right ends with the trees
column7: The worker's share automatically becomes a wage
column8: Musaqat must always yield a minimum profit
column10: Per the basis, termination rests on the Hadith "There should be neither harm nor malice", as the worker would be excessively harmed by working without compensation.

column4: After harvest, the dates of a Musaqat are stored awaiting sale. Absent any other term, who is responsible for taking care of them now?
column5: The worker alone, until they are sold, as he worked on them
column6: Owner and worker, each in proportion to his share
column7: Whoever holds the storage keys at the time
column8: The owner alone, from the moment of harvest
column10: Per 8/1, after harvesting the worker and owner take care of the crop in proportion to their shares; before harvest the worker does unless custom or contract differ.

column4: After the crop has materialized, the orchard owner prevents the Musaqat worker from continuing. What is the worker entitled to?
column5: A market wage only for time worked
column6: His share plus a market wage
column7: His stipulated share of the crop
column8: Nothing, as he did not complete the work
column10: Per 8/5, if the owner prevents the worker after the crop materializes, the worker is entitled to his stipulated share of the crop.

column4: A Musaqat worker waters the trees but refuses to pollinate, prune or control pests, saying only irrigation is his job. Is he right?
column5: Yes, unless the owner pays him an extra wage
column6: No, but the owner must pay for the pesticides
column7: Yes; his duty is limited to watering the trees, as that is what the contract names
column8: No; husbandry includes pollinating, pruning and pest control
column10: Per 6/1/1, the worker carries out plant husbandry: watering, pollinating, fertilising, weeding, pruning, controlling pests, harvesting and seasonal work.

column4: A Musaqat worker negligently fails to control pests, and part of the crop is lost. What is his position?
column5: He indemnifies the loss and forfeits his share
column6: He loses his entire share of the crop
column7: He indemnifies the actual loss but keeps his crop share
column8: He is not liable, as he acts as a fiduciary and a fiduciary bears no loss
column10: Per 6/3, the worker is a fiduciary; for misconduct, negligence or breach he indemnifies the owner's actual loss but remains entitled to his share of the crop.

column4: A Musaqat worker dies; the heirs decline to continue, and the owner completes the work. Once the crop materializes, what are the heirs entitled to?
column5: A share proportionate to his work, uncapped
column6: A market wage for the deceased's period, capped at his share
column7: Nothing, as they declined to continue
column8: The deceased's full stipulated share, since the crop materialized during the contract
column10: Per 12/3, the successor gets a market wage for the period worked by the deceased, not exceeding his stipulated share of the crop.

column4: A Musaqat refers vaguely to "some trees on the farm" without identifying them. Per the Shari'ah basis, why must the trees be identified and productive?
column5: To avoid Gharar; non-productive trees defeat Musaqat's purpose
column6: To determine the Zakat due before the contract
column7: To allow the owner to change trees during the term
column8: To calculate the worker's market wage in advance if the crop fails to appear
column10: Per the basis, identifying the trees and requiring them to be arable avoids Gharar; non-productive trees do not fit the purpose of Musaqat.

column4: After the crop materializes, a Musaqat worker quits. The owner hires a third party for 7,000 to finish. The worker's share later sells for 10,000. What does the worker get?
column5: 10,000, his full share
column6: Nothing, as he abandoned the work after the crop materialized and so forfeits his share
column7: 5,000, half of his share
column8: 3,000, his share after deducting the wage
column10: Per 8/4, a third party's wage is deducted from the worker's share after harvest and sale; any shortfall he makes up, and any surplus he keeps.

column4: Karim agrees to a Musaqat with a party whom he knows has usurped the orchard. The rightful owner reclaims the trees and produce. What is Karim entitled to?
column5: No remuneration at all
column6: His stipulated share of the produce
column7: Half of his stipulated share
column8: A wage at the fair market rate
column10: Per 11/2, a worker unaware of usurpation gets a fair market wage, but if he knew the trees were usurped he is not entitled to any remuneration.

column4: The agreed Musaqat term ends, but the crop has not yet materialized. What options does the worker have?
column5: Continue and claim a market wage for the extra time
column6: Demand that the owner extend at a higher share
column7: Stop, or continue without a wage until the crop appears
column8: Stop and claim a market wage for the full term
column10: Per 10/2, if the crop does not materialize within the term, the worker may stop working or continue without a wage until it materializes and then take his share.

column4: A Musaqat worker becomes unable to work for a reason within his control, and the owner revokes the contract. What is the outcome?
column5: He gets his full share and owes nothing
column6: He gets a market wage but indemnifies actual loss
column7: He gets a market wage and owes nothing
column8: He gets nothing and must indemnify the owner for the actual loss he suffered
column10: Per 13/2/1/2, he gets a market wage for the period worked but must indemnify the owner for actual loss suffered, as determined by experts.

column4: A worker knowingly worked usurped trees and is denied any pay. Which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite?
column5: "Overcharging a trusting buyer is Riba"
column6: "The Pen has been lifted from writing the deeds of three"
column7: "There should be neither harm nor malice"
column8: "Ill-gotten sapling shall have no right therein"
column10: Per the basis, a worker aware of usurpation is a transgressor, within the Hadith "Ill-gotten sapling shall have no right therein".

column4: A Musaqat worker hires two helpers to assist him with the customary work, and asks that their wages be paid out of the overall crop. What is the ruling?
column5: He may not hire anyone to assist him
column6: He may hire them, but their wages are his alone
column7: Their wages come from the crop before division
column8: The owner must pay their wages in full
column10: Per 6/2 and 8/3, the worker may employ others to assist, but if he hires others to do his work their wage is his sole responsibility, not taken from the crop.

column4: The parties to a Musaqat obtain Takaful cover for the orchard's crop. Nothing is agreed on who pays. How is the Takaful cost borne?
column5: By both parties, in proportion to their shares
column6: Equally, regardless of their shares
column7: By the worker alone, as manager of the work
column8: By the owner alone, as owner of the trees
column10: Per 8/2, the worker and owner bear the partnership's expenses, including Takaful insurance, in proportion to their shares unless agreed otherwise.

column4: An orchard owner signs a Musaqat with a 12-year-old boy as the worker. Which Shari'ah basis is cited for requiring legal competency?
column5: "O you who believe! Fulfil (your) obligations", the verse on contracts
column6: "There should be neither harm nor malice"
column7: "The Pen has been lifted from writing the deeds of three"
column8: "Muslims are bound by their conditions"
column10: Per the basis, legal competency rests on the Hadith "The Pen has been lifted from writing the deeds of three", including the child until puberty.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: How does the Shari'ah basis characterise the option to revoke owing to deal fragmentation?
column5: As a type of defect
column6: As a type of deception
column7: As a cooling-off option
column8: As a form of price gouging
column10: Per the basis, deal fragmentation is a type of defect; some Fiqh references categorise it under the option to revoke due to defect.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: A buyer discovers a hidden defect in goods, but meanwhile the goods were damaged in his possession. The seller refuses to take them back. What is the buyer entitled to?
column5: Return of the goods with a full refund
column6: Compensation for the defect (Arsh) only
column7: Return of the goods, less the damage
column8: Nothing, since the goods are damaged
column10: Per 2/6/2, if the item was damaged in the buyer's possession, he is entitled only to compensation for the defect, unless the seller accepts the damaged item back.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: After discovering a hidden defect in a delivery van, Ahmad keeps using it for his business for months without any excuse. What happens to his option to revoke?
column5: It continues, but the price is reduced
column6: It converts into a right to a new van
column7: It ceases, as his conduct implies acceptance
column8: It continues until he formally waives it
column10: Per 2/8/4, the option ceases if the buyer's conduct implies acceptance, such as continuing to use the item or delaying return beyond custom without excuse.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Ahmad bought land and built a house on it. He then discovers a hidden material defect in the land. What is his remedy?
column5: No remedy, as he has altered the land
column6: Return of the land and recovery of the building cost
column7: Return of the land with the house to the seller
column8: Compensation for the defect, as return is prevented
column10: Per 2/6/3-2/6/4, an attached addition not growing out of the item, like a building on land, prevents return; the buyer is entitled to compensation (Arsh).

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
