column4: An Istisna'a contract for a building includes a clause excluding the manufacturer's liability for any defects (sale "as is where is"). Is this clause permissible?
column5: No; excluding liability for defect is prohibited in Istisna'a
column6: Yes, if the price is reduced in exchange
column7: Yes; Bay' al-Bara'ah is valid in every contract, including Istisna'a for a building
column8: No, unless the buyer is a financial institution
column10: Per 2/2/4, a clause excluding the seller's liability for defect (Bay' al-Bara'ah) is prohibited in Ijarah and Istisna'a contracts.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: After buying a car, Ahmad notices a tiny mark that custom does not regard as a defect and that does not reduce its value or fitness. Does he have an option to revoke?
column5: Yes; any defect at all gives the option
column6: No, unless the seller hid it deliberately
column7: Yes, if he notices it within a week
column8: No; the defect must be material
column10: Per 2/2/1, a material defect is one that renders the item defective by custom, makes it unfit for purpose or diminishes its value.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: At contracting, Ahmad knew that part of a package of goods belonged to a third party and might be withheld. It is withheld. Does he have an option for deal fragmentation?
column5: Yes, as the deal is now incomplete and he did not receive everything he bought
column6: Yes, but only to claim compensation
column7: No; he must not have known the deal would fragment
column8: Yes, if the third party objects
column10: Per 3/2, the option to revoke owing to deal fragmentation is subject to the buyer not knowing that the deal would become fragmented.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: A car delivered as described is in good working order. Two months later, its condition changes so that it no longer meets the description. Does the buyer have an option for breach of description?
column5: Yes, if the description was in writing
column6: No; the breach must occur at or before delivery
column7: No, unless the seller caused the change
column8: Yes, within the customary return period, whenever the change occurs after delivery
column10: Per 4/2/4, the breach of description must occur at or before the time of delivery (actual or constructive) and must not be a subsequent occurrence.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: A man bought a servant, used him for work, found a defect and returned him. Which statement of the Prophet does the Shari'ah basis cite from this case?
column5: "No yield without risk taking"
column6: "No harm and no reciprocal harm"
column7: "Overcharging a trusting buyer is forbidden"
column8: "Muslims are bound by their conditions"
column10: Per the basis, the Hadith of 'A'ishah on a returned defective serf, where the Prophet said "No yield without risk taking", supports the option to revoke due to defect.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Part of a package deal turns out to belong to a third party. The buyer keeps the rest, which has no defect, at its share of the price, and claims extra compensation. Is he entitled?
column5: Yes, for the inconvenience and loss caused to him by the fragmentation of the deal
column6: Yes, equal to the third party's part
column7: Yes, as a fixed percentage of the price
column8: No; compensation applies only if what remains is defective
column10: Per 3/4, the buyer may revoke or accept the remainder at its portion of the price; he is not entitled to compensation unless there is a defect in what remains.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Ahmad bought a car described as automatic but received a manual one. He dies before exercising his option to revoke for breach of description. What happens to the option?
column5: It passes to the seller
column6: It transfers to his successors
column7: It converts into a right to Arsh
column8: It lapses upon his death
column10: Per 4/5, the option to revoke for breach of description can transfer to all types of successors and assignees.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Bank A sells Company X 100 cartons in one deal. Before delivery, 20 cartons are destroyed. Company X did not foresee this. What are its options?
column5: Accept 80 cartons and pay the full price, as the destruction was not caused by the seller
column6: Revoke only if more than half are destroyed
column7: Revoke, or accept 80 cartons at their portion of the price
column8: Accept 80 cartons and claim extra compensation
column10: Per 3/3/3 and 3/4, if part of the sold items is destroyed before delivery, the buyer may revoke or accept the remainder for the corresponding portion of the price.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Ahmad has taken delivery of a car and then discovers a hidden material defect. He wishes to revoke and return it. How is revocation effected?
column5: Automatically, upon discovery of the defect
column6: By mutual consent or a court order
column7: Unilaterally, by giving notice to the seller
column8: Only by the seller's free choice
column10: Per 2/5, if the buyer returns the item after taking delivery, revocation is effected by mutual consent or court order; before delivery he may revoke unilaterally by notice.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: A buyer knew in advance that a package deal would be fragmented. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does this knowledge remove his option?
column5: He should have bought from another seller
column6: Fragmentation is never a valid ground anyway
column7: His knowledge evidences consent, and the defect is not hidden
column8: Knowledge transfers the risk of fragmentation to the third party who owns the goods
column10: Per the basis, the buyer's prior knowledge is viewed as evidence of consent, and the defect is then not hidden or concealed.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Ahmad buys a used machine. Neither he nor the seller knew it had a hidden material defect, which later appears. Does Ahmad have an option to revoke due to defect?
column5: Yes; the seller's unawareness of the defect is irrelevant
column6: Yes, but only if the seller knew of the defect
column7: No; he may only claim Arsh, not revoke
column8: No, since the seller acted in good faith, without knowledge of the defect
column10: Per 2/2/3, the buyer must be unaware of the hidden defect at contracting, irrespective of the seller's awareness of it.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Ahmad buys a laptop, then spills coffee on it, causing a hidden circuit fault. He seeks to revoke the sale due to defect. What is the ruling?
column5: He may claim Arsh but not revoke
column6: He may revoke, as the defect is hidden and was not known to him when he bought
column7: He may revoke if he reports it promptly
column8: No option, since the defect was caused by the buyer
column10: Per 2/2/5, a condition of the option to revoke due to defect is that the hidden defect was not caused by the buyer.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Ahmad's contract specifies a red car; the seller delivers an identical white one. Ahmad decides to keep it. What price does he pay?
column5: Half the difference in market values
column6: The full price, with no compensation
column7: The full price less a colour discount
column8: The market price of a white car
column10: Per 4/1 and 4/3/1, if the item fails the description, the buyer may return it or accept it for its full price without any entitlement to compensation.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: Heirs of a buyer claim his option to revoke for breach of description. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does this option pass to heirs?
column5: All options pass to heirs without exception, being part of the deceased's estate
column6: It is a personal right of the deceased buyer
column7: The seller consented to it in the contract
column8: It falls within ownership of a physical asset ('Ayn)
column10: Per the basis, the option for breach of description transfers on death to heirs, general or special, because it falls in the category of physical asset ('Ayn) ownership.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: A car sold as "automatic" turns out to be manual, and it cannot now be returned. What is the buyer entitled to?
column5: A full refund while keeping the car
column6: A replacement automatic car at no cost
column7: A refund of the price difference between the two types
column8: Nothing, since the car cannot be returned and the option to revoke has therefore lapsed
column10: Per 4/3/2, if return is impossible, the buyer gets a partial refund equal to the price difference between an item fulfilling the description and one that does not.

column3: Options to Revoke Contracts Due to Incomplete Performance
column4: A buyer keeps a defective item and seeks Arsh. Per the Hanafi and Shafi'i view adopted in the Shari'ah basis, why is no Arsh due when he keeps it?
column5: Descriptions are not treated as part of the price here
column6: The seller's good faith cancels any Arsh
column7: Arsh is due only in Ijarah contracts
column8: The buyer waived all rights by taking delivery of the item and keeping it
column10: Per the basis, no Arsh is due if the buyer keeps the item, as descriptions are not considered part of the price, and the seller did not consent to a lower price.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: A credit sale contract is silent on any option. The buyer misses the payment date, and the seller now claims an option to revoke for non-payment. Is it available?
column5: Yes, but only by a court order
column6: Yes; it arises automatically on any non-payment
column7: Yes, if the delay exceeds the customary period
column8: No; it is valid only if expressly stipulated
column10: Per 3/1, options to revoke for non-payment are not valid unless they are expressly stipulated.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A buys goods from a supplier with a cooling-off option, planning to offer them to clients without any binding promise to purchase from them. Is this permissible?
column5: No; Bank A may not hold an option as buyer
column6: Yes; it may return the goods if clients do not buy
column7: No; Bank A must first obtain a binding promise
column8: Yes, but it may not return the goods later
column10: Per 2/8/2, the institution may stipulate an option when buying from suppliers to offer items to clients without a binding promise, returning them if clients do not buy.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A buys shares with a cooling-off option held by Bank A. During the option period, the company pays a dividend on the shares. Who is entitled to the dividend?
column5: The seller
column6: Bank A, in all cases
column7: Bank A, if it confirms the purchase
column8: Both parties, equally
column10: Per 2/6/3, an increase that is separate but grows out of the original, such as dividends on shares and rent from leased assets, belongs to the seller.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: A trader buys a commodity with a cooling-off option, intending to revoke if the market price falls during the period. Is this use permissible?
column5: No, unless the seller holds the option too
column6: Yes; protecting the buyer from price falls is the purpose of the option
column7: No; options may not be used to avoid price fluctuations
column8: Yes, if the period is under 3 days
column10: Per 2/8/5, it is not permissible to use cooling-off options to avoid price fluctuations during the option period.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad buys a car with a 7-day cooling-off option and test-drives it once to check its performance. Does this test drive cancel his option?
column5: Yes; any use of the item confirms the contract and ends the option
column6: Yes, unless the seller was present and agreed to the test drive
column7: No, but he must pay a fee for using the car
column8: No; testing cancels it only if repeated without need
column10: Per 2/4/2, the option owner may test the item without losing the right to revoke, unless he does so repetitively without need or acts as owner contrary to terms or custom.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: In a sale with a cooling-off option, the buyer voluntarily pays the price, but the seller holds back delivery of the item. What may the buyer do?
column5: Force the seller to deliver immediately
column6: Demand return of the price he paid
column7: Claim compensation for the delay
column8: Nothing; payment has confirmed the contract
column10: Per 2/4/3, payment and delivery are not required; if one party pays or delivers and the other holds back, the first may demand return of what it paid or delivered.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A sells land to Company X, with a cooling-off option held by Bank A alone. During the option period, who owns the land?
column5: Company X, from the moment of contract, subject to Bank A's right to revoke
column6: Company X, once it pays the price
column7: Bank A; ownership does not transfer to Company X
column8: Both jointly, in proportion to the price paid, until the option expires
column10: Per 2/5/1, if the option is held by both parties or only the seller, ownership of neither countervalue transfers and rights remain solely with the seller.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A enters a Salam contract and wants to stipulate an option to revoke if the buyer fails to pay. Is this allowed?
column5: No; it is not permissible in Salam
column6: Yes, if expressly stipulated
column7: Yes, if the period is specified
column8: Yes, in all deferred contracts
column10: Per 3/2, options to revoke for non-payment are permissible in contracts not requiring spot payment, but not in Salam and currency exchange contracts.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A buys 1,000 tonnes of wheat and wants a cooling-off option on only part of the deal. What must the contract specify?
column5: Nothing; the option may cover any part chosen later by the buyer
column6: The identity of the eventual end-buyer
column7: The percentage of the wheat to which the option relates
column8: The specific bags to which the option relates, identified by number
column10: Per 2/8/3, an option may relate to part of a deal; for differing items they must be specified, and for fungibles like wheat the percentage must be specified.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Under an either-or option, the period expires without the buyer choosing which item he will take. The seller has not revoked. What is the position?
column5: The contract lapses automatically and the price is returned to the buyer
column6: The buyer is legally obliged to make his choice
column7: The buyer must take all the items
column8: The seller picks the item for him, whichever he prefers
column10: Per 4/2/3, if the period expires without the buyer choosing, he is legally obligated to do so unless the seller chooses to revoke the contract.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Per the Shari'ah basis, why is a cooling-off option invalid in Sarf and Salam contracts?
column5: It contravenes the Qabd stipulated in those contracts
column6: They involve deferred delivery on both sides
column7: Their prices fluctuate too quickly for any option period to be workable
column8: Those contracts are non-binding by nature, so an option adds nothing to them
column10: Per the basis, stipulating such an option in contracts that entail taking possession (Qabd) is invalid as it contravenes the Qabd stipulated in Sarf and Salam.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: A buyer stipulates a cooling-off option without any time limit. Per the Shari'ah basis, why must the option be timed?
column5: The seller must know when to deliver, since delivery follows the option period
column6: Untimed options amount to Riba
column7: Options are valid only for three days, as stated in the Hadith of Khalabah
column8: An untimed option causes Jahalah that may lead to dispute
column10: Per the basis, an untimed option results in Jahalah (obscurity) which may lead to dispute; this is the majority view.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: A seller holding an option to revoke for non-payment dies. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the option not pass to his heirs?
column5: It is a readiness and willingness to act, not transferable
column6: All options lapse on the death of either party, whoever holds them
column7: Heirs must first obtain a court order
column8: The buyer's debt is cancelled upon the seller's death, ending the option
column10: Per the basis, the option to revoke for non-payment abates on its owner's death because it constitutes a readiness and willingness to act, not transferable to heirs.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad dies holding an either-or option over three items. Per the standard and its Shari'ah basis, what happens to the option?
column5: It lapses, like the option for non-payment, and the sale is cancelled
column6: It passes to the seller, who chooses the item
column7: It passes to his heirs, who must identify their selection
column8: It lapses, and all items return to the seller
column10: Per 4/3 and the basis, either-or options pass to heirs, since the deceased had established ownership in the items and the heirs need to identify their selection.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: An option holder offers the item to third parties, then actually sells it to one. Per the Shari'ah basis, why does the option lapse only upon the actual sale?
column5: An offer is a sale under all schools of Fiqh
column6: Offering probes the price; selling is disposal as an owner
column7: The seller's consent is needed for any offer made during the option
column8: Offering is permitted only after the option period has ended, never during it
column10: Per the basis, offering for sale probes the fairness of the price, but an actual sale testifies to acceptance, as the disposal is considered a disposal by owners.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad pays for a car bought under a 30-day cooling-off option, uses it for the month, then returns it and recovers his money, as planned with the seller. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as he exercised a valid option within its period
column6: Permissible, if the seller agreed in advance
column7: Permissible, if the car was returned undamaged to the seller
column8: Impermissible; a ruse for a lender's benefit on a loan
column10: Per 2/8/4, cooling-off options may not be used as a ruse to synthesise a lender's benefit, as when a buyer pays, uses the item and returns it within the period for a refund.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A and Bank B conclude a currency exchange with a 3-day cooling-off option for Bank A. Is the option valid?
column5: Yes, provided the period does not exceed 3 days and is fixed in the contract
column6: No, since only the seller may hold the option
column7: No; currency exchange requires spot payment of both sides
column8: Yes, as the cooling-off option applies to any financial contract between banks
column10: Per 2/3, cooling-off options do not apply to contracts requiring spot payment of both countervalues such as currency exchange, nor to Salam or non-binding contracts.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad holds a cooling-off option on a purchase and wants to sell this option to Karim for a fee. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, at a fair market price agreed between Ahmad and Karim
column6: No; options to reconsider may not be sold
column7: Yes, if the seller consents in writing within the option period
column8: Yes, within the option period
column10: Per 5/1, it is not permissible to sell or transfer options to reconsider.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad, holding a cooling-off option, decides to revoke and records his decision in his own files, without informing the seller. Is the revocation valid?
column5: No; the other party must know of the revocation
column6: No, unless a court approves it
column7: Yes, if made within the option period
column8: Yes; his decision alone terminates the contract
column10: Per 2/7/2, when the option owner revokes, the contract terminates, but it is required for the other party to know of the revocation for it to be valid.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A buys specialised equipment and stipulates that its outside technical consultant may confirm or revoke the purchase within 10 days. Is giving the option to a third party valid?
column5: No; only the buyer may hold a cooling-off option, never an outside consultant
column6: Yes, but only if the seller also holds the option for the same period
column7: No; only the two contracting parties may hold it
column8: Yes; the option may be given to a third party
column10: Per 2/1, cooling-off options give one or both parties or a third party the right to continue with or revoke the contract within a stipulated period.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad holds a cooling-off option on a car already in his possession. The car is destroyed during the option period. What is Ahmad's liability?
column5: None; the loss falls on the seller
column6: Only its cost, if he was negligent
column7: He is liable to pay its price
column8: Half the price, shared with the seller
column10: Per 2/5/3, if the item is destroyed in the buyer's possession while the buyer owns the option, he is liable to pay its price.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Which Hadith does the Shari'ah basis cite as the basis for the cooling-off option?
column5: "Muslims are bound by their conditions, except a condition that makes lawful unlawful"
column6: "Do not sell what is not with you, and no profit from what is not guaranteed"
column7: "No yield without risk taking"
column8: "Say: 'There shall be no Khalabah', then you have a 3-day option"
column10: Per the basis, the Hadith of Habban Bin Munqidh: "If you are concluding a deal say: 'There shall be no Khalabah', then you shall have a 3-day option".

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: A sale contract signed today gives the buyer a 15-day cooling-off option starting six months from now. Is this valid?
column5: No, because options may never exceed three days from the contract date
column6: No; the option period must begin with the contract
column7: Yes, if the buyer pays part of the price in advance
column8: Yes, since its duration is clearly specified at the time of contracting
column10: Per 2/2/3, the stipulated cooling-off period must coincide with the beginning of the contract period.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: A sale contract grants the buyer a cooling-off option that ends "when the commodity index reaches 500 points". Is this option valid?
column5: No; its time limit is indeterminate
column6: No, because options may not exceed 3 days
column7: Yes, if the index is reached within a year
column8: Yes, since the index is publicly known
column10: Per 2/2/2, the option must have a stipulated time limit; it is invalid if the limit is indeterminate, such as ending when an index reaches a particular value.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Under an either-or option, Ahmad takes delivery of three items priced 300, 600 and 900, to buy one. All three are destroyed in his possession. What must he pay?
column5: 900: the price of the dearest item
column6: 300: the price of the cheapest item
column7: 1,800: the price of all three items
column8: 600: one third of each item's price
column10: Per 4/2/1, if all items are destroyed and prices differ, the buyer pays the average price for the number purchased, e.g. one third of each item's price for one of three.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Bank A wants a 30-day cooling-off option when buying a building. A colleague says such options can never exceed three days. What does the standard say?
column5: No fixed minimum or maximum, unless contrary to custom
column6: The minimum is three days for any option
column7: The maximum is one month for real estate and three days for movables
column8: The maximum is three days, following the Hadith of the 3-day option
column10: Per 2/2/2, there is no minimum or maximum time limit except where it is contrary to what is customarily acceptable for the subject matter.

column3: Options to Reconsider (Cooling-Off Options, Either-Or Options, and Options to Revoke Due to Non-Payment)
column4: Ahmad, holding a cooling-off option on a property, offers it for sale to third parties to test the market price. When does his option lapse?
column5: As soon as he offers the property for sale
column6: Only once a sale to a third party is completed
column7: Once a third party makes a firm offer
column8: Only when the option period expires
column10: Per 2/4/4, the option owner may offer the item to third parties, and the option does not lapse until the sale is completed.

column4: Ahmad pays 'Arboun for a car, but the contract is silent on the option period. There is an existing local custom that specifies the option period for such sales. How is the period set?
column5: It stays open until Ahmad pays the remaining price
column6: By the seller, unilaterally, after the contract
column7: By the existing custom specifying the option period
column8: It is left to Ahmad, who may revoke at any time
column10: Per item 4, the option period must be specified by express stipulation of the parties or by custom where a custom specifies it.

column4: A customer concludes a Salam contract with Bank A and wants to pay 10% of the capital of Salam as 'Arboun, settling the rest within a week. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible: 'Arboun may not be paid in Salam
column6: Permissible, as Salam involves deferred delivery
column7: Permissible if the 'Arboun is refundable on revocation
column8: Permissible if the option period is fixed by custom
column10: Per 3/2, payment of 'Arboun is not permissible in Salam and currency exchange contracts.

column4: A buyer pays 'Arboun for equipment. The option period expires without him paying the remaining price, and the seller has not agreed any extension. What follows?
column5: The option period is automatically extended by custom
column6: The contract is revoked and the seller keeps the 'Arboun
column7: The contract stands and the seller may claim the balance
column8: The contract is revoked and the 'Arboun is refunded
column10: Per 5/2, the contract is considered revoked and the buyer is not entitled to recover the 'Arboun.

column4: A buyer takes delivery of goods under an 'Arboun sale. During the option period, the goods are damaged while with the buyer. What is the effect?
column5: The contract is void and the seller refunds the 'Arboun
column6: He may still revoke, but he forfeits the 'Arboun
column7: His option is canceled and he must pay the unpaid balance
column8: The seller bears the loss as the price is not fully paid
column10: Per item 6, after delivery the buyer is liable; if the item is damaged, his option is canceled and he must pay the balance of the price.

column4: Bank A proposes a currency exchange in which the customer pays 'Arboun and gets a period to confirm. On what basis does the standard reject 'Arboun in Sarf?
column5: 'Arboun may only be paid in kind, never in currency
column6: The exchange rate would remain unknown to the customer during the option period
column7: Sarf may be concluded only as a promise, not a contract
column8: It embeds a cooling-off option, while Sarf needs Qabd at the session
column10: Per the Basis, 'Arboun carries Khiyar al-Shart, impermissible in Sarf per the majority, as both countervalues must be possessed in Majlis al-'Aqd.

column4: Which narration does the standard cite as the basis for the permissibility of 'Arboun?
column5: The Hadith on paying in advance for dates by known measure
column6: Nafi' Ibn Abdul-Harith's purchase of a Mecca building from Safwan
column7: The Hadith "Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman"
column8: Ibn Umar's question on selling camels in Baqi' for dinars and taking dirhams
column10: The Basis cites Nafi' buying a building in Mecca from Safwan Ibn Umayyah: if Umar approved, the sale held; if not, Safwan kept 400 dinars.

column4: During the option period, the seller of an identified apartment sold under 'Arboun sells it to a third party. The first buyer refuses to ratify this. What is the status of the second sale?
column5: It is valid and the seller compensates the first buyer
column6: It is valid and the first buyer recovers his 'Arboun
column7: It is suspended until the option period expires
column8: It is void, being an unratified Fodooli disposal
column10: Per 9/1, the seller's disposal of an identified item is subject to Fodooli rules; if the first buyer does not ratify it, the second disposal is void.

column4: A buyer pays 'Arboun for an orchard, and it yields fruit during the option period. The standard treats this yield as part of the sale item. What evidence supports this?
column5: The Hadith "Gold for gold, silver for silver"
column6: The narration of Nafi' and Safwan on the Mecca prison
column7: The Hadith "Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman"
column8: The saying of Shurayh on voluntary conditions
column10: The Basis attributes separate growth and yields to the sale item on the Hadith "Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman": entitlement to revenue follows liability.

column4: Company X signs an agreement to buy a machine next month (a promise to sell, not a contract) and pays the seller 5% of the price with it. How is this payment classified?
column5: Not 'Arboun, as money paid with a promise is not earnest money
column6: It is 'Arboun, provided the agreement fixes an option period for the later purchase
column7: It is 'Arboun to be credited towards the price at conclusion
column8: It is 'Arboun that the seller may forfeit if Company X withdraws from the later purchase
column10: Per 2/2, an agreement to execute a contract in the future is a promise, not a contract; money paid with the promise is not 'Arboun.

column4: A seller under an 'Arboun sale of an identified car wants to deliver a different car with exactly the same specifications. When may he do so?
column5: Never, even if the buyer consents to the substitute
column6: Freely, since the substitute has the same specifications
column7: Only with the buyer's consent, and the payment stays 'Arboun
column8: Only if he first refunds the 'Arboun to the buyer
column10: Per 9/2, the seller cannot deliver a different item, even of the same specifications, except with the buyer's consent; what was paid remains 'Arboun.

column4: A buyer pays 'Arboun for a cow. During the option period, before delivery, the cow gives birth to a calf. Absent any stipulation, how is the calf treated?
column5: It is sold separately and its price divided equally
column6: It belongs to the buyer only if he later revokes
column7: It belongs to the seller since delivery has not occurred
column8: It is considered part of the sale item
column10: Per 8/2, separate growth during the option period, before or after delivery, is in principle part of the sale item, unless the liable party stipulates otherwise.

column4: Which maxim underlies the seller's liability for the sale item before delivery and the buyer's liability after delivery in an 'Arboun sale?
column5: Ownership passes at contract; liability follows Qabd
column6: He who voluntarily binds himself must honor the condition
column7: Al-Kharaj Bi al-Daman: revenue follows liability
column8: Contracts are interpreted by their intent and meaning, not by their words
column10: The Basis cites the maxim: ownership is established upon conclusion of the contract, while liability is contingent upon delivery (Qabd).

column4: Under an 'Arboun sale, Company X takes delivery of a machine during the option period and simply stores it in its warehouse. Has Company X confirmed the contract?
column5: Yes, any delivery during the option period confirms the sale
column6: No, taking delivery on its own does not indicate confirmation
column7: No, because delivery is not allowed during the option period
column8: Yes, since liability moves to it, the option ends
column10: Per item 7, the buyer may take delivery during the option period; this alone does not indicate confirmation unless his conduct shows acceptance.

column4: A buyer pays 'Arboun for a factory site and stipulates in the contract a refund if he fails to obtain licenses from the relevant authorities. Is this condition valid?
column5: Yes, a refund may be stipulated for specific situations
column6: Yes, but only if the seller agrees after the contract
column7: No, 'Arboun is non-refundable in all cases
column8: No, it turns the 'Arboun into a refundable deposit
column10: Per item 10, the buyer may stipulate in the contract a refund of earnest money in specific situations, such as failure to obtain licenses.

column4: Bank A concludes an Istisna'a contract with a customer for equipment to be manufactured, and the customer pays 'Arboun at the time of contract. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, but only if the 'Arboun is paid in cash, not in kind
column6: Yes, 'Arboun is permissible in Istisna'a contracts
column7: No, 'Arboun is not allowed where the item is described
column8: No, 'Arboun is limited to sales of identified goods
column10: Per 3/1, 'Arboun is permissible in commutative contracts not requiring spot payment, such as Istisna'a, whether the item is identified or described.

column4: During the option period of an 'Arboun sale, the sold car is destroyed in a flood before it is delivered to the buyer. What is the outcome?
column5: The loss is shared in proportion to the price already paid
column6: The buyer must pay the balance since title passed at contract
column7: The contract is void and the 'Arboun is returned to the buyer
column8: The buyer loses the 'Arboun as ownership passed to him
column10: Per item 6, the seller is liable before delivery; if the item is destroyed before delivery, the contract is void and the 'Arboun must be returned.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: The standard requires the revoking party to notify the other party. On what is this requirement based?
column5: The maxim that contracts follow intent, not words
column6: The agreed opinion of the majority of jurists
column7: Analogy to Iqalah, done without increase or decrease
column8: Abu Hanifah and Muhammad Ibn Al-Hasan, to avert harm
column10: Per the Basis, notification follows Abu Hanifah and Muhammad Ibn Al-Hasan, contrary to the majority, to avert harm to the unaware party.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A buyer holds a cooling-off option. After delivery, the sold item is destroyed by a natural disaster, and the buyer then tries to revoke within the option period. Can he?
column5: No, destruction after delivery is an impediment
column6: Yes, since he did not cause the destruction
column7: No, unless the seller agrees to share the loss
column8: Yes, since the option period has not yet expired
column10: Per 7/1, destruction of the sale item by a natural disaster after delivery is an impediment to revocation.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: Midway through an Ijarah, the lessee asks the lessor to waive his rights for the remaining lease period, and they agree a consideration at the time of waiver. Is this allowed?
column5: No, waiver of revocation rights is never compensated
column6: Yes, but only for debt transfer, not for Ijarah
column7: No, any consideration must be fixed in the contract
column8: Yes, in term contracts like Ijarah this is allowed
column10: Per 10/1, in contracts with specified terms such as Ijarah, a party may waive rights to the remaining period for a consideration agreed at waiver.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: Before delivery, the buyer, who holds a cooling-off option, damages the sold item so it is destroyed. He then seeks to revoke the contract. What is the ruling?
column5: He may revoke, as the seller is liable before delivery
column6: He may revoke but must compensate the seller
column7: He cannot revoke, even though it was before delivery
column8: He may revoke only if the option period remains
column10: Per 7/2, destruction of the sale item caused by the buyer, whether before or after delivery, prevents revocation.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A buyer with a cooling-off option revokes the sale of a sheep after delivery. Between delivery and revocation, the sheep gave birth to a lamb. Who owns the lamb?
column5: The seller, as revocation operates retroactively
column6: The buyer, as the growth occurred after delivery
column7: The seller, as the lamb is part of the sale item
column8: Both parties, shared in proportion to the price
column10: Per item 8, revocation nullifies the contract at the moment of revocation; separate growth after delivery belongs to the buyer, before delivery to the seller.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: Why does the standard say cooling-off options to revoke are stipulated only in binding contracts?
column5: Binding contracts cannot otherwise be ended
column6: Nonbinding contracts are void under the Shari'ah
column7: Only binding contracts involve a price or rent
column8: Nonbinding contracts are revocable by their nature
column10: Per the Basis, cooling-off options apply only to binding contracts because nonbinding contracts are by nature revocable by one or both parties.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A sale contract stipulates that the buyer will pay the seller a set amount if the seller waives his right to revoke. What is the ruling on this stipulation?
column5: It is not permissible in a sale contract
column6: It is permissible if agreed at the time of waiver
column7: It is permissible if the amount is fixed in advance
column8: It is permissible if the waiver is in writing
column10: Per 10/1, it is not permissible to stipulate payment for waiver of revocation rights in a sale contract.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: Ahmad buys a car with a cooling-off option and, within the option period, gifts it to his brother, who takes ownership. Ahmad then wishes to revoke. What applies?
column5: He may revoke but the gift remains valid
column6: He may revoke if he recovers the car from his brother
column7: Revocation is barred since a third party gained ownership
column8: He may revoke, since the option period is still running
column10: Per 7/3, conduct that transfers ownership and creates third-party rights, such as selling or gifting the item, is an impediment to revocation.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: Bank A's contract allows it to accelerate all installments. A solvent customer has missed one installment. Under the standard, may Bank A accelerate now?
column5: Yes, without notifying the customer beforehand
column6: No, it requires failure to pay two or more instalments
column7: No, acceleration is never allowed for solvent debtors
column8: Yes, any single missed installment is sufficient
column10: Per 11/3, a creditor may stipulate acceleration, after notifying the debtor, if a solvent debtor fails to pay two or more instalments.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A leased asset breaks down; the lessee chooses not to revoke and repairs it. Later it breaks down again from the same cause. Can the lessee now exercise his option to revoke?
column5: Yes, but only with the lessor's fresh consent
column6: No, because he repaired the asset at his own cost
column7: Yes, the option is not waived where harm recurs
column8: No, his first choice permanently waived the option
column10: Per item 9, if the harm from the cause triggering the option is recurring or continuous, the option is not waived.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A sale contract states that the buyer "may cancel the deal" if a stated event occurs, without using the word "revocation". Is this a valid cooling-off option to revoke?
column5: No, the technical word "revocation" must be used
column6: Yes, any form indicating the option suffices
column7: Yes, but only if confirmed later by a court
column8: No, the option must be agreed in a separate contract
column10: Per item 3, a cooling-off option to revoke can be stipulated in any form that indicates it; no specific word meaning revocation is required.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: Under a lease, the lessor adds a supplementary rental for maintenance, insurance and owners' taxes; the lessee refuses. The lessee had promised to purchase the asset. What may the lessor do?
column5: Enforce the promise only after the lease term ends
column6: Only continue the lease at the original rental
column7: Revoke and enforce the promise, adding the supplementary rent to the price
column8: Revoke, and enforce the promise without adding that rent
column10: Per 11/2, the lessor may revoke and demand performance of the promise, provided the supplementary rent for that period is not added to the purchase price.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A seller asks why he cannot stipulate in a sale contract a payment for waiving his right to revoke. What is the Shari'ah basis given?
column5: Analogy to Iqalah, done without increase or decrease
column6: The maxim that ownership arises at contract
column7: The opinion of Abu Hanifah on notifying the other party
column8: The rule that contracts are generally binding
column10: Per the Basis, the prohibition is by analogy to Iqalah, which must be done without any increase or decrease in considerations.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A credit facility lets Bank A revoke upon breach of a restrictive covenant. The customer breached it but fully cured the breach before Bank A sought to revoke. Is revocation valid?
column5: Yes, provided the bank notifies the customer first
column6: No, covenant breaches cannot trigger revocation
column7: No, the cause must exist at the time of revocation
column8: Yes, a breach at any time gives a permanent right
column10: Per 6/1, a valid revocation requires the cause triggering the option to exist at the time of the revocation.

column3: Revocation of Contracts by Exercise of a Cooling-Off Option
column4: A seller holding a cooling-off option decides to revoke the sale when the stipulated situation occurs, but never informs the buyer. What is missing for a valid revocation?
column5: Notification to the buyer as required by custom
column6: Refund of a penalty for revoking the contract
column7: A court order confirming the revocation
column8: Nothing, as the decision alone ends the contract
column10: Per 6/3, a condition of valid revocation is notification of the revocation by the option owner to the other party according to custom.

column4: Which of the following falls outside the scope of the standard on competitions and prizes?
column5: Competitions sponsored by the Institution
column6: Incentives to improve employees' performance
column7: Promotional gifts given upon purchases
column8: Prizes offered to investment account holders
column10: Per item 1, the standard does not cover incentives to improve performance of clients, employees and directors, job-related competitions or reverse auctions.

column4: Bank A runs a prize draw for credit cardholders but limits it to cards linked to current accounts, which holders cannot link to investment accounts. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if no fee is charged for the draw
column6: Permissible, if card fees during the draw stay ordinary
column7: Permissible, since debit and credit cards are alike
column8: Not permissible; prizes can't be confined to such cards
column10: Per 3/5/4/3, card prizes must not be confined to cards linked to current accounts where the holder cannot link the card to an investment account.

column4: Company X announces a reward for the winner of a cultural quiz it organizes. After the contest, it wants to withhold the reward. What is the ruling?
column5: Payment is binding only if participants paid fees
column6: Payment is binding on Company X, which committed to it
column7: Payment is binding only once a court confirms it
column8: The reward is a voluntary gift it may withdraw
column10: Per 2/2, a reward-based competition makes payment of the reward binding upon the party committed to paying it.

column4: Company X sells its own discount card for an annual fee. The fee covers only discounts on Company X's goods, with no other services. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the issuer is deemed a broker
column6: Permissible, as the discount is a Tabarru'
column7: Permissible if the fee is below expected discounts
column8: Not permissible, as it involves Gharar and Jahalah
column10: Per 3/6/2/2/2 Scenario (2), a card whose fee is exclusively for discounts from the same issuer is not permissible, as it involves Gharar and Jahalah.

column4: Bank A offers a draw-based prize to customers who use its fund transfer service. Under what condition is this permissible?
column5: No additional amount is charged on the service fees
column6: Only current account holders may enter the draw
column7: The customer pays a small fee to enter the draw
column8: The prize is paid out of investment account funds
column10: Per 3/5/3, a draw-based prize on financing, currency exchange or fund transfers is permissible if no extra amount is charged on fees for it.

column4: Which of the following does the standard cite from the Qur'an as evidence for the permissibility of competitions?
column5: The Bedouin's camel outrunning al-Adhbaa'
column6: Ayishah's foot race with the Prophet
column7: Yusuf's brothers telling their father they went racing
column8: The Prophet's horse race to Thaniyyat Al-Wada'a, as narrated by Ibn Umar
column10: The Basis cites Yusuf (Joseph): 17, where Yusuf's brothers told their father they went racing; the others are cited Sunnah narrations.

column4: Bank A's marketing team designs a competition, with a modest reward from shareholders' funds and due regard to public interest. What else is required before launch?
column5: Approval of the Bank's Shari'ah Supervisory Board
column6: A fee from each participant to cover costs
column7: A promise that every participant wins a prize
column8: Approval of the investment account holders
column10: Per 2/3/3/3, a competition organized or sponsored by the Institution must be approved by its Shari'ah Supervisory Board.

column4: Two competitors in a race each put up SR 1,000, and the winner takes the whole amount. Is this reward-based competition permissible?
column5: Yes, if the race is in a permissible activity
column6: Yes, provided a third party holds the money
column7: No, a reward from more than one competitor is barred
column8: Yes, since the two competitors contribute equally
column10: Per 2/3/2/2, the reward must come from a third party or one competitor; if offered by more than one competitor, it is not permissible.

column4: A telecom company runs a prize draw entered by calling a number billed above the normal tariff. What is the ruling on this draw?
column5: Permissible, since no direct fee is charged
column6: Impermissible, as it is an indirect entry fee
column7: Permissible, if all callers have equal chances
column8: Permissible, if the prize is Shari'ah compliant
column10: Per 3/3/3/5, charging a fee to enter a draw, directly or indirectly (e.g., raising call rates above the normal tariff), is impermissible.

column4: Bank A launches a prize draw open exclusively to holders of its current accounts. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible if paid from shareholders' funds and not from investment funds
column6: Permissible if the prizes are in kind, not in cash, and of modest value
column7: Permissible if winners are chosen by draw
column8: Impermissible to give prizes only to current accounts
column10: Per 3/5/1, it is impermissible to assign prizes exclusively to holders of current accounts (see the standard on Qard).

column4: Bank A offers prizes to investment account holders and proposes to fund them from the profits of those investment account holders. Is this allowed?
column5: No, they may be paid from shareholders' funds instead
column6: Yes, since the prizes go back to the same holders
column7: Yes, if holders consent in the account terms
column8: Yes, if the charity account bears part of the cost
column10: Per 3/5/2/1, prizes are not paid from investment account funds, their holders' profits or charity accounts, but may be paid from shareholders' funds.

column4: A company requires buying a coupon booklet to enter a draw, though it is reasonably known that customers buy it only to win the prize. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if all buyers have equal chances
column6: Permissible, since the booklet price is unchanged
column7: Not permissible, since purchase is only for the prize
column8: Permissible, if the prize is announced publicly
column10: Per 3/3/3/2, if customers would not buy except to win the prize, organizing the draw is not permissible.

column4: In a hotel loyalty program, a member lacks a few points needed for a stay, so he buys the missing points for cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible, since points are a Tabarru' only
column6: Permissible; using them pays part of the price
column7: Permissible only if the program has no fee
column8: Not permissible, as points cannot be bought for cash
column10: Per 3/6/3, a member lacking points may buy new points for cash and use them, as using them is deemed payment of part of the price.

column4: A store gives customers a free discount card, with no subscription fee, entitling them to reduced prices, though the exact discounts vary. Is it permissible?
column5: Yes, but only if a third party issues the card
column6: No, discounts must be fixed in a binding contract
column7: No, the varying discounts create prohibited Gharar
column8: Yes, as a Wa'ad to reduce the price on a Tabarru' basis
column10: Per 3/6/2/2/1, a fee-free discount card is a Wa'ad to voluntarily reduce the price (Tabarru'); ambiguity in Tabarru' is forgiven.

column4: A store gives buyers of a product a ticket for a prize draw, and prices that product higher than the same product sold without a ticket. Is the draw permissible?
column5: Yes, if the prizes are Shari'ah compliant and the draw is fair
column6: Yes, as the buyer still receives the product he paid for in full
column7: No, the price must not be raised for the right to enter
column8: Yes, if every buyer has an equal chance
column10: Per 3/3/3/1, the price of goods whose purchase qualifies for the draw must not be increased vis-a-vis the same goods without that right.

column4: Which text does the standard cite as evidence for the permissibility of prizes in competitions?
column5: The race of the she-camel al-Adhbaa'
column6: No prizes except on camelback, horseback or spear
column7: Ayishah's foot race with the Prophet: "this for that"
column8: The account of Yusuf's brothers going racing
column10: The Basis cites the Hadith: no prizes on racing except on camelback, horseback (or the like) or spear throwing; Sabq involves prizes.

column4: Bank A announces a prize of SR 50,000 for every SR 1 million placed in its investment accounts. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if paid from shareholders' funds
column6: Permissible, if the prize is announced in advance
column7: Permissible, as all holders have a chance to win
column8: Impermissible, as it guarantees part of the capital
column10: Per 3/5/2/2, prizes must not lead to guaranteeing invested capital or part of it, as with SR 50,000 for every SR 1 million.

column4: Bank A plans to organize a cultural competition and pay the reward out of the funds of its investment accounts. What does the standard require instead?
column5: Costs, including the reward, come from shareholders' funds
column6: Costs may be charged to the charity account
column7: Costs are shared with investment account holders in proportion to their funds
column8: Costs come only from investment account profits
column10: Per 2/3/3/1, competition expenses including the reward must be covered from the Institution's own (shareholders') funds, not investment account funds.

column4: How does Al-Mawardi derive the permissibility of racing from the account of Yusuf's brothers, as cited in the standard?
column5: The race was for a known distance without Jahalah
column6: Jacob ordered his sons to race as training
column7: Jacob did not object, and it was not abrogated
column8: The brothers won a prize, showing rewards are allowed
column10: Al-Mawardi said Jacob did not object to their saying, evidence of permissibility in his code which was not superseded by abrogation.

column4: A shop offers an unspecified gift with each appliance it sells. Under what condition is this promotional gift permissible?
column5: The price is not increased against the gift
column6: The gift is given in kind and never in cash
column7: The gift's value is disclosed before the sale
column8: The buyer pays a separate fee for the gift
column10: Per 3/6/1/2, a seller may offer an unspecified gift with a good or service provided the price is not increased against the gift.

column4: Bank A announces a reward-based competition but leaves its timing, location, tools and mode of operation undetermined. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as long as the activity is cultural
column6: Permissible if a third party pays the reward
column7: Permissible, since the reward amount is known
column8: Not permissible, due to Jahalah in the competition
column10: Per 2/3/2/1, a reward-based competition must be clearly defined to remove Jahalah as to timing, location, type, particulars, tools and mode of operation.

column4: Which narration cited in the standard's basis shows that the Prophet himself established racing competitions?
column5: Anas's account of the camel al-Adhbaa'
column6: Ibn Umar's report of races between horses
column7: Abu Hurairah's Hadith on prizes in races
column8: Ayishah's account of racing on foot
column10: The Basis cites Ibn Umar: the Prophet established a race between slender horses and another between ordinary horses, and Ibn Umar raced.

column4: A student claims that foot races between people have no precedent in the Sunnah. Which narration cited in the standard's basis answers this?
column5: Ayishah racing the Prophet on foot
column6: Anas's narration on the she-camel al-Adhbaa'
column7: Abu Hurairah's Hadith on camel and horse races
column8: Ibn Umar's narration on racing slender horses
column10: The Basis cites Ayishah: she raced the Prophet on foot and won, later he won and said: "this for that".

column4: Bank A offers a limited number of prizes to one subcategory of its investment account holders. How must the winners be chosen?
column5: By the length of each holder's relationship with the Bank, longest first
column6: At the discretion of the Bank's management
column7: By the size of each holder's investment, the largest holders being served first
column8: Through a draw open to every holder in the subcategory
column10: Per 3/5/2/3, every holder of an investment account or a subcategory must have a chance; if prizes are limited, winners are determined by draw.

column4: Bank A sponsors a sports competition timed so that participants are unable to perform the obligatory prayer. Is sponsoring it permissible?
column5: Yes, provided no reward is paid to participants
column6: No, it leads to failure to perform a Shari'ah obligation
column7: Yes, since sports competitions are permissible
column8: Yes, if the Shari'ah Supervisory Board is told later
column10: Per 2/3/1/2, a competition must not include or lead to anything prohibited, such as failure to perform a Shari'ah obligation like prayer.

column4: A service agent collecting rentals for a Sukuk also commits to make up capital losses, and charges a fee well above the market rate for similar work. Is this acceptable?
column5: Yes, if the fee is set in the service agency contract
column6: No, a service agent may never give such a commitment
column7: No, its fee may not exceed the prevailing market rate
column8: Yes, the extra fee rewards its undertaking
column10: Per 4/3/2/3, a paid service agent's fee must not exceed the market rate, to avoid a consideration for the undertaking, which must be voluntary.

column4: Why does the standard exclude opportunity cost from the investment manager's liability, even where misconduct is established?
column5: It is non-existing and unrealized Mal
column6: It is covered by the presumption of non-liability
column7: His possession of the funds is fiduciary
column8: Rab Al Maal has waived it by consent
column10: Per the Basis, opportunity cost is non-existing, unrealized money (Mal) and cannot lead to liability; realized profit is treated as capital.

column4: An investment agent claims a loss on a portfolio, while peer investments in the same market were profitable. Who bears the evidentiary burden in this case?
column5: No one, since losses fall on the investor
column6: The regulator, which must investigate the claim
column7: The agent, to prove the loss and no negligence
column8: The investor, as the party claiming negligence
column10: Per 6/3, circumstantial evidence (qara'in) contradicting the manager's claim, e.g., peers being profitable, shifts the burden to him.

column4: An investment agent managing a foreign-currency portfolio undertakes in the contract to bear any losses from exchange rate fluctuations. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if limited to part of the capital
column6: Permitted, since currency risk is beyond his control
column7: Permitted, if the agent charges no agency fee
column8: Prohibited, as a form of assuming the liability
column10: Per 3/5/2, an undertaking by the investment manager to assume losses from exchange rate fluctuations is a prohibited form of assuming liability.

column4: Rab Al Maal claims that the Mudarib's negligence caused a loss; the contract is silent on the evidentiary burden. Initially, who must prove the claim?
column5: Both parties equally, before an arbitrator
column6: Rab Al Maal, as the party making the claim
column7: Whoever holds the larger share of the capital
column8: The Mudarib, who must prove he was not negligent
column10: Per item 6, as an initial presumption, the burden of proving misconduct or negligence lies on the claimant, not the investment manager.

column4: A partial loss occurs in a Mudaraba. The Mudarib, of his own free will, then offers to make good the loss to Rab Al Maal. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, volunteering after a loss occurs is permitted
column6: No, any liability on the Mudarib is prohibited
column7: No, unless the loss resulted from his negligence
column8: Yes, but only if agreed at the time of contract
column10: Per 3/4, after a total or partial loss occurs, the investment manager may volunteer to assume the liability of his own free will.

column4: A Mudarib's misconduct causes a loss. Before it, the fund had realized a profit of 100; experts estimate a further 50 would have been earned. What does his liability cover?
column5: The capital plus the 100 and the expected 50
column6: The capital plus the 50 opportunity cost only
column7: The capital plus the 100 realized profit only
column8: Only the capital, excluding any profit
column10: Per 7/1, liability covers capital and profit realized before the loss, but not lost profit (opportunity cost) or unrealized expected profits.

column4: After a realized loss, a Mudarib voluntarily makes it good from his own funds. What basis does the standard give for allowing this?
column5: It is a public interest (Maslahah Mursalah)
column6: Benevolence: no blame lies on the doers of good
column7: It is his waiver of a right with his consent
column8: It is a third party's undertaking to donate
column10: Per the Basis, he does so out of benevolence in this specific case, and there is no cause for blame upon the doers of good.

column4: Six months into an investment agency, before any loss has occurred, the agent signs a side letter undertaking to bear any future loss. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, because no loss has occurred so far
column6: Yes, if the undertaking is implicit, not explicit
column7: Yes, since it is outside the original contract
column8: No, he may not assume the risk after the contract
column10: Per 3/3, the investment manager may not undertake, explicitly or implicitly, assumption of the risk after making the investment contract.

column4: When concluding a Mudaraba contract, the Mudarib offers on his own initiative to guarantee Rab Al Maal's capital in full. Is this permitted?
column5: No, volunteering liability at contract is not permitted
column6: Yes, if Rab Al Maal accepts it in writing
column7: Yes, since it is voluntary and not stipulated as a condition of the contract
column8: Yes, if it is limited to part of the capital
column10: Per 3/2, absolute liability may not be stipulated on the investment manager, nor may he volunteer to assume the risk at the time of the contract.

column4: In a Musharakah, the partners authorize Partner A to invest the partnership's funds. How does the standard classify Partner A's role?
column5: He is Rab Al Maal over the other partners' shares
column6: He is a service agent with no investment role
column7: He is a guarantor of the partners' capital
column8: He is an investment manager of those funds
column10: Per 2/2/3, authorizing (tafwid) one of the partners to invest partnership funds is a form of investment management.

column4: A central bank requires investment managers to bear the burden of proving losses and the absence of negligence. How does the standard justify complying with this?
column5: As an undertaking to donate by the manager
column6: As Maslahah Mursalah enforced by the authorities
column7: As the manager's waiver of his right by consent
column8: As the norm that the manager is presumed not liable
column10: Per the Basis, a burden imposed by a regulatory or supervisory authority is deemed Maslahah Mursalah enforced by ruling authorities and must be heeded.

column4: A Mudaraba contract requires the Mudarib to bear matters usually not carried by him, with the aim of making him liable for losses. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as Rab Al Maal may set any conditions
column6: Permitted, if it is stated clearly in the contract
column7: Not permitted, as it seeks to impose liability
column8: Permitted, if the Mudarib's profit share is raised
column10: Per 3/6, it is not permitted to stipulate on the investment manager what is usually not carried by him for the purpose of imposing liability.

column4: To protect Sukuk holders, an investment manager sets up a new company specifically to give a commitment covering capital losses. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the manager holds under 50% of it
column6: Not permitted, as it is an artifice (hila)
column7: Permitted, since the company is a separate entity
column8: Permitted, if the commitment is voluntary
column10: Per 4/1/1, as an artifice to the independence condition, setting up a company or legal entity specifically for this purpose is not permitted.

column4: An investment agent's misconduct causes damage to a commodity held as an investment, and its value changes afterwards. Which date determines the extent of liability?
column5: The date the loss or destruction occurred
column6: The date the liability is finally adjudicated
column7: The date Rab Al Maal files the claim
column8: The date the investment contract was concluded
column10: Per 7/4, for tangible assets, the date of the loss, shortage or destruction caused by the misconduct determines the extent of the liability.

column4: Rab Al Maal instructs the investment agent to sell an asset at 100. Without permission, the agent sells it at 90. What is the agent's liability?
column5: He bears nothing, as his possession is fiduciary
column6: He must recover the asset from the buyer
column7: He is liable for the difference of 10
column8: He is liable for the full price of 100
column10: Per 7/2, if the manager sells below the specified price without permission, he is liable for the difference between that price and the price sold.

column4: Why does the standard prohibit stipulating liability on an investment manager such as a Mudarib?
column5: It would create Gharar in the profit-sharing ratio
column6: It would contradict the rule on doers of good
column7: It would void any third-party commitment
column8: It would turn the contract into a benefit-bearing loan
column10: Per the Basis, stipulating liability on fiduciaries is a means to render an investment contract a benefit-bearing loan.

column4: A Mudarib invests Rab Al Maal's funds as agreed, without misconduct or negligence, but the market falls and 20% of the capital is lost. Who bears the loss?
column5: Rab Al Maal, as the Mudarib's possession is fiduciary
column6: The Mudarib, up to the profit share he expected
column7: Both of them equally, as partners in the venture
column8: The Mudarib, as he made the investment decisions
column10: Per 3/1, the investment manager's possession is fiduciary (yadd amana); he is not liable unless there is misconduct, negligence or breach of conditions.

column4: The Mudarib in Mudaraba Sukuk undertakes to purchase the underlying assets from the certificateholders at maturity. At which price is this undertaking permitted?
column5: At the face value of the Sukuk at issuance
column6: At a price specified when making the contract
column7: At the original capital plus expected profit
column8: At the net asset value at the time of purchase
column10: Per 3/5/1, an undertaking at a price specified at contract is prohibited; it is permitted at NAV, market value, fair value or a price agreed at purchase.

column4: A Mudarib enters a large project without a feasibility study, though the contract stipulates one. The project fails. How is the Mudarib's conduct treated?
column5: As ordinary business risk borne by Rab Al Maal
column6: As misconduct or negligence, making him liable
column7: As negligence only if he acted intentionally
column8: As a loss shared equally between the parties
column10: Per 5/3/2, not conducting a feasibility study despite its necessity by stipulation or custom is a form of misconduct and negligence.

column4: A third party commits to make good Rab Al Maal's capital loss, with a right to recover whatever it pays from the investment manager. Is this commitment valid?
column5: Yes, if the commitment is made voluntarily
column6: Yes, since the third party is independent of both the investor and the manager
column7: No, the obligor must have no recourse to the manager
column8: Yes, if recourse is limited to half the amount
column10: Per 4/1/2, the obligor shall have no recourse to the investment manager for what it has undertaken.

column4: Company Y offers to make good any capital loss to Rab Al Maal in a fund managed by Company Z. Company Y owns 60% of Company Z. May Company Y give this commitment?
column5: Yes, if it has no recourse to Company Z
column6: No, one party's holding in the other exceeds 50%
column7: Yes, since Company Y is a separate legal entity
column8: Yes, if Company Y gives it voluntarily
column10: Per 4/1/1, the third party must be independent of the manager; with common shareholding, one party's holding must not exceed 50% of the other.

column4: An investment agent, without intending to, exceeds the limits agreed in the contract when disposing of the funds. Does this count as misconduct (ta'addi)?
column5: Yes, but only if custom treats it as intentional
column6: No, misconduct requires a deliberate breach
column7: Yes, whether the excess was intentional or not
column8: No, unless it causes a loss above a set limit
column10: Per 5/2, misconduct is exceeding the limit authorized by Shari'ah and agreed by the parties, whether the exceeding was intentional or not.

column4: Bank A, as investment agent, is instructed not to invest in real estate but does so anyway, and the property falls in value. Is Bank A liable for the loss?
column5: No, unless the loss exceeds half of the capital
column6: Yes, but only up to the agency fee it received
column7: No, its possession is fiduciary in all cases
column8: Yes, because it breached the conditions
column10: Per 3/1, the investment manager is not liable unless there is misconduct, negligence, or breach of conditions; here conditions were breached.

column4: Bank A, as investment agent, breaches a condition of the contract. The contract has no clause on dismissal for misconduct. What is the status of the agency?
column5: It continues unless Rab Al Maal dismisses the agent
column6: The agent is dismissed automatically by the breach
column7: It ends once the loss is established by evidence
column8: It continues and Rab Al Maal cannot end it
column10: Per 7/6, the manager is not automatically dismissed for misconduct, negligence or breach unless stipulated; he is dismissed upon dismissal by Rab Al Maal.

column4: Funds paid to Bank A for its general pool were never actually added to the pool, yet the pool made a profit. Why is the investor still entitled to his share?
column5: Bank A volunteered liability after the fact
column6: Bank A's breach makes it guarantor of the profit, which it must pay him
column7: He is a partner by contract; commingling isn't required
column8: The profit compensates his opportunity cost
column10: Per the Basis to 7/3, the investor is a partner by virtue of the contract; pooling is not a prerequisite for profit entitlement or bearing loss.

column4: A third party's commitment to cover Rab Al Maal's capital loss turns out to be void. What is the effect on the underlying Mudaraba contract?
column5: It is suspended until a new obligor is found
column6: It turns into an investment guaranteed by the Mudarib
column7: It becomes vitiated (fasad) with the commitment
column8: It is not vitiated and remains in effect
column10: Per 4/2, default of the third party or voidness of its undertaking does not result in vitiation (fasad) of the investment contract.

column4: Why does the standard allow a third party to commit to make up capital loss, while the same commitment by the Mudarib is barred?
column5: It is an undertaking to donate, not a manager's guarantee
column6: The third party acts as a fiduciary like the Mudarib
column7: It is imposed by the regulator as Maslahah Mursalah
column8: The third party is paid a fee for bearing the risk
column10: Per the Basis, a third party's undertaking is an undertaking to donate; it does not turn into a guarantee by the investment manager.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Why does the standard prohibit a conditional sale and Khiyar al-Shart in gold trading?
column5: They make the promise tradable, which is barred
column6: They contravene the requirement of spot exchange
column7: They turn the sale into a loan with benefits
column8: They conflict with the option for defect
column10: Per the Basis, conditional sales and Khiyar al-Shart in gold trading contravene the Shari'ah requirement for spot exchange of countervalues.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A wants to buy gold through a Salam contract, paying the capital of Salam in currency at the session. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as Salam always defers the subject
column6: Permissible, as the capital is paid at the session
column7: Not permissible, as the capital may not be currency
column8: Permissible, if the gold is precisely described
column10: Per 5/2/2, gold may be bought through Salam provided the capital of Salam is not gold, silver or currencies.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Why may a pledgee not stipulate the right to use the pledged gold for its own benefit?
column5: Because the pledge must be sold at market value
column6: Because gold can be pledged only by certificate, not in physical form
column7: Because the pledgor bears the safekeeping costs of the pledged gold
column8: To avoid combining loan and sale; it would become a loan
column10: Per the Basis, this prevents combining loan and sale in one arrangement, as it renders the pledged asset a loan the pledgee is liable for.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An investor wants to pay a fee to acquire the benefit of a binding promise to sell gold held by another customer of Bank A. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the fee equals the Hamish Jiddiyyah
column6: Not permissible, as promises may not be traded
column7: Permissible, since the promise is binding
column8: Permissible, if Bank A consents to the transfer
column10: Per 8/4, trading in promises in any form is not permissible.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer deposits gold with Bank A as collateral against a loan he borrowed. Bank A wants to charge a safekeeping fee of 2% of the gold's value. What applies?
column5: The fee may not exceed the actual safekeeping cost
column6: No safekeeping fee may be charged at all
column7: The fee must be paid in gold of equal weight
column8: Any lump sum or percentage fee is permissible
column10: Per 5/4/2, safekeeping fees are permissible, but for gold deposited as collateral against the depositor's loan they may not exceed actual cost.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer exchanges 21K gold jewelry for 18K gold jewelry at a shop, on spot. What must be equal for the exchange to be valid?
column5: The total weight of the two pieces, including any other metals
column6: The karatage of the two pieces
column7: The market value of the two pieces at the time of the exchange
column8: The weight of pure gold in each countervalue
column10: Per 3/3/1/2, substances added for karatage are not intended per se; exchange must be spot and the pure gold weight in each countervalue equal.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A purchase orderer in Murabahah gives Bank A gold as Hamish Jiddiyyah, then breaches his binding promise. How is Bank A's deduction made?
column5: Actual loss only, gold valued at the deduction date
column6: The whole gold amount is forfeited as 'Arboun
column7: The bank's expected profit, at market value
column8: Actual loss only, gold valued at the deposit date
column10: Per 7/2/1, Hamish Jiddiyyah in gold is a trust, not 'Arboun; only actual loss is deducted, with gold valued at market price at deduction.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A and a customer exchange promises binding on both sides: Bank A to sell, and the customer to buy, a quantity of gold next month. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as no contract is concluded yet
column6: Permissible, if Hamish Jiddiyyah is paid
column7: Impermissible, as a bilaterally binding promise
column8: Permissible, if the price is fixed today
column10: Per 8/1, a unilaterally binding promise to sell gold is permissible, but bilaterally binding promises for sale of gold are impermissible.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A trader sells 100 grams of gold for 1,500 grams of silver, with both delivered in the contracting session. Is the sale valid despite the weight disparity?
column5: Yes, and delivery of the silver may be deferred until the next day
column6: Yes, disparity is allowed when gold is sold for silver
column7: No, gold and silver must be equal in weight, as in gold for gold
column8: No, unless each is first valued in currency
column10: Per 3/1/3, gold for silver is permissible regardless of disparity in weight, provided the countervalues are exchanged as required (spot).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Company X sells gold bars to a car dealer in exchange for cars to be delivered in three months. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible; gold may be sold only for currencies
column6: Not permissible; both must be delivered at the session
column7: Permissible only if the cars arrive within a month
column8: Permissible; spot exchange is not required here
column10: Per 3/1/4 and 3/2/1, gold sold for commodities other than gold, silver or currencies may be sold at any price with deferment of one countervalue.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer asks Bank A to apply the gold rulings to platinum that is marketed locally as 'white gold'. Under the standard, do the gold rulings apply?
column5: Yes, since all precious metals follow gold's rulings
column6: Only if the platinum is sold in ingot form
column7: No, they do not apply to platinum even if so called
column8: Yes, since it is called white gold in that country
