column10: Per 10/6, the gold rulings apply to white gold but not to metals such as platinum, palladium and nickel called white gold in some countries.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Why does the standard accept holding a gold certificate as constructive possession when ingots are sold for currency?
column5: The seller stays liable for the stored gold
column6: It equals physical possession in effect, incl. risk transfer
column7: Spot exchange is not required for ingots held in storage
column8: Stored ingots are no longer Ribawi items once held by the bank
column10: Per the Basis, a certificate is as good as physical possession in legal effect, transfer of risk and benefits, and ability to dispose.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An online platform sells customers unallocated gold ingots for currency, without the buyer taking physical possession. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible without physical possession
column6: Permissible, if the platform stores the gold
column7: Permissible, if the gold's weight is specified
column8: Permissible, since the price is paid on spot
column10: Per 3/4, it is not permissible to sell an unspecified (unallocated) ingot without physical possession.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Company X leases gold jewelry to a customer for an event, with the rent payable in arrears. Is this lease permissible?
column5: Yes, but only if the leased gold is ingots
column6: No, rent for gold must be paid in advance
column7: Yes, as its corpus is not consumed in the lease
column8: No, gold is a Ribawi item that cannot be leased
column10: Per 5/3/1, gold may be leased, as jewelry or ingots, if its corpus is not consumed; rent may be in advance or in arrears.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Why does the standard allow gold jewelry to be leased?
column5: Gold leased as jewelry is not a Ribawi item
column6: The lessee owns the gold at the end of the lease term
column7: Rent paid in gold is in lieu of the corpus, so the lease is a sale
column8: The lease is of usufruct; the corpus stays intact
column10: Per the Basis, leasing gold is permitted as the lessee uses its usufruct while its corpus remains intact; the subject is the usufruct.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An item that is 60% gold mixed with substances other than silver is sold for a commodity that is not gold, silver or currency. Is spot exchange required?
column5: No, spot exchange is not required in this case
column6: Yes, any item over 50% gold needs spot exchange
column7: Yes, unless the item is below 21K
column8: Yes, for the gold portion of the item
column10: Per 3/3/1/1 (second form, first type, c), when sold for substances other than silver or currencies, spot exchange is not required.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: In an importer-exporter gold deposit arrangement, the exporter used the deposit, so the gold is sold at market price. What is the stated purpose of this rule?
column5: To meet spot exchange at the contract's inception
column6: To prevent the deposit becoming a loan with benefits
column7: To compensate the importer's opportunity cost
column8: To avoid Gharar in the price of the shipment
column10: Per the Basis for 10/5, selling at market price when the exporter used the deposit aims to prevent rendering the deposit a loan associated with benefits.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Gold deposited with Bank A is damaged through the bank's negligence. How must Bank A indemnify the depositor?
column5: With equivalent gold of the same kind, if possible
column6: It is not liable, as it holds the gold in trust
column7: With its value at the date of the deposit
column8: With its value at the date of the claim
column10: Per 5/4/3, the depository indemnifies with equivalent gold of the same kind if possible, otherwise its value at the time of the damage.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A sells a gold ingot for currency and gives the buyer a certificate. Which certificate gives the buyer constructive possession?
column5: One that gives no right to physical delivery
column6: One for an ingot allocated by serial number, issued at T+0
column7: One for a specified ingot, issued two days after the sale (T+2)
column8: One for an unallocated quantity of ingots, issued at T+0 on the sale date
column10: Per 3/4, the certificate must represent a distinguishable (allocated) ingot, be issued on T+0 by recognized agencies, and allow physical delivery on request.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A opens an account in which customers deposit gold of a specific weight and karatage, as a current account. Which rulings govern this account?
column5: The rulings for investment accounts
column6: The rulings for joint ownership of gold
column7: The rulings for current accounts
column8: The rulings for Hamish Jiddiyyah
column10: Per 10/8, a gold-denominated current account is permissible and subject to the rulings for current accounts (see the standard on Qard).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Ahmad wants to exchange his old gold bracelet for a heavier new gold bracelet at a jeweller, on spot, paying nothing else. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes, since the new bracelet is unused
column6: Yes, since the exchange is made on spot
column7: Yes, if the jeweller agrees to the difference
column8: No, gold for gold must be equal in weight
column10: Per 3/1/1, gold for gold is permissible only if equal in weight, regardless of being new or old, with exchange as required by Shari'ah.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A agrees to sell gold to a customer, with the sale to take effect only if the gold price rises by 5% next week. Is this permissible?
column5: No, a gold sale may not be contingent on an event
column6: Yes, like a promise contingent on an index
column7: Yes, if the price is fixed at the contract date
column8: Yes, if both sides deliver when it takes effect
column10: Per 3/2/2, a gold sale contract may not be contingent on an event or occurrence, nor be a forward contract.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An item that is 70% gold mixed with copper is sold by Bank A for pure gold on spot. What condition applies to the weight of the pure gold?
column5: No weight condition applies to such alloys
column6: It must equal the item's total weight
column7: It must outweigh the gold contained in the item
column8: It must equal the gold contained in the item
column10: Per 3/3/1/1 (second form, first type), the pure gold must weigh more than the gold in the alloy, the excess being for the non-gold substance.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A buys a manufacturing company whose assets include some gold. Gold is not its primary asset and it does not trade in gold, silver or currencies. Must al-Sarf rules be met?
column5: Yes, the gold must first be sold separately
column6: Yes, spot exchange is required for the gold portion
column7: Yes, unless the gold is under half of the assets
column8: No, the sale is not subject to the rulings of al-Sarf
column10: Per 3/1/2, selling such an entity along with its non-primary gold is not subject to the rulings of al-Sarf.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An item containing 40% gold mixed with other metals (not silver) is sold for currency. Which treatment applies?
column5: No spot exchange, since it is not deemed gold
column6: Spot exchange is required as it is sold for currency
column7: The sale is not permissible at all, since gold is mixed with other metals
column8: The currency must be worth more than the gold it contains, to avoid riba
column10: Per 3/3/1/1 (second type), at 50% gold or less it is not deemed a sale of gold, unless sold for gold, silver or currencies, when spot exchange is required.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Selling a gold-silver alloy for heavier pure gold is allowed, the excess pure gold being in lieu of the silver. Whose view does the standard follow here?
column5: The Shafi'i School
column6: The Maliki School
column7: The Hanbali School
column8: The Hanafi School
column10: The Basis states that treating the excess pure gold as in lieu of the silver in the alloy is the view of the Hanafi School.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Company X deliberately sets up a portfolio for the specific purpose of trading in gold, and sells units in it on deferred payment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, as the gold is held within a portfolio
column6: Not permissible unless it complies with al-Sarf rulings
column7: Permissible, as the gold is an accessory to the entity
column8: Permissible, as the units are not gold themselves
column10: Per 3/1/2, it is not permissible to deliberately establish a portfolio for trading in gold unless it complies with the rulings of al-Sarf.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A holds the ownership certificates of a customer's warehoused gold pledged to it. When does this amount to possession of the pledged gold?
column5: Only if the gold is jewelry rather than ingots
column6: Only once the gold is moved to Bank A's vault
column7: When the owner can't dispose of it without them
column8: Never, as a pledge needs physical possession
column10: Per 7/1/5, holding ownership certificates is constructive possession as long as the pledgor cannot dispose of the gold without presenting them.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An item is mostly non-gold metal with a minority gold content, and Bank A does not treat it as gold. Which maxim does the standard rely on for this?
column5: In ruling (Hukm), majority is tantamount to the whole
column6: A promise cannot be the subject of a sale or purchase contract
column7: Gold paid as rent is in lieu of the usufruct, not of the corpus
column8: A certificate is as good as physical possession of the gold
column10: The Basis adheres to the principle of majority: in terms of ruling (Hukm), majority is tantamount to the whole.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A appoints Ahmad as agent to buy and take possession of gold. Afterwards, Ahmad buys that gold from Bank A by offer and acceptance. Who then bears liability for it?
column5: The supplier, until the gold is delivered again
column6: Bank A, since Ahmad remains its agent
column7: Ahmad, as purchaser in the latter contract
column8: Bank A, until Ahmad pays the full price
column10: Per 5/1/3, after purchase and possession the agent may buy from the principal by Ijab and Qabul, and liability transfers to him as purchaser.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: An importer deposits money with a gold exporter; a sale is concluded once a shipment is ready. The exporter has used the deposit. At what price is the gold sold?
column5: At any price the parties agree on that date
column6: At a price agreed when the deposit was made
column7: At cost plus a profit agreed in advance
column8: At the market price on the date of the contract
column10: Per 10/5, the price is normally agreed at the contract date, but if the exporter utilized the deposit, the gold must be sold at that date's market price.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer buys gold jewelry from a shop for currency, paying half the price now and half next month. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, since jewelry is not pure gold and is sold as a commodity
column6: Not permissible; both must be delivered at the session
column7: Permissible, since used jewelry is not Ribawi
column8: Permissible, if the full price is agreed now and secured by a pledge
column10: Per 3/2/1, in a sale of gold for currencies both countervalues must be delivered at the session, for gold of all purities, used or unused.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Company X pays gold as the capital of Salam to buy wheat for delivery in six months. Is this permissible?
column5: Yes; the Salam subject is not gold, silver or currency
column6: No, the capital of Salam must be paid in currency, never in gold
column7: Yes, if the wheat equals the gold in weight
column8: No, gold may not be used as payment in any deferred contract
column10: Per 5/2/1, gold may be the capital of Salam provided the subject matter (al-Muslam Fehi) is not gold, silver or currencies.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A shop sells wooden boxes decorated with a small amount of gold gilding, on deferred payment for currency. Do the rulings for sale of gold apply?
column5: Yes, spot exchange is needed for any gold content
column6: Yes, if the gilding exceeds the box's value
column7: No, such items are not subject to those rulings
column8: Yes, the gold must be weighed and priced separately
column10: Per 3/3/1/3, items with an insignificant amount of gold not intended per se, such as gilding and decoration, are not subject to gold sale rulings.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A jeweller sells an alloy of gold and silver containing 40 g of gold for 40 g of pure gold, exchanged on spot. Is the sale permissible?
column5: No, the pure gold must outweigh the gold in the alloy
column6: Yes, provided the silver is valued separately
column7: No, such alloys may be sold only for currencies
column8: Yes, as the gold weights are equal and it is spot
column10: Per 3/3/1/1, a gold-silver alloy sold for pure gold needs spot exchange and the pure countervalue must weigh more; equal or lighter is not permissible.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Why does the standard prohibit trading a promise (Wa'd) relating to gold through sale or purchase?
column5: The promise lacks spot exchange of the countervalues at the session
column6: A promise cannot be the subject of a commutative contract
column7: Trading it would render the deposit a loan
column8: The promise binds only one of the parties and so is unequal
column10: Per the Basis, trading a promise in any form is impermissible because a promise cannot be used as the subject matter of a commutative contract.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A charges a fee for a service that involves exchanging a customer's gold for other gold. How must the fee be set?
column5: At any amount the parties agree upon
column6: As a percentage of the gold's market value
column7: No fee may be charged for such a service
column8: Based on the actual expenses of the service
column10: Per 10/7, fees for safekeeping, allocation, minting and delivery are permissible; if the service involves gold-for-gold exchange, the fee is based on actual expenses.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Which evidence does the standard cite for classifying gold as a Ribawi item?
column5: The consensus of jurists on the permissibility of Salam with gold
column6: 'Ubaidah bin al-Samit's Hadith: gold for gold, like for like
column7: The maxim that the majority is tantamount to the whole in ruling
column8: The precedent of early jurists on endowing money
column10: The Basis cites the Hadith narrated by 'Ubaidah bin al-Samit: "Gold for gold... like for like... hand in hand."

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Company X pays gold as capital of Salam for wheat. Why does the standard find no Riba in this, unlike gold for silver?
column5: Each countervalue has a different Illah
column6: Wheat is a non-fungible identified item
column7: The gold capital is constructively possessed
column8: Salam is exempt from the rules of Riba
column10: Per the Basis, gold as capital of Salam (or as its subject) is allowed where the other side is not gold, silver or currency: different Illah, so no Riba.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer buys gold, and a latent defect appears later. The seller had not expressly absolved himself of defects. What right does the customer have?
column5: None, as the gold was exchanged on spot
column6: None, as options are barred in gold sales
column7: Option to revoke for defect and return the gold
column8: Only a price reduction, as the sale is final
column10: Per 10/2, unless the seller expressly absolves himself of latent defects, the buyer has the Option to Revoke Due to Defect and may return the gold.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A holds a customer's gold as Wadi'ah and, without his permission, commingles it with its own gold without allocation. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, if the deposit is recorded by weight
column6: Yes, since gold is fungible by nature
column7: Yes, if it later returns gold of equal weight
column8: No, it may not commingle it without allocation
column10: Per 5/4/1, gold deposits are held in trust; the depository may not use them or commingle them without allocation unless the depositor permits.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A takes a customer's gold as a pledge and stipulates a right to lease it out, undertaking to return it at maturity. Is this stipulation valid?
column5: No, even with an undertaking to return it
column6: Yes, since Bank A will return the same gold
column7: Yes, if the rent is credited to the debt
column8: Yes, since the pledgor agreed to it in the contract
column10: Per 7/1/4, the pledgee may not stipulate a right to sell, re-pledge or lease the pledged gold, even if it undertakes to return it.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Partners in a Musharakah agree to distribute profit in gold. At what value is the gold to be taken?
column5: Its average market value over the whole financial year
column6: Its value when the gold was first acquired by the partnership
column7: Its value agreed at the contract date, to avoid uncertainty
column8: Its market value at the time of profit distribution
column10: Per 4/2, the parties may distribute profit in gold provided it is at the market value of gold at the time of profit distribution.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer leases gold ingots from Bank A, and the parties agree that the rent will be paid in gold. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permissible unless the rent is paid on spot
column6: Permissible, even though the leased asset is gold
column7: Not permissible, being gold for gold with excess
column8: Permissible only if rent equals the ingots' weight
column10: Per 5/3/3, the rent (Ujrah) may be paid in gold even if the leased asset is gold.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A offers units in an exchange-traded fund (ETF) whose entire assets are gold. Which rulings govern trading in these units?
column5: The rulings for gold only above 50% purity
column6: The rulings for currencies
column7: The rulings for gold
column8: The rulings for shares of ordinary companies
column10: Per 10/3, Sukuk, investment fund units and ETF units whose entire assets are gold are subject to the rulings for gold.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: How does the standard characterize gold in principle?
column5: A fungible Ribawi item subject to the rulings of al-Sarf
column6: An ordinary commodity unless minted as currency
column7: A non-fungible item that may be sold on deferred terms
column8: A Ribawi item exempt from al-Sarf when made into jewelry
column10: Per item 2, gold is in principle a fungible item (measured by weight), a Ribawi commodity, and subject to the rulings of currency exchange (al-Sarf).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A customer buys gold for currency, with both delivered at the session, and stipulates a three-day option to return the gold and revoke the sale. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if the customer pays 'Arboun to secure the option
column6: Impermissible; Khiyar al-Shart is barred in gold sales
column7: Permissible, if the option period is specified
column8: Permissible, as the exchange was made on spot and both were delivered
column10: Per 3/2/2, stipulation of Khiyar al-Shart (cooling-off option) in the sale of gold is impermissible.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A buys shares of a non-gold company holding some gold, without spot exchange. Which maxim does the standard cite for exempting this from al-Sarf?
column5: A certificate is as good as physical possession
column6: A promise cannot be the subject of a sale
column7: What is barred in itself may be allowed as an accessory
column8: In ruling, the majority is tantamount to the whole in a mixed item
column10: Per the Basis for 3/1/2, the maxim: a thing not permissible in itself may be permissible as an accessory (and implicitly).

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Gold pledged against a customer's loan is kept in safekeeping, and the fee is capped at actual expenses. What is the reason the standard gives?
column5: Because the pledgee benefits from safekeeping
column6: To ensure fairness in the depositor's absence
column7: To keep the pledge in fiduciary possession
column8: To avoid charging Riba in a loan contract
column10: Per the Basis, the cap at actual safekeeping expenses for gold pledged against a loan is to avoid charging Riba in a loan contract.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Bank A wants to import gold by way of documentary credit, with the price payable 90 days after shipment. What is the ruling?
column5: Permissible, if Bank A holds the title documents until payment
column6: Permissible, if the gold is shipped on spot
column7: Not permissible; the price must be paid without deferment
column8: Permissible, as the documentary credit acts as a guarantee of payment
column10: Per 5/1/2, gold may not be bought by documentary credit unless item (3) is met, including payment of the price without deferment.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: A Rab al-Mal wants to contribute gold as the capital of a Mudharabah. What is required for this to be permissible?
column5: The gold is first sold for cash and the cash contributed as the capital
column6: Its value is set by the market price at the time of liquidation
column7: The gold is pure and in ingot form only
column8: Its value in the capital's currency is agreed at contract
column10: Per 4/1, gold may be capital if valued and its monetary value in the capital's currency is determined at the contract date by mutual agreement.

column3: Gold and Its Trading Parameters in Shari’ah
column4: Several investors store serial-numbered ingots in one warehouse and have not agreed on joint ownership. One investor's ingots are stolen. Who bears the loss?
column5: The investor who stored the most ingots
column6: That investor, as owner of his allocated ingots
column7: All the investors in equal shares
column8: All the investors pro rata, as joint owners
column10: Per 3/5/4, if ingots have distinguishing serial numbers, each owner owns his allocated ingots and is liable for their loss, unless joint ownership is agreed.

column4: A Mudarib sells assets to Rab al-Maal with a promise to buy them back at the original price, effectively protecting the capital. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, as it guarantees the capital
column6: Permitted, if both prices are spot prices
column7: Permitted, if documented in a separate deed
column8: Permitted, as it is a unilateral promise
column10: Per 5/1/5, the promise must not come from a partner, Mudarib or investment agent in a way that leads to guaranteeing the capital or part of it.

column4: An asset is resold, without collusion, to a party other than its original seller in a tripartite setting. What basis does the standard give for permitting this?
column5: A public interest in liquidity
column6: The absence of any 'Inah implication
column7: An analogy to Suftajah
column8: The buyer's retention of the legal deed
column10: Per the Basis, collusion-free, value-changed or tripartite repurchase is permitted due to the absence of Einah implication.

column4: Why may a partner in a joint enterprise promise to buy his partner's share at market value but not at a predetermined price?
column5: Market value reflects the partnership's profit or loss
column6: The partner is an outsider to the other's share
column7: Market value avoids a deferred Sarf between the partners' shares
column8: A set price makes the promise a contingent sale of the share
column10: Per the Basis, a predetermined price contradicts profit and loss sharing; market value reflects the partnership's profit or loss at execution.

column4: Ahmad sells a machine for cash. Months later, with no prior collusion or custom, he buys it back from the buyer at a higher deferred price. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as a deferred price above spot is 'Inah
column6: Permitted only if the second price is spot
column7: Prohibited, unless the machine's value changed
column8: Permitted, as it is free of collusion and custom
column10: Per 3/5/2/1, buyback is permitted, even if the deferred price is higher, when it is free of any collusion or customary practice.

column4: In a sale of land to Bank A, the sale contract stipulates that the seller will buy the land back from the Bank on a set date. What is the ruling on this term?
column5: Permitted, if a separate deed records it later
column6: Permitted, as both prices are disclosed to the parties up front
column7: Not permitted, as the buyback is stipulated in the sale
column8: Permitted, if the buyback is at a spot price at the later date
column10: Per 3/3, the second contract should not be stipulated within the first contract.

column4: Bank A sells bonds to Bank B for cash and buys them back in a month at a higher price, while Bank A keeps their yield and risk. How does the standard characterize this?
column5: A riba-based loan secured by financial assets
column6: A Tawarruq with a pledge of securities
column7: A valid sale with a unilateral promise
column8: A valid buyback, as both prices are cash
column10: Per 5/6/2, a conventional repo is a riba-based loan secured by financial assets; the price difference (repo rate) is interest.

column4: How does the standard justify characterizing a conventional repo as an interest-bearing loan rather than a sale?
column5: The assets are sold at a cash price
column6: The second price is set by an auction
column7: Contracts are judged by real intention, not form
column8: The buyer bears the risk of loss of the assets
column10: Per the Basis, the essential consideration is real intention rather than form; the sale is fictitious and the assets are only security.

column4: Bank A sells a commodity on deferred terms. The buyer later offers it in a public auction for cash, and Bank A wins the bid at a lower cash price. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited, as it is 'Inah through an auction
column6: Prohibited unless a third party outbids it
column7: Permitted only above the deferred price
column8: Permitted, even at a lower cash price
column10: Per 4/3, it is permitted to sell on deferred terms and buy back from the auction, even at a lower cash price.

column4: Why does the standard allow a seller to buy back his commodity in an auction, even below the deferred price?
column5: The seller's bid is a unilateral promise
column6: No collusion; the auction sets a market price
column7: The auction turns the debt into a spot sale
column8: The lower price means there is no excess
column10: Per the Basis, there is no collusion; others may buy it, and the auction mechanism sets a market price rather than a pre-determined one.

column4: Bank A buys listed shares from Company X, which keeps the legal registration of the shares in its own name. What does the standard require?
column5: Nothing, since registration decides ownership
column6: Transfer of the registration into Bank A's name before any buyback
column7: A guarantee by Company X of the shares' value at the buyback date
column8: A document, e.g. counter deed, confirming Bank A's ownership
column10: Per 4/2, if the seller retains legal registration, a document such as a counter deed must confirm the buyer's ownership; seller holds as trust.

column4: Why must ownership in a buyback pass by a contract made at that time, rather than by the mere lapse of a period?
column5: To let the seller keep legal registration
column6: To stop the asset's value from changing between the two sales
column7: Ownership needs a formulation; else the sale is contingent
column8: To keep the second price lower than the first in every buyback
column10: Per the Basis, ownership transfers only by a verbal or action-based formulation; automatic transfer would be tantamount to a contingent sale.

column4: Bank A sells an asset with a unilateral promise from the buyer to resell it to the Bank. Where must this promise be documented?
column5: In a deed separate from the first contract
column6: Only in the second contract, at performance
column7: As a clause in the first sale contract
column8: Nowhere, to keep it non-binding
column10: Per 5/1/2, the promise to purchase or sell must be documented in a separate deed from the first contract.

column4: In an investment deposit used for liquidity management, Bank A as investment agent wishes to tell the depositor bank about returns. Which statement is permitted?
column5: A guarantee of the capital in full
column6: An expected return, without obligation
column7: A guaranteed minimum return only
column8: A guaranteed specified return
column10: Per 5/6/3/3(c), the manager may not guarantee a specified return; it may state an expected return without obligation to realize it.

column4: Which of the following falls outside the scope of the standard on buyback?
column5: Repurchase from another to whom ownership passed
column6: Selling a usufruct, then repurchasing it
column7: Selling an asset, then buying it back at spot
column8: Return of an item through dissolution (iqala)
column10: Per item 1, the standard does not cover items returning to the seller other than by sale or rescission, like Wafa Sale and dissolution (iqala).

column4: In a joint enterprise, Partner A gives Partner B a binding promise to buy back B's share at a price fixed today, regardless of market value then. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since the promise is unilateral and the price is known
column6: Not permitted; it contradicts sharing risk and reward
column7: Permitted, as a normal feature of Diminishing Musharaka
column8: Permitted, if documented in a separate deed
column10: Per 5/4/2, such a promise at a specified price is not permitted; it is permitted at market value or a price agreed at performance.

column4: Bank A sells a commodity to Ahmad on deferred terms; by collusion, Bank A's 80%-owned subsidiary buys it back from him for less in cash. Is this a permitted scenario?
column5: Yes, if the second price is paid on spot
column6: Yes, as the buyer differs from the first seller
column7: No, the subsidiary is majority-owned by Bank A
column8: Yes, as the subsidiary is a separate entity
column10: Per 3/5/2/3, a different buyer is permitted only if neither party is wholly or majority-owned by the other.

column4: An Islamic fund's manager undertakes to buy back investment units from investors upon their exit from the fund. At what price is this undertaking permitted?
column5: At the unit's market value at exit
column6: At the price the investor originally paid
column7: At the face value of the units at issue
column8: At the original price plus expected return
column10: Per 5/5, the fund manager may undertake to buy units on exit provided the purchase is at the market value of the unit at the time of exit.

column4: Bank A buys a commodity spot from Company X and sells it on credit to Ahmad; all parties collude that Ahmad resells it spot to Company X for less. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since three parties are involved
column6: Permitted, as Bank A is not the final buyer
column7: Permitted, if each sale is a separate contract
column8: Not permitted, due to collusion among all parties
column10: Per 4/4, buying spot to sell on credit to a third party is not permitted if all parties collude to resell to the first seller spot for less.

column4: Under a known market custom of buyback, a seller sells a commodity for 100 spot and on a later date buys it back for a higher spot price of 105. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, if delivery took place in between
column6: No, it is a prohibited scenario under such custom
column7: Yes, since the buyback price is higher
column8: Yes, since both prices are paid on spot, with no deferment
column10: Per 3/5/1/4, with collusion or custom, selling for spot and buying back later at a higher spot price is a prohibited scenario.

column4: Company X and Bank A use a third party so that a commodity returns to Company X at a cash price lower than its deferred price. How does the standard view this?
column5: Permitted, as a tripartite setting excludes 'Inah
column6: Permitted, if the third party is independent
column7: A stratagem for 'Inah; the third party changes nothing
column8: Void only as a contingent sale
column10: Per the Basis for 4/4, it is a stratagem for Einah; engaging the third party does not change the essence of the transaction.

column4: Bank A buys a building from Company X, and they exchange promises binding on each of them: the Bank to resell and Company X to buy it back next year. Ruling?
column5: Not permitted, being a binding bilateral promise
column6: Permitted, if the prices are both spot
column7: Permitted, if recorded in a separate deed
column8: Permitted, since promises are not contracts
column10: Per 3/4, there must not be a bilateral promise (muwa'ada) binding on both parties to enter into the second contract.

column4: An investment deposit agreement gives all profit up to 5% to the depositor and any excess to Bank A as Mudarib. Is this clause permitted?
column5: Yes, as a performance incentive for the manager
column6: No, it may lead to cessation of profit-sharing
column7: Yes, if the 5% is only an expected return
column8: Yes, since the Mudarib takes only the excess
column10: Per 5/6/3/3(d), a clause giving all profits up to a limit to one party is not permitted; an incentive where both share profits first is allowed.

column4: Ahmad sells his car to Company X for 100 cash and, by prior collusion, buys it back for 110 payable in six months. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since the same asset is returned
column6: Permitted, since the first sale was for cash
column7: Permitted, if the car was delivered in between
column8: Prohibited, as it constitutes 'Inah
column10: Per 3/5/1/2, selling an asset for cash and buying it back at a higher deferred price, with collusion or custom, is 'Inah.

column4: Company X sells shares to Bank A, but the contract leaves all dividends and the risk of price falls with Company X until it buys them back. Is this buyback permitted?
column5: Yes, if the buyback is made in a separate contract signed later
column6: Yes, if there is no collusion on a higher buyback price
column7: No, the first sale must be real, with its consequences
column8: Yes, since legal title passed to Bank A at the time of sale
column10: Per 3/1, the sale must be real: the buyer is entitled to the yield, assumes price-change risk, and bears risk of loss on possession.

column4: In a Tawarruq where Bank A's debt is secured by a pledge of the customer's shares, Bank A stipulates a right to sell the pledged shares at will. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, though dividends may reduce the debt
column6: Permitted, since the shares are registered to it
column7: Permitted, if Bank A bears any loss on them
column8: Permitted, if the dividends are pledged too
column10: Per 5/6/3/4(d), the pledgee may not stipulate selling the pledged securities; parties may agree that dividends pay off or reduce the debt.

column4: Two banks agree to lend to each other on equal terms when either needs cash (back-to-back loans). On what basis does the standard permit this?
column5: Each loan is treated as a gift (Hibah) from one bank to the other
column6: It is a promise from one party alone to lend when needed
column7: It is a lend-me-and-I-lend-you condition
column8: The benefit is for both, by analogy to Suftajah
column10: Per the Basis, the benefit accrues to both parties, not solely the lender, by analogy to Suftajah; no harm is inflicted on either.

column4: Two banks agree a bilateral loans points system, with extra points to one bank as a penalty if the other repays its counter-loan late. Is this permitted?
column5: No, no party may receive extra or penalty points
column6: Yes, if points are never converted to cash
column7: Yes, if the penalty is agreed at borrowing
column8: Yes, since penalties ensure timely repayment
column10: Per 5/6/3/2(a), the points system must be fair; preferential terms or extra points, including as a penalty for late repayment, are not permitted.

column4: Company X sells Sukuk to Bank A with a unilateral promise from Company X to buy them back. Which pricing complies with the standard?
column5: Sale at spot, buyback at a higher deferred price
column6: Sale on deferred terms, buyback at lower spot
column7: Both the sale and the buyback at a spot price
column8: Both sales at deferred prices fixed today
column10: Per 5/1/1, with a promise to buy back or resell, both contracts (the first sale and the subsequent one) must be for a spot price.

column4: Bank A manages a flexible investment deposit for another bank as Mudarib and undertakes to buy the underlying assets at their face value. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if it is a separate deed
column6: Not permitted; it may promise to buy at market value
column7: Permitted, as a unilateral promise to buy the assets from the deposit
column8: Permitted, as the deposit is made for liquidity purposes only
column10: Per 5/6/3/3(b), the manager may not undertake to buy the underlying assets at face value; a promise to buy at market value is permitted.

column4: Which Qur'anic basis does the standard cite for permitting buyback free of stipulation, binding Muwa'adah or collusion?
column5: The Hadith prohibiting two sales in one and a sale with a loan
column6: The analogy to Suftajah between two cities
column7: Ibn Omar's narration on the 'Inah sale and following the tails of cows
column8: "Allah has permitted sale" and trade by mutual consent
column10: The Basis: contracts are presumed permissible, citing "Allah has permitted sale" and the verse on trading by mutual consent.

column4: Two co-owners hold a building in a joint ownership partnership. One sells his share to the other with a promise to buy it back at a specified price. Ruling?
column5: Not permitted, as it negates risk sharing
column6: Permitted, subject to the promise rules in 5/1
column7: Not permitted; only market value is allowed
column8: Permitted only at a price set at performance
column10: Per 5/4/3, in a joint ownership partnership a promise to buy back at market value, an agreed price or a specified price is permitted, per 5/1.

column4: Company X sells goods for cash and later buys them back at a higher deferred price payable in other goods rather than cash. Is this among the permitted scenarios?
column5: Yes, as the price in one contract is not cash
column6: No, a price in kind makes it a deferred Sarf
column7: Yes, but only if the goods changed in value
column8: No, any higher deferred price is 'Inah
column10: Per 3/5/2/4, buyback is permitted, even at a higher deferred price, if the price in one of the contracts is in a form other than cash.

column4: With prior collusion, Bank A sells a car to Ahmad for 120 payable in a year, then buys it back from him for 100 in cash. How is this classified?
column5: A valid Tawarruq, as Ahmad receives cash
column6: A valid buyback, as the contracts are separate
column7: 'Inah, which is prohibited
column8: A valid buyback, as the second price is lower
column10: Per 3/5/1/1, with collusion or custom, selling at a deferred price and buying back for less at spot constitutes 'Inah.

column4: A regulator's rules oblige any bank that receives a promise to buy back an asset to accept the buyback. Is such a promise arrangement acceptable under the standard?
column5: Yes, as the promise is from one party alone and the bank is not bound
column6: Yes, if the promise is recorded in a separate deed
column7: Yes, since a regulation is not collusion
column8: No, the promisee must not be obliged by regulation
column10: Per 5/1/4, the promisee must not be obligated to enter into the second contract by regulation, custom, collusion or the like.

column4: Bank A promised to sell an asset to Ahmad for 100 but repudiates. On the performance date Ahmad has to buy the asset elsewhere for 108. What may Ahmad claim?
column5: Nothing, as a promise to sell never binds
column6: 100: the full promised price
column7: 8: the purchase price minus the promised price
column8: The profit he expected from reselling it
column10: Per 5/1/7, for a promise to sell, actual damage is the purchase price on the performance date minus the promised price.

column4: Bank A buys a building for cash and renovates it extensively. Later, the original seller buys it back on deferred terms at a higher price. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, if the higher price reflects the asset's change
column6: No, the original seller may never buy it back on deferred terms
column7: No, any deferred price above the original spot price is 'Inah
column8: Yes, but only if the price is paid on spot
column10: Per 3/5/2/2, buyback is permitted where the price change is due to alterations in the asset's characteristics or value, not deferral.

column4: Ahmad repudiates his promise to buy an asset for 110 from Bank A, which cost the Bank 100. On the performance date Bank A sells it to a third party for 95. What may it claim?
column5: 10: the profit lost on the promised price
column6: 5: the cost minus the third-party price
column7: 15: the promised price minus the sale price
column8: 110: the full promised price
column10: Per 5/1/7, actual damage for a promise to purchase is cost minus the third-party sale price on the performance date; lost profit is excluded.

column4: Why is leasing a purchased asset back to its seller under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek not treated as 'Inah?
column5: Rent is for usufruct, a different subject from the sale
column6: The lessor's possession is held in trust
column7: The rent is fixed in advance and paid on spot at the contract
column8: The lessee owns the usufruct and may sublease it to third parties
column10: Per the Basis, rent is paid for the renewable usufruct, a different subject matter from the first sale; also time passes and value changes.

column4: By collusion, Ahmad sells an asset to Bank A for gold and later buys it back from the Bank on credit, paying in silver. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since gold and silver may be unequal
column6: Not permitted, as it results in deferred Sarf
column7: Permitted, if the silver amount is fixed today
column8: Permitted, as an asset stands between the sales
column10: Per 3/6, buyback must not result in deferred currency exchange, e.g., selling for gold or currency and buying back on credit in silver.

column4: Why does the standard prohibit repurchase at a deferred price exceeding the spot price where there is collusion?
column5: It makes the sale contingent on an event
column6: It turns the promise into a tradable right
column7: It amounts to a deferred currency exchange
column8: It amounts to 'Inah and two sales in one
column10: Per the Basis, it is tantamount to Einah and two sales in one (Bai'tan fi Bai'ah), citing Ibn Omar's and Abu Hurairah's narrations.

column4: Bank A buys equipment from Company X; the documents state that ownership reverts to Company X automatically after one year, with no further contract. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the price is paid on spot
column6: Permitted, as the reversion date is known and the price fixed
column7: Not permitted; the buyback needs its own contract
column8: Permitted, if Company X pays rent for the asset meanwhile
column10: Per 3/2, the subsequent purchase must be by an independent contract; it may not occur automatically upon lapse of a period.

column4: Bank A buys a factory from Company X and then leases it back to Company X under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if the rent is paid in advance for the full term
column6: Permitted, subject to the Ijarah standard's provisions
column7: Prohibited, as it is 'Inah in all cases where the seller leases back
column8: Prohibited, as a seller cannot become lessee
column10: Per 5/2, buying a tangible asset and leasing it to its seller under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek is permitted, subject to the Ijarah standard.

column4: Ahmad promised to buy back an asset from Bank A, but the asset is totally destroyed before the buyback date. May Bank A oblige him to perform the promise?
column5: No, unless the loss was under half its value
column6: Yes, the promise binds him regardless
column7: No, not after total loss of the asset
column8: Yes, but only at a reduced price
column10: Per 5/1/6, it is not permitted to oblige the promisor to fulfil the promise in case of total loss of the asset.

column4: A scholar argues that the creditor should first collect the debt, then sell it back to the same debtor. How does the standard's basis view such a requirement?
column5: As a valid form of set-off (muqassa)
column6: As needed to avoid riba al-nasi'ah
column7: As needed for the transfer of risk
column8: As a meaningless contriving formality
column10: Per the Basis, requiring the creditor to take possession of the debt and then sell it to the same debtor would be a meaningless contriving formality.

column4: Bank A places debts and tangible assets in a registered special purpose company and sells units in it. What minimum share must tangible and like assets form?
column5: More than 50% of the entity's asset value
column6: At least 25% of the asset value
column7: At least one-third of the asset value
column8: No minimum, as commingling has occurred
column10: Per 8/2/2, the ratio of tangible and like assets must exceed 50% of the value of the entity's assets.

column4: Why does the standard not require the debtor's consent for selling his debt to a third party?
column5: Because the debtor is deemed to be the possessor of the debt
column6: Because the sale is a separation of rights, not a sale of debt
column7: By analogy to Hawala; the creditor may claim via another
column8: Because "Muslims act upon their conditions" in all contracts
column10: Per the Basis for 5/6, analogy to Hawala applies, and the creditor may demand his right himself or through a party acting for him.

column4: A farmer owes Company X 1,000 kg of dates, and they agree he will settle it with dates of another type. Which conditions apply?
column5: Possession in the session; quantity may differ
column6: Any agreed quantity, delivered at maturity
column7: Equal quantity; delivery may be deferred
column8: Equal quantity, with possession in the session
column10: Per 4/1/1/1(b), where the consideration is of the same Ribawi kind as the debt, equality (tamathul) and possession in the session are required.

column4: Three partners split a single debt among themselves according to their shares. Why is this not treated as a sale of debt?
column5: It is a Hawala to each of the partners
column6: Such division is a separation, not a sale
column7: It is a form of sulh among the partners
column8: It is appurtenant to other assets
column10: Per the Basis for 6/1-6/2, dividing single or multiple debts among partners is a separation, not a sale (6/3 is treated as sulh).

column4: Ahmad simply repays part of his debt to Bank A, with no commutative arrangement involved. Is this governed by the standard on sale of debt?
column5: No, such discharge of debt is outside its scope
column6: Yes, if repaid before the maturity date
column7: Yes, as a sale of debt to the debtor himself
column8: Yes, as a sale of debt for cash at a discount
column10: Per item 1, the standard does not deal with discharge of debt by the debtor, in whole or part, not done through a commutative arrangement.

column4: In a new Murabaha with an indebted customer, the documents require him to sell the commodity on to a third party at once. Is this consistent with the standard?
column5: Yes, if he is a solvent debtor
column6: No, he must be free to keep it, with no duty to sell
column7: Yes, since constructive delivery suffices to complete the Murabaha
column8: Yes, if the third party buyer is not Bank A or its affiliate
column10: Per 4/1/3/4(b), the customer is entitled to take delivery, retain ownership and dispose of the item as he deems fit, with no obligation to sell.

column4: Company X sells its trade invoices to a factor for an immediate cash payment below their value. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the debtors are notified
column6: Permitted, as the factor bears collection risk
column7: Permitted, if the invoices are not yet due
column8: Not permitted: it sells monetary debt for cash
column10: Per 9/6/2, factoring is not permitted unless the invoices are bought for a commodity, usufruct or service with ascertained delivery.

column4: Before buying a portfolio of receivables, Company Y requires Bank A to arrange Islamic insurance (Takaful) on the debts. Is this condition permitted?
column5: Yes, but only after the debt has been sold and delivered
column6: No, the buyer must bear all the risk of the debts he buys
column7: Yes, a Shari'ah-compliant guarantee may be stipulated
column8: No, Takaful cannot cover sold debts
column10: Per 7/3, the buyer may stipulate that the seller secure the debt by a Shari'ah-compliant third-party guarantee, e.g., Takaful before sale.

column4: A customer owes Bank A compensation for damage caused by his negligence to a leased asset. Is this amount a 'debt' as defined in the standard?
column5: Yes, debt includes amounts arising from negligence
column6: No, debt arises only from a loan contract
column7: Only if it is acknowledged before a court
column8: No, debt arises only from commutative contracts
column10: Per item 2, debt is an established owed asset whatever its cause, including (i) a loan, (ii) a commutative contract, or (iii) misconduct or negligence.

column4: Bank A and a customer collude: the Bank pays cash now for oil to be delivered later, and on delivery the oil is replaced by a larger cash sum. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if replaced only after maturity
column6: Permitted, if the oil's value equals the cash
column7: Prohibited, as a legal artifice (hila) for riba
column8: Permitted, as a Salam followed by substitution
column10: Per 4/1/2, the transaction must not be a hila for riba, e.g., colluding to pay cash for deferred delivery then substituting more currency.

column4: Company X is owed a described transport service (mawsufa fi dhimma), not a specific one, and wants to sell this entitlement to Company Y for cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted to sell such a service debt
column6: Permitted, with the provider's consent
column7: Permitted, if the service is fully described
column8: Permitted, if sold for a commodity instead
column10: Per 5/4, a usufruct or service debt that is mawsufa fi dhimma cannot be sold, whether for cash, commodity, usufruct or service.

column4: An investor wishes to sell his Murabaha-based Sukuk to another investor for cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted at their face value
column6: Permitted, since Sukuk are securities
column7: Permitted once the Murabaha matures
column8: Not permitted for a cash price
column10: Per 9/3/1, it is not permitted to trade in Sukuk based on Salam and Murabaha for a cash price.

column4: Bank A sells a monetary receivable to Company Y in return for the use of a specific, identified office for one year. Is this permitted?
column5: No, usufructs are always deferred debts, so it is debt for debt
column6: Yes, since the usufruct's delivery is ascertained
column7: No, a debt may be sold only for a commodity delivered on spot
column8: Yes, but only with the debtor's consent
column10: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may be sold for a usufruct or service whose subject-delivery can be ascertained at the time of sale.

column4: Which narration does the standard cite for permitting the sale of an outstanding monetary debt to the debtor?
column5: Ibn 'Umar selling camels in al-Baqi' for dinars
column6: "Gold for gold, silver for silver... equal measure"
column7: "Muslims act upon their conditions"
column8: Imam Malik's report on Salam in the Muwatta
column10: The Basis cites Ibn 'Umar: no harm if at the rate of that day, as long as you do not depart without concluding the transaction.

column4: Why does the standard accept a new Murabaha for an indebted solvent customer, even if its proceeds settle his old debt?
column5: The new profit rate equals the old one
column6: It is independent; settling is the customer's choice
column7: The old debt is extinguished by set-off against the new financing
column8: A solvent debtor cannot give rise to riba
column10: Per the Basis for 4/1/3/4, the rules make it independent financing; any settlement is the customer's own disposition, outside the Institution's authority.

column4: Bank A sells a special purpose company holding debts and tangible assets, but undertakes to bear the risks of those assets after the sale. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, but only for the first year after the sale
column6: Yes, if tangible assets exceed 50% of the company's asset value
column7: Yes, if the company is registered
column8: No, the buyer must bear the risks of the assets
column10: Per 8/2/1, the sale must transfer ownership and risk to the buyer; it is not permitted to stipulate that the seller bears the risks at any stage.

column4: Bank A sells a receivable secured by a pledge. The buyer did not stipulate the pledge, and custom does not include it. Does the pledge pass to the buyer?
column5: Yes, if the pledgor does not object
column6: Yes, a pledge always follows the debt
column7: No, the pledge does not transfer
column8: Yes, once the debt falls due
column10: Per 7/2, a pledge or guarantee transfers with the debt only if the buyer stipulated it or custom admits it, absent a non-assignability term.

column4: After a Salam matures, the parties agree, with no prior stipulation, to substitute the Salam commodity (gas) with oil. Which condition applies?
column5: The substitute must be of the same kind as the gas and of equal quality
column6: The oil's value must exceed the gas's market value at the time of delivery
column7: The substitution must have been stipulated in the original Salam contract
column8: Oil must be fit as Salam subject for the capital; value not above the gas
column10: Per 4/1/1/3, after maturity the Salam subject may be substituted, same or other kind, if fit as Salam subject for the capital and not above its market value.

column4: A Salam contract for wheat stipulates that at maturity the seller may deliver barley instead. What is the ruling on this term?
column5: Permitted, since barley may be a Salam subject
column6: Permitted, as the substitution is after maturity
column7: Not permitted; substitution can't be stipulated
column8: Permitted, if barley's value doesn't exceed wheat's
column10: Per 4/1/1/3, substitution of the subject of Salam after maturity is permitted only without stipulating it in the contract.

column4: Bank A groups debts and tangible assets in an internal portfolio not registered with the authorities and sells it in one leg. Which rules apply?
column5: The rules for sale of debt to a third party
column6: The rules for ongoing operating entities
column7: No debt rules, since the assets are combined
column8: The commingled-entity rules, if assets exceed 50%
column10: Per 8/3, debts combined with assets without a registered entity (e.g., accounting separation, unregistered portfolio) follow item 5's rules.

column4: The basis for selling a registered entity of commingled debts and assets relies on a Maliki analogy of assemblage (tarkib). What is it?
column5: Usurped property sold to the usurper at its value
column6: Jewellery fixed on an ornament sold for that metal
column7: Salam over livestock sold before the buyer takes possession
column8: Camels sold for dinars with payment collected in dirhams
column10: Per the Basis for 8/2, the entity meets the Maliki assemblage condition for selling ornaments fixed with gold or silver for the same metal.

column4: A company whose assets consist entirely of debts, with no other assets, sells shares. Which rules govern the sale?
column5: The rules of the sale of debt
column6: The rules for sale of tangible assets
column7: The rules for Mudaraba-based Sukuk
column8: No restrictions, as the debts are ancillary
column10: Per 8/1, the exemption for ongoing entities applies provided the entity is not entirely composed of debt; otherwise sale of debt rules apply.

column4: A customer asks Bank A to buy Shari'ah non-compliant bonds for him and hold them for later sale. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if sold for a commodity
column6: Not permitted to trade in such bonds
column7: Permitted, if bought at a discount
column8: Permitted, if held until maturity
column10: Per 9/2/1, trading in Shari'ah non-compliant bonds, by sale, purchase, assignment or otherwise, is not permitted.

column4: A customer delays paying a matured USD Murabaha debt for three months, then settles it in euros. Which exchange rate must be used?
column5: The rate on the debt's maturity date
column6: The higher of the maturity and settlement rates
column7: The rate on the Murabaha contract date
column8: The rate on the actual settlement day
column10: Per 4/1/1/2(c), the settlement-day rate applies if the debtor delayed settling the debt when it matured.

column4: Company X holds a bill of exchange due in six months and wants Bank A to pay it now at less than its face value. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the discount is modest
column6: Permitted, as a sale of debt to a third party
column7: Not permitted to discount it before maturity
column8: Permitted, if the drawer consents
column10: Per 9/1/2, it is not permitted to discount a negotiable instrument, settling it to its beneficiary before maturity for less than its value.

column4: Why may a monetary debt be sold to a third party for a specific asset or the usufruct of a specific asset?
column5: Possession of any debt is constructive, so the sale is a spot sale
column6: The debtor's consent is presumed
column7: It is treated by analogy to Hawala, the assignment of debt
column8: Specific assets aren't debts, so it isn't debt for debt
column10: Per the Basis for 5/2, specific assets and their usufructs do not represent debt, so the sale is not one of debt against debt.

column4: Company X bought 500 tons of wheat by Salam and, before taking possession, sells that wheat debt to a third party for cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if sold for a commodity, not cash
column6: Not permitted before taking possession
column7: Permitted, if sold at its Salam price
column8: Permitted, as the wheat is precisely described
column10: Per 5/3, a commodity debt may not be sold before taking possession, whether for cash, commodity, usufruct or service.

column4: Ahmad owes Bank A 100 grams of gold. They agree that he will settle it with 1,400 grams of silver instead. What is required?
column5: The silver must be handed over in the session
column6: Nothing, as a debt may be substituted freely
column7: The silver may be delivered within a month
column8: The silver must equal the gold in weight
column10: Per 4/1/1/1(a), where the consideration is a Ribawi item of a different kind, it must be possessed in the session, even if quantities differ.

column4: Bank A sells a receivable to Company Y. When do the ownership and risk of the debt pass to Company Y?
column5: Only when the debtor pays the debt to Company Y in full
column6: Only on registration of the sale before a court
column7: By any means that customarily lets it claim the debt
column8: Only once the debtor consents to the sale and acknowledges it
column10: Per 7/1, ownership of the debt and its risk transfer to the buyer by any means that customarily allows the buyer to claim the debt.

column4: After a Sukuk issuance, tangible assets fall to 40% of the entity due to a supervening event acknowledged by the Shari'ah Board. What must the Institution do?
column5: Delist the Sukuk and stop all trading at once
column6: Redeem the Sukuk at their face value
column7: Nothing, since the ratio is above 33%
column8: Restore the ratio within a period the Board sets
column10: Per 8/2/3, if the ratio is lost due to a supervening event, the Institution must restore it within a period specified by the Shari'ah Board.

column4: At origination of a Murabaha debt, Bank A and the customer agree that the Bank will sell the debt to the customer at a future date. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since the debt is sold to the debtor
column6: Not permitted, nor is a bilaterally binding promise
column7: Permitted, if recorded in a separate deed
column8: Permitted, if the future price is a spot price
column10: Per 4/2, an agreement at origination to sell the debt to the debtor in the future, or a bilaterally binding promise, is not permitted.

column4: Ahmad owes Bank A USD 1,000 and agrees to settle it in euros. He pays half of the euro amount now and the rest next week. Is this permitted?
column5: No, the converted amount must be paid in the session
column6: Yes, if the remainder is secured by a pledge
column7: Yes, if the rate of the day is used for the whole amount
column8: Yes, since the debt itself was already due before the conversion
column10: Per 4/1/1/2(a), the substitute must be possessed in the session so that no part of the converted debt remains outstanding.

column4: Why may shares of an operating company with many receivables be sold without applying the sale of debt rules?
column5: The majority is given the ruling of the whole
column6: The debtor is deemed the possessor of the debt
column7: Appurtenance: what can't be sold alone may follow
column8: Supervening matters cannot be repelled
column10: Per the Basis for 8/1, the concept of appurtenance (taba'iya): a thing that cannot be sold independently may be sold consequentially.

column4: In a Salam, the agreed substitute asset is worth more than the Salam subject at delivery. Why does the standard's basis bar this?
column5: The creditor would profit from what he bore no risk of
column6: The substitute must be of the same kind and quality as the subject
column7: Salam may never be substituted after maturity under any rule
column8: The substitute was stipulated in the contract
column10: Per the Basis for 4/1/1/3, it would let the creditor profit without assuming risk and could become a loan yielding benefit.

column4: Bank A sells a USD 1,000 receivable to a third party for exactly USD 1,000 in cash. Why does the standard still prohibit this?
column5: The amount of the debt is unknown
column6: It involves riba al-fadl due to excess
column7: Equal amounts still involve riba al-nasi'ah
column8: The debtor did not consent to the sale
column10: Per the Basis for 5/1, unequal amounts involve riba al-fadl and riba al-nasi'ah; equal amounts still involve riba al-nasi'ah.

column4: Bank A holds Salam Sukuk and wishes to exchange them with the Salam seller, who is the debtor. Which rules govern this exchange?
column5: No debt rules, since Sukuk are securities
column6: The rules on sale of debt to a third party
column7: It is not permitted in any form
column8: The rules on sale of debt to the debtor
column10: Per 9/3/2, Salam or Istisna' Sukuk may be exchanged with the debtor following the rules of sale of debt to the debtor (4/1, 4/1/1/3).

column4: Bank A owes Company Y and directs it to collect the amount from Company X, which owes Bank A. How does the standard treat this?
column5: As a division of debt among claimants
column6: As an assignment of debt, not a sale of debt
column7: As a prohibited sale of debt for debt between the three parties
column8: As a sale of monetary debt for cash
column10: Per 5/1, an assignment of debt (Hawala) is not considered a sale of debt; see the standard on Hawala.

column4: Sukuk proceeds are used partly for Murabaha transactions and partly for tangible assets such as Ijarah assets. How is trading in these Sukuk governed?
column5: As a commingled entity, incl. the tangible ratio
column6: They trade freely, as an ongoing business
column7: They may trade only at their face value
column8: They may never be traded, as they hold debts
column10: Per 8/4, trading such Sukuk is subject to 8/2 (incl. the tangible asset ratio), provided the issuance guarantees nothing impermissible.

column4: Bank A and Bank B agree to swap their portfolios of receivables owed by their respective customers. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as a division of debt
column6: Permitted, if the portfolios are equal in value
column7: Not permitted, as a sale of debt for debt
column8: Permitted, if the customers consent
column10: Per 9/7, selling a debt to a third party for another debt owed to it by another party, e.g., swapping receivable portfolios, is not permitted.

column4: A Sukuk entity's tangible assets fall to 40% after issuance, yet trading continues while it is restored. Which maxim does the standard cite for this?
column5: Muslims act upon their conditions
column6: Contracts are valid and permitted by default unless prohibited
column7: The majority is tantamount to the whole in ruling
column8: What is overlooked in continuance is not at inception
column10: Per the Basis for 8/2/3, supervening matters cannot be repelled; what can be overlooked during continuance cannot be at inception.

column4: Ahmad borrowed USD 1,000 under a loan contract and now repays it in local currency. Which exchange rate applies?
column5: The rate on the day the loan was granted
column6: The rate prevailing on the day of settlement
column7: The rate on the loan's maturity date
column8: Any rate the two parties agree upon
column10: Per 4/1/1/2(c), discharge in another currency is at the rate on the settlement day if the debt resulted from a loan contract.

column4: Why does the standard permit a creditor to sell a debt to the debtor himself without first taking possession of it?
column5: The debt's risk is already with the creditor
column6: Debts owed by the debtor are not Ribawi
column7: Such a sale is an assignment (Hawala)
column8: The debtor is deemed to possess what he owes
column10: Per the Basis, the debtor is deemed the possessor of what he owes, like selling usurped property to the usurper already holding it.

column4: Three heirs jointly hold a single debt owed by Ahmad and agree that each will collect his own share of it. Is this permitted?
column5: No, a single debt cannot be divided among its joint creditors
column6: Yes, they may divide it in proportion to shares
column7: Only if the debt is first sold to a third party
column8: Only if Ahmad consents to the division
column10: Per 6/1, claimants in one debt may divide it among themselves in proportion to their shares, each reserving his share.

column4: Bank A sells a receivable to Company Y in a permitted form without asking the debtor; their original contract is silent on this. Is the sale valid?
column5: Yes, the debtor's consent is not required
column6: No, unless the debtor is notified first
column7: Yes, but only if the debt is secured
column8: No, the debtor must consent to any sale
column10: Per 5/6, the debtor's consent is not required for sale of the debt to a third party unless the debtor and creditor agreed otherwise.

column4: A debtor repays a currency loan at the rate of the loan date rather than the settlement day. Why does the standard reject this?
column5: It turns the loan into a Salam contract
column6: Past exchange rates are unknown to the parties
column7: It may raise or cut the debt, harming either party
column8: It breaches the debtor's right to consent
column10: Per the Basis for 4/1/1/2(c), other rates may increase the debt against deferment (harming the debtor) or reduce the creditor's right.

column4: Some debts in Bank A's securitized entity are settled, and the entity extends a new Murabaha to the same debtor. Does this count as turnover bringing it under 8/1?
column5: No; it is not turnover, and 8/2 still applies
column6: Yes, any new Murabaha counts as turnover
column7: Yes, as the debtor remains the same
column8: No, and the sale of the entity becomes void
column10: Per 8/2/4, substituting part of the assets or extending a new Murabaha to the same debtor is not turnover; 8/2 applies, not 8/1.

column4: Partners jointly own cash, tangible assets and debts. They agree that one takes the debts, another the cash and the third the assets. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted: debts can't be swapped for cash
column6: Not permitted unless the debtors consent
column7: Permitted only if each gets part of each asset
column8: Permitted by agreement among the partners
column10: Per 6/3, partners owning debts, tangible assets and cash may agree that some take debts, some cash and others tangible assets.

column4: Bank A holds a USD 1,000 receivable owed by Company X and sells it to Bank B for USD 950 in cash. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as Bank B bears the risk of collecting the debt
column6: Permitted, as the buyer is a third party
column7: Not permitted: a monetary debt can't be sold for cash
column8: Permitted, if Company X consents to the sale in writing
column10: Per 5/1, it is not permitted to sell a monetary debt against cash or for a monetary debt.

column4: Bank A sells a monetary receivable owed by Company X to Company Y in exchange for a car delivered on the spot. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if the car equals the debt
column6: Permitted, as the commodity is delivered on spot
column7: Not permitted; it can be sold only for cash
column8: Not permitted without the debtor's consent
column10: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may be sold for a commodity with spot delivery or for a usufruct or service whose delivery is ascertained.

column4: The debtor gives Bank A a unilateral binding promise to buy his debt, and the promised sale meets the rules for selling debt to the debtor. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, a unilaterally binding promise is permitted
column6: No, any promise to sell a debt is barred
column7: No, only a bilateral promise is valid
column8: Yes, but only if the promise is non-binding
column10: Per 4/2, if the rules of 4/1 are met in the promised sale, a unilaterally binding promise is permitted.

column4: Why may the seller of an entity holding debts and tangible assets not keep bearing the tangible assets' risk after the sale?
column5: It turns the sale into a Hawala between seller and buyer
column6: It shows the aim is the debts, not the assets
column7: It breaches the 50% tangible asset ratio for the entity
column8: It requires the debtors' consent
column10: Per the Basis for 8/2/1, the seller bearing the risk shows the buyer's intention is the debts, making inclusion of tangible assets superficial (shakli).

column4: In a Salam for gas, after maturity the buyer agrees to take oil instead, without this having been stipulated in the contract. What limit applies to the oil?
column5: No limit, as substitution is after maturity
column6: Its value must equal the original Salam capital
column7: Its quantity must equal the quantity of gas
column8: Its market value can't exceed the gas's at delivery
column10: Per 4/1/1/3, the substitute's market value must not exceed that of the subject of Salam at delivery time, and it must be fit as subject of Salam.

column4: Two partners hold three separate debts owed by different debtors. They agree that each will keep particular debts according to his share. Is this permitted?
column5: Only if the debtors consent to it
column6: Only if each partner takes part of every single debt
column7: Yes, multiple debts may be divided by shares
column8: No, it is a prohibited sale of debt for debt among the partners
column10: Per 6/2, claimants in multiple debts may divide them so that each reserves one debt or more based on his share.

column4: Bank A enters into a new Murabaha with a delinquent customer. What limit applies to the profit rate in the new Murabaha?
column5: It must equal the first debt's profit rate
column6: It may include compensation for the delinquency
column7: It may be raised to reflect his higher risk
column8: Not above his rate if he were not delinquent
column10: Per 4/1/3/4(d), the Institution may not compensate itself for the delinquency, and the rate may not exceed that for a non-delinquent customer.

column4: Ahmad owes Bank A 100, due today. Bank A offers to cancel it in return for a new debt of 110 owed by Ahmad in six months. What is the ruling?
column5: Prohibited as extinction of debt in debt
column6: Permitted, if the new debt is a Murabaha
column7: Permitted, if Ahmad is solvent
column8: Permitted, if Ahmad requested the extension
column10: Per 4/1/3/1, selling the debt to the debtor for a larger new debt is extinction of debt in debt (faskh al-dayn), prohibited by Shari'ah.

column4: Company Y buys a debt from Bank A and stipulates that Bank A guarantees it, with recourse for any unrecovered portion. Is this allowed?
column5: Only if the debtor was insolvent at sale
column6: No, a seller may not guarantee a sold debt
column7: Yes, the buyer may stipulate such recourse
column8: Only for debts sold to the debtor himself
column10: Per 7/4, the buyer may stipulate that the seller guarantee the debt, with recourse to the seller for the unrecovered portion.

column4: Why may early discharge of a debt in another currency not be stipulated, anticipated or customary?
column5: It would be a sale of debt to a third party
column6: It would become a deferred currency exchange
column7: It would be extinction of debt in debt
column8: It would involve excessive gharar
column10: Per the Basis for 4/1/1/2(b), such discharge would become a deferred currency exchange (sarf).

column4: Bank A sells a debt to Company Y, knowing that the debtor is insolvent, but does not tell Company Y. What right does Company Y have?
column5: A claim against the debtor's guarantor
column6: Recourse to Bank A for the full face value
column7: No right, as the risk passed upon sale
column8: The rescission option for misrepresentation
column10: Per 5/7, the buyer has khayar al-taghrir if the seller knew of the debtor's insolvency or procrastination and did not inform him.

column4: A customer owes Bank A a financing receivable. Bank A proposes using that receivable as the capital of a Salam with the same customer. Is this permitted?
column5: Yes, if the receivable has already fallen due
column6: No, a debt may not be made the Salam capital
column7: Yes, if the commodity is delivered at maturity
column8: Yes, as the money is already with the customer
column10: Per 4/1/3/2, it is not permitted to make a debt, such as cash loans or financing receivables owed by the customer, the Salam capital.

column4: Under a permitted new Murabaha, the sale proceeds are credited to the customer's account at Bank A. When may he choose to settle his first debt with them?
column5: Only after the new Murabaha matures
column6: Never, as proceeds can't settle the old debt
column7: After one working day following receipt
column8: Immediately, by automatic debit on receipt
column10: Per 4/1/3/4(c), the customer may freely dispose of the proceeds, including settling the first debt after one working day following receipt.

column4: Company X sells a debt to Company Y for a car delivered on spot, but neither party knows the amount of the debt. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, due to jahala of the amount
column6: Permitted, as the debt is established
column7: Permitted, if the debtor confirms it later
column8: Permitted, as the car is delivered on spot
column10: Per 5/5/2, lack of knowledge (jahala) of the amount of debt is excessive gharar, so the sale to a third party is not permitted.

column4: Bank A takes a car from an insolvent customer in place of his debt of 100, then sells the car back to him at 120 on deferred terms. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as the car is a real commodity and the sale a real sale
column6: Permitted, if the customer requested it
column7: Prohibited, being a form of 'Inah raising the debt
column8: Permitted, as the debtor is insolvent and Bank A took the car first
column10: Per 4/1/3/3, anything increasing the debt against longer tenure is prohibited, solvent or not, e.g., substituting a commodity and reselling it higher.

column4: Bank A securitizes its monetary receivables into tradable certificates. Against what may these certificates be traded?
column5: Other debt-based certificates
column6: Only a commodity, usufruct or service
column7: Cash at a discount to face value
column8: Cash, but only at face value
column10: Per 9/5/2, securities based on monetary debts may trade only against a commodity, usufruct or service with ascertained delivery, per 5/2.

column4: Bank A's financing contract stipulates that the customer will discharge his USD debt in local currency before its maturity. What is the ruling on this term?
column5: Permitted, if the settlement-day rate is used for the conversion
column6: Permitted, if the customer is solvent and agrees in writing
column7: Permitted, as early discharge favors the debtor
column8: Not permitted; such early discharge can't be stipulated
column10: Per 4/1/1/2(b), discharge in another currency before the due time must not be stipulated, anticipated, or a customary practice.

column4: Bank A wants to sell to a third party a debt that the alleged debtor denies, with no evidence to establish it. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted, due to excessive gharar
column6: Permitted, if the buyer accepts the risk
column7: Permitted at a deep discount for the risk
column8: Permitted, if sold for a commodity
column10: Per 5/5/1, selling a debt not established by acknowledgement or evidence involves excessive gharar and is not permitted.

column4: The tangible assets of a listed Sukuk entity fall to 25% of its asset value. What follows under the standard?
column5: Trading continues at market price while the ratio is restored
column6: They trade only under debt rules and are delisted
column7: Only new issuances of the Sukuk are restricted
column8: The Institution must buy back the Sukuk at par from all holders
column10: Per 8/2/3, below 33%, holders are notified that Sukuk are negotiable only under debt trading rules; listed Sukuk must be delisted.

column4: An investor buys shares of an operating Islamic bank whose assets are mostly Murabaha receivables. Do the sale of debt rules apply to the debts?
column5: No, the debts are ancillary to its ongoing activity
column6: Yes, since debts exceed half of its assets, as in a debt portfolio
