column7: Yes, unless tangible assets exceed one-third of its asset value
column8: Yes, so shares must trade at face value
column10: Per 8/1, an ongoing permissible entity may be sold whatever its debt ratio, as business debts are ancillary, unless it is entirely debt.

column4: A solvent customer owing Bank A asks for a new, larger Murabaha and may use its proceeds to settle the old debt. When is this permitted?
column5: If the profit rate is raised for the rollover
column6: If the Bank keeps the sale proceeds as security
column7: If it is independent financing with credit approval
column8: If the contract requires settling the old debt
column10: Per 4/1/3/4(a), the new Murabaha must be independent, not stipulated or required to settle the first debt, and given credit approval.

column4: Bank A uses a monetary debt owed to it by Company X as the capital of a Salam with Company Y for future wheat. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the wheat is precisely described
column6: Permitted, if Company X consents
column7: Permitted, as Salam allows deferred delivery
column8: Not permitted, as the wheat is deferred
column10: Per 5/2, a monetary debt may not be sold for a commodity with deferred delivery, e.g., making a third party's debt the Salam capital.

column4: How does the standard's basis characterize selling a debt to the debtor for a new, larger debt owed by him?
column5: 'Inah achieved through a third party who buys the commodity
column6: Riba al-jahiliyah: increase against deferment
column7: Riba al-fadl only, because the two amounts are unequal
column8: Gharar arising from an unknown amount of the new debt
column10: Per the Basis for 4/1/3/1, it is riba al-jahiliyah: sale of debt for a new larger debt, i.e., increase of debt against deferment.

column4: Why does the standard prohibit a bilaterally binding promise to sell a debt to the debtor?
column5: It turns the debt into Salam capital, which is not allowed
column6: It requires the debtor's consent
column7: It contains excessive gharar as to the price and the debt
column8: It is a means to achieve riba artificially
column10: Per the Basis for 4/2, a bilaterally binding promise in this form is a means to achieve riba artificially.

column4: A cash Waqf of 1,000,000 is invested and grows to 1,080,000. How is the 80,000 treated?
column5: As part of the Waqf asset itself, to be reinvested for growth
column6: As the overseer's remuneration for managing the investment
column7: As yield to be disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries
column8: As a return to the Waqif
column10: Per 2/4/13/1, any excess cash over the Waqf amount is the yield, which shall be disbursed to the Waqf beneficiaries.

column4: Which analogy does the standard use for spreading a revenue shortfall proportionally among specific beneficiaries?
column5: The 'awal reduction in inheritance shares
column6: Preference of a secured creditor
column7: The priority of a first-named heir
column8: Equal division in a partnership loss
column10: Basis 9/10/3: by analogy with the 'awal reduction of inheritance portions and with the creditors of a bankrupt.

column4: An overseer wishes to lease a Waqf shop to himself. How does the standard treat this?
column5: It is allowed at the fair rent if an expert confirms it
column6: It is allowed if he pays the full year's rent in advance
column7: It is barred, as it raises doubt of favouritism
column8: It is allowed if he informs the Waqif
column10: Per 3/8/3, the overseer is barred from favouritism or any act raising doubt of it, such as leasing Waqf assets to himself or his son.

column4: Bank A's board resolves to create a Waqf over some of its assets, subject to the approval of the supervisory authority. What is the status of this Waqf?
column5: Valid, as Waqf may be contingent upon a condition
column6: Void, since the contingency creates excessive gharar
column7: Void, as Waqf must always take effect immediately
column8: Valid only as a bequest within one-third
column10: Per 2/4/1/3, the presumption is immediate effect, but Waqf may be contingent upon a condition, e.g., the supervisory authority's approval.

column4: Which analogy supports paying for the preservation of the Waqf asset before other avenues when revenue is short?
column5: A lessor's rent is paid before the maintenance of the property
column6: A guarantor pays before the debtor
column7: A partner's capital is repaid before any profit is shared
column8: An estate pays the deceased's debts before the heirs
column10: Basis 9/10/1: by analogy, the estate gives preference to the rights of the deceased (debts, funeral costs) over the heirs' portions.

column4: The utilities of a Waqf building have been permanently cut off, making it impossible to use. What does the standard permit?
column5: Distributing the land among the beneficiaries in their shares
column6: Substituting it with a better asset of the same kind
column7: Ending the Waqf and returning the asset to the Waqif or his heirs
column8: Keeping it idle as Waqf cannot be changed
column10: Per 10/1/2/2, if utilities are suspended or usufruct is impossible, the Waqf asset may be substituted with a better asset of the same kind.

column4: Ahmad states: "I made this house a Waqf for myself and then for charitable causes." What is the status of this Waqf?
column5: Valid; the Waqif may stipulate himself as beneficiary
column6: Valid only if Ahmad is poor
column7: Void, as a Waqif cannot benefit from a Waqf he has created himself
column8: Valid only for the charitable part, the self-benefit being void
column10: Per 2/4/4/2, it is valid to stipulate that the Waqf beneficiary is the Waqif, e.g., a Waqf for himself and then for charitable causes.

column4: An overseer insists he would charge his own son full market rent for a Waqf flat. Why does the standard still bar leasing it to his son?
column5: Leases to relatives are void in all contracts under Shari'ah
column6: Human nature raises fear of favouritism to self or child
column7: A son can never be a lessee of any Waqf under any circumstance
column8: The son would become a Waqf beneficiary
column10: Basis 3/8/3: by human nature there is a fear of favouritism for himself or his child and of not choosing what is more favourable for the Waqf.

column4: Ahmad made Waqf of shares in a permissible company. The company later turned into a prohibited one. What must be done?
column5: Substitution is allowed but optional
column6: Shares are kept and income purified
column7: The shares must be substituted
column8: The Waqf ends and shares go to Ahmad
column10: Per 10/1/3, substituting Waqf assets is required if the subject turned prohibited, e.g., permissible shares that later turned prohibited.

column4: Ahmad dedicates cash as Waqf to be developed by turnover on commercial grounds, aiming at the Waqf's sustainability through its assets or their substitutes. Which type is this?
column5: Joint Waqf
column6: Private or Dynasty Waqf
column7: Specific Waqf Assets
column8: Investment Waqf
column10: Per 2/2/2/2, Investment Waqfs aim at development by turnover on commercial considerations, e.g., cash Waqf and Waqf companies.

column4: A Waqif set a sequence: orphans of Town X, then students of Town X. No orphans remain in Town X. Where does the revenue go?
column5: To the students, as the next body in the sequence
column6: To orphans of any similar town, as the Waqif's first choice
column7: To general charitable causes chosen by the overseer
column8: Back to the Waqif's heirs
column10: Per 10/2, on discontinuation of a beneficiary body, the Waqf goes to the next body if the Waqif arranged a sequence; otherwise to similar bodies.

column4: An overseer plans a 30-year Ijarah of Waqf land. What does the standard prefer for such a long-term lease?
column5: A rent below the fair rate, to secure a long-term tenant
column6: Variable rent linked to a benchmark, at least fair
column7: A fixed rent set once for all 30 years, to give the tenant certainty
column8: Full rent for 30 years paid in advance
column10: Per 8/4, long Ijarah needs evident interest; in long-term Ijarah, a variable rent linked to a known benchmark is preferable, at least the fair rate.

column4: Ten years ago Ahmad created a cash Waqf of 100,000. Inflation has since halved its purchasing power. What is the Waqf asset now?
column5: The inflation-adjusted equivalent of 100,000
column6: Nothing, as the Waqf ended when value eroded
column7: Whatever amount the overseer re-values it at
column8: The nominal 100,000 named at creation
column10: Per 2/4/13/4, the money nominated at creation is the Waqf asset; change in purchasing power has no influence on the cash Waqf value.

column4: Company X is a juridical person and wishes to create a Waqf over one of its buildings. What does the standard require for the creation?
column5: A court order authorizing the Waqf
column6: The written consent of all of the company's creditors and lenders
column7: A resolution of the owners or whoever has that authority
column8: The acceptance of the intended Waqf beneficiaries and the overseer
column10: Per 2/4/3/2, a juridical person's Waqf is created by a resolution from the owners or those with authority, provided it does not contravene laws.

column4: A cash Waqf is held in a foreign currency exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations. What does the standard direct?
column5: Use any market hedging tool available, whether or not Shari'ah compliant
column6: Leave it unhedged, as a Waqf bears its own exchange-rate risk
column7: Convert the whole Waqf into real estate
column8: Use Shari'ah compliant hedging to protect the principal
column10: Per 2/4/13/5, Shari'ah compliant hedging should be followed to protect the cash Waqf principal and hedge currency fluctuation risk (see SS 45).

column4: Ahmad holds interest-bearing bonds and makes them a Waqf for general charitable causes. When is this Waqf valid?
column5: Always, because the yield goes to charity
column6: If the bonds are substituted with assets of permissible yield
column7: Never, under any circumstances
column8: Always, provided the interest received is paid to the poor
column10: Per 2/4/10, Waqf over assets of prohibited yield (e.g., bonds) is valid if those assets are substituted with assets of permissible yield.

column4: An overseer prefers to redirect revenue of a Waqf for orphans to a mosque, as he thinks it worthier. No necessity exists. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, since a mosque is also a charitable cause
column6: Permitted if the Waqif's heirs agree
column7: Not permitted without necessity and authority approval
column8: Permitted at the overseer's discretion
column10: Per 9/3, the avenue of Waqf disposal may not be changed unless there is a necessity, and after approval from the relevant authorities.

column4: Ahmad asks why he may make a Waqf on himself. Which basis does the standard give?
column5: Analogy with charity given to oneself
column6: The Waqif retains ownership of the asset
column7: Analogy with a sale to oneself
column8: Necessity of the Waqif's maintenance
column10: Basis 2/4/4/2: self-Waqf rests on analogy with charity to self and hadiths such as "Start with yourself and spend it on yourself".

column4: A Waqf's revenue cannot cover all of: preserving the Waqf asset, employees' dues and beneficiaries' shares. Which is paid first?
column5: The relevant parties dealing with the Waqf
column6: Preservation of the Waqf asset
column7: The beneficiaries' shares
column8: The administrative employees' dues
column10: Per 9/10/1, in competition of avenues, preservation of the Waqf asset comes first, then obligations to employees and parties, then per the Waqif.

column4: Ahmad created a Waqf for his grandchildren. Years later, none of the designated beneficiaries exist any more. What happens to the Waqf?
column5: It turns into a Charitable Waqf
column6: It ends and the asset returns to Ahmad's heirs
column7: It passes into the ownership of the overseer
column8: It becomes void from the time of its creation
column10: Per 2/2/1/2, if the designated beneficiaries of a Private (Dynasty) Waqf no longer exist, it turns into a Charitable Waqf.

column4: An overseer manages two Waqfs whose revenues go to the same avenue of disposal. May he commingle their incomes?
column5: Yes, if both Waqifs are still alive
column6: Yes, and the two Waqfs then become a single Waqf in law
column7: Yes, though each Waqf remains independent financially
column8: No, incomes of different Waqfs may never be mixed in one account
column10: Per 9/9, incomes of Waqfs with the same avenue may be intermingled; each Waqf remains independent in financial status, overseer fees, etc.

column4: To which case does the standard draw an analogy when it prevents lending Waqf funds?
column5: Lending a deposit held in trust
column6: Lending from Zakah funds
column7: Lending funds of a Mudarabah
column8: Lending the funds of minors
column10: Basis 7: the prohibition rests on analogy with not lending minors' funds, as lending may cause loss, unless lending is more secure.

column4: Why does the standard require relevant authority approval for substituting tangible Waqf assets?
column5: To protect the Waqf under the state's public guardianship
column6: To allow the state to tax the substitution and collect a fee
column7: Because the state owns the legal title of all tangible Waqf assets
column8: Because overseers lack legal personality
column10: Basis 10/1/5/5: authority permission protects the Waqf, supports its interest, and establishes the public guardianship of the state on Waqfs.

column4: A Waqf building is destroyed by an earthquake. The overseer had managed it properly with no negligence or breach. Is he liable?
column5: Yes, as a guarantor of the Waqf assets even without any breach
column6: Yes, for half of the loss caused by the earthquake
column7: Yes, unless the building was insured against earthquakes
column8: No, as he holds the Waqf in a fiduciary capacity
column10: Per 3/7/5, the overseer has a fiduciary capacity and is not liable except for misconduct, negligence or breach of the Waqif's conditions.

column4: An overseer leased a Waqf asset at a flagrantly low rent, with no preferred interest. What follows?
column5: The lease stands, and nothing further is due from anyone, as the overseer had discretion
column6: The lessee alone pays a penalty to the Waqf equal to a year's rent
column7: He pays the difference and seeks termination unless rent rises
column8: The Waqif must compensate the beneficiaries
column10: Per 8/5, the overseer is liable for the difference and should demand termination unless the lessee accepts the increase.

column4: Ahmad makes Waqf of specific Sukuk for a period equal to their term. At cancellation, the issuer repays the principal amount (not a return). Who gets it?
column5: The Waqf, to be reinvested in new Sukuk
column6: Ahmad, the Waqif
column7: The Waqif and beneficiaries equally
column8: The Waqf beneficiaries as revenue
column10: Per 2/4/15/1(b)(3), if the Waqf period equals the Sukuk term, the amount paid at cancellation is for the Waqif, unless paid as a return (then revenue).

column4: A perpetual Waqf building is totally destroyed and nothing of the Waqf asset remains. What happens to the Waqf?
column5: It continues, as perpetual Waqf never ends
column6: The Waqif must rebuild it
column7: It passes to the overseer's liability
column8: It ends with the total loss of the Waqf asset
column10: Per 11, Waqf ends with the total loss of the Waqf asset, whether the Waqf is temporary, restricted, or perpetual.

column4: Ahmad bought a shop with an option to rescind held by a third party, then made the shop Waqf. The option holder later refused to authorize it. What is the result?
column5: The Waqf is null and void from the start
column6: The Waqf turns into a bequest of one-third
column7: The Waqf continues over the price Ahmad paid
column8: The Waqf is void only from the date of refusal
column10: Per 2/4/5/2, such a Waqf depends on the option holder's authorization; if it is not granted, the Waqf is deemed null and void from the start.

column4: Shares held as Waqf turn prohibited. Which hadith does the standard cite for requiring their substitution?
column5: "Muslims are held to their conditions, except those that make lawful unlawful"
column6: "Allah is Good, and He accepts only that which is good"
column7: "Start with yourself and spend on yourself, then on your family"
column8: "If you wish, hold the property as a Waqf and give its fruit as charity"
column10: Basis 10/1/3: a Waqf asset must be permissible, and the Prophet said Allah is Good and accepts only what is good; also by analogy with one repenting.

column4: An overseer appointed by the Waqif breached the conditions of the Waqf deed. Who else may dismiss him?
column5: Only the Waqif who appointed him
column6: The majority of the beneficiaries
column7: The judge or the relevant authority
column8: No one, as he was appointed by the Waqif
column10: Per 3/10/3, for misconduct, negligence or breach, the judge or relevant authority may dismiss the overseer, whoever appointed him.

column4: Fair experts value a proposed substitute asset as generating lower revenue than the Waqf asset it would replace. May the substitution proceed?
column5: Yes, if the overseer deems it wise in the Waqf's interest
column6: Yes, with the beneficiaries' consent
column7: Yes, if its market value is higher than the Waqf asset's
column8: No, the substitute may not be lower in revenue
column10: Per 10/1/5/3, the substituting asset shall not be less in value or lower in revenue than the substituted asset per fair experts.

column4: Which evidence does the standard cite for the validity of a Waqf created by a non-Muslim?
column5: The Prophet called Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām's pre-Islam charity a virtue
column6: Umar's Waqf of his land in Khaybar, on the Prophet's advice to him
column7: The Waqf of Banū Najjār's orchard
column8: Khālid keeping his armour and weapons for Allah's Cause
column10: Basis 2/4/3/5: the Prophet called Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām's charity in ignorance a virtue, showing a disbeliever's donation is valid.

column4: An investment Waqf company seeks Shari'ah compliant financing to expand its commercial operations. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted unless the Waqf asset is in ruin or has no revenue
column6: Permitted, if its revenues can settle the obligations
column7: Permitted only for necessary maintenance of the existing assets
column8: Not permitted without the Waqif's stipulation
column10: Per 5/2, investment Waqfs may incur debt for development under commercial practice, considering the Waqf's interest and adequacy of revenues.

column4: Why does the standard make the Waqf of a person interdicted for debt depend on his creditors' permission?
column5: Because the creditors own his assets
column6: Because debt removes legal capacity
column7: To repel harm from the creditors
column8: Because Waqf of debtors is a bequest
column10: The basis for suspending Waqf by one interdicted for debt until creditors permit it is to repel harm from the creditors.

column4: Ahmad acquired a building through prohibited means. He makes it a Waqf for general charitable causes and plans to live in one of its flats. Is that allowed?
column5: Yes, up to one-third of its usufruct
column6: No, he may not benefit from this Waqf in any manner
column7: Yes, since a Waqif may be his own beneficiary under the Waqf deed
column8: Yes, if he pays fair rent to the Waqf for the flat he lives in
column10: Per 2/4/9, one holding assets taken by prohibited means may make them Waqf for general charitable causes, but may not benefit from it in any manner.

column4: A Waqf deed over a warehouse says nothing about the duration of the Waqf. How long does the Waqf last?
column5: It is void for failing to specify a term
column6: It lasts only for the beneficiaries' lifetime, then reverts to the Waqif
column7: It is perpetual, as that is the initial presumption
column8: It lasts only for the Waqif's lifetime, then returns to his heirs
column10: Per 2/4/1/5, the initial presumption is that Waqf is perpetual; it is limited to a period only if the Waqif stipulates so.

column4: An overseer leases a Waqf below fair rent with no preferred interest. Which maxim does the standard invoke against this?
column5: An overseer's act depends on the Waqf's interest
column6: Certainty is not removed by doubt, so the first state remains
column7: Custom is a decisive authority where no text exists
column8: Hardship begets facility, so rules are relaxed in difficulty
column10: Basis 8/5: inna taṣarruf al-nāẓir alā al-waqf manuwṭ bi al-maṣlaḥa, the overseer's disposition of Waqf is contingent upon its interest.

column4: During the waiting period before distribution to beneficiaries, an overseer invests Waqf revenue. When is this permitted?
column5: Only in the overseer's own name
column6: Never; revenue must be paid out to beneficiaries at once
column7: Only if the Waqif expressly stipulated it in the Waqf deed
column8: When it does not affect distribution to beneficiaries
column10: Per 8/1, Waqf revenue may be invested if the Waqif stipulates it or during the waiting period, where it does not affect distribution.

column4: Ahmad declares his orchard a Waqf but does not name any beneficiary. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid, and its revenue goes to Ahmad's heirs by default
column6: Valid; the overseer or court directs it to charity
column7: Suspended until Ahmad names a beneficiary
column8: Void, as the beneficiary must be specified when the Waqf is created
column10: Per 2/4/1/6, an unrestricted Waqf is valid and is made available for charitable causes as deemed fit by the overseer or the court.

column4: An overseer used cash Waqf to buy an apartment. A more beneficial investment now arises. What may he do?
column5: Nothing; the apartment has become the Waqf asset and cannot be sold
column6: Sell it only if its usufruct is totally lost or the apartment destroyed
column7: Sell it, but only with the heirs' consent
column8: Sell it; the cash amount remains the Waqf asset
column10: Per 2/4/13/3, assets bought with cash Waqf are not the Waqf asset; they may be sold for a better investment, and the Waqf asset remains the cash.

column4: An overseer wants the Waqf to guarantee a supplier's debt. The Waqif did not stipulate it, it is not a Waqf purpose, and no authority permitted it. Is it allowed?
column5: Yes, if the supplier is reliable
column6: Yes, if the guarantee is for a short term
column7: No, the Waqf cannot guarantee it
column8: Yes, if the overseer bears the risk
column10: Per 7, Waqf cannot guarantee third-party debts unless stipulated by the Waqif, among its purposes, or in its interest with authority permission.

column4: A Waqif from a past century used an ambiguous term in his conditions. How should the overseer interpret it?
column5: By the customs of the Waqif's own time and place
column6: By its literal dictionary meaning, ignoring custom and usage
column7: As the beneficiaries prefer
column8: In light of today's customs in the place where the overseer lives
column10: Per 2/6/1, each Waqif's stipulated conditions must be read in light of the prevailing customs in his time and place.

column4: Ahmad argues he may take back his Waqf since Waqf is a voluntary act. Which evidence does the standard cite for its binding nature?
column5: Analogy with a bequest, which the testator may revoke at any time
column6: Consensus that gifts are revocable before Qabd, as with any donation
column7: The maxim that harm is to be removed, so owners may retract
column8: Umar's Khaybar land: not to be sold, gifted or inherited
column10: Basis 2/3: Umar (RA) gave the land in charity on condition it not be sold, gifted or inherited, showing the Waqf's binding nature.

column4: A Waqf's beneficiaries are three named persons. With authority permission and a preferred interest, the overseer wants to redeploy some revenue in the Waqf asset. What else is needed?
column5: The consent of the three beneficiaries
column6: Nothing further; the permission suffices
column7: A court judgment for each redeployment
column8: The Waqif's heirs' approval
column10: Per 9/6, if the Waqf beneficiaries are specific parties, their consent is required for redeploying revenue in the Waqf asset.

column4: Company X, a Shari'ah compliant trading company, is a Waqf. Its managers sell inventory and buy new stock in normal trading. Is this permitted?
column5: No, Waqf assets may never be disposed of
column6: Only for its real estate assets
column7: Yes, asset turnover is allowed under commercial norms
column8: Only with the relevant authority's approval each time
column10: Per 2/4/14/1, Waqf companies are investment Waqfs, and their asset turnover is allowed under the regulations and commercial norms.

column4: A Waqf deed names a committee, rather than one individual, as the overseer (nāẓir). What is the ruling?
column5: Invalid; the overseer must be an individual
column6: Valid; the overseer may be a group or a committee
column7: Valid only if a judge approves each member
column8: Valid only if the Waqif chairs the committee
column10: Per 3/1, the overseer may be an individual, a group of people, a committee, a ministry or the like.

column4: Bilal is the beneficiary of a Waqf house. The Waqif set no condition on how Bilal benefits. Bilal leases the house to a third party. Is this allowed?
column5: Only if the lessee is also poor
column6: Only with the prior approval of the relevant authority each time
column7: No, he must live in the house personally
column8: Yes, he may benefit through a third party, even by leasing
column10: Per 2/6/5, the beneficiary may benefit personally or through a third party, even by leasing, unless the Waqif stipulated personal benefit only.

column4: Why does the standard prevent pledging tangible Waqf assets?
column5: A pledge allows sale to repay debt; Waqf assets can't be sold
column6: Waqf assets have no market value so cannot secure a debt
column7: The overseer lacks any power to contract on behalf of the Waqf
column8: Pledges are prohibited in all donation contracts, including Waqf
column10: Basis 6/1: a pledge secures debt with an asset that may be sold to discharge it, whereas sale of the Waqf asset is not permitted.

column4: Which evidence does the standard cite for the validity of a Waqf of movable assets, such as weapons or equipment?
column5: Umar's Waqf of his land in Khaybar, a fixed real property
column6: Banū Najjār's Waqf of their orchard, offered to the Prophet
column7: Khālid kept his armour and weapons for Allah's Cause
column8: Sa'd's orchard given on his mother's behalf
column10: Basis 2/4/7: the Prophet said Khālid kept his armour and weapons for Allah's Cause; this is also the majority view and IIFA Res. 181.

column4: Which evidence does the standard cite for Waqf over a common share of an asset?
column5: Sa'd's orchard given on behalf of his deceased mother
column6: Banū Najjār's Waqf of their jointly owned orchard
column7: Khālid's armour and weapons kept for Allah's Cause
column8: Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām's charity during the pre-Islam period
column10: Basis 2/4/11: Banū Najjār instituted Waqf over an orchard they owned as a common share; Umar also made Waqf of shares in Khaybar.

column4: Company X wants to create a Waqf over its educational website and a set of digital applications. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if attached to real estate
column6: Not permitted; only real estate may be Waqf
column7: Permitted, as Waqf of movable assets is valid
column8: Permitted only as a temporary Waqf
column10: Per 2/4/7, it is permitted to create Waqf of movable assets such as vehicles, machinery, websites and digital applications.

column4: An overseer seeks financing to add a luxury wing to a tangible Waqf building. It would add benefit but is not essential. Neither the Waqif nor the authorities approved. Is it allowed?
column5: Yes, since it serves the Waqf's interest
column6: Yes, if the beneficiaries consent
column7: Yes, if the profit rate is fair
column8: No, as it is not for an essential purpose
column10: Per 5/1, debt against tangible Waqf for non-essential purposes is not permitted, even if beneficial, unless stipulated by the Waqif or authorized.

column4: An overseer appointed by the Waqif wishes to step down. What is the ruling?
column5: He may only with a court's approval after showing a valid excuse
column6: He may, with reasonable notice to the Waqif or authorities
column7: He cannot, since he was appointed by the Waqif himself and accepted
column8: He may only after finding a replacement
column10: Per 3/10/1, the overseer can dismiss himself, even if appointed by the Waqif, and should inform the Waqif or the authorities within a reasonable period.

column4: A Waqf's revenue this year is less than the overseer's remuneration, and the roof urgently needs repair. What is the correct treatment?
column5: Repair first; unpaid remuneration stays a liability on the Waqf
column6: The unpaid remuneration is forfeited
column7: Pay the overseer's remuneration first and defer the repair
column8: The Waqif must pay the shortfall personally
column10: Per 3/9/5, priority goes to maintenance and necessary expenses; the outstanding remuneration remains a liability against the Waqf.

column4: Which maxim does the standard cite on commingling Waqf incomes while observing each Waqf's allocation?
column5: Certainty is not removed by doubt, so the first state remains
column6: Hardship begets facility, so rules are relaxed in difficulty
column7: Repulsion of harm precedes acquisition of interest
column8: Custom is a decisive authority in matters without a text
column10: Basis 9/9: allocation must be observed if ignoring it wastes a specified Waqf, per the maxim daf' al-mafsada muqaddam alā jalab al-maslaḥa.

column4: While suffering from a terminal illness, Ahmad creates a Waqf over his apartment building. How is this Waqf treated?
column5: It is a Joint Waqf with his heirs
column6: It is deemed to be a bequest
column7: It is void for lack of legal capacity
column8: It is a perpetual Waqf binding immediately
column10: Per 2/4/3/4, Waqf during terminal illness is deemed to be a bequest.

column4: A Waqf lacks funds to repair its leased building. The lessee offers to carry out the repairs. What may the overseer do?
column5: Allow it only as a donation by the lessee
column6: Allow it, and transfer part of the building's ownership to him
column7: Refuse, as lessees may not repair Waqf assets
column8: Allow it; the lessee has priority to remain as lessee until he recovers his debt
column10: Per 4/3, if funds are insufficient, the overseer may allow the lessee to repair, and the lessee has priority to remain until he recovers his debt.

column4: Ahmad pledged his land to Bank A, then made the land a Waqf. A year later he settled the debt in full. From when is the Waqf enforceable?
column5: From the time of its creation
column6: From the date Bank A releases its title
column7: From the date the debt was settled
column8: It is not enforceable; it must be re-created
column10: Per 2/4/5/4, Waqf by the pledgor is valid; once enforced (e.g., by settlement of the debt), its enforceability is from the time of its creation.

column4: A financier and a Waqf develop Waqf land via Diminishing Musharaka ending in transfer of the buildings to the Waqf. What is the status of the land?
column5: It becomes jointly owned with the financier in proportion to the funds
column6: It is not part of the Musharaka; building rents are shared
column7: It is pledged to secure the financier's share
column8: It is sold to the financier and leased back to the Waqf for the term
column10: Per 8/6/2, the Waqf land is not the subject of Musharaka; building rental revenues are shared until the Waqf owns all the buildings.

column4: After meeting the Waqf's needs and the avenues set by the Waqif, revenue remains. What may be done with it?
column5: Invest it for the Waqf or give it to similar charities
column6: Add it to the overseer's remuneration as a performance incentive
column7: Return it to the Waqif or his heirs as the owner of the surplus
column8: Keep it idle until the Waqf ends
column10: Per 9/4, surplus revenue is invested for the Waqf, or disbursed in charitable causes similar to the Waqif's; otherwise to general charitable causes.

column4: A Waqif did not specify the overseer's remuneration, and the relevant authorities have set none. What is the overseer entitled to?
column5: A fixed 10% of the Waqf asset
column6: Nothing, as he is presumed a volunteer
column7: Whatever the beneficiaries agree to pay
column8: Remuneration at the prevailing market rate
column10: Per 3/9/2, absent the Waqif's specification and any authority's determination, the overseer receives remuneration at the prevailing market rate.

column4: In a Waqf for his children, Ahmad gives a larger share to his divorced daughter and his son with special needs. Is this permitted?
column5: No, all children must receive equal shares
column6: Only with the consent of his other children
column7: Yes, as there is a valid reason for the increase
column8: Only if done through a bequest of one-third
column10: Per 2/4/4/5, the Waqif may single out some children or increase their shares for a valid reason, e.g., divorcees or people with special needs.

column4: Why does the standard accept a Waqf asset that is not yet known but will become known?
column5: Gharar is allowed in all contracts
column6: Waqf is a sale, which requires later disclosure of the asset
column7: The overseer can fix the asset at will after the Waqf is created
column8: Ignorance is absolved in gift contracts, and Waqf is one
column10: Basis 2/4/5/1(a): ignorance can be absolved in gift contracts, and Waqf is one of the gift contracts.

column4: Ahmad's debts exceed the value of his assets, though no bankruptcy or interdiction ruling was issued. He creates a Waqf over his house. What is the ruling?
column5: It is valid, since no interdiction ruling was ever issued against him
column6: It is contingent upon the authorization of his creditors
column7: It is not concluded at all, like a prodigal's Waqf
column8: It is valid but treated as a bequest limited to one third
column10: Per 2/4/3/3, Waqf by one interdicted for debt depends on creditors' authorization; the same applies if debts exceed assets without a ruling.

column4: Ahmad leases a building for five years. The lessor has prohibited subleasing. Ahmad then creates a Waqf of the building's usufructs. What is the ruling?
column5: Not valid, as the lessor prevents him from subleasing
column6: Valid if the Waqf is shorter than five years
column7: Valid, as Ahmad owns the usufructs of the building during the lease
column8: Valid if the beneficiaries pay the rent to the lessor
column10: Per 2/4/12, a lessee may make Waqf of usufructs only if the lessor does not prevent subleasing and the Waqf term is not longer than the lease.

column4: An overseer records the Waqf's income and expenses inside the general ledger of his own trading company. What does the standard require?
column5: Nothing, if the totals are disclosed yearly
column6: Only an annual report to the beneficiaries
column7: Waqf accounts must be prepared separately
column8: Nothing, as the overseer owns the revenue
column10: Per 3/6/7, the overseer must prepare the accounts of Waqf separate from other accounts, under prevailing accounting principles.

column4: Ahmad made a perpetual Waqf of investment Sukuk. The Sukuk are now cancelled (redeemed). What happens to the cancellation proceeds?
column5: They are distributed to the beneficiaries as Waqf revenue at once
column6: They are reinvested in other Sukuk, units or income assets
column7: The Waqf ends upon the cancellation
column8: They are returned to Ahmad or to his heirs after redemption
column10: Per 2/4/15/1(a), on cancellation of perpetual Waqf Sukuk or fund units, the proceeds are reinvested in other Sukuk, fund units or revenue assets.

column4: A Waqf beneficiary owes an amount to the Waqf and delays payment. The overseer purports to waive it. Per the Shari'ah basis, whose debtor is the beneficiary?
column5: The overseer's, so he may waive it at his own discretion
column6: The Waqif's, so only he may waive it, and not the overseer
column7: No one's, as beneficiaries owe nothing
column8: The Waqf's, so the overseer cannot discharge him
column10: Basis 2/4/2: the beneficiary is the Waqf's debtor, not the overseer's, as the overseer cannot discharge the debtor from the debt.

column4: In his charitable Waqf, Ahmad stipulates that revenue goes first to the poor among his progeny, and the remainder to charitable causes. What is the ruling?
column5: Void, as it turns the Waqf into a Private Waqf
column6: Valid only if no other poor persons exist
column7: Valid, and the condition must be complied with
column8: Void, as charitable Waqf excludes relatives
column10: Per 2/6/3, the Waqif may stipulate that charitable Waqf revenue be disbursed first to the poor from his progeny, then to charitable causes.

column4: A donor gives cash to a Waqf as a gift, without intending it to be a Waqf. How is the cash treated?
column5: Owned by the Waqf, but not recognized as a Waqf asset
column6: Returned to the donor if not used within the financial year
column7: Treated as a Waqf asset in all cases, whatever the donor intended
column8: Treated as the overseer's property
column10: Per 9/5/3, if the donor intended other than Waqf (e.g., gift), the asset is owned by the Waqf but is not recognized as a Waqf asset.

column4: An overseer lets his friend, who is not a Waqf beneficiary, use a Waqf flat for free for a year. What is the consequence?
column5: It is allowed as a charitable act within the overseer's discretion
column6: Prohibited; the overseer is liable for fair rent
column7: It is allowed if the friend is poor and the use is temporary
column8: It is allowed for short periods without liability
column10: Per 3/8/4, lending the Waqf asset for no consideration to a non-beneficiary is barred, and the overseer is liable for the fair rent.

column4: A Waqf is created to fund a shop that sells alcohol. What must happen under the standard?
column5: It stands if the profits go only to the poor
column6: It stands unchanged, since Waqf is binding once it is created
column7: Its purpose must be changed to a Shari'ah compliant one
column8: It is void and the asset returns to the Waqif or his heirs
column10: Per 2/4/1/7, Waqf for a Shari'ah non-compliant purpose is prohibited; if created, its purpose must be changed to a Shari'ah compliant one.

column4: A Waqf consultant is asked which topic the Waqf standard leaves out, despite its semblance to Waqf in certain aspects. Which one is it?
column5: Detailed rulings of irṣād (state endowment)
column6: Conditions of each constituting element of Waqf
column7: Rulings on Waqf overseership and its management
column8: Means by which the Institution invests Waqf sources
column10: Per the Scope (1), the standard deals neither with detailed rulings of dynasty Waqf nor with irṣād (state endowment) or financial trust.

column4: On what basis does the standard hold that a change in purchasing power does not affect the value of a cash Waqf?
column5: Analogy with Murabahah deferred prices
column6: The Waqif's presumed intention
column7: Custom in currency markets
column8: Analogy with cash loans
column10: Basis 2/4/13/4: by analogy upon such assets not being affected in cash loans.

column4: A tangible Waqf building has no revenue to pay its utility bills and employees' dues. May the Waqf incur debt for this?
column5: Yes, but only by borrowing from the Waqf beneficiaries
column6: No, Waqf may never incur debt
column7: Yes, via Shari'ah compliant financing at a fair profit rate
column8: Yes, by pledging the building
column10: Per 5/1, tangible Waqf may incur Shari'ah compliant debt at a fair rate for necessary costs, e.g., fees, utility bills and employees' dues.

column4: Why is a Waqf valid even if the Waqif names no avenue of disposal?
column5: By analogy with absolute charity, vows and sacrifices
column6: Because the court becomes the owner of the unallocated asset
column7: Because Waqf requires no Waqif intention
column8: Because the overseer is the true beneficiary of the unnamed Waqf
column10: Basis 2/4/1/6: Waqf is alienation to seek Allah's pleasure; by analogy with absolute charity, vows, sacrifices and bequest, it is valid.

column4: A scholar objects that a Waqf deferred to a future date involves gharar. How does the standard's Shari'ah basis answer this?
column5: Gharar is lifted by registering the deed with the authorities
column6: Gharar has no effect in donation contracts like Waqf
column7: Deferral to a known date removes all gharar from the contract
column8: Gharar is accepted when the Waqif is wealthy
column10: Basis 2/4/1/3: the cause for barring suspension or deferral is gharar, which is non-effective in donation contracts such as Waqf.

column4: Ahmad makes a temporary Waqf of units in an investment fund. The deed does not say whether the Waqf is of the units or of their value. What is the Waqf asset?
column5: The value of the units at creation
column6: The periodic distributions only
column7: The fund's underlying assets
column8: Those particular fund units
column10: Per 2/4/15/1(b), the presumption is that the Waqf asset is those particular Sukuk or units, unless the Waqif stipulated that it is for the value.

column4: Ahmad makes Waqf of his shares in Company X. The company's Memorandum of Association restricts share transfers. How is the Memorandum treated?
column5: As irrelevant, since the Waqf rules override any company restrictions
column6: As overriding Shari'ah rulings on Waqf where they conflict
column7: As conditions of the Waqif, unless contrary to Shari'ah
column8: As binding on the overseer personally only
column10: Per 2/4/14/4, upon Waqf of shares, the company's Memorandum and legal framework are deemed conditions of the Waqif unless they violate Shari'ah.

column4: Ahmad created a Waqf over his shop last month. He now regrets it and wants the shop back. What is the ruling?
column5: He may resile, as Waqf is only a recommended act
column6: He may resile until the beneficiaries take possession
column7: He may resile if he compensates the beneficiaries
column8: He cannot resile, as Waqf binds him from its creation
column10: Per 2/3, Waqf is binding upon the Waqif from the instance of its creation, and he cannot resile from it.

column4: Shares held as Waqf rise in market value from 10 to 15 per share. How is the increase classified?
column5: As profit due to the overseer
column6: As a capital gain on the Waqf asset
column7: As revenue to be paid to beneficiaries
column8: As a gain returned to the Waqif
column10: Per 2/4/14/2, an increase in the market value of Waqf shares constitutes a capital gain on the Waqf asset and not revenue.

column4: Ahmad stipulated that his building is Waqf for ten years only. The ten years have now expired. What happens to the building?
column5: It returns to Ahmad or, if he died, to his heirs
column6: It remains Waqf, as Waqf is perpetual
column7: It is sold and the price is given to the poor
column8: It goes to general charitable causes
column10: Per 2/4/1/5, Waqf may be limited to a period if stipulated; upon maturity of the term, the asset returns to the original owner or his heirs.

column4: Ahmad, who has no grandchildren yet, creates a Waqf for his future grandchildren. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid only once the first grandchild is born
column6: Void, since the beneficiaries do not yet exist at the time of creation
column7: Valid only if it is converted into a Charitable Waqf at once
column8: Valid; a beneficiary need not exist at creation
column10: Per 2/4/4/4, it is not required that a Waqf beneficiary exists at the time of creation of the Waqf.

column4: A Waqf deed stipulates that the overseers may never be dismissed under any circumstances. What is the effect of this condition?
column5: It is valid unless the overseer is negligent
column6: The condition is void, but the Waqf remains valid
column7: The condition is valid and binding
column8: The whole Waqf is void because of it
column10: Per 2/6/4, a condition prejudicing the Waqf is void while the Waqf remains valid; e.g., stipulating non-dismissal of overseers in all cases.

column4: Ahmad makes Waqf of his current account balance held at Bank A. What is the ruling?
column5: Valid only after he withdraws the balance in physical cash
column6: Valid only if converted into real estate
column7: Valid, even though the balance is a debt owed by the bank
column8: Invalid, as a debt cannot be a Waqf asset
column10: Per 2/4/13/1, Waqf over cash is permitted even if it is an outstanding debt, e.g., current account balances.

column4: Ahmad's Waqf deed does not reserve a right to dismiss the overseer. The overseer has been negligent. May Ahmad dismiss him?
column5: Yes, negligence is a ground for the Waqif to dismiss
column6: No, only a judge may dismiss him, whatever the deed provides
column7: No, an overseer once appointed is permanent
column8: No, as the deed did not reserve that right to the Waqif
column10: Per 3/10/2, the Waqif may dismiss the overseer if so stipulated, if dismissal serves the Waqf, or if the overseer committed misconduct or negligence.

column4: Which report supports allocating a Waqf to some children, such as divorced daughters, for a valid purpose?
column5: Sa'd's orchard given for his mother
column6: Uthmān's Waqf of the well of Rūma for all Muslims
column7: Al-Zubayr's Waqf of houses for his divorced daughters
column8: Umar's Waqf of his Khaybar land for the poor and relatives
column10: Basis 2/4/4/5: al-Zubayr (RA) held his houses in charity for use by his divorced daughters, ending if a daughter remarried.

column4: Ahmad creates a Waqf over the yet-to-be-declared dividends on shares he holds in Company X. Is this a valid Waqf asset?
column5: No, due to gharar in the dividend amount
column6: Yes, as it is appurtenant to an asset he owns
column7: No, since the dividends are not yet owned
column8: Only once the dividends are declared and paid
column10: Per 2/4/5/1(b), the Waqf asset may be appurtenant to an asset owned by the Waqif, e.g., yet-to-be-declared dividends on his shares.

column4: An overseer wants to substitute a tangible Waqf building. Which approval is required?
column5: The authority's approval or a valid Shari'ah pronouncement
column6: Only the beneficiaries' approval, given by a majority vote
column7: The approval of the Waqif's heirs and the overseer together
column8: Only the overseer's own assessment
column10: Per 10/1/5/5, substitution of tangible Waqf assets should be per the relevant authority's approval, if any, or a valid Shari'ah pronouncement.

column4: A candidate for a Waqf overseership board is highly competent and sane but lacks moral probity ('adālah). Is he eligible?
column5: Yes, as a board member rather than as a sole overseer
column6: Yes, since competence is the only criterion for an overseer
column7: Yes, if the Waqif approves him
column8: No, moral probity is one of the eligibility criteria
column10: Per 3/5, the eligibility criteria of the overseer, as an individual or board member, are moral probity, sanity, discretion and competence.

column4: Ahmad declares his farm a Waqf to take effect upon his death. The farm equals half of his estate. How is this treated?
column5: As a binding Waqf from the date of the declaration
column6: As a void Waqf, since it depends on death
column7: As a bequest that cannot exceed one-third of his estate
column8: As a valid Waqf over the whole farm upon his death
column10: Per 2/4/1/4, a Waqf contingent upon the Waqif's death is a bequest; it takes effect upon death and shall not exceed one-third of his estate.

column4: Which reasoning supports the standard's acceptance of a Waqf limited by time?
column5: Perpetual Waqf is disliked in Shari'ah, so only temporary is valid
column6: Ownership cannot be relinquished forever
column7: A temporary Waqf is in fact a lease of the asset to the beneficiaries
column8: General Waqf texts cover perpetual and temporary Waqf
column10: Basis 2/4/1/5: some Waqf texts are general, applying to perpetual and temporary Waqf; Waqf is a donation whose scope is broadened.

column4: Under the standard, how is Waqf defined?
column5: Transfer of an asset's ownership to the poor for no price
column6: Appropriation of an asset and donating its benefit
column7: Donating an asset's ownership while the donor keeps its benefit
column8: Lending an asset for no consideration for a fixed period
column10: Per 2/1, Waqf is the appropriation (allocation for a particular purpose) of an asset and donating its benefit.

column4: Ahmad makes Waqf of his 30% common share in a building that is leased to tenants. What is the Waqf entitled to?
column5: Its share of the rent from the building
column6: Nothing until the building is divided
column7: Nothing, as the lease ends upon the Waqf
column8: The whole rent, as Waqf takes priority
column10: Per 2/4/11, Waqf over a common share is permitted; if the asset is leased, the Waqf is entitled to receive its share of the rent.

column4: A tangible Waqf building has validly incurred a debt for urgent repairs. The financier asks for a mortgage over the building. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted for up to half of its value
column6: Not permitted, even though the debt itself is allowed
column7: Permitted, as the debt was validly incurred for urgent repairs
column8: Permitted with the relevant authority's approval of the pledge
column10: Per 6/1, it is not permitted to pledge tangible Waqf assets even when availing a debt against the Waqf.

column4: A government proposes to pool all Waqf revenues into the public treasury and manage them with state funds. What does the standard say?
column5: It is permitted for Charitable Waqfs only
column6: It is permitted if the state protects the Waqfs
column7: Waqfs must stay independent of public treasury funds
column8: It is required, as Waqfs are public property
column10: Per 3/4/1, Waqfs must be independent of public treasury funds in administration, finance and accounting, while the state's protective role is regarded.

column4: A Waqf deed is silent about maintenance. The Waqf building now needs repairs. What does the standard provide?
column5: Repair needs consent of all beneficiaries
column6: Repair needs the Waqif's express stipulation in the Waqf deed
column7: Beneficiaries are paid first, then repairs from what remains
column8: Repair takes priority even without the Waqif's stipulation
column10: Per 4/1, maintenance or repair takes priority over other expenditures, and it is not subject to express stipulation from the Waqif.

column4: Ahmad makes Waqf of his share in a jointly owned plot. His partner then takes the share under pre-emption (shuf'a) rights and pays its price. What must Ahmad do?
column5: Deploy the price received in a similar type of Waqf
column6: Give the price to the partner's heirs
column7: Nothing; the Waqf ends and he keeps the price paid by the partner
column8: Refuse, as pre-emption cannot apply to a share already made Waqf
column10: Per 2/4/5/3, Waqf of an asset subject to pre-emption is valid; if it goes to the pre-emptor, the Waqif must deploy the consideration in a similar Waqf.

column4: A non-Muslim businessman creates a Waqf over a building for a public hospital. What is the ruling?
column5: Invalid, as Waqf is purely an act of worship
column6: Valid only after a Shari'ah board ratifies it
column7: Valid, subject to observing the rulings and conditions of Waqf
column8: Valid only where its beneficiaries are non-Muslims as well
column10: Per 2/4/3/5, Waqf by a non-Muslim is valid subject to observing the rulings and conditions of Waqf.

column4: Ahmad creates a Waqf whose revenue will go to poor persons and a university research centre. Based on the Waqf beneficiary, what type of Waqf is this?
column5: Joint Waqf
column6: Charitable Waqf
column7: Private or Dynasty Waqf
column8: Self Waqf
column10: Per 2/2/1/1, a Charitable Waqf is one whose revenue and benefit go to general charitable causes such as poor persons, research centres and universities.

column4: A Waqif creates Waqf by an act clearly indicating it, without the word "Waqf". On what basis does the standard accept this?
column5: Waqf is valid only when stated in writing before witnesses
column6: Silence is treated as an explicit offer
column7: Necessity allows exceptions to the form of the Waqf contract
column8: Contracts follow objectives and meanings, not words
column10: Basis 2/4/1/1: in all contracts, the intended objectives (maqāṣid) and meanings count, not words and forms, and custom is considered.

column4: The hadith "When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity..." supports which ruling in the standard?
column5: That Waqf is a recommended act
column6: That self-Waqf is permissible
column7: That Waqf upon death is a bequest
column8: That temporary Waqf is valid
column10: Basis 2/3: this hadith, with recurring charity understood as Waqf, is among the bases of Waqf being a recommended act.

column4: Ahmad's Waqf deed reserves his right to amend the Waqf's terms and conditions. What is the ruling?
column5: Void, since a Waqf is binding on creation and cannot be amended
column6: Valid, including the right to revoke the Waqf altogether
column7: Valid only for appointing the overseer
column8: Valid, if it does not prejudice the essence of the Waqf
column10: Per 2/6/6, the Waqif may stipulate the right to amend the Waqf's terms and conditions provided it does not prejudice the essence of Waqf.

column4: Ahmad declares his house a Waqf for his nephew Bilal. Bilal has not yet expressed acceptance. Is the Waqf created?
column5: Yes, Waqf does not require the beneficiary's acceptance
column6: No, not until Bilal takes possession of the house itself
column7: Yes, but it remains revocable by Ahmad until Bilal accepts it
column8: No, a specific beneficiary must accept it first, as with a gift
column10: Per 2/4/1/1, an offer from the Waqif creates Waqf; it does not require acceptance of the Waqf beneficiary, whether specific or not.

column4: An author creates a Waqf over his book's copyright, intending to appropriate that specific right as it is. Based on the Waqf asset, how is this Waqf classified?
column5: Cash Waqf
column6: Specific Waqf Assets
column7: Investment Waqfs
column8: Joint Waqf
column10: Per 2/2/2/1, Specific Waqf Assets aim to appropriate an asset as it is, and this includes Waqf of usufructs and Waqf of moral rights.

column4: Ahmad makes a three-year Waqf of specific Sukuk that mature in five years. What happens at the end of the three-year Waqf period?
column5: The Sukuk are sold and Ahmad receives the price
column6: The Sukuk become a perpetual Waqf
column7: Ahmad recovers the same number of Sukuk
column8: The Waqf continues until the Sukuk mature
column10: Per 2/4/15/1(b)(2), if the Waqf period is shorter than the Sukuk term, the Waqif recovers the same number of Sukuk at the end of the Waqf period.

column4: Critics say cash cannot be Waqf because the same coins cannot be retained. What is the standard's answer?
column5: Cash must first be turned into real estate before it can be Waqf
column6: Coins are not specific; their substitutes take their place
column7: Cash Waqf is merely a loan to beneficiaries
column8: Cash Waqf is valid only if the same coins are kept in a vault
column10: Basis 2/4/13/1: Waqf's objective is achieved in cash Waqf; money cannot be specific by identification, and its substitute will be in its place.

column4: Ahmad signs a letter to a charity: "I undertake to create a Waqf over my land for you." Has a Waqf been concluded?
column5: No, an undertaking to create a Waqf does not conclude it
column6: Yes, since Waqf may be deferred to a future date
column7: Yes, but it is treated as a bequest limited to one third
column8: Yes, once the charity accepts the undertaking and takes possession
column10: Per 2/4/1/2, the form of Waqf creation must be conclusive (jāzima); Waqf cannot be concluded with an undertaking to create Waqf.

column4: A Waqf is for four specific persons with defined shares. Revenue this year falls short. How is the shortfall borne?
column5: By the overseer from his remuneration
column6: Equally among them, regardless of their defined shares
column7: By the last-named beneficiary only, as the others rank ahead
column8: By all beneficiaries in proportion to their shares
column10: Per 9/10/3, if the Waqf is for specific persons and revenue falls short, the shortfall applies to all in proportion to their shares.

column4: A Waqf was created for the students of a particular school. The school has since closed permanently. What becomes of the Waqf?
column5: Its revenue is kept by the overseer
column6: It ends, and the asset returns to the Waqif or his heirs
column7: It remains valid and is used for similar charitable causes
column8: It becomes void from the date of creation
column10: Per 2/4/4/3, the Waqf remains valid if the beneficiary is discontinued; it will then be used for similar charitable causes.

column4: Bank A requires charge cardholders to deposit a cash guarantee and insists it be placed in a current account. What does the standard require?
column5: No cash guarantee may ever be requested from a charge cardholder
column6: The deposit must be placed in a current account, as it is a guarantee
column7: The deposit must be in an investment account
column8: Giving the option of a current or an investment account
column10: Per 4/3/2, the issuer should not stipulate depositing the guarantee in the current account; the holder chooses a current or investment account.

column4: Bank A's card advertising hides the fee amounts and urges customers to buy more than they need. Which requirements does this breach?
column5: Transparency and avoiding tempting excessive consumption
column6: Only the issuer's internal pricing policy for card products
column7: Only the card network's branding and logo use rules for issuers
column8: Nothing, as advertising is not regulated by the standard
column10: Per 5/9/1, the issuer must comply with transparency and disclosure, especially on fees and profit rate, and avoid misguiding and tempting excess consumption.

column4: Bank B provides Shop X with POS devices, organizes its dealings with the card network and recovers the card payments for it. Which party to the card is Bank B?
column5: The card network
column6: The Acquirer
column7: The card issuer
column8: The card acceptor
column10: Per 2/1/4 and 2/2/2, the Acquirer is the merchant's bank; it provides POS devices, organizes dealing with the network and acts as agent for recovery.

column4: Bank A lets its debit cardholders overdraw their balance against a monthly charge. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the charge is a fixed lump sum, not a percentage
column6: Permitted, for customers with good history
column7: Not permitted, as it is lending against interest
column8: Permitted, as the monthly charge is a service fee for the overdraft
column10: Per 4/1/1, a debit card must not result in lending against interest, like overdrawing the card against a consideration.

column4: An acquirer agrees with the card network to settle the amounts owed to it in a currency other than that of the goods' price. When is this permitted?
column5: When the exchange rate is known, with SS 59 conditions
column6: Only if the card network bears the exchange rate risk alone
column7: Always, without any condition, as it is a settlement of dues
column8: Never, as it is a sale of debt for debt between the parties
column10: Per 5/5/3, the acquirer may agree on settlement in another currency provided the exchange rate is known and 4/1/1/2 of SS 59 is observed.

column4: Bank A waives the card fee only for current account debit cards, while still charging the fee on cards for saving and investment accounts. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as a marketing incentive
column6: Not permitted
column7: Permitted, if the waiver is temporary
column8: Permitted, as current accounts carry no profit
column10: Per 4/1/2, the current account card fee should not be exclusively exempted or lowered if saving/investment account cards carry a fee.

column4: Why does the standard prohibit a card that rolls over the cardholder's loan through Tawarruq with the issuer?
column5: The card issuer cannot be a seller of commodities to its holder
column6: The commodity is never possessed by the cardholder or issuer
column7: Tawarruq is prohibited in all cases, even when properly structured
column8: It is an artifice to delay the loan with an increase
column10: Basis 6/3/2: revolving the debt via Tawarruq from the lender to settle the loan is an artifice to delay settlement with an increase.

column4: Bank A issues a card to Ahmad and keeps it valid for use, but Ahmad has not used it yet. How is the issuer-cardholder relationship characterized at this stage?
column5: Lending (Qard)
column6: Guarantee
column7: Provision of services
column8: Novation (Hawalah)
column10: Per 2/2/1/1, upon issuance the relationship is provision of services to the cardholder: issuing the card and keeping it valid for use.

column4: Bank A issues debit cards below their actual direct cost, but only to customers keeping at least 10,000 in their current account. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted
column6: Permitted, as debit cards involve no lending
column7: Permitted, as the bank may set criteria
column8: Permitted, if disclosed in advance
column10: Per 4/1/3, offering the card must not be contingent on a set current account balance if it is issued below actual direct cost.

column4: Why may an issuer not oblige a covered card holder to keep the cover in a current account?
column5: Current accounts earn no profit for the holder, so it is unfair
column6: Current accounts may not hold covers for financing at all
column7: It stipulates a loan within a commutative financing
column8: It breaches the holder's privacy over his own funds
column10: Basis 6/2: a current account is a loan, so obliging it in a financing combines a loan with a commutative contract (loan and sale).

column4: Ahmad cancels his new card a week after it was issued and asks Bank A to refund the issuance fee. What is the position?
column5: Bank A must refund it in full as the card was barely used
column6: Bank A need not return any part of it
column7: Bank A must refund it pro rata to the days left in the year
column8: Bank A must refund half of it
column10: Per 5/2/1, if the cardholder cancels the card after its issuance, the issuer may not return any part of the issuance fees.

column4: What is the basis for an issuer retaining service fees pro rata until a card's cancellation?
column5: The fee is earned only on actual usage of the services
column6: The fee is earned in full on signing the card agreement
column7: The fee is a security for future claims
column8: The fee is earned by enabling use of the usufruct
column10: Basis 5/2/2: the provider is entitled to the fee by enabling possession of the usufruct, estimated by the period elapsed since it was available.

column4: A Qard Hasan card charges issuance, renewal and cash withdrawal fees. Under which condition is issuing it permitted?
column5: Fees must be fully waived for all users, as Qard Hasan is free
column6: Its loan-linked fees may not exceed actual direct cost
column7: Fees must be paid by the merchant only
column8: Fees may be set freely by agreement between issuer and holder
column10: Per 6/1/2 with 5/1/1, a Qard Hasan card with fees is permitted provided its fees observe 5/1, so loan-linked fees stay within actual direct cost.

column4: Why does the Shari'ah basis make a seller who concealed a defect bear the return fees and exchange differences?
column5: He holds the goods in trust for the buyer until return
column6: He always bears all return costs
column7: He is the card issuer's agent and acts on its behalf
column8: He caused harm, and it is a discretionary sanction
column10: Basis 5/7: a seller who caused harm should remove it; he is charged the return costs as a discretionary sanction for concealing the defect.

column4: Ahmad paid a yearly fee for lounge access services on his card, available since issuance. He cancels after four months. What may Bank A stipulate?
column5: Refunding the whole yearly fee, since the lounge was never used
column6: Retaining the whole yearly fee, since services were available
column7: Retaining that fee pro rata for the four months
column8: Retaining half, regardless of time
column10: Per 5/2/2, the issuer may stipulate retaining fees for services other than issuance on a proportionate basis up to cancellation.

column4: Bank A, an Institution, plans a revolving credit card whose used amounts are settled in deferred instalments against interest. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted for Institutions
column6: Permitted if interest goes to charity
column7: Permitted if the interest is capped
column8: Permitted for non-Muslim customers only
column10: Per 4/4, Institutions may not issue revolving credit cards by extending a loan settled in deferred instalments against interest.

column4: Ahmad holds a Bank A debit card. Which of these uses mostly involves a fee to him?
column5: Paying a local merchant in the card's currency
column6: Paying online in the card's own currency
column7: Withdrawing cash at another institution's ATM
column8: Withdrawing cash at Bank A's own ATM
column10: Per 3/1/4, debit cardholders mostly bear no fees except for cash withdrawal at other institutions' ATMs or paying in another currency.

column4: Bank A issues Ahmad a card that deducts every purchase directly from the available balance of his current account with the Bank. Which card type is this?
column5: Prepaid Card
column6: Charge Card
column7: Credit Card
column8: Debit Card
column10: Per 1/1 and 3/1/1, a Debit Card is a settlement instrument linked to the available balance in the cardholder's account with the card issuer.

column4: Bank A's ATM charges other banks' cardholders 2 per withdrawal. It wants to charge its own credit cardholders 3 per withdrawal. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted to exceed the fee charged to others
column6: Permitted, as it owns the ATM and sets its own fees
column7: Permitted, if the higher fee is stated in the card agreement
column8: Permitted, since credit cards cost the issuer more to serve
column10: Per 5/1/2/4, an Institution that issued the card observes 5/1/1 and may not charge more than it charges other institutions' cardholders.

column4: Why does the standard bar waiving card fees exclusively for current account cards?
column5: It is gharar in the card fee, as the waiver is uncertain
column6: Current accounts are loans, so it is a loan with benefit
column7: It breaches the card network's pricing rules for issuers
column8: It discriminates against investment depositors, who bear more risk
column10: Basis 4/1/2: current accounts are characterized as a loan, and singling them out by waiver or discount turns them into a loan against interest.

column4: Bank A issues a lending-based credit card and sets its issuance fee well above the actual direct cost. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, if the card is not revolving
column6: Permitted, as fees follow the agreement signed with the cardholder
column7: Permitted, if the fee is disclosed to the customer in advance
column8: Not permitted; it may not exceed actual direct cost
column10: Per 5/1/1, fees charged by the issuer and linked to the loan in a credit card, such as issuance fees, may not exceed the actual direct cost.

column4: Abroad, a shop lets Ahmad pay in his card's currency, with conversion done by an independent entity at a rate above actual cost. May Ahmad choose this?
column5: No, he must pay in the local currency of the country he is in
column6: Yes, and that exchange need not abide by actual cost
column7: No, the rate must equal the actual cost incurred by the issuer
column8: Yes, only if his card is not lending-based
column10: Per 5/5/2, the holder may choose to pay in the card currency; the exchange is by an independent entity and need not abide by actual cost.

column4: On a lending-based card, the acquirer charges Shop X 2% per sale and passes part of it to the issuer. Bank A wants to recover this fee from cardholders too. Is this allowed?
column5: Yes, as the fee follows the agreement in the card contract
column6: Yes, if the amount charged is capped at the actual cost
column7: No, the cardholder shall not bear such fees
column8: Yes, if the card is non-revolving
column10: Per 5/1/2/1, the acquirer may charge the acceptor as agreed, with part to the issuer, provided the cardholder does not bear it in lending cards.

column4: Bank A plans to raise its card fee in return for a feature giving 2% cash back on all purchases. What is the ruling?
column5: Not permitted
column6: Permitted, if the fee rise is disclosed
column7: Permitted, as cash back is a gift
column8: Permitted if the cash back is capped
column10: Per 5/6/2, it is not permitted to increase card fees in return for cash back, a price reduction, a usage-contingent feature or one with no known limit.

column4: Bank A charged Ahmad one aggregate card fee without splitting it between issuance and other services. Ahmad cancels mid-year. What may Bank A retain?
column5: The entire aggregate fee
column6: Only the issuance part, as it estimates it
column7: Nothing, since the fee was not itemized
column8: A pro rata amount for the period since issuance
column10: Per 5/2/3, for an undifferentiated aggregate fee, the issuer may retain a proportionate amount for the period from issuance to cancellation.

column4: When a card issuer pays the merchant from its own funds, even though the cardholder owes it nothing and holds no money with it, how does the Shari'ah basis classify this?
column5: A restricted novation, which is void
column6: An absolute novation, which is permitted
column7: A loan to the merchant
column8: A sale of debt, which is prohibited
column10: Basis 2/2/1/2: if the issuer pays from its own funds, it is an absolute (unrestricted) novation, permitted even without a debt or funds held.

column4: Bank A gives its cardholders free air-miles and hotel booking discounts. The card's fees are not raised for these. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only on debit cards
column6: Not permitted, as gifts to borrowers are riba
column7: Permitted, as Shari'ah compliant free benefits
column8: Not permitted due to gharar in the benefit
column10: Per 5/6/2, it is permitted to give cardholders Shari'ah-permissible benefits for free, e.g., gifts, discounts, air-miles and cash back.

column4: Ahmad returns a defective item bought by card. The seller did not know of the defect. Bank A asks Ahmad for the exchange rate difference, per their agreement. What applies?
column5: Ahmad bears it and cannot claim it from the seller
column6: The seller must bear it, as the item was defective
column7: It is split equally between Ahmad and the seller
column8: Bank A must bear it as the issuer
column10: Per 5/7, the issuer may claim such fees per the agreement; the holder may not revert to the acceptor, even for a defect, unless it was concealed.

column4: Ahmad cancels a card the day after issuance and asks why the issuance fee is not refunded. What is the Shari'ah basis?
column5: The fee is a penalty for early cancellation of the card
column6: The fee is for a specific job already completed
column7: The fee is a gift (Hibah) to the issuer at issuance
column8: The fee is a deposit kept as security
column10: Basis 5/2/1: issuance fees are against a specific job done by issuing the card, and the provider is entitled upon completion of the job.

column4: On a lending-based card, Bank A adds a lounge access feature and raises the card fee for it. How far may the fee be raised?
column5: Not beyond the actual cost of the feature
column6: To double the actual cost of the feature
column7: To any level agreed with the cardholder
column8: Not at all; features must be free
column10: Per 5/6/2, in the case of a lending-based card, it is not permitted to increase its fees beyond the actual cost of such features.

column4: Ahmad wants to buy gold jewellery and pay with his credit card. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted only if paid within the grace period
column6: Permitted only with a debit card
column7: Not permitted, as gold requires cash at hand
column8: Permitted to pay the price of gold by credit card
column10: Per 5/4, it is permitted to carry out currency exchange and pay the price of gold and silver using debit, prepaid or credit cards.

column4: A card network offers Bank A incentive amounts for issuing cards managed by the network. May Bank A accept them?
column5: Only if paid in kind, not in cash
column6: No, as they amount to riba paid by the network to the issuer
column7: Yes, receiving such incentives is permitted
column8: Only if all of it is passed on to the cardholders as rebates
column10: Per 5/3/3, Institutions may receive incentive amounts from the card network for issuing cards managed by such corporations.

column4: A scholar objects that buying gold by credit card lacks immediate possession because settlement is delayed. What is the standard's answer?
column5: Possession occurs only on final settlement between the banks
column6: A settlement delay is excused by general public need and custom
column7: Possession is not required for gold bought by electronic means
column8: Possession occurs when the amount is held for the merchant
column10: Basis 5/4: card payment materializes possession by holding the amount for the acceptor at the time of use; settlement delays do not affect this.

column4: Ahmad's debit card account has a zero balance. He asks Bank A to let the card finance his purchases until salary day. What is the nature of a debit card?
column5: A credit instrument within a fixed limit set by the issuer
column6: A revolving financing instrument for the cardholder's purchases
column7: A settlement instrument linked to the available balance
column8: A credit instrument with a grace period
column10: Per 3/1/1, the debit card is a settlement instrument, not a credit (lending or financing) instrument, so it is linked to the available balance.

column4: Ahmad converts part of his prepaid card balance from the local currency into US dollars. Which rulings apply to this conversion?
column5: The rulings of Qard (loan) given by the issuer
column6: The rulings of ṣarf (currency exchange)
column7: The rulings of Hawalah (transfer of debt) only
column8: The rulings of Murabahah (sale with disclosed profit)
column10: Per 4/2/2, rulings of ṣarf apply on conversion of the prepaid balance or part of it to currencies other than the local currency.

column4: Bank A finds Ahmad using its card for gambling transactions. What does the standard provide?
column5: Bank A may cancel the card, as it bars such use
column6: Bank A may only charge a penalty fee
column7: Bank A must report but keep the card active
column8: Bank A has no right to intervene
column10: Per 5/9/2, the issuer must stipulate that the card not be used in prohibited transactions and has the right to cancel it in such a case.

column4: Bank A allows prepaid cardholders to spend beyond their balance, charging a fee proportional to the excess. What is the ruling?
column5: Permitted, as a prepaid card is not a loan
column6: Permitted, if the excess is settled within a month
column7: Not permitted, as it leads to lending on interest
column8: Permitted, if the fee is fixed in the terms
column10: Per 4/2/1, a prepaid card should not lead to lending on interest, e.g., allowing use beyond the balance (overdrawing) against a consideration.

column4: For its covered card, Bank A requires Ahmad to keep the liquidity cover in a current account. What does the standard require?
column5: Ahmad may choose a current or investment-based account
column6: The cover must be in an investment account earning profit
column7: The cover must be kept in a current account, as it is a guarantee
column8: No cover account may be opened
column10: Per 6/2/2/1(a), the holder should not be required to deposit the cover in a current account but given the option of a current or investment account.

column4: Under Bank A's Qard Hasan card with fees, how is the amount owed from card usage settled by Ahmad?
column5: In instalments with interest after a grace period
column6: In one lump payment at the end of the card year, with no increase
column7: In instalments with a profit margin added to the principal
column8: In equal monthly instalments, with no increase
column10: Per 6/1/1, the owed amount is settled in equal monthly instalments on set dates, without increase in the loan principal for instalments.

column4: Which evidence does the standard cite for allowing a lender to charge the actual direct cost of a loan?
column5: The hadith on accepting a transfer of debt (Hawalah)
column6: The verse that the debtor should dictate the debt
column7: The hadith on a sale combined with a loan contract
column8: The verse forbidding riba and consuming wealth wrongfully
column10: Basis 5/1/1: the verse "And the one who owes should give the dictation" shows the cost of writing the debt deed falls on the debtor.

column4: Why does the standard forbid raising card fees in return for a cash-back feature?
column5: It is gharar akin to gambling, with possible riba al-fadl
column6: It breaches the card network's rules on rewards and incentives
column7: Cash back is always a form of riba, whatever its basis
column8: Cash back is a prohibited gift from the issuer to the holder
column10: Basis 5/6/2: this is gharar, comes under a form of gambling, with the probability of riba al-fadl if the benefits are redeemed or decreased.

column4: In a lending-based card, why may the cardholder not bear the fees the acquirer deducts from the card acceptor?
column5: The acceptor is the true borrower, so the fee is its cost
column6: Part goes to the issuer as lender: a loan with benefit
column7: These fees are gharar for the holder as they are unknown
column8: The card network's rules forbid passing them on to holders
column10: Basis 5/1/2/1: part of these fees goes to the lender (issuer), so making the holder bear them makes it a loan carrying benefit.

column4: Bank A lets a covered card holder spend beyond the cash cover limit. Which fee rulings apply to that excess?
column5: No fee rules apply to the excess
column6: The rulings of the debit card
column7: The rulings for non-lending cards
column8: The rulings of the lending-based card
column10: Per 6/2/2/3, if the issuer lets the holder use the card beyond its cash limit, the excess takes the lending-based card ruling, observing 5/1/1.

column4: Ahmad pays Shop X with his debit card, and Bank A pays the shop out of Ahmad's balance with it. How is this relationship characterized?
column5: Bank A acts as the shop's selling agent
column6: Bank A guarantees the shop's sale
column7: Ahmad novates the shop to the card issuer
column8: Bank A sells the goods to Ahmad on credit
column10: Per 2/2/1/2, upon card usage the cardholder novates the card acceptor to the card issuer, which pays out of the cardholder's balance.

column4: Why must a covered card agreement state the issuer is not obliged to lower financing instalments?
